He said: When I left the Government in November, 1916, I had two courses open to me to pursue; one, in defiance of the well-established custom, to attack the Government, and to attack any measure they might introduce which I did not conceive to be in the interest of the service or of the country, and the other, to pursue a passive course, assisting the Government in every legitimate way I could, in the meantime withholding any criticism I might want to make until a later period. I might have been more or less vindictive towards a couple of my colleagues, but I chose to give them a friendly support in any way I could in reference to matters concerning their departments.
I could have given rein to ambition, Sir, and have exposed the Military Service Act, the registration fad, the Food Control scheme, and various other operations of the Government that certainly gave one opportunity to criticise if necessary. But, Sir, I checked my ambition 'and loyally assisted these gentlemen in any suggestion they had to make to me. I could have gone in for personal glory, ot I could have sharply criticised1 the operations and administration here, in England and at the front; but whether it was the Minister of Militia, the Minister of Naval Service, or any other

*ministers in the Government, anything I could do to help them in a quiet way was done, and my criticisms were confined, as far as 'possible, to legitimate action. I could also have exposed the outrageous loans and bad financing of the Government; but I contented myself with following the same line in regard to these matters. Everything was made subordinate to winning the war. I did make suggestions to my predecessor, as I say, but everything of *that nature had for its object the interests of the people of Canada. When the Military Service Act was brought forward I spoke to the Minister of Justice and endeavoured1 to point out to him that the tribunals' were just loopholes for having certain people escape service. I pointed out the weaknesses of that Act in as kindly terms as I could, but I regret to say my suggestions were not *much heeded. The Minister of Militia will bear me out in saying that in any communication I may have bad with 'the Prime Minister referring to anything at the front 'and which was of interest to Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig, General Currie, or any of the other officers, I invariably marked my communication as open to their consideration and sent each a copy. The same with General Turner. But now the war is over, Sir, I owe allegiance only to the constituents who for thirty years have loyally stood by me in political matters. Union Government has made no change in the principles of the old Liberal-Conservative party .of Sir John A. Macdonald. I have been carefully studying all the acts of the Unionist Government and I can see no acts worthy of consideration that were not embodied in the principles of the old Liberal-Conservative party of Sir John A. Maodbnald many years 'ago, and therefore I have loyally stood by those principles and quietly submitted to actions wdth which I could not agree. But others have not been so considerate in regard to me. I have seen my war plans set aside; I have seen my honour impugned; I have seen my friends in the service treated with injustice bordering on persecution; but worst of all I have seen the gallant four hundred thousand soldiers whom I had raised needlessly shot to pieces. Therefore I do feel keenly in the premises. I have long 'adopted the motto that next to : the honest convictions of my own heart and conscience I value the approval of my honest fellow-men and women. Therefore, knowing the facts; knowing the honest convictions of my own heart and conscience; this review- only a small fraction of the facts that

might be given in detail-is presented to Parliament and the country for the consideration of my fellow.
It is submitted:
1.	In full justice to myself and family of whom I >am rightfully proud.
2.	In justice to my many friends throughout the Dominion of Canada and the world at large. '
3.	In delayed justice to many a gallant and capable officer and man such as for instance:
Lieut.-General Sir W. E. Turner.
Colonel John A. Currie, M.P.
General Sir John Carson and Colonel Murphy.
To the memories of the splendid fellows resting peacefully beneath the golden lilies of France or the crimson poppies of Belgium.
To the hundreds of thousands of the returned lads and their friends in Canada.
And last, but by no means least, to Lieut.-Colonel Sir Arthur Currie.
Now, Sir, there are variouus forms of .calumny and slander. I do not know whether these have been indulged in during the recent war or not, but for the last number of years there has been a propaganda followed. Propaganda! I would like to see a definition of the word. But, Sir, there are various forms of propaganda. For instance, we have found:
1.	Indiscriminate praise of others undeserving.
2.	Calumny directly against the person concerned.
I have had the full limit of both forms from men whose motives' have been most unworthy. The man is a coward, unworthy of association with his fellow-man and woman, who unjustly and deliberately deprecates another:
1.	By promulgating what is false concerning him.
2.	By boosting others in untrue praise ~ with the object not only of helping the one
boosted, but to deprecate the other.
Truth, fair play, justice for all, must he the watchwords. He who wishes more is unworthy the name of soldier; he who deliberately plans for more or accepts more than truth, fair play and justice is a moral leper among the half million gallant Canadians who so heroically did their duty; but he who would wantonly by word or pen, or by silence dishonour the fair name of a comrade by permitting falsehood, misrepresentation or slander in deed or word, active or passive, should occupy the pit of infamy.
Injustice always breeds rebellion:
1.	In the person defamed or injured wrongfully.
2.	In the person deprived of credit for actions honestly done.
3.	In persons who see credit given to one who does not deserve it.
4.	In propaganda, camouflage and suppression of the truth to' advance untruth and hide the facts in order to advance another.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether my remarks will be very interesting to His Lordship and to the House, but I will pursue the even tenor of my way.
I was speaking about the propaganda which had been instituted concerning my actions and conduct both before the war and during the war. Now, that the war is over, I feel that I am justifying myself in placing these facts before the House and the country in order that a proper review may be had of them.
The propaganda to which I refer was active even before the war began. I do not



*wish to impugn the honour of any of the persons concerned in the premises, whom I shall name here as having been influenced directly by German money. But we now know that German gold in vast quantities had been distributed throughout the United States, Great Britain and Canada in order to create a public sentiment adverse to everything like preparation for war or the development of the defences of the country along proper lines. As Minister of Militia, and feeling as a result of my visits to Germany -that this war was coming on, it was my duty to prepare the country as quietly as possible for the struggle which I felt was impending. It was therefore more or less unpleasant, Sir, to find myself attacked by various organizations and journals. For instance, one of the most ardent journals in the matter was the Toronto Telegram. I was unkind enough to attribute the influence of that paper to the association of the then Finance Minister (Sir Thomas White) with it. The Toronto Globe was very bitter in its attacks upon my preparations. I never could understand the reason for it. But some years ago I found that the editor-in-chief of the Toronto Globe was receiving fifty per cent or thereabout of his salary-within a fraction of that percentage -from a peace society in the United States, associated with which was Ur. Starr Jordan of the Leland Stanford university of California. Subsequently, it transpired- absolutely unknown to the editor of the Globe, mark you; I have no hesitation in saying that-that peace society was supported by German gold. The people of Canada, myself in particular, were subjected to attacks from that paper because I was making preparations and getting ready for the war. The Montreal Mail and Evening News-established through the instrumentality of the then Finance Minister; at all events, the proprietor of it was a brother of the then Finance Minister-day in and day out attacked my policy, belittled me before the country and belittled my projects. The Winnipeg Telegram and Evening Post, for reasons of its own, also treated me to some consideration in this regard. In clubs, restaurants, prayer-meetings even, and on trains, the propaganda went on, all leading towards the same line-that my policy was wrong; that other lines should be pursued, and that we should not make the progress which we were making.
I regret to say that both Lord Shaugh-nessy and Sir Joseph Flavelle lent them selves in 1915 and 1916 to the policy of stopping recruiting. I understand that Lord 
Shaughnessy claimed that the war was going to be over by the 1st of June, 1916, and that the whole agitation to raise troops and .send them to the front was a fad of my own and had no foundation in necessity.
I wish to relate an incident that occurred in New York in March, 1916, when I was on my way to Europe to review the Canadian troops. Just as I was starting for the boat, I received a telephone call from one of the leading financiers in>
the city of New York who told me that undeT no consideration must I sail; that a conspiracy was afoot to destroy me. Thinking that he meant the German submarine campaign, I jokingly told him that I had arranged with the Kaiser that nothing was to happen to my ship, and that everything was all right. He said that this was a much more serious affair than that; that it was a conspiracy on the part of a couple of my colleagues in Canada to get rid of me. Knowing that I was the bulwark that .stood between Sir Robert Borden and some of the conspirators in and out of the party, they had conspired to destroy me in order that they might get rid of Sir Robert Borden also. I immediately notified Sir Robert Borden to this effect and stated that if any controversial matter arose affecting him or myself in any way, I would immediately return to Canada and defend him. I had scarcely got across the Atlantic when, through the instrumentality of certain gentlemen. who are now well known, an inquiry was commenced into the fuse contracts. In passing, let me say that no more searching inquiry than that was ever held, and never did men come through an inquiry with a cleaner record than, did the gentlemen concerned. Had that Shell Committee been permitted to continue its operations and to enter into similar contracts after the establishment of the Munitions Board, we could have helped them out. Mr. Russell, a protege, a creditor of the financial interests with which Sir Joseph Flavelle was asso-" ciated, had, on the first million- fuses he took, got a bonus of $675,000 over and above a fair contract price, and, as it was, when he found he could not load them, he got nearly $350,000 more for his first million fuses than did the Northern Electric Light Company of Montreal for an exactly similar contract. The scope, however, of the commission was not extended, although it may be at some future date.
On the evening before I spoke at the Toronto Empire Club in October, 1916, I had the privilege of being waited upon about eleven o'clock at night by a number of

leading Liberal-Conservatives of the city of Toronto. I may inform the House that in the city of Toronto the term " Liberal-Conservative " is still used. These gentlemen explained to me that the reason why they were out so late was because they had had a political meeting and the question had arisen whether the then Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) could get a seat in Toronto or not. They said that the meeting had unanimously decided that owing to his unpopularity in the city, he should not be nominated. The next day my staff officer came to me and said: " Something is wrong; last night we were told by these gentlemen that the Finance Minister was so unpopular here that he should not be nominated; now he is in everybody's mouth, it being said that he should become Prime Minister and that Sir Robert Borden, who is a weakling, should go."
I asked him who the gentlemen were who were carrying on the canvass, and in presence of two officers of the institution he pointed out eight men who were openly canvassing against Sir Robert Borden, demanding that the Prime Minister should go and that the Minister of Finance should succeed him. Each one of these gentlemen was associated with one or another of the commercial or financial institutions with which Sir Joseph Flavelle and the Minister of Finance were more or less directly connected. I shall not mention the names of the institutions. They are well known; they are known as the financial group in Toronto that has been manipulating the affairs of this country so long. That -was in October, 1916. I notified the Prime Minister of that and gave him the data so that he could verify it.
Then came the Borden-Bennett trip to the West on that national registration scheme, on which a lot of blotting paper and a good deal of money was wasted, but from which nothing resulted. During that trip Sir Joseph could not contain himself any longer, but must make a speech, and notification was given that he was going to make a speech and to drive Borden from the Cabinet. It appears from an 'article that came out in the Toronto Globe at that time that an effort was made on the part of the Prime Minister to induce Sir Joseph Flavelle to moderate his tone a little until Sir Robert Borden returned and not to come out so flat-footedly as he was reported to be intending to do. The effect of the Toronto Globe article was that a meeting was advertised in the interest of Sir Thomas White, to be held on a Monday evening, the evening that the
40J
article appeared, and that there was a charge of conspiracy against the Prime Minister. That meeting was suddenly changed; a startling announcement that was to be made did not materialize, and altogether the matter was more or less of a frost. The Minister of Finance was on the defensive rather than on the offensive, the cause being the exposure in the Globe of that day of the actions of Sir Joseph Flavelle.
Then followed that famous speech of Sir Joseph Flavelle, in which he relegated profits to a warmer climate than we have in Canada at the present time, but which caused people to inquire into the profits he was making on bacon and other commodities with a result which was not very creditable to him. After the Empire Club meeting, when I found this propaganda at work- and it was a revelation to me-I examined the system that I found had been in operation before the war, all through the formation of the Valcartier camp and all through the conduct of operations until the time that I left office, and I found the same friends were directing the show right through. At every meeting at Toronto or elsewhere the propaganda would be at work belittling General Bertram and the Shell Committee. I should like to say at this point as regards the Shell Committee, that when Lord Kitchener asked me to get a couple of hundred thousand shells-a quantity which at the time the war closed could be turned out in a few hours by half a dozen of our institutions-from the Bethlehem steel works, 1 told him I could get them. But I saw that dinner pails in Canada were not filled; that our men were out of employment; that the country was in danger of becoming bankrupt; and that it was questionable whether we could raise the money to send the first 20,000 men over. I, therefore, decided to make the 200,000 shells in Canada, and we summoned the steel men of the country to Ottawa, with the result that after a time we got them started making these shells, and thus money was brought into the country. For the first time in history we used our own basic steel instead of acid steel. I want to point out two things in connection with the manufacture of these shells. This was the first time that shells had ever been made outside of arsenals; we made them in our factories, and this was the first time that basic steel instead of acid steel was used in the manufacture of shells. The result was that millions, aye, billions of money came into Canada, and if we have prosperity to-day and can float our Victory

Loans, that is due to the fact that those industries were established at that time, and they kept the country prosperous and buoyant. This year some are out of business. Men like Mr. Russell and Mr. Lloyd Harris, who 1 regret to say is misrepresents [DOT]ng, or, to be parliamentary, is " representing " this country in connection with trade matters at the other side at the present time, were agents who were active in securing the destruction of the Shell Committee which was doing so much to help the Empire in the great struggle which has just closed.
Subsequently to the attempt to squeeze out the Prime Minister, another move was tried. A number of able statesmen in Toronto-I may mention their names, Mr. Rundle, an officer in one of the departments of Sir Joseph Flavelle; Mr. Ames, a financial broker; Mr. Gundy, a little broker, friendly with Sir Joseph Flavelle, and others -came down to Ottawa, where they met Sir Joseph Flavelle on a Sunday morning, and had a conference with him. They then went to visit Sir Wilfrid Laurier at his residence at twelve o'clock, had lunch with him, remained until four o'clock, and then subsequently met some other leaders of the Liberal party. I do not want to enter into any discussion. My object in all this is to show how I was handicapped and the organization of our forces was handicapped leading up to all these engagements, by the interference and misconduct of certain gentlemen who pursued lines that were not in harmony with those I was pursuing. I may not be h lawyer but I drew the motion up with the intention and expectation that it would give me scope to carry on, and I think I am within the limits. However, I am through with the Canadian end of it, and I will now take up the Old Country end, which has to do with the training of the troops oyer there.
In 1914 I arrived in England, from New York, on the same day as the troops. I found that the High Commissioner for Canada was there and my presence seemed very objectionable to him. He even went so far as to tell me "You do not pretend to control the troops." The same words were put in the mouth of Lord Kitchener, and when it came to Lord Roberts' inspection of the troops the plan was that he was to go to the inspection without me, but Lord Roberts informed Lord Kitchener that he would not go without me. When we got to the grounds Lord Roberts insisted with General Alderson that I should take a prominent stand in the review. I shall not dilate on this further, except to say that all the actions carried out in connection with the troops were interfered with by press agencies friendly to the High Commissioner's office, and that adverse criticism after adverse criticism, all of which was found to be groundless, was made of the Dominion of Canada.
There is another matter. In October 1914 I had called on Lord Kitchener and asked for the return of all our machine guns which we had loaned him at the beginning of the war, and I also asked him for the return of our field pieces, some sixty or seventy 18-pounders. He said he would be prepared to return them as they had ordered 300 more 18-pounders and 2,500 machine guns. I suggested that instead of that number he should have ordered 30,000 18-pounders and 250,000 machine guns.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, and I will take the proper occasion to tell the story. I do not question your ruling -in any sense whatever, Sir. I might point out that when we went over to England our motor lorries were thrown out and a propaganda was carried on there which I shall tell you about. Our wagons were thrown out on the ground, alleged by the officials who were attending to the business, that they could not turn in the narrow roads of France, as the English wagons could, when as a matter of fact an investigation showed that they could turn in three feet nine inches less space than the English wagons and that the Canadian wagons were in every sense better than the English wagons. This was a piece of camouflage, such as they carried on-from start to finish, in order that they might reject the things that we sent over there. I could go down through a long list of articles which were all thrown out, on the ground that they wanted uniformity at the front. I had taken the ground that Canada was a unit in herself, exactly the same as Field Marshal Haig was a unit under General Foch. I claimed that our forces were a unit under Haig in this great war. I regret to say that it was only at a later period that I could get any recognition of my contention, not by the British authorities, because Lord Kitchener, Lloyd George and all those prominent statesmen, when the matter was explained to them were prepared to concede it, but from the subordinate officers. These subordinate officers would reject everything we would send over there except our men. They rejected motor lorries, wagons, harness, collars, shovels, belts, rifles, bayonets, boots, clothes, field kitchens, tents, and machine gun batteries.
Later I found that an Order in Council had been surreptitiously passed by the Canadian Cabinet-I was not once consulted about the matter, although I was present at several of the meetings-giving General Alderson full control over the appointment of officers without consultation with any person in Canada or with myself.

mental officers were made, and were never interfered with.
Under the former conditions, it is understood the appointments took several weeks to finally go through but the officers selected acted num the date of their nomination. Thus there would not be more than two or three days' difference in time in any event between the two systems.
Under the new plan, the proposal regarding all appointments and promotions at the Front is that they shall be submitted to Colonel Sir Max Aitken, as the General Representative for Canada at the Front, and be, by him, taken up with the War Office, while the more important ones should be informally talked over by that "officer with the Commander-in-Chief, or his representative, before any action be taken. In all probability positive agreement could be reached through this informal conference without any hitch whatever.
Regarding promotions, etc., in England:-The plan is that those shall be sent through the various corps to General Carson who, with Sir Max Aitken, will consider them; and then both they and those from the Front will be by the latter officer submitted unofficially to the War Office and officially to Canada. *
By pursuing this course it appears evident that any possible friction will be reduced to a minimum. The presence of the General Representative at the Front, who will be advised by the Canadian Minister of Militia and Defence without any delay as each important appointment or promotion presents itself, will: obviate the possibility of the action proposed in the last paragraph of the letter of Mr. B. B. Cubitt. Hence, the statement therein contained that " it will therefore not be desirable that vacancies should be left over until the concurrence of the Dominion Government has been obtained" cannot be accepted by Canada, the matter of cabling from the Front to the Minister of Militia and Defence for Canada on the one hand, or to the Secretary of State for War in England on the other being a difference of only a few minutes.
Moreover, the question of appointments to important positions on the Staff and Brigades, Divisions and Corps is one which would especially come under diplomatic consideration between Canada's General Representative at the Front and the Commander-in-Chief, or his representative. These appointments being important and there being many members of the Canadian Force who are well qualified for them, it would be most desirable that the consultation and agreement should take place in the preliminary stages rather than later. However, where parties are actuated by the supreme welfare of the Empire and by the most honourable and patriotic motives, and where no personal or local interests find place, there should be no trouble in amicably settling any and every possible difference that might arise.
Further, it would be very undesirable that any such appointments should be temporarily filled. It would be a very delicate matter to remove an officer once he were so appointed. In justice to our own deserving officers Canada respectfully asserts the constitutional principle that these appointments shall be controlled by her; and that as she has officers competent to fill any of these appointments with credit, capability, and honour, it is essential that such Canadian officers be given first consideration

and that among them selection be made on the basis of merit and fitness alone.
I may point out I have a double object in placing these facts before the House. One is to dispel the misapprehension which has been caused in the country by the speech delivered by Sir Edward Kemp last session in which he claimed that this position had not been taken until he himself had taken it some time previously. I point out now that away back in 1915 and 1916 I had laid it down as a principle, and asserted it from the very beginning; also demonstrating that it would have a very great effect in the developing of our troops and keeping lip that splendid spirit with which they entered the war and which continued until the end.
I now come to an article written, I think, early in 1918, by Lord Rothermere in the Sunday Pictorial on " The Menace of a Seven Years' War," and I quote from it the following:
Lessons of Passchendaele.
Now, as to the future; it is imperative for the Allies not to be recklessly wasteful of manpower in the field, no matter how great their numbers may become.
No nation, certainly not Germany, has been so prodigal of man-power in the battle line as Great Britain has been. France learned her lesson early. We have not learned it thoroughly even now. Our operations have been conducted as though we had an inexhaustible reservoir of men. As most men know the evil consequences which flowed from Passchendaele directly contributed to the break through near St. Quentin last March, which placed France and the Allied cause in jeopardy.
There has been far too much secrecy in official statements with regard to these battles.
The British tradition appears to be that while admirals and commanders of ships must suffer for grievous blunders, generals can do no wrong. This should not continue. A measure such as M. Clemenceau has introduced in France, by which military commanders, however exalted, may in future be tried by court-martial so constituted as to include not only generals, but also eminent members of the Senate and Chamber, and the head of the highest French legal tribunal, should be adopted.
In the fifth year of the war it is time that British generalship was not necessarily taken for granted. It should be submitted when necessary to close, competent, and ruthless scrutiny, in the interests of the real fighting men. The range of selection for the highest commands should be widened.
Now, in connection with this matter, I wish to say a few words concerning Lieut.-Gen. 'Sir E. W. Turner, V.C., of Quebec. Turner went to the South African war and won there the South African medal, the Distinguished Service Order and the Victoria Cross. In 1914 he enlisted for the recent war. He sought to serve in a subor-

dinate capacity in the Princess Patricia's Regiment, offering to take command of a company. I declined to allow him to serve in that capacity and at Valcartier gave him command of the Highland Brigade. At St. Julien, at the second battle of Ypres-which I think in some respects was the greatest battle of the war, owing to the fact that it was the first time the horrible poison gas was used by the Germans-this officer practically had entire command of the whole defence system. General Alderson, it is true, was in reserve; he was in the rear, as commanders usually are, ten or fifteen miles away, and was therefore not in actual touch with what was going on. Turner was actually in the firing line and had command of the whole force, of the entire line, some battalions of the 2nd Brigade and some battalions of the 1st Brigade, as well as the entire Highland Brigade, being placed directly under him, so the general control of the whole fight devolved upon Turner. He carried that fight through all Thursday afternoon and night, Friday and Friday night and Saturday, and retired only late on Saturday night, when the British troops came in to help him out. I think I am right in the date and that he had the general command up to Saturday night. Further than that, in 1915, about a month later, he ' distinguished himself at the battle of Festu-bert. Although the attack as a whole at that time was not a success, Turner's part, the Canadian part, of it was a complete success. The troops on either side of him encountered machine gun positions which the reconnaissance of the Imperial forces had not disclosed, the troops on each side being Imperials. The machine gun nests held the Imperials up, but Turner got through and maintained his position until he was relieved by Imperial troops. When the second division was being organized in 1915, General Steele not being fit to take command owing to having been injured twice, I recommended Turner for the command. Now, Sir, in justice to General Turner and in justice to the late Lord Kitchener, I must point out that there was an agitation at that time, or, rather, there was a feeling that only Imperial officers should command divisions. Even when the Valcartier camp was formed the idea was entertained by some that colonels of our regiments should be taken from the Imperial service as far as possible. I repudiated that.
The next thing was the command of the brigades. I did not find any fault with those who recommended appointments contrary to my views, no doubt their motives
were absolutely honest, but I insisted that our own officers should be placed in command of our brigades. Then when the Second Division was formed I felt that General Turner was entitled to recognition and should have it, so I stood up for him. He had distinguished himself in South Africa and also at St. Julien-the greatest battle in many respects in the history of the world-and also at Festubert. Sir Robert Borden reached London the day before I did, but I did not see him on the morning of my arrival. I immediately called on Lord Kitchener at 8 o'clock, as previously arranged, and discussed with him General Turner's appointment. He recommended some excellent English officers but as he had not given them anything above a brigade in the British Army, I did not think we should give them the command of our division. When I asked him why Turner was not put in command, he said that Turner was insubordinate at Festubert. I inquired, "How insubordinate; he won Festubert." Lord Kitchener said, " When the order came to him to take Festubert he said, "What, more bloody murder!" I said, " What would you have him call it? Was not that * a very proper description?" I assured him that no staff officer of any decency would ever report what was said by an officer when an order was handed to him. I had been a staff officer and had carried orders, but I never thought of reporting what an officer said. Officers always damn the orders they receive, but I thought it was beneath my dignity to report their remarks. However, this had been reported to General Alderson, and by him reported to Kitchener. Alderson was against Turner from start to finish and used his malign influence for all he was worth. I stood out for Turner's appointment. Kitchener asked me to see him again in an hour's time. In three-quarters of an hour he telephoned to me to come to him. He said: " I have seen His Majesty the King, who said, ' I pinned the South African medal on Turner's breast, I pinned the Distinguished Service Order on Turner's breast, I pinned the Victoria Cross on Turner's breast, and I want Turner to command the Canadian Second Division.' '' Kitchener then said that Turner would command the Second Division. Turner took over the command and held it with great credit until he was removed and brought back to England to act as staff officer to the Overseas Minister of Militia- one of the greatest blunders in the history of the war.

About this story of Jack Currie and the Snow dugout- a story which is common to-day-a colonel recently returned from the front, a Highland brigade colonel, too, said to me: "There is no use in your telling me anything different; I know it was Jack Currie who was kicked out of Snow's headquarters." I took the position that the following advantages would accrue from having the two corps. There would be greater rest for the men; it would be a complete system running in bunches of three; there would be honest rivalry between the two corps; it would require no more men than for one corps because the same length of front was always to be held, the men would be exposed to the same fire; there would be the highest efficiency when we had two corps instead of one, and there would be no vendetta with England. Anybody going from England to France or from France to England at times had to take his life in his hands because there was so much bad blood between the two places. Finally the Prime Minister got the parties together and the trouble was smoothed over. There would be no swash-buckling, and no using of the Canadian corps as a " bouncer." If there was a nasty job, it was a case of " send for the Canadian corps." All that the Canadian corps was entitled to do was to take its place in the fighting line, and it was not entitled to be regarded as a " bouncer " for the army. There would not be nearly such heavy losses, and there would be an opportunity for efficient officers. Let me point out here that the Canadian force has developed thousands of splendid officers. There were in England hundreds upon hundreds of excellent officers who could not get to the front; hundreds of them came home, and we hear men from their places in the House taunting officers because they did not go to the front and fight, when these men would have given their last drop of blood .to be permitted to go, but they could not go except as privates, and they were too old for that. We had at the front any number of boys who were fit for promotion. There was young Rogers of Toronto who was competent to command a division, and there was Colonel Allan of Toronto, now deceased. These are only two of hundreds I could name if I could take the time. There were many fellows who would make excellent divisional commanders- take McBrien, no man would have ever made a better divisional commander than he. There are our friends Griesbach and Peck in this House, and they are no exception to the rule; there are hundreds like them who would have made the best of
brigadier commanders, staff officers, regimental commanders that it was possible to find. Yet, under the closed corporation of one unit, there was no opportunity for these men. I have no hesitation in saying, with all kindness to certain of the gentlemen who held these high positions, that they were not superior to men who were serving under them, and it would have been a great thing for the service if there had been six divisions instead of five eighteen brigades instead of nine, and so on right down the line. Sir Edward Kemp, in his speech, pointed out the terrible increase in cost which he said would result from the adoption of such a scheme. The cost, however, would not have been greater. These men were drawing almost the same pay, if not higher, than they would have got at the front, in whitewash jobs in England where they were rolling over each other, in the way, breaking their hearts- but they wanted to serve their country in some way, and so they took these jobs in England. Had my scheme been adopted, recognition of worth would have been possible; publicity of facts would have resulted, not propaganda. I could give a chapter on that, but I shall not detain the House. There would have been no closed corporation. Inefficient officers would have been weeded out; blunders would have been avoided, and there would have been a larger force at the front training instead of deteriorating at the base. I shall not enter the details of that, but can give the figures at any time they are needed. There would have been a comparison of command which was not otherwise possible. Hundreds of good officers for the staff could be found in the force, both at the front and in England; more officers and men would have been trained, so that hundreds of officers and men who have returned without service would thus have had it. Junior officers at the front would have had promotion; competition would have eliminated weak senior officers, and there would have been no actions such as Lens, Passchendaele and Cambrai. At the end of 1916 there were enough recruits in uniform to keep six divisions at strength until the end of the war. There is not one argument against six divisions and two corps, and not one argument for only four divisions in one corps under one command.
I was going to take up the question of the dual ministry, 'but I will save that for another occasion, and will simply say that there was very bad blood between England and the front. I was also going to take

Tip the question of control of generals, but that comes under another heading, so I will defer it.
We come to the time of the retreat of the Germans, and I want hon. members to picture this in their mind's eye. These are my ideas, and while I may be wrong, in many things I came pretty close to what happened. The line from Nieuport on the North sea to Verdun, is an air line of 200 miles; the trench line between the same points is 260 miles in length. From Chateau Thierry, the south point of the German advance, to Namur in Belgium, is upwards of 100 miles. The funnel is thus 200 to 260 miles at the mouth with a depth of 100 miles and at Namur the neck that the Germans would have to retreat through is about 30 miles wide. The whole German line, 260 miles in length, had to retreat 100 miles and then go through that thirty mile neck. If the line were broken perceptibly at any one point, a large part of the force, if not the whole force, might have been cut off, and that was Foch's game, to pin them up against Sedan at the right, to smash them off to the left, and to smash them in the centre. His plan was to cut off two small salients from Rheims to Soissons and from Noyon to Arras. Some people thought that if he had adopted the big plan better results might have been had, but his plan succeeded very well. The centre of that funnel was Douai, Cambrai, Le Gateau, and Hirson. I might point out that on my maternal side I had associates in the city of Valenciennes and Oambrai which I visited thirty years -ago or more and in which I took a great interest. It is the centre of the funnel and any one could understand that the- German army, in order to save itself from annihilation must on one side hold the centre of the funnel by the best forces, and the Canadian troops which were against them, as they did on every occasion faced fearlessly and manfully these soldiers. The world never before has seen soldiers like these Canadians. The river Meuse runs from Verdun northwest to Charleville and Mezieres, and there is a splendid road, which I have had the opportunity of travelling over on three or four occasions and down which the Germans had to get all their heavy material. In order to hold themselves on their line they 'had to get their impedimenta and munitions of war back through this funnel as fast as they could, and in order to do that they had to hold the positions all along the front. The Meuse runs north west to Charleville 
and Mezieres, then north -to Namur, then northeast to Liege.
The causes of the retreat, in general terms, were the splendid advances made by the Yankees. They had brought millions of troops into France, and their entrance into the war and their advances in attack was one factor; secondly, there was the disruption and discontent ill Germany, and for evidence of that you have only to read I.udendorff's story. Thirdly, the front German line had two salients, one from Rheims to Soissons, and the second from Noyon to Arras, and any break in any part of the line endangered the whole line. I have no hesitation in saying, from the viewpoint of the student of military history, that Luden-dorff, in retiring his army as he did against these splendid assaults of the British, French and other Allied forces, made what must be admitted by military men to be one of the most masterly retreats that has ever occurred in history. The Germans had, to hold these positions in order to avoid disaster, and I maintain that any general must have known that in going up against these positions he could expect to hit a snag and he should be prepared for it.
We have read a great deal of the qualities of soldiers in times gone by-of Horatius and his comrades holding the bridge; of Leonidas and his three hundred men at Thermopylae, of the charge of the Light Brigade at Balaclava, but we must remember that all these men were inspired by the enthusiasm of personal combat and the impelling glory of a cavalry charge. The heroic cavalry charge at Balaclava, for instance, was accompanied by sounding trumpets that inspired the men to brave deeds, but in this war, again and again and again men have walked silently up to almost certain death. They could not see their enemy once in a thousand times, for he would be hidden in some dugout, firing with a machine gun from some unseen position. The history of warfare shows nothing more glorious than the cool bravery of our men.
The retreat of the German army was begun at Chateau Thiery. I happen to know intimately a Yankee officer, who, with his battalion, was surrounded. He did not know that the Germans were so close to him, but when he saw the Germans behind him he realized there was only one thing to do and that was to shoot. " We were good shots," lie said, " and we trimmed them to a finish; we would have run like good fellows if we had only known, but there they wTere behind us and we had to fight our way out." And so it went on. They got there fighting

little by little, until finally the Yankees made a good showing with the French to the south. Some two divisions of Americans also made a good showing with the British to the west. The conduct of the soldiers at. Arras, Parvilliers, and elsewhere was magnificent. I have had questions put to me regairding the lose of the 32nd British division which was attached 'to the Canadians, and which was almost wiped out of existence-needlessly, the British officers claim. The Drocourt-Queant line was smashed; a tremendous artillery fire preceded', the tanks smashed through and the infantry followed up. At the same time the British claim that their naval divisions .broke through a little farther to the south. The Canadians did their duty fearlessly and well, following out their part in the general plan of attack. I might refer to a letter which the Prime Minister has in his possession, and which I wrote away back in 1915, and again to the same effect in 1916, protesting against these blanket attacks running up against trenches. It was only a waste of men, and I suggested that the narrow front and a smash through with tremendous force, then mushrooming -out, was the only plan of attack. Ludendorff admits that this narrow yet deep attack Is effective. On November 27, the British had advamced- to Cambrai. Considerable criticism has been made that I was wrong in my statements in regard to Cambrai. What I said in my letter, which appears on last year's Hansard, was that it entailed a "needless loss of men," was "foullheaded," and that there was fighting in "suburban villages." I have here maps which were taken off a German officer, stained with his own gore, and good rich blood it seems to be. I have scores of reports from lieutenants, corporals, captains, majors, and colonels who were on the field of Cambrai, and some of them are not unknown to this' House. These facts have been furnished me in justification of my position in this matter. I shall not weary the House by reading them, nor divulge the names of my informants. Incidentally, I might say that in South Africa I never divulged the name of any person who informed me of anything. In this war 1 had considerable difficulty on that account with some of my colleagues. I pointblank refused to divulge the name of my informant in each and every case in matters concerning secret missions and things of that sort. I would not divulge these things to any human being. Any information given me I treat as sacred, but lest some
one should say "Oh, it was Jones sent him that, or Brown," I want to point out that they have done nothing of the kind. These reports have been sent to me by men who held them and who have been discharged from the army. I have scores upon scores of original orders and reports justifying the position I 'took as regards Cambrai where for example, in one attack, one whole company reduced to the command of a lance-corporal, was shot to pieces inside of two hours.

The Canadian force lay with its right on the Amiens-Oambrai road, and its left extended beyond the Arras-Oambrai line. On the 28th of September the British and Canadians met at the village of Fontaine, having failed to take it. Subsequently it was taken by a Canadian infantry brigade. The high command replied that this was not so, and refused to have artillery fire upon the church tower. I am not called on to give names. I am assuming responsibility for my statements here to-day. I am not going to stoop to giving names. We have seen that game played many a time

here. Sam Hughes assumes responsibility for any statements he makes. I said that it was in the early morning and foggy, and the artillery did not know they were so close to St. Olle. As the main line of the Canadians had been advanced and the right wing curved back, they thought the linh would be farther up, and the first thing they knew they were shot down and lay wounded in the suburbs of St. Olle for half a day. St. Olle was taken that evening and they were relieved.
St. Olle is a suburb of Cambrai and machine guns were in a church tower at St. Olle. The word was sent back that the machine guns were there but the higher command said " there are no machine guns there;, go on." That is not disputed, if it is disputed I will give the data.
I met Major Edgar when the Princess Patricias were here, and I said in the presence of Mr. Smellie, a barrister of Ottawa: " Edgar, I do not want you to open your mouth; I am going to do the talking; you are not talking; you notified the higher command on the night of the 28th that you were up against wire entanglements, but the higher command replied that there were no wire entanglements there and instructed you to go on." Edgar said " There are wire entanglements over a mile long and sixty yards in width " but the higher command said: " No, go on."
Mr. GRIB9BACH:	Who would be the
higher command-the brigade commander, the divisional commander or the corps commander?
The hon. gentleman knows the routine as well as I do.
No, pardon me; the hon. and gallant member is too subject to inferences of that kind. I desire him to say whom he means-the brigade commander, the divisional commander or the corps commander.

I do not presume it went back as far as the Field Marshal but I would expect a brigade commander would consult the corps commander before he would order any one to go up against wire entanglements like that.
That would eliminate the divisional commander?

When the command came to these boys to go on, the higher command was responsible no matter where it might be. On the night of the 28th the artillery was ordered forward after one o'clock in the morning 6,000 yards to their positions before they were to fire the bar-

rage*. On the 29th the Canadian division passed through a narrow passage left in the wire entanglements, deployed outwards and took their positions. Inside of three hours they were shot to pieces. Lance-corporals in some cases were in command of companies. Colonel John Thompson of Ottawa came out with less than 100 men. The Highland battalion came out with less than 150 men, another battalion came out with 40 men, and other battalions met similar terrible losses. Next day two tanks started up, punched through the wire entanglements and in less than an hour one of them destroyed 59 German gun positions with the loss to the tanks of one man slightly wounded. In one instance it was a question of sound judgment and in the other it was a matter of sending splendid and gallant Canadian soldiers up against machine guns. There were machine gun nests every nine or ten yards and our battalions were mercilessly sent up against these and shot to pieces. That is what happened to Major Toipp's company of the 42nd Highlanders. I gave him the data-I did not get it from him-and he had to admit that it was correct. The losses on the 29th September were simply terrible. On the 30th the tanks came forward.
On the morning of the 1st of October I wrote a letter to the Prime Minister of Canada. I had seen- by the reports how the boys had been handled and I protested. I immediately sent notice to General Currie, to Field Marshal Haig, and to the overseas minister, and inside of a week after Ramillies had been taken an order was issued that there should be no more concentrated attacks, but that there should be, to use the words of General Foch, "peaceful penetration;" that is, penetration after heavy military fire-smash them to pieces and then advance. Our machine gunners also had been rushed forward on the night of the 29th to try and occupy positions.
Colonel PECK, V.C.: I would ask the hon. gentleman if he could give us any map reference as to the location of the German lines where the machine guns were, or anything else, because I have been trying to follow him closely. As far as I can find out the artillery seem to have been ahead of the infantry-something that I have never heard of before.
(Sir SAM HUGHES: I have maps here which I am not going to bother the House with because all the members could not gather round and see them. On October

1, when the magnificent battalion, so splendidly led by my hon. friend (Col. Peck, V.C.) fell back, I am free to s>ay the artillery was not ahead of the infantry. They were up on the line that had been left that morning, and the artillery, the camp equipage and everything of that kind had to he retired precipitately to the rear, something it had not done before. They feared that the Germans were following up, but fortunately the Germans were not strong enough to follow them. Up north of St. Remi the hon. gentleman's battalion retreated from Ban-tigny. I do not reflect on anybody. Fighting such as that had never occurred in the history of the world, but the occurrences showed lack of proper discretion on the part of some person in the rear in failing to make sure of the position, with the result that thousands of men were rolled up between the marshes of'the iSensee canal and Cambrai. It was criminal to send men blindfolded and empty-handed against positions like that. On the 30th September they sent the tanks in and cleared the German machine gun nests out. They had no proper barrage of any kind on the morning of the 29th. As I say, they had not sufficient artillery barrage and on the 1st October the 16th battalion, commanded by the -hon. member for Sheena (Col. Peck) was badly shot up, and the remnant of the battalion in the end had to retire with the loss of one complete company and the balance badly ishot up.
Col. PECK, V.C.: I would like to correct that statement; it is not the fact. I might inform the House that my battalion did not retire then and never retired in the war. I was ordered to keep in touch with another battalion, but in coming up we were left with a flank of two or three miles. The Germans came through in behind Avecourt and my battalion, along with others, having reached their objective, were forced not to retire but to move to the right and form the flank on the right.

I do not wish to
detract from the credit to which any particular battalion or regiment is entitled, simply because it had to retire. I never knew of a battalion yet that had not to retire at some period or other of its history during the late war. What I have to say is that the gallant 16th Battalion had to retire or had to go back in an oblique direction, and the flanking British troops on their left were caught by the fire of the Germans posted in the marshes along the Sensee canal. One company of the 16th Regiment was
practically wiped out and the balance badly shattered were retired southwesterly to the position held by the Canadians in the morning. There is no glory in saying that any particular battalion did not retire. The best soldiers in the world have had to retire again and again. As one officer said to me speaking of his experiences, " I came back much faster than I went in." The point I want to make is that on the 29th there was not sufficient preparation. On the 30th there was proper tank preparation and a good artillery barrage. Still they first attempted to make the dash without that proper preparation and came to grief. They did not capture the place until the 10th of October. I wrote my letter on October 1, and the statements I made were absolutely true.
There was at St. Olle, St. Remi and Petit Fontaine fighting in the suburbs and bull-headed work all along the line. On the 30th more adequate preparations were made and more was gained with the loss of only one wounded man than was achieved with such terribly heavy losses on the 29th. On the 1st October an infantry attack developed north of St. Remi with the result as my hon. friend (Col. Peck) points out that the 16th Battalion had to retire obliquely to save itself. I think I am safe in saying that at least one company of the 16th was wiped out and the balance badly cut up as is' proved by my records and also the German records. But that is no discredit to the men. I say that better fighting was never displayed in the history of the war. These men went on to certain death again and again and there was no protection for them. I wonder at the higher command permitting such a thing and allowing the men to go on. I want to point out that in one instance Lord Cavan took full responsibility early in the war for not advancing and declined to make the attempt, notwithstanding the order of his superior officer, because he knew the reconnaissance that had been made was wrong and there was no proper barrage. I know that the 27th Regiment was cut up early in the war because of failure to disobey. At St. Eloi I know that four colonels followed my instructions. I had given them orders "Unless there has been a proper reconnaissance don't put yourselves at the mercy of any fellow over you; do not sacrifice one man's life needlessly unless you are absolutely sure that you are right." Those instructions were followed by four colonels. One pooT fellow who did not follow these



instructions lost some 827 odd men of his battalion oh the battlefield of St. Eloi.
I do not want to dilate on the affair of Moos, or say anything here that will not do the highest justice to the gallant officers and men concerned; they had to live up to their general instructions. As I said at the time, my one object was to save the lives of these gallant men and to use brains instead of something else. My object in writing that letter was absolutely justified. Inkerman was a soldiers' battle, tout every battle in this war has practically been another Inker-man. I tried to do justice to all without doing injustice to any; but justice delayed is never the same as justice rendered at the time. As to Mons, I have data here (I will not weary the House with it at the present time) showing that the general officer commanding the Canadian Corps congratulated the troops at 10.50 o'clock that morning on the capture of the historic city of Mons. I want to point out that the Canadians were eight miles beyond) Mons on the north and more than abreast of it on the east. I saw a tetter written by General Morrison, in which he stated that the night before the [DOT]armistice smoke was going up from fires started by the Germans preliminary to their retirement. So that the Germans were retiring, and anyhow Mons was not a city of any great importance; I would not give the snap of my finger for it. It is a nice little place, but to sacrifice the lives of Canadians on the eve of the armistice was quite out of place and more of a piece of bravado than an attempt to help the great cause of human liberty at an acceptable time.
There are some other matters that call for consideration, but I must take the privilege of dealing with them on a future occasion. At present I shall not detain the House any longer.
