subsubtopic: MOTION ,BY MR. PRIPP AS TO POSITIONS FOR RETURNER SOLDIERS.
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, all persons who have served overseas in the Canadian Expeditionary Forces, including British Reservists from Canada, are entitled to be placed in as good circumstances financially as before enlistment by being (a) restored to their former positions by their employers; (b) appointed to all positions in the outside and inside branches of the Civil Service of Canada if possessed of the necessary qualifications without passing any
fSir Sam Hughes.]
academic examinations and in priority to all other applicants; and (c) given an annuity for a limited period sufficient to augment their present earning capacity reduced by disability arising from such service, to equal the amount earned at the time of enlistment. And further, that the necessary legislation to provide for the purposes of this resolution be passed at this session.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution was introduced by me at the last session of Parliament, in March last, as the result of personal interviews with a great many returned soldiers. I do not know whether any other hon. gentleman has had the same opportunity as I have had to receive and interview many of the men who served us so faithfully overseas. Whether it is because this is the Capital city or not I do not know, but we certainly do receive a very great number of returned men in Ottawa. As a result of my interviews I came to the conclusion that this Government had not up to that time, that is, in March, 1919, taken such practical steps to rehabilitate the returned man as they ought to have and might have taken. Since I introduced this resolution I have received thousands of letters from all parts of the country, and some of them I would like to place upon Hansard.
I imagine that every hon. gentleman-will agree with the preamble stated here) that the members of our overseas forces are entitled to be placed, as far as this country can place them, in as good a position as they were in before the war. That is not such a very big order if it is considered properly and fairly. What was the position of these men when they came back home last year? As far as I can find from these personal interviews as well as from the letters I have received, their position amounts to this: A large proportion of them find that the positions which they held are not now open to them; and the first proposition which I asked the House to consider is that those men should be restored to their former positions by their employers. I am not unmindful of the fact that perhaps this Parliament has not sufficient jurisdiction to enact that an employer shall reemploy his former employee; that is possibly a matter .that the local legislatures must deal with, because it may come under " property and civil rights;" but I do think the Dominion Government can restore returned men to their positions in the Government service, and from the correspondence I have received it appears that that has not been done. I think it is important that this House should affirm the principle,

subsubtopic: MOTION ,BY MR. PRIPP AS TO POSITIONS FOR RETURNER SOLDIERS.
speechtext: No, read them.

subsubtopic: MOTION ,BY MR. PRIPP AS TO POSITIONS FOR RETURNER SOLDIERS.
speechtext:
-and come to the part which is pertinent. He states:
I am a returned boy of twenty-five months' service in France and over three years in khaki. 1914 I obtained my qualifying certificate for a Railway Mail Clerk, and having no prominent friends at that time was naturally unsuccessful in obtaining an appointment. Since the war the appointments are made direct from Ottawa and not from the various M.P.'s-
This will meet the approval of a great many hon. gentlemen because the writer goes on to say that appointments should be made by members of Parliament and not by the Civil Service Commission.

subsubtopic: MOTION ,BY MR. PRIPP AS TO POSITIONS FOR RETURNER SOLDIERS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: MOTION ,BY MR. PRIPP AS TO POSITIONS FOR RETURNER SOLDIERS.
speechtext:
He continues:
I am not asking any favours, holding the necessary qualifications as I do, and with your resolution an accomplished fact, we may get the appointments, which in the past seemed to be impossible for a boy such as myself, with no people here in the country to help me along.
Now, Mr. Speaker, that is a straight, honest letter, which would not be written without cause by any man who had served his country as faithfully as did the writer of it.
Another statement appeared in the Toronto Globe which I shall read because it is short, because it expresses the idea embodied in nearly all the communications which have come to me. The words of a returned soldier are quoted as follows:
We won the war, but I as a veteran do not want any cash won in that way. Like many of my chums, I am a citizen and a taxpayer of Canada as well as a soldier, and I know that every dollar raised by Canada comes from our

pockets, and that we cannot hoist ourselves by pulling on our own boot-straps.
We all want a chance to get a good Job-as good or better than we left behind us. If the chaps doing all this talking were busy working they wouldn't have so much time to spend looking for so much easy money.
Again I ask, why should a conscript get $2,000 of our taxes because he was forced to go to Prance when the war was finished?
There are in Ottawa to-day, I have no doubt, at least five hundred returned men out of employment-although Ottawa and the Government at Ottawa have done excellent work in providing positions as far as possible for returned men; and that is much to the credit of the Government here. In The Veteran, published by the Great War Veterans' Association, it is estimated that fifty thousand men will be out of employment this winter in the larger cities. What do we propose to do about it? It is true that this matter of the re-establishment of the soldier has been referred to a parliamentary committee, but I am sorry to say that there is one notable feature about that committee-those who represent the majority of the men who rwent to the front are not represented on it. I hope that thiat will not cause the committee to fall short of dealing with this matter thoroughly. A large body of men who went to the front, eighty per cent of them, were labourers and mechanics from the large cities. Toronto did its duty nobly; I believe that that city alone sent 75,000 men overseas. But there is no representation of members from Toronto on that committee; neither is there any in respect of Winnipeg, Ottawa or Hamilton. I mention this only to express the hope that the House will strengthen 'the hands of that committee by adopting this resolution so that those on that committee who are not as much in touch with the condition of the returned men as we who represent cities will, nevertheless, do their part in giving effect to *such legislation as may be necessary to .rehabilitate returned men.
I think I have said enough about the employment end of the resolution. I have somewhere heard the expression-and it seems to me most apt-that a Government that is strong enough to take a man out of his job and put him in the army ought to be strong enough to take him out of the army and put him hack into his job. That is a principle which any Government might well adopt in dealing with the question of restoring 'to these men, as far as possible, their former positions.

Then, I ask fih'ait all persons who have served overseas in the Canadian Expeditionary Forces be 'appointed to all positions in the inside 'and outside branches of the Civil Service, if possessed of the necessary qualifications, without examination. That suggestion ought to be accepted unanimously 'by the House. Any hon. member who will read soTne of the questions put to candidates for poisitions in. the lower grades *in the Civil Service will see at once how absurd they are. Had I known that this resolution was to come up 'this afternoon I would have brought with me some examples of these questions, for the benefit of hon. gentlemen who have not seen them. One question, for instance, was: "What is St. Petersburg noted for?" Evidently that examination .paper was written before the name of the Russian capital was changed to Petrograd. Candidates were also asked to name several cities in India where certain 'articles are .produced or manufactured -'and all this for a man who is going to earn $800 a year. Then, there are questions in arithmetic; the applicant is .asked to multiply twenty-eight figures by twenty-eight figures, and so on-questions that were submitted by a gentlemen who then held a position on the Civil Service Commission. I suppose they (were his idea, coming as he did from .a university not far away, of 'the best way to get at the proper qualifications of a postman, a letter-carrier or messenger. Any returned 'Soldier, who, as the result of an oral examination, can show that he has enough common sense to perform such work in 'the lower grades *as I have mentioned1, ought to get the .position without having to write any examination.
The last clause of 'the resolution involves, perhaps, a more difficult question; it asks that we augment 'the present earning capacity of the soldier, which has been reduced by disability arising from service. That, of course, is a very big order. I have considered the matter seriously, and I do think that we ought to augment the present earning capacity of the returned man so that it will be made at least equal to his earning capacity before he went overseas.

subsubtopic: MOTION ,BY MR. PRIPP AS TO POSITIONS FOR RETURNER SOLDIERS.
speechtext: Do you mean the wounded man?

subsubtopic: MOTION ,BY MR. PRIPP AS TO POSITIONS FOR RETURNER SOLDIERS.
speechtext:
The wounded man, the partly disabled man, and the man who has been rendered unable, by reason of his having taken part in the war, to hold the position that he held before. Let me give you a single example. Not long .ago a

young man came to me and said: "Mr. Fripp, I would like to get a position in the Government." "Well/ I said, "what was your position before you went to war?" He said: "I was a qualified plumber. I was shell-shocked. When I came hack I went to my old job, but I find I cannot do the work that I did before. I cannot go on a high building; I cannot do plumbing work at any considerable height from the ground, so that all I can earn now is what I can get as a plumber's helper." He put the question to me: "Why should I lose, after my service of four years overseas, the difference between the wage that I was able to earn when I offered my services to my country and wihat, through no fault of my own, is the most that I am able to earn now?" That is only one case out of thousands of the same nature. Many returned men are not quite fitted for the positions that they held before, and the question arises, what are we going to do about it? My judgment is that we have to deal with these returned men practically as individuals, not as a class. If the Department of Militia and Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment are doing their d'u'ty, they have a complete record of every man who went overseas. They ought to know what his former occupation was; what disability, if any, he suffered or is suffering; what his earning capacity was before he went away, and what his earning capacity is to-day. Having that information, it would not be difficult for us to take hold of these men individually and find out exactly what can be done for them. In my judgment, with all due respect to those w'ho think differently, the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment is a very expensive piece of machinery for the amount of good that it is going to do or is doing. If I remember rightly the figures given by the President of the Council (Hon. Mr. Rowell) the other day-of course, I am subject to correction in this-he said that 22,000 returned men were being re-trained. That is an excellent and very essential work, no doubt, but there are thousands of men who cannot take the training that is necessary to fit them for better positions in life.
If, as I understand, we are paying out of the treasury for the Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment Department $30,000,000 or $40,000,000, it seems to me that is too expensive for the results we are obtaining from it. Would it not be better for us to take each soldier individually, and to say to him: We will offer you a position; we will help you to secure such a position as you are able to fill? These men are the wards of the Government, and it is the duty of the Government to take them individually and to see that their present condition is, at all events, as good, if not better-and we would all like to see it better-than when they went overseas. There are many men whose positions are better to-day than they were when the men went overseas. We can eliminate them, but there are many men whose present positions are much worse, and such men must be attended to by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, or some other organization, and money is required for that.
I am satisfied that we must either deal with the problem in the way I suggest or give them a cash bonus or gratuity such as that with which the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Currie) dealt in this House some days ago. We must face the situation one way or the other, and that will require money. As regards the money part of the matter, I am not one of those who may toe or are pessimistic about it. There are large sources of revenue yet untapped for the returned soldier. I do not say that we could raise such a sum or should shoulder such a responsibility as that which was suggested as regards giving them $2,500 and $2,000 each; but there are in this country many people who have not made any sacrifice whatever, and they could raise a large sum of money which would pay the interest on a larger sum. If, for example, we put a special soldiers' war tax on every man, woman and child in Canada, we could raise a large sum of money. We could raise very much larger sums from men who are not yet, through the income tax, paying their fair share of the burden of this war. Of course, my first proposition would be to put a tax on our farmers., who have not yet, I think, contributed their fair share to the war. I am sure all hon. members are of opinion that there are sources of revenue from which we can obtain such a sum of money as will be sufficient, in part at least, to mete out to those young men who have come back to us some such measure of civil re-establishment as will give them a fair start for the future.
Then there is the alien question. This Government lost thousands of friends in this country by not taxing the alien. The time is not yet too late, and there is no reason in the world why we should not pass legislation compelling the employer of the alien to deduct every day or every week a certain proportion from his earnings so that he may pay his share of the war. I do not see any serious difficulty in that respect. In Australia and New Zealand the Governments are moving along the lines I suggest with regard to compelling em-

ployers to take back soldier employees if they are able to do the work. We have a " Master and Servant " Act in this province and in every other province, so why should not a soldier be able to go in a simple way before a magistrate and lay a complaint that his employer refuses to take him back and say to the magistrate: You can decide whether I am to be taken back or not? That would be a very simple remedy.
There are many ways in which we can deal with the problem to. the advantage of the returned men. I do not want to detain the House any longer, because I presume this resolution of mine will go to the committee .that is now dealing with the soldiers' civil re-establishment. My sole desire is that it will go to the committee so that their action may be as wide as it is possible to make it for the purpose that we have in view, namely, the re-establishment of the returned man in civil life. I am satisfied that the committee will deal with the matter seriously if they realize that the House is in earnest-and we are in earnest and the Government must realize that. Any man who has anything to do with the returned men must know that there is amongst those men a current of feeling that they have not received justice. I know no body of men in the Dominion of Canada who say less about what they should have and what they think they should have than the returned soldiers. The returned soldier is the most modest man I have ever had to deal with, and as you know, Sir, during the time I have sat in Parliament, I have had to do with thousands of persons wanting Government employment. I have never yet met a class that equals the returned man in his humility, modesty, want of braggadocio, any attribute that would lead one to believe that he was expecting more than he thought he ought to get. On the other hand, I find they expect less than we ought to give them, and it is our duty to face the situation and to see if we cannot put them back as nearly as possible where they were before they , made the great sacrifice and did so much for Canada and future generations of this great country.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MOTION ,BY MR. PRIPP AS TO POSITIONS FOR RETURNER SOLDIERS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as the resolution moved by the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) raises questions very much of the nature of and 
cognate to, those which are at present engaging a committee of this House appointed to consider the Bill dealing with soldiers' civil re-establishment, and acting upon the suggestion of the hon. member himself- without undertaking at present to express an opinion one way or the other upon his proposals-I beg to move that the resolution be referred to the said committee.
iMr. SPEAKER: That motion could not be entertained at this stage except by consent.
Motion agreed to. [DOT]

M,r. LEVI THOMPSON (Qu'Appelle) moved:
That in the opinion of this House, it is
desirable that a limit should be placed on the time that may toe occupied by members in addressing the House and Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think it will be agreed that this House transacts more important business than any other institution in Canada. One would, therefore, naturally expect the business of this House to he transacted in the most 'business-like way. But no one, I -think, will claim -that it is so conducted. I -think most people will agree that the work of this House is transacted in a more unbusiness like- way than that of any other business institution in Canada. That certainly should not be the ease.
There may be some reason for this, but to-night I shall deal with only one. The length of time occupied by many hon. members of this House in making speeches on different questions, and the frequency with which they address the House, is becoming both a public and a private nuisance. It is a public nuisance in that it wastes the * money of the country. I do not purpose giving an estimate of the amount of money wasted by unnecessarily long and frequent speeches. Estimates have been made, however, of the cost per day, and even per hour and per minute, of the cost of conducting the business of this House. There is no doubt that the sessions are unduly prolonged by reason of these lengthy and frequent speeches, and I do not think it requires much arguing to make it plain that this practice, which is daily becoming worse, does constitute a public nuisance, if for no other reason than that money of the country is unnecessarily expended in carrying on the work of the House.
It constitutes a public nuisance also because the business of the House is

unnecessarily retarded, and in consequence, important measures are left over from session to session. There may sometimes be other reasons why measures are left over, but the main reason, in my opinion, is that so much time is unnecessarily taken up in discussion that the Government are discouraged from bringing forward the legislation they would like to present.
The practice is also a private nuisance, because it compels members of this House to remain here longer than is necessary. It is in the interests of the country, I believe, that men who want to conduct the business of the country in a businesslike way, promptly and with despatch, should be encouraged to seek seats in this House and to keep those seats so long as they are able. At present men of that type are discouraged from entering Parliament. The last thing this country needs is orations. We need, rather, business men from all walks of life-the business labour man, if you will, and business men in every other line. We require men who believe in conducting the business of the country with promptness. But the time that is now wasted in making speeches discourages these men from entering the House. Further, from the beginning to the end of the session, the voices of a great many members of this House are hardly ever heard, and they are silent largely because of the length of time taken up by others. I believe that the views of some of these men who are conversant with the subject under discussion would be more useful to the House and the country than the views so frequently and fluently and freely expressed by others, but these men are silent because they feel themselves outclassed by orators, or near-orators, or those who think they are orators, who are anxious to address the House on all subjects that come before it whether they are posted on them or not.
I want to refer briefly to the Debates of the session of 1918, the last session for which we have a bound volume of Hansard. I have made a few calculations, and while I would not lender take to say how much of the time of the House each member occupied to air his views-I am referring to private members, and that does not necessarily include the Speaker of the House or the Chairman, the Prime Minister, the leader of the Opposition or his desk mate, nor any one holding a portfolio under the Government-I find that there were 204
private members, and that nine of them took up twenty-five per cent of the time occupied, as nearly as I could figure it-
Name them.

and that over
half of the time was occupied by twenty-five members. Those hon. gentlemen may consider that their views are so important that they are entitled to that proportion of time, but I do not think the majority, of hon. members would agree with them. To make matters worse some of these gentlemen who took up this extra time were new members, and when we think of what may happen when they become thoroughly familiar with the procedure of the House and " get into their stride," the prospect gives us cause for serious reflection.
It is proposed that we shall express ourselves in the terms of the resolution I have moved. We are only asking for an expression of opinion. No plan is being proposed except, if the House should express itself favourably to this resolution, we would expect the Government, or the House, in some way to take action upon it because there is very little use in expressing the view of the majority of the House unless action is taken. I do not want to suggest any particular way in which this plan could be worked out, but one thing that strikes me is that if we think favourably of this proposal a parliamentary committee should be appointed at the beginning of next session which would take the matter into consideration and decide upon some plan which it would ask the House to adopt. It would be useless to take the question up at this late day in the session, but it seems to me that it would be well to take it up at the beginning of next session.
While, I say, we are only asking the House to adopt the principle, I would suggest that it would not be out of place for me to make some suggestions that have occurred to me, and I make them merely as suggestions. It seems to me that if we were adopting such a rule we would have to make some exceptions. Necessarily, it would go without saying that the Speaker and the Chairman of Committees, the leader of the Government and the leader of the Opposition, would be excepted from the rule. If a time limit were fixed for each member, it would be only reasonable that certain members should be allowed a greater time than others, for instance the heads of departments or the holders of portfolios in the Government. The work of the Opposition, no matter which party is in

opposition, constitutes a very important part of the work of this House, and I believe that it would be necessary, if any such rule were adopted, that the, leader of the Opposition should be allowed to select a certain number of persons whom he would call his lieutenants and who would be given additional time. These are merely suggestions.
There is another thing that occurs to me. According to present appearances, in the next Parliament we may not work on the old two-party basis; we may find ourselves with additional parties in the House. That possible fact would have to be taken into consideration if we were framing any plan.
There is another thing that I have not brought to the attention of the House in particular although I think it would be a very important consideration. If the time were limited we would have condensed speeches upon different subjects, which would be very much more interesting than some of the unboiled speeches we hear at the present time.
Oh, oh.
Boil down the speakers.

Perhaps I should
say uniboiled-down speeches. These are merely suggestions. All we are asking for is that the House give an expression of opinion on the principle involved, which, I hope, in the interest of the House, in the interest of the country and in the interest of humanity generally, will be favourable.

speakeroldname: Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is not the first time that this subject has been ventilated in the House. I am not going to say that it partakes of the quality of the proverbial chestnut, but similar ideas have been floating around within the halls of Parliament ever since my entrance into Parliament in 1882. I do not think there is any doubt at all that a good might be gained if the doctrine of self-restraint were practised by each individual member. You can often get a man to put a rein upon himself who would be restive under a rein put upon him by a second or third party.
Then the hon. gentleman is not a prohibitionist.

A school for teaching proper methods of conducting business in legislative and parliamentary assemblies might be a very good thing and every member of Parliament and prospective member of Parliament should be obliged

to take a course and get a diploma from that school. A great deal, I think, conceivably might be accomplished in that way; whether we could practically carry it out or not I do not know.
Then again I think there is quite as much waste of time in Parliament-not speaking of any others now but our own-by the intrusion into the parliamentary arena of subjects the reason for 'the introduction of which it takes a good deal of ingenuity on the part of the common-sense-minded man to unravel. If we had some kind of censorship, some sieve through which all these things should be put, or some sort of questionnaire, which would eliminate altogether irrelevant and altogether irreverent subjects which are often brought to the attention of Parliament, I think we might gain a good deal of time and in public respect as well.
But when you begin putting the throttle on, you always have the right of the individual to contend with. The individual represents his constituency, .and you run the risk of the accusation that you are trying .to cripple and shut out the voice of the great electorate in so far as that constituency is concerned by tying down the man who represents it and not giving him the free use of his speech, his powers of oratory and his power of thought. You have to take that into consideration. The individual member, the representative of a constituency in Parliament, has a pretty good platform upon which to expatiate-almost as good as has the newspaperman when he hurls his anathemas against any attempt to restrict the freedom of the press and to prevent the voice of the people from being heard through that medium.
As far as this motion is concerned, it asks for an expression of the opinion of the House, and if an expression of the opinion of the House is given on the principle that we should try in some way or other to place limits on the extraordinary usage of time, we, the Government and the House itself, through its proper machinery, must take cognizance of that wish and try to devise some way by which, by amendment of and addition to the rules of the House, less time may be wasted than is wasted now. We will include all of ourselves as being wasteTs of time. In these later years I do- not take up very much time, bu't may be if we went back far enough those with memories as persistent as my own must recall a period when I took up a considerable amount of the time of the House myself.

But coming down now to what really may he said of the -question, I think it is possible for us to make of ourselves a more efficient and more respected body than we are at the present time by putting some restraint upon the misuse of time to -which we must all, in the course of long parliamentary careers, plead guilty at one time or another. It is true that of late there have been deep questionings in refer- . ence to the efficiency of parliamentary institutions not only in our own country but in other countries. It may be that we are considerably to blame for these questionings in the outer world; and that if we did really put ourselves down under reasonable restrictions which would enable us to do business more efficiently in shorter time and to the greater satisfaction of the public, parliamentary institutions might not be attacked as much as they are. It may be that the proposals of alternatives which are so disastrously advocated to take the place of parliamentary institutions of the past may have been to a certain extent aided by the misuse of time in legislatures and parliaments, and that we would exercise a wholesome influence upon the growth of what you might call the direct political action if we made ourselves a more efficient body. Now those thoughts just come to my mind. I am an old member of Parliament and my time in parliamentary life is drawing towards its close. Those that are about me are younger, they will be responsible for the future work; but I cannot help but be very strongly impressed with the fact, and with the idea, that parliamentary institutions may have made arguments against themselves by the lack of efficiency and method and purpose with which they have applied themselves to their task. I have always found that when a man is limited to time he will draw upon his best resources, and he will put himself on his best behaviour-he will marshal his facts and his arguments so that the time that is at his disposal may be most advantageously used. And I am entirely of the opinion that shorter speeches, debating speeches, speeches which do not have for their main object an object outside of the House itself, are most effective in parliamentary work and conduce to the better understanding of the subjects which are being discussed.
There is no objection at all to this motion -this is a proposition for the House. If the House thinks it is better that we should put ourselves into a position of thought and possible action as to how we may best
economize our time, but which in a larger sense is the people's time and for which the people pay, I think that some method can be found by which that opinion, that laudable wish and recommendation, can be carried into effect.

The right hon. gentleman (Sir
George Foster) has touched, I think, if he will allow me to say so, on the central point, or kernel rather, of the situation. He says it is for us to make ourselves a more respectable body. How can we do that, Mr. Speaker, when but a short time ago, when the question of patronage arose, we committed political and moral hari-kari by stigmatizing ourselves as a crooked bunch-the most extraordinary scene that was ever enacted in this House, or probably that ever occurred in the annals of -Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hope the hon. gentleman will not fail to adhere to the subject before the House which has purely to do with the length of time consumed in making speeches.

That being the case, Mr. Speaker, it would be impossible for us to consider length of time. Length of time would have no place in the matter at all, and we ought to be snuffed out at once;- we set- ourselves by ourselves, and we ought to know.
Then the right hon. gentleman has touched upon representative institutions. There are only two institutions, or sorts of institutions, in the country so far as I understand-those that are representative and those that are not. Even the Russian 'Soviet is simply the saifie -representative institution in different hands. The word "Soviet" means a council; and in Russia they have the village councils, the district councils, the general councils, and the national councils (which is only another name for Parliament), and they are representative. The confusion of the revolution is -simply due to the fact that the people have lifted up the mighty burden and overthrown what is in existence-they have not overthrown the principle. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that our representative institutions should not be tampered with-either the freedom of speech or the freedom of the press-and that if we would allow ourselves to enjoy a reputation which every respectable man ought to wish to enjoy-that is -some belief and regard for his reputation for probity, and not stigmatize himself as a crook-then I think we would have done
very largely that which the resolution seeks to attain.

As a young member who -spoke perhaps on more than one occasion last session, I rise with a certain amount of diffidence after the weighty words pronounced by the member (for Qu'Appelle (Mr. L. Thomson) and I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that my remarks shall be very brief. I recognize, and I think all recognize, the wisdom of the words which fell from the lips of that famous parliamentarian (Sir George Foster) who is leading the House to-night; but let me say this, that as a new member I have been deeply impressed by the fact that we do a tremendous amount of our most important business-that is the passing of the estimates -and expending of 'the people's money-without, in my humble opinion, anything like adequate discussion -and adequate examination. I do- not wish in a family talk of this sort to be unduly critical of the -Government, but my short experience has led -me to- the belief that very often a great number of important Estimates are only brought down -at -an hour of the session when it is practically impossible to dea-l with -them ias -they should be dealt with. -Now, should- we limit by the rules o-f -this Chamber the right of members -to speak -a certain time? I remember a story of a curate who, having preached a sermon of a length of on-ly -ten minutes, asked his bishop, who had listened to him, whether he had not done well in making such -a short sermon.

Was he -a Presbyterian?
Mr. M-cMASTER: The -name "curate" implies, to those who understand the different deno-minatio-rus into which the Protestant church is divided, that he was not a Presbyterian. Well, this curate asked his bishop whether the sermon could not be commended upon the grounds of shortness, and the Bi-sho-p replied that it was one of the most tiresome as well -as shortest, sermons *he had ever listened to. Some speeches are tiresome -that only occupy ten -minutes. Other speeches -are much more interesting although they -may. occupy an hour and -a half.
But are there not other methods which we could adopt besides the method of individual self-restraint which has been commended to us by the Minister of Trade and Commerce? I think there are. For instance, there is a rule of this House that if a Bill is not com-

pletely passed in one session it has to be taken up de novo the next session. In the recently published life of Sir Edward Clarke he tells us of his efforts to introduce into the British House of Commons a rule whereby if a Bill went as far as its second reading and was then shoved aside by pressure of other business, it should not be thrown into the waste paper basket, but should at the next session of the same Parliament be resumed at the committee stage. These are suggestions I throw out as a short and, I hope, not tiresome contribution to the discussion.
Mr. D. D. (MclvENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria): Mr. Speaker, I fully agree with the idea of the resolution, that we should waste no time. A certain amount of time is necessary for the proper conduct of the business of this House. The problem is to draw the line between where we use our time well and where that time is wasted. One thing is certain, that every member elected to this House should realize that he is coming to an assembly where there is sympathy and good will, where there are no austere rules, and where the representatives of the people are expected primarily to present their views to the public, if you please, and, in a secondary way, to the House of (Commons.
Whether we are in the schoolhouse, or on the farm, or in a business-whatever position in life we occupy, there is much to be gained by the example set by our teachers or principals; and I would suggest not only to this Government, but to all governments, that much time might be saved by the Government itself being ready with its business and putting it forward with every possible despatch. Much time is wasted for which Governments are to blame by reason of their not being ready with their business, which unreadiness invites long speeches and dilly-dallying while they are preparing something to throw into the mill. Very few hon. members will continue with* a long speech if they find they are impeding Government business and that the Government has really live business to bring on. I would therefore suggest that hereafter the heads of departments should have their business ready when Parliament meets so that it will be manifest to the House that there is work to do and no time to waste.
A.-j far as freedom of speech is concerned, Sir, I am absolutely opposed to trammelling any member who has anything to say. I think a good example can be set by the leaders of the House not talking away

from the subject, and their followers being kept as close to the line as possible. I would like to bring to the notice of the leader of t)he House (Sir George Foster) that last year, during his absence- I presume he would not tolerate such a thing if he had been present-we had the closure applied after two hours' discussion of a Bill; and after the Government had taken that course five pages of closely printed matter were added to the Bill. That is going to the other extreme, and while I am not in favour of any waste of time, I must necessarily, as a Liberal, I suppose, be absolutely in favour of the fullest opportunity being accorded to every member to express his views. It may be a mistake to allow that latitude at times, but it is certainly keeping on the right side, and, after all, perhaps it is the best use that we can have of wasted money. I do not wish to tantalize my good friend the leader of the House, but I was very much amused tonight when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) was speaking to notice my hon. friend listening very attentively until he discovered that the hon. member was not criticising the heads of departments, when he immediately exclaimed: "Name those long speechmakers." He felt he was safe.
My hon. friend gives .me credit for more shrewdness than I possess.

There are advantages in long speeches from hon. gentlemen like my right hon. friend who leads the House. His speeches contribute, much to our literature, for they are conspicuous examples of splendid English, fine thought and lambent wit, and are a source of inspiration and education to us, as they will be also to those who cOme after us. In cases of that kind it would be a pity to restrict the scope of the speaker's eloquence, imagination and learning on public matters, which are to the advantage of this House and of succeeding generations.
I have only one remedy to suggest, Sir: That those of us who realize the difficulty should set an example, and endeavour to develop a public opinion in this House against too lengthy speeches, and that public opinion will undoubtedly prove thoroughly effective and salutary.
Mr. JEAN J. DENIS (Joliette): Mr. Speaker, the atmosphere of the House tonight gives one the impression that hon. members are opening up their hearts in the direction of effecting a reform, and in that
line I cannot help but add my small contribution. During last session I had occasion to oppose a motion which was made by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) that the House should sit during the remaining days of that session every Saturday and every forenoon. In so far as I remember, I was the only one who dared oppose such a motion, because, at that time every hon. member was very anxious to go back home, especially when the session dragged into the sultry days of summer. I said then that it was totally impossible for hon. members to do their duty to their satisfaction-at least, I was speaking for myself-and I contended, as I still contend, that with my humble attainments it is absolutely impossible for me to follow the sittings every day, six days in the week, in the forenoon, in the afternoon and at night. The occasion does not arise now for a protest on my part, but I am simply taking this opportunity of warning the Government that if we are going to have a free Parliament they should take the necessary means to convene the next session at a sufficiently early date to allow business of the House to be transacted during reasonable hours. This question, I understand, is not irrelevant to the motion under discussion, which has for its object the limiting of the time to be occupied by hon. members when addressing the House, and so, incidentally, limiting the time during which the House sits. A man of ordinary physical strength cannot sit in the House all night and still be in a position to assist in a reasonable way in the passing of legislation-legislation, at any rate, which has been duly weighed in the estimation and conscience of every one.
During this session hon. members have not been very busy. Only one important matter has come before the House-the ratification of the Peace Treaty. And what happened? Hon. members are called upon to cast their vote on that subject before an opportunity has been had for free discussion in this House. I take the responsibility which goes with my words; I say that the Treaty was adopted before a free discussion had been allowed. For it is not a free discussion in any Parliament when the members of that Parliament are called upon to vote on a certain subject at a time which has been fixed. In this way hon. members are debarred from expressing their views freely on a given subject. Upon this one important subject with which we were called upon to deal this session we were asked to vote at half past one in the morning,

when several members had no opportunity of expressing their views with regard to it. Well, Sir, I think that the Government should take the necessary measures to provide that the House should sit only during reasonable hours. I would isay that only under very exceptional circumstances should the House sit after midnight.
Hear, hear.

There is no reason why the House should sit until one, two or three o'clock in the morning.
Further, if the Government wants to bring about such a reform as that of which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) spoke a while ago, they should establish the principle that the House should not sit during the summer months-in July, for instance. During the war that was all right enough. If the House had sat twelve months in the year, no one would have complained; those who were here at the time realized that it was necessary. But now that the war is over, there is no reason why the House should sit during the months of July and August, and I appeal to the ministers who hear me now to convene the next session of Parliament sufficiently early so that we shall finish the business which has to be done not later that the middle of June.
During the last two weeks of the last session I came into this Chamber day after day, sitting after sitting, and saw on your left, Mr. Speaker, perhaps ten or twelve members, and on your right fifteen-just enough to make a quorum, although the House was, perhaps, discussing a most important measure. Estimates were passed by the millions and scores of millions, yet hon. members had no control over them at all; it was physically impossible for them to have any control over them. Hon. members would stand the strain for a day or two and then walk out disgusted; some of them would go home, saying: "We have had enough of it." A reference to this condition was on the lips of many during the latter part of last session, both inside this House and outside of it.
Now, Sir, if we are to have reforms, if there is to be a limitation of the length of speeches, I do not object. If other reforms have to be made, I am ready to help the Government as much as I can. But certainly there is a reform to be made in the matter of which I speak; the abuse was referred to on many occasions during the last session as well as after its close. Im-[Mr. Denis.1
mediately after the session closed I read an article on this subject in the Ottawa Journal, which certainly is a supporter of the Government. Had I known that this subject was to come up to-night I would have had that clipping with me. The Ottawa Journal said it was a crime to cause Parliament to cease to exist through these long sittings. I hope, therefore, that the Government will accept the advice which has been given them from the other side to-night and see that some reform is accomplished.

Mr. Speaker, when I heard the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. L. Thomson) make the speech supporting his resolution, I went to the library of the House and looked up the Hansard which contains the report of the proceedings of the House at a time when the hon. member was not so shy as he seems to be now.
I find that in those days when the hon. member was not straddling the fence, as he is now, he covered many pages of Hansard in the addresses which he made to this House. In 1914, on the occasion of the Address and in reply to the speech from the Throne, he covered about eight pages of Hansard. In 1915, on the Budget, his speech covered about the same number of pages. In 1916, on the Prohibition question, his speeches covered pages 1479, 1480, 1481, 1482, 2557, 2883. On the Military Service Act in 1917-coming closer to the present-his speech covered nine pages, and his speech on the Budget of that year covers pages 976, 977, 978, 979, 980, 981, 982, 983, 984, and 985. May I suggest that the reason why the hon. member is not making any speeches now is that he is in such a position that were he to rise for the purpose of . addressing the House he would probably be obliged to make long speeches of criticism of the Government? My hon. friend probably thinks it is better for his health that he should sit down and not air his opinions at the present moment, and that is probably the reason for his continence.

Mr. Speaker, I have hesitated very much to intervene in this debate, as I was anxious that my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. L. Thomson) for whom I have great respect, should receive some measure of support from those who agree with him. It follows from what I have already said, Sir, that I do not find myself in absolute agreement with my hon. friend.

The hon. gentleman, as my hon. friend (Mr. Archambiault) has pointed out, made to-night what is perhaps his shortest speech on record. I certainly think it was the worst speech of his that I ever heard-not because of its brevity, but because it contained so little. He said, so far as I can remember, that there is <a great deal of time wasted in Parliament, that long speeches are the cause of it ; and without going into detail, having made his diagnosis, he proceeded to the treatment, which of course was the suggestion that the speeches should be curtailed. Well, that is a very summary way of dealing with"this question. One has, in such a debate, Sir, to speak with one's watch in one's hand.
The very points that my hon. friend mentioned in his speech which seemed to reveal a feeling on his own part that the subject was defective are those which he should have elaborated. He said that he was not going into detail. Now, that is a pity, because if he was going to curtail speeches, he should at least have given us some idea of the point to which he would allow the speeches of those who are not heads of departments or ministers to go. He did not mention any time limit that he himself would put on. Another great defect in the speech, so far as I may be allowed to judge it-and my good friend will allow me, I know, because he and I have always been on the very best of terms, and will continue so, even though I venture to differ from him on this subject-was that he failed utterly to take note of the fact that a large variety of subjects come before hon. members of the House.
Mr. Speaker, it is perfectly obvious to the youngest member of this House that there are some subjects which naturally lend themselves to brief speech, and I have heard in the House debates in which no speech exceeded a very few minutes, because of the nature of the subject being dealt with. The debating was, from my point of view, admirably varied and spread over the whole House. I have known other subjects come before this House which naturally lent themselves to be dealt with by hon. gentlemen who had given perhaps a lifetime of study to those subjects and the very nature of which caused the speeches of these hon. gentlemen to occupy a large proportion of the time. I repeat that I wish my hon. friend had gone more into detail and that he had taken note of that other matter. In supporting his resolution he ventured a long way in criticism of his fellow-members. He practically classified
this House, so far as it has an existence outside of himself, and the classification took this form. He gave some very interesting figures about hon. gentlemen who spoke a great deal in the House, and then he went on to express the opinion that there were a large number of hon. gentlemen who never speak at all, who did not open their mouths, yet could speak at least as well or perhaps better than the speaking gentlemen. In other words, he seemed to classify the House as consisting of speaking nonentities and dumb philosophers. I am quite at a loss, and I am sorry that my hon. friend did not enlighten us, as to how he arrived at an opinion of the ability of the dumb gentlemen. That is a matter which is a very great puzzle to me at the present moment. It must have been because they have taken him into their confidence in private, and then, I suppose, they must have spoken, and it is possible after all for members of Parliament to waste a great deal of time in private conversation when they ought to be attending to speeches, short or long, within this chamber. I could not help thinking that when he was forming his opinion of the amount of wisdom that is contained within the heads of the hon. gentlemen who seldom or never speak in the House, he was a somewhat more superficial observer of men than Shakespeare was. Shakespeare, you remember, Sir, said:
There are a sort of men, whose visages Do cream and mantle, like a standing pond ; Who do a wilful stillness entertain,
With purpose to be dressed in an opinion Of wisdom, gravity, profound conceit;
As if to say, " I am Sir Oracle,
And, when I ope my lips, let no dog bark! "
Well, the poet, so far as he describes the kind of members of the House-I do not describe them-as they appeal to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Levi Thomson), has described them; but in the subsequent lines, if my recollection is correct, the great student of human nature goes on to utter about this dumb people some further sentences which are by no means complimentary, because you, Mr. Speaker, who are a student of Shakespeare, will very well remember that he goes on to say that if these dumb gentlemen did but speak, their speech would so horrify the community that their brothers would wish they were dumb. That is my recollection of the subsequent portion of the poem.
I want, without exceeding my time limit and in a single sentence, to enter a serious protest on behalf of the only speaking animal upon the face of the globe. We have,

from the jelly fish, up through the insects and the worms and the reptiles and the molluscs and the birds and the fishes and the quadrupeds, an infinite variety of animal creation; but it so happens that the only animal capable of articulate and well-reasoned speech is the human being, and I want to enter a modest plea on behalf of the head of the animal creation on this globe. I should be very sorry to vote for the resolution in the form and shape in which it stands. I find myself almost in entire accord with the very wise words that fell from the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie). There is a certain waste of time in Parliament, though it is a very pleasant place to spend one's time in. I am a confirmed believer in Parliamentary institutions, and I enjoy seeing those Parliamentary institutions in operation, even when they lead to Parliamentary speech. There is a great deal in what the leader of the Opposition said about the methods by which Governments do their business. He did not, I think, for a moment want us to believe that that applies to any one Government in this country or in the Old Country upon whose great Parliament our parliamentary institutions are founded. The fact is, Sir, that in this connection certain broad traditions have gathered around Parliament, and one of these days, especially when our people are in such a businesslike frame of mind as I believe them to be at the present moment, when our people are looking for some product from Parliament for the benefit of (he people, it will be necessary for some party, composed either from the old traditional parties or by an unparalleled .and swift growth on the part of the cross benches in this House, to see to it that those traditions are abolished, broken through, and that when we meet for business, the Government of the day, Which after all is responsible for governing the country and for the running of Parliament, .shall bring its business before us in a businesslike manner.
In previous discussions, I have heard the rules of the House blamed upon this question. I would say in regard to that, emphasizing what was said by the leader of the Opposition about the importance of free speech, merely that those rules have grown not only through generations hut through centuries of practice of the Parliamentary order of debating and deliberating, and that I should be slow to blame those rules. Nearly all of them are 9 p.m. framed originally to curb arbitrary power on the part of mon-ardhs and governments and to preserve the 
rights of the people. They may be improved, and they are being improved from time to time by the Acts of Parliament itself and by 'the rulings of Speakers in the Chair. I do not think my hon. friend was successful in making out a good case for voting for so abstract a resolution as the one he has brought before us, and if it went to a vote, I for one would certainly vote against it.
In addition to the very practical and wise suggestions which fell from the leader of the Opposition, we must 'all have been impressed with the equally wise suggestion which fell from my right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) who is leading the House on this occasion, namely, that a wise restraint upon the part of the individual would help very much. There are other restraints, of course. At every general election the public applies a restraint, because I believe it is a fact that, one-third of the House disappears at every general election, and I am not at all sure that in that disappearance the speakers fare any worse than the dumb philosophers. The public is a wise restraint and a purifying process in that way. And the members of the House have, after all, their own methods of controlling any undue tendency to speak on the part of any individual member. Cbm-mon sense in my humble judgment, may be trusted in this matter to control us. Of course, I may remind myself and the House of the three wisest rules I know of in regaad to public speaking which were once pronounced in a famous address on the subject by a former Governor General of Canada, Lord Dufferin. Lord Dufferin gave rules for public speaking which, if we followed, would at once make needless such a resolution as that we have before us to-night. He said to an audience of young men once, " Never rise unless you have something to say. When you rise, say it. And when you have said it, sit down."
Motion negatived.

For a copy of all correspondence relating to the dismissal of James Conner from the dual positions which he held at Snowflake, Manitoba, under the Departments of Customs, and Immigration and Colonization.
He said: When the Estimates of the Customs Department were under discussion last session I brought to the attention of the House a little matter that I thought required ventilation. I referred to a member of the

Civil Service, James Conner, who was appointed a preventive office at Snowflake, Manitoba, about twenty-one years ago. He first was appointed to guard the public domain in the matter of timber, for which he got about $200 a year. Later he was appointed Customs officer at a very small salary. After from fifteen to twenty years' service, he was receiving a salary of $600 a year. About eight years ago when the immigration movement began from the United States, Mr. Conner was asked to look after the immigrants, and $100 a year was added to his salary. So he received for this dual position the magnificent sum of $700 per year. I have known Mr. Conner for some thirty .years. He is a man of sterling character, devoted to the public service. He guarded the boundary for a considerable distance as faithfully as if the country belonged to him. During the eight years in which he received $100 for performing his immigration duties he spent many a night from sunset until eleven or twelve o'clock doing all in his power to perform those duties, and he lived in a tent in order to do it. I looked up the records and I read the report of a Government inspector who went down there and reported to the Government that Mr. Conner was a faithful officer and had done his duty efficiently. Mr. Conner has brought up a family of ten children in that country. They live there yet, and have added greatly to the wealth of the country. They farm something like eight quarter-sections of land. That man has laboured on the farm as very few farmers have ever done. I was moved when I was member for Lis'gar, because of his faithfulness and industry as a man, to suggest to him that he might look after the timber for the Government and become a preventive officer. He did so and received this small salary. I have not represented that constituency for a great many years, but I know this old Scotchman, and he wrote me a letter about a year ago saying that he had just received notice on October * 4 that he had been summarily dismissed as on the previous 30th of September. I was naturally indignant at an action of that kind on the part of the Government, and especially on the part of the Union Government, so I wrote to the Commissioner of Customs, the late Mr. McDougald, and he replied that the dual positions which Mr. Conner had held had been combined and Mr. Conner let out on the grounds of economy.
I want to preface what I am going to say by stating that I am not blaming the Minister of Customs or the Minister of Immigration because they knew absolutely nothing about this. I took the trouble to inquire into the facts, and I discovered that although one of the reasons assigned for Mr. Conner's dismissal was that he was an old man, there had been appointed in his place to do this immigration work a man from Winnipeg fifty-seven years of age, at a salary of $650 a year. Through a little contemptible wire-pulling on the part of some officers in the departments, for which they should be dismissed, they got this fine old farmer fired from the Customs Departs ment, giving the dual position to this Mr. Nesbitt at a joint salary of $1,200-on the ground of economy, mark you!-whereas Mr. Conner had done the work of preventive officer for $600 and immigration for $100 a year. Any hon. member with a sense of justice would naturally be aroused at a contemptible action of that kind. I found by inquiry that the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) knew absolutely nothing about it. It was done before the Government of which he is a member took office. I inquired into the reasons for the dismissal of Mr. Conner from the Customs and the other department. The matter was very properly referred by the Minister of Immigration to the officers of his department, and one of these officers, Mr. Scott, Superintendent of Immigration, reported-I hold in my hand a copy of his report-that Mr. Conner had been discharged because he was inefficient; and a more efficient man appointed in his place. Inefficient, mark you. Now, Mr. Conner only received $100 for performing his duties as immigration officer, and during the eight years in which he performed his work we had the heaviest immigration into this country from the United States that we ever had. We shall never in all probability have such a heavy immigration again. And although Mr. Conner had performed this work during all these years up till the time immigration absolutely ceased, he was dismissed on the ground of inefficiency. It annoyed me still more to have these peti*- officers who conspired to put a decent man out of business make a lying report kv the effect that he was inefficient. I read the report of a Government officer who inspected the work of Mr. Conner at the time and he reported that he was entirely efficient. Now, to add insult to injury, these petty conspirators put forward the claim that Mr. Conner was inefficient and they had to get another man to take his place; and, just think of it, on the

ground of economy, forsooth, when the new man is drawing double the salary that was paid to this old gentleman, Mr. Conner. In writing to me, Mr. Conner said that he would not have minded at all if the job had been given to a returned soldier, but it was a different matter when the position was given to an official sent out from Winnipeg, because there was nothing for him to do in the Winnipeg office and because wires had been secretly pulled to undo him. I inquired very carefully into this matter, because it interested me, and I am not able to see that any member of the Government even knew about it, but in the correspondence I was able to -examine I found one letter that gave me a slight clue to what probably occurred. Here is a letter which Mr. Cory, Deputy Minister of the Interior, sent to Mr. John McDougald, late Cbmmissioner of Customs. He says :
Mr. F. H. Nesbitt, Immigration Inspector at Snowflake, Manitoba, who draws a salary of $1,050 per annum could do the Customs work as well.
He was to get $1,050 to do the immigration work whereas Mr. Conner had done it for the years when there was immigration coming into the country for $100 a year. This man was to get $i,050 when there were no immigrants coming into the country. If Nesbitt was getting $1,050 as the immigration officer and $600 for customs he was being paid a pretty handsome salary. What business was it of Cory's to conspire against this splendid old officer who had done his best for the Government for twenty-one years?
I believe that your officer at that point is very old, and, from what I can gather, very inefficient. The commissioners, who have been investigating our immigration service recommend that the duties of the two departments be combined and that Mr. Nesbitt be -placed in charge; the cost of the service to be apportioned between the two departments.
This is the matter about which I spoke to you over the telephone. Will you please let me have confirmation of this arrangement?
That is a very suggestive statement. This man Cory speaks to John McDougald over the telephone in order to conspire against this prime old officer who, after twenty-one years' service, receives a letter Sn the 4th of October saying that he is summarily dismissed. This is most contemptible conduct towards any officer. Here is the copy of a report that Mr. Scott, Superintendent of Immigration wrote to the hon. the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) after I drew the attention of the Government to it last session. Mr. Calder asked for a report. I will read from it.

Mr. McLeod, a lawyer in Morden, took up their case on appeal for their release. The case went before a judge at Morden; as no one appeared from the Government to prosecute they were let free and deported.
If this report of the Superintendent of Immigration has any effect at all in condemning Mr. Conner for letting in these gypsies, how comes it that neither he nor the department thought it worth while even to send somebody to prosecute them when they were in the jail? The Government, or the department, must have treated the matter with entire indifference before these people were let go. Nevertheless the commissioner uses that as a pretext for the ignominious dismissal of this officer.
Mr. Scott says they were gypsies: I find nothing in the immigration regulations respecting gypsies; one of them, a well informed man, told me they were truck farmers and had negroes working for them down in the State of Georgia.
Mr. Scott says in his reply to Hon. Mr. Calder on the 12th September, 1918-you sent me a memo, asking that I ascertain whether P. H. Nesbitt, our officer at Snowflake, had been appointed customs officer. The Commissioner of Customs replied to say that Jas. Conner, sub-collecor of customs would not be acting for the Customs Service after the end of Sept. 1918, and that the Customs Dept, would utilize the services of P. H. Nesbitt and would pay $600 towards his salary. Now the question arises who recommended Jas. Conners' sudden dismissal from the Customs?
That is one of the questions I have been working on, and I have come to the conclusion that it was a little put-up job on the part of the understrappers and officials to get rid of this man and obtain the place for some favourite of their own.
Mr. Conner has just sent me this memo, with regard to the work he had to perform and his remuneration. He says:
On page 73, part 1, trade report, Department of Customs, 1917. Revenue collected (Man.) Snowflake-

Remember, Conner got a salary of only $600.
Revenue collected at Snowflake $2,066.33.
Now at Crystal City, which is supposed to be a much more important port the revenue collected was $1,398.30. Yet the collector at Crystal City received $1,000 a year salary from the Customs, and James Conner who collected far more revenue, received much less salary. The mam at Crystal City who collected $1,398.30 received a salary of $1,000 from the Customs Department, whilst Jas. Connor, who collected at Snowflake $2,066, only received a salary of $600, and yet Connor is the man that is dismissed. It just looks to me, Mr. Speaker, that it is precious funny conduct to display to the most decent and efficient officer in that part of the country- to dismiss him on the ground of economy.
I was wondering if the Civil Service Commission had anything to do with a case of that kind. Is it possible that a little conspiracy can be hatched on the part of a few understrappers that the head of a decent man may roll into the basket because of this conspiracy and how are we to guard the interests of men of that type? I got no satisfaction last session when I brought this matter up. As in the case of the old Presbyterian minister the Government looked the difficulty squarely and savagely in- the face and passed on. Therefore I have brought the case up again, and I want to know what is going to be done .about this ignominious dismissal of Mr. Conner? Is this Union Government going to rest under the stigma of even being in existence whop ia man as decent as that is summarily dismissed without notice, without a thank you, and under such circumstances as I have described, or is he to be reinstated? I want to know if these things can be done in this year of grace 1919 and no redress forthcoming to this decent man? What (incentive will /any civil servant ever have to serve the Government faithfully if just because of that faithful service he is to be summarily dismissed without any notice being given him-in fact, Conner was dismissed and his salary stopped before he got his notice of dismissal. I would like a declaration from the right hon. gentleman (Sir George Foster) who is leading the House, a man to whom we all look up and who is the acme of wisdom, and I take it also of justice. I would just like him to tell the House what ought to be done in the

case of a man like Mr. Conner. Mr. Conner does not even know I am bringing up his case, but my sense of justice was outraged;
I felt I would keep at this thing to find out whether justice could be obtained in a case of this kind. If the position had been given to a returned soldier, probably Mr. Conner would have been perfectly satisfied and so would I. I am not trying to get a job for him but simply to have some little consolation offered to him for the manner in which he has been treated. Now I pause for a declaration from the Government as to what it will do in this case.

I will try my very best to give a declaration after what the hon. gentleman has been good enough to say about me. I do not know the least thing about the case except that I have heard the story of my hon. friend. I am not impugning that at all; it is, I dare say, correct, but I think I will have to ask my hon. friend to await an answer from the responsible head of the department-it is very dangerous work mixing in with the business of colleagues. The papers in this case will be brought down in answer to the request of my hon. friend. I have no doubt at all that the interested ministers will give my hon. friend a fair answer and if injustice has been done they will take the proper steps to remedy it.

I would like to point out to the leader of the House that I was just as emphatic in my observations and presented the case just as perfectly last session. The responsible minister, Hon. Mr. Calder, did not propose any remedy or offer any suggestion, and I do not at present know whether or not any measure of justice will be accorded this dismissed officer.
If the right hon. leader of the House will say that when the papers come down, if he is leading the House at the end of the session, he will make a declaration, I will subside at once.
I can do that right away. A declaration will be made either by the responsible minister or by myself.
All right.
