On the motion of Sir George Foster the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution; Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
That it is expedient to amend subsection seven of section ninety-five of The Canada Grain Act, as enacted by section three of Chapter forty of the Statutes of 1919, by providing that if in any year after the crop year ending on the thirty-first day of August, 1919, the total surplus of grain found in an elevator upon taking stock is in excess of one-quarter of one per cent of the gross amount of the grain received in the elevator during the crop year, such excess surplus shall be sold annually by the Board of Grain Commissioners and the proceeds thereof paid to the said Board. Such proceeds to be applied towards the cost of administration of The Canada Grain Act in such manner as the Governor in Council may direct.

Will the minister please explain the necessity of the amendment?
Mr. A. It. MACLEAN: The purpose of this resolution is to found a Bill thereon amending an Act of the last session of Parliament in relation to the Grain Act. Hon. gentlemen will remember that last session a Bill amending the Grain Act provided that overages at terminal elevators should not exceed one quarter of one per cent. I had the direction of the measure during its passage through the House, and from the representations made to me at the time it was apparent that the intention was that the Bill should first be applicable to the present cereal year. The purpose of the proposed Bill therefore is to make it clear that the provisions of the Act of last session shall not apply to grain in terminal elevators at the end of the last cereal year.
Will the hon. gentleman tell us briefly the number of elevators to which this law will apply, and how many of them are Government-owned elevators and where they are situated ?
They are all terminal elevators at the head of the Lakes.
All Government-owned?
Government and private-owned elevators situated at the head of the Lakes, the Georgian Bay ports, and Montreal.

Are those the only
elevators to which this law will apply?

There are also
three elevators in the interior to which this will apply. It does not apply to any

elevators in the Maritime Provinces-if that is what my hon. friend has in mind.

I do not think there
are any elevators there.

Do I understand the
hon. gentleman to say that this amendment does not apply to any elevators in the Maritime Provinces and west of the Great Lakes?
I said it applied to the terminal elevators, and that there were no such elevators in the Maritime Provinces.
Is there not one at St. John?
The question of overages would not arise there.
It has just as good an opportunity to arise there, I think, as at other points.
I do not think so. The question does not arise at Montreal.
Does the word "interior " bar them?

It would apply
to interior elevators.
And also on the Pacific coast?

Yes.
Resolution reported, and concurred in.
Sir George Foster thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 17 to amend the Canada Grain Act.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.

On the motion of Hon. A. K. MACLEAN, the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend The Civil Service Act, 1918, and'therein to provide:-
That the provisions of the said Act relating to temporary employment, dismissals, resignations, hours of attendance, annual reports, regulations, examinations, classification, appointments, promotions, transfers, and compensation he amended, and that provision be made for reclassifying the Civil Service and for any additional expense which may result from such re-classification.

Mr. Chairman, after the very interesting discussion which we have had to-night as to the undesirability of unnecessary talking, I hope that the committee will not require any lengthy
CMr. A. K. Maclean.']
address from me at this stage of the measure. I am anxious to make progress in the matter, in the first place, in order that I may have the Bill introduced and printed and, in the second place, that I may be in a position to distribute the copies of the classification of the Civil Service, which is the principal matter referred to in this Bill.
The resolution, hon. gentlemen will remember, was under discussion during the last session, but for various reasons the consideration of the Bill based upon it was postponed until the present session. During recess some amendments have been made to the printed classification as presented to Parliament last session. I think that the classification as it now stands will be much more readily understood by hon. members because of the publication of a list of classes grouped by services and the division of various services into ranks. I hope the committee will allow me to proceed and have the Bill introduced so that I may have the copies of the classification distributed.

I am told upon what I regard as fair authority that this Bill, which was before the House last session, and on which we made some progress, was submitted to a committee appointed by the Government for the purpose of considering it; that they had made a report and that some amendments and some reconstruction of the classification are proposed. It will be interesting to know what that report is and to ascertain wherein the Bill has been improved so that it may now be satisfactory to the Civil Service.
I assume that my hon. friend refers more particularly to the classification than to the Bill.

Well, I believe that
the Bill as submitted last session was entirely unworkable, and if the improvement in the classification or in the Bill is such as to make it workable and satisfactory to civil servants it will be a victory for the national policy, so to speak. We had in Ottawa for over a year gentlemen who were imported into this country from the United States who called themselves experts and to whom very large amounts of money were paid by the Government for the bringing about of this classification. I am told that they produced a piece of machinery so difficult of understanding, so complicated and so far beyond the comprehension of the Government and of the officials of the various departments that the thing was en-

tirely unworkable, and some ordinary minds had to go to work at it with a view to providing machinery that a very ordinary Government could understand. When I used the expression " national policy," I mean home talent, and I am glad indeed that this home talent, these men of our own who took hold of this Act, have apparently been able to put it in such shape that we shall be able to put it through. I hope that the minister, before he asks us to go very far with the Bill, will have this report printed and distributed, so that we may see exactly what changes were made and what recommendations are sent to us by this committee. I do hear a great many expressions of opinion to the effect that the Bill should go through this session. I trust that it is in such shape and that there is such accord on the subject among members of the Government themselves and their supporters that the Bill will become law during the present session.
I shall endeavour to give my hon. friend the information he desires. I think I shall have it in my possession on the second reading of the Bill.
I notice that this resolution is rather narrow. Will provision be made to enable us, when the Bill is brought down, to discuss the question of enlarging the Civil Service Commission?
It will be open to any hon. gentleman to propose an amendment.

But if an hon. member proposes an amendment to that effect, a reference to the resolution as adopted will show that no provision is made in it for the enlargement of the commission. The hon. gentleman will see that it does not provide money for that purpose.

The Bill as presented to the House last year made provision for the enlargement of the Civil Service Commission. At present, however, it is the view of the Government that there is no good ground for the extension of the personnel of the commission and the consequent increase in the cost of administering the Act. However, if the judgment of the House is otherwise, I am sure that the Government will not interpose any objection.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Hon. A. K. MACLEAN thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 18, to amend the Civil Service Act, 1918.

Explain the Bill.
Mr."A. R. MACLEAN: It is my intention to explain the Bill on the second reading. In the meantime, I propose to distribute the printed classification.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF POWERS, DUTIES AND RIGHTS-ALLIED PURCHASES OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
There might
really have been no necessity tor this legislation. The Board of Grain Supervisors was appointed in 1917 under the war power which the Government possessed. They have been carrying on their work during two grain seasons, but the active work of purchasing and receiving grain ceased on the 15th of August last. There are always ends of business to be looked after and settled up and it is quite probable that some transactions in the way of settlement or final disposition-not in the way of the purchase or reception of grain-will remain to be carried out by the board during the remaining months of this year and probably during a part of next year. The powers of the board are good and sufficient until the ratifications of peace have been effected, and it may be that these ratifications will not all be finally made until the board shall have completely finished its business. But the Government did not care to have them carry on further operations under their powers conferred by virtue of the War Measures Act after the war was practically over; they preferred to ask Parliament to confirm such of those powers as are necessary to enable the board to wind up the business with which they were entrusted and which they have been carrying on.
The resolution refers to certain Orders in Council. I am laying copies of these on the Table, and I am sending a copy to the leader of the Opposition. As no new powers are asked for and as it is necessary that the board retain such powers as will enable them to wind up the operations of 1917-1918 and 1918-1919, I imagine that there will be no objection to the resolution. Hon. gentlemen will be able to see the Orders in Council, and I shall be pleased to give any other information that may be desired on the second reading of the Bill.

speechtext: Wbait I wish to bring to the notice of the minister is that, as I understand the provisions of the War Measures Act which was passed in 1915, it contains within itself all the powers that the parties acting under the minister would require for the winding up of the business. We had that question under discussion here the other day, and if I properly understood the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), he quoted the provisions of the War Measures Act when read together with the Interpretation Act of the Revised Statutes of Canada as containing in themselves sufficient ipower to enable any board or any person who has started the transaction of any business under an Order in Council to finish that business regardless of whether a declaration of peace is made or not. We had that matter under discussion last session when the then Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) introduced a Bill for the continuance of powers in connection with an inquiry that was in the hands of a commission as to the business existing between the pulp mills and the newspapers. We passed that Bill, but the then Minister of Finance, as a lawyer, agreed with me that there was sufficient power in the Act itself. I am not raising any objection to this, but there are many Orders in Council and a large volume of business outstanding that was instituted under those Orders in Council and that must be carried to completion. If the Department of Justice thinks that there is in the War Measures Act itself ample power to carry forward those transactions, a great deal of time and labour would, be saved if proceedings were continued under the terms of that Act, thus avoiding the necessity of coming here for a special Bill for every matter that may arise unuer the various Orders in Council. I bring this matter more particularly to the notice of the Minister of Justice, because, if we can avoid multiplicity of Bills and arrive at the same result, that would be desirable.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF POWERS, DUTIES AND RIGHTS-ALLIED PURCHASES OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
We went through the Orders in Council vrith a view to determining which of them it might be desirable to continue in force. We arrived at the conclusion that there were, after all, but comparatively few with regard to which it might be desirable to make clear beyond perad-venture that they continue in force. Among the latter are those that are now being dealt with in order that there may be no question about the power of the board. We thought it more desirable that, even though the war

be still continuing because peace has not been ratified, when what might be described as war conditions have ceased, so far as that might be possible, any operation that would- be deemed necessary to be carried on should be carried on under appropriate legislation not depending for its effect upon the War Measures Act. I quite conceive that there may be some of these Orders in Council under which power may be exercised, where the public convenience may necessarily require that such power should be exercised under them so long as they continue in force in virtue of the War Measures Act. But where that could conveniently be done, it seemed to us desirable that we should make it quite clear that any power that was being exercised was being exercised1 under direct authority of Parliament. It is to make that quite clear with regard to these particular orders that this legislation was introduced.

speechtext: The Minister ot Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) referred to certain operations that were carried on and stated that they had resulted in a surplus and that there was a proposal for the disposal of that surplus. If that be so, that establishes the contention of the farmers that they are paying rather excessive charges for the handling of grain in this country. speechtext:
My hon. friend must remember this, that in normal times the cost and charges of handling grain from the primary station to the place of consumption must always be incurred and must always be paid for by somebody. They are never, I imagine, paid out of the pockets and fortunes of the grain dealers themselves, but they are really taken in the shape of profits or surplus charges on the grain, sufficient in the mind of the dealer to bring him out square. Therefore, we must always take-into account that somebody has to pay the charges of the whole handling of the grain from the initial station until it gets to the point of consumption. This ivas undertaken and carried out entirely by the Board of Grain Supervisors, and consequently costs and charges were provided for, for that body alone. I have not the least doubt that, if an investigation could really be carried out-and it is difficult tt>
do it-if it were a matter of an alternative between the handling of grain as it was done by the Board of Grain Supervisors and
the handling of grain in normal times, when those cost and charges were deducted with profits by the different handlers and purveyors of grain, the balance would be in point of economy to the handling of grain by the supervisors. The Board of Grain Supervisors were not speculators. They did not have to make any arrangements for profits. Handling grain in normal times contemplates not only charges for transportation, storage, freight, insurance, interest and everything of that kind, but it must also be loaded by a certain amount for profit to the handler, because these things are not simply done out of a benevolent spirit. So looking at it in the light to vrhich my hon. friend has drawn attention, if you take it for granted that the farmers' wheat has to pay these costs and charges, the cost to the farmers was less under the Board of Grain Supervisors than under the dealers.

speechtext:
Some of us in the West have contended during the last few years that while the charge has to be carried

back and the producer really pays all the overhead charges until the grain is delivered in terminal elevators, it is not fair that the amount received from overcharge against the grain should go into the Consolidated Revenue. Our contention is that if there is an overcharge this year on a certain line of work and a surplus accumulates, the surplus should be retained in the hands of the Government, who are carrying on the work, and he applied in the way of a reduction of the charges next year. Then the producer would be paying the full charge, and no more, for delivering the grain to the terminal elevator. It certainly is not fair that the money should go into consolidated revenue. You cannot distribute it back for the past year, so it should be used for the benefit of those who sell to the board next year.

subsubtopic: CONTINUANCE OF POWERS, DUTIES AND RIGHTS-ALLIED PURCHASES OF WHEAT.
speechtext:
The system of handling grain from the producer to the consumer, whether in Canada or foreign countries, is not the work of governments. It is the work of long business experience in every country where wheat is a commodity of exchange. So far as I can judge, the experience of this country has not been that governments can handle wheat to better advantage or more cheaply than can commercial bodies who have been trained in that work. The first year the Government handled the crop-and this is proved by the legislation which the minister will bring down by a subsequent resolution-there was a tax of three cents a bushel which had to be paid not only by the man who sold wheat, but also by the Eastern farmer who grew only sufficient wheat for the requirements of his own family. A miller was liable to a penalty for grinding a farmer's grist unless he collected a tax of three cents a bushel. Whatever majy have been the experience in handling the last crop, the Canadian Grain Corporation, which is going to handle this year's crop, have decided that three cents a bushel is not sufficient, and they have notified every miller in Canada that he will be penalized for grinding the wheat of any farmer, whether or not it is ,required only for his own family and in Eastern Canada there are many farmers who grow sufficient only for their own family needs, unless he taxes him fifteen cents a bushel. It seems to me that should convince the minister, who is of an economical turn of mind, that this system 
of handling the wheat does not appeal to the Eastern farmer. The result is that many millers throughout Eastern Canada to-day, having been advised of the amount of red tape that has to be gone through, have decided not to bother with the farmer's grist. Any of them in a position to do commercial work prefer that to bothering with the intricacies of the cumbersome system provided by the Canadian Grain Corporation for handling this year's crop.
Another feature of the Government system of handling the grain of this country that is having a disturbing effect throughout Canada iis the 'preference that the Grain Corporation give to the exportation of grain rather than the products of grain. Now if there is one industry that is natural to this country it is the milling industry, and everything goes to show that this Government are doing everything possible to throttle and destroy that industry in this country. I think I shall be able to convince the minister of that. It is quite true that in the early days of the wot the millers made enormous profits; they could not help it, for whatever they paid for wheat to-day it was worth more to-morrow, the governments of Europe were scrambling for it and running the price up on themselves. Any miller with a stock on hand to-day naturally benefited if the price went up tosmo-rrow, but on the whole it has been shown that when the 'Government took over the business and dictated the millers' profits, the profits' of the millers of Canada on the business done was very much less than the profits on the turnover of other industries in this country. In July of this year the Government, through their grain agents, made a large sale of wheat to Greece. After the sale had been arranged the Government discovered that they could not get the wheat, that it was not in the country, except in the hands of the millers; so the Government commandeered one-half the stock in all the millers'' hands in Canada. What was the result of that?
The grain was shipped out, the mills were shut down and consequently the price of bran and shorts went up because they were scarce. Notwithstanding the howl there is throughout the country and the palliative statements of the Board of Commerce that the price of bran and shorts must oome down, the real problem, to-day is not a matter of price, but of obtaining a sufficient supply for the demand. There is not a supply of bran and shorts commensurate with the demand's of the trade, particularly for the feeding of stock, and that is why the

price of these commodities is high. It seems to me that if the Government had stood aside and allowed the business to take its natural course; if, instead of shipping out our raw material, the manufacturers had been allowed to mill wheat in Canada; if the Government had said to Greece: " We cannot sell you wheat, but you may have flour," then we should have had bran and shorts for our own stock, and there would not have been ia dissatisfied protest throughout the country at the price of milk and pork.
The minister can see very well that it would be much better for us to manufacture our own products in Canada, for we should not only have the offal, which is essential for the dairy and stock-raising industry, but we would have the immense advantage accruing from the necessary labour. The labour involved in the manufacture of a barrel of flour represents a certain monetary advantage to this country, and it must therefore be obvious that if we manufacture our own wheat into flour in Canada rather than export the grain to Greece and Rou-mania to be manufactured by the native there we shall be benefiting our own people. The same conditions are prevalent now as obtained in August. The Grain Corporation is selling wheat; no flour is being sold for export to-day by Canadian mills. I do not know where the screw is loose-if I may use a vernacular expression-but statistics show that the United States millers are making large sales in the export of flour, and we know that wheat to-day is worth more across the border than in Canada. Now, while these two resolutions are due for consideration, I may express the hope that the minister will make a statement of policy in regard to the handling of this year's crop. I should be pleased to know whether the Government will favour the policy of exporting wheat, or will encourage the manufacturing of wheat in our own country, so that we may have the advantage of the labour, and the use of the offal or by-products of the wheat to build up our stock and dairy industry. 1 should like ia statement also as to how the 15 cents a bushel tax on the handling of the crop will operate. Will the grain corporation insist that a farmer taking wheat to 'the mill to be ground for exclusively private use-for the purposes of his family and not with a view to commercial profit-shall pay 15 cents on every bushel that goes to the mill; and, if he pays the 15 cents per bushel-which in the aggregate, as has been pointed out by previous speakers, will amount to a considerable sum- what will be done with the money at the end of the cereal year?

On motion of Sir George Foster (Minister of Trade and Commerce), the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution; Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
That it is expedient to provide that the powers, duties and rights of the Canadian Wheat Board appointed by the Governor in Council under the provisions of the Order in Council of the thirty-first day of July, one thousand nine hundred and nineteen, P.C. No. 1589, as set forth in the said Order in Council and in the Orders in Council of the seventh day of August, one thousand nine hundred and nineteen, P.C. 1659, and the eighteenth day of August, one thousand nine hundred and nineteen, P.C. No. 1741, and the Executive Committee, Chairman and members of the said Board and of the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, be continued in full force and effect for the period of eighteen months from the date of the passing of this legislation, and that the Governor in Council shall have power during such period to fill any vacancies in the chairmanship or membership of the said board, and to make any regulations that he may deem necessary or convenient for the extension, conduct or management of the business of the said board.

Will the minister be good enough to give the Committee some explanation on this?
Sir GEORGE E. FOSTER: I am going to ask the House to pass this resolution in committee, if it can see its way clear to do so, and reserve certain information, * which I have not at my hand just now, for use when we come to the second reading of the Bill. This is a hoard which assumes duties similar to and largely cognate with duties which were assumed by the

Board of Grain Supervisors for the two preceding years. The powers that have been vested in it have been vested by virtue of the War Measures Act, and are practically similar powers to those that were exercised by the Board of Grain Supervisors.

Is it a permanent proposition?
Sir GEORGE E. FOSTER: I may as well set that point at rest at first. It is not a permanent proposition. It is simply effective for tills year. The Government would have been very much better pleased if, in the two preceding years, as well as during this year, the grain trade could have taken its normal and usual methods. My hon. friend opposite, who has just spoken, is quite right in calling the attention of. the House to the fact that there has been, there is, and we hope there shall continue to be, a prosperous, thriving and well ordered system of disposing of the crop of cereals which are raised by the farmers until they find their way into the homes of the consumers. Several businesses combine, co-operate and lend their efforts one to the other in that whole business of great and growing importance. There is the producing interest, the farmer himself. He is primarily interested in getting rid of his Wheat as early as he possibly can, and at the best price that he can possibly get. Millers may come and millers may go; transport companies may exist or they may go to pieces. The farmer is interested in these to a certain extent but his primary interest is, as I said, to get rid of bis wheat at the earliest possible opportunity and at the best price 'that he can get. The millers come in as a secondary and subsidiary operation, and they provide for the domestic requirements of this country, absorbing such grain as is necessary from the producers of grain, putting it in shape for the consumers of the country, and carry on besides a more or less large and thriving trade. I't 'has its vicissitudes, of course, in what we call export business. Its aim, after supplying and whilst supplying the domestic interests of the country, is to sell as much of its product as it possibly can and at the very best possible rates to outside countries who wish ft and who are able to pay for it. It is a legitimate industry, has been long established, and will be a very large and important industry in our country, I hope, as long as our country exists. Then there are numbers of people whom we may designate as the handlers of grain-those who buy the crop

from the farmer at different points and at different stages of the transit of grain, see to its transport and finance its cost and its charges, and in the exercise of their [DOT]wisdom and shrewdness put upon this grain about what they think is necessary in order to give them an immunity of loss and a fair and reasonable profit for the work that they do. That is a large, a distinct, and a very important interest; and if you take by and large these three interests connected with the grain trade, they all have very great importance; and I am one who believes that in their co-operation and free existence, one with the other and in the general interest, you will get probably the best solution of the grain business and the food business problem of this country in so far as that business is derived from cereals. Over and above that, there is the supervising interest which the Government has undertaken in its system of investigation, of examination, of .certification, and of storage; and under the Canada Grain Act a system has grown up which, whilst it may have its faults, still, I think, has gone on from good to better from year to year and has established itself as a useful, and I am inclined to think necessary, factor in the general economy of the grain trade of the country. Now it may be that these interests clash one with another to a certain extent, and it may be that all of these interests in abnormal times are not able to function as they would like and to the extent that they would like, and as they do in normal times. The experience has come to us in these last four or five years; and I think we all-whether we are producers or handlers of grain or whether we are millers and exporters of grain, whatever we are-have been taught that in these abnormal, times all these interests could not have just the play and just the extension that they would have liked for their own individual advantage and gain. Now my hon. friend in criticising- but before I go further let me say this, and it is something in 'answer to the 'hon. gentleman who questioned me a moment ago: That the Government would very much have preferred if during 1917-18 and 1918-19 the ordinary and normal methods of conducting the grain business in this country could have been followed. The operations which were carried on under the Orders in Council for the grain supervisors, as also which are being carried on under the Orders in Council for the Canadian Wheat Board, with respect to the crop of
those years are organizations and methods which the Government, after careful consideration, thought were necessary under the present abnormal conditions; but it is not the wish and not the intention of the Government to carry out those systems outside of the emergency period which we limit to the present crop year of 1919. These different interests-particularly the handlers and the exporters of grain-had their legitimate, their lawful, and their proper business largely interfered with during the years 1917-18 and 1918-19. All of these different interests bemoaned the necessity for the measures taken, but they submitted, I think, in a truly patriotic and reasonable way, to what was dictated by the necessities of the times.
This year a peculiar situation confronted the Government and the grain interests of our country-a situation that prevails all over the world-not only with reference to the methods of handling the grain, but with reference very particularly to the financing of the grain, to the providing of the credits which are necessary where the cash cannot be found. And it was with that peculiar situation confronting it, which, as I said, is not peculiar to Canada, but is 'world wide, that the Government decided, after mature consideration, to give the management of the present year's crop into the hands of a board consisting of practical and approved men. Therefore the Canadian Wheat Board was instituted. Its membership is known to the House and to the public. What the Government tried to do was to get practical men, those who had had the experience and who were trusted and approved as business men in their different capacities, to handle this business as a board, and I think we were successful in getting together a board which has the general approval of the' country, provided it be agreed that the business should be handled by a board at all. The producing interest is well represented on the board, as are also the transporting interest, the consuming interest and the milling interest, and it is the representatives of those four great interests who are carrying on this business under approved principles
My hon. friend puts to me certain questions as to why they do this and why they do that. I am not able to answer his questions. The Government is not managing this business. The Government has put the business into thj hands of the board, and the board must be trusted to carry out its work in the most practical, the most economical and the most efficient way. That,

I believe, it is trying to do. But any information that my hon. friend asks for, and that I can get by communicating with the board, I shall be only too glad to give to him and to the House, because T am sure the board would desire that such information so far as it is possible to be given should be given.
Now, I want just discursively to mention one or two things that were brought to my attention by my hon. friend, because I am not arguing this question on any set plan. He says: "You are doing a wrong to the milling interests and to a certain extent to the live stock interests of this country, because what is best for those interests is that every bushel of wheat raised by the farmers shall be milled in this country, and that this country shall get the added profit upon the milling from the country to which we export over and above what is necessary for our own domestic consumption, and that there shall be the largest possible quantity of bran and shorts available for distribution among our live stock interests." I agree that it would be on all those grounds a very excellent thing if the
200,000,000 bushels, or whatever it is, of surplus grain over and above what is necessary for our own consumption could be milled in this country and disposed of in foreign countries in the milled form so that we would have the benefit of the subsidiary products. Yes, that would be a good thing, but this year it is an absolute impossibility for this country to accomplish it. It is a thing which in any year is probably impossible of accomplishment in completeness, but this year it is an impossibility. My hon. friend has instanced one example, and it happens to be an example with which I am familiar. He says: "This board, or the Government, instead of selling flour to the Greeks and keeping these subsidiary advantages in Canada, has actually sold to them some 12,000,000 bushels of wheat. Now, they should not have done that, for it is against the milling interests and the live stock interests of this country." All I have to say to him in answer to that is this. I know as a matter of fact that neither he nor the whole Dominion of Canada could have sold to the Greeks one single barrel of flour of that 12,000,000 bush-les of wheat. The Greeks wanted wheat, and wheat only. If they do afterwards want flour, then they will negotiate for it. But it was an absolute condition of that sale that it was to be made in the shape of wheat or it could not be made at all.
Now I come back to the farmer, and I put him alongside the miller and let them argue

it out. I am sure of the conclusion that a third party would make, that under those circumstances, the Government, through its commission, had nothing else to do but to see that the farmers got rid of that 12,000,000 bushels of wheat, even though it did not filter through the subsidiary and fructifying processes of the millers of Canada in their different operations. Am I not right absolutely in that respect? My hon. friend would be right if it had been possible to make that sale to the Greeks in the shape of flour; it was not.' And I may go further than that, I may say that the very same difficulty arises with reference to the other European Powers who are negotiating for our products. Go to Great Britain and study the conditions there. My hon. friend whom I have in my eye now understands those conditions thoroughly; so do others of our friends sitting in this House. If any country in the wide world has a famine for food for its live stock, it is Great Britain to-day. Look at the prices she is paying when she wants a bit of feed for stock which is being raised for the market. The price is almost fabulous. Great Britain has also flour mills. Her interest is twofold; she wants to get the offal in order to sustain her live stock industry; she wants to get the grain in order that her mills may grind it and give her that food. And neither my hon. friend, nor all his friends alongside him who 'belong to the milling interests, can go into Great Britain to-day and dictate the purchase of our cereals, as to whether it shall be in the shape of flour or in the shape of the grain itself. That decision is for Great Britain to make for herself. She will buy all the wheat she can for these subsidiary benefits that I spoke of just a moment ago. She is justified in doing it. Canada would do the same thing if she were in the same position. Consequently Great Britain's interests must be borne in mind. But that does not imply that Great Britain is not also going to buy flour from our millers. She will do so. There is not the least doubt about it. But we cannot dictate to her or to any other European Power that any of them shall take the wheat product and shall not get from us the grain itself out of which the products are made for the sustenance of their people.
Now, I happen to know those circumstances, because I was in the negotiations which led up to the purchase of the grain by the Greeks, and these are conditions, without labouring the subject any further, that obtain outside, and Canada must not feel, as I am sure she does not feel,

that she is the only and the supreme arbiter as to how our cereals shall go out to the countries that have borne the bloody burdens of an exhaustive war, and whose people in their homes and in their activities are put to it as never before to reconstruct themselves into comparative happiness and comparative prosperity.
We cannot leave that side of the question out of our thoughts when we are talking about what we would like to have done.
My hon. friend has said that the United States is paying more for wheat than we are here. The United States fixed the price of the crop for this season at $2.26 a bushel. The initial payment made by the Canada Wheat Board to the farmer the moment that he brings his wheat to the station is $2.15 a bushel. Whatever may happen as a surplus when the wheat is finally disposed of, after costs and charges have been accounted for, is divided among the original sellers of the grain. If the wheat nets $2.26 the original sellers will get $2.26; if it nets $2.30 they will get $2.30; if it nets $2 they will still get their $2.15, and the Government will pay the difference. They get what a competent wheat-selling board gets for the product on the markets of the world, less costs and charges. On the other hand, the seller in the United States gets $2.26, no more and no- less. If the surplus is sold at $2.50 he gets no more for the grain than $2.26. That is a fair statement of the case as between the two systems.
The question of finance was really the governing question in the Government's reaching a decision as to the medium through which the purchase and disposition of the grain should be made this year. I am not going very fully into the matter at this moment; questions will probably be asked and we may discuss it later. The farmer could not sell his wheat unless there was somebody to buy it, and that somebody could not buy it unless he had the cash to pay for it. It was that idea and that consideration which determined the Government to adopt the method it did in order to provide that the very moment the farmer got his wheat to the station-no matter whether it was the last of August, the last of September, the middle of October, or any other time-he would get $2.15 as a basic price. The market was made absolutely certain, and the price was made absolutely certain up to $2.15. Thus governments have to do with governments, and finance was provided for.
Now, I do not want to go into, the matter any more fully at this time. I am not able

to give all the whys and wherefores as to what the Canada Wheat Board is doing; it is doing that business, not the Government. But I shall be quite glad to give all proper information that may be asked for when we come to the second reading of the Bill.	'

With the personnel of the Canada Wheat Board I have no fault to find. I hope that later the minister will make some statement with regard to the reason for the fifteen cent tax and what is going to be done with that money at the end of the year.
Now, the minister has made an excellent plea on behalf of the exportation of Canadian products in the raw state-raw material-and of the manufacture of our products in other countries. The minister points out that Greece would not buy one pound of flour; she would buy wheat. Very well, if Greece would not -buy flour, Finland would. The minister contends that the real object of the Government was to help the farmer to get rid of his wheat and to get paid for it. But the farmer had already got rid of the wheat that was sold to Greece; that wheat had been paid for and was held by the Canadian millers who were prepared to mill it and take chances on what they would do with the product.

How much wheat did
the Government commandeer from the millers at that time?

They commandeered just
fifty per cent of the wheat stocks in millers' hands; I understood the total to be about
12,000,000 bushels. I suppose my hon. friend will not contradict that in view of the assertion just made by the minister that 12,000,000 bushels were sold to Greece.
But that 12,000,000 bushels sold to Greece runs over the year.

We will not argue about the number of bushels; the fact remains that the Government took away from the millers one-half of the wheat that they then had in stock. The minister will not dispute that assertion.

No. But let me put the thing to my hon. friend from a humanitarian as well as from a patriotic point of view. Suppose we had an opportunity to sell 12,000,000 bushels of wheat to Greece provided we could get the millers to give us a portion of their surplus wheat

to fill the first order. If we put it to the millers whether they should keep more than they really required rather than give us a certain quantity which they could make .good by future purchases, should not the milk of human kindness cause the millers to say: We do not want you to miss that good offer. We have a surplus here; you take half of it and we will make it up afterwards?
We are not discussing the humanitarian point of it.
We are all human.
What I am trying to point out is that the minister is reversing the policy he preached for years.
Not at all.
Were actual sales of wheat made at that price?
And to what extent?

I have not before me the figures as to the extent, but there was trading and wheat sold at $2.45, and it was

bought and sold by the men who had been buying and selling for years, by the same men to whom my hon. friend (Mr. Henders) sold his wheat before he was able to sell it to this Government, and, I imagine, sold it at just as great a profit.

It was to a
limited extent that sales were made, and the wheat was bought in some instances, maybe in the major part of instances by brokers or parties on the other side of the line w'ho had no entry into the United States for Canadian grain to the extent of a single peek. The United States has a surplus of grain; it fixed the price at $2.26 for its own farmers; it, therefore, had to put around its border an 'absolute prohibition of wheat going into that country to interfere with its own national operations.
The United States fixed a minimum price of $2.26.
Oh, no, an absolute price.

I hold in my hand the Winnipeg Free Press of September 27, .and these are the quotations in Minneapolis for cash wheat:
No. 1 dark Northern, $2.65, $2.95.
No. 1 Northern, $2.60, $2.70.
Everybody along the line knows to-day that Canadian farmers who are adjacent to the international line are taking their wheat into the United States and getting more money for it than they are getting in Canada. Will any western man dispute that statement right now?

Will my hon. friend be perfectly frank about the matter and inform the committee about what proportion of the total crop of Canada that is marketable is allowed into the United States under those conditions?

If the promise made to the farmers of Western Canada by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) is of any good at all, the whole crop can go into the United States, because the Government represented to the western farmers that there is reciprocity in wheat, and with loud acclaim they told the farmers they had all the advantage of the American market.

Without going hack to musty arguments, will my hon. friend answer my question? What proportion of the grain of Canada which is to be sold and is.looking for a market is allowed to go in on farmers' wagons? Never mind

what old theories have been' or anything of that kind.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce apparently -wants to run away from the argument.
I think there is another man that wants to run away. He is getting his seven-leagued boots on.
I will be quite frank with the Minister of Trade and Commerce. There is . a very limited portion going in.
Yes.

The farmers are doing only a retail business, a peddling business, and why? Because the hoard appointed by my hon. friend have passed certain regulations, and they are working in harmony with the board in the United States; they are allowing in wagon-loads; a farmer can draw his wagon-load into the United States and sell it, but he cannot ship a carload as that is prohibited by the regulations. As I am not familiar with the inside history, I do not know whether it is the United States that is prohibiting the shipment of carloads or whether it is the Canadian Government; but I know and I make this statement- and if I am not right, I want the minister to correct me-that wagon-loads of wheat are going into the United States all along the Canadian border and that carloads cannot be shipped into 'that country.

My hon. friend is absolutely right. How many wagon-loads are going in, I cannot tell, but even those are under regulation. But Uncle Sam appears to be big enough to say: Whilst I have an absolute policy for my great grain production, I am not so bigoted but that I will allow a poor Canadian farmer that lives within a few miles of the border to take his wagon-load over, and I will say nothing about it; but he is not allowing the importation of Canadian grain into the United States, not on your life.

But he is allowing all that the farmers can draw in on wagons. Where does the Canadian Government come in as regards that? Does the Canadian Government permit this traffic to go on without protesting when it sees a man, say fifty miles from the line, at a disadvantage of fifty cents a bushel as compared with his Canadian brother farmer who lives nearer to the line?

He has the advantage of geographical position. This, the
43J
first protest I have heard against this comes from a miller in Eastern Canada and not from a farmer in the West.
My hon. friend is endeavouring to place a mis-construction upon my words. My protest is that the Government prevents all the farmers of Western Canada from taking advantage of that market.

There is an assertion, that the Government of Canada prevents all the farmers of the West from taking advantage of the American market in this year 1919. I deny that absolutely, and I challenge my hon. friend to the proof. It is patent to any man that when you have a country which has fixed an absolute price which it will pay for the surplus grain in the United States to its own producers, the Government of that country is not going to allow hundreds of millions of bushels to be imported into the United States and the seller to get the same advantage as the men who are citizens of that country itself have. It must protect its own surplus. This is not to be thrown as a fault upon the present Government or upon any Canadian Government. It is absolutely the policy of the United States, and not a barrel of flour nor a bushel of grain under that policy in the large is allowed to entrench upon that United States' market.

I have not, under my hand to-day, the proof of what this Government are doing, but I have under my hand proof of what this Government were doing only a few months after they introduced reciprocity by Order in Council and advertised throughout all the West that they were going to give the farmers of Western Canada the advantage of the United States' market. I have here a letter dated February 11, 1918, from the" Canadian Food Control regarding the exportation of flour. It states:
I am in receipt of your letter of the 8th instant and beg to inform you that the exportation of flour in quantities of 25 barrels or over is absolutely prohibited to the United States, as per memorandum No. 2147 B enclosed herewith.
That was an Order in Council of the Government. They were the people who then stopped the information. I do not know who is stopping it to-day. Let us get on with this story.
It is a story.

I told the House a few moments ago that the Government policy early in July was for an open market, and that

as a matter of fact they did have an open market. When it was announced to the trade in Canada that there was to be an [DOT] open market, the Winnipeg Grain Exchange sent to England Professor Magill whom, 1 am sure, the Minister of Trade and Commerce will acknowledge as an expert in his particular line of business, no matter what others may say of him. It was my hon. friend himself who selected Professor Magill as the head of the grain handling business of Canada. Subsequently, he left that work and became associated with the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. After his return from England he made a report to the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, in which he says:
I was one of those who believed (and I still believe it) that the sooner we could get back to commercial methods in handling our business, the better it would be for our country, ourselves and everybody concerned.
Now let us see what he says of conditions as he found them in England. The Canadian High Commissioner and Doctor Robertson took the matter up with the British authorities. Professor Magill says:
They had an interview with the Royal Wheat Commission on June 13th. I want to speak of that interview for a moment. There were present on behalf of the Government of Canada, Sir George Perley and his secretary, Mr. Griffith, and Dr. Robertson, and on the other hand the Royal Wheat Commission. I was not asked to be there; I had no right to be there. That interview was on June 13th. What happened? Mr. Griffith sent me a letter stating what happened. I will read it to you.
I shall put this letter on Hansard so that all members of the House may have this statement from the man who was handling the grain business over there at that time. The letter is as follows:
Dear Dr. Magill:	Following the conference
with the Wheat Commission a letter has been received from the secretary stating that it is impossible at present to outline any specific buying policy, partly owing to the crop situation in both consuming and producing countries still being subject to large variations, and partly because it is not yet known how far the responsibility of the Royal Commission may extend in making purchases on behalf of the Allies. The Royal Commission, therefore, is unable to state what proportion of the new Dominion crop it will desire to buy, but as the Commission is alive to the fact that the Wheat Export Company was necessarily a hindrance to the normal conduct of the export trade during the war, and they desire to revive the activity of commercial enterprise, they propose to liquidate the Wheat Export Company (Winnipeg) as a trading concern so that complete freedom may be restored to the Dominion grain trade to sell its produce in the simplest manner without restriction of destination, during the ensuing year.
It is added that the Commission, as at present advised, will probably make its purchases

on an f.o.b. basis as and when stocks are wanted, and it will probably prove advisable to establish an office at the Canadian seaboard to ensure promptness in the correspondence which must take place between London and Canada. The Commission believes that an early announcement that the Wheat Export Company (Winnipeg) will cease to operate and that trade will be able to resume some normal courses, will remove the element of uncertainty which we deprecated.
Tours faithfully,
W. N. Griffith.
Referring to this letter, Professor Magill goes on to say:
That is from the High Commissioner's office. What does it mean? It means that the Royal Wheat Commission on behalf, of the British Government undertook to buy our crop from the Canadian Grain Trade at the Atlantic seaboard f.o.b	They said in
substance " We will buy it in quantities as we need it. As we need it, we will furnish the ships and pay for it f.o.b. We will not interfere with your selling to neutral countries-sell to them on a commercial basis." These neutral countries have their own tonnage and they are wealthy. They have money to pay for wheat without credits, and Germany is said to be buying through them. That was the proposal of the Commission-that we should sell to neutral and enemy countries direct and to the Royal Wheat Commission at the Canadian seaboard f.o.b.
I think the minister will accept the statement of Professor Magill that he did not anticipate any trouble in selling or financing the crop. My complaint with the minister to-day is that the Government, through their methods, are not helping the trade, but are rather injuring it. If the Western farmers who live along the border are able to sell a portion of their grain to the United States at 50 or 60 cents a bushel above our prices, what is to hinder them from carrying that wheat to within five miles of the international boundary and hauling it over as fast as they can by teams? Is there anything to hinder them?
They would very soon have a customs officer after them.

We have not noticed any of that yet. I hope the minister will make a clear statement and tell us that we are going to be rid of this government control of industry. It is not good for the country. I am sure the minister himself must be bothered night and day with these restrictions. I think it is better that the trade should be open. Let us get down to sound business principles. That is the only way to build uip any industry and build up the country.

I wanted to say a word about the fifteen cent tax. The farmers have to pay this tax on the wheat they bring to

the grist mill for gristing. The millers in my constituency have made representations to me. They object to this tax. The farmers also object to it very much. These farmers do not sell their wheat to the millers; they only bring it to the grist mill for gristing. If they sold it, I understand from the minister, that they could he given a participation receipt for this fifteen cents a bushel that they have to pay, and they would get the balance later on. When they bring their wheat to the mill for gristing they want the flour and the offal back. It is a disadvantage to the miller to have to charge this fifteen cent tax, and I hope the minister will make representations to the Wheat Board with a view to having this tax abolished as far as gristing is concerned.
' Sir GEORGE FOSTER: I will have it looked into. I will take it up later.

I am sure we all have a distinct recollection of the agitation throughout the country by those interested in the growing of wheat of a few months ago before the Wheat Board was appointed. After the board was appointed and a minimum price fixed a great many of these same people were dissatisfied that the Government had moved in the matter. I can readily understand how much easier and more agreeable it would have been for the Government to have let business follow its usual channels rather than undertake the difficult problem of handling the wheat for the farmers of Canada.
There is a mistaken idea, I believe, on the part of many people that a tax is being levied on wheat, particularly where grists are taken to the local mills, and even where wheat is purchased in small quantities for feed purposes. I hope that when the minister speaks on this point to the committee his statement will reach everybody throughout the country. It is essential for the farmers of Canada to grow wheat, and to find a market for their wheat abroad. We are all prone to lose sight of the fact that success in agriculture demands the application of scientific methods, as well as industry and skill, and is not a mere mechanical process. Agriculture is undoubtedly ^the greatest industry in Canada, and it is not by raising grain or some other such product and disposing of it in its crude unmanufactured state that we shall reap the maximum profits. When it is borne in mind that a large part of Canada is comparatively new agriculturally, and that for centuries there has been stored up in its soil richness and fertility, which in many
sections has for years been exploited, it requires no great stretch of imagination to picture the result if the present practice that obtains in many parts of the country is continued. In the district in which I lived when I was, a young lad, there were in all the small towns grain warehouses, one after the other in succession, all along the railway siding. These warehouses were provided for the storage and shipment of grain, but to-day not a bushel of grain is shipped from any of those towns in that district. On the contrary, thousands of tons of feed are purchased and fed on the farms. By the application of scientific methods, and in the manufacturing of raw materials and shipping finished products, such as live stock and dairy produce we achieve our greatest success. The fertility of our soil cannot be maintained under the system which generally prevails at present-and I am particularly referring to western Canada, because the system now in vogue there no longer exists in the older provinces. My hon. friend from Huntingdon has referred to the question of the disposal of by-products of wheat and in view of the statement of the minister that the demand abroad is for our wheat and not for our flour, I think I may deal with this matter for a moment. I believe that the transportation charges have a good deal to do with the present state of affairs. Reference has been made to the farmers of Great Britain and some other countries, I believe that there are in Great Britain a class of farmers who are superior to those in any other part of the world. They have developed their business on strictly scientific principles, and are [DOT]able to produce to-day crops such as they were never able to grow in years gone by. In the old country the fertility and productivity of the soil is being increased rather than depleted, as a result of the development of the livestock industry, which has been cultivated to a remarkable degree. Our greatest handicap consists in the method by which we dispose of the produce of our farms in many districts. I admit that no effective remedy oan be undertaken as regards the present crop. The matter presents a problem which has to be worked out, and I believe that this discussion this afternoon will be one ol the most valuable contributions of Parliament if it will serve to stimulate a real interest in the question of transportation charges on wheat and flour. I hope I shall live to see the day when every bushel oi wheat in the country will be manufactured

into flour, and the bran and shorts or byproducts fed to the live stock in Canada. When we reach that condition we may rest assured o! a prosperous agricultural. community. Until then, we shall be far short of the acme of our industrial attainments; and ruined lands will be the portion of those who persist in the present practice. The difficulties are largely attributable to the cost of transportation. Wheat is a convenient ballast for steamships, and I think a preference in transportation charges is given in its favour over flour. If it were necessary, I believe it would be in the interests of this country to secure enougli ocean carriers to take the crop overseas and place it on the markets, so that there might be no discrimination as a result of charges, and there might be a preference in the carrying of flour as against wheat. I think that the day is not far distant when Canada, in its own interests, will adopt such a policy. The member for Huntingdon said that the by-product of wheat is hardly obtainable in this country, and that some of the wheat in the millers' hands had been commandeered by shipment to Greece. The minister has pointed out that only a very small proportion of the twelve million bushels has so far been shipped, so that it appears that this has not affected to any great extent the supply of mill feed in Canada. It is a fact, however, that bran is practically unobtainable in the part of the province from which I come. There is a greater demand at present than has existed before in many years, but strange to say you can purchase any quantity of shorts, and as a matter of fact there is a difference of ten dollars' per ton between the prices of bran and shorts. Shorts today is simply bran ground fine. The millers do not want to sell plain bran but they are delighted to sell it in the shape of shorts as long as they can get ten dollars a ton moire for it. This is one of the things that have a very important bearing on some of the questions that are agitating the. minds of the people tenday-the high cost of living.
Who fixed the price?
I hope the hon. member will discover 'file person who fixed the price and have him held up before the public gaze, if such a price as I have referred to has been fixed.
There is the prioe fixer right in front of you.

Let me say that whoever is responsible for the difference in price
[IMr. Sutherland.]
between bran and shorts must see what a harmful effect it has. To-day the millers are grinding the screenings, which contain a small proportion of cracked Wheat, and mixing it with bran in order to bring it up to the requisite standard:. That is precisely what is being done with regard to bran and shorts'. The quantity of weed seeds that are being ground up and mixed with bran and shorts represents to the farmers of the country tens, yes, hundreds of thousands of dollars annually through the poison that is being sent out in this way, to say nothing of weed seeds that are being scattered throughout 'the land.
Do you purchase shorts at all? Don't you buy everything under the name of middlings?

It is really a distinction without a difference. There was a time when we considered shorts as shorts, but to-day there is another by-product of wheat which iis commonly called "red dog'' or low grade flour, which is really the old form of shorts which the farmers were able to purchase a few years ago and which is commanding a very high price to-day. Bran and shorts are scoured to-day to such an extent that it will not come up to the standard required, and in order to make this possible, wild buckwheat and screenings containing small bits of cracked wheat are ground up. There is sufficient of this cracked wheat and buckwheat included to bring of the bran and shorts up to the standard called for. This is quite obvious to every one engaged in stock-raising in Canada. Bran and shorts are essential food stuffs required by those engaged in the breeding and producing of stock and for dairy produce. Take up the newspapers and see what prices are quoted for mill feeds at the present time. You will find that corn meal is now quoted at from $80 to $82 per ton or a trifle over 4 cents per pound. Now what is the effect of the high price of feed? It is this: that in many parts of the older provinces, at least, wheat is being ground up by the farmer and fed to the stock rather than take the chance of buying some of the dirty, foul, poisonous mill feed, bran and shorts, that are being sold off by the millers Thousands of animals are dying yearly <as the result of being fed on this stuff. Yet under the laws of the country the millers are permitted to engage in the sale of this adulterated product and do it from year to year. I have a Bill before the House dealing with that subject and I .am not going to refer to what I hope the House

will consider or do with regard to it; but let me remind the hon. gentleman (Mr. Robb) that the millers of this country have justly earned for themselves the censure-
I was going to use a harsher expression than that-but they certainly are deserving of the censure of the people for the policy which they have pursued in the adulteration of these two important by-products of wheat.
Why not expropriate them along with the railways?
I am one who believes in competition. I think that governments have quite enough to do without interfering in matters that can much better be conducted by the people themselves-
Hear, hear.

-and if we have public ownership of railways in Canada 1 do not think anybody will say that it has been from a desire or any particular effort on the part of the Canadian people; it has come as a result of existing conditions and we have it whether we want it or not.
Now I do not intend to say anything further on this subject more than this: The agitation that was carried on before the Wheat Board was appointed, and the dissatisfaction expressed after that board's appointment, is somewhat significant and remarkable. Strange to say, it is very largely the same people who were agitating and objecting in both cases, which goes to show that it is absolutely impossible for the Government to try to please all the people-that is out of the question. However, I do want to emphasize the need for the Government to exercise great care with regard to this matter because wheat is the one commodity above all others-above even gold, which regulates the standard of living and prices in Canada as well as any other country. I do not think ' there is any getting away from that, it is conceded by every one who has studied the question; and I am not too sure even yet, in view of the fact that the wheat crop of Canada is not likely to he anything nearly as great as it would have been under more favourable conditions, whether it would not be advisable to let this cereal reach the consumer through the usual channel.

I would like to say two or three words in connection with this discussion, The first is that under these unusual conditions in regard to the supply of wheat and of flour, and the measures that have had to be taken by the
Government on the other side and the Government here, one outstanding feature was the elimination of speculation in wheat from the Chicago market and from our Canadian markets. I think that was a good thing for the farmers of Canada and I do hope that lesson will in some way be continued. We have had better prices for wheat during the war, of course there was another reason for it, but without speculation in wheat by reason of the exchanges in Chicago and Winnipeg. That has been beneficial and if an advantage has been derived from it, let us continue the practice. Another thing has come out in this debate and that is that in these times-while speculation has been stopped as far as the grain exchange is concerned-there have been enormous profits made by the millers of this country in grinding. Now, are we watching those profits? Are we, in these times of stress and of great need of money Jor carrying on the business and the affairs of- the country, watching those profits of the Canadian millers, and are we getting our fair share in the way of -a profit tax? I think that should be looked into. My hon. friend (Mr. Sutherland) referred to another thing and that is the price of mill feed. That is a matter that I have had farmers come to see me about. Only on Friday last I had a long talk with a farmer whose main grievance was the high price of mill feed. He is also a milk producer and he referred to the Board of Commerce then sitting in Toronto dealing with the price of milk. He inquired: "Why does not the Board of Commerce which is regulating the price of our milk see we get mill feed at a fair price, and ilso get real bran and shorts," as pointed out by my friend from Oxford " and not some adulterated feed"? The farmers have grievances in all these matters and those grievances ought to be removed. We ought to so arrange our national policy that if it be possible to sell the flour and keep the bran and shorts in our country for the live stock industry we ought to do it. I agree with the Minister of Trade and Commerce that in connection with this sale to Greece we could not do that, perhaps it could not be financed in that way; but the national policy of Canada ought to be as the member for Oxford said, on the line of encouraging the shipment of flour in preference to wheat, and in that way have the benefit of the mill feed for our own country so as to encourage the Canadian live stock industry which is a great source of revenue to our farmers. Of course you cannot always dictate to the buyer what

he must take. That brings up another question, which was also referred to by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sutherland), that we can develop our railways just as much as we like, we can spend all the money we like in creating a national system of railways, but unless we have steamships under our own control in connection with our national railways, we will never be able to get the best advantage and dictate to the greatest extent the character of the export of our grain, whether it shall go as wheat or whether it shall go as flour. All this is on the line of national policy; I hope that the policy of the Government, the policy of this Wheat Board, and the policy of this Board of Commerce, will have in view on every occasion the securing of such prices and such handling of the profit as will be for the advantage of the country, and will see to it that the making of a great business out of speculating in wheat in this country shall not continue. Furthermore, if the millers are to make large profits out of the handling of our grain, reasonable taxes on those profits should be taken for the benefit of the treasury of the country. I hope that the Board of Commerce which is now fixing prices will see that when it is fixing the price for the farmers' milk-and the board is telling the farmers that they must not sell their milk beyond a certain figure-will also see to it that the millers are regulated in the prices they charge for mill feed, and that mill feed shall be of some kind of guaranteed quality.
If that is done it will be a benefit to the whole farming industry of this country. I quite agree with the minister that he has put forward a very fair case to justify the creation of this Board. I am not at all of the belief though that is to be the end of control of grain and other food products. The best security for the farming business of this country will be a constant regulation of the price of wheat, I believe, and, connected with that, an averaging of the price by years. I believe that a real substantial uplift will be given to farming, and especially to the production of wheat, when we can keep three crops of wheat in store, if that is found to be feasible-and I believe we can do it-coupled with a fixed price, and " valorizing," if I may use that word, in connection with such fixed price. If we can do that it will result in a real benefit for the country at large. We must also see to it that speculation is eliminated and that no unfair profits are made by the milling interests, but that the man who raises the wheat shall get every cent he
[Mr. W. P. Maclean.!
ought to get out of his industry as a grain grower.
the Government closed the market when it was an ascending market?	.

This has developed into a very important discussion, Mr. Chairman. Apart altogether from setting the price of wheat, whether it sells at $2.10 a bushel or $2.50 a bushel, I think a very important point was brought out by my hon. friend the member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) in his very excellent speech, namely, that tens of thousands, yes, I believe hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of stock has been poisoned by the action of the millers in mixing poisoned seeds in the stock feed they have sold throughout the country within the last few years. Last year a number of farmers brought to my attention the loss of their hogs from some mysterious complaint. One of them, after he had lost several hogs, had a sample of the feed sent down to the department here for analysis, and he received a very comforting reply to the effect that they did find poisoned seed in the sample, but they would not say that it was sufficient to kill a hog.
They did not know the hogs tenacity of life.

Every farmer handling feed put on the market, particularly during the last five or six years, has been paying for so-called shorts which was only ground bran, oat-hulls and every kind of dirt which the miller could add to the mixture and sell it as shorts. I do not know, but perhaps the millers also mix straw in what they sell as shorts, but they undoubtedly mix oat-hulls, corn cobs, with a sprinkling perhaps of corn, and many other things, with a trifle of cotton seed oil or oil cake to give the feed on analysis a showing of protein, and so practically rob the farmers. It is a very serious condition of affairs, Mr. Chairman. I do not like to charge the millers with the intention of deliberately going out to rob their patrons, but I will say that they deliberately deceive the people when they pretend to sell a commodity that is not at all up to the standard which the purchasers might reasonably hope to expect.
Six or eight years ago I introduced a Bill and it was placed on the Statute Book, which required the miller to put on the outside of the bag or other container an analysis of mixed feed. That regulation was observed to a certain extent, but not as rigidly as it should have been, and it seems to me that it is important that something should be done in the near future to absolutely prevent the sale of these mixed fraudulent feeds, and above all to prevent the sale of any feed containing a percentage of poisonous seeds. There is no reason under heaven why a miller should be allowed to mix in his stock feed seeds that are poisonous. Therefore I would like to ask the minister to take this into serious consideration and see if something cannot be done to prevent such a practice in the future.
Mr. MoOOIG: I agree with much that has been said by gentlemen who have spoken this afternoon, and have no doubt ithalt the discussion will be productive of good effects. I am glad that the minister is paying so much attention to the con>
plaints that are being made with regard to these matters. Complaints are heard from all parts of the country concerning the class of feed that is being sold at large prices throughout Canada, and anything that can be done to remedy that -condition will meet with the general approval of producers of stock.
It is complained by the farmers in m-any rural sections that they have been unable to sell their wheat. In my section of the -country we are receiving $1.94 for our wheat, but in many cases the- farmers are unable to get a market for it. The- present regulations seem to be having the effect of closing the elevators in the smaller centres; only in the large centres will the millers or grain buyers purchase wheat. If the operations of the Wheat Board -are -having -any bad effect in this regard the -minister should direct their -attention to the matter and see that this unfortunate state of -affairs is remedied. Would it not -be -advisable for this board-which, no doubt, will -be a grea-t expense to the people-to take into consideration the advisability of regulating the prices of agricultural -implements that -are absolutely necessary in the production of wheat? If the board would go thoroughly into this matter the fanners would he better satisfied, because they would feel that they were not the only class of the community whose products were being regulated as to price by Government or by a commission.
M-r. BOYCE: As one who has occasion to purchase considerable quantities of cattle feed, I wish to express my approval of some of the remarks that have been made this afternoon with regard to these feeds. I do not think that some of the millers are as had as they have been depicted, but I know

that sometimes they have been pretty bad. Three years ago we paid $20 a ton for bran; now we pay $50. If it was good feed, I would not object so much, but I have actually got bags of some kind of seed from this bran. I do not know what kind of seed it was, but I know that it was very bad indeed. There is no question about its being poisonous; I have seen hogs refuse to eat it. Of course, the cattle have to eat it because it is mixed with ensilage and such other feeds, but as food for hogs it is .poison of the worst description. Cattle are very expensive; you cannot get a cow for less than $150 or $200, and anything so valuable as that should not be fed with stuff that is apt to injure it. The Government, therefore, ought to investigate this matter and prevent such rubbish from being put on the market, at the same time fining the offenders so heavily that it wall be a lesson to others not to repeat the offence. The sooner this state of affairs is done away with the better for all concerned. The cost of everything is high now, and the farmers cannot afford to throw away their money in the purchase of stuff that is of no use to them.

The member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) raised a question with regard to the milling in this country of all our own wheat. I wish to point out that Great Britain takes an average of 75,000,000 bushels of our wheat yearly. She has a large population to feed. She grows a large quantity of wheat, but it is of a type that does not make the quality of bread that the British people want to eat. Britain, therefore, has to go to some otheT country for a wheat to blend with her own in order to bring the flour up to the standard required by her people. She has discovered that Canada is a producer of the kind of wheat that she requires. Other countries produce the same type of wheat; Siberia produces it, and so does Northern Russia. The price paid by Great Britain for the surplus wheat that she requires regulates in large measure the price of wheat on our own market-in fact, in the markets of the world. If Great Britain, therefore, because of our adopting the policy of grinding all our wheat in this country and selling simply the flour, is prevented from securing ill Canada the wheat which she requires she will go to Russia or Siberia for that wheat. That would mean that each year we would have this 75,000,000 bushels of wheat on our hands without a market. Furthermore, it would take out of our hands the very commodity that fixes the price we secure for the rest of our crop.
IMr. Boyce. 1
