Can we afford to let that happen? Britain must have that type of wheat. We ought to be the very first to see to it that we secure that market for our wheat.
Some hon. members who have sipoken this afternoon have made reference to the kind of work that is being done by the millers and the kind of offal that they are sending out. Suppose we force the .millers to grind that 75,000,000 bushels of wheat yearly that ordinarily goes over to the Old Country, and they have to find a market in the Old Country for the offal from this 75,000,000 bushels of wheat. If they supply to the Old Country the same kind of offal that they supply to our own trade, what effect would that have upon our market in the Old Country? Not a very good effect, I am sure. But my main point is that the wheat that we send from this country is a determining factor in fixing the price that we receive lor the whole of our crop. We must keep production in this country in a healthy condition; otherwise we may put ourselves in such a position that we will have to go out of wheat production.

I do not think that we should depart from what is a good policy for this country simply because the people of some other country require some of our wheat.
If we in this country are the sole producers of an article that must be had in other parts of the world, if other nations must have our goods, we must not, to the detriment of our own people, and to the extent of causing the production of poison for the hogs of this country, send wheat out of Canada. The minister is very sympathetic for men in Greece who may want wheat and for the cows in Greece that may want by-products. I do not see why his heart should be so tender for the Greek cow as against the Canadian, cow.
As a matter of fact, it was a British cow.

The Canadian people
who use the products of the cow require the by-products in this country, and if a Canadian is able to buy that by-product and if he has the money to pay for it at a reasonable price, I do not see why it should be put beyond his reach and sold to a man who cannot buy it at all, we ourselves being obliged to come to the fore and to furnish the money to the Greek who wants to buy the wheat and who takes it out of this country. By this process, we put the price away up in the clouds in this country for our own people; in fact, we put ourselves

in such a position that we have not the article at all, and I do not understand that to be good business. When the people of any country produce an article and there is in that country a fair price for that article under fair competition, I do not think it is the duty of a Government to interfere and to furnish money to a foreign country to buy that article and, by so doing, put the price beyond the normal and to make it difficult for our own people to exist. That is not good business, and that procedure should not be allowed to exist in this country; but that is what has been done, not only in wheat, but in clothing and various other articles. We find in this country clothing, exceedingly high in price and difficult to buy, because every shred of cloth that could be available in Canada is bought up, made into garments and sent out of the country, bought up by the money of the Canadian people. That is a policy which for the last few months I have been protesting against as much as I can, but my protests are of no avail, and we are dealing with ourselves and sending the result of our purchases out of the country and bringing no advantage whatever to the Canadian people.
I wish particularly to refer to this charge of fifteen cents that appears to be imposed upon grain in parts of Canada where we may say there is no grain trade at all. In the province from which I come the farmers raise for their own use what may be regarded as a fair quantity of food, but such a thing as exporting grain or flour or selling grain to any noticeable extent, is not known to our people at all. Within the last few years there have been established in Nova Scotia a few mills for the grinding of wheat, just as good mills and producing just as good flour as mills in the West or in Ontario. That has brought about the growing of more wheat, so that many farmers in Nova Scotia to-day produce sufficient wheat to furnish their own flour. There are only two or three of those mills in that province, and (the (farmers go to those mills with that wheat and have it ground; but I confess I never heard before of this impost of fifteen cents on every bushel that every farmer in Antigonish or Victoria or any other county in Nova Scotia may bring to a mill for the purpose of furnishing flour for his own family, and, by the way, getting the by-product of that for his stock. I wish as emphatically as I can to protest against any tax of that kind. Whatever benefits may inure to the farmer who is in this trade in the far West and who sells
grain and gets the benefit of this tax because it is necessary for sending his wheat to market, that does not in any way touch the farmer who may have a small quantity of wheat which he brings to a mill and has ground for his own purposes. He does not tax the railway; he does not tax the elevators; he has not the benefits of any of the machinery that is set up for the purpose of handling the larger quantity of grain. The minister should differentiate between the man whose business or living is the handling of grain and the farmer who raises a few bushels and who handles them entirely and exclusively for his own purposes and not with a view to entering into competition with anybody who is in the business of raising wheat or other grain for the purpose of selling for export or otherwise. If this tax is applied now, or if it is being collected now at the mills in my province or in the other Maritime Provinces where they have no grain worth speaking of to sell, steps should be taken to differentiate in the matter and to see to it that the tax is no longer collected.

I will have that looked into and will give my hon. friend the information. Might I ask the committee to pass the resolution and to let me have my Bill introduced, and the discussion can be taken up and continued on the second reading of the Bill? I have not replied to several questions which have been put to me, because I want a little fuller information before I endeavour to give to the House just what is involved in some of these technical alternatives that they are making in the course of procedure.

Will the minister when
lie is making his explanations, be good enough to remember what the hon. member for Oxford South (Mr. Sutherland) said regarding the spread in price between bran and shorts?

I have a note of that.
Resolution reported, and concurred in.
Sir GEORGE FOSTER thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 21, respecting the Canadian Wheat Board.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

subtopic: BOARD OF COMMERCE-SALARIES OF THE COMMISSIONERS.

speechtext: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 12, to amend the Board of Commerce Act.

subtopic: BOARD OF COMMERCE-SALARIES OF THE COMMISSIONERS.
speechtext:
In view of the prominence that has been given to the actions of the board during the past few days, I think it is very important that we should have some further information with regard to the effect of their attitude and what their policy is going to be before we consent to pass this Bill. The Board of Commerce have been given very wide powers indeed under the Act, and efforts have been made on a number of occasions during the past week to ascertain what the members of the board are doing. Apparently, members of this House here in session are not in a position to advise those who have sent us here as to the extent and effect of the xulings that are being made by this board. Some one may say that I have been rather too persistent in attempting to obtain information during the past week as to the Board of Commerce reported rulings on milk, etc., but I come from a county that is affected possibly to a greater degree than any other county in Canada, and I was endeavouring to look after the interests of my constituents. The ruling was made by a member of the board -by the vice-chairman, I understand, though I am not sure, and he seems to deny it-but we have an admission by the leader of the Government (Sir George Foster)this afternoon that the order was rescinded. It affected, as I have already pointed out, an industry that is highly developed, particularly in South Oxford-an industry of about five million dollars per annum for that county alone, and one that is rapidly growing. The province of Ontario to which the ruling applied produces more than one half of the total dairy products of the Dominion of Canada, which amounted in 1917, the last year for which we have the figures, to somewhere in the neighbourhood of $100,000,000. At the time when we have a Bill before the House fixing the salaries of the members of this board who are given such extensive powers, we have a member of the board meeting the people in a glib and flippant way and making a ruling on which we are unable to obtain any definite information. I should like to read a statement which appeared in the Toronto papers, and I believe in other papers throughout the -country, on September 27, as follows:
That Man O'Connor Ties His Own Hands. Issues Reply to Critics and will let it go at that.
The sarcastic criticism to which he was subjected a few days ago from members in the House of Commons called forth an answering statement from Vice-Chairman W. F. O'Connor, 
K.C., of the Board of Commerce, at yesterday morning's sitting of the board at the City Hall. He emphatically declared that the speakers to whom he referred had dealt with "things that were not so."
The statement was as follows:
"Some days ago in the House of Commons certain observations were made affecting myself as to my character, disposition, attainments and otherwise. Certain of those who made these references to myself of the peculiar personal touch mentioned thought they were making them of a judge. This is a court, but not of judges, although these observations were made by those thinking the members were judges and therefore could not answer, as a judge is not allowed, nor is it considered proper for him to make any observations.
"To this board are given functions of an administrative and judicial nature combined. As to the observations regarding myself as to the things I have said or I have done, I say the things that I have been alleged to have said, I have not said, and those things that I have been said to have done, I have not done.
"The statements that the newspapers have published certain things that I have been alleged to have said or done is wrong. No paper ever published them. From the be. ginning to end every speaker dealt with things that were not so. But if everything was said which had been said, and if everything was done which I was alleged to have done, I would have an absolute and perfect right to do that thing.
"With respect to the gentleman who exhibited knowledge as to my earnings, and with peculiar appropriateness I mention him last, my earnings previous to 1914 were larger than they are now. If I chose to go out into the world my earnings would be larger than they are in the position I now All, and which I refused four times before accepting it on the fifth. While I am here I intend to do my duty and pay no more attention to any of these remarks.
"Those who wish to make any remarks like this in the future are making them of a man who has tied his own hands, and not of one whose hands are tied by either law or custom."
Well, if his hands are tied, he has shown the people of this country that his tongue, at all events, is not tied. He does not give out very much edifying information in this statement which he is alleged to have made in the city of Toronto a few days ago.
I picked up The Toronto Globe on Saturday morning and noticed in the middle of the third page a small paragraph of four lines which intimated that the Board of Commerce had passed a ruling of some kind which would be found in another column. I searched the paper carefully, page by page, but was unable to locate the ruling. I went over it again, but failed to locate the ruling, although I noticed a statement that the Board of Commerce had met and an account of what they had done, but there was no reference whatever to the order that had been issued at Hamilton, when Mr. O'Connor, according to newspaper reports,

threatened to fine and imprison any one who would dare to increase the price of farm produce during the next forty days. After going over the paper a couple of times, column by column, I found on the social page under a large half-inch type heading "What Women are Doing," in a column at the top of which was a prayer, Lord make it fit the article, but after reading it I was unable to understand what change the board had made, and that was the reason why I was anxious, if possible, to have an answer this afternoon to the question I was justly entitled to put to the leader of the Government. We now have the admission that the order has been rescinded.
Was that in answer to the prayer at the head of the column?

I presume it was; 'however, this is the condition of affairs. Now, I regret exceedingly that the press of this country has given as much prominence as it has to certain things that have been done or are alleged to have been done by these gentlemen-and not publish the fact that the injunction had been rescinded. I was rather amused to see in some of the papers a photograph of the two commissioners coming down the steps of a building-I think it was in Montreal-with large calabash pipes in their mouths and satchels in their hands, beneath the picture being the terse allegation: "Nothing to do." They had evidently straightened out all the trouble in connection with the cost of living; there was nothing else for them to do; and apparently they were two of the most contented men one could imagine.
An hon. MEMBER; They were in Montreal.

I believe that is where the picture was taken, but they were not in the district where the vice chairman, Mr. O'Connor's ruling applied. His ruling applied only to the provinpe of Ontario. Right across the river from here you find a different condition entirely. I believe that in the city of Ottawa milk is selling higher than it has been in almost any other part of Ontario. Why have the board singled out one particular province, and what is the real condition of affairs to-day? These are questions which I think this House should know or have some definite information on in regard to the operations of the board, and a statement should be made concerning what they intend to do. We desire to know something as to the effect of their ruling in connection with dairy produce in this country. Any one who
knows anything about agriculture realizes that at the end of the summer season, when the pastures are dried up, when the cold weather approaches and stock have to be stabled, feed is much more expensive than it is under other conditions, That is the situation now, and you will find in almost every section of Canada that there is an increase in prices at the beginning of October. Yet one of these commissioners threatens to tie up this industry which, as I have pointed out, amounts to about fifty millions of dollars in this province. They threaten to take this drastic step regardless of the effects it will have on production in Canada, which, is pre-eminently the panacea for our present, chaotic difficulties. It is not by ill-considered restrictions issued without due consideration as to its effect by a well paid Board of Commerce that you will reduce the cost of living, for such restrictions will only tend to put an end to production.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

When the House rose at six o'clock I was referring to the possibility of the object sought for when, the Board of Commerce was appointed being defeated by reason of the course that members of the Board are pursuing. I feel very strongly that, whatever be the -aim of the board, the course they have followed during the past week is likely to have that result. I think the opinion of the country was unanimously in favour of the purpose sought to be accomplished when the Bill creating the Board was passed. It was the desire of the people of Canada to see that profiteers, those who were charging undue prices, should not be permitted to continue to do so. That, I think, was clearly Parliament's object when the board was appointed. I made some reference before six o'clock to what the hoard have been doing during the past two weeks-particularly to the operations of the vice-chairman of the board, and the ruling which he is alleged to have recently made-and to the lack of information before this House as to what the board are really doing. I also referred to the fact that in order to overcome the difficulties with which we are faced, and in order to meet the obligations that have to be met by this country, it is important and absolutely essential that the production of Canadian exports should be very greatly increased rather than curtailed in any way. That, I think, is quite

evident to every one who has looked at this question seriously and who sincerely desires that we should be placed in the best possible position.
Now, the situation is one which makes it necessary to deal with personal matters, which is not a very pleasant thing to do namely, the salaries of the men who have been appointed to the board, this being the subject dealt with by the Bill now before the committee. I would not say the salaries in question were too large if we had the right men to conduct this work; but we have had what I believe to be absolutely convincing evidence that the members of the board have made a wrong start, that they are not following the lines that Parliament desired they should follow, and that they are not likely to accomplish the purpose contemplated when the statute in question was enacted. That being the case, Mr. Speaker, I want to refer more particularly to a ruling which is alleged to have been made by Mr. O'Connor either in Hamilton or Toronto. In order to do so, let me quote from what the newspapers have published on the subject, and up to now that is all the evidence in the matter that this House has before it. In the Toronto newspapers of September 17, I find the following:
Stop Upward Move.
This is not the time for an increase in prices. Prices should go down from now on. In this connection I wish to announce now that all vendors, from the farmer who increases prices on milk or anything else, will be guilty of an indictable offence punishable by a fine of $1,000 and two years' imprisonment."-W. F. O'Connor at Hamilton.
Mr. Speaker, these are very heavy penalties to impose on a'ny one who might think he was carrying on a legitimate business and endeavouring to do so at a very reasonable profit and it might be at a loss. An order, or injunction, is issued and a threat implieed that if the parties concerned do not comply with it the penalties mentioned will be enforced. Now, I would like to know from the minister who is leading the House whether this board has the power to impose any such penalties or not? I think it would be in the interest of all concerned to know whether we have placed such absolute powers in the hands of the board. If it is true, then instead of passing the present Bill I think we should certainly see that the measure does not proceed any further.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The power of the board is not for the imposing of punishment on their own authority. When they make an inquiry and find that a person in their judgment has been guilty of unduly en-
|}Mr. Sutherland.]
hancing prices, or has committed the offences set out in the Act, it will then become their duty to make a finding. A report of that finding would be submitted to the Attorney General of the province and a proceeding' might be instituted, but the punishment would finally be imposed by a court.

What about the
penalty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: At the moment I have not got the Criminal Code before me and the precise penalty to which a man may be liable for an offence committed under the Act I am not prepared to state; but it does not belong to the board to impose a penalty for an offence of that kind. The result of their report, following any inquiry, would be that, the matter being so referred, a prosecution might be instituted, and the court before whom the trial would take place would fix the penalty to be imposed for such an offence. Perhaps I might suggest that if it is a matter of giving information-and I am most anxious to give that information as far as it lies in my power- we could deal with that feature of the subject more conveniently in Committee than would be the case at present by interrupting the hon. member's speech.

I can hardly understand a responsible commissioner making a statement of that kind, and I hope that is one of the statements that Mr. O'Connor will deny having uttered. I notice in the papers to-day that the board has also decided to fix the price of pork and pork products at the level at which they stood a year ago. It will be remembered that about a year and a half ago Mr. O'Connor, who was then on the Cost of Living Commission, made a statement with regard to the profits that certain packing houses were making, and as to how they should be regulated. Well, as a result of the ruling that has been made in Toronto with regard to the price of pork and pork products it will be found that it will not be the packers who will suffer, but that it will again be the producers.
Now, I would ask those hon. members who have an intimate knowledge of conditions throughout the rural districts during the past twenty-five years whether there has not been a continual movement from those districts to the urban centres? Is it not a fact that the greatest difficulty we have to contend with as the years pass is how to prevent the young people and the middle-aged leaving the farms and going

into the towns and cities? If you go through the old-settled districts, Mr. Speaker, you will find empty houses everywhere. During the debate on the advisability of the Government doing something to solve the housing problem, I often thought that we have in the rural districts ample housing accommodation to take care of a great many more people than are in those districts to-day. I believe that the rulings the Board of Commerce are now making will have a tendency to further aggravate that situation. As I mentioned this afternoon, I believe in competition, and I further believe that where you eliminate competition and fix prices, you are doing something that is not in the public interest, something that is bound to defeat the very object you have in view. If you once start out to fix the prices of certain commodities it will become absolutely necessary to fix prices all along the line. That is the difficulty I see with regard to fixing an eight-hour day and a minimum wage scale, for once you do that you have to carry that out in every branch of industry, and it can not be done in agriculture.
Now, what has been the result with regard to the very industry that this Board of Commerce ruled on in Toronto but a few weeks ago?-I refer to the dairy industry. During the war it is well known that as a result of the difficulty in securing shipping facilities the price of our cheese was fixed by the British Food Control Board, and practically exists to-day. The result of that price-fixing is that in the old districts where cheese factories have been established for fifty or sixty years they are closing up one after another. In order to bring that home a little more forcibly I want to refer to a statement which I noticed in the local press of Oxford a few days ago. A "statement, made by a well known cheese buyer in the city of Woodstock, who a few years ago came there from one of the adjoining counties, was as follows :
The cheese industry will soon toe a thing of the past in the province of Ontario. In the vicinity of Woodstock alone during the past few years thirty cheese factories have been closed up, and in the district from which I come-

which, I believe, was St. Thomas, in
the county of Elgin

over one hundred cheese factories have been closed up during the past few years.
That is one of the things we have to face largely as a result of the fixing of prices and the low price of cheese. The price of
cheese is not keeping pace with the price of other dairy products. The same remark applies to butter. In fact, the majority of dairymen in the county from which I come buy their butter; they do not make it for the simple reason that they are selling their milk to better advantage.
It is now proposed to step in and to close up some of the channels or avenues of trade that have been developed and are proving profitable. You would be surprised to know, Sir, the millions of dollars that are being invested in this country by what is known as the. American Milk Produce Company. Large condenseries are being established here by the parent firms in the United States with branches scattered all over the country. Some of the British firms aTe also establishing factories in this country. As a matter of fact, this is one of the most profitable branches of dairying that we have to-day. And that is the reason why I was so anxious that we should have some announcement from the Government as to whether the order passed by the Board of Commerce on the 16th instant was to apply to all dairy products, because prices are fixed at about the 25th of the month to apply on the following month. I am not very clear even yet as to the effect of that ruling, and I think that is one of the un* satisfactory features of having ,a commission doing the things that ought to be done by Parliament itself. I am absolutely opposed to delegating to irresponsible commissioners the duties that ought to be performed by the people's representatives and by the Government. To me it does not seem to be in keeping with responsible Government because in the final analysis I will be held responsible by the people who sent me here for the absolutely irresponsible acts of these men whose salaries we are asked to provide in this Bill.
A sensible speech.

I want to say further, Mr. Speaker, that I have evidence that another branch of this industry, the butter branch, is being adversely affected by the Board of Commerce. It is not very long ago that we permitted oleomargarine to be imported and to be manufactured in this country and to incorporate butter into it to deceive people so that it would give the grease or tallow that the packers were manufacturing into oleomargarine the flavour of butter. As a result of that action, I believe, we have done much to destroy a branch of the dairying industry; and now we propose to' permit a board such as I have

referred to to destroy another branch. Evidence was given by the packing interests before the Cost of Living Committee appointed at the last session of this House, land the general manager of one of the packing companies-I believe it was the Davies Company, but I am not sure as to that-stated when questioned as to ithe quantity of butter they held in cold storage, "Why, we buy up all the June butter that we possibly can." "Why June butter?" he was asked, "Because it is so highly coloured that it will colour oleomargarine and make it look and taste like butter," he replied. That is what the packers are doing. By Act of Parliament we provided that they must not put any colouring into their margarine, and in order to get over that difficulty they buy highly coloured butter and incorporate it with tallow, thereby accomplishing their purpose and defeating the very object we had in view when framing the law, that of preventing colouring being added.
I referred to the fact that the population in the rural districts was gradually being reduced and I want to make some further reference to that, because I regard this as a very serious matter. You may say that the farmers are reaping undue profits at the present time; I say that there never was a greater feeling of unrest in the rural dictricts of Canada than there is to-day. Why is that the case? Not because they are not getting pretty fair remuneration for their labours but by reason of the fact that they have to do more work than should be necessary on the part of any one, for labour is not to be had. By working long hours, early in the morning and late at night, they have been able to carry on, but they have in many instances come to the conclusion that the game is not worth the candle. They have got tired of it. We have passed, or permitted to go into effect, what is known as Daylight Saving which has further aggravated the situation. Agriculture to-day requires not only industry but the application of scientific principles. You who have made a study of what the successful agriculturists of this country are doing will Teadily appreciate that. There are many who, knowing little or nothing about what the farmers are doing or what they have to contend with, think it is merely a matter of sowing the seed in the spring, taking off the harvest in the fall and then sitting around all winter and waiting until springtime comes round again. That is not the case. I believe a prosperous, contented and happy people is the nation's greatest asset, for if there is

one lesson taught by history it is that the permanent greatness of any country must ultimately depend more upon the character
of its country population than upon anything else; no growth of cities, no growth of wealth, can make up for a loss in either the number or the character of the farming population. It wrnuld be a calamity to have our farms occupied by a lower class of people than the hard-working, self-respecting, independent and manly men and women who first settled in this country.
The words I have just spoken are not wholly my own; they are quoted from recollection from a speech of the late Theodore Roosevelt. He was speaking of the United States, but his words, unfortunately, apply equally to Canada, and not to Canad-a only but practically to every country in the world. We ought to be very careful indeed to see that we do not do anything, or permit any commission which has been appointed by this House to do anything that will further aggravate the situation. If you look . over this country with its vast extent of nearly four thousand miles from ocean to ocean and realize its enormous agricultural resources, and possibilities you can come to no other conclusion than that the very foundation upon which we must build for the future and to meet our obligations is the agricultural industry. Yet you permit this industry to be attacked by this commission at the very outset. Why did they not go after those people who, it is claimed, have been profiteers? Mr. O'Connor alluded to the packing industries of this country. Why does be not get after them if they are the profiteers he alleges they are in place of going after the producers?
Mr. CAHILL; Because the Government will not let him.

I think the hon. gentleman will -agree with me that the Government have not very -much control o-ver them, -and that is the reason why I want this House to be very careful indeed before they pass this Bill to fix the salaries of men, one of whom at least it is apparent is unfit to carry on the duties that we have entrusted to him. I do not -blarhe the Government altogether in this -matter. There was a clamour throughout the length and breadth of the country that Mr. O'Oonnor had been removed from office by the Government as the result of certain things which he sai-d about Sir Joseph Flavelle a.n-d the Davies Packing Company. That feeling was quite evident. It was general throughout the county from which I come,

and I have no doubt that hon. gentlemen have been bombarded from all quarters to have this man O'Connor reinstated. I want to put on record a letter I received from the County Council of Oxford under date of April 24, 1918:
The following is a copy of a resolution passed by the County Council at a special session held on the 22nd day of April, 191S :
Moved by Councillor Lilllco, seconded by Councillor Denton, and resolved:-"That this Council desire to express their regret that Mr. O'Connor, Cost of Living Commissioner, should have resigned and that his resignation should have been accepted.
" Mr. W. F. O'Connor has shown himself an independent and fearless official, and we are of the opinion that when found, such a man should he retained in the service of the country: and that a copy of this resolution be forwarded to the representatives of the county in the Federal House."
Carried unanimously by a standing vote.
Certified,
N. E. Birtch, County Clerk.
I am not going to say to the House what the opinion of some of these people is in regard to Mr. O'Connor to-day. He has trod on their toes a little sooner, evidently, than they had expected. If there are profiteers to be found among the farmers or any other class in this country I hope they will he shown up and punished. As soon as the chairman of the commission arrives here and consults with his colleague there is a stay of proceedings and the ruling or injunction assured by Mr. O'Connor is not put into effect. It appears that the order has been rescinded and that a very substantial increase in the price of milk has already taken place. The price cf milk in some of the cities-in Toronto at least- for an eight-gallon can, containing 80 pounds was $2.55. Since the new ruling has been made, 1 understand, the price has been increased to $3.10 per eight-gallon can, or $3.87J per hundred. There is absolute proof that this man, O'Connor, issued the first order without giving any consideration as to the merits of the case and without evidence. The fact that a substantial increase has taken place condemns the attitude, actions and threats of that commissioner. In the face of that condemnation by the chairman, as well as by himself, are you going to say that he is worth $8,000 a year to this country? If that conduct is pursued it is going to cost this country hundreds of millions of dollars instead of being a benefit to the country. There is no getting away from that.
I thought at the time, and I still think, tha* we have, or ought to have, in the various departments of the Government
the machinery to put into effect all that we are expecting this board to do, and we could then hold the departments or the Government responsible for what they were do'ng. I still think that would be much better than the course which we are pursuing.
I do not wish to take up any more of the time of the House with regard to this matter* but I want to place myself on record as being absolutely opposed to paying the salary of a man, or the salaries of men who, I am satisfied, will, as a result of their unfitness for the position of carrying on the work which we intended they should do, cost this country millions of dollars.
Before the hon. member takes his seat, I should like to ask him a question. If his speech is to any purpose, I think he should move an amendment, to give this measure the six months' hoist.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The hon. member has submitted no question whatever.
Mr. SAMUEL F. GLASS (Middlesex East): Mr. Speaker, I am sure the House and the country will feel indebted to the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) for having presented this matter in the form he has to the House. The Bill before the House has to do with a proposed increase in the allowance or salary which shall be paid to each of the members of the commission who in their proper sphere have very important functions to perform. We would naturally think that the first important requirement would be for the men who were appointed to that commission to have given some demonstration of their efficiency for their important duties. It may not be fair for me generally to criticise the fitness of the members of this commission, and I do not intend to imply that I am criticising their fitness, because 1 believe, from what I have heard of the gentlemen who occupy positions on that commission, that they are men of ability. As the hon. member for South Oxford has pointed out, from all parts of this country came the call to this Government to recognize the outstanding fitness of Mr. O'Connor for just such an appointment. But it might have been well had that commission had on it some outstanding figure representative of the great agricultural productive interest of this country, so that he might have been a stay and a guide to them in considering the important matter of production.
This is not a new thing in this country. There is an ample reason for the condition



in which we find ourselves to-day, and the same condition exists in all parts of the world. If there be one thing that is more important than another, and the importance of which is realized by other countries, it is that if we are to get down to lower levels, that can be accomplished ultimately only by a greater production from the resources of the soil. The hon. member for South Oxford has referred to the importance and the stability of rural life, to the splendid men who have been raised on the farms of this country. He has well and rightly said so. The quotation he gave from remarks of the late President Theodore Roosevelt, was appropriately duplicated by Mr. Lloyd George in July last when, meeting a deputation of the Agricultural Committee of the House of Commons, he said:
I do not think there is an industry in mis land which is as important to its life, to its health, to its strength. It is the place to grow men. The mines of South Weirs would have been derelict, they would have had to be worked by black labour, if it had not been for the big, brawny men brought up in the agricultural districts of Wales and Somerset and the Western Counties. This nation has been living on its capital in more way than was imagined, It has been living on its capital in strength. These people brought from the agricultural districts are its capital in vitality; and that has been eaten up by the industrial life the country without anything being put into the bank again. On the contrary, it has been drained and drained and drained; and unless we put our backs into this I think the prospect will be a serious one, and it will show we are not a nation which can understand a lesson when it is taught us, when it is written by the finger of Providence clearly for us, even in the blood of our own children.
Proceeding, Mr. Lloyd George made this important statement:
Therefore I think it is important that we should, during the next year or two, immediately put our minds on the best methods of developing the agricultural resources of this country, and bringing the population hack. I can see in France what a difference it makes now; it gives them a sense of security. When you talk about Bolshevism, M. Clemenceau says, you must remember half our population is on the land. You cannot make a Bolshevist on the soil; it is not the place to make him, especially if you give him some sort of an interest in it. Therefore I think it is right, and as far as I am concerned I need no convincing about the overwhelming importance of this problem, but it has got to be done thoroughly; and I am very sanguine, from my experience of those who are on the land, that they are going to look at It from a patriotic point of view.
We know that what Mr. Lloyd George said on that occasion is equally true in this country of ours, namely, that the farms have been drained, not only through the war, hut through decades past. The very

best of our life-blood has been drawn into the cities to engage in industrial pursuits of various kinds, and we are not giving back to the soil, to the farm, any of that brawn and sinew which have been the strength of our agriculture in years past. This country must face that situation. We cannot get on; we cannot meet the enormous responsibilities of this nation nor solve the problem of the enormous debt we have to face unless some unusual effort is put forth to stimulate production on the farm-. How are we going to do that? It seems to be one of those problems that, even during the war, it was impossible to solve. During the war we induced our industrial community, our town life and our city life, to get out on to the soil; we interested the women, and they responded nobly in their efforts to assist in production in this country; but just as sure as the night follows the day, unless we can solve this problem of greater production, we are not going to solve the problem of cheaper living. And we are not going to do this by commissions such as we have if they commence by striking right at the very, base of production. If a commission were appointed, or if sober men were to set themselves to a consideration of the important problem of how best to stimulate production, how best to carry on that propaganda which was so effective during the long years of the war, the result might be a much earlier reduction in the prices of the necessities of life. There are functions for this commission to perform in connection with that.
I am of opinion that one of the greatest difficulties, and one of the greatest causes of unrest and increased cost, is the inordinate greed of the distributor. There are, of course, different kinds of middlemen. There is the middleman who, at an opportune time, when production seems to be short and when the prospect of prices ascending seems certain, corners supplies of food stuffs and holds them in cold storage to await the higher values that are bound to come. These are illegitimate middlemen who should not be allowed to exist, and wherever in this country there are cold storage plants holding large supplies of food for higher prices, there is a root of evil at which this board can well strike and eradicate altogether. The man who is engaged in -trade as his regular calling in life is in a different position, but nevertheless it is just as necessary that he should be carefully watched and not be allowed to extort exorbitant prices from the people of this country.

The price of milk has been under discussion this evening, and the case has been well put before the House by my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland). I am glad that at last he had the opportunity of putting this matter squarely before the House, because I have observed that during the past few weeks he has been consistently thwarted in his efforts to get some information on this important subject. A high price for milk is not peculiar to this country; it is the same all over the United States and Great Britain. I have in my hand a copy of The London Times of September 12 last, and these are the words of Mr. G. H. Roberts, M.P., Food Controller:
Fears and apprehensions had been expressed by many persons as to the future price of milk. He had been advised that he must not allow milk to reach a certain figure, otherwise there would be universal discontent. On the other hand he was told that unless he largely exceeded that figure, no milk would be produced. For a month or two past he had been going through all sorts of reports from all standpoints, and he could say that the cost of producing milk was three times that before the war.
He had reluctantly, therefore, come to the conclusion that the price of milk this winter must be three times the pre-war cost.
That was to him a very alarming prospect, for it might place milk beyond the reach of large sections of the poorer people. Yet, if milk could not be produced and sold at a reasonable profit below a certain figure, then that figure had to be granted. He wished to emphasize that the prices issued by the Mini-try were maximum prices and they could be modified in many districts.
The report says further:
The Director of Milk Supplies has written a letter to Mr. Harry Binner, of the Industrial Reconstruction Council, in reference to a statement by Mr. Binner that there was no excuse for the high price of milk, if supplies were sufficient to permit of " strapping male adults " drinking large glasses of milk in the tea shops. He states:-
"Milk is an extremely valuable food, not only for children, but for adults, and at times when there is an adequate supply for everyone there can be no objection to adults consuming milk. Even at the present high prices, milk is a relatively cheap food."
In Great Britain they made an effort to conserve their cream by forbidding it to be used for any other purpose than that of making butter. The fixing of milk prices in Great Britain brought out its production cost, and the Commission that was appointed to investigate the matteT came to the conclusion that the cost of producing a gallon of milk in the summer time was Is. 4jd., that is, 33 cents. I cannot conceive on what grounds we could assume that the cost of producing milk in this country is
less than in Great Britain, where they have splendid pastures and the cows give heavy milking. The foodstuffs for cattle there do not cost any more, I presume, than here, and therefore in view of the ascertained cost of producing milk in Great Britain can any one say that the price of milk in this country has been inordinately high? Let me point out-I am speaking more particularly of the western part of Ontario- what has been the factor that has regulated the price of milk there during recent years. It 'has been the price that the condensing factories or the evaporated milk factories could afford to pay the farmer for his supply. If the condensing factory finds that it can raise the price of milk to $3.25 a hundred pounds, it must necessarily follow that if the farmer has to choose between selling his milk to the distributor in the city at $2.50 or $2.75 a hundred pounds, or to the condensing factory at $3.25, he is going to sell his milk to the condensing factory. And if you are going to put a board between that man and his market, what is going to happen? He is not going to produce for that lower price. He is going to shut off production at once. The effect of the board's action will be a largely decreased production of milk.
I find by the last issue of the London Times received here that they have fixed the price of milk in Great Britain for the coming winter. How did they do it? They did not set a fixed price for the whole winter, but graded the price according to the season and the varying possibility of production. They fixed the price to the consumer for a quart of milk as follows: October, lid., or 22 cents; November, December, January, February and March, Is., or 24 cents. With the return of spring in April and the possibility of pasturage, milk drops back to lid. No regulations are made covering the following months. The wholesale price per gallon from the producer is fixed at 2s. 2d. Our price here is fixed at 39 cents. Even after paying the exorbitant price to the profiteer-farmer, as they have called him, 39 cents is away under the price authorized to he paid to the producers in Great Britain. The wholesale price to the producer in Great Britain has been fixed as follows, per gallon: October, 2s. 2d., November 2s. 8d., December January and February, 3s. 3d.; March, 3s. 0d.; April, 2s. 2d. When we compare those prices with the prices here I do not think there is any reason why this board should endeavour to undermine at its very base the milk supply of this country.
It takes more than that.

If that be so, then I presume we make better cheese and the percentage of butter fat is greater in our milk. But, even assuming my hon. friend to be correct, it shows that the cost of production of cheese in Great Britain is around 40 cents a pound.

I am safe in saying, however, that it must cost considerably more than that because the price the Government pays the producer is 48 cents a pound. On the other hand, our farmers here are offered 25 cents a pound, and the purchasing of New Zealand and Australian cheese makes it possible to bring the average cost down so that the British Government can sell to the wholesaler at 31 cents ia pound.'
I think these facts clearly indicate the disadvantage of the farmer here as compared with producers in Great Britain. A oareful and scientific study has been made of the cost of production by men who know, and if it costs 40 cents to produce a pound of cheese in Great Britain I do not see how there can be excessive (profit in production in this country at 25 cents a pound. The farmers have said all along that these prices for dairy products do not give an adequate return and reasonable encouragement, and in addition to this unfavourable condition the farmer is confronted with the element of uncertainty in regard to his market. My hon. friend from South Oxford referred to the large reduction in the production of cheese. This is due to some extent to the uncertainty of the market, and also, in a measure, to the fact that the condensing factories can afford to pay a higher price for milk than the cheese maker can in order to sell cheese at the world's market prices. We have to meet this situation, and at this juncture I might refer to the comments made in the Farmers' Advocate of Saturday last. The Farmers' Advocate has observed the movements of this commission, and it says-:	[DOT]
The logical place to begin is at the beginning, and trace an article through the various channels of production and distribution to its ultimate destination, the consumer.
No one will deny the truth of this statement.
Already the agitation amongst consumers has given rise to a whole series of investigations by governmental agencies. Great Britain, the United States and Canada are each making strong efforts to reduce the costs of food-stuffs, and the effects are already noticeable. The man who noticed them first, however, is the farmer; just as he is the last to gain by any increases in values. When hogs took a sudden drop in the United States market, due to a combination of consumer, government and packer, it was some time before a reduction of price was noticeable in retail stores.
History repeats itself -and right in this country we are experiencing that condition at the present time.
Nevertheless, the price has stayed down for the farmer in spite of the same exceptionally

high cost of production. This phenomenon is being repeated in Canada, where, due to a combination of circumstances to which United States and Great Britain have contributed, prices of hogs have suddenly and seriously declined. Here is where the Board of Commerce, which has such full powers, might do some permanent good in the interests of the consumer and producer alike. Last year, with bran and shorts around $40 to $45 a ton, oil-cake in the neighbourhood of $70, and prepared hog feeds in the vicinity of $60 per ton there was not enough difference between market prices for live hogs and the cost of production to encourage farmers to increase their output. Bran and shorts, since then, have risen to about the $60 plane, oil-cake is in the neighbourhood of $85 when it can be obtained, oats are worth between $2.80, and $3 per hundred, depending upon whether they are new or old, and prepared hog feeds have been climbing up towards $70 per ton	
A more complete analysis of the situation reveals several important facts. A combination of these feeds, such as have just been mentioned, will range around 3$e. per pound, and it requires about five pounds of grain to make a pound of gain. It will, therefore, cost in the neighbourhood of 16c. per pound for feed alone to produce hogs ; but it has been demonstrated at the Central Experimental Farm, that the feed cost is only 67 per cent of the total cost of production, so that on the basis of these figures, hogs should sell for $20 and over.
The farmer says that at present prices there is no encouragement to increase production of hogs, and I think that this view is only in accordance with the truth and the facts as they have been clearly demonstrated. In view of the present high prices of food stuffs he will not be justified, with the falling price of hogs, in increasing his production. The markets of Great Britain are glutted with bacon, some of which is spoiling on the wharfs and in cold storages by reason of difficulties in transportation and so sorth. At present there is a cessation of importation from this country, and as a result the farmer who has produced hogs on high-priced food stuffs now finds himself bound to sell in a depressed market. If we are to have a satisfactory and stable production we must have a steady fixed prices. Great Britain is fixing the prices of wheat for next year, and it has also fixed the prices for many other commodities. No country has more fully realized the need of increased production to the limit of possibility than Great Britain has done during these serious years of war, and she is not relaxing her endeavours at present. By various means she is' encouraging production for next year, and has appointed a commission with a view to ascertaining how best agriculture may be stimulated. During the wa*r the Department of Agriculture in this country issued to the farmers a pamphlet which was brimful
of patriotism. It presented the situation that prevailed throughout the world and eloquently pictured the urgent need there was for a miximum of production. Even in our towns and cities, by means of back gardens and otherwise, an effort was made by local committees with the result that there was an enormous production. What happened last year? As soon as the Armistice was signed the farmer, unable to gauge world conditions as was possible in countries where a minimum price was guaran-ted by the Government, had no encouragement and necessarily became pessimistic. He was afraid there would be a reaction in prices which might drop to such a level that he could not produce at a profit.
Sir, I say now, as I said a few nights ago, I think it was incumbent on the Government at a time like that to give leadership. The Department of Agriculture of this country were pretty well aware of what the conditions were, and if that same effort to stimulate production had gone on amongst the people in the rural parts last year we would now have had a much larger production than has been the ease. I point this out, although not so much in criticism of what was done last year, in view of the opinion of the world's statesmen, such as Lloyd George and other men who thoroughly understand the situation, that the duty incumbent upon the Federal Department of Agriculture, and of the Department of Agriculture of every province in Canada for the next year is to get at the very root of the matter and see by what means and by what efforts they can best stimulate the greatest production of foodstuffs in the coming year. Talk as they may, and appoint commissions as they may to regulate matters, the law of supply and demand is going to count in the matter of the prices of food. And, Sir, all the commissions this Government can employ or can appoint will not, by any system of reasoning or argument, or by any orders which they may promulgate, encourage the farmer to greater production by limiting his prices. As I have said before, the farmers of Canada at their meetings throughout the country have declared: " Leave us alone. We are willing to take our chances on the world's market." Great Britain does not take that attitude, but that is because Great Britain needs a big production at home in order to conserve her tonnage. The more foodstuffs she can produce there the less she has to import and the less shipping she has to provide. But our farmers say:	"Leave us alone.
We will take the world's prices, we will take our chances. Do not hamper us and throw

bring their little production of an acre or two acres of flax to the scutching mill, and Mr. Larose would scutch it for them and deliver the fibre. They took the fibre back to their homes and there with their old loom and hand spinning-wheel made it into linen. I am told that the farmers down there spin a very nice quality of linen which is used for cloaks for the clergy and for other purposes. Now, Sir, this man in connection with scutching-and this is the part. I wish to emphasize to show how much native wealth is lying idle-had accumulated four tons of what we call tow, that is the waste when they are getting the shell from the straw and extracting the fibre. In years gone by it was used mostly for upholstering furniture. This man had not been able to find a market for it, but the flax expert of the experimental farm, Mr. Hutchinson, who happened to be down that way and had seen the quality of flax, asked why he did not market all this good tow. The man replied, "I do not know where to sell it." Mr. Hutchison said to him, "Give me a sample and I will find you a market for it." He took a sample, and in a week got an offer of 28 cents a pound, $560 a ton, or $2,240 for the four tons of waste lying in the man's barn, its value not appreciated. Of course, at present high prices the value of that tow would be very much greater. My friends in the province of Quebec grow as good flax as anywhere in the world. Why don't they get going down there, why don't they get up steam and show us what they can do in the way of greater flax production? I hope to be able to aid in such a way that we may give them that protection which they are so fond of and encourage them to develop this industry. I am told that already in the province of Quebec there are three thousand acres under contract for the production of flax next year.
What about the price ol milk?
Well, I got away from milk.
Oh, oh.

I am rather inclined to agree though with every word of my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland). 1 am of opinion that the present prices of milk are not inordinately high. I cannot say whether those prices give a decent profit to the farmer, but I do say this, Sir, that it is an extraordinary thing, that notwithstanding the statemens that have been made on behalf of the farmers in the dairy
districts, unless they have cows of the highest producing capacity they are giving up their herds, and unless a cow produces more than 4,000 pounds of milk her owner cannot afford to keep her at the present prices of feed.
I do not take the position my hon. friend did and say that these commissioners are not worthy of their hire, or that the salaries we purpose to give them are inordinately high. They are men of outstanding capacity, Mr. O'Connor is a man of peculiar fitness as an accountant and for ferreting into facts and figures, and I believe he will prove a useful member of the commission. But I think, Sir, the discussion in this House may have, indeed, I believe it has already had, its effect in leading the commissioners to believe that they were working along unsound lines when they commenced to attack the producer. Therefore I hope that as a result of what has been said in this House, and with 'the little experience the commissioners have had, they will desist from taking any further action against the producer, and instead will try to solve correctly the problem of increasing production.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make one or two observations on this subject, and I promise not to take more than two or three minutes. It does seem to me that this discussion has wandered very far from the Bill before the House. I cannot help thanking that our good friends the member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) and the member for East Middlesex (Mr. Glass) have become unduly exercised and are labouring to make out a case in favour of the farmer. So far as I can see no blow has been struck at the farmer by this Board of Commerce. It is perfectly true that an order was talked about or passed by one of the members of the board, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) informed the House this afternoon that that order has been rescinded. As a matter of fact, that is the only evidence, if it be evidence, that can be brought against the board by those hon. gentlemen, who probably are making a laudable effort to stand pat with their farmer constituents. I represent a great many farmers in my constituency, but I would dislike do take the position that a fanner should not bear his burden as well as any other member of the community.
Now, let us glance at this matter for a minute. All our people were clamouring, practically unanimously, against the high cost of living and demanding that the Government should make some effort to control

prices or to limit profits, and even threatening that certain things might happen if it did not make such an effort. Yielding to public opinion the Government appointed this Board of Commerce. For myself-and 1 think my opinion was shared by the majority-I never thought that this board could control prices, I never thought it was desirable that it should make the attempt to control prices; but I believed it could be effective in limiting profits, and. I am satisfied that the great majority of the people also believed that the board could be effective in limiting profits, <and that it ought to be effective in doing so.
The next question was, who should constitute this Board? When the matter was before the House T took very strong ground against the appointment of too many lawyers. However, when the name of Judge Robson was suggested I said that he was exactly the man we should have.
Is he a lawyer?

I have known Judge Robson for a great many years. He rendered magnificient service to the Province of Manitoba as Public Utilities Commissioner. He is a man, in my judgment, whose heart bu^ns to serve the people, and when his name was proposed I did all I could to secure his appointment. While I am on that subject I may refer to his salary. Judge Robson, I understand, was drawing $15,000. a year when he agreed to accept this position. He gave up that great salary in order that he might be of real service to the people. So you can see he is the identical man for the office. With regard to Mr. O'Connor, I had my own reservations; I feared that he lacked the necessary discretion and ballast; but I believe that if the people had been polled as to who should occupy the position of Vice-Chairman on that Board, Mr. W. F. O'Connor would have received a great majority of the votes. I was pleased to hear my honourable friend the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) pay tribute to Mr. W. F. O'Connor the other night when he spoke of him as a worthy and efficient man. I happen to know that Mr. O'Connor made the statement that he was earning a larger amount of money annually than is provided for in this Bill. It is true that Mr. O'Connor was charged with making statements in Toronto as ViceChairman of the Board, and when they were published I believe the general opinion was that they were indiscreet. I happened to meet him about a week ago, and he absolutely denied that he had made the statements that were at-
tributed to him in the newspapers. But I do not think we are going to cavil as to whether he made them or did not make them. Let us admit that he might have been indiscreet in that one particular. But, he has come under the influence of Judge Robson, they are now sitting as a united board, and I will venture the guess that you will not find that W. F. O'Connor will be indiscreet in the future. I think he is a man who would like to be of service to the public, and, while I would not probably have appointed him myself, I am hopeful that he will make a satisfactory member of the board.
Let me take one instance. I notice that the board has made an order that, as I read it, the price of bacon be reduced on an average of from two to six cents a pound. Well, that at least is something. If you take the consumption of bacon in Canada and take an average reduction of three cents a pound, you will find that it will be a very considerable saving to the public. I did not hear our hon. friends from South Oxford and East Middlesex denounce this regulation in regard to the reduction on bacon because one would at least expect them to say that this interferes with the price to the farmer.
It does.

Our hon. friend (Mr. Smith), one of the dumb philosophers of the House, says that it does interfere with the price. I would rather think not, because bacon in the city from which I come was selling as high as 70 cents a pound, and if the farmer was only getting 17, 18 or 20 cents a pound for his pork, I should think those who made the profit were the manufacturers of bacon-the pork packers, f believe that the order of the board is not aimed at the producer of pork, but at the profiteer and the manufacturer. Anyway, somebody's ox is sure to be gored, and no [DOT] matter what this Board of Commerce may do, it is sure to be criticised. There is a quotation that I frequently make, and it seems to apply in this case.
You'll be damned if you do,
You'll be damned if you don't.
But we have a board, 1 believe, that will prove eminently satisfactory to the people of Canada. I think they ought to be given a chance. I do not think that every time they make an order, be it small or great, the members of the Parliament of Canada should rise up and denounce them. How are you going to get service from anybody

if you are going to keep on harping upon their acts, criticising, and tearing them down? Surely the people's representatives should stand by something! Let us be constructive, let us make some progress, let us support these men.
I believe that if you ask the people of Manitoba they will be a unit in saying that Judge Robson is the very highest type of man. He will give the very best service he can, and if you want a commission of the highest efficiency, he is the best man that could have been selected to conduct its work. Then, in Heaven's name, let us support him loyally. If this board does something absolutely wrong and inimical to the public interests, it will be time enough to criticise it. But this House has got into the habit of criticising and carping at everything that is done, and if we keep on we are going to rock the boat and it will go under. If there is one thing that is needed in Canada more than another at the present time it is to try and prevent rocking the boat. With our enormous commitments and responsibilities, if this policy is continued, ultimately the ship of State is bound to be wrecked. It is only, in my judgment, by the most careful steering, by pursuing the most judicious course, by husbanding our resources and by endeavouring to stand by what appeals to the best judgment of the people as being right and in the best interests of Canada, that we can succeed in saving the ship at all.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. W. JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the debate has wandered very far from the question before the House, which is the fixing of the salaries of the members of the Board of Commerce. That is the matter which should engage the attention of the House, and nothing further. I have very little sympathy with the Government which is responsible for bringing on this debate. There was no necessity to have brought this matter before the House. The Government was given power at the last session, when the Bill was before the House originally, to fix the salaries of the commissioners. The Governor in Council had the power to fix the salaries, and why we are now called upon to discuss this whole question again is something that passes my poor understanding.
I must deplore the criticism which has been levelled at the Board of Commerce by the members seated on your right, Mr. Speaker. With the exception of the lion.
member who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Richardson), and who condemned the board with faint praise, there was not a * single member on the Government side who had a good word to say about the Board of Commerce. I was not very much enamoured of this board when the question was first mooted in the House but I was willing that it should be given a chance. To-day we have a number of gentlemen representing the farming community who, finding that possibly the actions of the board may interfere with there profits, are furiously attacking the personnel or membership of the board. I think it is highly improper on the part of members in the House to criticize the composition of the boiard in -the way that they have done. This is not the proper place to discuss milk prices and agricultural economics. The proper place to do it is before the Board of Commerce, before Mr. O'Connor and Mr. Justice Robson. But here we are discussing before this House a matter ex-parte with no one on the other side to say a word in defence of the board. I have no sympathy at. all with the Government who find themselves in the position of having a quarrel in their own family, inasmuch as it was not necessary for them to bring this matter before the House at all.
I would like to say a word or two in regard to a matter which was brought before the House by one of the members when discussing the effect of the rulings of the board upon agriculture. I would like to relieve his mind, if I can, as to any fears which he may have that the rulings of the board are'going to affect his particular business. If he will refer to "the Act itself, he will find t-halt the board has practically no power at all. The Government has surrounded the board with barbed wire entanglements and made it impossible for the board to do anything. The Government has seen to that. If hon. gentlemen will refer to section 41 of the Act, they will notice that:
The Governor in Council may, in his discretion, either upon petition of any Person interested, lodged within one month after the making: of the order, decision, rule or regulation, or within such further time as the board under special circumstances may allow, or of his own motion, at any time, and without any petition or application, vary or rescind any order, decision, rule or regulation of the board.
That is to say, the Government itelf may, without any complaint whatsoever, rescind any order of the board. The board really has no power at all. Its claws were drawn before it was brought into existence.

Furthermore, we find that when any order is made by the board, nothing can be done by that board beyond making the order, they are impotent. The board send the 0'i'der to the Attorney General of the province in which the alleged offence was committed, and it is for the Attorney General to pigeonhole it or not just as he thinks fit, but the matter at once falls into the jurisdiction of the Attorney General of the province. Therefore, hon. gentlemen have no reason to be frightened; nothing is to be done to their business; they can charge any price they like for their milk, cheese, butter, beef or any other commodity, so that all this talk is really to no purpose at all. And, when I listened to one hon. gentlemen after another taking up the time of the House, I was rather inclined to agree with the resolution introduced here last night by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Levi Thomson) who stated that most of the speakers in this House developed into public nuisances. I do not wish to attach any such expression to the hon. gentlemen who have spoken to-day; I do not think they ore public nuisances. For instance, I was rather interested in the remarks which1 fell from the lips of the hon. member for East Middlesex (Mr. Glass) who regaled us with an interesting speech upon the price of milk in Great Britain and the price of flax in Quebec. I find that every time I come into this House I learn something from hon. gentlemen who talk with so much intelligence upon every subject- that comes before us.
The hon. member for. Springfield (Mr. Richardson) paid a very high tribute to Mr. Justice Robson, with -which tribute I wish to 'associate myself. I am very glad that Mr. Justice Robson's ability has been brought before the House in such a striking manner, and I am sure the Government ought to be congratulated on the appointment of Mr. Justice Robson to this high and important position. Everything the hon. member said about him I can heartily endorse. I was, however, rather sorry to think that the hon. member should have stopped there. He said that there ought to have been no criticism of the board; that they should have been given a -chance; that their efficiency is going to be affected throughout the country if we criticise them in the way in which we have done. Then in the same breadth he told us that he did not know anything about Mr. W. F. OfCb-n-nor, but he rather thought he was an indiscreet gentleman, but under the influence of Mr. Justice Robson, for I do not

know how long, he might -perhaps develop into a useful official. Then we were told that the board talks too much. I wonder what the opinion of the board is with regard to members of Parliament, whether they reciprocate that view or not.
We have already appointed to this board three gentlemen, one of whom is merely a locum tenens. When the Bill, creating the board was introduced into this House at the last session, I raised the question that it was highly necessary and proper that a French-speaking man should be appointed -as a third member of this Bo-ard of Commerce, -and I s-till make th-at pretension. I took the view that in this country, where more than twenty-five per cent of our people are French-speaking, who do not understand the English language as they do their own language, it is essen-ti-al that the third member of the board should be a Frenchspeaking man. It may be, of course, that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the Government feel that the whole province of Quebec is so free from profiteering and from excessive charges in matter of products that there is no necessity at all for having any sittings in that province; but perhaps there is -another view, -and I think it would be a s-afe thing -at all events, to appoint some person from Quebec who would be conversant with the Frencli tongue and at the same time would render useful service to the board by his ability to speak the English language.
What makes me believe that the Board of Commerce is at present rendering useful work to the community and to the country is the fact that we have such a chorus of disapproval in this House from members representing the farming community. You know,' Sir, the old saying that when you throw a brick down a dark lane at night and you hear a howl, you know you have struck something. That is the view which I think the community generally will take. I think the board is doing excellent work in investigating everything, not only the farming community, but the pork-packers and others. Every interest ought to be investigated by this board, and I trust they will be. The farming community who are not yet affected by any order of the board should wait before they lay their complaints before the House. One gentleman went so far as to say that he felt that the-	*
Mr. MoCREA:	Would you investigate
the lawyers?

I do not think the lawyers require investigating. I think it will he

found in the case of most lawyers that, when they come to give up the ghost either their estates are insolvent or their relatives accept the estates under the benefit of inventory. That is the best proof that they are not profiteers. In any event, I think the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. MoCrea) would prevent them from . becoming profiteers, even if they wanted to be, at his expense.
One hon. member-I do not remember from what constituency he hails-said that this discussion ought to do good, as it would teach the men who are on the board just what their duties should be and should not be. I cannot take that view at all. It seems to me that those men who are appointed to. the board should proceed with their work in no manner affected by any views to which expression may be given in this House. We know that, in our courts of justice, any attempt made to affect the views of a court or a judge is treated as contempt of court, and punished accordingly, and we in this House have no more right in that respect as members of Parliament than we would have as private members of the community going about our daily avocations.
I ran across Mr. O'Connor on Sparks street to-day, and he assured me that, as a result of the operations of the board, they have already caused a reduction in the price of beef of ten or twelve cents per pound. I have not yet felt the effect of that myself, but I hope I shall in due time. He also told me about the price of pork, but for obvious reasons I was not interested. So far as I am concerned, I only hope the price of that article is put up to a prohibitive degree in order that the members of the community may not be permitted to eat of the unclean animal.
I trust that we shall hear nothing further about the conduct and action of this Board of Commerce. Let them continue on their way. Let us see what they ai'e able to do, and if, at the next session, we find that we have made a mistake in creating this board the same body.-the Parliament of Canada- that brought this court unto existence can give it its coup de grace. But I bespeak for it the support, not only of the members of this House, but of the whole of the country, and let us see if something cannot be .done towards reducing the cost of living, a consummation devoutly to be wished by every one of us.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think any ihon. member can class me as one of those who take up the time of the House
with long speeches, and I invite them to look over the pages of Hansard for the last ten or twelve years and see how the record bears out my statement. I w.as very much interested in the remarks of the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), who was loud in his condemnation of the hon. members for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) and East Middlesex (Mr. Glass), who, as he put it, were voicing the sentiments of their constituents and of the farmers of this great country.
I ask the House to think of the remarks of the hon. member (Mr. Jacobs) and ask themselves if he was not voicing the sentiments of his own constitutuents as loudly as any other hon. member did this afternoon.
Only on the pork question.

His whole speech was a condemnation of the farmer and the price of foods stuffs. Why, in every paper you picked up during the last few months you saw the price of eggs and of butter and of bacon complained of, and the Government was bombarded to appoint a commission to bring down the high cost of living. The high cost of what? Boots and shoes and clothing? No, of butter and eggs and food stuffs generally. If we are to judge by the reports that have appeared in the papers the last day or so, this is no Board of Commerce at all, but a board to control the price of food. I have nothing to say against the personnel of the Board, but I do say that the great agricultural interests of his country should be represented on the Board by at least one member.
