Prom forty to fifty per cent of the people of this country live on the farm, and are producing the stuff that is going to pay the war debt of this country if ever it is paid, and yet a board is appointed to look after the interests of the. consumer, and the forty to fifty per cent of the people of this country who are producing and upon whom the consumer is dependent for his very life, have no representative on the Board. That is what I protest against. I also'protest against the members from the great cities and urban centres crying down the farmer and saying that he is the man who should be throttled. I .say to those hon. members that this is a broad and vast country, nearly four thousand miles across, with millions of acres of virgin soil. Go and tell your constituents who are shouting about the high cost of living, "Canada has millions of .acres of virgin soil. Go and produce for yourself the eggs, the butter the cheese

and the milk that you need". If they did that, there would be no cause for complaint about the high cost of living. But hon. members from the city will not tell them that, and a hoard is appointed to fix the price of food. Why, to my mind, it is the most absurd thing under Heaven. I was amazed to hear my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson) say that lie did not know that fixing the price of bacon influenced the price of hogs. Has he read the market reports for the last few weeks?
Sure.

Then he must have seen that the price of live hogs has gone down from 5 to 7 cents a pound. Has he not seen the papers from the great city of Montreal announcing, sometimes under big headlines, what this board has accomplished?

The hon. member
would not say that the fall in the. price of hogs was due to regulating the profits of the manufacturer.

I would not say it was due to regulation, because I do not believe any bacon should sell at 70 cents a pound. I am not here to protect the profiteer, but I am here to protect the honest producer, in his interest and the interest of Canada. When I was home a week ago I had farmers ask me "What are the prospects for the prices of hogs next spring?" I said "Do not ask me. Ask some one with a greater knowledge of those things than I have." 1 have been a producer, of hogs for forty years, and I say that if you set the price at 15 cents live weight, you cannot make anything at it to-day with the present price of wheat and other cereals, and if that price is fixed, instead of having $40,000,000 or $50,000,000 of bacon to export you will have the same condition we had a few years ago with regard to butter and mutton and lamb, and the like,-we shall be bringing these things in from New Zealand, and eggs from China, and all the rest of it.	*

My hon. friend admits that 70 cents for bacon is an outlandish price. If the board set the price at 60 cents, does my hon. friend say that that would mean the price of hogs would be 15 cents? The board is not setting the price of pork at all. .
When you fix the price for the product of the hog you set the pTice for the whole hog.
Then you would justify 70 cents a pound for bacon?

No. I know that price has been often quoted. I might say that for a little piece of Windsor bacon $1.50 might not be out of the way. Let me explain. It is only a very small part of the hog that sells at 70 cents, but judging by the papers you would think every part is sold at that figure. You do not have to pay 70 cents a pound for the shank or many other parts. When you get a choice piece of 'bacon specially cured with all the bone taken out, the rind taken of, and cut in slices one-sixteenth of an inch in thickness, done up in a quarter-pound package and delivered at your house, do you think 70 cents a pound is too much for that? I repeat, it is only a small part of the back that sells for that figure, but the whole hog is held up to scorn on account of that price. Foodstuffs are not the only element in the high cost of living, and if this Board has been appointed especially for the purpose of bringing down the price of foodstuffs and is going to act along these lines alone, it will strike at the very foundations of the greatest industry of this country.
When I have gone up and down the country I have tried to point out to the people that the only thing for us to do is to produce more. Before the war Russia was producing about one-third of the world's wheat supply, running over 1,000,000,000 bushels every year. The world's consumption of wheat was a little over 3,000,000,000 bushels a year, and up to 1911 no country in the world had come near Russia's production. But in 1911 or 1912 Providence provided a bounteous harvest in the United 'States, and for the first time in her history she equalled Russia's production of wheat. Russia also produced 700,000,000 bushels of rye, over 52 per cent of the world's production. Eggs and butter from Siberia were pouring into Great Britain, and other parts of Europe. That supply has all been cut off. Belgium and France and other parts of Europe have been laid waste for five years by the most dastardly war the world has ever seen. A starving Europe looks to this Continent for bacon, butter, eggs and other foodstuffs. Only two years ago practically every school teacher, clergyman, and member of Parliament in this country was out on the side lines and back lanes begging people, even the boys at school, to own a pig and produce bacon. "Produce, produce, produce!" was the cry; "give us bacon to feed our armies." The farmers rose to the

occasion. Did we not export some $52,000,000 worth of bacon during one year of the war? And now the ho-n. member from Montreal, because he represents a city riding, is clamouring to have the screw put on and prices kept down.
In conclusion!, Mr. Speaker, I would give this advice to the members of the great city ridings of Canada: If your food is too dear and your people are clamouring, tell them that God has provided a great and bounteous land for them, with millions of acres between the Atlantic and the Pacific, on which they can make a living honestly and uprightly, and bring up their families under God's open heaven far better than they can in any slum in the city-land on which their children may grow up to be men and women eminently fit to bring Canada to the forefront and make her a nation whose name will be glorious throughout the world.

I am in favour of a commission of this kind for the purpose of regulating the cost of living which has been hearing heavily upon the people not only of Canada hut of Great Britain and the United States. The authorities have regulated the prices of foodstuffs in Britain with some success, and in the United State's an active campaign has been launched. Here also we are taking steps to reduce the cost of living, and I sincerely trust that our efforts will meet with -appreciable success. I agree with my friend from East Peterborough (Mr. Sexsmith) in the view that the -cost of food is not the only matter that needs to be regulated; it is necessary also to regulate the prices of manufactured goods, including clothing, boots, e'tc., and I hope the Commission) will pay due attention to this matter. In considering the high cost of living -we naturally ask ourselves the question: What is the justification of commissions such -as these and of investigations? Well, the justification lies in this, that publicity is given as to th-e conditions that exist -and facts- are brought Out on which reasonable action may he based. Let us take -the question of milk which we were discussing this -aftem-oon, and which is one of importance to the city of Toronto and to the farmers who live -in the townships I happen to represent. It has been revealed that the farmer -at best receives 7 cents -a quart -for his milk. Milk produced in the neighbourhood of Toronto is sold wholesale by the farmer to the milk dealer a-t 7 cents, (whereas the city dweller pays	14 cents for
it. In other words,	there is	an
astounding spread. All the investigations that have taken place in Europe, in the United -States and in Canada are bringing various facts to light, and the great economic fact is that the matter for gravest complaint in -Canada on the part of those who live in cities is the difference between the price paid the producer 'and that which the consumer is charged when the product finally reaches him. I do not think that we ought to pay 14 cents for our milk in the city if the farmer gets only 7 cents, and it is obvious that there is an economic difficulty of some kind that demands a remedy. This spread in -prices exists to a greater extent in connection with hog products. Hogs run from 20 cents to 25 cents a pound live weight, and bacon and ham and pork have gone from 40 cents to 60 cents a pound. Such a discrepancy in prices should not exist; there is a profiteer somewhere who ought to be curbed. I do not say it is the fanner, but it is in the interests of the public that all these facts should be established, and if there is anything wrong-and certainly there is, so far as the people in the cities are concerned-an effective remedy should be applied. I think, therefore, that a board of 'this kind is n-ecessary. While perhaps they may have made mistakes at first, they are bringing out facts and getting results; and the predominant fact witli which the people of this country and those of tile Unitted States are now acquainted, as a result of investigations into the cost of living, is that there is an injustifiable difference between the price which -the producer of the food receives and that which is paid by the consumer. As a result of investigations in the United States the farmer i-s not being hurt, but the profiteer is being haled before the bar of public justice and made to reduce h-is profits, with the result that prices are going lower. That is one phase of the operations which justify the board in the United States, and I believe that similar proceedings have been taken in Great Britain. We must find a way in Canada of dealing with this exorbitant spread between the producer's price and the consumer's. This matter is worthy of the attention of Parliament. It is worthy of the attention of a high court of some kind, and it should receive the support of the Government and of every member of this House. In doing what it has done Parliament has in a measure responded to a great public demand.
In regard to the personnel of the Commission I agree that the farming element ought to be represented. The farmers know a great deal about the production of the

necessities of life, and the board should include a representative of agriculture, as is the case in connection with the Board of Commerce in the United States. I should like to deal with some other questions to-night, but time does not permit. But the disclosures that have been made in the United States have justified the investigations that have taken place there. The public have obtained better treatment, and we must see that similar results are attained here.
The only other criticism I would pass upon the board, and it is a strong one from my point of view, is the fact, as the hon. member for Montreal said, that there is not a real enforcement of our law as in the United States. There they have a federal enforcement of a federal law. I have spoken already on this matter in the House, and I believe that the Government differ considerably from me in that respect. But if we have a strong commission and a proper enforcement of the regulations that are made, we shall have better results. As was said this afternoon, we want some one in the House who can be held responsible for the enforcement of these regulations. We ought to make the Government responsible for the enforcement of the law, and I have said before that the Attorney General ought to be the responsible official. He should be able to employ various assistants, attorneys and special agents to investigate the matter of prices, and should have at his disposal proper experts to advise him. Let there be accountants to ascertain whether there is or is not an unfair spread; and if there is unfair profiteering let us take adequate steps to eliminate both these elements. It will not be done in a day.
Have you any information as to the prices of hog products in the United States as compared with Canada?
There is a very substantial reduction of prices in the United States.
That is not the question. Are our prices higher than in the United States?	i
Yes.
I doubt it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Live pork is cheaper
in the United States to-day than in Canada.

Live pork?
[Mr. W. F. Maclean.l

Yes. The price of live pork is higher in Toronto than in any other place in America. It has been so for several years, and the price of meat products has been higher in Canada generally. The great fact that 'has been brought out by the investigations in the United States is that there is a substantial reduction in the cost of living, the benefit of which the people are feeling. There are two large classes in this country, those who work on the farms and those who work in the cities; and between them there is a third class who do not produce but sell to the consumer. These are the packers, and in the United States and Canada this class of the community is under public investigation. The general opinion is that their prices are altogether unfair, and the net result of this Commission will be, I trust, some relief to the public.
In the same way there are unfair charges on manufactured goods in this country by reason of combines and organizations of that kind, and these must be investigated; it is not quite fair to the farmer that his products should be the only products to be investigated. I have been charged with being a protectionist. Perhaps I am, perhaps I am not, but what I wish to say is that you cannot justify the exorbitant profits that have been made in connection with manufacturing industries in this country; you cannot justify the prices of clothing in some cases, or of boots, or of many other manufactured articles. Take the building trade and it will be found that the prices in Canada to-day are so high for builders' 'hardware that notwithstanding the duty, it pays to import these goods from the United States. Now a protective tariff is not justified in that case. We want investigation into all these matters; we do not want them set aside and the clamour of the people not attended to; we have got to have an investigation, we have got to bring out the facts and ascertain if there is any such spread in prices and any such profiteering as we believe there is in many lines. My objection to the Board of Commerce is that it has not enough members and they are not directing their energies in a sufficient number of directions, unless they go into the high cost of manufactured goods.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: During the days of the [DOT] Food Board was not the spread of prices regulated?

I do not know whether it was or not, perhaps the hon.

gentleman oan tell us, but the fact I am pointing out is that the people of Canada are up in arms against the high cost of living, and against this unjust spread in prices and this unjust profiteering; they are not against the farmers, but they want fair treatment in this matter. Let me point out what happened in the United States. President Wilson has just returned to Washington, more or less ill, after an effort that he made to explain to his fellow-countrymen the meaning of the League of Nations and the Treaty of Peace. Before he went out on that expedition he sent a friend of his to swing round the circle and advise him as to whether it was advisable or not for him to take this discussion to the people. But before he went out he was advised by his friend, and his friend, I think was a good judge, "Never mind the League of Nations; devote your energy to a reduction of the cost of living." The president has undertaken the two things, and he has put the whole resources of the United States Government behind an investigation into the high cost of living. And ho has got results. A good deal of money has been spent in connection with it. but there is a very powerful commission at work over there. The Government has strengthened that commission; they have put any number of attorneys, prosecuting lawyers and experts to work on the investigation, and, as I say, they are getting results. The question for the people in the United States is the high cost of living just as it is here; and we must have a commission that will bring out the facts, that will bring out the amount of this spread1-as it is called-between what the producer gets and what the consumer pays, and if it is unfair there has got to be Government, regulation in some respects, especially in war time, or in the times that follow war. There is one economic condition that exists at the present time and more or less interferes with the situation, and it is this: If the high cost of living is increased unnecessarily, there is an increasing demand for wages and as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Glass) quoted from an English authority, it is a case of just going round in a vicious circle; first, it is a case of raising wages, then it is a case of raising the cost of living -the cost keeps going up and no relief is afforded. Therefore, we must have these investigations. You are not going to improve the conditions of labour unless you reduce the cost of living, so that we have to reduce both the high cost of living and exorbitant profits.
Why not investigate the cost of high living?

I do not object to that. Let the cost of high living be investigated for there is a good deal of it in this country. If my hon. friend will start a movement in that direction, or if he will lay information against the high livers, perhaps Mr. O'Connor will take the matter up and some facts will be disclosed in regard to it. But the great fact is that we have got to deal with public opinion here. Public opinion is crying out against the high cost of living, and expects Parliament to do something. The Government are doing something, they have made a start. They have not gone as far as I would like to see them go, but inasmuch as they have made a start I have no object to the passage of this Bill. I would not only make the remuneration to the members of the board adequate, but I would make the board still more efficient by legislation that would strengthen their usefulness and achieved the desired results. What they should achieve, and what I think they will achieve later on, is a substantial reduction in the high cost of living.

It is true that I do not worry the House very much, but I have had a fairly long parliamentary experience and I have had time to think over two or three things since I was accused of being a " dumb philosopher. " One of the things that I thought of occurred during the session of 1918 when a certain honourable gentleman coming from the riding of Springfield (Mr. Richardson) made a speech and in half an hour apologized for doing so.
In connection with the present Bill it is possible that an extreme view may be taken. In some respects I might hold that it was unnecessary to appoint a Board of Commerce, but considering what we have passed through during the past four or five years it was possibly a wise course for the Government to take. Having appointed such a Board they certainly were justified in having on it the very best men they could find in Canada. As far as the two members of that board are concerned, I do not think any exception can he taken to them, although it is true that some of my friends of this side have objected particularly to Mr. O'Connor. I notice in the press to-day that a suggestion has been thrown out that a returned soldier from Montreal shall be appointed as a third member. Now, I agree entirely with every-

thing the honourable gentleman (Mr. Sex-smith) has said that upon the Board of Commerce there should be at least one farmer. Upon that point I might say-and I make the statement for the information of the Government-in the case of all the commissions that have been appointed the farmers have been practically overlooked. From my knowledge of agriculturists-living and working amongst them as I do, because I happen to be a farmer myself-it occurs to me that surely in all common sense the Government might have been able to find, throughout this broad land, one farmer qualified to sit upon that commission. If we appoint good men on the Board of Commerce, I think it is only fair that they shall be well paid for their services-I do not object in any particular to that. The point is being made in connection with the Board of Commerce that they can regulate if they can do nothing else.
The farmers of Canada during the last three of four years have been told that they must produce and keep on producing. What was the object of that advice? It was in order that increased production might lower prices to those living in cities and towns. But unfortunately, and I say this with full knowledge, many of those living in the cities and towns are trying to-day to increase wages and shorten the hours of labour. The resr.lt is that the price of manufactured articles must necessarily go up, and what the farmer has to use for production is thereby greatly enhanced in price. Now there come in between the producer and the customer those who are retailing,-and take my word for it, their profits never vary; they are as large on the last day of December as they were on the first day of January-they never in any shape or form decrease. The hon. gentleman from Springfield (Mr. Richardson) surely must know that if the prices of bacon and of live hogs go down, it necessarily follows that the farmer does not get as much for his work I need not labour that point, because it is only common sense. To-day we farmers think that we can run our business to suit ourselves, and we realize that we are perhaps not very far from a crisis. Labour cost has not gone down-it cannot very well go down for a considerable time-and the result necessarily follows that the profits of the farmer must be less.
We hear a great deal to-day about the farmers not only in the province of Ontario but in the other provinces. And for the Jife of me I cannot see what they want to unite for to-day with the prices we have

had for the last four years. The farmers of Canada never had four such years as they have had since 1S'14. But if the farmers of Canada had heard the discussion this afternoon and to-night they certainly would think it unnecessary to have this House composed of actual farmers. If there is one thing I am proud of, Mr. Speaker, it is that I am a farmer, but even if with that feeling of pride I have to act the part of a "dumb philosopher"; when the interests of the farmers are at stake, it is possible that my voice may be raised in their defence.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. H. KEEFER (Port Arthur and Kenora):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As representing not a farmer's
constituency but a city constituency, Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with those representing rural constituencies in the criticism of this Bill, against any talk about fixation of prices, be it of farm products or anything else. It is rather interesting to listen to the discussion that has taken place from time to time on this question, and then to remember the slams, to use a slang expression, that the poor old Food Board got during its short regime. Hon. members will remember that when the late Mr. Hanna was appointed to the position of Food Controller the cry went over the country:	What don't you fix the prices?
Everywhere that was thrown at him. Fortunately he was a man of parts who was not going to be misled by the hue and cry and the first thing he did was that which has been advocated by the hon. member for York (Mr. Maclean) and by other members, he gathered around him business men who had experience in these subjects, and his investigations soon convinced him of the impossibility of fixing prices. As soon as the cry went out that the price of milk was to be fixed by the present Board of Commerce telegrams came down from my constituency protesting against it, and rightly so, when it was pointed out what was the price for bran and shorts. How could you expect the farmer, Sir, to produce the milk and have his price fixed if you did not fix the price of the feed that went to make the milk, and so forth?
Price fixation is as old as the hills; there is nothing new in it. In the olden days trading was merely a case of barter and exchange with no price. That was found inconvenient and the Romans introduced the piece of money " Praetium "-something that passed between. How absurd it is to attempt to tie one end of that piece of money and leave untied the other end! It cannot be done without causing econo-

mic disorder. The very fixation of the price of wheat resulted in this, that we were informed on the Food Board that it was cheaper for the farmer because wheat was fixed at $2.20, which was thought to be a very high price, at the time to feed his wheat to the hogs and sell at good prices his oats or say his flax at $4.50 a bushel, and we had therefore to pass an order prohibiting the feeding of wheat to hogs. That simply shows the futility of trying to fix the price of one article unless you fix the price of all other articles, and I do hope that this Board of Commerce will endeavour to profit by the experience of men like the late Hon. Mr. Hanna, or Mr. H. B. Thompson, who gave long study to this question and gathered the best practical men around them to arrive at a satisfactory solution.
Take the price of milk; that is no new question. The Canada Food Board called in the milk dealers from all over the country and had them in session here several days, with the result that a report was issued on the milk question which is practically a classic on that subject, citing one of the western towns as an example to follow, that town having lowered the price of milk to the consumers during the war and yet increased the price to the farmer. It is largely a question of distribution. It was shown that in the city of Toronto, for instance, on Spadina avenue there were probably fifteen or sixteen milkmen delivering milk-fifteen or sixteen overhead charges for drivers and wagons. It was shown that here in the city of Ottawa milk was cheaper. Why? Because one company has practically almost a monopoly, and that company said, " Give us the whole city and we will even lower the price again.'' It was the cost of distribution, not the cost to the farmer.
I sincerely hope that we will have less of these scare headlines. There 'is a member of the Board of Commerce who fairly revels in publicity; he thrives on it. And what is the effect? It is simply stirring up ithe unthinking people, and it is very hard to get them to again look at things correctly. If we are going to have a Board of Commerce let them try ;to get down to the kernel of the matter and not gO' off on these side questions. With regard to what the hon. member for York (Mr. Maclean) advocates, that the Government should administer these laws, that is not correct. The popular idea is that the Minister of Justice is the policeman of the country. That is not correct.
Sir iSAM HUGHES: He was at ithe time of the Military Service Act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Attorney General of each province is the policeman of his province. One attorney general made the remark: "I am not a policeman." He was. It was his duty to enforce the law. The provinces draw their subsidies for the civil administration. Our criminal law is a Dominion statute, but it is enforced by the provincial authorities. We had that same difficulty up in the Food Board. There the ground was taken that these Orders in Council should not be enforced by the provinces, but by the Dominion. At once we saw that if we attempted that we would have an army of men from one end of the country to the other, a lot of new officers in conflict with existing officers and consequent confusion of authority. We came to the conclusion that it was most inadvisable to promulgate such a doctrine, and instead of that Mr. Thompson wisely called in the chiefs of police of the different parts of the country for a conference. After that conference they stood loyally behind the Board, they did their work well. To remunerate them we put through an Order in Council saying that all the fines should go to those instituting the proceedings. If they were municipal, the municipality profited; if they were provincial, the province profited. These things might be solved in that way should difficulties in enforcement arise.
Then, as regards the question of spread, as my hon. friend from South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) indicates, that is the keynote of the whole problem. I asked him the question: "Was that spread fixed?" It was. The food board did not advertise, it did not have scare headlines, but all the ti'me, after Mr. Thompson was chairman, and during the war up to the Armistice, we had the spread in Canada fixed; the wholesalers' spread was so much, the retailers' spread was so much. We did not have to prosecute. There was a remedy. How? We made each dealer take out a little license to do business and required him to pay a trifling fee of a couple of dollars. With these fees we paid the whole of the board's expenses, and we had a surplus when we got through of $37,000, which was paid into the Receiver General of Canada. That license was the key to the situation. If we found a dealer violating the spread, we simply notified him that if it occurred again we would have to cancel his license.



He lived up to the transaction after that. But we did not have any scare headlines.
You remember the prices of food during the war-we were only regulating the prices of food. But the same system might have been applicable to clothing, and so on, if such also had been under the board. The prices of food were much lower during the war in Canada than they were in United States with the exception of four or five articles that were peculiar to the United States. We regulated the spread, we controlled the number of transactions for the benefit of the community and yet we were criticised and condemned in this House from A to Z. One reason for that was that we did not make public everything we did. We kept right on with the work and we got no thanks for it. But we are getting our thanks now. The criticism that is now being heard through the country is the best commendation of the work which the Board did.
Why were prices rising? That is not difficult to ascertain. During the war the Allies-not the neutrals-came seeking our products. They wanted our cheese. France was bidding against England for our cheese, Italy was bidding against France for our condensed milk, and prices started _ to climb. We said: "You are acting against your own interests and against ours; you must stop competing in our markets for goods; form an Allied purchasing commission amongst yourselves so that this Allied Purchasing Commission. can buy all this produce and distribute it amongst yourselves; you will get your produce cheaper and there will not be any unnecessarily enhanced prices." We did our best to increase the supply, with the result that people went up and down the side lines just as a previous speaker said-including boys and teachers-every one preaching the gospel of increased production. We spent considerable money advocating increased production with the result that farm products increased two-fold or from about $300,000,000 to $600,000,000.
Sir SAM. HUGHES:	How about the
quantities?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
And the quantities also. The price did not vary so much, with the exception of that of wheat. The reason why they did not vary was that we held control through the Allied Purchasing Commission.
Then came the Armistice. The old countries wanted at once to get away from these restrictions and they said:	"We will go
back to normal conditions." They dissolved 
their Allied Commission, and this Government saw fit to abandon any further food control in view of the unjust criticism of the board. What was the result? Immediately these allied nations began bidding against one another and the prices started to climb. What was the next result? Neutrals who, prior to the Armistice, could not purchase, entered the field upon the signing of the Armistice and prices climbed higher. Then, under peace conditions came the enemy aliens who also are starved for leather, clothes and goods of whatever class was lacking. So long as this bidding goes on outside of the country; so long as the production of this country is insufficient to meet the demand, prices have got to climb until you get to the apex. We may talk until we are black in the face in this House but we oannot regulate prices unless we dislocate the entire economic conditions of the country.
Furthermore, you cannot properly bring down prices unless you do one of two things -either make some arrangement among the nations to do their buying collectively or increase our production to such an extent that the demand is less than the supply. If we do not do either of these, prices are bound to rise. I think it is high time for all of ns to do our best to inculcate in the minds of the people the real causes of these increased price-s and to point out that they are not due so much to profiteering and all that sort of thing as to economic law's. There is a small amount of profiteering which may be controlled by regulating the spread. Mr. Thompson and bis associates on the Food Board did that. I had the pleasure, during the war, of receiving from one of the largest milling concerns a cheque for over $9,000, representing undue profits which that company had made on bran and shorts and which amount they wrere obliged to pay into the Treasury of Canada.
You might control the profits by regulating the spread, and this the Board of Commerce has power to do.
Now, as to this Bill providing for the salaries of the Commissioners, let us pay them a decent salary, let us see that they do t'heir work, and if they do not, then let us put other men in their places who will.

Mr. Speaker, there is
one thing that I would wish to point out to the minister, and possibly it would not be amiss at this stage. There seems to be considerable confusion about the orders that are made, and perhaps might have been made by this board. I think the minister

will see the necessity of having these -orders filled somewhere. I do not know that any one department more than another has to do with this board. I presume that it is supposed to be absolutely independent of any department of the Government. Nevertheless, I think there should be some connection between this board and some department-possibly the Department of Labour or the Department of Justice. It js not for me to say, but I think there should be some department of the Government in which the orders made by this board should be filled so that the farmers, the manufacturers and others who are concerned in the orders made and the decisions reached will know where to find them.
Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-salaries of Chief Commissioner and other commissioners.
Is it the intention of the Government in the near future to appoint a third member of the board?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I think in a day or two there will probably be an announcement of appointment.

I suppose the recommendation made by the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) that a French speaking gentleman be appointed to the board, will be taken into consideration by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When the organization
is completed, I think it will be seen that the necessity for the French language being thoroughly understood has been given consideration and has been provided for.

This clause fixes the
salaries of the commissioners. How has the Government arrived at a salary of $10,000 for the chairman and salaries of $8,000 for the other commissioners? I know other employees of the Government in other departments holding very responsible positions and performing very valuable services who are being paid very much lower salaries than are named in this clause. I do not understand why there should be this difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is difficult to lay
down an exact basis upon which one fixes a salary of $10,000 or $8,000; but with regard, for instance, to the Chairman of the Commission, we had to press him to abandon a larger income. We wanted a gentleman whom we could regard as being most
45J
highly competent, and we found that most highly competent gentlemen, to take one instance, earning more than $10,000, and I think the hon. gentleman himself will hardly doubt that a man competent to perform the duties of this very important office, where he is called upon to deal with the most difficult as well as the most important problems, is in view of what similar salaries are paid in other walks of life, not overpaid at $10,000. I cannot go into a comparison with all the other salaries in the whole * Civil Service and endeavour to say why one ought to be lower or ought to be higher. The nature of the work that is to be done and the capacity that ought to be brought to the doing of it, in the judgment of the Government fully justified the fixing of the salaries as proposed, and I do not think I can go more into detail than that.

In the original Act as it was passed in July of this year, section 9, which is amended by the present Bill, provided that the chief commissioner should be paid such annual salary, and each of the other commissioners such, annual salaries, as might be determined by the Governor in Council. I do not, therefore, see that we are justified in passing the present Bill as the matter of fixing salaries was left entirely in the hands of the Governor in Council under that Act. It might be easier to get rid of some of these men if they should not discharge their duties as they ought to do if the Act were left as we passed it in July. I do not want to criticise the chairman of the commission at all. From all that I learn and hear and from the attitude of the other commissioners since the chairman came back from the West, I have good reason to believe bis judgment is sound, and we shall not be entertained with some of those freak judgments or injunctions that we have been treated to during the past few weeks, and that have agitated and upset the business of the country to a greater degree than possibly most members of this House realize. I personally would imagine that the matter would be quite safe in the bands of the Governor in Council, it being left exactly as it was in the original Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I might just say that 'there was in the Governor in Council power to fix the salaries, and in the view of the Governor. in Council, these salaries would have been proper salaries to fix; but it was thought more desirable that Parliament should be asked to deal with the matter, and that it should be made a matter of statute. That is the entire difference. If

?08
we liad fixed the salaries, we would have fixed them at precisely these amounts, and that would haive implied precisely the same contract with the gentlemen whom we appointed as to the permanency of their salaries as the statute does; but we submit the matter to Parliament and we make the salary a statutory salary. That does not alter the power to remove if there were sufficient cause -to remove. The most that might be suggested is that it might modify any power, if we had power, to alter the salary; but I do not think it would be suggested that, even although it remains with the Governor in Council to fix the salary, if we ask the gentleman to leave another occupation and appoint him for a fixed period at a fixed salary, the Governor General would be justified in altering that salary. He might, if there were proper cause for removal, and there were power to do that, remove the incumbent; but I do not-think it would be suggested that he ought to hold over the gentleman's head the power of changing the salary in order to exercise an influence over him. We want this Act carried out reasonably to attain the purpose for which it was intended. But it is impossible that a board of this kind should be constituted with th-e idea that the Government is to stand over the members of that -board, and let us -suppose that the hoard pronounces a judgment or comes to a decision which the Government d-oes not -approve, there is a remedy -by -appeal. But leaving that matter of the right of appeal to the Governor in Council aside for the moment, such a board must not be in a position of rendering its decisions under supervision of the Governor in Council, and with perhaps a suggested power to change their -salaries if we do not like their judgments. An element of independence is, I think, essential to -the satisfactory working of any board .of this kln-d.
Did I understand the minister to say that there is an appeal to .the Privy Council?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is an appeal to the Governor in 'Council, which appeal was referred to this evening. It -is in that regard precisely -the same provision that is made with regard -to the Board of Railway Commissioners. It is a reserved power seldom exercised, but it is thought wise to give the same power as is given in- 'the case of the Board of Railway Commissioners.

I realize the force of the argument -advanced by the Minister

of Justice (Mr. Doherty), but I think he will admit, -and the members of the committee -will agree, that it is rather unfortunate that we should be called upon to fix, by Act of Parliament, the salaries of the members of this board, in view of the exhibition that we have had -as to the absolute incompetence of a member of that board to carry out the duties with which he was entrusted. That is admitted -by the action of the hoard in rescinding the in-, junction that was issued a few weeks ago. despite the threat that wa-s made to the people of this country that if it was not observed a penalty would be imposed. I do- not think you could have clearer evidence than -that of the unfitness of the commissioner for his position, and it seems hard for me to agree to fixing the salary of a man who has given ample and abundant evidence of his total unfitness for the position to which he was appointed.

I wish to say
in the first instance in connection with the clause before the committee that I was personnally gratified to learn that the thought expressed when the Bill was going through the House in July that the -salary of the Chairman of the board would be fixed at approximately $8,000 has been -changed, and that the Chairman of the Board is to get $10,000 and the commissioners $8,000 each. I believe that no group of men has ever undertaken a -more important work in this country than that performed by the Board of Commerce. They have in the statute bringing -them into existence very wide powers, given to them very largely as the result of the wide-spread feeling throughout the country that some means should be taken to control profiteering, if such existed, and -at least to stabilize public opinion. If men of the right kind to carry out that work are to be -secured the salaries named are not too great.
The next point is with regard to making the salary statutory. It seems to me that no -more dangerous condition could exist with regard to any judicial pr semi-judicial body than for them to he placed in the position suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Sutherland), where the Government might tamper with their salaries if the Board's judgments did not at all times satisfy them. We hope at least that the judgments of the Board will be free from political bias. They could not he looked upon throughout the country as free from political control if a condition such as that suggested was imposed, whereby the Government might reduce the salary of a man in the hope

that he would get tired of his job and quit, because he was not performing it to their satisfaction. You might as well say that in the case of the judges of the Supreme Court if their judgments did not suit the Government their salaries should be reduced.
Reverting to what has been referred to by my hon. friend as the "admitted incompetence" of one member of the Board,
I have been forced to the conclusion, having read the greater part of the discussion that has taken place and also listened to a part of it, that there is a certain hysterical feeling abroad with the work of the Board of Commerce. It may be due to the nervousness that the country seems to be suffering from that is permeating all classes of men. They accept the startling headlines in some morning or evening paper, and without digging down into the facts take if for granted that the headlines tell exactly what happened. That is one of the troubles through which this country is passing. If my hon. friend, and those who have repeated on the floor of this House statements similar to those he has made here to-day, had taken the trouble to find out just what the Board of Commerce did when sitting in Toronto-
I cannot find out.

You could if you had made an effort. This is what took place with regard to the milk question. The Board of Commerce did not arbitrarily fix a price which could not be changed for forty days. What they did say was this, that the price of milk should remain as it was for forty days, or pending an investigation that might take place to determine whether a rise in price was justified or not. In carrying out that principle what did they do? They appointed a Fair Price Committee upon which were representatives of the producers, the distributors, and the consumers, to go intd the whole question and report to the Boar-d of Commerce. The result was that the producers, the distribu

tors and the consumers agreed upon what they considered to be a fair price and reported to the Board of Commerce, and the the BoaM of Commerce issued an order making that the legal price for milk in the city of Toronto. What else could they do? It is true the information was not given to the public. I do not know why, and I am not going to make any assertions as to the reason why but I have given the facts.
Let me give another instance. Perhaps hon. members read in the Toronto papers
published yesterday morning that the Board of Commerce-and in this case His Honour Judge Robson was sitting as Chairman-had issued an order, or were going to issue an order, reducing the price of certain articles of food 6 or 8 or 10 cents a pound. No such order was made; no such order, apparently, was ever contemplated. What the Board did do, after considering the question, was to say that prices would go back some time between now and the 15th of October - providing conditions with regard to the raw product of that particular industry remained as they are to-day-to the level of the 15th of March last, when the price was about the same as it is today. That was a perfectly reasonable order to make, but the country is agitated apparently by the scare headlines in the newspapers, and that agitation is creeping into the House of Commons.
I think it is only fair to give the Board of Commerce a chance. Surely none of us can deny the fact that from one end of this country to the other there was an agitation amongst all the people, and I know of nothing for which the Government was more universally condemned by those who wanted to find fault with it, than that they were not making some comprehensive effort to control the spread in prices. The Government enacted the legislation bringing into existence the Board of Commerce, and in doing that, went further than any other country in the world. I believe that they exercised the greatest possible care in selecting the commissioners. Their judgment may not have been right; time alone will disclose that. Mr. DONALD SUTHERLAND (Oxford South) moved the second reading of Bill No. 7, to amend the Adulteration Act (respecting bran and shorts or middlings)

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. member should give some explanation of this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I shall make a few observations in regard to some of the objects which I had in view in introducing this Bill.

It may be contended that the Adulteration Act of 1906 and subsequent amendments thereto make ample -provision against the adulteration of the by-products of wheat in the milling of flour. Unfortunately, however, for those who would so argue the adulteration of these commodities has been and is the practice of nearly all the milling companies of Canada to-day. It is a glaring and flagrant outrage that these things should be permitted, particularly in view of the fact that our present legislative enactments enable the millers to do that and still remain beyond the reach of the law.
Some reference was made yesterday to the value of these by-products -and to the necessity of using bran and shorts in large quantities in connection with -the raising of stock. Young and growing stock -are in great need of bran because of the protein, fat and other food qualities which it contains. The best breeders and feeders of live stock in the old- land feed enormous quantities of bran to their growing stock. In the feeding of d-airy stock also, the use of large quantities of this commodity i-s necessary. I have repeatedly pointed out that stock raising in this country should receive greater attention at the hands of the farmers than it has done in the past, because it is the only -possible means whereby the fertility of the soil can be maintained and increased. The truth of this contention will he conceded by all who are engaged in agriculture. It is, therefore, very important and most essential that these products should reach those who purchase and feed them, in a pure state.
I regret that steps were not taken many years ago to -accomplish the objects that I had in view in introducing -this Bill. Some hon. members may recall that in 1913 I spoke as strongly as I could with regard to the spread of weed seeds throughout the country and the l-ack of any effort on the part of the Government to control that menace to agriculture.
it is a very singular thing that even in those by-products of wheat weed seeds should be found in tremendous quantities and should thus be sent broadcast throughout the country. Every one who understands the milling of wheat into flour knows that it is thoroughly cleaned and put through several processes before the wheat "is ground into flour. Consequently, there cannot be any appreciable quantity of weed seeds or anything except pure wheat when it is milled. Therefore, if anything be found in the bran
or shorts other than that, it must have been placed there deliberately by the millers or others, and that is what I seek to have remedied by this Bill. If you go back a few years, you will find that the Act as it was originally passed contemplated the preventing of just such things as have been taking place during recent years. On May 3, 1911, an amendment was passed to the Act, and I will read the words that were included with regard to bran at that time. The section as originally passed read:
Bran is a product of the milling of wheat or other grain and contains not less than 14 per cent of proteids, not less than 3 Per cent of fat, not more than 10 per cent of crude fibre.
This is what was added on May 3, 1911:
And must be free from vital seeds of any of the noxious weeds defined toy the Governor in Council.
What does that imply? It cannot imply anything other than that the miller is permitted to put almost an unlimited quantity of ground weed seeds into the bran and shorts as long as the vitality of those seeds is destroyed. I should like to know what pressure was brought to bear and who was agitating for any such legislation as was placed on the statutes at that time. Why is the word " vital '' mentioned? That very word ** vital " implies that if the vitality be destroyed, no exception would be taken to the mixture. The result has been that immense quantities of weed seeds have been ground up fine and mixed with the bran and shorts, and no complaint can be lodged on that account against the millers of this country, as this amendment implies this can be done. More recently, however, further legislation was passed with regard to this matter. On December 10, 1917, it will be found that another clause, clause 17, was added to the definition of grain products :
The presence of presumably vital weed seeds in any form of feeding stuff shall be held to constitute adulteration under the Act, when more than 25 seeds per pound, as enumerated in the Seed Control Act of 1911, are present in the feed.
Step by step, this continued until in 1917 an Order in Council was passed permitting further adulteration by having as high as twenty-five vital weed seeds per pound in addition to all the ground stuff that the millers saw fit to place in the bran and shorts. What has been the result of this? The result is that there is not a department of the Government connected with agriculture, the Department of Trade and Commerce, also the Department of Inland Revenue, when -it was in existence, but had

numerous complaints from farmers throughout the country and from branches of the provincial Departments of Agriculture pointing out that large numbers of stock were being poisoned and had died as a result of this stuff being fed to them. That being the case, the House can readily understand that a great and serious injury was being done to a large proportion of the stock which might not have died but whose health was impaired as a result of eating this mixture. But in view of the fact that those complaints were being continually made and were on file with the departments of the Government, I say that the Government were lax and recreant in their duty in not seeing that some steps were taken long ago to eradicate this evil. Further, if the Board of Commerce desire to do something in the interest of the people of this country, they will immediately get busy on this matter.
There is a very wide range of weed seeds that are termed noxious. I am not going over the list; but in addition to that, there are many seeds that are not termed noxious and it is quite permissible for the millers to put as much of this in the bran and shorts as they see fit. The law prohibits more	than	twenty-five vital
noxious weed seeds per pound, but you can dump into it as much of the other stuff as you see fit, and the law cannot interfere with you.
I should like very briefly to refer to something which happened before a special committee of this House at the last session cf Parliament when we had before the special committee that was dealing with the cost ol living in this country evidence given by Mr. Hedley Shaw, managing director of the Maple Leaf Milling Company; Mr. William Allan Black,'representing the Ogilvie Milling Company, and Mr. W. W. Hutchinson, vice-president and manager of the Lake of the Woods Milling Company. In answer to a question that I put' to Mr. Hedley Shaw on that occasion, he said:
Bran and shorts are better with the screenings added thereto. If you take it out, it would reduce the quality of the bran and shorts.
It is well known that in the cleaning and the milling of wheat there is a certain proportion of cracked wheat that is broken into four quarters. This is left with the wild buckwheat and other weed seeds that are taken out of it, and by reason of the fact that there is a certain quantity of flour in wild' buckwheat and in this cracked wheat, the millers can scour the bran and shorts so fine that it would not come up

to the standard required, the one to which I referred to a few minutes ago which requires 14 per cent of proteids, 3 per cent of fat and so forth; 'but by reason of the fact that they are permitted to incorporate into those by-products this other stuff that should properly be termed as screenings, they are enabled to bring up the standards of bran and shorts.
The result is we have another by-product of wheat on the market to-day called Red Dog, a low grade flour, which was formerly considered as shorts or middlings. The bran and shorts to-day are of such poor quality without the addition of the wheat and the buckwheat in the screenings that they do not come up to the standard. One of the objects I had in view in introducing this Bill was to remove this very serious defect. When Mr. Black, of the Ogilvie Milling Company was before the committee, I questioned him with regard to the practice they were pursuing and pointed out some of the results. I asked him whether it would not be advisable and in the public interest for them to dispose of their screenings as screenings, because they would have a commercial value if the seeds were taken out. He replied:
I think it is rather a puttering thing to do to take it out and separate it and work it oft. It would he a good deal of a bother and a great deal of a nuisance to start out with. Of course, it is entirely up to the Government to say what we can do and what we cannot do. If the Government says nothing can go in except pure bran and shorts, of course, we will have to abide toy that.
So the millers were quite within their rights in doing what they did. A little further on, Mr. Hutchinson, replying to a question I had put to him said:
Might I make a suggestion, if it is as serious as you have brought out to-day?
Mr. Sutherland :	Yes, certainty.
Mr. Hutchinson:	Why does not the Government make it illegal altogether?
That was a straight honest statement from the general manager of one of the biggest milling companies in this country. So the blame is not on the milling companies entirely, but rests on Parliament and the Government for having permitted such a practice to be pursued. Let me qualify that by saying that it has been during the last year and a half that the most serious legislation has been enacted enabling the millers to carry on in this way. Instead of endeavouring to remove this nuisance the Government through the Department of Agriculture have contracted for what is termed reeleaned screenings to be disposed of by the department to the farmers of

Canada. During the past year 16,889,450 pounds of this stuff had been purchased by the Government and disposed of to the farmers of this country, *much of it unground. More than 10 per cent of that stuff was wild oats, and about 2 per cent of it was made up of noxious weeds of the very worst kinds1-mustards and others. This stuff has been sent broadcast all over Canada, and I say as emphatically as I can that some one in the Government is to blame for having permitted such a thing to be done. The greatest possible injury that could be done to agriculture in Canada has been done through the action of the Government in this regard. I say further, it may well be asked whether the Minister of Agriculture for the Dominion of Canada during the past year and a half considered himself to be in the employ of the people of Canada or in the employ of the Grain Growers' Grain Company.
I wish to refer to a document published by the Government, Bulletin No. 412, from the laboratory of the Inland Revenue Department, prepared by the chief analyst, Dr. McGill, relating to the inspection that has been taking place. speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Bill of my hon. friend the member for South

Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) proposes to amend the Act respecting the adulteration of food and other articles. As my ho.n. friend has said, the administration of that Act has been transferred to the Department of Health, and the proposed legislation comes under the jurisdiction of the department over which I have the honour for the time being to preside. The matter brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for South Oxford is undoubtedly one of great interest to the agricultural community. It is important on the one hand to keep the soil free from weeds and on the other to see that the live stock im-dustry does not suffer from the character of the feed provided.
There is no doubt upon the facts disclosed in the bulletins already issued by the head of this branch, Dr. McGill, that the existing law has been violated by those engaged either in the production or the _ sale of certain classes of feed. My hon. friend has read certain extracts from some of the publications issued by the department, and they do disclose a seed weed content far beyond what is permitted by the regulations. The administration of the Act has only been transferred to my department in the last two weeks, and therefore I am simply speaking from information received from the chief of the branch, Dr. McGill. As I understand the situation, it is not possible as a practical proposal to have feed absolutely free of foreign matter, that grain even when cleaned is not absolutely pure. The amount of weed seed residue may be very small, but there is always a certain residue. Unfortunately it happens that to-day the grain is not so free from weed seed as it was perhaps a few years ago, and there is an increase in the weed content of the grain grown in many sections of the country. Of course, methods are adopted for freeing the grain as far as possible of these weed seeds; and in the grinding the seeds in a large measure become pulverized and the number of vital seeds that pass through should be very limited. Then in the case of bran and shorts fed to cattle or sheep, my information is that the method of mastication should still further devitalize the seeds that may be left in such cases. But whatever may be the facts in reference to the present situation, the law authorizes the Governor in Council to pass regulations governing the matter, and regulations have been passed to which my hon. friend has referred. These regulations were issued in the year 1917, and they define the character of the 
feeds to which my hon. friend refers. They are as follows:
14.	Bran is a product of the milling of wheat or other grain, and contains not less than fourteen (14) per cent of protelds, not less than three (3) per cent of fat, not more than ten (10) per cent of crude fibre and must be free from vital seeds of any of the noxious weeds defined by the Governor in Council under "The Seed Control Act."
15.	Shorts or Middlings is the coarser material sifted out from the products of a second treatment of the grain by crushing the coarsely ground material that is sifted out from the bran after the first grinding; and contains not less than fifteen (15) per cent of proteids, not less than four (4) per cent of fat, not more than eight (8) per cent of crude fibre and must be free from vital seeds of any of the noxious weeds defined by the Governor General in Council under "The Seed Control Act."
16.	Chop Feed is whole grain of one or more kinds more or less finely ground, and contains not less than ten (10) per cent of proteids, not less than two (2) per cent of fat, not more than ten (10) per cent of crude fibre and must be free from vital seeds of any of the noxious weeds defined by the Governor in Council under "The Seed Control Act."
17.	The presence of presumably vital weed seeds in any form of feeding stuff shall be held to constitute adulteration under the Act, when more than 25 seeds per pound, as enumerated in the Seed Control Act of 1911, are present in the feed.
As I understand the matter, if there is a smaller weed seed content than 25 seeds per pound, the presence of these weed seeds is not considered as adulteration under the Act, and any person handling such feeding stuff would not be subject to the penalties prescribed for selling adulterated feed; but if the product contains more than 25 of these seeds per 'pound, those manufacturing or selling it would be liable to the penalties.
That is vital seeds?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. Now, it is quite true that as a result of the investigations by the department they have found that *a weed seed content beyond the maximum permitted is present in many of the samples taken, and they have instituted prosecutions against the parties selling such adulterated products. As soon as the matter was brought to my attention I gave instructions that proceedings should be instituted in every case where the law was being violated. In addition, if the large milling concerns do violate the law, not only should they be punished, but the widest publicity should be given to the fact that the products of those concerns are being manufactured and sold in violation of the provisions of the Adulteration Act. Dr. McGill is now considering methods of giving wider publicity to the fact that convictions have been registered against certain firms for such viola-

tions of the law. I can. say to my hon. friend that so long as I am responsible for the administration of this Act, I intend, to see that the law ds carried out and that adulteration is prevented as far as possible. I believe that Dr. McGill has been working -most industriously and faithfully along these lines with a view of putting the law into motion against those who either manufacture or sell adulterated feed.
Dr. McGill informs me that the present legislation i-s sufficient. If the 25 vital seeds per pound is too high a number to permit, then the provisions of the Order in Council can be changed. According to the information he has furnished me, -an examniation of a large number of samples which contain this number or less showed that -there was no deleterious result so f-aT as -the stock were concerned, but where a larger number of vital seeds was found there were in some cases at least unsatisfactory results from the use of such feed. But there is power under the existing legislation ito reduce the number of these vital weed seeds, and if an investigation proves that that number is too high

and I know some of the officers of the department -have reported- that in their judgment that number should be reduced-J can see no reason why i-t should not be reduced to a minimum consistent with what would be the reasonable -and proper requirements of the trade.
I do not know iny-self, I -am only speaking on the information -that has been f-urn-ished to me, -but I am informed that it is not po-ssihle to get feed- -absolutely pure. My instructions -are that the amendment, as my hon. friend has put it, if carried out to the letter would be unworkable, inasmuch as weeds and intermixture of other grain in the field, is inevitable. There -is no such thing known to commerce as wheat bran entirely free from material other th-an wheat, or corn bran entirely free from other than -maize products, that in all cases there is some of the weed content in the grain, and that it would not be -commercially possible to carry the law out to the very letter. I had the matter looked into -and I received this information to-day. In view of it I would suggest to my hon. friend that instead of pressing the Bill to the second reading he should let it stand over until the next session, -and I undertake, as head of the department, to go into the whole matter very carefully in the interval with a view to remedying the conditions to which my hon. friend (Mr. -Sutherland) has referred.
He has rendered a public service in directing attention to the importance of this matter; the whole question is as to the best method of dealing with it. I would have no objection to the second reading of the Bill were it not that I am instructed by officers of the department that, on a strict interpretation of the Bill, it is not feasible to carry out its provisions; that it would have the effect in some cases of preventing the sale of ordinary bran and other animal food of that kind. What we all have in view is to accomplish a certain result in the public interest, and, having regard to the information at hand, it appears to me that the course I have suggested would be the more likely one to secure the best possible results. Any violation of the present regulations will be prosecuted to the limit of the law, and the names of the offenders will be made known so that the public will be fully advised as to what firms or corporations are violating the law. Then, if the present weed seed content permitted under this Order in Council is too high and it can be lowered without serious prejudice to normal business operations, I shall be very glad indeed to see it lowered.
In fairness to my former colleague, the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. T. A Crerar) who is not here to-day, I wish to add that in whatever he did in connection with regulating the work of his department, I am quite sure that he was guided solely by what he believed to be the public interest.
Mr. GEORGE BOYCE. (Carleton):	Mr. Speaker, the hon. member says that it is not possible to have bran pure. I agree that it is pretty hard to have it pure, and in that connection I wish to draw attention to a matter that I had personal knowledge of. On one occasion I received a consignment of bran, and in the carload there were two bags of seeds. How did those seeds get there? 1s- it not fair to assume that they were gathered together for the purpose of mixing them with the bran that we are paying $65 a ton for? We are paying a great deal for the tricks of the people who are producing this stuff. It is necessary that this commodity be pure, because we are paying for a good article; besides, it is a very serious thing for the people who use milk in the cities, especially children and aged persons, if the dairymen who supply the milk feed their stock with stuff that is poisonous. The sooner this matter is taken in hand, the better for all concerned. The member for South Oxford
deserves great praise for bringing the subject to the attention of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with much interest to the remarks of the member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) on this subject. The milling industry is one of the important industries of Canada; it is growing and expanding and improving from year to year. The member for South Oxford would seem to be in favour of drawing the line so closely that every miller in the country would be open to prosecution on evidence of there being something in the bran which was not of wheat, but which was grown with the wheat. I have had a great many years' experience in the milling business, and a number of years' experience in the handling of grain. To my knowledge-leaving the hen out of consideration-there is no machinery manufactured that will separate certain kinds of grain or weeds from wheat. The report read by the hon. member showed that traces of wild oats were found in bran. A great deal of the wheat grown throughout the West contains from eight to fifteen per cent of wild oats, and I do not think it is possible-anyhow, it is impracticable-to clean out all traces of the wild oats before it passes through the rolls. Kernels of that wild oats will remain, and although it does not go into the bran without being crushed, the presence of the hulls shows that there is wild oats in the bran. Buckwheat, too, will go through the screens; it is hardly possible to take it all out. No machine has been manufactured up to the present that will separate barley from wheat. But under the Bill presented by my hon. friend, if a trace of barley, of oats, or of seed is found in bran the miller is liable to be hauled up and prosecuted for something that it is beyond his power to remedy. As the President of the Council (Hon. Mr. Rowell) has suggested, it would be well for the hon. member to allow his amendment to stand until the next session and give the minister in charge of the department an opportunity to enforce the law which is already on the statute-book. I think that the present law is about as far as we can go without having impracticable legislation. There is no doubt in my mind that the mills have been injecting seeds into the bran and shorts, outside of what was in the feed when it went through the rolls. By close inspection of the feed by officials of the department, a few examples might be made which would soon cause the practice to stop. I support

the suggestion that this matter be allowed to stand over until next session.

Mr. *Speaker, the member for Saskatoon (Mr. J. R. Wilson) suggests that itjs not practicable to prevent buckwheat and wild oats from getting into bran. If buckwheat and wild oats were the only things that went into the bran there would be very little complaint. In fact, I would not complain at all; I would be quite satisfied even if there was a large percentage of buckwheat in the bran. But there is no difficulty in separating from the 'bran the other objectionable seeds my hon. friend did not refer to; any ordinary fanning mill will take them out. I refer to small black poisonous seeds, which are worse than useless.
We would not object very much to paying for something that was useless if it was not harmful, but this is both useless and harmful; in fact, it has caused the death of scores upon scores of animals. There is an excuse for the hon member for Oxford South (Mr. Sutherland) dealing leniently with the matter of wild oats, but there is no excuse with regard to black poisonous seeds, they can be taken out without any difficulty at all. There are, however, other things that go into bran. If you get a sack of bran to-day in Ottawa, I venture to say that if you take a handful and hold ii't up to the light you will see a growth of the finest fuzzy whiskers on that bran you have ever seen in your life; you can see a small fuzz all over the top of it. There is something more than seeds in that; it looks as though all the sweepings and screenings and everything else that it was possible to gather up around the mill had been thrown together and ground up in a simplex grinder and sold as'food under the guise of bran. This is something that should be looked into. Personally, I have not had a pound of bran on my farm for the last fifteen or eighteen months, because I came to the conclusion that I was far better without it entirely even if it had almost beentgiven to me. Unless something is done, serious consequences will arise.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have very little to say with regard to the Bill that is now before us for our consideration. I have listened with a great deal of attention to the speech of the hon. member for Oxford South (Mr. Sutherland), who has given evidence of having gone very fully into this question and who has produced and placed on Hansard very strong reports

aud e\idence in support of his contention that some steps should he taken to put an end to the sale of what he says is poisonous or deleterious animal food. I take it for granted that the facts as put forward by the hon. gentleman are sustained. While I do .not profess to be very familiar with the Act that is now on the statute-book, we have an Act which comes pretty close to the subject, if it does not cover it altogether. If we have an Act which could be enforced and which could put an end to what is complained of, that Act should be enforced; but if the Act itself is deficient and does not cover the ground or does	not give enough authority	to
the Government officials to put an end to whait is complained of, I should be in favour of providing that remedy at the earliest possible moment. I do not speak with authority as to what the old Act contains; but if it is lacking in any particular, or if it falls short of furnishing the machinery necessary to put an end to this evil, we should not allow this fall to pass by and permit people who are producing-this kind of food to do more mischief. I think the Bill should be passed, and then if it be required, it is available; if it be not required, it can do no harm; but a great deal of harm may inure to the people of this country by reason of the fact that we have no legislation to deal with the subject which is provided for in the Bill of the hon. member.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mighlt I juslt answer the question of my hon. friend? I myself think that the Act at present gives sufficient authority, and it is a question- of the exercise of that authority by regulations passed by the Governor in Council. Section 3, of the Act provides:
Food shall be deemed to be adulterated within the meaning of this Act.
And-	[DOT]
"Food" includes every article used for food or drink by man or cattle-
And so forth. The Act provides that food shall be deemed to be adulterated within the meaning of the Act-
(a)	if any substance has been mixed with it so as to reduce or lower or injuriously affect its quality or strength;
(b)	if any inferior or cheaper substance has been substituted wholly or in part for the article ;
(c)	if any valuable constituent of the article has been wholly or in part abstracted.
The latter will not apply, but I should think both (a) and (b) would apply if the
46J	J J j
bran contains weed seeds as that is certainly contrary to the provisions of that clause. If it contains a mixture such as the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) has referred to, I should certainly say that it contains an inferior or cheaper substance which has been substituted wholly or in part for the article. Then (f) would also apply:
(f) if it contains any added poisonous ingredient or any ingredient which may render such an article injurious to the health of persons or cattle consuming it.
Under one or all of those three clauses (a) or (b) or (f), I would think that regulations might be made by the Governor in Council to cover this. Pursuant to those provisions, regulations have been made which I have read to the House, and under section I, subsection 17, if the article contains a minimum of twenty-five of these weed seeds per pound, it is considered adulterated. As I said before, it may be that that should be changed and the number reduced. But I think under the existing legislation there is power to deal with the matter.

Is there any provision for
inspection?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, the Act provides for inspection, and the Adulteration of Foods Branch has certain inspectors. It may be that more attention should be paid to inspection. I speak with a very limited knowledge of the matter, but I know Dr. McGill is deeply interested in the whole question and in seeking to put an end to these practices and to get the best results, because he has already discussed the matter with me.

By common consent,
the hon. member could ask a question. I

It is not exactly a question.
