speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I thought I had made that point quite clear.
Perhaps the minister did.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I intimated that I had already taken the matter up with the Dominion analyst, Dr. McGill, who has been working at it under the Department of Trade and Commerce under the minister in charge of that department, and it is the intention to pursue the subject to the end with a view to putting a stop to the practice which undoubtedly has existed, which the departmental reports show exists to some extent at the present time, not only punishing to the limit of the law the men who are guilty, but making known to the public the fact that these firms have violated the law and are selling for animal use foodstuffs that are contrary to the law. Further, it is the intention to have the whole situation examined with a view to seeing if the existing regulations should not be more stringent than they now are in order to meet the situation to which the hon. member for Oxford South has drawn the attention of the House, and which is certainly a most important one. I believe the publicity which this discussion has given will focus public attention more and more on this important question.

That will apply to all
stock feed, I suppose, not merely to bran and shorts?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend is aware that there is a special Act dealing with other classes of feeds, known as the Act respecting Commercial Feeding Stuffs, under which parties desiring to sell this feeding stuff must register and get a number. The stuff can only be sold under that number and the sale must comply with certain conditions. The Chief Analyst passes upon these commercial feeding stuffs. Under this Act also the necessary proceedings are being taken to prevent feeds containing deleterious substances being sold for animal use.

At the outset of
my remarks in moving the second reading of the Bill I said that some might argue that the present Bill makes ample provision for remedying the very thing I seek to remedy by this amendment. I pointed out that it was a common practice with nearly all the milling companies in Canada to do what I have described. I would point out that the Adulteration Act is not the only one that has a bearing on this matter. The Grain Products Act and other Acts and Orders in Council have a bearing on it. Those Orders in Council in my opinion have made the enforcement of the Act more difficult. I also pointed out the effect of the amendment to the Grain Products Act of May, 1911, which contained the words "and must be free from vital seeds of any of the noxious weeds defined by the Governor in Council under the Seed Control Act." No provision was made there for excluding seeds other than noxious weed seeds. Let me give another analysis from Bulletin No. 412, from which I have already quoted. In a pound sample from the Ogilvie Milling Company in the Vancouver District there were 864 lamb's quarters seeds, and in the same district another sample there were 528 lamb's quarters. These are not noxious weed seeds, and they are not covered by the Grain Products Act. The very fact of the amendment being made to that Act implies that weed seeds other than noxious weed seeds were quite permissible. The regulation made in 1917 went even further and provided that vital weed seeds in excess of twenty-five per pound would be considered as adulteration. So all these things have a bearing on the Adulteration Act.
The difficulty in enforcing the present law is so great that I do not think this Parliament would be justified in deferring action on the matter. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Wilson) has pointed out that it would be absolutely impossible to clean wheat so that it would not contain a certain percentage of weed seeds or words to that effect, and he referred to wild oats and wild buckwheat. Now the milling companies admitted in this very building at the last session that wheat was put through seven different processes before being ground into flour, that it was made as clean as it was possible for them to make it, and that only a very small percentage of any kind of seed, or grain of any other kind than wheat, could possibly get through to be milled into flour. I think that is the belief of every one who knows anything about the milling processes. An odd kernel of barley would be more likely to get in than buckwheat; because I can see

no reason why every buckwheat seed should not be taken out in these seven processes. The wild oats could also be taken out very easily because they are so light. I venture to say that you would not find one kernel of wild oats ground up in a whole barrel of flour. That being the case, you can rest assured the inspectors will never detect the very very small percentage that might get through. The general managers, of the milling companies all admitted that this stuff is piped back into the bran and shorts deliberately. They say: "We purchased it in the wheat and there is sometimes from four to ten per cent of it." In Western Canada this year there are large sections where the crop has been very poor indeed, but it is a remarkable thing that no matter how poor the crop may be, there will be a rank growth of weed; weeds grow without any encouragement. I believe there will be a very great percentage of weed seeds in the grain this year in those places. There is no reason why more than a very small percentage of that stuff should * ever reach the elevators or the mills. The millers pay for their wheat according to its cleanness. We have a very large number of men engaged in farming operations in Western Canada and I doubt if there is one of them *who will not admit that you could very easily put a sieve in a separator which would remove practically all of the small black seeds. Some wild oats and barley might get through it, but the more dangerous weed seeds could very easily be taken out. But the thresher does not want to do that. He is threshing by the bushel and wants to have as big an output as possible, and he will not take very good care to see that the wheat is kept clean. The result is that to-day this stuff is considered a marketable commodity, and has been distributed by the Government all over the country during the past year. I have already spoken of the way it is disposed of. The Government purchased, that stuff at $35 a ton, and sold it to the farmers of this country. It has become a commodity in which the grain growers are very much interested, and they are anxious that it should be disposed of in this way rather than be taken out by the separator when the grain is being threshed, and burned on the farm which is the only proper thing to do with it. I do not wish to be unreasonable, and I do not think that I have been, in view of the fact that I have been patiently referring to this matter for the past six years, and on more than one occasion have received the promise that the departments were looking into it and hoped that some
redress would be found. I would ask the minister if he will undertake to reimburse the farmers of Canada who suffer losses as a result of feeding this stuff to their stock in the meantime. I would also ask if he will undertake in the meantime to take off the hands of the farmers in this country the bran and shorts they may purchase in which is found a large percentage, not of vital weed seeds, but of ground weed seeds, which will be quite permissible unless this amendment to the Act goes through.
You have placed in authority in this country a Board of Commerce who have been going around threatening with a fine of a thousand dollars and imprisonment any farmer who dares to increase the price of his produce during the next forty days. This was the mandate issued a short time ago. I understand that it has since been partially rescinded, but it shows the disposition of the men who comprise the Board of Commerce. Notwithstanding the fact that a plain, straightforward question was asked here last night as to whether the third member of the board had been appointed, we find in the press this morning that this appointment has been made and that the man who has been chosen has no particular interest in agriculture in this country, quite the contrary. In view of the fact that this adulterated commodity is to be found all over the country to-day, I think it is only fair that wherever a farmer has it on hand he should be provided with some recompense or relief. With the spread of price between bran and shorts to-day, if delay takes place in remedying the present condition, the milling companies will reap an enormous advantage by being permitted to grind up the bran into shorts and dispose of it in that way during the next few months. It is not to be wondered at, Sir, that bran is almost an unpurchaseable commodity in Canada to-day under these conditions, and in face of the regulations that are being enacted against the farmers who are being held up now that they have to purchase large quantities of mill feeds. As I pointed out before, I doubt whether in the whole history of the province of Ontario feed for stock was ever before so scarce and dear as it is at the present time, and I also pointed out that thousands, yes, tens of thousands of cattle are being disposed of, to be slaughtered and cut up as canners, as a result of this condition. I do not think it is fair to the people engaged in this great industry. The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Wilson) has stated that the milling industry is one of the greatest in the coun-

try. Well, I say, without fear of contradiction, that agriculture is the greatest industry of Canada, and it is the industry that is apparently receiving the least consideration. In view of all the circumstances, therefore, I do not feel justified in withdrawing this Bill, at any rate at the present juncture, because I consider that the evidence I have submitted is absolutely authentic and cannot 'be controverted. I therefore respectfully decline to withdraw the Bill.

Mr. W. D. EULER (Waterloo North Riding) resumed the debate on the motion of Mr. McKenzie for the appointment of a parliamentary committee to investigate the alleged manipulation of soldier votes in the general election of 1917.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the resolution which is before the House on the motion of the leader of the Oppoisition has elicited what in my opinion was a most remarkable speech from the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Meigben). The feature of that speech which attracted my attention most particularly was the enunciation of a new *code of political morals which must come with a shock to the moral sense of the people of Canada. The motion of the leader of the Opposition is based u-pon a certain telegram purporting to have been signed *and sent by the Minister of the Interior to the Prime Minister of Canada during the fall of 1917, or, 'to be precise, in December of that year while the Dominion elections were in progress. That telegram is dated at Winnipeg, and reads as follows:
Would like one thousand soldier votes at large for Manitoba, of which 300 for Selkirk, balance divided between Provencher, Macdon-

aid, and Springfield, or same proportion or division no matter what our allotment may he.
Mr. Speaker, viewing that telegram carefully, I contend that, on the face of it, it is obvious that the motion of the leader of the Opposition is -absolutely in order. 1 do not think it can be disputed that a case has been made out which requires the strictest investigation. What does the telegram mean on the face of it? Does it mean that the Minister of the Interior is merely expressing a desire that the -Prime Minister should supply him with -a thousand votes or so, which might be thrown into any constituency in which the opposition candidates appeared dangerous, or in which their election seemed probable? I do not think we can gather that from the telegram. It means more than that. There is no doubt whatever that it indicates that there was a stock of votes somewhere that was at the disposal of Unionist candidates. That presumption is borne out by the very significant word "allotment" in the telegram. That word "allotment" implies that there is a supply of a certain commodity on hand which may be drawn upon at the will or discretion of those who wish to avail themselves of it. I do not think that any other explanation would -satisfy any member of the House. I am quite sure that none of the members -are so credulous tir innodbnt as to imagine that anything else was meant than that there was an allotment of votes which could be used practically at will to defeat any candidate of the Opposition who seemed likely to win his election. I had thought that possibly the Minister of the Interior would disclaim all responsibility for sending the telegram, but he does not do so. I did not believe, however, that he would actually justify the sending of a telegram of that kind or the object that it sought to attain which was nothing less, than to defeat the will of the people. When the Minister of Interior s-ay-s that it was a perfectly lawful proceeding that these votes of the soldiers should be applied, to use his own cynical expression, where they would do the most good, I did not think he would also justify it by any contention that it was -a right and decent and proper thing to do in a democratic country.
He has a special mentality.

The minister does not deny sending the telegram. He does not remember that he sent it but- he does -say that the Prime Minister did not receive the telegram. After -all that has no very great

significance in view of the fact that the minister claims that it was a perfectly lawful and proper proceeding. I was disappointed at the attitude of the hon. member for Red Deer in his speech on the resolution. I have a high regard for that hon.' gentleman, and his sentiments are usually not only couched in admirable language, but they are also of a very lofty and noble standard. If it is his view that it is well to forget all, to bury the matter altogether, I cannot see eye to eye with him; I cannot understand his position. Perhaps it should be remembered that it is the traditional practice of the members of the medical profession to desire as quickly as possible to bury their mistakes, say, about six feet deep, in preference to calling in 'the coroner to investigate and establish the wrongdoing if such there be. I was still nore [DOT]disappointed when, throughout the whole '.of his speech, he gave the impression that he subscribed to the vicious doctrine that the end justifies the means. I contend that t-haJt is what bis speech implies. While he admitted-perhaps not in so many words- [DOT]that things which had taken place during the election were not just what they should have been, ye't, after all, he took the position that they bad brought .about the desired result and that all was .well. I do [DOT]not believe in the policy of hushing up 'matters, nor in the doctrine that the end justifies the means. If that be the principle, then may we expect this country to enter upon an era of corruption such as has never been known. I venture to say 'that there never was .a government, bad 'as it may have been, that did not believe that it was about the best government 'the 'country ever had. It necessarily follows that, believing that the end justifies the means, that they will naturally act upon that- principle and adopt any plan whatever that may bring them back into power. Surely the hon. gentleman does not desire that.
' The hon. member also stated that that which was irrevocable might as well be forgotten and the dead past be permitted to bury its dead. I do not subscribe to that policy iu all cases. If 'that is a good principle to follow then we might as well abolish the criminal law entirely. If the man who slays his fellow man shall be allowed to escape simply because the life of his victim cannot be restored to the body, then, I say, we may as well do away with our criminal law altogether. It is not difficult to imagine the results which will flow from
the policy that exposure and punishment shall no longer follow wrong-doing.
It may be well under some circumstances to let bygones be bygones. Perhaps some of the things which have been discussed in this House might very well be treated in that way. But, Sir, when a shameful wrong has been perpetrated upon the Canadian people, when their constitutional rights have been set at defiance, when a minister of ithe Crown practically glories in what has been done and attempts to make wrong appear right, black appear white, then I think it is the duty of the Canadian Parliament to disavow the wrong that has been done and to reaffirm its belief in the principles 4 p.m. of democratic and responsible government. We have heard, Sir, a good many startling revelations since the election of 1917 as to how the election was won by the Union Government. We have heard of perjury, subornation of perjury, personation, plural voting and the coercion of soldiers. I think every member of this House could add his quota of evidence to the charges that have been made in regard to that election. 1 do not propose to go into these details but to confine myself very largely to the attitude that was taken by the minister in regard to the legality and propriety of the placing of soldier votes. The minister states that the telegram in itself implied nothing that was not perfectly lawful. If that is the case it means that it was legal in this country to use certain votes that were cast by non-Canadians in an election to defeat the will of the bona fide Canadian people in the various constituencies and that the Government could destroy its opponents at will. If that be true then the law is a great deal worse than I thought it.
According to my reading of the Military Voters Act it was entirely the duty of the voter himself to designate where his vote should be placed. There was no provision whatever that he should vote by proxy or that he could assign his vote to some one else, not even the Union Government. Yet on the face of that telegram there can be no reasonable doubt that these votes were appropriated to use not at the behest of the voter himself but at the behest of the Union Government committee. That argues such a departure from what, in my opinion is fair, just and decent, that it strikes at the very vitals of democratic institutions.
I hope, Sir, that I am not Pharisee enough to claim higher standards of conduct than those of the ordinary good citizen who has

a definite code which he lives up to in a more or less successful way. I assuredly make no such pretence. But, after all, such a broad and well defined line runs between what is essentially right and what is essentially wrong, that it is incomprehensible how men can mistake one for the other.
I stated a moment ago that if the law gave the right to any other than the man who actually voted to place that vote where he desired, then the law was a good deal worse than I had thought. The Minister of the Interior the other dtay in his address made the statement that the Opposition .through their representative overseas had striven to give ithe impression that .all soldier votes could be placed wherever the Government desired. I do not know whether or not that is the case but I do know that a similar impression tv.as in the mind of at least one member sitting on the other side of the House. I will give the instance with which I am most familiar. Shortly after the election of 1917, and during the first session of this Parliament, I had the pleasure of a conversation with an hon. member on the other side of the House. We discussed the election. During the course of the conversation he made the statement that both the leader of the Government and the leader of the Opposition had the undoubted right to place the soldiers' votes wherever they pleased. I thought at first, Mr. Speaker, that he said it as a joke and I said so, but he adhered to what he had said.
He stated, " I can prove it, because our organizer came to me and said, ' Mr. So and So, how many soldier votes do you want? ' I told him I wanted about two or three hundred." I have no doubt that he got them. Now, Sir, I would not'speak of that if it were not for the fact that i.t is evidence of the comprehensive plan indicated in the telegram. I do not know whether the minister based his statement that the procedure as outlined in that telegram was perfectly legal on anything else but wihat is in the Act itself. It may be, Sir, that among the multitudinous Orders in Council which have gone forth from the Union Government. there is an order -which makes it legal to treat those votes in that manner; I do not know.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what did it mean if it was lawful that those votes could be used in this manner? It meant that it was within the power of the Union Government to compass the defeat of any Opposition candidate anywhere. There were, I understand, something like 10,000 or 12,000 votes [Me, Kuler.]
available for use in this way, and which I suppose, according to the wording of the telegram, " no matter what our allotment may be," could be thrown into any constituency where there was a likelihood of an Opposition candidate being elected. There was not a single constituency in all Canada, I should judge, in which the vote could not he " fixed " beyond peradventure. The Opposition candidates were not at the mercy of their electors; they were at the mercy of the Union Government Committee. Any man could be defeated with almost absolute certainty whether his own individual riding gave him a majority or not. The Opposition candidate was practically in the position of the man who sits in a card game while his opponent has the winning card up his sleeve ready to play it whenever he needs it-that .surely is the very negation of representative government. The Prime Minister in the first session stated that in his opinion the election of 1917 was the fairest election ever held in this country.
The most honest.

I believe, Sir, that it was the most unfair election ever held in this Dominion. Indeed, in my opinion the term " election " is a misnomer. It was not an election at all. In the language of the times, I would say that we might describe it as the " parliamentary selective draft." Sir, was it not true that the members of this House were drafted at will according as it was desirable to elect one or defeat the other? I am quite serious when I say that I consider it little less than a miracle that some of us are here at all. In Ontario and the West apparently there were a few cases of miscalculation, or perhaps a saving sense of shame on the part of our opponents, because eight of us from Ontario and two from the West were allowed to be returned. Under the ingenious system so warmly defended by the Minister of the Interior, a non-Canadian voter had greater power in Canadian elections than the genuine Canadian himself. The real Canadian had to east his ballot in a certain constituency, as I read the law. If he should happen to come from the city of Toronto, or some other Unionist hive, he was obliged to cast his vote there, although he might be well aware that it would be practically wasted. But the soldier who was not a Canadian, who came under the description of " voter at large," could cast his eye over the whole Dominion, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and then place his vote as he pleased, with the result in some

cases that he thereby would defeat the will of the people of the constituency itself. Of course, this privilege was more apparent than real; a kind and disinterested Union Government relieved him of the necessity of making a choice. Again in the words of the minister " it placed the votes where it would do most good." Mr. Speaker, surely it is not an exaggeration to say that if such views prevail the very foundation of democracy must crumble. They are based on the free franchise of the bona fide Canadian citizen. When you destroy that, the superstructure must fall. If, Sir, it is indeed right that men can obtain membership in this House by any means other than the will of the actual residents of any constituency, then I say democracy has departed and we may as well own up to the sham and know ourselves for what we are.
Mr. Speaker, I judge from the remarks of the Minister of the Interior and his friends that the request of the leader of the Opposition for an investigation will not be granted. But, Sir, outside the walls of this Parliament the great jury of the Canadian people is sitting in judgment. During the last five years they grimly bore many things which were abhorrent to them, but which they thought were unavoidable. They closed their eyes, sacrificing much of lifelong conviction and of principle while their sons were engaged in the deadly conflict overseas. But the war is over, Sir, and the people are going to hold this Government responsible for its actions. I do not believe the people endorse the shameful things of the election of 1917. I do not believe either that they will subscribe to the new political doctrine enunciated by the Minister of the Interior. Indeed, Sir, if I believed that they did I would be ashamed to be-a Canadian.

I do not intend to take up very much time, Mr. Speaker, on this subject, because I realize the truth of the Prime Minister's declaration some time ago, that in his judgment the election of 1917 was one of the fairest ever fought in the Dominion.

Members may smile, but let me say in regard to Springfield that the civil majority was between 1,200 and
1,500, and that the legitimate soldiers' vote, votes cast by soldiers who came from the constituency of Springfield, ran the majority up to considerably over 2,000, and that 525 soldiers' votes for myself were cast at large. Soldiers appeared anxious to give an old friend a lift and so voted in Springfield. They were, however, disallowed by the returning officer. Had it not been for improper misrepresentations by men like Mr. Preston and others, those 525 votes might have been distributed in other constituencies where possibly they could have been of some advantage. But the legitimate majority in Springfield was considerably over
2,000,	*and I do not think I have any apologies to offer.
It will never be that again.

It is not necessary for me to go any further than the figures furnished toy the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) the other night, when he pointed out that of the 82 constituencies in the great province of Ontario only four could possibly have been influenced by the soldiers' vote, and that if the same proportion of soldiers' votes had been cast in these four constituencies as were oast by the civil vote, the members1 returned would have been elected. The story is practically the same throughout the entire Dominion. If hon. members will look up the returns they will find that candidates in Manitoba supporting the Union Government were returned by a sufficiently large majority to wipe out the minority of Government candidates, in a very large number of constituencies in the province of Quebec. Why, the majority of the hon. gentleman who represents Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Andrews) was something like 23,000 or 26,000. As a matter of fact, the people were overwhelmingly in favour of conscription, overwhelmingly in favour of the union of the two parties in order to carry the great war to a successful issue. I have always marvelled at the position taken by some hon. members of this House in criticising the result of that election. I would have thought that after seeing the verdict of the people, after reading the figures, such hon. gentlemen would have been satisfied to retire quietly and maintain a discreet silence with regard to this election.
The hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Euler) spoke of the election as a parliamentary selective draft. I would reply to that by saying that we on this side who were in that selective draft have reason to bt:

proud. As for those who for personal motives stayed at home rather than devote their energies to the preservation intact of our country and the empire-well, if they are satisfied, I think we also have perfectly good reason to offer no complaint.
After all, the great point-and I sometimes wonder why our friends on the other side have failed1 to grasp it-is that a mighty struggle, the greatest in history, was going on. The people of Canada, the most important Dominion of the Empire, were heart and soul in that war. They realized that the liberties of the world were gravely at stake and they resolved to spend their all in order to carry on their part in the great struggle. As a result of that election the resources of the Dominion were placed at the disposal of the British Empire. I need not relate here or emphasize the part that Canada took in that great war; it is a matter of history that it was the Canadians who broke -the Hindenburg line. But we hear hon. gentlemen, instead of expressing themselves as proud of the achievements of our Canadian forces, constantly carping and criticising the election that enabled that great fight to be carried on by our own people.
I do not agree with the member who has just spoken that our friend from Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) took the position that the end justified the means. I can easily understand, however, that honourable men, good citizens of Canada, might think that in a great crisis such as that with which the country was then faced, almost any methods to save the liberties of the world would be justified.

One of. the reasons why I intervened in this debate was because of some remarks that fell from the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) with regard to the position taken by Sir Wilfrid Laurier on the question of political corruption when he was leading the so-called Liberal party. The leader of the Opposition quoted some remarks made by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, as well as some remarks of the then former member for West Toronto, Mr. Osier. I happened to be a member of the House when the remarks which the hon. gentleman quoted from Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. E. B. Osier, were made. I well remember that celebrated debate, and there are members of the House -I do not see them in the Chamber this

afternoon-who also were members of the House at that time. I want to give a little of the history of this case, because I took a very deep interest in it.
The debate occurred on what was known as the Brockville and West Huron byelections. These two by-elections had been held in 1899 to fill two vacancies, one for Brockville and one for West Huron, and it was charged in the House by the present Prime Minister, then Mr. R. L. Borden, that the grossest corruption had taken place in both. An inquiry was held before the Committee on Privileges and Elections in 1899, and although the evidence offered was of a most important, convincing, and I might add, disgusting character, the partisan majority of that committee failed to make a report to the House in accordance with the evidence; it merely reported the evidence and left the matter for the House to deal with. In the following session Mr. Borden, who was then the lieutenant of the leader of the Opposition, Sir Charles Tupper, re-introduced the subject, and asked that the ease be again referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections. But notwithstanding the evidence that had been adduced, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his following-and I was one of them-resisted any reference back to the Committee on Privileges and Elections. Day after day passed and the debate was continued; member after member on the Government side spoke against any further investigation into those elections.
Now, I dislike very much to read when I am addressing the House, because I know it is apt to distract the attention of members and to cause them to lose interest in what is being said. But for the purpose of making out this case and of making it so that there shall be no possibility of any mistake with regard to what occurred, I am going to read a brief extract from the speech which Sir Robert, then Mr. Borden, made upon that occasion with regard to what was proved before the Committee on Privileges and Elections. I sat day after day in the Committee room and can vouch for the truth of what the present Prime Minister then said. I quote:
Now, the next question is: What did X undertake to prove when I made this motion before this House during last session and what did I prove? I undertook to prove, in respect to one polling section, No. 4 Colfoorne, that 43 or 44 electors had deposited their ballots in favour of Robert McLean-
He was then the Conservative qajididate. (Reading):	'

and that at the conclusion of the polling, when the ballots were counted, only 30 ballots

for Robert McLean were to be found. I proved by distinct evidence before the Privileges and Elections Committee, that at that particular polling subdivision, No. 4 Colborne, 98 ballots were cast, that none of them were spoiled, that at the conclusion of the polling 68 ballots were found to be marked for Robert Holmes, and 30 were found to be marked for Robert McLean. I brought before the committee 43 men who distinctly and unequivocally swore that they had marked their ballots for Robert McLean at that election, that they had handed their ballots to the deputy returning officer, and that they believed he had deposited them in the ballot box. I also showed that 125 ballots had been delivered in the first instance to the deputy , returning officer, Donald Cummings, and that twenty-seven were unused. I need not go into the various minor irregularities of the appointment of four scrutineers for Mr. Holmes at that polling place, and the disregard of the provisions of the election law in regard to giving information during the holding of the poll as to what electors had voted and what electors had not voted.
Mr. Borden then went over the evidence of Donald Cummings, one of the deputyreturning officers. Fourteen ballots were produced. They had been deposited in the box; they bore the initial of this Donald Cummings, the deputy returning officer, and they were supposed to have come off the ballot pad. As you, Sir, and every hon. member must know, these pads are cut with a cleaver, and they could not vary in width one hair breadth. Yet, those fourteen ballots were about one-eighth of an inch wider than the ballots on the official pad from which they weie supposed to come. In addition to that the ballots were twice as thick as the ballots on the stub from which they were supposed to be taken. There was produced before the committee a paper expert from Eddy's mills, Mr. Harvey, and he placed his micrometer on the bogus ballots which he declared were twice as thick as the ballots belonging to the regular pad. I sat by and heard this Donald Cummings first swear that the initials on the ballots -were his. He was not so definitely sure about that later on when he was cornered up, but he had to take some position, for there is no doubt that the ballots bore his initials. They, never came off the pad; they were switched in and placed in the ballot box by some nefarious operators, and in that way the worst possible fraud as practised in that election, the same as in Brockville.
I have one more extract which I think I ought to read to the House. In that election, there was employed a man named Pritchett, a man whose name was a household word throughout this country because of its notoriety in connection with those two by-elections. , It would be unfair for me to place this case before the members
of the House without reading the most important portion of the affidavit as made by Mr. Pritchett, and I am going to do so:
To wit:
I,	John G. Pritchett, of the city of London, in the province of Ontario, contractor, at present of the city of Detroit, (make oath and say:
1.	I have for several years taken part in municipal affairs and in politics in the said city of London, and have acted as deputy returning officer in municipal elections, and also in the elections for the Legislative Assembly.
I always acted -with and on behalf of the Liberal party. In 1898, I was elected an aider-man for ward No. 6, in said city of London.

3.	From my experience in the various elections

Mark this. This is really worth while.
-I formed the opinion that elections could be more easily and surely won by the manipulation of ballots than by buying votes; and after the said general election, I, in conversation with friends used words to that effect.
4.	Thereafter, at the request of John O'Gorman, of London, I took part on behalf of the Liberals in by-elections, my special duty being to instruct deputy returning officers in the method of manipulating the ballots so as to win the election whatever the vote might really be.

Will the hon. gentleman be kind enough to tell me how he connects this with the telegram sent by the Minister of the Interior? What has this to do with the present case?

I now propose reading an extract from the speech which Mr. E. B. Osier, to whom the leader of the Opposition referred, made in connection with that debate. He says:
I am prepared to say without any hesitation that X had a great deal of sympathy with the Liberal party, before the last elect'on. I felt that the other party had been perhaps too long in power, and I had a sort of half belief that the promises and professions of honesty and honour which the Liberal party made before they came into office would more or less ibe carried out. But have we seen one single solitary instance of this? Certainly not since *I have been in this House.
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries: You have seen honest government ever since.
Mr. Osier: I have not. I have seen a government that has made me ashamed of my country.
I contrast that with the statement from the hon. gentleman's speech which the leader of the Opposition made. Now I want to read a brief extract from a speech I my-, self made and I would especially commend it to the hon. member for George Etienne Gartier (Mr. Jacobs). He will be especially interested in the position I took. I was under the impression that the hon. Mr. Oliver, who was then a member of the House, also took the same position but I do not find his speech recorded in Hansard, although I am satisfied from conversations I had at that time that he very largely shared my view. Let me read what I said:
I attended almost every session of that committee and for my part I was absolutely satisfied that the greatest corruption was practised in the election of West Huron and Brockville.
Bear in min'd, Mr. Speaker, that I was a supporter of the Liberal Government.

I examined that ballot pad very carefully, and I claim that the conclusion ws.3 irresistible -that those fourteen ballots never came off that pad at all. If my memory serves me correctly, there were some 150 ballots on the pad, and -the majority were torn off, but these fourteen ballots-and I took the trouble to compare them very carefully-were a shade wider at the perforated line than the good ballots, about which there was no dispute. I made that examination two or three times and perfectly satisfied myself. If there was any possible dispute as to these stubs and ballots, surely a silent instrument could make no mistake in its register. We had an expert from the Eddy mills who came there with his micrometer. He -tested every stub left on the pad, some 150, I think.
Mr. Borden (Halifax) :	One hundred and
twenty-five.
Mr. Richardson: and if my memory serves me correctly, there was not the slightest variation with regard to these stubs. Am I right?
Mr. Borden (Halifax) : That is right.
Mr. Richardson: Then he took the ballot that had not been torn off and we found that these ballots corresponded exactly in thickness with all the stubs. Then he took the ballots about which there was no point raised, that they were not good ballots, and he found that these billots were identical in thickness with the possible exception of one with those on the stubs. Then, in reference to the fourteen ballots, about which there was a dispute, and that I have satisfied myself never came off that pad, he found that they were 4-1000ths of an inch in thickness, while the others were 2-1000ths in thickness, so that the fourteen ballots were double the thickness of the other ballots. Is any man going to ask me to say or can I be expected to say that these fourteen ballots were good ballots, and that they came off that pad? It is flying in the face of reason, of honesty, and I might almost say of decency, to expect me to believe anything of the kind, and I absolutely decline to do so.
Mr. Borden (Halifax) : I might also say that this expert proved that the paper was made on a different machine.
. Mr. Richardson: Yes, I had forgotten that point, but he doubtless stated that. . . .
Then there was the other point as to the initials on those fourteen ballots. I think, and I speak subject to correction, that Mr. Cummings swore in the first case, that- these initials were his. I think in cross examination he said that they looked like his. The conclusion is irresistible that if those initials are his, John Cummings could not possibly be an honest man. If these initials are his, and the ballots never came off that pad, then the irresistible conclusion is, that Cummings initialled these ballots before he went to the poll. And if the affidavit made by Pritchett, in regard to the wholesale initialling of ballots by deputies in the electoral division of Brockville, is correct, this furnishes the sequel that the ballots were initialled in advance in West Huron.
I concluded with these remarks:
It is surely inconsistent with the best traditions of Liberalism that we should fail to pursue and' punish these crawling creatures, these slimy assasins of our liberty, together with the greater criminals who inspire, lay the plans, and pay for the execution of these crimes. Unless we throttle the monster, he will assuredly throttle us and we shall deserve the fate which
is sure to overtake us if we fail in what the people of Canada will regard as our clear duty. Let the Parliament of Canada strike with deadly intent at political corruption, and its action will meet with the hearty approval of a grateful people who would welcome such a course. That in my mind would be the best political move and the best political tactics which any party could adopt in this country. For every heeler whom it would alienate it would gain scores of friends. What the people most need is to be honestly led, and to the party which so leads, their gratitude, when they realize the results, will not be in stinted measure. For these reasons, unless such a judicial investigation as I have outlined is promised, I shall feel compelled to vote for the motion of the hon. the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Borden).
As I said at the outset, the Government set out to resist itha-t inquiry and the debate dragged on day .after day for a considerable time. The idea was tih-at no inquiry would be granted. The debate had kept on until about two or three o'clock in the morning when there was evidence that members supporting the Government would vote for the resolution of 'the hon. member for Halifax unless the Government granted that inquiry. Then between two -and three oclock in the morning, Sir Wilfrid made a complete volte face. He rose in -his place an-d denounced in the roundest terms all kinds of political corruption. I have his remarks here and I shall he gl-ad to read them if .any hon. member would like to hear them. I do not want to take up any -more time than is necessary. Sir Wilfrid denounced in the strongest language political corruption -and -announced that the Government had decided to have a complete and efficient investigation into electoral irregularities, but he added that not only would they inquire inlto the Brockville and West Huron elections, but they would go into the electoral corruption that had occurred in both parties extending back for a number of years. Then Sir Charles Tupper, in- -a manner characteristic of himself, rose and twitted the Government with having hacked down because they were afraid of having -a revolt in their own ranks. When- it was found that they would inquire into the misdeeds of both parties, the fat was in the fire. I never was able to discover really what happened but I could fancy I heard our old friend, the late Jim Sutherland, whip of the Liberal party, talking to the managers of 'the other party .and saying, " We would be blankety-blank fools would we nolt, if we .appointed a judicial committee to inquire into the scoundrelism of both parties." Jim would tell the other side that the country would spew -both parties oult li-f they did .anything of that kind. Therefore, you can understand why

nothing happened. The thing died right there. It was just 'as if a depth bomb had fallen and bit it on the head. It never afterwards wias heard of.
In regard to my own position, I always felt that that was the time when I committed the unpardonable political sin with regard to the party with which I had been associated almost from childhood. I then became what the member for Brome would describe as a. "separated brother." Communion was withdrawn from me and a little later on, when the House was dissolved and we appealed to the country, 1 found that I 4id not get the nomination. The wires had been pulled against me. I had offended. I had endeavoured to stand upon the plane of common honesty, common sense, and common decency and I had tried tto adopt such an ethical standard as ought to warm the heart of the hon. member for Brome. According to the ethics of the then party you were sure to become a separated brother if youpreferred principle to party. I would say to the hon. member for Brome that he talks well, that, of course, 'his ethical standard is all right and of course he is associated with a group-I am not going to call it the Liberal party-that he thinks is all right. He talks like that and I give him full credit, but let him vote once against his party. Let him do so just once and, in the language of the street he will receive a rude jolt; he will find that he has become a "separated brother" quicker than he imagines it possible. That is what makes separated brethren on that side. I 'have no doubt it would have been 'the same with the Old Tory party. If you stand up and talk principle, and if you vote against the supposed interest of the party, you 5 p.m. are fired out of the synagogue without delay and without ceremony.

May I ask the
hon. gentleman a question?
Certainly, I think 1 would like to hear it because there might be a come-back.
I would like to ask my hon. friend if it was on account of principle that he did not vote on the titles question two years ago?

Well, I have not time to answer such a puerile question as that. Let me point out a few instances. The hon. the president of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) has taken the position of differing from the party with which he was

formerly associated and he is now a "separated brother". The hon. the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) has followed suit and he is also a "separated brother". The hon. member for Park-dale (Mr. Mowat) and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), following their consciences and standing by conscription and the war have also been placed in category of ".separated brothers." The hon. member for Shelbourne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) and the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Pardee) did not seem to possess the necessary courage to stand until the end. Instead of becoming separated brothers, they crawled quietly back to the fold. Let us hope that they will find peace, happiness and contentment therein.
The hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) always interests me. There is a certain frankness about him that appeals to most people. I think he believes in his code of ethics, and I fancy he honestly thinks there is a higher code of ethics on that side of the House than on this. Perhaps, as far as he himself is concerned he would like to practise as high a code of ethics as possible. I trust he will be able to succeed. He bubbles over with the exuberance of political youth and it is interesting to sit here and listen to him, because one cannot help but think that he is in deadly earnest. I sometimes think he will have an awakening somewhat like poor old Jim McMullen had. You know Jim, in the old Liberal Opposition, used to discuss pen knives and other extravagances, and when his party got into office he found that there were even more pen knives, and more extravagant things done because the country was growing, old Jim subsided and finally went into the Senate and we never heard anything more about him. That may some day be the fate of the enthusiastic and exuberant member for Brome. Speaking of higher political standards, some who are more indifferent than I am towards him, might suggest that the hon. gentleman takes the position of the Pharisee who stood in the temple and said, " Lord, I thank thee that I am not as other men "-not even as this rather indifferent bunch of publicans that sit around me.
I believed for a great many years just as the hon. member for Brome seems to believe. I had an abiding conviction that if we could just get the Liberal party into office all the ills of public life would disappear. I believed the Senate to be a political excrescence. I know the appointment of members of Parliament to office was

most vitiating. I believed every vestige of protection should be wiped out of the tariff. And I advocated these things. I thought ours was a party of political purity. I ought to have known better. This is rather a reflection on my common sense, because as a young newspaper jman I ought to have been able to see that morally there was really not a tittle of difference between the men sitting on one side of the House and the men sitting on the other.
They are pretty much tarred with the same stick. I had lessons that should have convinced me. I remember one-and seeing that I have turned this into an experience meeting I am going 'to tell it. I remember sitting in a committee in South Winnipeg in the old days when I was a very enthusiastic young worker. I took charge of a polling subdivision-

I was going to say-
