All right, Jacques. I was just going to say, Mr. Speaker, that I ran as as an Independent candidate, but the Conservatives in the constituency supported me very largely. I had no idea generally who the workers were. But after I was elected by a large majority I took issue with the Conservative party at the following session of the House on a very important railway matter touching Manitoba. Mr. Bourassa, then the member for Labelle, supported me, as did also Mr. Charlton and some other members, but I offended the 'Conservative organization. So they conspired with Mr. Sifton, who was Minister of Elections in the Government, and with Bob Rogers, who was Minister of Elections on the other side, and they decided to have me unseated-
Mr. MdMASTER: They are both now on the same side.

-and of course they succeeded in getting some obscure party heelers, whose names I did not know and had never heard of, to swear that teams were hired. Two judges heard the case. They are dead now and have gone to their reward either down or up-I suspect down -and therefore I can criticise them. A bribe was dangled before those two judges whilst they were considering their verdict. One was to be appointed to the Supreme Court, and the other to the Chief Justiceship of Manitoba. As a result those judges, notwithstanding the flimsy and absurd nature of the evidence, gave their decision

against me and they both received the respective official bribes of promotion shortly after they rendered their iniquitous judgment.
Order, order.
-and I was unseated.
Order, order.

That is all. Now,
before I sit down, I am going to say something that will probably appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite. If I were to suggest that electoral corruption had been or was confined to one party or the other in the old days I do not think I would deserve the respect of fair-minded men. I think the " honours " (putting quotation marks on the word) in the matter of electoral corruption have always been about even between the old parties. It was a case of scoundrelisin on both sides. Having referred to electoral corruption in elections where the old so-called liberal party was concerned, I want to say that later on I ran at a by-election in the electoral division of Macdonald.
Hear, hear.
Yes, they will say " hear, hear." You see, it all depends on whose ox is gored.
No, we do not want him.

When you say some little thing and it pleases one side they will all giggle and say "hear, hear;" and ditto with the other side: the middle course is the correct one. I ran in the Macdonald by-election as an Independent and as a supporter of reciprocity, in which I strongly believed at that time, and still believe. I am free here to confess that I do not think the records of Hades could be searched for a class of electoral scoundrel-ism such as was practised against me in that election. Why, Sir, men went about armed with a bundle of blank warrants a night or two before the election, and if they found anybody working for me or likely to be of any use to me they just filled in the man's name, gathered him in, and then a day of two after they filled in the crime of which he was supposed to be accused.
Two men were caught personating in that election-caught red-handed. They were seized by the police and taken to the police station, and their trial was set for eleven o'clock the next morning. Well, would you believe it?-the magistrate, who stood in with the gang at that time, had these men

brought before him at nine or ten o'clock the next morning, long before the time set for their trial. He imposed nominal fines upon them and let them depart, which they hurriedly did. When the lawyers on the other side came along later and were wanting to inquire into the matter, and one of the under-strappers was giving some particulars, the magistrate stopped him with the exclamation: "God Almighty, you are giving the whole snap away !" I just mention that to show that I want to be perfectly fair in denouncing election crookedness. Election corruption is bad, no matter where it is found or by whom practised. I have tried in my humble way to oppose election corruption; I believe that it is a dangerous thing for the country and a very dangerous thing for the party that indulges in it. I believe that such a thing reacts upon the party which has anything to do with it. I believe that a party will receive more votes and have a much better chance of success if it does the square thing on the occasion of the holding of elections.

speakeroldname: Mr. JACQUES BUREAU (Three Rivers and St. Maurice):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to devote any time to answering the remarks of the member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson), because he has been discussing matters which are far afield from the motion which we are now considering. I suppose that my hon. friend felt the necessity of making himself believe that he was alive, (because he quoted from remarks that he made twenty years ago. I congratulate him upon having the courage to go back that far. I am always afraid to look back that far; time seems to pass very quickly and I would much rather look ahead than look behind. But whatever his political conduct may have been; whatever his remorse may have been-
No remorse.

Then my hon. friend is a more hardened sinner than 1 thought he was. Whatever his actions for the future are to be is a matter for my hon. friend himself to settle.
The question before you, Mr. Speaker, is embodied in a motion calling upon this House to recommend the appointment of a committee to investigate " the existence of a widespread system of manipulation of votes, under the direction and with the approval of ministers of the Crown, for the purpose of defeating the will of the Canadian people as expressed at the polls." That is the question at issue.
47i	[DOT]
The motion gives a reason for this request for a committee of investigation when it goes on to say:
*Such scheme of manipulation involves not only the honour of the ministers concerned, but the constitutional rights of the people.
I would be willing to exonerate the minister if he only were concerned, because he is only one man, and one man is very little when it comes to considering a whole country. But there is the question of the constitutional rights of the people. You know as well as I do, Mr. Speaker, that for some time there has been- an impression among most of the people of the country that the last election was not carried on as it should have been. Some of the people are convinced of this-they are the people who have had a chance to talk with those who are conversant with the facts. There are others who are certain that the election was stolen-I use the word advisedly-that the election was stolen, and that the result did not actually represent the wish or will of the people; and those who know this are the men who were the actors in the conspiracy to steal the election.
Now, we are asking that this matter be investigated. The Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Meighen) answers: You have not made a prima facie case, and the time to make it is now-this with a great tragedy gesture. We must first show that ballots have been (switched and that there has been manipulation of the voters who went to the poll to express their views.
The Speaker of this House is the First Commoner; he it is who guides the proceedings and guards the honour of this House. For the purpose of winning your sympathy, Mr. Speaker, and in order that you may see fit to advise the Government to grant this committee, I shall refer more particularly to those votes which are most familiar to you. I want to show that there has been manipulation, and I shall do so by relating certain facts, giving a few examples of the votes as they were cast, and stating how they were cast in the county of Cumberland, Nova Scotia.
Captain W. H. Burke was the deputy presiding officer at Ashdown in the county of Surrey, England, on the occasion of the last election. The ballot box number was 175. Now, certain evidence with regard to the polling in this constituency is under the control of the House, or can be obtained if the House wants to obtain it. I do not want to weary the House with unnecessary deitails; I will give a few names and figures for the benefit

of those who may be inclined to doubt She correctness of the statements which I make but which I am prepared to prove from the public records.
A certain number of votes were polled and counted in Cumberland', Nova Scotia. First let me take the Act as interpreted and explained to the House by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) himself. He said that there was a certain class of soldiers who in the last contest had the right to choose the constituency in which they should vote. You will note, Mr. Speaker, that the soldier had that right, not the deputy presiding officer or any one else. (Reading):
They were those who being British subjects had not resided for any four months of the year preceding enrolment in a particular county and who besides had never at any time lived in Canada. If a man had resided for four months or more in any electoral district, there his vote could count and nowhere else. If he could not specify an electoral district wherein he had resided for the time mentioned but could specify a place in a certain constituency in which he had at any time resided his vote could count in that constituency and nowhere else.
If he was a British subject and had at no time resided in this country, there was no place to which Parliament could with propriety allot his vote and the only way to give him the franchise was to permit him-
I want to underline the word "him," because there lies the whole thing. It was not the deputy presiding officer, not the minister, not the military officer, who had that right, but the soldier himself who came to cast his vote, who 'had had no residence in Canada, but who was a British subject and bad the right to vote. (Reading):
The only way to give him the franchise was to permit him to select his constituency. Will hon. gentlemen suggest any other way of giving that soldier the franchise? Did hon. gentleman suggest any other way in the session of 1017?
I do not object to that, Mr. Speaker. There was the law. The minister said, while putting up a so-called defence, that the impression had 'been created abroad that any soldier could throw his vote wherever lie pleased, and as evidence of this impression going abroad and being entertained by men of prominence, he cited the case of Isaac Campbell, of Winnipeg, a prominent lawyer, who took the trouble to telephone the minister and ascertain whether in reading the Act he had not failed to see something which would justify this impression. The minister said: No, there is nothing.
The minister says that he was not the sponsor of the Bill, but he must have been acquainted with every detail of it, because

lie took a very active part in the discussion at that time. Although the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Doherty) was the sponsor, the Minister of the Interior must have had something to do with the Bill. No man knew better what the Bill meant, what it was intended to convey, to what extent the soldiers would have the right to vote and in what manner they should cast their votes.
It was the duty of the Government to protect every one of the deputy presiding officers or presiding officers at that election; to instruct them in their duties, so that the soldiers could not be misled and so that nothing wrong could be done. My hon. friends may yell " corruption," as a common thing; they may say whatever they please; but this Act was an Act of Parliament, and Parliament had entrusted the Government through its officers to see that the Act was enforced honestly and legally. Therefore, I conclude that all these officers must have received from the Government, or from the proper authority, such instructions as would permit them not only to guide but to force the soldiers to live within the law and to cast their votes according to the law.
The minister says: Come out now and show us the telegram, and where is the fraud ? I will come to that in a little while. What I want to show now is the switching of the ballots. In order to do that I must give the number of the ballot box, the name of the deputy presiding officer, the number and name of the soldier, the residence of the soldier as ascertained from the records of the Militia Department, where he enrolled, and how he voted. I take the county of Cumberland.
No. 9481, F. A. Finnimore, swore that he resided in Springhill. When we come to ascertain what this is, you find that the real name is W. G. Parsons, 3 Mark street, Toronto. This man voted in the county of Cumberland, N. S.. The next is No. 183232, F. Withip, who swore that he resided in Springhill. Upon looking up the records of the Militia Department, we find that his residence is given as Calgary, Alberta. No. 1245, J. Stott, swore that he resided in Springhill. The Militia Department records show that he was from Toronto. No. 709917, J. Ellis Gagne, swore that he resided in Springhill. He is from Albert county, N. B., and enlisted in Sussex. No. 183268, E. Alfred Hayball, swore that he resided in Springhill. Upon looking up the records of the Militia Department, we find his residence to be given

as Calgary. No. 120345, W. Watson, swore that he resided in Springhill. The records show that he resided in Sherbrooke. No. 835021, Leonard Owles, swore that he resided in Springhill. The records show that he resided in Kingston, Ontario. No. 901087, E. L. Skerry, swore that he resided in Springhill. The records show that he resided in Colchester country. No. 417502, P. E. Vermette, comes from 880 Dorion street, Montreal. Yet he voted in Cumberland.
His vote would do the most good there.

I have pages of this.
This is as far as Springhill is concerned. Let us see how votes were polled in Amherst. These are some of the names that are given: No. 457723, J. H. Skinner, swore that he resided in Amherst. On looking up the records of the Militia Department, we find that Mr. Skinner is a resident of Montreal, Q.ue. No. 406212, Sgt. Wiseman, swore that he resided in Amherst. We find that his residence is in Brantford, but that he enlisted at Hamilton, Ontario. No. 736956, A. Russell, swore he resided in Amherst. We find from the records of the Militia Department that his residence was in Lethbridge. No. 802638, Henry Edgett, swore that, he resided in Amherst, but his residence is given as Ealing, Ontario, and he enlisted at London, Ontario. No. 725523, J. R. Wood, swore that he resided in Amherst. The records show that his residence is in Fenelon Falls, Ontario.
What is the name, please?
Mr. J. R. Wood, Fenelon Falls.
That is in my constituency.
That is one of your votes.
He ought to he all right.

I do not say that these men are not all right, and that is the reason why I say that a committee should be granted. Every one of these boys was all right, but he was induced to vote all wrong through all sorts of threats and misrepresentations, and that is why we are asking for this committee.
How does the hon. member know that Wood did not vote for me?	*

He may have voted for the hon. member; but if the hon. member goes to ballot box No. 175, with Deputy Presiding Officer Captain W. H. Burke, he will find that a man by the name of J. R. Wood, bearing number 725523, who enlisted, voted in Cumberland, Nova Scotia; but when you take the same number and the same name from the records of the Militia Department, it will be found that this gentleman is from Fenelon Falls, Ontario. It is not up to me to explain that. I am sorry my hon. friend was deprived of that vote, because I am satisfied it would have - been a fairer vote given in the proper place and perhaps for the proper man-who knows?
He could not return to Fenelon Falls to vote. Was he not entitled to vote at the place where he was stationed?
Why was he not?
Yes.
Because the law says so.
I understood the law gave a man the opportunity

No, I just read the law as explained by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen). Perhaps some other gentleman may be interested.
The next man was No. 198813, Mr. A. Wolmsley, who swore that he resided in Amherst, in the county of Cumberland, and whose residence appears from the records of the Militia Department to he Dryden, Ontario. No. 625333 is another Wood, Mr. G. H. Wood, who came from Alberta. There is no particular place of residence given, but he swore that he resided in Amherst. No. 907720 is John Young, who came from Regina, Sask., and so on. As I said, I do not desire to weary the House with all these things; but the Speaker being a man interested, I thought I would take a few of those names out of hundreds, that he might go to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), the Acting Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and insist that they should 'tell their supporters to grant this investigation.
I have another list from Oxford in the same county. Perhaps I shall find some names of mien coming from ridings of some of my hon. friends who think they have been cheated out of their votes.
Was that vote for Cumberland county polled in England or Canada?

I could not say. It was polled in the presence of Captain W. H. Burke, Deputy Presiding Officer. I understand that he is a relative of Mr. Speaker, a brother-in-law, or a cousin, or some other relation. He seems to have been very sympathetic, even if not related. All I have here is the number of the ballot box, the name of the Deputy Presiding Officer, the names of the men who voted, the residence they swore to, and the actual residence according to the records of the Militia Department.
In the case of that gentleman who had the honour of coming from Victoria County, he was stationed at Amherst, I presume. Where else could he have voted hut at Amherst?
Physically speaking he could have voted nowhere else, but the law allowed him to apply his vote in the county where he resided.
How do you know he did not?

He voted for the candidate in Cumberland county. That is why he swore he resided there. I could not vouch for it, but it is the fact that the vote was actually polled in England. Here are the names of other men who swore they resided in Oxford, but whom the militia records show as living somewhere else. Sergeant Sweet, No. 54147, swore he resided in Oxford, whereas the military records give his residence at London, Ontario. Pte. G. B. Harris, No. 113276, swore he resided in Oxford, whereas his residence is given as in Peterborough. He enlisted at Ottawa. Pte. D. A. Robertson, No. 412847, swore he resided in Oxford. He enlisted at Lindsay, Ontario. There are others who swore they resided at Tidnish, but whom the record shows were residents of. Hamilton, Val-cartier, Regina, Toronto, Brandon or Edmonton. Others swore they resided at Jog-gin Mines in the county of Cumberland, whereas their residence was at Pembroke, St. John, New Brunswick, London or Montreal. Others swore they resided at Shulie, whereas their residence was at Montreal, Toronto, or St. Catharines. Others swore they resided at Nappan or Pugwash, but not one of them resided there.
I think we have shown that there was something done with the ballots. Now, let us see the manner of allocating the votes of

military electors to constituencies other than where they were legally entitled to vote. Take the roster of the 208th Battalion. The number of names on this list is 656. The military electors whose addresses we have been able to trace with the limited means at our disposal, and who voted in constituencies other than where they were entitled to vote, number 240. This official roster was issued in May, 1917. At the date of the election Lieutenant-Colonel W. P. Malone, of Owen Sound, was commanding officer and presiding officer. There were 766 votes polled by this battalion, of which 541 were apparently fraudulently switched to different Ontario constituencies. Of course, the discrepancy between the names on the list and the number of votes polled may be explained away by saying the men were transferred to this battalion, but that is not satisfactory to me.
Let me summarize. I find by this roster that constituencies received switched ballots as follows: First of all, I will take the officers: South Bruce, 1; South Essex, 2; 'South Oxford, 2; Kent, 2; total, 7. Now the men: South Bruce, 34; South Essex, 42; South Oxford, 67; Kent, 28; North Waterloo, 27; South Waterloo, 7; North York, 27; South Ontario, 2; South Renfrew, 1; Brant, 3; Ottawa, 1; Durham, 1; total, 240. That is the number we have been able to ascertain. I have got the name and number of each man who voted, his country of birth and residence. Surely these men, who had been in Canada, should have voted where they resided. The names and addresses of these 240 men can all be verified by the records of the Militia Department. These people refused to answer questions 6, 7 and 8. In order to connect the authorities', my friends the ministers, and those they were instructing with the whole scheme I shall read a letter which was written by Mr. W. P. Purney, in England, as follows:
47 Victoria Street, S.W. 1, 2Sth January, 1918.
To Special Returning Officers and Clerks at London, appointed under the provisions of the Military Voters' Act, 1917.
Having been requested for a decision where questions 6, 7, and 8, on the voters' envelopes are unanswered, but question No. 9 fixes an electoral district, I decide that in all such cases, such envelope shall be allocated to the electoral district thereon named.
W. P. Purney,
Assistant Clerk of the Crown in Chancery for Canada. London, 28-1-18.
I do not see how the Government can evade the responsibility, so far as that is concerned. Either this man was particularly

instructed or he was not, and if he was not it was his duty to get particular instructions.
Talk about influencing voters ! There was a conspiracy among men immediately under the control of the Government to influence voters, and they influenced them not only without reprimand, but were promoted for so doing. I hold in my hand a circular letter addressed " To My Comrades in Canada," by H. A. Machin, Lieut.-Col. late O.C. 94th Overseas Battalion, and late O.C. 1st Canadian Labour Battalion B.E.F.
This Lt.-Colonel Machin, Mr. Speaker, was the very gentleman who I believe was charged with the oversight and proper enforcement of the Military Service Act so far as the province of Quebec was concerned.
He was the director.

He was directing the enforcement of the Military Service Act, a legal procedure which we were assured was carried out without bias or prejudice, and with an eye single to absolute justice to all. We were told that the enforcement of the Act would be carried out in such a manner as to merit no criticism whatever, but events have shown how vain were our expectations in this regard. I shall not read the whole of the circular because I have no intention to cumber Hansard. But let us see how broadminded and fair, how scrupulously just was this gentleman-who of course, had no sympathy with any particular party and was actuated with nothing but a keen desire to see the Act properly enforced and fair play done to all. Let us see what this just and unprejudiced man said:
If I.aurier wins (which God forbid) what will be the result? Tour wounds and suffering were in vain-your 30,000 comrades asleep in [DOT] Prance and Flanders all died in vain-their widows and children have suffered in vain-. all the hardship, suffering and sacrifice endured will have gone for naught-for a vote for
I.aurier, or any one of his candidates, is equivalent to a vote for the Kaiser himself.
Shame!

(Reading):
Laurier would quit, the war-he'd take a referendum-what an insult and mockery to you and our dead. 'Shun! You're warned for duty. Your last Duty-on the 17th December, 1917.

He was an officer
of the Government.

This, Mr. Speaker, was the gentleman who was supposed to be a fair and impartial judge appointed to administer the Military Service Act, and
who was kept in office after this circular had been issued. I am satisfied that no reasonable person will doubt that the Government was aware that this circular had been printed. I am satisfied in my own mind, and I am confident that any reasonable and rational man with the least modicum of intellect who does not care to allow his prejudice and bias to run away with him is also satisfied, that this was done with the full knowledge of the Government. But there must have been some inducement for the writer of the circular to pen such a fervent appeal on behalf of the cause it advocates.
Now, I .submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that having shown that ballots had been tampered with *- and I have addressed myself particularly to the First Commoner so that he may exercise his influence to see that the House shall take proper action in granting a committee;- having shown that those who were under the immediate control of the Justice Department,^-because I consider that Lieut.-Col. Machin came under that department, -were acting as they did, trying unduly to influence the ballots;-having shown all this, and the fact that this could not be an isolated case but must have been the result of an organization, what conclusion can we come to? Why, Mr. Speaker, the conclusion naturally forces itself upon us that the organization that undoubtedly influenced these matters was the creation of the Government, presided over by whom? By the gentleman who sent the telegram, of course. As I said a moment ago, no man was more conversant with the details of the Military Voters' Act than was the Minister of the Interior. Now what does the telegram say? My hon. friend from Waterloo (Mr. Euler) said just now that the minister asked for votes at large, but where, in the Act, did he find even the possibility of such a thing as a vote at large? There was absolutely none. But as the hon. member for Waterloo remarked, the climax is reached at the end of the telegram when the minister asks for a division of the votes or the same proportion "no matter what our allotment may be". *
Now, Sir, by virtue of what authority could, a member of the House-at least an honourable man who desired to be scrupulously just -have an allotment of votes "at large" made in his favour? The act distinctly laid it down that the voter himself should indicate the place where he would vote; and there is a further provision-I am speaking from memory, but I have a recollection of it-

whereby it was incumbent on the presiding officer to use every endeavour to ascertain precisely what the will of the soldier was, so as to preclude any possibility of his vote toeing switched. I think, Sir, that a prima facie case has been established beyond any shadow of doubt. You do not have to produce the evidence that a man has committed murder before you may empanel a jury. If a man is charged with an offence a proper tribunal is constituted to establish his guilt or innocence, and you cannot try an offender unless there is a tribunal. Now we ask for a tribunal and if it is granted we will adduce the proof. Surely that is sufficient justification for one. What is the answer? My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior, who invariably is very adroit, dancing on one foot and 'then on the other, begins with the unsatisfactory and vague assertion:	" I do not
remember sending the telegram." Well, Mr. Speaker, I am not very familiar with the proceedings of petty courts in one particular respect, but I am informed that this is the precise answer that is made to the presiding dignitary in the morning by the man who happened to be boisterous the night before in the condition when his head feels rather too big for his shoulders:	"I don't remember." But supposing-so argues the minister-supposing he did send the telegram, what of it? " Supposing I did send the telegram? I would not send it to the Prime Minister." That, Sir, reminds one of the man who says: " Even if I do get full you cannot smell gin on me; I take rye." This sort of contention does not become an honourable man. The minister does not deny the fact that the telegram was sent. On the contrary, he tacitly admits it, and in that admission he pleads guilty to the charge. We are not even bound to make out a prima facie case-although we have done so in no uncertain way-because the honourable minister pleads guilty. But he goes further, and it is just here that he corroborates the arguments of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie). He says, speaking about the telegram:	" If it ever existed,
it may have been sent by some one under the authority of the general committee-I do not know. If it was sent by the organization, then I have no desire to repudiate the message; none whatever." "If it was sent by the organization" -that is what we claim, Mr. Speaker. We say that there was an organization, and our contention is that the moving spirit of i't was the Minister of Interior. He does not repudiate the organi-
zation, yet he says: Produce the telegram! I repeat, Sir, that it is not incumbent on us to produce our evidence except before a competent tribunal. Every member, the Minister of Interior first of all, will bear me out in this doctrine. What defence does he make? His sole defence is a patriotic ebullition of intense fervor, in which he takes the opportunity to throw some of his slimy aspersions on hon. members on this side, whom he calls slackers. I have been opposed to conscription. It was said that such opposition was cowardly. Well, Mr. Speaker, in the presence of my God I am proud to say that I bad manhood enough, notwithstanding every allegation of cowardice made against me, to stand firm by my conviction. I have no Charge to make against any man. It has always been my belief that every man should be free to act as he saw fit under such circumstances, and I believe so still. But in 1914 when war was declared the Minister of the Interior was then 38 years of age. Mind, Sir, I do not say this in order to>
disparage .the hon. member. But the fact is that the minister was going about the country proclaiming that he wanted 'the 'last man and the last dollar obtainable in the country, and everybody had eyes upon him. He was a prominent figure in the Cabinet and in this Chamber and he was a light in the country, so much so that one day, rightly or wrongly, rumour went abroad that he had enlisted. And I am told that he was flooded with so many telegrams of congratulation, starting from the Canadian C'lub in Winnipeg, that he was perplexed and knew not what to do. "I have nothing to say against the minister in 'this respect, 'Sir, hut when charges are being made that certain people are slackers and are white-livered, these statements being made to reflect on the honour of those against whom they are directed, then I think I aim justified in saying that the Minister of the Interior must bear in mind that the country is aware of the tact that he was bom in 1876, and knows that when he -was, with such great enthusiasm, calling for men throughout the country there was something else for him to do' besides screaming such epithets ais "white-livered slackers" at 'his neighbours. I repeat, Sir, that I do not reproach any mian with failure to do his duty by his country; but I want the country to know the state of affairs1, 'that is all.
A line of argument has been adduced that has surprised me. We are fighting in regard to this matter not on account of electoral corruption but for'a principle; we

are fighting.for the very basic principle of democracy, liberty and free institutions. If we are to fight for these things we want to take conditions as they exist and we want a fair fight. I think the statement which has been made with regard to the Minister of the Interior has made plain these conditions. May I add that when he says that we are at the other extremity of the patriotic thermometer, his patriotic currency has been largely discounted by me ever since I looked at the Parliamentary Companion and found how old he was and what his history had been.
The most unspeakable of all crimes is to violate the sanctity of the grave and to lay profane hands upon the dead. When there is an earthquake, a fire or a civil disturbance, with loss of life in some great city, the order first to be given and most readily obeyed is to shoot down without mercy the ghoul found looting the bodies of the dead. But the ghoul who merely takes a few pennies from the body of a stranger lying dead upon the street is a petty offender in comparison with the vampire who breaks into the sacred tomb of the honoured dead and seeks to filch from the departed his good name and reputation. In every well conducted cemetery men are employed to drive away and exterminate the loathsome animals that defile and despoil the mounds that mark the last resting place of the dead. The police run down with vigilance, and the law summarily punishes, the grave robbers and the body snatchers. Why have we no fitting punishment for the more obscene and degraded malefactors who violate the scancity of the grave? Now, 1 want, to refer to , some of those who have gone down to to the cemetery and opened the grave of one for whom we have the greatest reverence for the purpose of trying to make a political argument. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) quoted the late Sir Wilfrid Laurler as having said:
Well, no great mistake could be made if the Grits should undertake to fight the enemy with the devil's fire.
That cannot be found in the speech delivered on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne in 1906 by the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. My leader asked the hon. member for Red Deer this question:
Mr. McKenzie:	Would the hon. gentleman
mind giving me the page of Hansard and the subject in connection with which Sir Wilfrid Laurier said he was no purist?
The hon. member for Red Deer replied:
It was in the debate on the address in the year 1906. I have not the page, unfortunately.
He says further:
I was comparatively a stranger in this country when I read that statement, hut I must say it horrified me considerably. I think I understood Sir Wilfrid as well as most other men.
It was not to establish the position of the hon. member for Red Deer in this House that he made that quotation. The quotation was made, whatever his protestations may have been, for the purpose of hurting the feelings of the men who sit on your left, Mr. Speaker, and who have the greatest reverence for the memory of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier as they had the greatest reverence for himself when he lived. I repudiate the aspersion that has been cast upon the memory of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the fact that such an argument is resorted to is one reason for granting us a committee. The side issues which have been introduced to gratify various instincts and to serve as an answer to the charge which has been made are not only flimsy but unworthy of members of Parliament.
At six o'clock the House adjourned.
Thursday, October 2, 1919.
The House met at Three o'clock.

Major-General MEWBURN:	It is presumed that the hon. member has reference to No. 120591, Pte. Benoit Bougie.
There is at present a credit balance of $35.34 in favour of this man's estate. Mrs. Bougie was overpaid $210 separation allowance on account of her other son, No. 3166935, Pte. Leo Bougie. subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: Is the Bill distributed? I have not a copy of it.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
Yes, the Bill is
distributed. In considering many Bills I must admit that in my experience there is no advantage in discussing the Bill in Committee of the Whole; but I anticipate there will be more or less discussion on the principle of this Bill and the Civil Service Act of 1918, which this Bill purposes amending. Therefore, probably it is in the interest of orderly debate that the discussion, if any, take place upon the second

reading, and at least the few observations which I desire to make had better be made now.
The principal and important feature, of this Bill is that it purposes asking Parliament for the ratification of the classification of the Civil Service, a work delegated to and imposed upon the Civil Service Commission by an Act of Parliament passed in the year 1918. The classification so-called was presented to Parliament at its last session and near its end, and the Government deemed it advisable not to push forward the Bill at that time, but to postpone its further consideration to this special session which was then in mind.
I assume that in the meantime hon. gentlemen have had an opportunity of perusing the classification, and that it is unnecessary for me to attempt to go into the minutiae of the very voluminous report, which contains so many details of a varied character.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: Do I uriderstand that there has been a re-classification of the classification report which was distributed to hon. members last session?

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
The classification which was submitted to Parliament last session has been amended, and the amended report has been submitted to Parliament and distributed to hon. members. The classification submitted to Parliament last year was not in every case an object of commendation from the public, from the Civil Service, or from members of Parliament. Obviously and inevitably a work of that character was bound to -contain weaknesses and errors:. I cannot conceive that a work of that kind could possibly be carried out'by any man or group of men without containing defects which are subject to correction. As I have already said, it was the view of the Government that members should have an opportunity of studying the classification submitted last session, and it was also deemed advisable to postpone its consideration in order that during the recess its provisions might be considered further by the Civil Service Commission. Shortly after the prorogation of Parliament last session a committee, known as the Board of Hearing and Recommendation, was set up by the Civil Service Commission. The Chairman of the Board was Mr. Jameson, of tire Civil Service Commission, and he was aided by departmental representatives	-and representatives of	theCivil	Service, one of whom	was
a returned soldier. The board held many meetings during the recess and while it did

not have an opportunity of considering all the classes contained in the classification they made many recommendations, and the classification as changed in consequence of their deliberations was submitted to Parliament two or three days ago and has been distributed to hon. members.
I suppose it will be said that the classification as amended and now before Parliament is not entirely satisfactory. I should not be astonished if that is the case, nor would any reflecting man, I trust, because it is humanly impossible to expect a classification of the 'Civil Service of this country, comprising about sixty thousand persons, to be free from criticism.
I have frequently heard it said that the classification is the subject of much criticism by the Civil Service. Naturally, the Civil Service are interested in the matter. It is quite proper and legitimate that they should be, and that they should have every opportunity of submitting their objections to the proper authorities. However, I do not believe the classification should be condemned because some members of the service do not approve of it. The Civil Service is entitled to justice in this matter, and I feel sure that every hon. member of this House will do his utmost to see that justice is extended to that very-large body, who after all are very largely interested in the administration of public affairs in this country. I think, however, I may safely say on behalf of the Civil Service of Canada that 99 per cent of them desire the adoption and 'approval of the classification by Parliament this session, and in its present form. Many of the organized branches of the Civil Service have expressed to me the view that while they appreciate the classification contains defects, and while they realize it may not be possible at this short session to give consideration to all the details, they prefer its adoption now rather than have it go over to another session.
I am much interested in what shall be the procedure in the consideration of this Bill, and I should like the very frank advice and direction of Parliament. If it is given, I shall endeavour to sense it in the very best way I can, and 1 shall follow what seems to me to be the wishes of the majority of hon. members, for after all any matters affecting the Civil Service are fundamentally and primarily as much a matter for Parliament as for the Government, and perhaps more so. Hon. gentlemen realize that it is impossible for me to attempt to explain all the minutiae of the classification. I could not possibly do it, and I am
sure hon. gentlemen will not expect me to attempt it. I should require an army of assistants upon the floor of the House, and even with that aid I fear it would take very many months before we could dispose of the matter if we were to go into all the details. It appears to me, therefore, and I wish to .submit my own view frankly to the House that there are only two ways of dealing with this matter: Either accept the classification, as it now stands, in its entirety, or refer the same at once to a special committee of about twenty-five members who would give consideration to the matter and have the advice and assistance of the Civil Service Commission and their assistants, and hear from the Civil Service, from the public, and any body or bodies interested as to the principles involved in the classification. There is much to be said in favour of either course, and I am willing to accept whichever Parliament desires. There is this to say in favour of the adoption of the classification as it now stands: It would enable us to dispose of this particular item of business quickly and reach prorogation shortly, which I assume most hon. members desire as early as is reasonably possible. In making that statement I have a further view which I must give to the House, namely: that the Civil Service Bill, the second reading of which I am now moving, contains a provision that the Civil Service Commission may add to, take from, or amend the classification as it now stands, subject, of course, to the approval of the Governor in Council.
And behind that, of course, there is always to be remembered the fact that the Civil Service classification is inoperative and of no effect unless Parliament in the future votes the money with which to pay the civil servants. If the House is in favour of the reference of the Bill to a special committee I earnestly hope that we shall be in a position to do so at the close of to-day's proceedings in order that we may make some progress.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am not unconscious of the fact that there is a great deal of criticism of the Civil Service Act of 1918 and all that it involves. I have been just a little too long in public life not to have anticipated that criticism, not to have heard it and not to have clearly realized tne reasons for it; and it is all, of course, quite natural to me. The Civil Service Act of 1918 was truly revolutionary.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: What is that? Revolutionary?

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
Yes. It was truly revolutionary, 'but it should stand, if Parliament has the same view concerning it as was entertained in 1918, when the measure was passed. I trust that the view of Parliament then still holds. I desire to recall to the House the fact that in the general elections of 1917 the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) issued a statement to the public enunciating his programme, in which there was contained a reference to Civil Service reform. I think I should read the statement in regard to that point:
Civil Service Reform, with a view to extending the principle of the present Civil Service Act to the outside service, and thus to abolish patronage and to malre appointments to the public service upon the sole standard of merit. The Civil Service Commission has already been directed to make a report to the Prime Minister as to the necessary steps for that purpose. Such arrangements will be subject to the existing regulations, which give preference in appointments to returned soldiers who are duly qualified.
In pursuance of that pledge to the public, in the session of 1918, the Civil Service Act was introduced and was adopted by Parliament, and I think it is only fair to say that the measure received the almost unanimous support of this House.

speechtext: Does the Bill refer to promotion?
