speechtext: The Bill of 1918?

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
I refer to the statement which the minister is making now with regard to the Bill. He says that the basic principle of it is merit. Does that refer to
promotion?	[DOT]

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: Yes. It refers to merit in the personnel of the Civil Service. I was about to say that the Bill met with the unanimous approval of Parliament. The Opposition, I think, without exception approved of the principle of the measure, and I assume that their attitude is the same today.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: There were some clauses which we fought pretty hard.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
Yes, but I am referring to the principle of the Bill. On the Government side of the House, while there was some criticism as to detail, the measure in principle was accepted, and I think it is greatly to the credit of the supporters of the Ministry that they took the position they did in relation to that important measure. I am sure any one who has been in public life for any length of time realizes how natural it might be for members of

Parliament supporting a Government to have some disinclination to divest themselves of a long-established power of recommendation to office. Now, what did the Civil Service Act of 1918 mean? It meant, Mr. Speaker, that the Civil Service Commission was given the power of appointing to office the members of the Civil Service, and the Commission has since 'been operating to that end. The effect of the measure was to deprive members of Parliament of the power of recommending appointments to office, thus abolishing the practice of patronage, or whatever you wish to call it, which was long known in this country to be an attribute of members supporting the Government of the day.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: Was that a power or a privilege?

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
It matters not
what the definition may be; the effect was practically the same. The Civil Service Act of 1918 was passed, and the classification is merely following out the direction of the statute; and therefore there is in my judgment very little reason why a consideration of that classification itself should involve very much time on the part of the House. The wisdom of that legislation may be questioned by some, and one can very readily realize how it may be attacked. I have no doubt it will change wonderfully party organization, and probably give colouring to the future politics of this country. Yet, I submit that the principle of the measure is sound, and has the approval of the country; and I am sure that the Parliament of Canada will never presume to alter that principle in the future, in the main, at least.
The Act has been in force for one year under the direction of the Civil Service Commission. Now, I know that the commission has been the subject of a great deal of criticism. Its members are not supermen and are not infallible, but I can say of them that they are good, faithful public servants who are doing as much and as good work as any other men in the public service of this country to-day. Naturally the Civil Service Commission will come in conflict with the wishes or views of members of Parliament, of members of the Government, and of great sections of ihe public; and so long as they are discharging a public duty which brings this about they are natural-, ly open to very much criticism. I make this remark regarding the commission because I feel that they have been the subject of criticism which has not been alto-

gether fair. The commission is an independent body; if it were not it could not properly discharge its duties. I think therefore that Parliament should stand behind it or else abolish it altogether.
I know that supporters of the Liberal party will say that the Civil Service Commission is not doing its duty because in a certain case perhaps an applicant who hap' pens to be a Liberal is not appointed.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: In all cases.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
I beg to differ
from my hon. friend. On the other hand, it follows that some supporters of the other party who do not receive a favourable consideration of applications in which they are interested for appointments to public office may be inclined to feel that the judgment of the commission is unsound. It is of course obvious to every hon. member who chooses to reflect upon the matter that it is utterly impossible for the Civil Service Commission to please every applicant for public office. If they were able to do that they would indeed be supermen.
The Civil Service Commission has been criticised for employing as assistants in the classification work a firm belonging to the United States. I have seen it in the press, I have heard it from some hon. gentlemen in the House, I have heard it outside of the House. But, I must say that it is criticism that I have never been able to appreciate. It was not possible to get in Canada one single person who had the slightest experience in the classification of a Civil Service and I commend the judgment undertaking the classification of the Service, undertaking the classification of the service, in going out into the world and getting the best and most experienced men they could get no matter what it cost or from what country they came. They did secure the services of an experienced firm in the United States and, at considerable expense, they have since been assisting the Civil Service Commission. I think it would be a small position for public men to take if they would deny the right to the Government, or any body created by the Government to perform a special duty, to go outside of the country and purchase experience and wisdom if they could not obtain it at home. Such, I say, was the condition of affairs. I hope, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that the Civil Service Commission will not be subjected to criticism by reason of the fact that they brought to their aid experienced men who were not resident in Canada.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: Does the minister think that it would be . proper and in the interest of this country to disclose to the citizens of another nation all the inside workings of this Government?

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
I think it would not be quite proper to disclose the inside workings of this Government to any foreign government or to any body but I do not see any objection to disclosing to the entire world the internal economy of our Civil Service. Many cities in the United States and many of the states have classified their civil services just as we are proposing to do and my hon. friend, or myself, by making a request, could obtain the book containing all the information.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what does classification mean? After all, that is the main feature of the Bill inasmuch as it asks Parliament to approve of the report of the Civil Service Commission upon classification. There is nothing else of much importance in the Bill, although I shall come to that later. Classification is simply an effort to standardize the public service of this country. In other words, it is an attempt to establish on a business basis the work of those engaged in the Public'Service of Canada. It is an effort to do what is done in well organized and well directed business concerns to-day. The purpose, I think, is laudable, and whatever be the future wish of Parliament as to the manner in which persons are appointed to the Public Service, surely there can be no objection to the classification fo the Service.
I do dislike reading to the House. It is not easy for the one who undertakes to read and it is not usually very interesting or intelligible to those whom he asks to listen while reading. But last year there was submitted to the members of Parliament, a report accompanying the classification in which the Civil Service Commission attempted to present the principles which guided them in making the classification and the purposes and objects which they sought to accomplish by it. I have had prepared a typewritten statement gathered entirely from the report and I ask the kind permission of hon. gentlemen to read the same to them. It is simply a digest of what is now in the report-a report which I trust all hon. gentlemen have read, or if they have not, I hope they will do so as early as possible. That report indicates the reason why the classification was commenced, the principles which guid-

ed the commission in the making of the classification and the objects which they had in mind. If hon. gentlemen will be good enough to give me fair attention while I read this, I think it will make clear to them the purpose of the classification much better than I could do it myself. It is as follows:
(a)	The Civil Service Act of 1918 specifically called for a classification of the Outside Service. Section 52 (1) provides.
"The Commission shall, as soon as practicable after the passing of this Act, . . . - Prepare schedules containing lists of the positions and the duties and salaries attached thereto and the salaries and increases or other remuneration that in the opinion of the Commission are necessary and proper, .... and, upon the approval of the same by the Governor m Council, and by resolution passed by both Houses of Parliament, such schedules shall come into operation."
It was clearly the intention of Parliament that the 50,000 positions in the Outside Service which constitute about 85 per cent of the entire service, should be studied and classified as the first step in the application of the extended Civil Service Act. The classification as submitted constitutes such an analysis and complies in a practical way with the requirement that "the positions and the duties and salaries attached thereto" be "listed."
(b)	In order to make possible a practical administration of the Act with regard to examinations a classification of positions is essential. The law under, "Duties of Commission" section 4 (1) (a), reads:
"To test and pass upon the qualifications of candidates for admission to and transfer and
promotion in the Civil Service	
and in section 38, part III, the matter of tests is prescribed in the words:
"Appointments to positions in the Civil Service shall be by competitive examination which shall be of such a nature as will determine the qualifications of candidate for the particular positions to which they are to be appointed. . ."
Obviously the Commission cannot pass upon the qualifications of candidates to fulfil the duties of particular positions unless they know what the duties of these positions are. If they are to wait until a vacancy is to be filled to ascertain the duties not only will a serious delay be introduced but a separate test of applicants wiil have to be conducted for each vacancy, which is an absolutely impracticable method. Only by a system of classification by which positions having substantially the same duties and calling for the same qualifications are grouped together can examinations be held in advance and lists of qualified persons be secured and maintained. Then when vacancies occur, appointments can be made without delay from those whose names are on the appropriate list and examinations need be held only when lists need to be replenished.
(c)	The provisions of the Act respecting the organization of departments also impliedly called for a classification of positions. Section 9, part II of the Act requires the Commission, after consultation with department heads, to prepare plans for the organization of each department of the Civil Service, and particularly provides in clause 4, page 5:
If, after such organization and classification

has been effected, the number of officers, clerks, and employees in any portion of the Civil Service, or in any class or grade thereof, is greater than the number allowed under such organization, the remainder shall be supernumeraries-*
Clearly, if the Commission is to indicate what classes of positions and what numbers of each class are required for the work of any department, it must be able to refer to a classification and scheme of nomenclature by which the duties of given classes are prescribed and designated.
The fact that the country was, and had been for more than three years, engaged in war, with a resulting increase in prices and a corresponding decrease in the purchasing value of the dollar caused an unrest in the public service which could >be properly met only by a most thorough-going consideration of the duties of the various positions in the Civil Service and the compensation which should be provided for these positions in order to effect uniformity and provide for just and equitable compensation throughout the service.
The Civil Service Act of 1918 greatly extended the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission. It not only turned over to the Commission the administration of the Outside as well as the Inside Service, but at the same time made imperative a classification of the Outside Service

I think I am correct'in saying that under the provisions of the Civil Service Act of 1918, a classification of the Outside Service was directed.
The standardization of compensation, the preparation of plans of organization for departments, the organizing of the commission's staff, the examinations of applicants for recruiting the Civil Service, the preparation of regulations, and other matters of equal importance.
In order that the commission might not be distracted from giving its attention to the current needs of public business, it decided to retain special temporary assistants for its organization Branch to make the investigations and formulate the recommendations, upon which a classification might be based. Inasmuch as this work was of a permanent character and of the highest value to the country, and as the time element was most important, it was considered inadvisable to train a special staff for this temporary purpose. After a thorough canvass of the professional field the commission found that the firm of Arthur Young and Company was engaged in this highly-specialized line of work and well able to furnish experts of the kinds and numbers needed. It was found that this firm maintained an organization of civil service specialists, employment experts, efficiency engineers and accountants, thoroughly experienced in classification work, had been established in business for some twenty-five years, and had been retained over a period of years by the British, French, and American Governments on important commissions.
I remind the House further that while some of the Civil Service indulged in criticism of the classification report and of the work of the experts which the Civil Service Commission have secured, they themselves -the Civil Service-have employed experts from the United States in the matter of

classification and brought them to Ottawa to study the subject.
The staff thus secured was assigned the work of the permanent staff of the organization provided under the general direction of the commission. Its work was carried on according to principles and policies approved by the commission.
The next paragraph of the statement reads as follows:
What the Classification is.
Classification is the bringing together of like things. This particular study has endeavoured to bring together positions of like nature. The basis of the classification has been the duties and responsibilities of the positions existing in the Civil Service. Positions having similar duties and responsibilities were thus brought together in what is called a class. All such positions were then given a standard title, a standard definition of duties, standard qualifications and requirements, suggested lines of promotion, and a standard salary range. By this process the sixty or more thousand positions in the Civil Service were grouped into approximately 1,600 standard classes. These classes further gathered together into thirty-four occupational groupings called services-
To which I will refer later.
-and within the services they were grouped, on the basis of responsibility, into ranks, the classes of lesser responsibility being placed in the lower ranks, and the classes of greater responsibility in the higher ranks. The classification does not attempt to present an ideal classification. The attempt has been made to classify the positions now existing in the service whether such positions indicate good organization or bad organization.
The principles and policies adopted as a basis for the recommended schedules of compensation were as follows:
1.	That rates of compensation should be uniform for the same work. This means the same hours and the same pay should apply to all positions of the same class, and automatically to the incumbents of such positions.
2.	That rates of compensation should be relatively right for the different classes.
3.	That the rate for each class of employment should be equitable, that is, fair to the employee and fair to the tax-paying public.
4.	That the schedules of compensation should provide for an absolute minimum and an absolute maximum and intermediate rates in this range. The minimum is to be that compensation to which an employee should be entitled immediately upon his appointment, it being assumed that he is qualified for the place. The maximum compensation is to be the figure representing the limit of usefulness which the employee, no matter how experienced or efficient, can reach by reason of the limitations inherent in the employment or in the work he is doing. The intermediate rates are to make possible a regular advance from the minimum toward the maximum as an employee's proficiency and consequently the value of his services increases.
5.	That the salaries proposed should not be based on the depreciated value of the dollar at the present time. Conditions are not now stable. Economic conditions the world over are in an unsettled and uncertain state, and to
found a salary revision on what may prove to be temporary conditions might involve the necessity of a downward revision when conditions return toward the normal. On the strength of these considerations it was decided to base the general level of salary schedules on what would have been normal conditions for 1918 had the tendencies of the period prior to the war continued and had not the war occurred.
6.	It was thought that for certain classes at least a special war bonus should be paid to employees in addition to the salaries provided by the schedules.
What the Classification Accomplishes.
The classification accomplishes six distinct desirable ends, thus furnishing six reasons why it should be adopted. They are as follows:	.
1.	Equitable Compensation:	The state of
affairs with regard to the compensation of positions discovered in the course of the classification work was exactly that which invariably develops in any service administered under a decentralized system and without regard for sound and scientific employment principles.
(a)	In many cases highly qualified employees were found to be as a class under paid.
(b)	In other cases employees were found who had no scruples in holding sinecures and drawing salaries large or small for doing nothing.
(c)	' Throughout the service there was serious lack of uniformity in salaries for persons performing the same work. In one branch of one department of seven employees doing identically the same work, two received $600, one $900, one $1,200, two $1,300, and one $1,350. In another branch where duties, responsibilities, hours of work, and personal qualifications were found to be identical, one employee was receiving $600 per year, and another $1,800.
(d)	In many cases it was found that supervision has not been recognized in the amount of salary received. One striking case of such injustice involves an employee who has been receiving $1,000 while of the fifty-five employees under his supervision two receive $1,400, one $1,300, two $1,200, and several $1,100.
(e)	Considerations of humanity one often finds to be a prolific source of over payment. One official was found of advanced age who at present is practically incapacitated but is retained at a very substantial salary and doing purely nominal duties.
Such anomalies will, through the proper administration of the classification, disappear within a few years. It is the plan to raise to the minimum provided for each class the salaries of all persons in such classes which are at present below the minimum. This action will go half the way by giving incumbents of all positions at least what the minimum of the class calls for. The other half of the standardizing process, namely paying no more than the maximum provided for the class, will take some time for the accomplishment, as according to the proposed Bill incumbents receiving more than the maximum of their positions will not be reduced, but will be allowed to retain not only their present compensation but also be permitted to advance to the maximum of their cItss obtained under the 1908 classification. When such employees retire from the service, however, their positions will be filled at the minimum rate.
2.	Advanced Employment Administation: Inasmuch as the classification provides not only standard compensation but also a uniformity of nomenclature, the Civil Service Commission and the employers, that is the department heads,



are enabled to deal with each other in a uniform and standard commodity, that is to say the titles of positions are standard throughout the service. The department may requisition six clerk-stenographers, one assistant chemist, one hydrometric engineer, two statistical clerks, and one office boy with the assurance that the Civil Service Commission will send to them appointees having qualified for these particular classes, and therefore having the standard qualifications, and toeing able to perform the duties prescribed for these respective positions. This decided advantage in making requisitions and appointments is manifestly just as advantageous in connection with advancement in compensation, promotion in position, and transfer from department to department.
3.	Standard Employment Conditions: From the viewpoint of the man on the street seeking to enter the civil service, or of the employee already in the service, the classification presents standard employment conditions throughout. A study of the classification volume, particularly of the sequences of positions as set forth in the rank and service groupings will indicate to the prospective or present civil servant just what his chances are for entering or having already entered, promotion in the civil service. He finds that the positions are set forth under standard titles. In the definitions of the respective classes, he finds the duties and responsibilities of the position for which he seeks appointment clearly set forth, and also the minimum qualifications which he is expected to have upon taking the examination clearly specified, so that if he does not already possess these qualifications he may take steps to secure them. In addition, he finds that standard compensation rates for the various positions have been set up and he may accept am appointment with the assurance that he is getting at least what the position is worth and also that upon the performance of efficient work he may be advanced from rate to rate within the range, until he reaches the maximum. The promotion examinations provided for will make it possible for an employee possessing the required qualifications to attain any position in the Civil Service.	-
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not think I need read further from this statement, which, as I have already intimated, is a series of extracts from the report of the Civil Service Commission which accompanied the classification submitted to Parliament at the last session. This report is a very interesting document, and 1 hope that it will be read by hon. members. I do not expect concurrence in all the views expressed therein-I certainly do not concur in all of them myself. But I think 1 can truthfully say that it contains much matter of great interest to any person interested in the welfare and efficiency of the Public Service. The statement which I have just read gives almost unanswerable arguments in support of the necessity of the classification which is now submitted to Parliament, as well as of the classification itself.
I do not know whether hon. gentlemen have examined the classification report which I tabled two days ago. It is pracfMr A. K. Maclean.]
tically of the same size and same number of pages as the classification submitted at the last session. However, the classification is improved by the inclusion, in the latter portion of the book, of a grouping of Oivil service positions into classes. At page 787 of the classification you will find a grouping of all those engaged in the service of the country, Inside and 'Outside Services, into thirty-four classes. There are, for instance, the following services: Natural science service, engineering service, postal service, book-keeping, accounting and statistical service, legal service, physician service, chap-"lain service, instructional service, commercial development service, police service, marine navigation service, marine engine-man service, marine skilled labour service, and so on. Inat simply means that the commission were able to group into thirty four divisions all those engaged in the Public Service, and having done that they believed they were in a position to recommend that the compensation to the various ranks within eacn of these services be standardized and fixed.
Following this list of classes grouped by services, you will find that each service is divided into ranks and the minimum and maximum rates of compensation for each rank are stated. For instance, I have before [DOT]me the page which refers to the agricultural research and development service. This service is divided into six ranks, beginning with: " Canning Specialists " and ending with " Plant Disease Investigator," the minimum salary being $75 a month and the maximum $120.
In reference to the designation or nomenclature of the positions, I may say that the classification does not introduce any new positions; it simply attempts to classify positions that are now in existence. The fact that positions are given a title sh.uld not destroy the value of the work, as has been argued' by critics of the classification. There are in the Civil, Service men or women, boys or girls, carrying out the duties of the positions set forth under these different services and their various ranks. Although the positions may be designated by terms different from those by which they have been generally known, still, the effort of the commission has been to designate each position according to the duties to be performed by the one who holds it.
Rank 2 of the agricultural service commences with " Assistant Apiarist," and ends with " Supervisor of Illustration Stations," the salaries running from $120 to $150 a month.

Rank 3 commences with animal husbandman and ends with tobacco specialist, the salaries ranging all the way from $160 to $200 per month. Rank 4 commences with the position of animal pathologist and ends with the supervisor of agricultural instruction, with salaries ranging from $185 to $225 per month. Then follow ranks 5 and -
6.	All the services are divided into several ranks, and most of them are, I think, limited to about six different ranks.
It will be found that the post office service includes nobody other than those engaged in that service. If you take another service such as the engineering service, that will apply to many in the Outside Service and in the Inside Service. It will apply to positions in the Marine Department, the Department of Public Works and other departments of the public service, where engineering services are required. This is an effort to pay the same compensation for the same work no matter in what department of the Government a civil servant may at present be employed.
It might be interesting to hon. gentlemen present if I should give a few more illustrations of the inequalities in compensation in the Civil Service. It was a matter of fair criticism in the past that members of the Outside Service in particular had never received justice as regards compensation. I know in my constituency of Halifax of great inequalities, and I know very well just how they occurred. It would happen that when one political party was in power, friends of that party would receive some consideration from the sitting member or from some members of the Government and would receive promotions and increases in compensation while those in the service belonging to the other party would be entirely neglected. I think I can say this very frankly to the House, because hon. gentlemen are just as well aware of it as I am, and it was a weakness as boldly disclosed by one party as by another. It would be impossible to find a body of intelligent men who would dedicate themselves to the public service if they were not to receive fair treatment from Governments, regardless of their political affiliations.
In the public service to-day there are a number of assistant archivists, and the salaries at present run from $500 to $1,950, although the duties are practically the same. The commission recommends that the salaries range from $1,080 to $1,320. The minimum will be higher in that case, while the maximum will be lower, but I believe it
will do justice to those employed in that class of work. Assistant district inspectors of customs are paid salaries ranging from $1,000 to $1,900 and the duties are, so I am informed by the person who prepared the statement for me, practically the same. The commission recommends a range of compensation beginning at $1,500 and going up to $1,800. Assistant immigration agents get from $900 up to $1,800, although their work is practically the same. The Commission recommends a range of from $1,200 to $1,500. Baggage examiners are to-day paid all the way from $750 to $1,400. The Commission recommends a minimum of $1,080 and a maximum of $1,500. Computing clerks are now in receipt of salaries ranging from $900 to $1,600. The proposed range, as contained in the classification, commences at $1,320 and rises to $1,800. The salaries of customs examiners at present range from $600 to $1,700, and that is, of course, based on no basis of reason or business at all. The classification proposes a range beginning at $960 and going up to $1,440. So, I might proceed giving hon. gentlemen many illustrations of great divergencies in compensation paid to employees in the public service where the duties and responsibilities are practically the same. I do not, however, purpose wearying the House with a further explanation of the details of the classification.
Just a few words as to the Bill itself, the second reading of which I am now moving. The important feature in the Bill is, after all, the clause approving the classification. I should like, however, to read to the House that section of the Bill which authorizes the Civil Service Commission to re-classify new positions in the future and to amend existing classifications, that, of course, being subject to approval by the Governor in Council. Section 42 reads :
The Commission shall hereafter, as it may from time to time deem necessary, establish additional classes and classify therein new positions created or positions not included in any class established in the said classification and may combine, alter, or abolish existing classes. Each such class shall embrace all positions similar in respect to the duties and responsibilities appertaining thereto and the qualifications required for the fulfilment thereof, and shall be given a classification title indicative of the character and rank of the employment.
Possibly it might come to 'the minds of hon. gentlemen that it is asking too much of Parliament to allow the Civil Service Commission to re-classify the service. On reflection, however, I think hon. gentlemen will see that there is not much objection to that. Parliament has always given to

the Government the power of classifying the service as regards salaries and duties. By that I mean that members of the Civil Service are placed in the positions they occupy by direction of the executive; the salaries they have been receiving are entirely due to the initiative of the Government; the Government simply comes down to Parliament and asks Parliament to vote the money, and Parliament has always done so. I think, therefore, this provision is, in the first place, necessary, and secondly, desirable in all respects. It was by virtue of that .provision in the Bill that I presumed to say to hon. gentlemen at the beginning of my remarks that we might very well pass the classification as it is without an incursion into the minutiae of the thing, or we might assign it for consideration to a special committee, asking them to go into the general features of it, because they possibly cannot consider all the details. The Bill also provides that the classification shall come into effect on the first day of Aipril next. The Bill as introduced last year did not contain that provision. In fact, it provided that when the classification was approved by Parliament it should date back, so far as compensation was concerned, to the first day of the present fiscal year, namely, April 1, 1919. Since the prorogation of Parliament, however, a special bonus has been granted by Order in Council to members of the Civil Service, both Inside and Outside, and the Order in Council provides that the bonus shall continue until the end of the present fiscal year.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: Does that bonus apply to all the Civil Service, or not beyond a certain salary?

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: It does not apply to all; there are some exceptions. I have not read the Order in Council for some time, but I laid it on the Table a few days ago. It provides, however, that those to whom it does apply shall receive the bonus until the beginning of the next fiscal year. Therefore, it would not have been fair to the country to enact that the classification, so far as compensation is concerned, should date back to the beginning of the present fiscal year.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
Was that Order in
Council passed under the authority of the War Measures Act?

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
I think it was. I do not think there was any other authority, except this: Parliament voted $10,000,000 for the purpose of this bonus, and to that extent we had the authorization of 
Parliament. The mode of distribution was settled by the Government, and if they did not have inherent powers which I think they likely would have under the vote, they would have authority under the War Measures Act. I think, however, they had inherently the right under the vote.
The Bill before the House does not contain two provisions which were in the Bill introduced last session. The Bill introduced by me last session contained a clause empowering the Government to enlarge the membership of the commission from three to five, and provided a method whereby the membership might be automatically reduced in course of time to three. The view had been strongly pressed upon the Government at that time that the commission should be enlarged so as to permit of direct representation-upon it of the returned soldiers. At that time rightly or wrongly there was also considerable complaint manifested both outside and within the House that the returned men were not securing appointments in sufficient numbers to the public service. Whatever may have been the merits of that criticism then, it cannot possibly be urged to-day. I fancy there is no country in the world doing so much for the returned men, so far as appointments to the Civil Service are concerned, as Canada is, and I think we can say that of Canada generally in respect to all matters of justice and fair treatment to the returned soldier. I am informed by the commission that !i5 per cent of those being appointed to the Civil Service to-day are returned m'en; in fact, nearly all those being appointed are returned men. No other country has gone so far as we have in this respect, that we have by statute directed that returned men shall receive preferential treatment in examinations for admission to the Civil Service, and further, we have provided no age limit for entrance. I assume that some time Parliament will take this matter further into consideration. As it stands to-day, it reads as if this preferential treatment would extend forever, and I frankly say I think it works an injustice in some respects. I would be just as anxious to see appointed to the Civil Service the qualified dependent, the widow or the child of the man who had fallen in France, as the soldier who was fortunate enough to come back. I think in many respects we have gone too far altogether in our restrictions, and have shut out possibly a very deserving element which has a close relationship to the returned men. However, that pro-

vision bad been in effect by Order in Council long before the Civil Service Bill was introduced, and that I presume is the reason why it went into the Bill just in that form. If Parliament thinks that provision should be amended, I shall be bold and shall not hesitate a moment to make an amendment if it seems light so to do.
Coming back to the membership of the Commission, by reason of the facts which I have just related, the Government were of the view that there was no necessity for enlarging the personnel of the commission at the present time, and I think the position of the Government should receive the endorsation of the House. I have reason to believe that it has the approval of the many representatives of the returned men at the present time. However, this is a matter upon which the Government are not inflexible, and if anybody can give very good reasons for enlarging the commission they will receive the consideration they deserve.
The Bill of last year also provided that the members of the Civil Service Commission should have the status of deputy ministers, That wias left out in the printing of this Bill, but it will be inserted as an amendment. It is a matter upon which I should like to hear from the House. Personally, I think it is only fair that the members of the Civil Service Commission should receive that status. They are a hard-worked body. I cannot conceive of any body in the public service, with possibly few exceptions, which is obliged to do the volume of work the Civil Service Commission is obliged to do, Furthermore, it is a disagreeable duty they have to perform, involving the constant hearing of complaints, having accusations made against their motives and actions, and finding themselves opposed by persons of influence. I think on the whole, being members of a body which should be entirely independent, they should have the rank and status of deputy minister. It involves only a very small financial consideration.
I have been discussing a matter which perhaps is not very interesting, but I .am very grateful for the exceedingly kind attention -which iso many lion, gentlemen have .shown' me to-day. At present there is nothing further I desire to say, except to move the second reading of the Bill.

speechtext: Will the minister indicate in the Bill wherein the amendments differ from the law as it at present stands?

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite right in asking that question. Possibly I should have referred more in detail to the Bill.

speechtext: If I remember rightly, in 1918 there was a provision in the Bill we passed then that when the classification was made no employee should be put in a class with a salary lower than that which he might he receiving at the time of the classification. It seems to me that that clause is repealed by the Bill presented to-day, and I should like an explanation.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
On page 2 will be found certain clauses in reference to temporary employment. Clause 23 empowers the Commission to employ, by reason of a temporary pressure of work, extra assistance on a written report of the deputy head that such extra assistance is required; and subsection 4 of section 23 is- as follows:
(4) When employees are required on short notice for emergency work outside the city of Ottawa, the responsible agent or officer of the department requiring such extra assistance may engage the necessary employees, and the said agent or officer in each case shall forthwith report to the Commission through the deputy head of his department the names of the persons so employed. No such employment shall extend beyond thirty days unless approved by the Commission.
The purpose of that section is to enable some administrative head in. the outside service at any distance from Ottawa personally to employ any assistants who are urgently needed temporarily. It frequently happens th^t at some place, say Vancouver, it is necessary for the marine agency to employ someone for some temporary and unforeseen work, and it would occasion in some instances endless delay and embarrassment if 'the officer at Victoria, for instance, were obliged to write to Ottawa for permission to^employ such persons. It .is provided, however, that persons so employed shall not be continued for more than thirty days.

Nothing in this Act shall be construed to prejudicially affect the status or the present salary or rights to future increase of any officer, clerk or employee, whether permanent or temporary, who is dn the Civil Service on the date of the coming into force of this Act

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: I feel it my duty to remind the House that we are not in committee and each hon. member is limited to one speech. The hon. member for Halifax (Hon. A. K. Maclean) has the floor at present, and while a great deal of latitude has been allowed in the putting of questions, I submit that they are in the main relevant to matters of detail and have nothing to do with the principle of the Bill. I shall therefore ask the House to conform more strictly to the rules of debate, leaving questions of detail to be discussed in committee.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
Do I understand that this Bill-is to be referred to a special committee? If it is, then the House will be debarred from a discussion of its varioris clauses. As usual, it will go to a special committee, whose report will be submitted and carried.
Mr. A. It. MACLEAN: The report of the special committee if it is decided to send the Bill to one, will come back to the House and in due course be referred to a committee of the whole House, when all details may be discussed.
However, I am anxious to give any explanation of the Bill I can. The next clause in the Bill, which is new and to which I would like to ask the attention of hon. gentlemen, is to be found on page 3 and it refers to examination:
(1) The examinations held by the Commission to establish lists of persons eligible for appointment may be written or oral in the form of a demonstration of skill or any combination of these, and shall be of a character fairly to test and determine the relative fitness and ability of candidates actually to perform the duties of the class to which they seek to be appointed.
The purpose of that is to make the examination a test of the duties of the work to be performed by the applicant. This is an answer to the criticism of the Civil Service examinations which I heard somebody in the House making the other day. I think it was on your left, Mr. Speaker, but I am not certain as to that. I think that the provisions of the Bill should meet with the commendation of hon. gentlemen. There really is no important departure from the Civil Service Act of 1918. In most respects the amendments are very trifling. Of course,

the clauses with respect to classification, compensation and promotions are new, hut in other respects the amendments are not very important, and I think they might with more satisfaction be discussed in Committee of the Whole House.

speechtext:
It is provided by section 43 of the Bill that:
Appointments to the Civil Service shall be upon competitive examination. Whenever a vacancy in any position in the Civil Service is to be filled, the deputy head shall request the Commission to make an appointment.
I was under the impression that in the old Bill returned soldiers had the preference.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: If I understand the statement of the hon. the minister (Mr. Maclean) the Bill is to go to a committee, but he asks the House to put through the classification without the examination of the schedules.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: I meant that the classification should go to the committee too.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
I am very glad to hear that, because I have only had this classification book upon my desk within the last hour, and I have not been able to look it over. There were such gross errors in the first classification that one would naturally be a little bit suspicious as to what this present one may contain. I have no desire to unduly criticise the members of the commission, but I think I ought to draw the attention of the House to at least one or two things in the classification that was sent down to us last year and which would justify us in giving some care to any document that they might present for our consideration. In the report transmitting the classification of last year we read:
The staff thus secured was assigned to work with the permanent staff ot the Organization Branch under the general direction of the Commission. Its work was carried on according to principles and policies approved by the Commission, and each step in the programme was considered and sanctioned before it was taken.
I gathered from that statement that the commissioners had read the classification and that they knew what the book contained. I am not sure whether I am mistaken in that but if we are to understand that they had examined this classification.
then all I can say is that they sent us a most extraordinary document. I find some statements set out here that somewhat astonished me in view of the experience of the chairman of the commission. I have just had time to notice that they have been corrected in the classification that we have had presented to us to-day. As an example, we read in last year's classification that the duties of the Clerk of the Privy Council are to attend the meetings of the Privy Council, take minutes of the proceedings, and so on. I can only conclude, after reading that definition of duties, that the commissioners, and especially the chairman of the commission, who at one time was a member of the Privy Council, could not possibly have given any consideration to the document that they sent to this House to be adopted. It makes it imperative that we should go into this classification with a good deal of thoroughness.
I find, in so far as I have been able to look into this book in the few minutes during which it has been available to me, that they have corrected some of these things but there is one particular place where I find that a correction has not been made.
I have some knowledge of the printing business and I was surprised to find that the superviser of composition gets $2,640 while the superviser of press work gets $2,400. There is no question that the latter is a much more highly skilled man and requires greater technical knowledge than the former. That remains as it was before. I shall refer to another point and then I will drop this side of it. I find that the maximum salary for translators still remains at $1,680. That is about the salary a man gets for driving a street car in the city and it does not seem to be at all adequate. With such things as these in the classification, I think it requires examination page by page and clause by clause. If a committee is going to undertake that, as I think it ought to, it has a pretty big job on its hands.
I have been wondering by what authority the commission spent $100,000 on this classification. Was there any vote of this House or any Order in Council providing for that amount to [DOT] be spent, or did they spend it on their own responsibility? I have been endeavouring to ascertain, but I cannot find any specific authority having been given for such a large expenditure.
I am among those who entirely disagree with the employment of experts of the character who have been engaged on this work, and the proof that something better might have been done lies right before us in the

new classification. Their finished work was submitted to the members of the Civil Service, and it was submitted unofficially to the general public through the columns of the daily papers in the city of Ottawa. In fact, Mr. Speaker, it has been submitted practically to everybody in the country except the members of this House. The representatives of the people are the only ones who have not yet been consulted, or been advised in any way, as to what was being done. So far it has not been found worth while to get their opinion, and I think for that reason we should go into this matter very thoroughly.
The minister thinks it is a small position to take that we should not go outside Canada to engage experts for this work. I would agree with him that if no person could be found in Canada to do the work then we should go where competent experts could be found-

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: That is what I said.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
But I entirely disagree with the idea that competent persons are not to be found in the Dominion of Canada. Furthermore, I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that more competent men than the Chicago experts could have been found in our own civil service. The fact that those experts have been compelled in the last analysis, by the faults of their own work, to submit that work to members of our own service sustains my position, I think, absolutely.
I have just another point or two to touch upon, and as the Bill is to go to committee and we will have opportunity there, I hope, to discuss the measure in detail, I will not at present occupy the time of the House at very great length. Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a remark or two with reference to this Bill and the classification which has been tabled, although at this stage I shall not do so at any great length.
I 'have in the past advocated the principle underlying the appointment and operation of the Civil Service Commission, and I have done so honestly with a view to our getting rid of patronage. I have to the utmost of my effort supported the commission and I am still strongly of the opinion that 'the principle aimed at is a good one. The principle aimed at is largely to abolish patronage, particularly the improper exercise of, patronage; and to the suggestion that such a thing is desirable I am sure that every one in -this Dominion who is interested in good, clean, honest Government will say ''Amen."
I wish to express also, with all the emphasis at my command, my desire to support the principle of merit in promotion. If we were to incorporate in the enactment respecting the Civil Service Commission a provision laying down the general principles applicable to promotion by merit and then compel the commission to adhere to those principles, we would do far more, in my judgment, than we shall do by trying to settle every minor detail; for it is absolutely impossible to do that with any measure of justice. All the difficulty, all the objection, so far as I can see, in connection with the whole work of the Civil Service Commission rests in the

fact that they have attempted what it is humanly impossible to do, that is, to effect a uniform standardization of various activities of emplyoment and energy in the whole field of civil service labour. For any body of men to address themselves to the task of standardizing, with equity and justice and with an honest regard for the principle of proper remuneration, sixteen hundred different activities, embracing all classes, men and women, various professional labours and other kinds of work, is but to court absolute failure at the start. They have, I say, attempted too much. I wish to refer to one or two instances in the new classification which have just come under my notice.
If you turn to page 798 you will see, under Rank 1, that " Physician " receives a maximum salary of $125 a month, whereas "Junior Law Clerk" receives $140, and "Senior Prison Guard" $140. That demonstrates at once the absurdity of any such classification when it makes any attempt to professional standardization.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: " Physician " in that case would be probably one employed in a penitentiary, not as a convict, hut as a professional gentleman attending the convicts.

speechtext:
If he does it at that salary, he could hardly do justice to the prisoners; I should be sorry for the men who would come under his medical care, whether they were prisoners or not. However, I do not wish to be hypercritical in this matter. I sympathize with the idea of progressing slowly towards the Utopian object which the Government have set before them in this attempt. And to some extent also I sympathize with the member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) in his advocacy of a limitation of the application of standardization in this case until we make somewhat equitable the standardizations which are already in working order.
By way of opposing the application of this effort to such a broad field, let me give you an illustration. The Government are building in Toronto a new custom house, which is to cost somewhere in the neighbourhood of one to two millions of dollars. It is such a building that any Minister of Public Works would be justified in taking prid? in its construction and character. Even the local member who was supporting the Government at the time of the erection of the building might be excused if he pointed to it with pride as the

work of an honest and earnest Government. The plans have to be approved by the Government; the contracts have to be let under the direction of the Minister of Public Works, but when itr comes to seeing that the contracts are properly carried out and the requirements of the specifications lived up to, I think I am correct in saying that the clerk of works or the officer who performs this duty is placed in that position by the Civil Service Commission; the Minister of Public Works has nothing whatever to say about it. Any one who raises a question or finds fault with the manner in which the contract is being carried out is told that the matter comes absolutely under the control and direction of the Civil Service Commission. I make that statement after a consultation which I had last year with the then Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Carvell), on the occasion of my putting some questions to him with regard to this matter. He said to me then: " Well, that is now altogether under the Civil Service Commission." If such be the case-and I believe it is-the House will agree with me that it is an extension of the work of the Civil Service Commission and of the modus operandi of the whole Utopian scheme which goes far beyond what either the public or Parliament or the country ever intended. I think, therefore, that the whole matter should receive not adverse criticism, but careful, sympathetic consideration on the' part of a special committee of the House which will be large enough and broad enough to deal with all the questions that may be raised.
One word more and I will take my seat. I am strongly in sympathy with the idea that a woman should be placed upon the Civil iService Commission. We have much to thank the women for in connection with the administration of labour and in all spheres. I want to say this-and I say it without fear of successful contradiction, and I speak now as a scientific man and a physiologist-that a deliberate wrong, an injustice, will arouse the unquenchable ire of a woman and her energies in which she will persevere to the end, far more easily, more quickly and better than it will a man. If I am going to ask for plain, honest justice I will appeal with the utmost confidence to the natural tendencies, instincts and integrities of the woman. For that reason, I think, when employment is concerned, when we have a large number of female employees in the service of the Dominion, we secure to them at least a measure of justice in having
a woman on the Civil Service Commission. There are in the service of the Dominion enough female employees to demand that.
I wish, moreover, to emphasize the necessity and justice of having a soldier representative on the Civil 'Service Commission.
1 do not'think, when all the questions come up relating to the employment and promotions of soldiers, the difficulties under which they labour regarding promotions and the questions in reference to faults that may be raised in employment, we can do to the returned man the full measure of justice which we in this House desire to do unless we have on that commission some one who is fully in sympathy with the returned man. These are only a few 'thoughts that come to me en passant.
We should, moreover, have in this Bill a clause providing within broad lines how examiners are to be employed. We find that almost anybody can be chosen to be examiners. A question came up in the House regarding certain gentlemen who were appointed examiners, and I do not think it was fully brought out that the examiners had the qualifications to examine. Where it is necessary for the Civil Service Commission to refer a question in dispute to examiners, there should be imported into this Bill some instructions which will, in a broad measure, define what qualifications the examiners must necessarily have. I hope that the whole Bill will be referred to a large and representative committee of this House, and that it will receive very careful study and consideration before the classification as it is brought down is adopted.

I see. I shall go on with a couple of other cases. The Supervisor of Char Service in the Government buildings who, from the description in the book is the man who supervises the women who clean up the rooms, sweep and dust, and so forth, is to receive a salary of from $1,680 to $2,160, while a junior translator (p. 800) who has to speak two languages and have a high school education I believe, gets from $75 to $100 a month. I give these instances simply to show the tendency in our country to minimize the importance of educational requirements. I think the committee which is appointed to deal with this matter should take up this question. I believe that those who are required to have a high school or university education should be given some consideration. Otherwise, we are simply belittling the value of education, and we certainly should not do that.

I wish to put myself on record as being strongly in favour of the principle of this Bill. The classification is far from perfect. The minister admits that, and everybody knows it, but at the same time I think the attempt is very well worthy of the support of the House, in order that we may have some regularity and system in the handling of the Civil Service. Everybody who has only a smattering of knowledge of the Civil Service knows what a great number of irregularities there are. One man will be getting $600 and another man as high as $1,800 for doing exactly the same kind of work. That lack of system is attempted to be corrected ultimately by this Bill, and I believe the principle is sound. I am also in favour of the principle of abolishing patronage as we knew it in the past-, except that, in making certain appointments, if anybody in a district has to be consulted, I think the proper person to be consulted is the member of Parliament. Where no such consultation is necessary I think examination by an impartial commission is the fairest and most honest method of making appointments. I repeat, however, that where somebody must be consulted the proper person to consult is the member for the district, whether he be a supporter of the Opposition or the Government.
Last year there was a great deal of dissatisfaction among the civil servants I happened to come across over the classification, and one of the reasons why I should like to see the Bill given a fair support this year, is because I have yet to hear any civil servants saying they do not wish it to go through. There may be many, but I have not happened to meet them. On the other hand, I have received a .number of telegrams and letters from various Civil Service organizations asking me to support the Bill, and I have received no communications to the contrary; so apparently the classification is satisfactory to the Civil Service. Mr. .T. W. EDWARDS (Frontenac):	I

have more than they can attend to now in connection with the Inside Service. That is not the

That is right. Then it is the fault of the Government, and it should be rectified at the earliest possible moment. Let me give another case where the Commission may or may not be at fault. The largest penal institution in the Dominion of Canada is that situated at Portsmouth. The position of warden of that institution has been vacant for some time. The position of physician to that institution is also vacant,

and has been for a short time. Why are these positions not filled? Would I be right in blaming the Commission if they are not filled? From what branch, would he be taken? ho matter from what branch of the Civ'] Service 'he might come he would be an expert in his particular line and would be no better than any one else so far as effective representation of the other branches are concerned.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I am gliad that this matter is being handed over to a special committee, because I believe that there are very many inequalities and injustices whidh call for rectification. lianment, which will afford us plenty of time to pass definitely upon it.

speechtext:
When the Bill was introduced in 1918 I was one of the strongest supporters of the minister who brought it in on that occasion and who is now introducing this Bill in amendment, and I have seen no reason whatever for changing my opinion expressed at that time. In fact, I think that the change from the old system to that which is now in operation is one of the most important improvements that have been made by this Parliament. A measure of Civil Service reform was promised in the election platform set out by the Prime Minister, a platform which we supported on this side of the House; and although that reform did not constitute the principal issue in the election of 1917 it formed a very considerable ground for discussion at the different political meetings that were then held. And the approval with which the discussion was received, and the opinions expressed regarding this policy, showed that the country was quite prepared for the change. That thjy approve of the change that has been made is, I think, undoubted. But it is evident from the remarks of several hon. members that the old idea that a member of Parliament should take a hand in local appointments is not by any means dead. Some hon. members have grown up in an atmosphere fraught with this idea and have therefore come to regard it as a privilege or prerogative to have some participation in the making of appointments, and to some extent they have been looked up to by their people in the filling of vacancies to the public service. This, however, seems to me to be a principle which should not influence us here.. It is of pre-eminent importance to give the public a good Civil Service, and I venture to say that in a very few years a Civil Service appointed by merit as well as personality will so discredit the old system of patronage that members who yet have a liking for it will infallibly see that they were wrong. Now, in order to have a good Civil Service it is necessary that you should have educated and self-respecting civ,i.l servants who are under no particular obligation to members of Parliament or to politicians, so that they may be entirely unhampered by fear and may be able to devote their full time and energy to the service of the public. Eventually there will grow up in Canada, as in Great Britain and the United 'States, a very much improved Civil Service. We must get into the Civil Service ladies and

gentlemen who will be content and free to devote their time to their public duties, having no irrelevant matters to worry them, such as anxiety to please politicians. I have been told by a civil servant since this Bill came in that they now consider themselves free from bondage under this system. I think that was the expression that was used. If that is so, is it not highly probable that the civil servants, imbued with this spirit, will undertake their duties with increased vigour and interest and give ithe best of their lives to the service of the public? I think the object of the Bill is to obtain a good Civil Service, and in principle I support it and adhere to the opinions I expressed when the matter was first introduced. I think that, if it is given a fair chance, in a very few years we shall see that no mistake was made when this important change was effected.

speechtext: I desire to say a word or two, not upon the principle of the Bill, nor directly in relation to any of its clauses, because, when the Bill comes before the Committee of the Whole House, as it is bound to come sometime or other, I hope to be able to make inquiries of the Government regarding certain of its sections. However, I want to place myself on record as being opposed to a reference of the Bill to a special committee. The time has come when some action must be taken with reference to the Civil Service. The civil servants throughout the country were led by the Government to believe that immediate and urgent action would be taken by them. We are now informed that the opinion of the Government is that it would be preferable to refer the Bill to a special committee. But it is well known that we are now in the dying days of the present session, and the labours of the special committee would cease concurrently with the conclusion of the session, with the result that the Bill would of necessity fall. I think that the better way-and I suggested to the minister-would be to refer the Bill to a Committee of the Whole House in order that we might dispose of it one way or the other.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
In making a few observations upon the Bill, I may say in the first place that I have never had the opportunity to exercise patronage in my riding and probably never shall. But I have made a fairly exhaustive investigation in different parts of the country and I must say that the conclusion has forced itself upon me that this Bill is not wanted by either the members of the House
or the country at large. I think we may as well be honest about the matter, because hon. members

if you can believe their opinions as expressed in the corridors and in the lobbies-are absolutely opposed to the measure, while my experience and that of others, as it has been expressed to me, shows that a member cannot divest himself of responsibility for what occurs in his riding. When you tell them that the Civil Service Commission does it, they will not believe you and they ask you point blank: ''What good are you any way?" I think we might as well be honest about it. Every member in this House knows that what I am saying is true. There is no use in trying to camouflage it any more. I think the principle of handing the patronage of this whole Dominion over to three men who are responsible to nobody is- wrong. It is not getting away from patronage; it is only transferring it from a responsible head to an irresponsible one. I have an open mind on this question. I have not taken part in any further discussion. But this is the impression that I have got from members of the House and from talking with people in different parts of the country that I have visited. I, like my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), think that this is too big a question to start in upon now. I have looked over the classification somewhat and I find that there are undoubtedly glaring inequalities in it. I do not think this Parliament is capable of rectifying them in the ten days or two weeks that it is likely to be in session.
The question has been brought up again to-night, as it was before, about having a soldier on the Commission. On two former occasions in this House, in. May, 1918, and also in 1919, I brought this question up and it was brought up by others. We were practically promised on both of these occasions -in one case by the Prime Minister-that this appointment to the Commission would be made. I am not saying that things, would be any better, but I am saying that the presence of a returned soldier on that Commission would be in the interest of the country, because it would allay dissatisfaction. The soldiers would feel that they had some one to whom they could appeal and we could tell them, when they came to us with their complaints, that they might see Mr. So-and So. We could say to them: "There is a member of your own organization on that Commission and we believe that he is anxious to look after your interests and will do so." I believe it is in the interest of peace in this country and that it is in the

interest of the Government. I have investigated these things, I have discussed the question with members of this House, I have discussed it with people in my own constituency, I have discussed it with judges in the country, and the impression I have gained is that the country does not want this method of making appointments to the Civil Service. The people want their member to be responsible for what goes on in his district and they want to hold him responsible for it. I do not know how you are going to run political parties-and we might as well be honest about it-if you are going to take away from the member every privilege he has except that of standing up in this House and speaking and voting. The member ought to have some say in the running of this country and in appointments in his own constituency. We cannot divest ourselves of responsibility, because the people will either not believe us or else they will tell us that we are absolutely no use and they had better get somebody else to represent them.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I realize that it is perhaps a little late in the day for me to express the view which I am -about to place before the House concerning the principle of divesting ministers and members of their responsibility and placing it upon an irresponsible commission. I was always opposed to the Civil Service Commission and much more so since the authority of the Commission has been extended to the outside service as well as the inside service. I think if is wrong in principle and I am sure it is undesirable in practice.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: Was not my hon. friend a member of the Government when this principle was adopted?

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
I am not discussing that now. I admit that it is a little late but I feel it to be my duty to express the conviction which I hold upon this question. I s.ay that I have always been- opposed to the principle of* divesting ministers and members of their responsibility for appointments to the Civil Service' and placing it upon men who are irresponsible. It is wrong in my opinion ,in theory and it is unsatisfactory in practice. It is contrary to the first principle of responsible government. The Government is -supposed to be responsible for these appointments. The members are regarded as being responsible for appointments and ought to be in my judgment, in order that the people whom

they represent, through them, may have something to say -about the matter.
- In practice, has there been any improvement in the character of the Civil Service since the Civil Service Act of 1908 was enacted? Who are the best men we have in the Civil Service to-day? I am -speaking now of the in-side service. Are they men who were appointed under the old system? Almost every one of them. I undertake to say that there has been no improvement, since the Civil Service Act of 1908 w'as passed, in the character or efficiency of the Inside Civil Service and that amongst the best men that we have in -that service are the men who were -appointed under the old system where the Government was responsible to Parliament -and the members were responsible to their -people. Under that system the -people had some protection.
Take -a concrete -case. An important vacancy occurs in- your constituency. You are looking forward to the next election. You know that the press has its eye upon you, you know that the public has its eye upon you and you know that the great majority of the electors in your constituency are not looking for public positions but that they are demanding that there shall be in -the public service men of ability, of efficiency, of character and that you dare not recommend to the Government the appointment of a scallawag to that position because [DOT] you know that the general public would not support you in the next election.
To-d-ay, under the present system, while the member has nothing to say about it, while the minister has nothing to say about it, the appointments- are not, to put it mildly, more satisfactory than they were under the old system. Whose recommendation is accepted now? What is the -modus oper

an-di? The Civil Service Commission advertises a certain position and -applicants are notified that they are required to sen-d in the names of three references. These names -are sent in- -and the Civil -Service Commission writes to each of the three men named an-d they are guided by their report. Now get down to practice. Suppose a position of some importance were advertised and you desired it, and knew that you would have to send in the names of three men and that they would be communicated with by the Civil Service Commission, whose names would you send in? Would you apply to independent men or would you try to find three friends of your own-friends politically, or by reason of church, or other affiliation? You would

probably try to find out from each of them what kind of report he would make. "Will you report favourably on me?" You might ask, " Well, I have known you for several years, John; I am afraid I could not report very favourably on you." "All right," you say to yourself, " I will not send your name in. I will find some fellow who will probably report favourably on my application;" and the Civil Service Commission in its innocence and simplicity, are controlled to a very large exent by what these three or four men who are given as references say about it. Why those of us who have had any experience in life would not give a brass nickel for a bushel of recommendations or testimonials sent in by friends. If you will pardon me one moment I would like to give you a little personal experience. I was in a position for seven years where I might have done something for some of my relatives or some of my friends, as many others have done. During the whole of that seven years I never recommended a relative of mine to a position in the public service, although I had lots of them. I said: "You cannot get any help from me, there will be no nepotism so far as I am concerned." I never recommended a relative for a position in the Civil Service during the seven years, and no such one has ever been appointed to either my department or any other. Further than that, I made it a principle when I had some influence in that direction, never to recommend a man for an important position who applied for it-speaking generally. There are exceptions, I realize, but speaking generally the man who is looking for a position in the public service declares by that very act his inability to work his way in the open fields of competition; and, during my time I never recommended a man to a position of any importance who asked for it. Let me illustrate: The best office, perhaps, in my constituency, became vacant owing to the death of the previous holder, and you can imagine that I had a great many applications for that position. The war was on at the time. Several of the -applicants were men of military age, several of them had sons of military age, but there was not one of them, or a son of any of them, proposing to fight for his country. I said, of course to myself, " I will not recommend one of you." I looked around the constituency. I said: " There is a man who is well qualified for this position. He has only two children in the world, and they are both fighting in France.
If he will accept this position I will recommend him. I wrote to the man
in question and he accepted the position and has filled it in a manner perfectly satisfactory to everybody. Afterwards I got twenty-four letters from as many Conservatives, some of them being men who had applied for the position themselves, saying: " That is the best appointment you ever made." I got eight letters from leading Liberals in the city of a similar character. When the next election came around, of those who wanted the position, some voted for my opponent, some would not vote at all, and some voted for me. I think at least five Liberals in my town voted for me, by reason of that appointment, for every Conservative I lost. Mr. Speaker, you can trust the plain people of this country
