speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
-and if you have in your mind the public interest in making these appointments, as you always should have, the public will support you. You are responsible to the public, the public feel that they are making these appointments through their representative, and I see in the new system no improvement on the old. It is wrong in theory, unsatisfactory in practice, and has been no -more satisfactory than the old system. Can any one of you point to a man occupying a position to which he was appointed under the old system who is a scalawag?-a postmaster anywhere in this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, a collector of customs, or a collector of inland revenue? You cannot point to one. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, and I want to repeat now-it is a little la^te for me to speak about this matter, although it has long been my desire, I have always been opposed to it, and I am opposed to it now. The present system is not working any more satisfactorily than the old system, and I think it will work out less satisfactorily as the years go by, because the Civil Service Commission cannot, in a big country like this, know personally anything about the applicants for positions in the service. If a janitor is required for the post office in Vancouver ana he is to be appointed by the Civil -Service Commission in Ottawa, who is going to advise them about the character of this man? wno ought to advise them, who is interested in advising them, who protects the public at Vancouver in making the recommendation? ihe member; and when you get a man-a member of Parliament, a minister, or anybody else-in a position where he cannont benefit



himself without benefiting the public, the public is pretty safe.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Bill respecting the Civil Service was before the House at the last session of Parliament I expressed myself in favour of keeping the Civil Service out of politics, and I have not since had any occasion to change my opinion in that regard. I do not agree with those who have said that the putting of the outside Civil Service under an independent commission is wrong in principle; I believe that it is right in principle, although it may be weak in some of its details. But I do not think we have any good reason to complain if the Act has not got down to as smooth a working basis in one year as we might have hoped it would. It is like every other innovation; it will take a little time to get it working smoothly. I believe that if the Civil Service Commission is given a reasonable chance it will improve the Civil Service and relieve politics of a good deal of the odium that has attached to it in times past.
My personal experience has not been that of those who know of no case where a man who has been appointed through political agencies to a position in the public service has not been fitted for the position. As a matter of fact, my experience has been the very reverse. I can recall the names of a considerable number of men who were appointed not because they could give efficient service in any sense of the word but purely because of the service that they could give at or near election day.
It has been stated that the country has been almost universally opposed to the placing of the Outside Service under the Civil Service Commission. A member of Parliament might use that argument at a ward association meeting, but I question very much whether many members of this House would go into Massey Hall, Toronto, and make that assertion, or would make it at all before the public generally. If I have understood anything of the political situation in this country, there was, prior to the last general election-indeed, there has been for the past ten or fifteen years-a definite demand on the part of the public that patronage should be taken out of politics. I believe that in this Bill we have an honest and sincere effort to accomplish
TMr CrofherB.]
that end, and for that reason I am going to support it.
I wish, however, to be frank. In the short time that I have had an opportunity of glancing over this book that has been placed in our hands I have discovered some anomalies which will ultimately require to be corrected. However, I do not want to see this measure passed over to another session of Parliament, whether in the hands of a special committee or otherwise, because I know of a large number of men in the Outside Service who are subjected	to injustice	on	account of
their	waiting for this reclassification to be put into effect. I shall refer to only one class, the railway mail clerks. I believe I am within the mark when I say that increases which in the ordinary course should have been made to these men twelve months ago are still pending, awaiting the putting into effect of this classification. In my judgment it would be preferable to put the re-classification into force at once and then, if necessary, amend at a future session the anomalies to which hon. members have referred. If this is done, those who are justly entitled to increases which will come to them under this re-classification will get them. I believe that the country will back the Government up in putting this legislation into force.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is a rule of order that when a member expresses an opinion decidedly against a measure under consideration, he shall not be put upon the committee appointed to consider that measure. All those members, if I am right, who are expressing a hostile opinion to this Bill are therefore excluded from the committee, and the consequence is that the committee, being composed of men who have expressed a favourable opinion, will necessarily bring in a favourable report.
Putting the Outside Service under the Civil Service Commission means a vast expense to the country. A few illustrations will show what I mean. A member told me this afternoon of the case of a postmistress, located 130 miles north of Kingston, in the backwoods, and receiving $80 a year, who [DOT] resigned. It was necessary for the post office inspector to go to that locality and make inquiries. Had he been permitted to do so, he could have inquired of the member for the constituency and had the whole question decided for next^to nothing. But he went to the locality and. back to Kingston; then he went to the locality again and back again to Kingston. Three or four

times he had to make that journey, with the result that the expense ran up to hundreds of dollars. In my own constituency a postmastership in the back country-a trifling affair, but a very great convenience to tourists and others who visit that district in the summer time-became the subject of inquiry in the same way. The inspector kept racing back and forth, whereas if he had inquired of me he could have dealt with the whole situation in a few minutes.
If the member is not fit to make a suggestion about a matter of this kind, why, put the member out. The principle of a member representing his constituency and being asked various things in connect ion-with it for the benefit of that constituency is perfectly sound. That there are some members who are unfit to give an opinion, may be possible. Well then, bring in a Bill to prohibit those members from having anything to say about such matters-or leave it to the people, who may be trusted to rectify the matter in very short order.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: The member is responsible to the people.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
The member is responsible to the people; the people have elected him on that understanding; and for the central authorities in Ottawa or anywhere else to go sneaking round and making inquiries from all sorts of irresponsible persons in the constituency is disgusting, it is insulting, and it cannot work. It cannot last and it won't last; no such principle as that can possibly continue in existence very long. No self-respecting member, no man who has any respect for himself at all, would put up with it. I quite understand why it is that there is such seething discontent in the House; members are beginning to realize what they did when they put the mark of the beast upon themselves.
To exclude women from this commission is an absurdity. Women comprise at least half of the electorate of the country; women are in the Civil Service. It naturally follows that they should have representation on the commission. The soldiers and labour may be left to take care of themselves; they are well able to do it, and they certainly will do it. But I make the plea for the poor member that he be represented on the commission. The poor outcast-do let him, Mr. Speaker, be represented on the commission, because if he is not fit to be consulted in such a trifling matter as this, why should he presume to give an opinion upon the business of the country? It is
49J
an absurdity. We are here-what?	A
gathering of men declared morally unfit to do the business of the country-not only to do the business of the country, but to do the most trifling things connected with the various constituencies that we represent. Certainly this is a matter that ought to be looked into and the principle recognized that the people of this country, including members of Parliament, are respectable people unless they are shown to be otherwise.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
Mir. Speaker, the more we discuss this Bill, the more unpopular it seems to become. It is not necessary for me to make comparisons as to the various salaries in the classification; but there seem to be great inequalities, and however often we revise it,, it will never be satis factory. Experts or specialists were brought in from tlhe United States to classify the various employees of' the Government. After that classification; was completed, there was a good deal of criticism, and it was thought that a further revision might be undertaken by a commission of Canadian experts or Canadians who had had experience in the Civil Service. But, notwithstanding their expert opinions and revisions, the classification is still unsatisfactory, and it is now suggested by the minister that we refer it to a special committee for further revision. It will then come back to the House, and the natural result will be, of course, that it will be still further revised. If we could cut out many of those things to which we object, by the time we got through revising, there would be nothing left but the outside covers.
During the latter part of 1917, when the classification of the Civil Service was a plank in the platform of the Unionist party, it had many supporters. I thought myself that it might be a good thing, and during the first session in 1918 I stated that I thought it was worth while to give the matter a trial. But I was rather suspicious that it would not be a success and would not prove to be satisfactory to the public generally, and I 'believe it has worked out in that way. People who at that time felt that this was a move in the direction of reform have changed their minds. It will be noticed that under this new condition of things the reform party or association or the Conservative Association or any other association that calls for gatherings cannot attract a corporal's guard at any of them. Formerly if the Reform Association or the Conservative Association or any other simi-

lar body sent out a notice of a meeting, hundreds, sometimes thousands, would respond. Why is there that change in the response? Under the old conditions, the selection made upon the recommendation of a representative of the people, who was a responsible person, almost invariably proved successful ; but the strong feeling now is that something has been inaugurated for the benefit of the people but it has proved to be a failure from many standpoints, and the new condition of things has grown unpopular, and those who receive notice to attend a party meeting say: It is not worth while to respond to this notice and attend the meeting. The feeling would express itself about in this way:	Under the old conditions I, or some one of my friends might be an applicant some time for a position in the Government. They looked forward to that and they were anxious; they were ambitious; they attended; they enthused. That is not the condition to-day. They stay away; there is nothing to look forward to except to get out and work hard. While it may appear that this is a good thing to have out of politics, I venture to say that if you divide the members of this House outside on this measure, the majority would condemn it and would go out of existence; but as it has been introduced by the Government, some members would be slow to express a candid opinion. Many have already expressed their candid opinions and they have not been in favour of this Bill. Under the system of examinations, a position may be advertised to be filled by competitive examination, and many young men may apply who have no special qualifications, who have no special ambitions, who are not so energetic, but wfio can pass an examination. There is another young man who, perhaps, cannot go successfully pass an examination, but who, if selected by a representative, might prove to be far the better man; he would be more industrious, more energetic and more anxious to make a name for himself as against the young man who has always been a drone and who would be one upon the Government if selected by the Government as passing the necessary examination and given a position. We might venture to say that in many cases he would not prove a success, but when he is once placed in that position, it will take a'good deal of strenuous work and energy to displace him. Therefore, even under present conditions, I do not think we get the best results, that is to to say, the best men for the positions.
[Mr. T. Foster.!
It has been suggested-and I think the minister is disposed to accept the suggestion-that the commission should be enlarged. It has been suggested that a returned soldier, or a woman or a labour representative, should be placed upon the commission. I am very strongly in favour of placing upon the commission a returned soldier with the proper qualifications. As to the women, their interest should be well looked after, and I believe if we had a fair expression of opinion of the women themselves, they would prefer to have their interests left in the hands of the men rather than have a woman represent them on the commission. But since there are two members to be selected, a labouring man might be selected as one of the commissioners. We are giving a great deal of attention to the labouring interests; we are trying to create harmony between labour and the industrial world, and this is an opportunity, where labour is all labour. This is not a manufacturing, commercial industry that we are considering to-day; it is labour from " A " to " Z." The employees all report to their positions at a certain hour and retire at a certain hour, and they give their best services. It is said there are some fifty or sixty thousand of these employees, and it is only fair to say that those fifty or sixty thousand who are labouring every day for their living might reasonably be represented by a labour representative. Therefore, the minister in giving this matter his further consideration,. should consider, with the question of appointing a soldier representative, that of appointing a labour representative on the commission. This Bill is a very important one, and it has been suggested that it should be referred to a special commitee for further consideration. Perhaps that is the best thing we can do, but I think it might be as well before sending it to a committee to have a division just to find out w.hat the feeling of the House is on the Bill. I venture to prophesy, from the murmurings I have heard among members for many months now, that this measure is so unpopular that a vote would .mean the end of the Bill. The Outside Service, if they had an opportunity to express themselves, would be found to fee entirely against coming under the Civil Service Commission, and there are many thousands in the Outside Service. There are hundreds of cases where injustice has been, done in this classification, and if we went on with it I am sure that very few members of the Civil Service and very few hon. members would be satisfied when we had finished revising it. A great many members, appar-

ently, are reluctant 'to give their candid opinion of this Bill on 'the floor of the House, but if they would only get up and express themselves freely I am sure it would be found that the Bill had very few supporters here. From my knowledge and experience I think the classification is unsatisfactory and unpopular, and if we revised and revised it, it would still be unsatisfactory. I think it would be well to withdraw the Bill and let at stand over for another session. In the meantime we should have an opportunity to study the latest classification.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
I fear that I shall be in that class just referred to by my hon, friend from East York (Mr. Foster)-one of the very few supporters of the Bill in this House-because what I have to say to-might will be, comparatively speaking, in favour of the pill. I am not aware that the question before us for consideration in this Bill is the wisdom or otherwise of the abolition of patronage and the putting of the Civil Service entirely under the control of the Civil Service Commission. If this Bill were defeated on a vote, as prophesied by imy hon. friend from East York, it would not mean the return of patronage to him or to any other member. This is a step further in the direction than was taken by this Government when the Outside Service was placed under the Civil Service Commission. No great step like that, which was a revolution in the Civil Service, could be expected to be thoroughly successful within a year or *two; we could not expect it to be entirely relieved from criticism within that time. When Great Britain took a similar step, criticism continued for at least fifty years, and it is only within the last ten or fifteen years that the British Civil Service Commission has been largely relieved from criticism. In Great Britain the Commission passed through the very same stage that our Civil Service Commission is passing through now. The United States Civil Service has been under a Commission for ten or twelve years. That Commission also has passed through the very same stage that our Commission is going through now. We must expect the Commission to be criticised for a number of years longer until the people of Canada and their representatives in this House become accustomed to the changed conditions.
I do not think that the conditions which arose and existed under the old system of patronage have very much to commend them. The chief evils that exist in the
Civil Service to-day are the evils that developed and continued to exist under the old system. What are some of these evils in the Civil Service to-day? Last session we had a special committee appointed to investigate the working of the Civil Service, and I would commend to the reading of every hon. member of this House who has not already read it the evidence taken before that committee. While the evidence was taken hurriedly, and there was not time to go into the matter fully, many things were revealed that should be known to every member of this House and to the people of this country. One evil that we found to exist, and which ought to be remedied, was the vast amount of time lost through civil servants being absent from duty. Civil servants are allowed, in addition to the statutory holidays , three weeks' holidays every year; but we yet found in some of the departments an amazing amount of time lost through civil servants being absent from duty over and above their regular and statutory holidays. In the Department of Agriculture, for instance, the average number of days absent over and above regular and statutory holidays was 14.4; Immigration and Colonization, 14.2; Interior, 20.9; Militia and Defence, 12:6; Post Office, 20.8; Railways and Canals, 15.4; Trade and Commerce, 13.9, and so on. In the year 1918 the days absent from duty on the part of civil servants in Ottawa made an aggregate of 94,633, which is equal to 315 working years. Resolve that into dollars and cents, and what do we find? The average salary of civil servants is 8800, so it means that about $250,000 a year was lost owing to civil servants being absent from duty over and above their regular and statutory holidays.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: Were these conditions due to the method of appointment?

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
That was the condition
that existed under the old methods of appointment.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: Have those conditions changed?

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
They ought to be changed, and that is one of the reasons. I intend to support this Bill. These conditions have existed for many years, and it is time they were changed. The first step taken to change them was to place the Civil Service under the Civil Service Commission. Further steps will have to be taken by the Commission, and I am sorry they are not taking them a little more rapidly; but we know that they have been overloaded with work ever since

their appointment, and they have been asked to undertake a task which no>
three men should be expected to undertake and accomplish in such a short time.
We also found that the Civil Service was overmanned, and in order to relieve the service from this overmanning and to improve conditions generally, the first step to be taken is the passing of this Bill and the adoption of this classification, which will strengthen the hands of 'the Commission in carrying out the reorganization of the service.
I regret that we are expected to get through with the matter as quickly as the minister evidently anticipates. If I were the minister I would not allow myself to be influenced to too great an extent (by the clamour of some of the civil servants for a hurried passage of this Bill. The matter is one of great importance. It is a business matter that deserves very mature consideration, and any action taken by this Parliament in connection with it should he well considered. The responsibility rests not with the civil servants but with this Parliament for putting into effective operation a system which will improve present conditions and remove the imperfections of the Civil Service as it exists. So that when we are asked to shoulder this responsibility I think it is our duty to see that the work is well done in order to avoid as far as possible any criticism in the future. If the Bill does not pass and become law this session, I trust it will when next parliament meets. But I do think that before it is passed this classification should be gone into thoroughly by a special committee, whether it requires a week, or a month, or even six months; however long it may take to deal with it let us see that the whole subject is considered in all its phases; let us make sure that the work is properly done before we ask Parliament to give its approval to it.
I desire to call attention to another matter which, so far has not been mentioned in the discussion and which, I think, may appropriately be considered at this moment. One thing that is indispensable to a satisfactory condition of affairs is a scheme of superannuation. The committee found in its investigations last year that there were a great many-I can hardly say how many, but there were at least from one hundred to four hundred-employees in the Civil Service who, owing to age or physical disability were incapable of giving the best service which the remuneration they received entitled the country to expect. It

is difficult to dispose of these civil servants by merely dismissing them and turning them out on a cold and uncharitable world, but they could be dealt with, to the advantage of both themselves and the country at large, by a proper scheme of superannuation, and I had hoped that when the Government introduced this Bill they would announce their intention of adopting some scheme that would relieve the Civil Service of its older and disabled members to permit of the promotion of younger men, at the same time removing from the service many of younger years who are physically incapacitated for hard work.
I trust that this Bill will receive due consideration, and that it will be referred to a special committee which will give adequate time to a thorough investigation of the matter; and when that committee reports to the House I sincerely hope that hon. members will see that it is to the advantage not only of the Civil Service- which after all is a secondary consideration -but to the whole of Canada to pass the Bill, adopt the classification and continue in operation a system of filling positions in the Civil Service without reference to the old practice of patronage.

I heard some hon. gentlemen advocating very strongly that there ought to be a woman on it, but upon inquiry I find that those who support that suggestion so strongly are bachelors. However, there is one part of the Civil Service which has not received the consideration that it is entitled to. That is the rural mail service, including the country mail carriers and postmasters. I said a few words in regard to this in the course of the

I went on several occasions to the Postmaster General, but he told us he could not do anything until the law was changed. I hope that this House, in justice to these men, will see that they get a fair remuneration for the work they do. Take a country postmaster; many of them only get $50 or $75 a year. Men are paid less than $1,000 a year for carrying the mails sixty or seventy miles. Those men, considering what it costs them to keep their teams, and the time they give to the service, are not being fairly [ aid. Some provision to improve the position of these members of the public service should be incorporated in this Bill.
Whether the Bill is disposed of now or left over until next session, I do not think matters very much. Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of taking the Public Service of this country absolutely out of politics, and mainly and in the first place for this reason: I have had a rather long connection with recommendations from the political point of view. My experience has taught me that if a person goes into the Civil Service he ought to have recognition of his merit, if he shows merit, and I believe that a commission of this kind, guided as it must be more or less by the experience of the different departments, will recognize merit and give it promotion. That is a principle which should be recognized more

than anything else in connection with this new Bill. The most satisfactory appointment that has been made in the city of Toronto since this new Act came into force was the promotion of the deputy postmaster to the postmastership. If you ask the citizens of Toronto, irrespective of party, you will find that they endorse the principle of the recognition of merit as exemplified by the promotion of the deputy postmaster, an officer of long experience, to the position of postmaster of Toronto. I want to see the same rule adopted in regard to the customs and every other department. I believe that throughout the whole service there should be a recognition of merit in the way of promotion when it is deserved.
But, I have another reason for favouring the recognition of this principle. I believe in the nationalization of railways and we have heard a good deal about it in this country. We have turned our railways over to a board of directors. I might prefer that there should really be a board of experts to run our railways, but I should have no hope whatever for the public ownership of railways if the operation of railways was to be made a political consideration. The great thing in the administration of publicly owned railways is that a man's merit will be recognized and he will be promoted irrespective of politics. The one thing that is creditable to the whole railway administration of America and of the Old Country is that they have recognized merit; the man at the top of every railway administration in this country has risen from the ranks. That is a great principle, and if we propose to undertake the administration of 20,000 miles of railway, politics must be eliminated to get the best results.
I wish to refer to what the hon. member for West Elgin, the ex-Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) said in regard to responsible government and his assertion that if you carry on the administration of the public service by a commission you do not have responsible government. I deny that. The greatest example of responsible government in the world to-day is in the Mother Country where they have de-politiealized their civil service. They have promotions there. The men who make the promotions are held responsible, and the public men of Great Britain, I. think, are glad that they do not know of such a thing as being responsible to their constituents for the administration of the civil service. The United States is coming to it. It takes a long time, as an hon. gentleman has already said, to bring these things about.

There have been mistakes made in connection with our public service. The departments have been overloaded. Perhaps they are more or less overloaded now; but certainly to my mind the path leading to better things is in the direction in which we are now moving.
When we are talking about the public service there is one thing that I want to say; I referred to it the other day. We have to change our way of constructing administration buildings. We cannot have any more of these gothic buildings with the small rooms; we must not neglect to do what modern administration of business affairs suggests to us.
If you want to have a most efficient public service you have got to change your buildings, you have got to get the new kind of administration 'buildings. You have got to have large buildings, with lots of light, with big rooms where you have your departments under heads who are in the very rooms. It is an absurd thing to run up big administration buildings and cut them into small rooms, and then expect to get a chance to recognize ability in those employed. You want large rooms, you want lots of light, and every member of the service there ought to be under the eye of the chief. Even the dhief ought to be under the public eye more or less. They do not divide up modern administration buildings now into small offices with two or three clerks in a room; large open buildings with large flats are constructed. You can go into any modern administration building 'and see the opportunity that is given for recognition of ability. Under such conditions those who give good service can be given consideration. We have got to get that business principle in the administration of the business affairs of this country.
Having had experience in exercising patronage-and while I did exercise a good deal of it in connection with the administration of public affairs in Toronto, I turned it over in every case to committees of the party, and took their recommendation-but after my experience I have to say that I am glad to get rid of it. It may be different with other members, and it may be more or less identified with party considerations. I do not dispute the position of those members, but I do hope we are gradually growing out of it, and that we will get a better system. Lots of faults and mistakes will be made; but if there is responsibility on us as public men, there is also responsibility on public officials, and when they do not do right we still have
the responsibility to us in Parliament, more or less, and we can hold everybody responsible just as well under the new conditions as we did under the old. I believe the public opinion of this country, on the whole, is in favour of the recognition of this principle of taking the public service out of politics, and, with that making the underlying principle of the administration of the departments the recognition and promotion of merit, and using it now as a means for recognizing the returned soldier. Nobody can do it better than the commission appointed for that purpose who will be held responsible for what they do.

The point which the hon. gentleman has just made with regard to the railway administration is one which was in my own mind and which I had intended bringing to the attention of the House. I cannot conceive of anything more disastrous that could happen to the state-owned railways, or to any successful administration, than to allow the patronage system to enter into the appointments.
In connection with the administration of our national railways a board has been appointed with powers independent of the Government or Parliament, and I am satisfied that a degree of efficiency is being attained in that administration which would not otherwise have been possible. To look back upon the appalling inefficiency that existed in connection with the administration of the Intercolonial railway during a period of thirty or forty years is surely enough to cause hon. members to look with disfavour upon a continuance of the old system.
For thirty or forty years the appointment of a Collector of Customs at Winnipeg was one of political patronage. While I do not wish to impugn the integrity or reasonable efficiency of many of those who have held that position, I am satisfied that they do not equal in any way the efficiency of the recent appointee. For the first time in the history of Winnipeg the Collector of Customs of that city has been appointed by the Civil Service Commission, the appointment having been made by the promotion of Mr. Allan, one of the most efficient officials of the Customs Department in Winnipeg, who has served in that department for some thirty or forty years. Now, that could not have happened under the old patronage system. The great drawback about the old

system was that appointments and promotions were usually the result of political pull. When the better positions, as well as many of the minor offices, are, as was the case under the old system, filled by means of political patronage and on the recommendation of members, civil servants ard deprived of any incentive to continue their work or to do their very best. Under the old system they knew that it did not make any difference how efficient they were; unless they had political pull they would not receive promotion. Under the present system that is all changed.
I recall, as a resident of the West for many years, that in the early days, before the provinces there were organized, the West was made a stamping ground for political heelers and men who had rendered service to one political party or the other.
I recall one instance-I shall not mention the name of the gentleman concerned, but the appointment was made by Sir John A. Macdonald; it must have been forty years ago; I remember the man very well.

As the member for South Perth has said, and as everybody knows, civil servants have three weeks holidays besides all the other legal holidays which occur throughout the year. In addition to that, the committee found that in practically every department whenever civil servants felt disposed to have a day off they reported sick and not fit for duty-and their time went on just the same. One of the causes of unrest in this country to-day in the farming communities and among labourers generally is the fact that civil servants are being fairly well paid, with very short hours and little work. I am not complaining about the pay. I would not even object to increasing the pay of civil servants, but I would want them to increase the work which they do to the extent of about a hundred per cent. I would want them to double the labour, and I would give them a small increase in wages. If the Civil Service were reduced by about fifty per cent and reasonable work exacted from them, they would not even then be overworked. That would be in the interest of the country and of everybody, in the interest of allaying the unrest that is now rampant throughout this country. The ordinary hours of labour for the Civil Service are, I understand, in summer 51 hours and in winter 6i hours. If they were giving every one of those hours to diligent and attentive labour, the condition would be better than it is; but if you go into any department, you will find it is a place of visiting-come in late; go out early; do practically as they like. This Government would be well advised and would act very wisely if they would take the necessary time to study out a plan and then appoint a commission of the best men they could get to try this out and see what the Civil Service would be under a commission that would look after it properly.

Several hon. gentlemen have said that members of Parliament have suffered an indignity through the power of recommendation for appointment to the Public Service being taken away from them, and that this power should be restored. Now, I do not think the House can say that I was not frank with them this afternoon, because I did say that the legislation of 1918 was revolutionary, but in the right direction, that it was in pursuance of the pledge of the Prime Minister, -and that I believed it had the moral support of the Canadian electorate. I said further that I believed it would in the future meet with the approval of all classes. I am personally glad to have been associated with this work, 'and I hope to see this legislation a permanent thing in the political life of this country. I am not, however, surprised that there is opposition to the Bill. I can understand the feelings and the hearts of members of Parliament who may feel that a great factor in political organization has been taken from them. I think, however, they can overcome these difficulties to their own advantage and to the advantage of the country. I shall touch on that later. The point I wish to make now is that this Parliament in 1918 solemnly and deliberately placed the power of appointment to office in the hands of an independent commission, and this Parliament without a single protest voted for the classification of the public service. The Government, in obedience to the direction of hon. gentlemen, have had the same prepared through the commission, and it is now presented to Parliament for approval.
I do not accept the proposition myself- and I want to be generous to the men who think differently from me-that it is part of the duties of a member of Parliament to recommend to office. The hon. member for West Toronto suggested the restoration of this power to the hon. members, and my hon. friend from Prescott (Mr. Proulx), who was a little more credulous than I thought he would be, accepted the statement of the hon. member for West Toronto that the Opposition members would participate in the power of recommendation. answer the hon. member for West Toronto gave, and apparently accepted his statement as one likely to work out in practice. Now, there is no doubt in the world that if the power of recommending appointment to public office is restored and the [DOT]old practice is continued, that power will rest with the members supporting the ministry. It would be absurd to expect anything else, and the man who did so would be demonstrating conclusively bis incapacity and unfitness for a seat in Parliament- and quite properly so, for if the proposition is sound, that power should only rest with members supporting the ministry.
The hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) objected very strongly that the power of appointing a postmaster in some place in his constituency, where tourists resort for a few days in the month of August was taken from him. I am sorry the hon. gentleman is not in the House, because I should like to say to him, whom I know to be a distinguished member of Parliament, a man of intellect and vision, who conceives and studies ideals and endeavours to put them into practice in this House, that I should be surprised if he seeks the support of his constituents upon the ground that he desires to fulfil the duties of nominating persons to small country post offices. I am sure the hon. gentleman is qualified for much nobler and more important national work than that while he is a member of this Parliament, and I hope he will not rate himself so low in the future.
I think there are two other important reasons why it is desirable that the poiwer of nomination, once resting in members of Parliament, should foe placed in an independent commission at the present time. The hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) referred to the policy which this country, rightly or wrongly, is embarking on of state ownership and operation of railways. It is a serious policy for any country to embark upon, and one which has given me a great deal of anxiety as to its outcome. I say that you cannot have government ownership and operation of railways in this country and at the same time have the Civil Service appointed other than by an independent commission, such as the Civil Service Commission. It is utterly impossible to- conceive of appointments to the Civil Service by members of Parliament, and appointments to a state-owned and state-controlled railway system

by a railway board or any other management.

speechtext: Is it the intention to apply this classification to the railroads?

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: I was just going to remark that railway employees do not come under the operation of this Act. I do not know of any way in which that could be done practically. I say that the effect of making appointments to the Civil Service by an independent commission has made it possible for the Canadian National Railway Board to operate the .'National Railway System and select their own employees free from political interference, and I make this statement that if you take from the Civil Service Commission the powers they now possess under the statute you will immediately have a reversion to .political appointments upon our national railway system.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: CLASSIFICATION OF THE CIVIL SERVICE DISCUSSED ON SECOND READING OF BILL.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman says, " no," but I have had experience in that connection in the Maritime Provinces where we had Government ownership and operation of railways, and it would be impossible for any hon. gentleman, no^ excepting myself, if he had the power of nominating persons to public office, not to intrude himself and his influence, if he had any, upon the management of the Canadian state-owned railways. The Canadian National Railways to-day have 42,162 employees, and the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk have 30,185 altogether 72,346, and upon that ground alone I say to you candidly that it became absolutely necessary that the power of appointment to public office should be placed in the hands of an independent body. Otherwise appointments to the state owned railway system would be largely political, and that would mean the bankruptcy of the roads.
There is another reason why I think that hon. gentlemen should be glad to be rid of this power of recommendation. Under the statute returned soldiers have preferential treatment in appointment to office, and it is a fact that at the present time practically every appointment goes to a returned man. In the circumstances I cannot conceive of any hon. member wanting to distinguish between the merits of rival applicants to public office when they all come from the same class. What would be the tendency? If I had the recommending power-and I venture to say that this assertion will be applicable to all others-I would desire
to support a soldier who I thought was politically friendly to me to-day or might be to-morrow if I were continuing in public life-a soldier who would support my colleagues and my Government. But the soldier would not submit to that, because it .would be an unfair proposition to say to a soldier who chanced to be a political opponent of mine that he was not entitled to public office and was not to have an opportunity to such appointment. And the result would be that members of Parliament in the end would refuse to exercise the recommending power if they had it; and if they did exercise it they would do it partially, which would be unsatisfactory to the soldier. So that I think it would produce a condition of social and political disorder which would not be acceptable to any one. Some one has said that it is jiot democratic to have appointments to public office made by an irresponsible commission. Well, I do venture the assertion that if there is anything democratic in the world it is the very system which we are discussing to-night, because it is designed, and on the whole I think it works out that way, to give an opportunity to every one; and democracy, if it means anything at all, means an equal opportunity for all. Where appointments to public office are in the hands of the Government in power they naturally go to the friends of that party. Experience indicates that. So that, after all, that practice is not very democratic, because an opportunity comes only to those who happen to be friends of the ministry. I venture to make the prophecy that a few years will demonstrate the fact that the Civil Service Act of 1918 was an expression of wisdom on the part of hon. gentlemen who upheld the principle of the measure. As I said this afternoon, it will have some effects upon our political life. It will give greater prominence to real issues. A great many of the shibboleths of party which we heard a great deal about in the past during elections have gone, and, I trust, forever. Issues and men will count for something in the future politics of this country, and nothing that happened before 1914 will count for anything. Considering the great economic burden now resting upon this country, and the necessity for the business affairs of Canada to be administered in a real business way as far as possible, I think it was important that the principle of the Civil Service Act should have been adopted. I trust it will be continued, and I have no doubt that in the course of a few years it will have the approval of the leaders

of all political parties then prevailing in this country, and that there will be no desire on the part of any to revert to the conditions which prevailed prior to 1918.

Debate on the proposed motion of Mr. McKenzie for the appointment of a Parliamentary Committee to investigate the alleged manipulation of soldier votes in the general election of 1917, resumed from Wednesday, October 1.

subsubtopic: DEBATE .RESUMED ON MOTION FOR PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock yesterday I had put on Hansard a certain number of names of soldiers whose votes had been "switched", to use an expression that has been used since the commencement of the debate. I stated

at that time that I did not want to put any more names on Hansard but I desired to make the statement that I had hundreds of the names of soldiers whose votes were not polled in the constituencies where they resided and where they ought to have been polled. I also yesterday cited a circular that was sent out by Lieut.-Col. Machin to show that there was a general organization-I might say a general conspiracy-which was carried on with the knowledge of the Government to try and influence such voters. I stated also that Lieut.-Col. Machin was the man who was charged with the carrying out, I might say, of the Military Service Act. We were assured in 1917, when the Military Service Act was before the House, that it would be administered with equal justice to all. During the debate, when the other day the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) put up his so called defence, he stated that he was not the sponsor of the Bill but that the hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) was. I would like to give to the House a few-I will not say the assertions-but promises made by the Minister of Justice that this Act should be properly administered. If you take Hansard of the 20th August 1917, page 4688, you will'find that the Minister of Justice said:
The principle of the Bill is that our soldiers should toe afforded an opportunity to vote at the coming election and that adequate provision should be made to enable them to register their vote, precautions, however, being taken to ensure the regularity, fairness and genuineness of that vote.
That was one of the guarantees that was given to us by the sponsor of the Bill as to its provisions and as to how they were to be put in force. In 'view of the suggestion made by the then member for St. John, N. B. the Hon Mr. Pugsley, that under the provisions of the Bill there was a possibility of grave fraud being carried on and that therefore the Bill should be administered by an impartial tribunal the Minister of Justice said, page 4742:
I do not think I am making a profession of any superior virtue, or being particularly unctuous, when I say I desire to work out the measure on as fair a principle as it can be worked out on, but while I desire to do that, I am not prepared to accept the suggestion that, with regard to this election, and to the law which should govern the election, this Government should abdicate the functions which belong to it, and which have belonged to the Governments of Canada so long as there has been an election law. We must be responsible for this law.

I gather from that, that Parliament was responsible for the law, but it was suggested or stated by those who took part in the debate that the Government was responsible for the administration of the law. In whatever manner the law is administered, they have to take the responsibility. In this case I charge that this law was wrongly administered. I charge farther that, from the facts which I have brought forward and putting the circumstances together, the law was wilfully wrongly administered and we are asking for this committee to show exactly that the statement I make now that the law was wilfully wrongly administered for party purpose is true.
If you want any further professions of faith on the part of the Minister of Justice you will find that on the same date, August 21, page 4708. he says:
May I point out that the number of votes that will be covered by this provision with regard to men who have not previously resided in Canada will not be very considerable?
Fifty thousand of them have been thrown out. Thousands in addition to those of the voters whose names I cited yesterday were switched and put into counties where the. men did not reside. The measure was passed for the purpose of providing for a number of votes which would not be very considerable. I cite these facts to show that this system could not have gone on unless there had been a general organization to carry it on and there could not be a general organization without the Government being aware of its existence. As I stated yesterday the Minister of the Interior said that if there was an organization that was carrying on the switching of votes throughout this country he was willing to take the responsibility and he had nothing to repudiate.
On the same page of Hansard the Minister of Justice said:
If you take the men who could not define their constituencies and all the men who never resided in Canada and crowd them all into the places in which they were enrolled, you would in regard to many constituencies take these constituencies boldly out of the hands of the people actually resident in them and transfer the control of them to these men who gathered there accidentally merely for the purpose of voting.
I admit that the Minister of Justice was right. If we had determined that the soldiers should vote in the places where they were enrolled it would have been unfair and it would have defeated the will of the residents of the county where the vote was taking place. But in this case it is not only at certain points of enrolment
that this was done but it was spread all over the Dominion of Canada wherever the 'Government were in doubt about a constituency because they were taking not only those men who did not reside in Canada or who could not define the constituencies wherein they had lived, but also the men who actually knew where they came from and instructed them to apply their votes in one constituency or another. The examples I cited in Cumberland, Nova Scotia and the few names I read into Hansard were designed to show that we had the infoimation-number, name, place of residence, where he was born, where he enrolled, in what county he voted, and where he swore he was living for the purpose of voting.
At page 4720 my hon. friend again says:
Are we going to hive all the votes in the places where the soldiers happened to have enlisted? Is that fair to the constituencies where the largest enrolment took place?
I am with him and the reproach that I make to the Government is that when the measure was before the House they explained exactly what they wanted to guard against. They explained that they wanted the soldier to vote-we all agreed with that-and that they wanted the soldier to be master of his vote and not to be coerced to vote in one place instead of another.
On page 4722 of the same Hansard, on the same day, the Minister of Justice said:
The only man who is to have the chance to indicate where he desires to vote is the man who neither knows the name of the electoral constituency nor is in a position to name a place or places in which he resided, or from the naming of which the constituency can be ascertained... There is no ground to apprehend
difficulty in so far as regards a man who knows where he lives-whether he knows the name of the constituency or not, that man will vote in the constituency in which he lives.
I will not quote any more of these statements. The intention of those who were the sponsors-to use the term of the Minister of the Interior-for this legislation are very clear; the idea was to give the man a vote where he lived, and to give the man who had no residence in Canada a vote somewhere but where to be indicated by the man himself. There was no contemplation of any "vote at large," there was no contemplation of any "allotment," to any particular constituency under the Act by any one whomsoever, and the words "at large" and "allotment" in the telegram show exactly, and constitute evidence per ;e, that there was an organization and that there was an army going across the seas and all over America allotting votes and dis-



tributing them to meet the purposes of the parties interested. And who were they? Surely it was not the Opposition who wanted the Union Government to be elected3 The parties interested were the Union Government and those uho were organized by them, under them, and for them.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I spoke about the feeling that was general in the country, and I said at the time that this feeling was sufficient to justify the Government-no, not justify the Government but force the Government-to grant the committee of investigation which we are now seeking. Allow me to read a letter which was received from a sergeant-major, and what he has to say ahout this matter. Among other things he says:
Well, I see by last week's paper that the overseas elections were the subject of a controversy in the House of Commons the other day-

From my own experience, first as an agent at the polls and later as a special returning officer, counting and allocating the votes, I have no hesitation in saying that it was the biggest travesty on the franchise of a supposedly free people and the most barefaced steal ever perpetrated in the name of the sacred ballot.
Now then, Mr. Speaker, Ithat has reference not SO' much-

I have no comment to make because this comes from a soldier who was thei;e and saw what was going on. He was a sergeant-major.I will not give his name but he will come before the committee, if you will grant one, and he will tell

about this dirty work that he is speaking of and some more.

speechtext: At what poll and in what country was he acting in the capacities mentioned?

speechtext:
He was ia special returning officer counting and allocating votes, he does not say where. He was not a civil special returning officer because there was no allocation of the civil votes
10 p.m. that were counted by the regular returning officer. That was only done-I hope so, although it may have been done elsewhere-in the case of soldiers. If my hon. friend wants to crossexamine me now, I will give him a chance to cross-examine the man himself if he will vote to grant the committee for which we are asking. Here is another statement. Mr. Speaker, one that was made publicly by Doctor (Major) Cryus McMillan, Professor of McGill university, Montreal. Speaking publicly in Prince Edward Island he said:
Shortly after he was sworn in he received a letter from General Embury asking him to inform the soldiers that if the Government was sustained they would get three months' furlough. Major McMillan also says that he and other deputies were instructed to hurry up the polling, and then to make a return of the number polled, with a list of names and addresses of those not polled, and that they were to be voted (personated) at the base.
At the base, How could they be voted there? They could be personated. Now, Mr. Speaker, if that does not constitute a conspiracy to switch votes I want to get all the best authorities in this country to give me a definition of conspiracy, for I do not understand the word. Let me give another example and I quote further from the statement made by Major Cyrus McMillan. He also said:
Many English and Americans did not wish to vote in Canada, and were voted or personated in this way.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that Major McMillan intends to write his experiences having to do with elections overseas, and to publish them in a pamphlet for the edification of the public of Canada and show how much and howr hearty was the support of the Union Government at the last election1.
I have another letter here from Lieut. A. C. Campion, who was a poll clerk at Carlisle in Scotland, but -I will only read a part of it. I want to establish my case showing conspiracy and that we are en-

titled to this committee. Lieut. Campion says:
We were advised by wire from London ot constituencies where the election would be close and would have the voter vote in that riding. A voter was supposed to be able to vote in any riding he chose if he weren't quite sure where he voted before at the previous election
Now I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is that the intent, or is that the wording of the law, and are those the instructions that were sent to London to be given to the presiding or to the deputy presiding officers? I read last night, and I produced a letter of Mr. Purney, who was giving his opinion and saying that those who did not answer questions 5, 6, and 7 ought to be counted as voters. This was reversed afterwards but reversed and the Government were satisfied they had done enough switching, stealing and personating to win the election without the 50,000 votes. This lieutenant further says:
A voter was supposed to be able to vote in any riding he chose if he weren't quite sure where he voted before at the previous election. So this afforded, an opportunity to switch the votes to any riding and if the voter were not quite sure of the candidate he wished to vote for the name of one of the close ridings before mentioned was suggested to him.
Was suggested to him! He did not suggest where he wanted to vote, but it was suggested to him. By whom?
By the officer in charge and the voter, as a rule, marked his ballot so that the officer could see that he voted for his man.
I do not want to go on further. I have got statements like those I have quoted by the stack, and I do not want to encumber Hansard because I have enough confidence in the judgment and honour of the House to believe it will grant the committee believing as I do that I have made out a good case.
In the earlier part of my remarks I alluded to the tragical gesture of the Minister of the Interior when he demanded the production of this telegram and asserted that the time to produce it was "now-now." I do not see that this telegram has to be produced, and I say this for two reasons. Your warrant does not issue on the evidence as adduced to convict ia man; you make out a prima facie case by swearing that you have reason to believe that the man is guilty. But let us talk about the telegram. The Minister of the Interior says:
The message might have been sent; it might have been sent by me; it is a message which might have been sent by any honest man.

Well, here I pause. Where is the honest man who, in the ordinary course of business, sends an honest message for an honest purpose to another honest man and uses a code cipher? And on what occasion would such a message be sent if the cipher was not in the possession of and agreed upon between the sender and the receiver?

subsubtopic: DEBATE .RESUMED ON MOTION FOR PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE.
speechtext: Did the hon. member ever receive a cipher telegram? If he ever did, was either the sender or the receiver a dishonest man?

subsubtopic: DEBATE .RESUMED ON MOTION FOR PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE.
speechtext:
I have received cipher telegrams the purpose of which was to shorten the wording of the message and reduce -the amount to be paid to the telegraph company. It is for this purpose that codes are employed in sending cablegrams; it is for this purpose that codes are adopted for the ordering of parts from automobile factories. It is agreed between the sender and the receiver that a certain word means a certain part, and orders can be sent without the use of lengthy messages. But in ordinary business like this, why should you use the cipher? Because you did not want it to be known to the people through whose hands the matter was passing. If this was an honest transaction, why should you hide it from the telegraph operators or from those who might hear it on the wire? It is not a matter of business about which you do not wish your neighbour to learn; it is not a price you are quoting which you do not wish your neighbour to know. You are asking that a certain provision of the law be put into force. Well, every man is supposed to know the law; why should you use a cipher? The words "at large" and "allotment" are the two crimes perpetrated by this telegram-then there is "amphibio-logioal" and certain other words that would scare an army of soldiers. But would that cipher telegram be sent if at the other end they could not decipher it? That in itself is evidence that he who sent it and he who received it knew the cipher and had an agreement between themselves as to how it should be used.
I do not see that the production of the telegram would better conditions any. The Minister of the Interior said:
But if a man, however vaguely or obliquely-

answer is itself rather oblique .(reading) :
-alleges wrong-doing, surely the onus is on him to produce the facts; surely it is on him to establish the truth of his allegations; surely it

Here is another affidavit in proof of the same statement:
I, the undersigned, No. 2245525, Pte. Audy, make the following statement:
While a private with the 43rd Forestry Battalion at Sunningdale the Adjutant of the same battalion called me in his office and said to me

"Audy, are you going to vote for the Germans or for the Government?" To that question, I answered, "Sir, I am going to vote for Laurier." The saidi Adjutant then said: "If you do vote for Laurier, you will immediately be transferred to an English infantry battalion; you lsnow that you are afraid of an infantry battalion by the fact that you cannot drill." I answered: "Sir, you can send me anywhere you like, but I am going to vote for Laurier just the same...," you can put me in the clink if you care to do so, but you cannot change my vote and I am going to vote for Laurier." Then the Adjutant sent me back to my hut. After a few minutes, Sergeant Lalende came to see me and addressed me in this way: "Audy, do not make a fool of yourself; vote for the Government, andi everything will be all right and you will stay with us." I answered "You can do and they can do what they like, but I am going to vote for Laurier." Sergeant Lalende then took me to the Adjutant's office and this last gentleman told me: "You know that there is nothing like a secret vote here" (pointing out the reserve space marked No. 2 on the ballot). The adjutant giving me an order, I was forced to vote and I did vote for the Government. After that, the said Adjutant told me, " Now, Audy, get ready, for you are already transferred to the 156th Battalion, where I am now."
I do not know whether the 156th was in the trenches, whether it was a fighting unit, or what it was. My hon. friend is in a better position to know. Anyway the man was transferred, and I do not suppose he was getting a promotion after having repeatedly stated he was going to vote for Laurier no matter what happened. It goes on:
The same intimidation was given to many soldiers for getting their votes for the Government and some of them Were transferred to some infantry battalion.
After explanation made to me of the said declaration and knowing that the said declaration has the same effect as one taken under oath, I have signed.
(Signed) Joseph Audy.

E. B. Bastien,
I56th Canadian Infantry Battalion.
If that is not coercion I do not know *what it is. If I put a pistol at your head [DOT]to make you sign a deed, and anybody has the gall or the consummate nerve to say that your signature was the free act of a man who wanted to sign that deed, he is welcome to his views because he does not belong to my gang. I think I have made a case, and I do not want to detain the House any longer, but before I resume my seat let me quote a paragraph from a newspaper which has supported Union Government very strongly, the Toronto Star. In its issue of September 27, 1919, it has this paragraph:
Representative Institutions on Trial.
When representative institutions are under fire-when it is said that they are of little value to working people, and that direct action [Mr. Bureau.!
should 'be substituted for political action-it is of the utmost importance that ministers and members of Parliament should uphold the dignity and independence of Parliament and the most scrupulous fairness in elections. It is of course right that a charge of fraud or unfairness should not be taken as equivalent to proof.
We are willing to take our chances if we cannot prove what we say. We are not asking for a verdict, but for the constitution of a tribunal which will pronounce a verdict upon the evidence adduced. It goes on:
But it should be treated in a manner which shows that the House attaches importance to freedom and fairness in elections, as if it set a high value upon free institutions.
There is no force in the plea that neither party is free from the reproach of abusing its power by practices which defeat the will of the people. The offences of the past were punished or ought to have been punished. They are to serve for warning, not for example or excuse. Especially is it necessary that our representative institutions should be above reproach today, when they are upon trial and subjected to attack as useless and undemocratic.
I close with these few remarks. To-day there is a condition of unrest in the country. This condition of unrest is due to the fact that the people of this country have no longer respect either for Parliament or the Government. They have not respect for Parliament, because Parliament has been unable to maintain and hold its own privileges. They have been taken away from Parliament time and again by the Government. They have no respect for the Government because the Governtnent is under a cloud, with accusations and suspicions of their conduct coming from every quarter, not only in the matter of elections, but in the matter of patronage, in the matter of the expenditure of public moneys. It is to these things the unrest is due, and I say it is high time that we, the members of the House of Commons, following the examples of the nations which I have cited, get up and tell the people "We are willing that you should scrutinize our conduct. We are willing to .appoint men who will listen to every one of you. Every man that has a grievance let him come forward and submit it. Those who are guilty will be punished, and those who are innocent will be so proclaimed, and those who have accused falsely will bear the odium of having 'persecuted men who were innocent." It is not a question with us of making political capital. We do not care for that; we do not require it, because this Government is defeated already in the opinion of the people. I see smiles on faces of hon. gentlemen opposite who will

never smile again in this House after an election, because these men will never come back. We are asking for this inquiry because we want to show people that if the men who have been covering themselves with the mantle of the war are not sincere, we are; that if they are not democratic, we are. We stand for liberty and free institutions, for the free expression of the will of the people at the polls, the same as for the free expression of the thought of hon. members in this Parliament. We have brought forward facts sufficient to connect at least one member of the Government with the organization. He pleads guilty. He is a self-confessed member of that organization, and he ought no longer to sit in the Government if the facts which we allege are proven true, and if his connection with this organization is as stated by my honourable leader. Brigadier-General W. A. GRIESBAOH (West Edmonton):' Mr. Speaker, I should like to say at the outset that I know nothing about the conditions which prevailed in Canada, in England, or in France, outside of the Canadian corps, during the last election. But within the Canadian corps I do know the facts, and I feel it my duty to lay them before the House, inasmuch as there were 100,000 men included in the corps and nianv gallant officers whose reputation has been aspersed by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. I shall confine my observations to only one aspect of the uis-cussion, I refer to the statement made by the leader of the Opposition that officers from the rank of general downwards threatened men under their command that if they did not support the Government they would be sent to the front line. Now, I was a candidate myself in the last election, and I was also a general commanding a brigade. In passing, I may say that a good deal of interest was taken in the election, purely from the point of view of the question of conscription and the securing of the reinforcements that were so urgently needed. I did not see anybody, I did not meet anybody, I did not hear of anybody throughout
the whole of the Canadian corps who had any intention of voting against conscription and in favour of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House.
And when out of that one hundred thousand men it was discovered at the close of the polls that some two or three dozen had voted for the Opposition every one was somewhat surprised and wondered where those votes had come from. I was a candidate but I did not canvass any one. I did not ask any man for his vote, nor did I issue any orders. I said nothing to any soldier calculated to influence his vote, but on one occasion when I went down to my old regiment for the purpose of presenting some decorations that had been won, in the course of a conversation concerning the military situation and training that was then being undertaken for operations that were in prospect I was asked, as the men were all present, to express an opinion in regard to a piece of propaganda which was in circulation at the time to the effect that if the men of the Canadian corps would vote against the Government and defeat conscription, then the corps, for lack of reinforcements, would be taken out of the firing line and set to work on lines of communication. I need scarcely say that there was not very much doubt in the mind of any man there as to where that propaganda had originated. As I say, I was asked for an expression of opinion concerning the matter, and I was also asked to state whether or not I thought that the brother of a man who had volunteered who was at home supporting a family could be conscripted. Upon these two points I gave my opinion, and that was the only occasion on which I had anything to say in connection with the election.
Now the charge is made by the leader of the Opposition that Canadian officers, from generals down, threatened their men with transference to the front line if they did not support the Government. Well, Sir, the front line is not such a fearful place after all, and it has no particular terrors for the soldier. Thousands of men lived more or * less cheerfully in the front line and many of them died there willingly. So that there is no particular dread for the soldier in connection with the front line, and the only officer who would dream of making use of such a threat is a man who would himself be impressed by the threat,- in other words, a man who is himself a coward. And the threat, to be at all effective, would have to be addressed to men who were cowards. It could not otherwise be advantageously used, and I desire to say

to the leader of the Opposition that the number of officers who were cowards in the Canadian corps were mighty limited-the same remark being absolutely true of the men. The statement is therefore an insult to the officers and men of the Canadian corps. It is one which is based upon a conception of cowardice and could only be used by cowards. It could only influence cowards, and I make bold to say that it can now be repeated only by cowards on behalf of cofcvards.

But the ghoul who merely takes a few pennies from the body of a stranger lying dead upon the street is a petty offender in comparison with the vampire who breaks into the sacred tomb of the honoured dead and seeks to filch from the departed his good name and reputation.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Three Rivers read that. statement in order to fasten on the hon. member from Red Deer the charge of having misquoted the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier. It is not necessary for me to defend the member for Red Deer; he is perfectly capable of taking oare of himself, and I have no doubt that in due time he will give answer to the allegation
[Mr. Nicholson.!
which the hon. member for Three Rivers has made.
I repeated what the hon. member for Three Rivers said in order that I might, if I could, bring him to a realization of the position in which he and the members surrounding him are placed in connection with this whole debate. Mr. Speaker, this country of ours has hosts of honoured dead. We may trace our history back three hundred years, and in all the pages of that history we find records of men whom we are privileged to honour. But in the whole of that host of honoured dead there is no element that will command the veneration and pride of this country throughout succeeding generations in the same degree as will that host of honoured dead who lie to-night in the fields of France and Flanders. What do hon. gentlemen opposite think of the ghouls who open up the graves in France and Flanders in order to take from these men, who stood facing the Hun, and holding the line in order that this country might remain free that the member for Three Rivers might have the privilege of speaking in a free parliament, the reputation that went with them from this country as respectable and honoured citizens?
What is the charge? It is simply this: That tens of thousands of Canadian soldiers who are to-night sleeping in France, in the performance of the last civil act that it was their privilege to perform, committed perjury, personation and all kinds of political crimes, some of them utterly unspeakable. And what did honourable gentlemen opposite add to that charge? I do not hear quite so much cheering from honourable members opposite just at the moment. Let me repeat that I trust that their cheers of a few moments ago give evidence of a soul-awakening that will make them realize something of what the awfulness of this war has meant.
