I quote again from the remarks of the honourable member for Three Rivers:
it was not to establish the position of the hon. member for Red Deer in this House that he made that quotation. The quotation was made, whatever his protestations may have been, for the purpose of hurting the feelings of the men who sit on your left, Mr. Speaker.
The feelings of honourable members on the other side are very tender. I wonder if they realize what the feelings of the thousands of Canadian fathers and mothers, wives and sisters, must be when they hear

the charge hurled back and forth in this House, bandied about by men outside the House whom honourable gentlemen opposite themselves would not believe on their oaths, that the last civil act that these soldiers were privileged to perform was an act of perjury or personation?
I wish to refer to something that was said by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) as reported on page 565 of Hansard, September 24 last. I quote:
Their own commanders and officers and every one under their thumb and control, officers who were preaching to these men only the Sunday before the election in such term's as these: " Gentlemen, we do not want 99 per cent of your votes; we want 100 per cent " ? That was the exhortation of generals, colonels, and others from the top to the bottom.. . The soldiers were told if they would not vote as told 'by their officers they would be immediately sent to the trenches, where likely they would be killed.
The member for Erontenac (Mr. Edwards) drew attention to that and asked the leader of the Opposition to define clearly what he meant, because, like every other decent man in this House, the member for Frontenac was loth to believe that any man could be found anywhere who would make a charge of that character against the soldiers who were fighting our battles overseas. Whom did thd hon. member mean by the "generals, colonels, majors, captains and lieutenants?" One of the generals is sitting in this House. One of the colonels has the privilege of occupying a seat in this House. Did he mean either of these? Did he name any one? No; he simply made a blanket accusation that every general, every colonel, every officer in the Canadian forces gave his men to understand that if they did not vote as he desired he would send them to the front line trenches, where they would be shot. We have from time to time heard many startling accusations against people in this country with regard to what took place at the time of an election, but it remained for hon. gentlemen opposed to assert that there was any man in this country so low that he would say to another: You will either vote as I tell you to vote, or I will have you shot. What is the meaning of that? It simply means that the officers were going to send to the front line trenches men to be shot who otherwise would not have had to go to the front line trenches at all. It means that or it does not mean anything.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what are these charges based on? The leader of the Opposition says that he has a telegram. Whether it is a bogus telegram or a stolen telegram-a document secured from some one-he is not willing to produce it or tell the House who obtained it. We have had the privilege of reading from Hansard statements that were made in this House in 1918 on this same subject, and we have the right to assume that this case was built up in the same way as the case presented then by the member for Westmorland (Mr. Copp) was built up. What did he base that on? The unsupported statements of the most completely discredited political blackleg that ever disgraced the politics of this country. Let me repeat it again-a man that the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) himself would not believe on his oath. That is the basis for this whole charge. If I said to you, Sir, that this whole case from beginning to end was a fabrication of miserable falsehoods, I have not the slightest doubt that you would declare that I was out of order. If I said that the whole case from beginning to end was a miserable, contemptible slander, I believe again that you would declare that I was out of order.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with great attention to the speech just delivered by the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Nicholson), and I will pay the hon. member the compliment of saying that my remarks in answer to his speech will be very brief. During the war the Germans introduced into warfare several new methods. They sank ships carrying women and children; they sent out poison gas; but to the horror of the civilized world, in the dying days of the war, the Germans placed lines of women and children that they had taken from French cities, in front of their army, so as to keep the Allied armies from firing upon themselves. The method adopted by the Germans in the field has been adopted by the Government and by the hon. member for Algoma East in this debate. When we call upon the members of this Government and of this House to answer to the country and to the people of Canada for their conduct and behaviour during 1917, they place before themselves the noble army of Canadian boys, and they say: If you fire on us, you fire on them.
At this late hour, I do not wish to detain the House very long; but on this side of the House we have a very high admiration for our Canadian army, and our admiration may be better founded than the admiration that is boasted of on the other side, because we have more disinterestedness; we are not always talking about the soldiers; we are not always talking about the boys at the front. We want to be judged on our own merits, and we have never called on the boys who were at the front to win any battle for us in this Parliament. As regards the hon. member for Algoma East, I have heard him several times in this House viciously attacking the members from the province of Quebec, and particularly attacking myself.

I can only say to the hon. member for Algoma East that if his remarks made to-night are not an attack on my province and on the members from my province, the hon. gentleman does not generally know what he is saying when he gets up in the House to talk. English is not my mother tongue; my mother tongue is French, but I know enough English grammar, and I have read and learned enough English to understand from the hon. member that he was attacking this side of the House when he spoke a minute ago, and when he did speak, he attacked us viciously and bitterly. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Griesbach) addressed this House. I have nothing to say as regards the military record of that hon. member. I admired his career at the front; I followed his promotions at the front, and I think every member of this House is proud of the military record of that hon. member.
But if the hon. member for Edmonton is a noble soldier whom everybody in this .House admires, he still may not be a good parliamentarian. He knows everything about the military art. Whenever he made an attack it was made in accordance with the hest rules of warfare, but I have some advice to give to my hon, friend: Let him learn the rules of parliamentary warfare as well as those of actual warfare. If he had known those rules I do not think he would have taken any part in this debate.

He is a gentleman who was elected over the Hon. Frank Oliver, although the civilian voie gave Hon. Frank Oliver a majority of over 800. The hon. member's election was contested. Fraud was alleged. There were seventy-three different charges of fraud against the hon. member, and I think that in a debate of this kind the noble and gallant member for Edmonton .should have remained silent.	,
I said that I did not wish to address this House very long. But 1 want to say a word with regard to the campaign waged by a newspaper, called The Montreal Gazette. The Montreal Gazette is a paper printed and published in the city of Montreal. It represents the Tory ideas in their most advanced form. The Montreal Gazette, like any other newspaper, has a right to combat for and defend any principles it chooses to advocate, but I say that The Montreal Gazette and any representative of The Montreal Gazette in the press gallery of this House has no right to insult the members of the House. I do not care who writes for The Montreal Gazette nor who represents The Montreal Gazette, but a principle which the journalists in Ottawa as anywhere else should never forget is that when they are admitted to hear and report the debates of this House they owe some respect to the members of the House. The Montreal Gazette says that in this debate the Liberal party is only bringing on a discussion which is a slur on the soldiers. We are not making any slurs on the soldiers, but we say that if the Government of Canada, or the officers of the Canadian army in France, forced the soldiers to vote in a way they should not have voted, the Government of Canada and the superior officers of the Canadian army should be brought before an investigating committee and every fact ought to be known.
The Montreal Gazette says that the Liberal party in this debate is trying to air old grievances. These are not old grievances. As far as the members for the province of Quebec are concerned, we are not afraid of the stand we took during the war. The stand we took during the war was the stand that we considered Canadian. We might have been wrong, but we were sincere, and I think that is more than lots of other people can say. The Montreal Gazette says that we are bringing on a debate which is nothing but petty politics.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: DEBATE .RESUMED ON MOTION FOR PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE.
speechtext:
The gentleman who writes these articles and the members of this House who say "Hear, hear when I mention petty
politics seem to be ignorant of the history of the constitution of England. They seem to forget that at the basis of this very .question we are discussing there is the great and eternal question of the freedom of the people.
I have heard members on the other side of the House on several occasions ask: "Why should the member for Dorchester discuss matters of this kind? He only had six military votes in his county." Mr. Speaker, the time has come for me to make a brief explanation as far as my county is concerned. In 1914 when war broke out, who represented the county of Dorchester in this House? Was.it your humble servant, Mr. Speaker? No. It was Hon. Mr. Sevigny, who was then Deputy Speaker, or Speaker, of the House of Commons. He was the man responsible to the Government of Canada and to the people of Canada for the conduct and behaviour of his people. I was then member for the Local House. I had nothing to do with enrollment or enlisting as far as federal laws or federal politics was concerned. Not only did Mr. Sevigny, the colleague of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), not do anything in 1914, but when the Minister of Militia of that day, Sir Sam Hughes, wanted to mobilize the 92nd Battalion, which is the battalion of Dorchester, Mr. Sevigny interfered and told him not to do it, because it would hurt his political chances. The war went on, and the situation became more and more serious. What did the then member for Dorchester do? We have in the House to-night the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid), and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), who were colleagues of the Hon. Mr. Sevigny at that time, and I defy them or any member of this House to say that the then hon. member for Dorchester in 1914, 1915, 1916 or 1917 ever held a single recruiting meeting in the constituency of Dorchester which he represented. But it is against me that the reproaches are made; it is against me they direct their attacks. As I have already said, I was then member for the Local House, and whenever the Premier of my province, Sir Lomer Gouin, proposed anything to promote the cause of the Allies I always gave him my vote, because I believed in the sacredness of our cause. Then, in 1917, Mr. Sevigny, on account of his patriotic efforts which I have just related, was chosen by the Prime Minister of this country to be a minister in the Borden Government. A byelection took place, and I resigned my seat in the Local House to run against Mr. Sevigny. Why? Because I thought that his

past history precluded him from properly representing the people of Dorchester, and from advising His Majesty the King in the troublesome times we were passing through. I resigned my mandate and said to the people of Dorchester that a Nationalist should not 'be chosen. I ran against Mr. Sevigny, and the Government directed all their efforts towards my defeat. The sum of $100,000 was spent. Never in the history of Canada was such a fraudulent election carried on. I was beaten, but when I went down to defeat I could say that my honour was still safe, because I had done nothing that I could reproach myself with. Mr. Speaker-and I call the attention of the ministers to this fact-in those days Iron. Mr. Sevigny 'proclaimed on every hustings in Dorchester that never would there be conscription, because he had the Prime Minister's word for what he was saying. The colleague of hon. Mr. Sevigny at that time, a man who ran in two constituencies in Quebec and was defeated, hon. Mr. Blondin, who was rescued from disaster by a benevolent Government that sent him to the Senate, said in the parish of Ste. Rose in the presence of npy hon. friend from Rimouski (Mr. d'Anjou):	"Never
will we have conscription. But if we should have conscription why worry about it? The American border is close by; you will go to the United States and escape the law." Mr. Speaker, in this debate, when we ask that the honour of Canada and the honour of Parliament be safeguarded, I hear men like the hon. member from Algo-ma (Mr. Nicholson) make the charge: "You are not patriotic." Well, my answer is-and it is an answer given long ago- "Very often patriotism is hut the last refuge of a scoundrel."
I do not wish to detain the House at any great length, but-

speechtext:
The member for Trois
Rivieres had a few things to say about the member	for Red Deer (Mr.	M.
Clark) and I shall not add very much to what he said. But I will say this-and that gentleman can read it in Hansard-that when he gets up in this House and gives us his lessons in English history, I challenge him to show me, in justification of such conduct as that which we are now discussing, one line, one word, one syllable that can be found in any of the speeches of those at whose knees he is supposed to have learned his politics- Bright, Cobden, Gladstone, all those great Liberal statesmen. It is a great thing to say, " I represent Liberalism:	I know
what Liberal principles are, and I enunciate those principles for you to follow." It is easy enough for the hon. doctor to get up in this House and change the roles and become schoolmaster, hut I will refer him to a French author whose name was Mol-iere, and who said many years ago: " Medecin, gueris toi toi-meme"-Doctor, cure thyself.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the last member to whom I shall refer, the last but not the least, is the Minister of the Interior

(Mr. Meighen). I say candidly, Mr. Speaker, that I admire that hon. minister. My hon. friend from Three Rivers does not seem to have as high a degree of admiration for him as I have, but I do admire his talent and his eloquence, and I admire his legal knowledge. But I will tell him one thing, and that is that this Parliament is a serious court of justice, and.if he wishes his talent to be admired in the future he must come before this House with serious arguments worthy of his own capacity. The hon. minister said: " Tt may be right, it may be wrong. It may be anything at all." He uttered the watchword, " Patriotism," and wrapping himself in the Union Jack he turned to his supporters and said: " Cheer! cheer! I represent Great Britain and the British Empire." Mr. Speaker, the speech of the minister may be summed up in a few words. According to him, the end justifies the means. Would that hon. gentleman or any other member of this House say that rape was excusable because it was a process to motherhood? Mr. Speaker, I can say to this House that the minister has no right to talk about patriotism after the conduct of the Government during the last election. I have seen soldiers who came back from the other side. An hon. member on the other side said that we had no soldiers in Quebec. Well, I have seen-soldiers from my constituency, I have seen soldiers from Quebec, and there were soldiers from my own family, and I know what took place on the other side. Official canvassers appointed by this Government went to the soldiers overseas and told them to vote in favour of the Union Government so that they might be enabled to go back home. Is that patriotism? Patriotic motives.
Mr. Speaker, very often in this country we hear of profiteers, and the greatest war profiteers that we have are the members of the Government.
If it had not been for the war they would not have been in office. Since the armistice they have only remained in office on account of the war. I am not surprised that we have not yet ratified the treaty with Bulgaria. This Government is in no hurry to terminate a state o>f war, it is its only safeguard and protection, its only means of remaining in power.
When we say anything, 'these hon. gentlemen cover the heap of iniquity with the Union Jack and say, "We are at war; be careful; do not say anything; the British Empire is in danger; we are saving the Empire; do not interfere with our work".
The people are getting sick and tired of seeing you gentlemen saving the British Empire. New doctors will have to he called in.
The question before the House may be summed up as follows: The action of the Minister of the Interior is either legal or illegal. If it is legal why should the Government object to an investigation; why should -the Government refuse an investigation to enable the Opposition to prove something that is lawiful and legal? If it is illegal, not only is an investigation useful, but it is necessary. I do not wish 'to go into the details of this case. You have heard the facts .as they have been brought before the House. We have a prima facie case of fraudulent conspiracy. An investigation should be granted. Moreover, if we have this investigation, if it is shown that, according to law, as the minister contended, he had the right .to send the telegram he sent, it is high time that the law should be changed. If he had no right to send that telegram, it is high time the minister should be punished.
I will finish these few remarks but I will ask these hon. gentlemen on the other side to remember the day when in this country we fought for the freedom and the liberty of the ballot. The last principle to be conquered was that of the freedom and the secrecy of the ballot. That principle has come to the people of this country as a result of the effort of the Liberal party. If there is .anything essential to the constitution of the Canadian people it is the independence of Parliament from interference by the executive. Go back to the history of England, to the time when Sir Robert Walpole was premier, to the time of the placemen, when the executive used to choose the representatives of the people; go back to the time of the Duke of Newcastle; .go to the time of the Georges when the executive used to choose the members of Parliament. England in those days was suffering because of a lack of parliamentary freedom. But her institutions have been improved. To-day her executive does not tamper with the choice of the people's representatives. At this last election the Government of Canada did interfere, and if we have an investigation, if the facts are brought forward, if a report is made, the new electoral law that will be brought in will be an electoral law of such a nature that two elementary principles will be safeguarded-the freedom of the ballot and the independence of Parliament.



Hon. NEWTON W. ROWELL (President of the Privy Council): Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to enter upon a lengthy discussion of the matter before the House but I desire to draw attention- to the terms of the resolution submitted by the hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Me-Kenzie). After reciting the telegram alleged to have been sent by the hon, -the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) the resolution proceeds:	.
-and, whereas, the said telegram indicates the existence of a widespread system' of manipulation of votes, under the direction and with the approval of ministers of the Crown, for the purpose of defeating the will of the Canadian people as expressed at the polls, and
Whereas, such scheme of manipulation involves not only the honour of the ministers concerned, but the constitutional rights of the people.
And that therefore this committee should be granted.
I desire, Mr. Speaker, to draw the attention of the House to the terms and basis of the resolution. The basis upon which a parliamentary committee is asked is that the telegram discloses a scheme for the manipulation of votes and involves the honour of the ministers concerned.. There is no question that the resolution directly challenges the honour of the Prime Minister who is said to have received the telegram, -and of the Minister Of the Interior who is said to have sent it. That is the basis of the resolution -before the House-. There is a well understood and thoroughly constitutional practice, .as was pointed out by the Minister of the Interior, when any hon. member desires to impugn the honour of another member of the House, and particularly of a minister of the 'Crown. If the 'leader of the Opposition had, upon his responsibility as a member of the House, made a charge impugning the honour of a member of the Government, he would be entitled, as a matter of course, to a committee of investigation. The hon. member has not done that but has based his charge upon this telegram.
It has been suggested .that if the -law permits such a telegram, such a law should no longer continue in existence. The law under which the vote was taken was the Military Voters Act. It was passed by this House in the year 1917. It was the law for taking the votes of soldiers overseas -and in 'Canada in the General Election of 1917. That law is no longer in operation. It has -ceased to be effective. It no longer

affects any election that may be held. If the desire is to secure a change in the law, that cannot be accomplished by this motion for the Jaw has ceased to be effective.
Hon. members may challenge the law; they may say that the provision of the law whereby men who had no settled residence in Canada were given the vote should not have been -adopted. That was a debatable question. That question was debated in this House in 1917 and the House decided that these men should have a vote. Therefore, under this law, these men became entitled to vote. We cannot now pass under review that legislation. It was there for better or for worse. We must take it as it stood. Then the only question that arises now is whether that law was honestly administered in so far as 'the ministers of the Crown were -concerned, and that is the question raised by this motion.
The question is whether the Prime Minister and the Minister -of the Interior acted honestly and in pursuance of the law of the land, in any action they took or were guilty of some fraudulent conspiracy, as the hon. member has said, to defeat the wiLl of the people by acting contrary to the law.
. I was not in the House in 1917 when the law was passed. I did follow the discussion in the House and gathered something of the meaning of that legislation; and I want to say that in respect of no Act that passed this Parliament in recent times has there been more widespread misunderstanding than in respect to this particular piece of legislation. I know it because of the enquiries I received from candidates contesting constituencies in the province of Ontario and from men representing both sides of the House. The opinion appeared to be widespread that there was some power somewhere in the Government to allot ballots to particular constituencies, and I received communications from different candidates, from some members of the House even, asking me to see either that ballots were allotted in favour of certain candidates, or that ballots were not allotted against some other candidate. I had to reply, and was glad to reply, that the law made no provision for any such thing, that there was no right to allot ballots to any candidate in any constituency but the voter himself must determine the constituency in which he desired to vote. There was no right of -selection unless he had no previous residence in Canada; if there was no previous residence in Canada, then he had the right

to select his constituency. There were some ten or twelve thousand voters, it was said- I do not know how many there were-who had this right of selection. There is no use shutting our eyes to the fact that so far as those ten or twelve thousand voters were concerned, men on both sides would seek to persuade them to place their ballots in the constituencies where they thought they would do the most good.

But whether we take one view or the other, that was the law, and the Prime Minister, the Minister of the Interior, or any member of the Government, in carrying out that law, so long as they did it honestly and fairly, are not open to any censure or criticism at the

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: DEBATE .RESUMED ON MOTION FOR PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to keep the House for more than a very few moments. What my colleague, the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) has just said sums up very fairly and clearly the real position with regard to the motion before the House. We have travelled, with the aid of the magnificent imaginative powers of hon. gentlemen on the other side, a very great distance away from this telegram, and we have had flights of eloquence and denunciations of practices of all kinds and a most admirable quotation describing the sanctity of the ballot box. Hon. gentlemen in this House have evidently been roused up to a very high pitch of indignation by a number of things that we have been told about in the course of this debate that have been made to rest, in some instances, on anonymous letters, or letters of gentlemen who did not like their names to be given, and in one or two instances upon the affidavits of particular soldiers who seemed to think, if they had the grave

complaint that their affidavits set forth, that, instead1 of going to those in authority over the military officers who are charged with having done this wrong of threatening the soldier if he did not vote in a particular way, instead of going to the superior officers of those men, who have it in their hands to do them justice, it was a wiser and more effective way to hand those letters in to hon." members of the Opposition who have also apparently thought that the wiser way to have those wrongs rectified was to keep those letters in their pockets until they could use them in support of a motion directed not against the people who threatened the soldier, not against the people who perpetrated the wrong that is alleged to have been perpetrated, but until they could use them in support of a motion in itself based upon the flimsiest of grounds and one directed against the honour of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) of this country and against the honour of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen). Hon. gentleman who have [DOT] been able to connect these isolated cases, to which they have referred as the basis for their eloquent indignation, with anything that is contained in the telegram, have proved themselves certainly masters in the field of imaginative deduction. What have they done and what has this motion given them? It has after all, roused, in this House a feeling which does not make for that concord between the people's representatives which ought to exist at the present time and be an example to those people themselves that we might hope that they would follow, as we certainly ought to appeal to them to follow it. Surely the present time is no moment for the opening up of old sores in a manner whiefi can have no effect but one, that is to say, to rouse what there may be of latent feeling of animosity in the breasts of any or all of us, arising out of incidents of the last election. Surely this is a time for us to be ocupying ourselves with those things that may bring us together in co-operation in the building up of this country; and surely the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) should not have expected this House to be in a disposition of mind to waste its time in acrimonious discussion about what happened in the recent election.
Mr. Speaker, let me not be misunderstood. I am not standing here deprecating any practical method that might be taken to bring to justice any man who was guilty of any offence in connection with the carrying on of the election, whether that man be soldier or civilian. But there are ways

of enforcing the law, and there are ways of using unfortunate incidents, that may be discovered to have happened in. the course of a general election that took place upon two continents, for the sole purpose of rousing political passion and making an appeal to the people oi this country for the purpose of discrediting men who, as has been so eloquently pointed out by the President of the Council, have, for the last four or five years, but especially for the last two years, given, without hesitation, unstintingly of the very best that is in them in the service of the country. And we are asked to do that on what? On an inference, on an interpretation of a telegram. I am not going to deal with that phase of the thing. The President of the Council has, i think, sufficiently pointed out how this telegram is perfectly susceptible of a perfectly innocent interpretation. Hon. gentlemen said:	Rut it was on the 30th of
November and voting had been going on long before that. True, voting had been begun, but voting went on until the 17th of December, and surely there were thousands, and thousands, and thousands, of votes amongst the soldiers on the other side and on this to be polled when the intimation was made that the sender of the telegram would like, that, in the requesting and direction of voters anxious to know where they should vote, one thousand should be asked to cast their votes in the province of Manitoba. We have had some discussions of different standards of ethics. For my part, I entirely fail to see what reproach would have been made to the leader of the Opposition if he found himself in face of soldiers entitled by law to vote at the place that they selected, either they asking him for advice or he not waiting	to	be	asked	for advice
because he, in the patriotic conviction that the interests of this country demand the return to power of the .party of which he is a distinguished member-face to face with those electors entitled to select a place of voting-had felt that it was his patriotic duty to advise them to cast that vote in the place where it would be most effective to produce what he believed to be the patr riotic purpose of having returned to power the party in which he had confidence.
Certainly I would not reproach him if he acted so, and certainly-I do not know whether I am going to condemn myself in the eyes of hon. gentlemen on the other side- I would have had no qualms of conscience in giving that advice. Surely if we go into public life and engage in an electoral contest earnestly convinced-and I believe with
regard to this side of the House and the other that as a rule the men who do present themselves to do as a rule with the honest conviction that the party whose flag they are carrying is the party whose election will be most beneficial to the country-I have always believed .that the man who undertook that task owed not merely to his party but to his country the exertion of every honest effort of which he was capable to assure the triumph of the party which in his belief would best serve his country. Unless it can be shown to me that there is something dishonourable in saying to a man to whom the law of this country gave the right to select a constituency in which he could vote, unless it can be shown that there is something dishonourable on the part of one who honestly believes that the success of the party to which he belongs is essential to the good of the country, and that it is a dishonourable thing for the man so placed to give advice which will lead to that vote being used in such a manner as to produce the largest effect of which it is capable in bringing about that result which the adviser believes to be the best result for his country, then I wish to say for myself that an honourable man taking up that telegram and reading it will not see anything evil in it. It takes an ingenuity-and there has been more ingenuity than ingenuousness bestowed upon the interpretation of this telegram-it takes an ingenuity of which I confess I am incapable to read that telegram as necessarily implying anything dishonourable, and if there had been no other circumstances than that the telegram in itself was at least susceptible of an innocent interpretation that in itself should have been conclusive to any man who knows the man to whom it was addressed and the man whose signature it bore, that that was the proper interpretation to attach to it.
Something has been said about the law, and I have been spoken of as sponsor for that law. I have no desire to deny that I put that law through the House, and I have no apologies to make for it. If ever the Parliament of Canada did a thing that under the circumstances was a rightful thing to do, it was when it passed that Act that secured to the men whom we thought good enough to fight for Canada the recognition that they were good enough to vote in Canada. In the face of such criticism as has been addressed to that law, I am quite prepared to say that I happen to be the man who conducted that Bill through the House,

and if it were to do over I would do it again with the same confidence that I was doing the right thing which inspired me when I did it in the past. Let me add that, though at the outset when that Bill was introduced there was a good deal of questioning and carping criticism, 'before we were done with it the Bill went through this House practically unanimously. It went through with the common consent that every possible effort should be made to secure the vote to the soldiers. We were all equally agreed, too, and none shared in that opinion more heartily and more honestly than myself, that the vote should be surrounded by every safeguard which it was possible to attach to it under the circumstances under which it had to be taken.

speechtext:
I am not discussing that Act, but the Military Voters' Act, and I think if the hon. member will carry his memory back he will recall that in the last stages of that Bill there was practically unanimity. I want to pay a tribute to hon. gentlemen who sit on the other side of the House with regard to that Bill. When I introduced the Bill I told the House that I looked for unanimity on the principle that the soldier should have his vote, and we got that unanimity. I told the House further that I recognized the very great difficulties attached to surrounding that vote with proper safeguards, and I appealed to both sides of the House for suggestions. Valuable suggestions came from the other side of the House and were adopted, and the Bill left this House with the operation to be carried on under it surrounded by the best safeguards that the best minds in the House at that time could suggest. We all recognized that there were dangers-, and that you could not secure the same absolute control and supervision -that you could secure in an election carried on under normal conditions. But I think we all agreed at that day that that if the cost of giving the soldier the vote he was entitled to was the taking of the risk of irregularities, we would all willingly take them. We did take them, and there were irregularities; nobody disputes that; we have had instances. The hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) about a year and a half ago entertained us with an enumeration of irregularities, and he has come back to the charge in this debate. All these irregularities have been dealt with, but- he comes back and tells us now that he does not agree with the com-
[llr. Doherty. ]
missioner who heard the evidence upon the charges that lie saw fit to make; he does not agree with him as to what constitutes perjury, and whether -those men were guilty or not. To dispose of that subject right off, in the first place it has no connection with this motion. In the second place, -the hon. gentleman is full of indignation. For eighteen months he has nursed his wrath to keep it warm. And what was he wrathy about? He said that he not only knew, but that he had in his hands the evidence, that certain soldiers and officers in St. Johns were guilty of perjury and that the commissioner who heard the evidence had not done justice and had come to a wrong conclusion. His heart filled with just indignation in the face of those criminal offences going unpunished. With the courts of his province open to him to lay his charge of perjury and subornation of perjury; with all his confidence that the honourable judge who sat as commissioner was wrong, and with his absolute conviction that a series of crimes had been committed, he just sat by for eighteen months, and now comes into this House which can afford him no remedy. If these men were guilty there was a place where he could easily obtain a remedy, and that was in the courts of the country. To pass from that, however. I say there were irregularities. Under the law they were possible and we knew it. But there were many causes which contributed to those irregularities, and one of those causes was the persistent misrepresentation of the Act that was indulged in throughout the country by people speaking in the name of the party which the hon. gentleman leads. Why, in my own constituency and throughout the constituencies adjoining as well as throughout the province, so far as I came in contact with it, I encountered an honest, earnest and sincere belief that under the law every soldier had a right to vote where he liked; and wherever I came across that belief I inquired:	" Where did you get that impression?" and was told in reply "Every Liberal candidate and every Liberal leader is thundering accusations against you as the author of that law. You are being accused of having enacted the nefarious law allowing every soldier to vote where he liked." Leaders of this kind persuaded the people and persuaded the soldiers that they had an absolute right to vote where they chose. They so persuaded them because they thought that in such misrepresentation of the law they found an effective arm of attack against myself and others who were responsible for the law. Well, the

argument has proved a boomerang in the sense that it very widely or largely created that belief on the part of the soldiers. I cannot of my own knowledge speak of conditions on the other side, but some instances were given of representations made there. But I do know what the conditions were upon this side, and to-day,' having created and fostered that belief, those opposite ask us to establish a drag-net commission to go out and see what we can find out-how many soldiers we can find who were deceived in that way, and what soldiers we might possibly find who intentionally violated the law. In so far as the result of the election is concerned, as it was pointed out time and again, no useful purpose can be served by a sweeping investigation of the kind suggested. The hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) read us affidavits-and I cannot help asking myself why it is that neither before military or civil authorities did those people who suffered that awful injustice have recourse, as was their right. Among the superior officers of that adjutant referred to, I have not the slightest doubt, it would have been easy to find one who would have meted out the justice that man deserved; but so far as we see, no endeavour was made in this direction. On the very face of it evidence produced in such a way certainly does not commend its sincerity to those to whom it is presented. But as I have said, and as the President of the Privy Council has said, if there are cases of that kind let them be dealt with as individual cases. Let the names of the culprits be given and there will be co-operation to the end that they may be punished; but let them not be used for the purpose of seeking to rouse indignation in this House and among the public generally against the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Interior who are sought to be connected with it by nothing but a series of imaginative constructions of possible combinations of circumstances. To do that, I submit, is unjust and unfair. Denunciations of violators of the ballot boxes have no application to the members of this Government or the members of the House, who find it their duty to do justice to the two ministers, against whom in my judgment and, I am satisfied, in the judgment of the majority of the members, absolutely no case has been made justifying an inquiry. They ask for an inquiry directed against the Prime Minister of the country and the member for Three Rivers stands up and says: "I have made out a prima facie case because there was an adjutant in France who told a soldier -that if he did not vote a certain way he would be sent to the front line or the trenches."	On	that	statement ofa soldier	the	hon.	member	says
he has made out a prima facie case that the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Interior were engaged in a nefarious conspiracy to interfere with the liberty of the soldier. Can inconsequence go further?

Speaking in the province of Ontario on December 17th, 1918, in explanation of another speech which he had made during the election, I find this passage which appealed to me:
These magnificent results-
Referring to the results upon the battlefield.
-will have a decisive effect upon the whole course of our history. They were made possible not only by the courage and patriotism of our army in Prance, but also by the courage and patriotism of the people at home who put country before personal or party considerations in the hour of our country's need.
Did the President of the Privy Council put patriotism before personal interest, or love of country before party interests, when he said to-night, speaking with the reputation which he has in his native province, "the soldiers had a right to allot their votes"? Why, every child in this country knows that by this time. But he did not say-mark well-that the officers had the right to allot the soldiers' votes. No, he was too guarded about that. The soldiers had the right to vote but the charge is that the officers allotted certain votes which were not regularly put into the ballot boxes; and the Pre-
1 a.m. sident of the Privy Council who uttered the words that one must put country above party, and above personal considerations, stands up and approves of that conduct because, forsooth, he has confidence in his leader.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to detain the House, nor was it my intention to take part in this debate. But, Six, when I heard those utterances to-night-and I hope that I am not more honest than the hon. gentleman is, I trust that I am as honest-I hope that he has never stooped to anything disloyal in elections. I certainly, Sir, have been brought up in a county where we did not know-to the best of my knowledge I say it,-where we did not know, since the days of Confederation, of political dishonesty and corruption. That county has been represented by Liberal and by Conservative, and, Sir, to-night speaking with my fullest responsibility as a member of this House, and speaking in the name of the county that I represent, and in my own personal name,

I want to say as emphatically as I can, if that is the code of morals of the President of the Privy Council, if his morals are such that he can palliate, and 'endorse such action, then, Sir, so far as I am concerned, I want to place it upon record that I am opposed to all such methods, and if I were voting I would vote with the leader of the Opposition.

That is the position they have taken. They scout the idea of any one taking exception to that position.
The Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Doherty) says: I have passed a law knowing that I was giving votes to soldiers who had no stake in this country; I also passed a law enabling the officers, of my department and of the Government to place these votes just where they pleased, absolutely regardless of what the will or the wish of the voters might be-because the voters were not to have any will or wish; they were to be subject to the will and wish and direction and control of the Government and the officers of the Government. That is the position of the Minister of Justice, and he gets particularly warm because in construing the same law and in construing the duty of an officer of the law as high up as the Minister of Justice I take sharp issue with him and say that if he passed such a law he did something that he had no business to do; that if he puts such- a construction on it he did something that was absolutely wrong and unconstitutional, and that if he authorized officers to carry out such a law, he did

-which was this Bill, I differed largely with my party. For myself, I was against it all the time, absolutely against it, and my speeches will show that. I got the majority of the votes of the soldiers in my county who had the privilege of voting-a large majority. But overseas, where there were more than seven or eight hundred voters for my county, I got the magnificent number of thirty-five votes, because the votes of the soldiers there were switched and manipulated by this machine. Their fathers, their mothers, sisters and brothers and the soldiers at home were voting for me; do you mean to say that the boy who was away and whose mother and father were writing him and telling him to vote for McKenzie, would not vote for me if he could? Of course he would, but he could not; so that out of from seven hundred to a thousand votes I got only thirty-five-and that was by some mistake; it was not intended that I should get even that number. That indicates what sort of machine was doing the work.
The difference between the Government and myself is this: I say that no individual or aggregation of individuals, I care not who they are if they be anything short of angels, should have any power or right 'to interfere with the rights and privileges of the people. I say that no honest machinery is capable of being contrived by which the Prime Minister or any other minister, when votes were being taken on two continents separated by thousands of miles, could honestly pick out three hundred votes here, three hundred there, a thousand somewhere else, and place them
here and there all over the country as they wanted them. There is only one way of doing it, and that is the way it was done. These votes were falsely marked; they were put in one pile and then they were divided as you would divide a hundred bags of oats. Hon. gentlemen get quite hot under the collar about this thing; I never saw so much heat in the Minister of Justice since he came to this House as I saw in him to-night-because, forsooth, gentlemen differ with him on the construction of a statute. We are all wrong, it would seem, because we take a different view of that law. I say to the minister, I say to every honest man in Canada, and I will say to the people of Canada when the opportunity presents itself, that 'the implementing of that telegram-which hon. gentlemen opposite admit was sent; which they admit is correct; which was sent in code in a most dark and mysterious way from one minister to another-was absolutely incapable of performance in an honest way.
There is not a member of the Government, not a man sitting in this House who can more readily get out of an -awkward situation than the President of the Council (Hon. Mr. Rowell). Knowing his ingenuity and willing that he and his friends should have the benefit of the answer to it, I put a question to him.
Just after he had sent this telegram saying that three hundred should go to Selkirk, and so many to another place, and so many to Macdonald-aye, Macdonald, the pious, God-fearing man from Macdonald-they were going there-I asked the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell): With this voting going on throughout two continents promiscuously, how could you devise machinery by which you could place so many of them here and so -many of them there? Once in his life the acrobat from-I do not know where he is from-was non-plussed and could not tell. Nor any other man in creation could tell; it cannot be told. There is only one way of doing this: Those ballots were got together; they were marked just as they pleased; then a group of some kind of officials

I do not know who they were- got around them and divided them as they would divide a hundred bushels of -potatoes or twenty bushels of oats, of something like th-at. That is the way in which the thing was done. The story is quite easily told, and it is quite easily understood. If that sort of thing is all right, then I am all wrong. All I can say is that the people of Canada, in the innocence of their hearts, did not think that- that was the purpose of

the War-time Elections Act, nor of the Military Voters' Act. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) says that when he put the law through-and he is proud of it; he will do it to-morrow again-he knew it was capable of that thing and he knew the thing would happen.

subsubtopic: DEBATE .RESUMED ON MOTION FOR PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE TO INVESTIGATE.
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) said1 that we lay on our oars for a year and a half without bringing forward any charges of this kind. The Minister of Justice remembers well that the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Copp) in this House about a year and a half ago produced scores of affidavits sworn to by soldiers, and the oath of one soldier is sacred; I suppose, the oath of any soldier is sacred. These soldiers in their affidavits duly sworn to stated that they were tampered with in many ways; that they were not allowed to vote as they wanted; that they were threatened, and all the rest of it. That was laid before the Minister of Justice and the Government very emphatically in this House, and that is all we could do. The Minister of Justice at that time refused to do anything in regard to that charge. Does it then lie in the mouth of the Minister of Justice tonight to come back to us and say that we are too late; that we have slept on our rights, and that we have no business to

revive these things to-day? We revived them a year and a half ago and now we are reviving them again; but it is enough for the minister to say: You laid an investigation a year and a half ago; I refused to accept it; now you are reviving it again; I will consider it out of date because you are too late I would not take it at any time, but now you should not do anything about it and you are only reviving old spleen. I would be afraid that the tremendous heat which was indulged in on the other side of the House might spread across to myself, were I not determined that not one word would escape me that would in any way reflect upon the Prime Minister or the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen). I laid my case before the House on the day that I moved my motion, and I leave it to the House to say if I touched the hem of their garments in the slightest way. I kept strictly and absolutely to the facts of the case, saying nothing personal whatever. In reply or in response to that, I have the thanks for my care from the Minister of the Interior who said that I was the lineal descendant of the miserable thief that stole the telegram. That is who I am. That is a miserable Fletcherism of something that took place more than half a century ago in the House of Commons of England. It is not new; ft is not fresh, and it did not touch me at all If the statement were original with the minister, I might have thought it clever; but when he had to go (back to nearly a hundred years ago in the English House of Commons to find out something that was said about a very distinguished English statesman-and I should be proud to be put in his class because the reference was to Disraeli, the statement being made by the distinguished Irishman, O'Connell- the statement was not new; it was so stale and flat that I paid no attention to it. As to the question whether we should let these things drop and pay no more attention to them, I simply say as I have said before that we have brought them up before; that we have: pressed them as hard as we could upon the oaths of members of the service on the other side-I do not know whether they were officers or not; they were at all events private soldiers-and the Minister of Justice refused to comply with our request. We are pressing him again and he now comes badk and the whole Government comes back and says: There is nothing wrong; this telegram is all right, and the minister had a perfect right to send it and the Prime Minister of this country had a

right to he a conduit, a chute with a great many holes or arms in that chute by which means , votes were to be " chuted " here and " chuted " there, and shot to the other place. That was the 'kind of octopus the Prime Minister was going to be, and telegrams were coming 'from all parts of the country, while he was continually turning this crank " chuting " votes throughout the country. That is the position in which the Prime Minister was put. I am not at all surprised that he is tired and sick and wants to go away for a rest.
The matter would not be so very serious if these were only what is called " votes at large," that is, men in Canada who had no domicile here, who never lived in Canada. If those were the only tmen inr terfered with or whose votes were to be corralled, or " allotted " is the word, as is pointed out in this telegram, it would not be so serious. But the Minister of Justice and other members of the Government will see the facility with which mills were erected throughout the country making this sort of a vote. All that had to be done was to get a soldier to leave unanswered two or three questions and immediately that man became a soldier at large-he could go anywhere.
At Chambly and Vercheres 400 or 450 men were made to say that they did not know where they should vote. Imagine, men who swore before the commissioner that they were bom and had lived all their lives in Toronto, Ottawa, 'Montreal, or other towns and cities in the two great central provinces, swearing, in order to vote, that they did not know where they lived. The commissioner said there was no harm in it, but that is what they did. The Minister of Justice says it is all right, and the commissioner found it all right for a man who had lived in the city of Toronto and enlisted there as a soldier to go down to St. Johns in the province of Quebec and swear he did not know where he resided in order that he could vote in that constituency. The commissioner says that is all right, and the Minister of Justice and the whole Government back up the commissioner and say " Certainly, that is all right." That was all that was necessary in order to make as many votes at large as you please. There may have been ten thousand or only a few thousand, but you could multiply it up to 100,000 or 200,000 simply by the process of getting the men to answer in that way. That is what I object to.
We have no knowledge-I do not think the Government has any knowledge-how
this voting was done. Take the county of Provencher, for instance, some votes were required for that constituency. Would it not be a proper thing for the people of Canada to know how the soldiers voted whose votes were transferred to that constituency, and so put this trouble to rest forever? What machinery was used to put the votes there, and how did they get there? If the Government can show that everything was all right let us have the actual facts. But they take the contrary course. They say it was all right to do it any way at all since the votes were put where they would do the most good. It has already been said that the good or the bad in connection with an election depends upon party, that if the Liberal party is running everything that would assist them is a good thing, if the Tories are running everything that would assist them is a good thing. Is it proper that either party should have the deciding of what is the right thing, and then be given power under an Act of Parliament to take votes and apply them to that thing which they decide is the right thing?
I said on the day that I introduced my motion that the marking of the ballot Is a judicial act which one should do for himself. If he cannot do it for himself, he should not do it at all. It is an abuse of the privilege of the franchise for a man to vote who does not know anything about the matter at issue. If he does not know enough to decide for himself he certainly should not be allowed to exercise the franchise. We differ entirely on this. I say that what was done is capable of being absolutely wrong. The Government says it is capable of being absolutely right. The people of this country must decide for themselves with their own votes the destiny of their country. Honourable gentlemen opposite say that in the stress and storm of war they can do what they please. Imagine, Sir, a man setting fire to another man's barn and when called to account for it saying, "Oh, well, he was a slacker, he and his boys. They sent nobody to the war. I and my boys went to the war, so it's all right to set fire to his barn." That would be miserable logic, but it is just as bad to say that anything wrong can be done in connection with an election provided the intention is the sustaining of the Government that it is believed would be the most favourable to the prosecution of the war.
It is unnecessary for me to elaborate the consequences of corruption in elections. If the Government can keep themselves in power by switching votes, the corruption

speechtext:
The actual membership of the Board of Commerce has been completed by the appointment of Mr. Murdock. I may add that a French-speaking gentleman, Lieutenant-Colonel Lafleche, thoroughly qualified in * every respect, has been appointed to be the chief examiner and advisory expert to the Commission. I am sure the hon. member will recognize his competency, and the very many reasons which justify that appointment. I am satisfied that with the organization of the board so completed the hon. member will realize that the statement of mine to which he has just referred has
been fully implemented. The hon. gentleman is mistaken in saying I had made a promise that a French-speaking gentleman would be appointed to the board. If lie will re-read what I said he will find that what I said was that when the organization was complete it would be found that the necessity of providing within that organization for the perfect understanding of the French language had been considered and provided for. Provision has been made in the way I have mentioned.

subtopic: QUESTION AS TO APPOINTMENT OF FRENCH SPEAKING MEMBER.
speechtext: May I ask what is the salary of Lieutenant-Colonel Lafleche?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
