maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext:
On motion of Hon. Mr. Rowell (President of the Privy Council), Bill No. 22, to .amend the Royal Northwest Mounted Police Aot, was read the second time, and the House wen-t into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On Section 1-Name changed.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It might be well for the President of the Council to explain this Bill. As I understand it, I believe it amalgamates the two forces.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
As I intimated on the first reading, the Bill provides for the amalgamation of the Dominion Police with the Northwest Mounted Police. The continuing force will be the Mounted Police, and provision is made in this Bill whereby the Dominion Police may enlist in the Mounted Police, notwithstanding their age, and become entitled to the benefits of Mounted Policemen under the terms of the Bill. That will give to the Dominion Police the benefit of the pension provisions now available for members of the Mounted Police. Up to the present time there has been no pension fund for the Domin.on Police. Some of the mem-for the Dominion Police. Some of the mem-reacned the age at which, under the terms of the Act relating to the Mounted Police, they would be entitled to retire from the force and draw pension. It was considered that it would not be right to provide that,

upon joining the Mounted Police, they should have the right to immediately retire and draw pension, and it is therefore provided that they must serve for five years in the new force before they shall become entitled to retire voluntarily and receive pension. ilf a member of the Dominion Police were retired for grounds which, under the Mounted Police Act, would entitle a man to pension, he would then become entitled to it under the new Act. The Bill substantially improves the existing status of the Dominion Police and provides one Federal police force for the whole Dominion. The Bill further amends the clause of the Act which fixes the headquarters of the police force in the Western Provinces, and authorizes the Governor in Council to determine where the headquarters shall be. When the Bill goes into operation there is no doubt that the headquarters will be established at Ottawa and the force will be administered from this city. I think that this fairly outlines the purpose of the Bill.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Will the uniform of the amalgamated force be that of the Dominion Police or of the Northwest Mounted Police, or will a new uniform be provided?
Mr. BOWEL-L: The general uniform will be that of the Mounted Police; 'there will be no Change in that respect. Probably it will not be necessary or desirable that the uniform of that section of the police which is in charge of the Government Buildings in Ottawa should be changed from what it is at present. That particular matter has not been considered, but the present general uniform of the Mounted Police will be continued.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
This matter is a very important one and should be thoroughly understood by the Canadian people. In the days prior to the organization of the entire northwest into separate provinces it was commonly understood just what the service of the Northwest Mounted Police was. That service was unquestionably a very valuable one, and members of the Northwest Mounted Police as a body have won fame for themselves as a result of the excellent service they have rendered the country. But when the great Northwest Territory was divided into distinct provinces- Manitoba long ago, and more recently Saskatchewan and Alberta-taking up practically all the country over which the Northwest Mounted Police held sway, then of course these areas came under the control of the provincial governments which were

responsible for the enforcement of law and order within their own bounds. I do not see why the province of Alberta, for instance, or British Columbia, or any province west of tlhe Great Lakes has a right to a force of mounted police any more than Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec or Ontario. The same responsibility rests upon every governmental machinery for the maintenance of Jaw and order within the limits of the province. If I remember correctly, an arrangement wa.s made a few years ago by which the provincial governments in the West contributed some money towards the pay of these forces. I do not know whether that policy is still in practice; at any rate, I have heard nothing about it for some time. I am quite familiar, at least from hearsay, with the work and establishment of the Northwest Mounted Police, but I do not profess to be equally conversant with the Dominion Police Force, which appears to be a distinct body discharging separate functions. Now the two bodies are -to be amalgamated. -We have received -no explanation from the -minister as -to what the services of the new body thus formed will be, and it is desirable that -certain questions should be -answered. For instance, do they belong to any particular -province or territory; -and what will their functions be? Again, what is their jurisdiction and what law of Parliament -are they supposed to enforce? These are very important questions, and we would expect that, with the amalgamation of the two existing forces, a smaller number of -men would accomplish the duties ait present discharged by -them respectively, with some resultant economy. I should think fewer men would suffice, with fewer departmental heads, than in the pas-t. How -many men does the minister intend to have in the new force; wh-at is the nature of the organization; what officers *are to be put in -charge of -these different bodies; where are the forces to be located; -and what -service generally are they rendering and -will they render to the people of Canada? Further, what is the necessity for them? I submit that when a province takes upon itself responsibilities -as such it necessarily -assumes also the responsibility for maintaining all the 'm-a-chin-e-ry that is requisite for the general administration of justice -and the proper observance of order and good government. Why should we have a body somewhat analogous to an armed force in aid of civil- authority when there is no trouble or disturbance of any kind? There -are no wild men in the

West so far as we can see, and it seems to me that it is .a very expensive luxury for the Canadian people 'to maintain these forces unless tlhere is an imperative necessity for them.
The different provinces of Canada should assume the responsibility of looking after their own affairs. If there are any outbreaks in sight in the West, of course, that should be provided for, hut as far as I know, no indication is present of any trouble of that kind. It seems to me that there is some argument in favour of effecting economy by cutting down these forces or disposing of them altogether and letting the provinces look after their own affairs. The minister should explain what is to become of the various officials whom we had in connection with these two establishments. It is to be hoped that we are not going to carry on under one head all the officialdom that we have had under two departments. At this time when it is so keenly felt that we should save not only every dollar but every five cents that we can in order to keep within out national income and follow the principles of proper economic government, we should economize in every possible way. I trust that the minister will explain the exact position with- regard to these forces.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
My hon. friend is correct in saying that some few years ago agreements existed between the Federal Government and the Governments of the three prairie provinces under which the Mounted Police performed certain police duties in those provinces and in return the provinces paid a cash contribution to the Dominion Government. During the war those agreements were'Terminated, because it was considered that in view of the duties which devolved upon the police from a federal standpoint, their whole time would be required for these purposes during the war period. The most important branches of their work related to aliens and alien communities in Western Canada, the policing of the international boundary, and the general safeguarding of our interests in time of war. The agreements, as I have said, came to an end and there is now no written agreement in existence between the Federal Government and the Government of any of the provinces in reference to this work. Each province is responsible for the maintenance of law and order and for the administration of the criminal law within its own jurisdiction.
Much of the information my hon. friend has asked for to-day was given in the House
last session when I submitted an amendment to the then existing Mounted Police Act. That Act enlarged the jurisdiction of the Mounted Police, extending it throughout the whole Dominion. The amendment which is before the committee to-day does not enlarge the jurisdiction of the force; that is covered by the legislation which existed prior to last session and amendment of last session to which I have referred. The duties of the Mounted Police comprise the performance of such services as they may be called upon to render in relation to the enforcement of federal laws which affect the federal revenue, questions relating to customs, the international boundary, inland revenue, Indian settlements in Western Canada, and the post office-some very important work has been done by the Mounted Police in connection with trouble . that has arisen through robberies of the mails. They give attention also to certain work in connection with the Government system of railways. In addition the Mounted Police constitutes a reserve force which the provinces may call upon any time to assist in the maintenance of law and order. The Government considers it to be a matter of some importance that there should exist in this country at this time such a reserve force; and we are satisfied that that is the feeling of the people. This Bill does not increase the strength of the force; authority to increase the strength was given last session, The present authorized strength of the Mounted' Police is 2,500; the actual strength is somewhere between 1,600 and 1,700. The permanent Dominion Police make up a force of something less than 200, so that even when the Dominion Police, if they all choose to do so, enlist in the Mounted Police under the provisions of this Bill, the total strength will still be less than the present authorized strength of the Mounted Police.
I believe that there will be a reduction of expense in administration by reason of the amalgamation of the two forces. The iormer chief commissioner of Dominion Police, Sir Percy Sherwood, has resigned; the position has not been filled and it will not lie necessary to fill it. Under the new legislation the combined forces will be un-Jer the direction of the commissioner. The present Comptroller of Mounted Police will, under the new Act, be made financial comptroller and so long as the present incumbent holds that office he will receive the salary and hold the rank of deputy minister, as at present. That is the same provision as was made last year in con-

nection with the Deputy Minister of Agriculture, who was transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce to take charge of the Trade Marks and Copyright branch.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What are the duties of the financial comptroller?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The words themselves give an indication of what the duties will he-questions of pay, the purchase of supplies, equipment, accounts. In fact, the financial side of the administration will come under the financial comptroller.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I thought there was to be a purchasing commission some day?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Yes, but there must be a man in the department to look after the accounting side. '

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: My hon. friend said there would be an officer who would purchase.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: If I used that language, I did so inadvertently; I meant an officer who would look after the purchasing. There must be in each department an officer who is charged with the responsibility of recommending what should be purchased in that department. With a force of 1,500 to 2,500 men, the question of supplies to be purchased and of the general financial management of so substantial a force will require the care and1 attention of a responsible officer. That, generally, describes the duties which would pertain to the office of the financial comptroller.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Did I understand the President of the Privy Council to say that the present comptroller would continue in office as financial comptroller, with the status of a deputy minister.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: He will be re-appointed; at present he is comptroller. This Bill provides for the office of financial comptroller, and he will be appointed, under this measure, to that office with the rank and status of a deputy minister. That is the intention.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The statement was made by the President of the Privy Council a few minutes ago that after all these arrangements had been completed, the probabilities were that the headquarters of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police would be removed to' the city of Ottawa. This is of very direct interest to me because I happen to live in the city of Regina which has, for probably thirty-five or forty years, been the headquarters of this magnificent force, 
and I would like to know what is meant by the statement. Does the minister mean that the administrative officers will be moved to this city, or is he going to bring to Ottawa the whole of what has been heretofore regarded as the headquarters of that body? I might say that we expended out there probably a million dollars in providing barracks, training grounds, etc., and there are about two hundred acres of land in the city of Regina which the force has had the use of for that time without taxes, and everything has been done to assist it. I fancy that what is contemplated is the removal to Ottawa of the purely administrative officers, is that not so?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
That is entirely satisfactory to me. I would like to say a word or two further while I am on my feet, if the President of the Privy Council will pardon me. The leader of the Opposition made reference to the Mounted Police, and suggested that probably there was no necessity for it in Western Canada any longer. Let me say that I think there is such necessity and that it probably will continue for at least twenty-five years to come. I do not think the entire cost of discharging duties that would be, and have been, discharged by the Mounted Police, should yet be thrown upon the provinces. Let the leader of the Opposition understand, as I think he must, that the Dominion Government has thrown into the province of Saskatchewan alone in the past ten years probably 250,000 foreigners, none of whom before they came here knew anything about the Government of Canada or the conditions under which they -vyould live in this country. These men do not know Canadian law and they have to be taught it. They have been thrown largely into colonies where they do not come into contact with Englishspeaking people at all. They will, I believe, in time make the very best citizens. Their sons and daughters will also be good citizens, but the whole of them must be properly trained, and trained in a way to respect [Canadian law. I know of nobody in Canada or elsewhere that can discharge that duty as efficiently as can the Royal Northwest Mounted Police. The force, in fact, has already done so. These foreigners do not fear the Mounted Police at all, they respect them, and that is why the police have been as successful as they have. Now, as I have lived for some thirty odd years in the city where the headquarters of this fine body is located, I have naturally

taken a great deal of interest in it, and I for one, like everybody else I think in Western Canada, was very much displeased when the movement was started to disband this very excellent force. However, the decision was given to re-establish the police, and we have been watching them very carefully this last year to see what the result would be. I wish to state as emphatically as I can, that I am exceedingly pleased with the progress that has been made in getting this force into its old condition. The type of men in the force in the olden days was of the very best.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The police were an intelligent lot of men, they were of good social standing in every way. Men of splendid physique, and they were just the kind of men that were wanted. Latterly some hundreds of new men have been taken on the force, and I for one have been in a position where I could see the type of recruits that were being enrolled. By reason of the increase in salaries which was made last session, and further by the good judgment of Commissioner Perry, we have today in the force at the headquarters in Regina a body of men as fine as we ever had, and I am satisfied that in the course of another year the force will be back to its old-time condition and will once more enjoy its former prestige. That is the reason-because of the necessities of the situation and because the Federal Government should not thrust upon the provinces the cost of maintaining law and order and educating a foreign people for which the Dominion authorities are responsible-I think this body should be continued and in the manner suggested; but I do hope that the Government will not think of moving the headquarters of the force from the city of Regina at the present time-I think that would be a great mistake.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Just in answer to my hon. friend's question. (He is quite icorrect in his understanding of the situation. We will move the administrative officers who will direct the operations of the force. I have no doubt that all the buildings and equipment now at Regina will be required for the force stationed there, and will continue in use substantially as at present.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: All right.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
As I recall it, the present Comptroller of the Northwest Mounted Police was appointed
by commission. Now I understand he will be reappointed as Financial Comptroller, and I would therefore ask as to whether in his new position this officer will be reappointed by commission.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The Bill as drawn probably does not require the issue of a commission. However, there is no intention of derogating from the status of the present Comptroller, and if it is necessary to provide that "by commission" should be added, I have no objection to inserting these words in the Bill. I intended to ask the Law Clerk about the 'point later, and if necessary that addition can be made.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I am in the judgment of the minister, I merely wished to draw the point to his attention. I am tremendously interested in the splendid body of men known as the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, because I have been associated with them for about twenty years on the frontier. I have seen them carry on their duties in policing a vast territory approximating 200,000 square miles in extent find sparsely populated', and I think it is difficult for men living here to appreciate what the traditions, of the Royal Northwest Mounted Policemen are to that vast territory north and west of the lakes. The uniform of the members of this force has been a terror 'to evil-doers and would-be evildoers in the West from the boundary line to the Arctic ocean. The mere appearance of a yellow-striped constable in a mining camp, where there are men who would be likely to cause trouble if there was no restraining force in the vicinity, is sufficient, so wonderful is the tradition of this force throughout that vast territory. I am glad to know that the uniform of the force is to be retained, because it means a very great deal to people who live in that northwestern country. I think it is a good idea to amalgamate this force with the Dominion Police. As to the retention of the uniform of the Dominion Police in the Capital, or even in the East, where the Dominion Police are better known and the Mounted Police are not as well known, that may be a right thing to do, but I am not in a position to judge or to criticise the proceeding.
Some hon. member referred to the cost of administering this Force. I have no illusions in regard to it at all. It is going to cost more, for the simple reason that the force under the amended Act will be a larger force than we have ever had. As I recall it, the Royal Northwest Mounted Police never numbered more than 1,000 or

1,200 men during tthe last fifteen or twenty years. The Act, as I understand it, provides for an establishment of something like 2,500 men. I do not regret that; on the contrary, I welcome it, for it opens up another career for some of our young men who desire to participate in that form of national work.
It might be of interest to the committee, Mr. Chairman, for me to state the difference between the policing of the Yukon Territory of 200,000 square miles, with comparatively few people, and the policing of the District of Alaska with an area of 600,000 square miles. I do not suppose that at the present moment we have in. the Yukon Territory fifty Northwest Mounted Policemen, and at times that number is decreased perhaps to twenty-five and even less. I .have not the figures to present to you, Mr. Chairman, but I believe I am well within the mark when. I state that the United States Government to-day have in the District of Alaska between. 1,500 and 2,000 men-not ,as policemen, but as soldiers in military posts through that vast territory in the North which is under the Stars and Stripes. The Governmental authorities of Alaska admit that our system of policing, administering and governing a frontier country is very much superior to that in. vogue in. Alaska. I am satisfied myself that it is very much less expensive to police the Yukon. Territory per square mile or per capita of population than it is costing the Government of the United States at the present time with their system in, Alaska. They have from time to time studied our system, and efforts have been made to get the United States Government to create for their territories an establishment similar to our Northwest Mounted Police, but up to the present time they have not been successful. We have had many encomiums from men. who are prominent in the Republic to the South when they compare the two systems in the Yukon and in Alaska.
One word touching the cost of this proposed Force. As I say, I have no illusions in regard to it. This larger force is going to cost a lot of money, hut the expenditure will be worth while. We will have a mobile force spread across the country within easy striking distance of the various centres where unrest may from time to time occur. And, I assure you, Mr. Chairman, when the new force is properly organized we need fear very little trouble from prospective law-breakers. It will cost several million dollars more than it is costing now to keep this augmented

force equipped, provisioned and trained.
I am not quite sure how my
4 p.m. hon. friend the Minister of Militia (Major-General Mewburn) conducts his department, but I have in mind that the financial side of the Militia Department is under a separate head from the military side, and I would suggest to my hon. friend the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) the advisability of placing the financial part of this organization under a financial head. I take it that the President of the Privy Council will make Commissioner Perry head of the amalgamated body. And let me say here, Sir, that I have great pleasure in offering a tribute to that gallant officer for the excellent work he has done for the Royal Northwest Mounted Police Force. I know of no better man, and I know many officers of the force, who will uphold the traditions of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police with greater honesty, integrity and efficiency than the present Commissioner, Colonel Perry. However, he will have his hands full with what might be called the purely police or military part of the organization, and as a matter of administration I would suggest that it might be worth while to make the financial head independent of the military head, as I notice that this Bill provides for placing all matters under the control of the Commissioner. The Minister of Militia perhaps might inform us as to the custom in his department.
Major-General MEWBURN: The Deputy Minister of Militia, like the deputy minister of any other department, is directly under the minister and responsible to him.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
That is not exactly the point I raised. I know that the deputy minister is responsible to the minister.
Major-General MEWBURN: The deputy minister has charge of the civil and financial side of the department.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: That is the point I am making. I am not quite clear as to the line of responsibility here. Do both these gentlemen, the Commissioner and the Financial Comptroller, both have the status of deputy ministers? Of course, they are each responsible to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in answer to my hon. friend, I would say that the Bill as drawn provides that the Commissioner is to be the head of the force and responsible for its administration. The Bill provides for the appointment of a

Financial Comptroller, and so long as the present Comptroller shall occupy the post he will have the rank and status of a deputy minister. The duties of the Financial Comptroller will, under the' terms of the Bill, be defined by the Governor in Council. I do not think it is desirable to set them out in the Bill, for the reason that the view of the Government is that when the piesent Comptroller shall cease to hold this office it may be found possible to dispense with the title and add the duties to those performed by the commissioner.
I do not say that that can be done, but it is our present view that it may be done, and therefore the question of definition of the duties under the Bill should be made by the Governor in Council.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Do I understand that this Bill provides for the appointment of a new officer to be known as the Financial Comptroller?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: We have a comptroller now, but under the Bill he will be known as the Financial Comptroller, and instead of the duties of the comptroller being as extensive as they are now they will be limited to financial matters,.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
It looks to me as if the office might be abolished altogether, because there appears to be very little for a financial comptroller to do, according to the description given by the' minister. The financial management of the Mounted Police Force is a very small matter, there being only 2,200 men to be paid, and a clerk in the department could do it just as well as a financial comptroller. Therefore, I see no reason why we should pay the salary of a deputy minister for the performance of services that seem to be so simple. I would like to impress upon the minister the necessity of economy in connection with this department, and I think this is one way in which he can economize. I do not think he has at all made out a case for the appointment of this financial comptroller. We all know that in the Yukon and in the North west Territories we require a Mounted Police force; in fact, it is indispensable, and, of course, on both sides of the House we agree that that force will have to be maintained.
It is not clear, however, that they should be used for domestic work in the provinces. I do not think a very good case has been made out for that by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Cowan), or by the minister who has charge of the Bill. The minister tells us that the members of the force are now devoting themselves to looking after
infractions of the customs, inland revenue and post office law's. Why should we have that force engaged in that work in the Western Provinces when that is not necessary in the Eastern Provinces? As regards infractions of the customs laws, the seacoast is the place where there is the most danger, where there are the greatest facilities for smuggling and other breaches of the customs laws. If the ordinary customs officers are able to maintain the customs laws on the eastern and western coasts of this country, I do not see any good reason why we should spend large sums of money in assisting customs officers in the three Prairie Provinces. It will be necessary for the minister ito make out a stronger case than he has made on that score. My idea would be to reduce the staff of the Northwest Mounted Police to the capacity that would be necessary to * police the Northwest Territories and the Yukon and to let the three Prairie Provinces look after their own affairs.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. H. KEEFER (Port Arthur and Kenora):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, coming from a riding which is not of the Northwest Provinces but of that portion of the old province of Ontario called New Ontario, I wish 'to point out that there is something more in having this force well up to strength than merely in order to administer the laws of which he speaks. If you take -a point somewhat isolated, say four or five hundred miles away from any place where 'there is a laige number of trained men, of any force at places, for instance >at the head of the lakes, like Fort William, where the Government have wisely seen fit to establish a headquarters, the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) cannot realize the feeling of confidence existing there now since those men have been established at that point. Prior to that a very large proportion of our population was from the different parts of Europe, strange to our ways and to our language, and in times of excitement the situation amongst those of us who lived there was considered very critical as we did not know at what minute these people might flare up. I have seen riots;
I have seen times when we had to bring the militia from Winnipeg there in order to carry on the transportation, not only of the domestic business, but of the business of the whole of Canada. You have there three transcontinental railways; you have there elevators with a capacity of 53,000,000 bushels; the whole of the Northwest business is dependent upon what takes place there, and it is not

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry
to find the able-bodied representative for Port Arthur so frightened of foreigners.

Down in the province from which I come we have thousands and hundreds of thousands of all classes and descriptions of men from all parts of the world, not only by land but by sea. We live at seaport towns where we get all classes of people in the world. If you go into any small town in Nova Scotia with a population of ten, fifteen or twenty thousand, you will find two boys in bluecoats going along the streets, the same two men doing night and day duty without the slightest trouble, and everybody sleeping soundly when sleep time comes, nobody afraid.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What about strikes?

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
In times of strikes we never require outside help. Our own men take care of the situation. The sight of a Royal Northwest Mounted policeman would be a curiosity in our province. Nobudy would think of asking for their help. Of course, we are all slow to part with any luxuries we may enjoy, and the Northwest Mounted Police are undoubtedly a luxury to the western people. No province wili undertake to provide its own police so long as it can pass the burden on to the Dominion Government, and so long as the President of the Privy Council continue? to pay for policing the West the Provincial Governments there will be perfectly happy to let him do it, and in the meantime will not appoint a force of their own. They will not organize, form districts, appoint councillors and get a proper grasp on the situation themselves. Naturally they say "Why should we concern ourselves about that? We can use our money in another way. Ottawa is looking after this matter and paying the taxes." I do not doubt that it would be regarded as most extraordinary if the city of Sydney, or Halifax, or St. John should ask this Parliament to tax the people of the West for policing any of those cities. My good friends from the West would not stand for it for a moment. They would say, and quite properly, "Let those cities and the provinces of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island anti New Brunswick do their own policing in their own way. We are not called upon to furnish money for policing their cities." Now the West has very much larger cities than we have in the East. The magnificent cities of Calgary, Edmonton, Winnipeg and others put to shame our little establishments down by the sea. Why should not these great cities with all their wealth and influence and civilization and society. do their own policing? I think it is extraordinary that
people from the other provinces should be called upon to put their hands in their pockets to pay for policing the West, and it will continue so long as this Government sits back and pays the bills, and does not stir up the provincial authorities to look after their own affairs. The Mounted Police do nothing that cannot be done locally by the provincial authorities, if they would only get down to it. My hon. friend (Mr. Keefer) tells us that in this great magnificent province of Ontario with all its wealth and population, educational facilities, and potential resources, the people of his district had to send for mounted policemen to keep order in a corner of the province around Port Arthur. Ii I had not heard him say so, I could not have believed that any corner of this great province would come to the Dominion Government for police to maintain-order and good government within the province. It is a discovery that I never expected to make, and I would advise my good friend at once to insist upon the sleepers at Queen's Park waking up and providing proper police protection for the province to which he belongs, and let the resit of Canada look after themselrves.
It is all very well to talk generalities, but I want to say that >1 am making these observations seriously and with the earnest desire to see a proper administration of law and the maitenance of good order and adequate police protection in every nook and corner of this great country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and the best way to accomplish that is to throw the responsibility for the administration of these matters upon the local Governments. My good friend from the Yukon, who in his early days had the benefit of all we could give to a youth in the great province of Nova iScotia, knows that in that province we never had occasion for protection- of this kind, and I am surprised that he got accustomed to such protection in the far West. I should' like to see the foreigner in the good province of Nova Scotia who would try to boss around our Irish and French and Scotch people down there. He would find out where he was pretty quick. We have full control. We never give way to any foreigners. The foreigner has to make his conduct conform to our laws, and in no province in the East do we look for the protection of mounted police. I repeat, that as long as the minister continues to keep up this huge machinery and pays the bills for the local Governments and cities and towns of the West, so long will he find them coming back to him and



their representatives in Parliament saying what a magnificent man the minister is. what magnificent officers he has appointed, how well lie is treating the West, and what magnificent results 'they are getting. It costs them nothing to say that, and when [DOT]this Government- pays the bill the taxpayer in, the West is relieved of his legitimate obligation of maintaining law and order there. If the foreigner does not behave himself properly, let the local authorities police the district and make the foreigner pay for the policing. That would soon bring him to his senses, when he found he had to pay for any disorders he created. It is said that if you want to touch a Scotchman on a tender spot, touch him on the sporran, but I know of no better way of bringing men to their senses as a rule than by touching their pockets, and giving them to understand that if they do not obey the law they must take the consequences and pay the penalty. The minister knows that in 1906, immediately the two new provinces in the West were organized, there was a change in the old conditions. The new Governments formed in the West realized that a new era had dawned and that they had taken upon themselves provincial responsibilities, and those responsibilities they had to discharge. The burden which the Dominion Government had carried for a great many years was shifted to other shoulders. Now, some twelve or fourteen years afterwards, I cannot understand why we should be going back to those old responsibilities. We should have advanced, and conditions should be very much 'better than they were in 1906, when these two new provinces were formed. 1 hope that the minister, who loves economy, or at least professes to do so, will carefully consider what I am saying, for I was never more serious about anything in my life than I am in this statement, that while I desire to see order maintained in Canada and progress made in every province, I think that the responsibilities which the Constitution casts upon every provincial government should be left to that government to be discharged, and that we should perform our own duties that devolve upon us. The member for Antigonish and Guysborough has pointed out that we have a very expensive machinery in connection with this matter. Now, I can understand that when two departments are amalgamated the minister may have some difficulty in disposing of officials, but in such circumstances those officials should be subsidized, or some*other satisfactory course should he 
taken in order to have matters conducted in a businesslike way. It is exceedingly unbusinesslike to put half a dozen governmental families into one house and maintain them under their old heads and with their former wages. What is the good of such amalgamation? Every business amalgamation that occurs in the country is made with a view to economy. If two banks are amalgamated you do not find two presidents and two managers. The sole purpose of the amalgamation is a greater expedition in business and an improvement in the matter of economy, and if we are going to put these two departments together I trust we shall follow the same principle. Why should this force not be under the control of some existing department that has the proper machinery at hand ? The Militia Department have to deal with thousands of men outside. I do not know that they have any financial agents or officers outside of the department, but the entire business, at least in normal times, is managed from the department. This police force might very well be placed under the. control of the Department of Immigration and Colonization. That department is in touch with the West and knows the conditions that exist there. It is not a busy department by any possibility, for, as far as we can see, it has had nothing to do for the last three or four years. Indeed, if I were asked to mention anything that has been done by that department I should be entirely at a loss to do so. Why not therefore give it something to do? Put the force under their control and wipe out all the unnecessary machinery that we have been maintaining merely for the control of one or two thousand men working in the West. I am confident that this department would not he overworked if the force we.re put under it's control. At any rate, the Northwest Mounted Police must not exist for more than a few years, because the time is coming when every province will have to take care of itself as regards the enforcemnt of law and order. Let no one imagine for a moment that I have anything but the highest praise for the Northwest Mounted Police. But no matter how good they are, when the day arrives that their services 'are no longer required by the Carfhdian people they must go. They must be provided for if necessary. At all events, they will have the profession and do something else, and there is plenty for them to do in this great country. These are my views on this subject, and I am particularly of the opinion

that the provincial governments and their officials must do their own work and shoulder their full responsibility as prov-' inces. The sooner we appreciate the importance of that principle the better.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
My hop. friend has drawn a touching picture of the peacefulness and somnolence of the villages in Nova Scotia, and of the two constables who have nothing to do in North Sydney, I suppose. He has also shown us generally how the affairs of the province are looked after and how capably they are attended to by the village Dogberries of that district. The hon. member, however, must bear in imind that we sometimes get different accounts of Nova Scotia, and especially of Cape Breton, that indicate that the province is not always free from the industrial troubles and riots which have afflicted other parts of the country. My hon. friend as a lawyer will know that a leading case in connection with the calling out of the militia for the suppression of trouble arose in the particular corner of the province from which he comes, and it bears directly upon this question; for by such an act as this we may avoid any riot in that very peaceful corner oif Nova Scotia. There it was necessary to call out the militia to suppress the trouble. A Highland regiment, the number of which I have forgotten'-any hon. friend from Guysborough no doubts knows it-was called out, which was a very improper thing to do. The militia is not for the purpose of interfering in labour troubles, and everyone will agree with this statement. Interference of this kind only gives the militia a bad name amongst the people against whom they are called out, but if there is no police force there is nothing to do but to call out the militia. The case in question arose from the fact that my hon. friend's townsmen or neighbours requested the militia to suppress a riot and the regiment was constrained to go to the courts in order to collect their pay for the very strenuous work they performed. Now, the Northwest Mounted Police have found a place deep down in the hearts of the people of this country. For years and- years we have known how, by their system of stern, yet benevolent, justice they have been able to exercise a widespread authority and influence over the great territory that has hitherto been our ward. I hope that in time the provinces there will come into all the natural resources that are theirs and may then be able to finance matters of this sort. As my hon. friend from Yukon has said, the Northwest Mounted Police, by reason of 531
the wholesome fear which they have inspired in the rough and rude men of the West, have effected such a perfect state of discipline and such a respect for authority that one man can fearlessly enter a camp of desperadoes or refractory Indians-at any rate if he is afraid he admirably conceals his fear-and quell any trouble that exists, and arrest the most desperate man in the crowd. The moment these men see the uniform they realize that it is useless to resist the authority of the police. When a murder occurs among the Esquimaux on the Arctic ocean two or three men go out, and, taking their lives in their hands, bring the offenders to justice. Even if it takes a year to attain that end, the people in those regions know that the Northwest Mounted Police will stick with dogged tenacity to their purpose until crime is expiated, and we hope to see such implicit respect for law and order prevail throughout the country. Now, I do not agree that there will be any extra expense as a result of the amalgamation of the forces. The very reverse will be the effect, for we shall be able to abolish the position of the Commissioner of Dominion Police, now filled by Sir Percy Sherwood at a salary of $6,000 as deputy minister, and we shall have one commissioner at the head of both forces. The work will be co-ordinated and the result must necessarily be a great improvement and economy. We must have an administrative department to conduct tne business end of the force, and the present controller apparently is to be made financial controller. So that we are bound to have economy instead of extra expense. Altogether, therefore, I think the minister deserves the support and commendation of the House when he introduces a measure like this to perpetuate the efficient work of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police in regard to which so much excellent sentiment exists.
Mr. \\ HIDDEN: I should like to say just a word in favour of this clause and this Bill. I do not think it can be very easily shown that the Bill favours a sectional luxury; I rather think that it favours a national necessity. If I did not believe that the enactment of this legislation would be in the national interest I would not be as much interested in it as I am or as ready to support the Bill.
The question is not simply what the Northwest Mounted Police has dona for Western Canada as such; it is what that body of men has done for the whole of Canada, even though it has operated very largely in one part of the country. The sooner we get away from the sectional idea

of the benefits to be received from such organizations as this the truer our view will be. I am not inclined to disbelieve the possibility of an occasional Northwest Mounted policeman having been of great value if he could have been procured in that part of Nova Scotia from which it was my privilege to come, a good many years ago; I am not so sure but that an occasional Scotchman and Irishman needed to be brought into line, especially on election nights. But be that as it may, the fact remains that the newer parts of Canada are only beginning to be developed. There are the northern portions of the four western provinces; there is the new section of Ontario itself. Indeed, I should not be surprised if sufficient foreigners came into the good old Maritime Provinces to make the presence of a few red-coats welcome down there some time in the future. As for extravagance in continuing the Comptroller in his present office, I do not think there is an argument there at all. The President of the Council has given us ample assurance that such further adjustments will be made from time to time as are fair and reasonable and in the interests of this merged or combined force-a force to be known not as the "Royal Northwest Mounted Police" but as the "Royal Canadian Mounted Police." This Bill is worthy of our largest sympathy and our complete support.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I am not quite clear *on the question of jurisdiction. Suppose a mail robbery occurs in Ontario; would it he in order for the Mounted Police to take Initial action in that case or would their jurisdiction be in the way of supplementing the work of the provincial police-

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The primary responsibility for the enforcement of criminal law rests upon the governments of the various provinces, and in the case of any violation of the criminal law it is the duty of the province to see that the violator is prosecuted under the provisions of the Criminal Code. In such a case as that which my hon. friend mentions it would be quite competent, however, for the Federal Government, which is particularly interested in such a matter as that of the robbery of the post office or the mails, to put its own police on that case with a view to following up and capturing the criminal. That has actually happened in certain cases in Western Canada. The most cordial relations exist, I believe, between the heads of the Mounted Police and the Attorneys General

of the different provinces. I have made it perfectly clear to the Attorneys General of the provinces that this Government does not intend to relieve them from their prim- -ary obligation to maintain law and order in their own provinces. This force will give their attention, to the enforcement of the various federal laws to which I have referred and which affect the revenues of the Federal Government.
I want to make it quite clear that the Mounted Police will perform also the very important function throughout Canada of being a reserve force available when called upon by the Government of any province to assist in the maintenance of law >and order. In every country a certain force must be maintained for the preservation of law and order. If we had not the Mounted Police, we would have to have a larger permanent military force in Canada. The existence of such a body as this will render it unnecessary to maintain as large a permanent military force as otherwise would be required for the maintenance of law and order and of constitutional authority.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: My hon. friend is aware that we have doubled the militia force?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: We have not doubled it yet.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: We passed legislation to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Authority has been
granted to do that, but it has not been acted upon as yet. The point I am making, however, is not with reference to the strength which is authorized; it is with reference to the actual force that should be maintained. I think it is wiser to have that reserve in the form of police force rather than in the form of a larger military force than we need otherwise maintain. It will tend to the preservation of law and order and it will be less likely to give offence and create irritation if the force available for maintaining law is a police rather than a military force. May I illustrate that point by mentioning the unfortunate strike that took place in Winnipeg last summer and the situation which resulted therefrom? It was no part of the duties of the Mounted Police to interfere in any way with the progress of that strike or take sides with either employers or employees.
The Mounted Police took no action until the mayor of the city and the Attorney General of the province stated that they were no longer able to maintain law and order, and requested the assistance of the

Mounted Police. The fact that the Mounted Police were there -at. that -time and did take prompt -and effective -action when called upon to assist in the preservation of law and order when disturbances occurred undoubtedly prevented v-ery serious bloodshed, and the possible loss of life and property on a serious scale. They re-es-tabli-shed law -and order in the course of a day or two after the trouble broke out. So that in -addition to the peculiar federal purposes which have been mentioned this force will be a reserve available at the call of the provinces to assist in the maintenance of law and order in case there is necessity for. their so doing. Such is the reputation of the Mounted Police; such is the regard in which they are held wherever they are known, that the very fact of their presence in a given locality prevents many an outbreak which might otherwise occur. The value of the services rendered by the Mounted Police, therefore, rests not only upon fheir active assistance if called upon in case of a disturbance, but also upon the fact that their being available for the preservation of law. and order constitutes an important safeguard against -serious disturbances.
I agree with the leader of the Opposition, that we should not relieve the provinces of their -primary responsibility for the administration of the criminal law and the maintenance of law and order in their own provinces. There is no intention to relieve them from the responsibility-this force is merely complementary to theirs and is maintained in the interests of the whole Dominion.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What is the actual strength of the force?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The present strength is between sixteen and seventeen hundred.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: May I ask also the number of men that are stationed in each province at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The principal divisions
at the present time are the Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia divisions. What is called the Manitoba section of the force includes the detachment at Fort William as well as the forces in Winnipeg, Brandon, and Portage la Prairie. Winnipeg is the headquarters for the administration of the Manitoba division but the reserve squadron-that is a squadron available in the case of need-is stationed at Brandon, Manitoba. Regina is the prin

 cipal headquarters of the force in the province of -Saskatchewan and the main body
of the -police of that division is stationed there, but there are detachments in certain other important centres of the province. In Saskatchewan also an important force is maintained at Prince Albert and from that post an important section of the Northwest Territories is administered. In the province of Alberta there is the northern section with headquarters at Edmonton and the southern force with headquarters at Lethbridge, a substantial number being maintained at Macleod where we have suitable barrack accommodation for them. In the province of British -Columbia the main force is stationed at Vancouver but we have limited forces in Victoria and at certain points in the interior. Vancouver will be the headquarters for the force in that province.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: To be perfectly clear on the point I raised a minute ago. Take for illustration an ordinary robbery, do I understand from the minister that it is primarily in order for the provincial police to look after the matter, but that the Mounted Police may take action of their own volition if they wish, without being called upon by the provincial force?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: A-s I understand my hon. friend's question, it is this: Would the Mounted Police take action without being called upon by the provincial authorities to do so? Is that my hon. 'friend's, question?

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I asked, would they
have the authority to do so?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
They would have the
authority, in fact the right, to do so, -as I understand the law and the powers given them under this Act, but whether they would do so or not is a question of policy, and the general policy is n-o-t to intervene except at the request of the province.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
That is the point I
wanted cleared up.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Is it the intention of the Government to station any of the Mounted Police in the eastern provinces?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The distribution of the
force when the amalgamation is completed has not been decided upon-. When the amalgamation is completed then the question will be taken up for consideration. I cannot say at the present time that there will be any portion of the force stationed in the East, and yet it is quite within the powers given by the Act of last session, and by this Bill to place a limited number of the force there if it was considered in the public interest

to do so. Of course there are certain Dominion Police in the East at the present time who will now become Mounted Police, and to that extent the force will be represented.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: This Bill provides for the appointment of two chief officers, a Commissioner and a Financial 'Comptroller. I understand that the salary of a deputy minister is $6,000 and that the Financial Comptroller is to receive that amount. Will the minister state what salary it is proposed to give the commissioner?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Order. Before the
minister answers the question I must draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that we are not proceeding regularly this afternoon. maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Perhaps I can
get an answer to my question now

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The Commissioner oi
Police now draws a salary of $4,000 as provided by the Act and the usual allowances granted to an officer of the Mounted Police. It is contemplated that that amount will be increased, in view of the increased responsibilities imposed upon the Commissioner. maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The practice or procedure by which the militia are called out in aid of the civil authonties is well established under the Militia Act. Will the Minister explain rwhat machinery is provided under his Act by which the civil authorities can call out this body of police to their aid if they should require it. A soldier who used his .gun or bayonet in quelling a riot without the authority of the mayor of the municipality or of the local authorities, would be acting unlawfully, but if he has [Mr. Rowell. 1
such authority from the authorities he is protected in anything he may do. Supposing that in the city uf Winnipeg or the city of Toronto, it is found necessary to call out this body that we are now creating in aid of the civil authorities, what is the legitimate way of going about it so that these men would have authority and would be protected in whatever they might do?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The policy which has been adopted, and which I think has been found to work satisfactorily, is that we require a request from the Attorney General of the province before the Mounted Police are allowed to intervene in support of law and order. Of course, we do not require such a request in connection with the enforcement of certain Dominion laws in which the Dominion Government is particularly interested. It is not statutory, it is the result of a common understanding between the Dominion authorities and the Attorneys General of the different provinces.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Does the province incur any liability upon making such a request?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: This House has to vote the appropriations for the maintenance of the Mounted Police, and we have not asked the provinces to make any contribution under those conditions.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: As the minister is aware, the municipality where a disturbance takes place is liable to bear the expense of policing by the military. The proposal now is, as I understand it, to allow the municipal authorities a choice between the Mounted Police and the military. It appears to me that the minister's idea is that sometimes the military might be called out, and at other times the Mounted Police, to assist in quelling disturbances. I would like to know if the chief magistrate of a municipality has that choice? There is no doubt as to the practice in regard to the military. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) has referred to that. When a request is made by the chief magistrate of the place where a disturbance is taking place it is the duty of the military to assist. I would like to have some explanation on that point. .

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The situation is not quite as my hon. friend has suggested. As he has pointed out, the conditions under which the military interfere are well understood and laid down in the statute, and there is no proposal to interfere with that practice. As the law stands, the mayor of any muni-
>
cipality, under the conditions prescribed in the Act, inay ask for the assistance of the local inilitia in maintaining law and order. Where that assistance is given it necessarily means a more or less substantial expenditure of public money to provide for the maintenance of the militia while they are under arms. But the Mounted Police are in regular service all the time. It does not cost any more for them to assist in the maintenance of law and order, as, for instance, in the Winnipeg riots, than it costs the country to maintain them in barracks ready to be called out. In other words, the calling out of the police in a case like that did not add appreciably to the financial burden of the country. Therefore, so far the Government has not asked any province to make a contribution in a case that called for the assistance of the Mounted Police. We have not recognized the right of the head of a municipality to call for the assistance of the Mounted Police. We have always insisted that that assist-
5 p.m. ance would be given only upon the request of the Attorney General. We think in that way we are more likely to maintain that cordial co-operation which is so important in the administration of law and the maintenance of order throughout the provinces.
I will illustrate the situation by an actual incident. Some time last spring, as I recall it, we received a request from a certain point in British Columbia, stating that a strike was on, riots were occurring, and neither life nor property were secure, and asking that the Mounted Police be sent in. This reply was immediately sent: " Have you requested the Provincial Government to assist in maintaining law and order? If the Provincial Government require our assistance, and wire that they wish the Mounted Police to be sent in, then the Mounted Police will be sent in; but they will not be sent in unless the Provincial Government requests it." That has been the policy pursued up to date, and so far as I ain aware that is the policy which would be pursued in future.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The minister did not, perhaps, appreciate my point; at all events he did not answer iit. Supposing a mounted policeman comes into the city of Winnipeg, and in doing what he thinks is necessary to restore order he kills a man, and is charged with murder, wdiat is his protection? That is my point. If he were a soldier brought in by the mayor of Winnipeg under the Act he was practically the same as if at war, and if he killed a man in the discharge of
his duty his answer would be: He was called out under the Militia Act and acting in the discharge of his duties. That is the protection of the militia man. But here comes the mounted policeman, and in the discharge of his duties at the request of the mayor he happens accidentally or necessarily to kill a man, and he is charged with murder, what is his defence? I submit that it is noit a defence for him to say that the head of the Mounted Police Force told Him to come at the request of the mayor; there must be some statutory authority.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I overlooked the point my hon. friend has mentioned. He is quite correct in saying there should be some authority justifying such action. That authority is found in the Mounted Police Act itself. I turn ;to the amendment of the Act passed last session, which is now known as Chapter 69, 9-10 George V, and I find the duties and powers of the police are there set out, and in the respect to which I am now referring I do not think they differ materially from the law as it stood before the amendment. subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
The purpose of the
amendment is simply to correct an error that crept into the dispositions which prohibit the carrying of firearms. There are two dispositions, one of general application, which prohibits the carrying of such firearms as are susceptible of being concealed on the person, and the second applicable only to aliens, which was intended to make a prohibition of the carrying of firearms generally without the proper license. In the second section as it stands in the Code the words " as above described " were introduced which produced the result of limiting the disposition to the class of firearms the carrying of which was generally prohibitive. The purpose of this amendment is simply to strike those words out so that with regard to firearms generally the prohibition will apply to aliens, who will be required to have a license to carry any kind of firearms. At present the general law requires a license only for the carrying of such firearms as are susceptible of being concealed on the person.

On the Orders of the Day:

I have before me a copy of the Toronto Daily Star of October 1, which contains some statements concerning myself to which I desire to refer. It says:
He comes forward as an offended military genius whose advice was not taken by General Currie, as it was not taken by Lord Kitchener -and many others. His advice appears to have been at the universal disposal, yet was not used.
Never in my lifetime have I offered advice to General Currie. I have offered suggestions tp Lord Kitchener and to the British War Office. With your permission, Sir, I will refute the statements here, and I -am sure the Toronto Star will be the first to regret its mistake.
Leaving out anything in regard to the South African war and colonial assistance in European wars, I should like to say that I made suggestions to the British Government in regard to straight rifle shooting and rifle shooting wa.s encouraged in Britain and in Canada -for years before the war. We were fortunate in having the "Old Contemptibles," or the "Old Eeliables" as we choose to call them as well as the Canadian soldiers thoroughly up in rifle shooting when the war broke out.
In 1912 .and 1913, I had proposed the sys-tern of trenches near the border, and on- the night war broke out, I proposed 'that system practically on the order of the Prime Minister of the Dominion. The matter came up when war was declared, and the Prime Minister asked me what the chances were.
I told him that if the plans as laid down which I happened to know were followed out our men would during the first three months get the most severe trimming men ever got. He asked me if anything could be done to prevent that, and I said that it could be stopped by the1 use of trench positions. He urged me to send a cablegram to Lord Kitchener and Lord French, and that I did, and to-day the trench system is credited all along the front to your humble servant.
In March, 1918, when the retreat was going on from St. Quentin, I took the liberty of drawing Lloyd George's attention to the matter, and while I am not saying that this was done on my suggestion alone, at all events Lloyd George adopted that suggestion, and the trench system with untrained soldiers was utilized to withstand the onrush of the Germans. fSlr Georgo Foster.]
In the cablegram which I sent in 1914, I proposed trench diggers which we had been using for some time here, and they were adopted by the British Government in 1915.
I. may point out that I recommended the shield-shovel in- 1914, but it was not adopted by General Alderson or the British War Office, but it was used by some Canadian officers and men and was very effective in saving many a life, and if generally adopted would have saved thousands and thousands of lives on parapet work at night. They were the fore-runners of the steel plates used by all the Allies. The British Government, as well as France, Eussia and Italy, adopted thorn.
Armoured machine gun motor batteries were adapted by us in 1914, and they were used with some effect in 1918. The system of hidden machine gun positions in rear of trenches I recommended in 1914, and after the battle of St. Julien- I took the liberty of cabling Lord Kitchener to know why they were not ready for that fight and received his answer; but after that the system of hidden machine gun positions was adopted by the British service.
I might point out that I also recommended the use of palmite powder in 1914, a very high explosive and very safe to handle. We used it here in Canada in making experiments with it until the supply was used up, and it proved very effective.
I recommended the use for the first time of cotton hose filled with explosive for destroying iparapets and wire entanglements, and I also recommended iron pipe filled with explosive, both of these to be used for the destruction of wire entanglements. They were used with great effect until the tanks came in when, of course, the tanks supplanted everything else. The methods of throwing hose and pipe so filled were suggested by us.
In 1914 I devised a trench mortar and handed it over to the British Government, and tens of thousands of them were used all along the line; in fact I believe about a hundred thousand of them were used.
I also recommended a direct-fire gun in October, 1914; I had one prepared, and in 1916 both the British and the French adopted it- I have letters from the British Minister of Munitions and General Joffre adopting the suggestion. The guns they used were somewhat heavier than the one I suggested, but they turned them out and they did splendid service until the tanks came in when they were carried on the tanks.
As regards the convalescent hospital system, the system we established in 1915 was

adopted three or four months later by the British War Office and by the Allies also.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am inclined to think
the hon. member is making what is in effect a reply to a charge or a statement contained in the Toronto Star. It is quite competent for the hon. member to make a denial and to explain his position, but I hope he will not pursue the course of making what is in effect a reply to certain statements.

I thought it was
competent for me, not merely to give a bald denial, but to show what I did. I may say, with all frankness, that I do not purpose letting any person rob me of any credit due to me. I have not urged this before the country; I would not urge it now had it not been pointed out that it was claimed that none of my suggestions were carried out by the British Government, when the fact of the matter is that every one of them has been carried out. The transport and supply system which I recommended in 1915 and the fish rations system which I recommended to the British Government were also adopted by the British War Office. The direct system of recruiting which we adopted in 1915 was later on adopted by Lord Derby as far as the British municipal systems would permit. The utilization of commercial institutions as well as arsenals for the manufacture of shells was first adopted by your humble servant, and every Government in the world followed suit.
The refining of copper and zinc and the manufacture of T.N.T. and gun cotton were first introduced into Canada during the war. The use in war of the leading commercial, business and scientific men as honorary officers was first introduced during the war by your humble servant, and I need not say what splendid results have been achieved in Canada and all other countries which followed suit. The Forestry 'Corps was established under the direction of General Alexander McDougal, and the British Government is still retaining his services in the old land to straighten matters up. The Railway Corps was established under the direction of General Jack 'Stewart, and the British Government took over the whole system.
The dental corps was established in defiance of all military rules and against the wishes of the British War Office but they accepted it and nothing could have done more to promote the comfort and efficiency of our men at the front than the work which this dental corps did. The disinfecting and
cleansing . service, through the medium of creolin, etc., was also taken care of.
Our plan for brigades, divisions and corps were adopted by the British. Our sysiteSh of administering the medical corps, with reference to the business end of it, was adopted by the British Government in 1915. We also instituted reforms in our Pay Cbrps. With regard to the aeroplane and zeppelin service, I pointed out to the British authorities the need; and some days ago showed what Colonel Grant Morden had done. In 1914 Mr. Fessenden showed me his plan for detecting submarines and locating artillery by photographing sound waves. I sent him to England and it was his invention that proved so useful in locating artillery and submarines. The University of Toronto, at my request, took up the matter of tetanus toxin. I understand that it was from the University of Toronto, the work being taken up at the instance of your humble servant, and it being recommended by me to the British War Office, that large supplies of tetanus toxin were procured and utilized greatly to the advantage of the men.
After the first gas attack in the battle of St. Julien I was waited upon by Mr. Le-Sueur of Ottawa. I had him submit a report with regard to certain methods of using gases and I have the data to show that the British Government appreciated his report very highly.
May I 'point out that I did intrude, much to the dissatisfaction of some gentlemen, in seeking to save the lives of our Canadian boys in the Ypres salient? I recommended in 1915 that the line should be straightened out; I also recommended in 1916 that the line should be straightened out; and in 1918 it was straightened out, much to the advantage of the defensive forces. I recommended in 1915 and also in 1916 that in place of having the blanket attacks that were being made they should go in for narrow and deep penetration. If you read General Ludendorff's report on the succesful British attacks in 1918 you will see that it was by the system of narrow and deep penetration that the Allies were able to smash the German lines.
I had the honour of discovering Max Aitken and although it took me three months to get him recognized by the Canadian Government, no man, according to General Ludendorff, did more to win the war.
In 1914-15 I recommended the system adopted in connection with the Canadian national loans. I had the honour of point-

ing out that we should make these loans from the Canadian people, using the money that we had in reserve in Canada, obtaining it, not at high rates of interest and not making the income exempt from taxation. I would not have taken up the time of the House
Go on.
I could go on talking for an hour-but in justice to myself, the Toronto Star and the Minister of Propaganda in this Government, who evidently inspires the Toronto Star
