On section 1 : Operation of provisions respecting the disposal of surplus grain. Postponed until after crop year ending 31st August, 1919.

I explained the purpose of this amendment when introducing the resolution on which the Bill is founded. At the last session of Parliament

a Bill was enacted, being chapter 40 of the statutes of that year, and 'section 3 of that Act provided that in the month of August in each year stock should be taken of the quantity of each grade of grain in the terminal elevators, and when the total surplus was found to be in excess of one-quarter of one per cent of the gross amount, the grain received in those elevators during the crop year, in excess of that surplus should be sold annually by the Board of Grain Commissioners and the proceeds thereof applied to the purposes of the board. It was clearly the intention of Parliament that that amendment to the Act should not apply to the cereal year ending August 31, 1919, only to the present and future cereal years. I am sure this was the understanding of Parliament and of those who were interested in the proposed Bill, the measure being in my charge during its passage through the House.
Mr. McKENZIE r Do I understand the minister to say that the Act has not yet come into effect?

The Act is in effect and as it now stands empowers the board to take any surplus of grain in excess of one-quarter of one per cent of the surplus of the last cereal year which ended on August 31, 1919, in so far as the elevators are concerned.
When did the Act go into force?

On the 7th of July, 1919, and1 it was the intention that this provision should only apply to the surplus grain in the terminal elevator beginning with the cereal year 1919-20, that is beginning September 1.
The provision is only to take effect on the 1st September, 1919?
Yes.

Purely that.

I had a preliminary report from the Board of Grain Supervisors with reference to receipts and expenditures, and just from the figures that were given, I think I made the statement that there 'was a surplus of receipts over expenditures, the larger proportion of which had gone to the diminution of the price paid by the Allies for the grain which had been purchased; but. the accounts scarcely bear that out. I stated to the House, as well, that the Government would not be called upon for any guarantee. That statement remains good; but un-

til the whole of the accounts are adjusted it is impossible to say what surplus there will be and how it will be distributed. We will have that information at the next session of the House when the affairs of the Board of Grain Supervisors shall have been ultimately settled. Some of these are matters of negotiation and adjustment-they are not all finished.
Mr MeKENZIE:	Is the minister sure
there will be a surplus on the right side?

I am assured
there will be a substantial surplus.

There is another matter the minister might clear up for the information of the country. It has been widely stated that in Great Britain at the time the British Government guaranteed the ninepenny loaf the price of wheat was fixed at $1.80 cents a bushel. We guaranteed a price considerably over that to the Canadian grower. Does the purchaser in Great Britain pay us the cost of the wheat to the Government, .that is, the price guaranteed by the Government, plus interest, storage and transportation charges, or do we make certain allowances to Great Britain on its purchases?

The regulations approved by the Board of Grain. Supervisors provided for carrying charges, as my hon. friend will notice, if he has read the various orders which were issued. So that in the guaranteed price the carrying charges were provided for, and there is no loss to the Board of Grain. Supervisors with reference to those items. The British Government sells the wheat to the British miller [DOT]at a price which guarantees the ninepenny loaf, and bears whatever the cost may be in that regard. Of course, my hon. friend knows that for a whole year or more the British taxpayer has been subsidizing the bread production in Great Britain in order to keep down the price of bread to the ninepenny rate, which has involved .a heavy cost. But that cost is borne entirely by the British people through the British Government; it does not fall upon the producer on this side of the water.
Mr. J. H. .SINCLAIR: Mr. Chairman, I think this would be the proper place to get some information from the minister in regard to a paragraph which .appears in. the Auditor General's Report, Volume 1, page 24. An Order in Council seems to have been passed on.. the 12th of October, 1917, empowering the Grain Board to collect from millers, exporters., etc., a fee not to exceed

four cents a bushel, so as to create a fund for the purpose of defraying the cost of carrying wheat in store or for any other purpose .which the Board might deem expedient. Up to July 31, 1918, the Board had collected for this fund the large sum of $5,987,883.28 including ($43,122.92 bank interest. Then the Auditor General proceeds to say that the Board declined to pay this money into the Consolidated Revenue Fund, claiming that they had a right to deal with it without any parliamentary control. The letter of the Auditor General from which I have extracted this information does not appear to have been, answered, and I would like to know from the minister how that matter was dealt with and if the Consolidated Revenue Fund did get possession of that large sum of money.

No. The Consolidated Revenue Fund could not by any possibility get possession of that large sum of money which my hon. friend (Mr. Sinclair) has mentioned, amounting to five million dollars odd. The fund referred to had to carry the whole cost and charges of the grain-interest, insurance and everything else -and was to a great extent disbursed for those purposes. It was not something which came in as a perquisite to the Board of Grain Supervisors; it was, as my hon. friend will see if he will read the orders of the board, a fund constituted for the purpose of meeting the expenses of carrying the grain from the point of production until it was taken charge of by the Allies. It would be impossible, of course, for that money to be put into the Consolidated Revenue Fund as something belonging to the Dominion itself. As I have stated, until all the accounts are adjusted and paid we shall not know exactly how the matter stands and just how much the surplus will be.

Mr. Chairman, the reason why I ask the question is that the Auditor-General takes the ground that this money does belong to the Consolidated Revenue Fund; but from the minister's explanation I understand the Government has taken the opposite ground and has sustained the position of the Board of Grain Supervisors.
I have not seen the correspondence and do not know whether there has been a reply made or not. I will make inquiries and inform my hon. friend in reference to it.

Are any commissions paid by the Trade Mission handling our commodities on the other side? For in-

stance, on the Roumanian and Greek business?	'	i
What does my hon. friend mean by commissions?

Any commissions paid by the Trade Mission or by any one concerned therewith. In short, I may as well state what I understand, that considerable commissions were paid to agents in connection with the Roumanian business. Of course, as is well known, the Roumanian Government is not paying us cash; this Government is advancing the money on the security of Roumanian bonds and so on, which are worth sixty to seventy cents on the dollar in the open market. T understand that commissions have been paid to agents for securing this trade, and I would like to know what are the facts.

" I think it has been already explained to the House, at least, questions have been answered which carry the information, that the Canadian Trade Mission in London and the branch here in Canada in connection with it are empowered by an Order in Council to take a percentage on the contracts which are entered into in London, which percentage is paid by those who hold the contracts in this country, and that percentage goes to form a fund which bears the expenses of the Trade Mission in London and the Trade Commission here in carrying on their operations. That fund is subject to audit, and if there is a surplus after all the operations are through, it will remain in the Consolidated Revenue Fund. But no commissions are paid either by the Trade Mission in London or by the Trade Commission in Canada. Both are simply agencies through which what is required by European Governments or buyers is brought to the attention of those in Canada who supply those requirements.
Who fixes the prices, for instance, of the commodities that go to the Roumanian Government?

The price of
wheat, for instance, is to be at the current market rates. As it was an impossibility to foretell what the deliveries of wheat would be worth from month to month through the year, the price had to be put upon an indeterminate basis, and therefore arranged that the Roumanian Government should pay the current market rates from time to time. As regards other contracts-
Building paper, for instance?

The specifications of anything that is required by the Roumanian Government are given, and the Trade Mission bring those to the attention of the manufacturers or producers in Canada who work along those lines. The matter is then one of adjustment between the purchasing party on the other side and the selling party on this side; the price is agreed upon and the contract signed.

Some phrases in the last line of section 2 require some explanation. As I understand it, we are guaranteeing the man who sells ithe wheat against any loss by reason of the failure of the foreign Government or the British Government to complete the bargain, take delivery and pay for the goods. Have there been any cases of failure to purchase or to complete the contract? Are there any claims outstanding as against foreign governments? The last time we were discussing this Bill the minister told the committee that we had had no losses; he tells us to-day that, perhaps, he was a little premature in making that assertion.

No, not as to
losses; my statement still holds good so far as that is concerned. The Board of Grain Supervisors fixed the price of wheat and sold the surplus on that fixed price. The buying power last year was really the Wheat Commission in London, which bought through the Wheat Export Company here. There was no trouble in connection with failure to take delivery; in fact, the surplus of last year was not so large as to equal the quantity -which was needed by the commission. So that the general statement holds good that the guarantee which was given by the Government will not involve Canada in any loss. The other statement, I think, is also correct, that, without committing oneself to the amount, there will be a surplus when the operations are all completed.
The Auditor General's Report shows that the Wheat Export Company got- $2,500,900 by way of proceeds from these operations last year. What is the Wheat Export Company? Who are its members?

Mr. James
Stewart was the head of the Wheat Export Company. This company was the medium which bought for the Allies the wheat which the Board of Grain Supervisors, on behalf of Canada, produced for purchase. They



were the agents, or buyers, of the Wheat Commission-that is, the representatives of the three Allied powers for whom this wheat was bought and to whom it was distributed.

At the last session an amendment was made to the Grain Act providing for the appointment of an appeal board. That board has not yet been appointed, yet in no year in the history of the West has there been greater need for such a board as there is this year. Have any steps been taken looking to the appointment of that board, and if not, what is contemplated?

The legislation was to go into operation on. proclamation of the Governor in Council. The Governor in Council,- having in view the expense which would be entailed in the establishment and employment of a board of appeal who should give their whole time to the duties involved in the opera-
4 p.m. tions of such a board, and having regard to the small number of appeals that were actually made during preceding years and the small number of these which were adjudged against the primary decision, came to the conclusion that the matter might well stand over for another year and be a little more closely examined into before the legislation should be brought into effect.

I do not think that the excuse of the expense involved should be made in this case. The Grain business has always carried itself; it has been no charge on the country in any way. If i.t should be any charge on the country, the fault would be that of the administration. It was amply demonstrated during the discussion at the last session that the fact' that there were very few appeals was not a proper criterion to go upon. The cumbersome nature of the board that has had to deal with these things practically prohibited any appeals being made; the board was so constituted that it was almost impossible to get it together. The considerations which the minister has mentioned should not, I think, carry weight; -in the interests of grain producers and the grain trade that board should be appointed very shortly.

We on this side will surely approve the attitude now taken by the minister in recognizing the need for economy. The very opinion the minister has just expressed was voiced from this side of the House when the legislation was going through last session, when it was pointed
TSir George Foster.!
out that appeals were comparatively few. I am glad to know the minister has taken the sensible view, and that one department at least of the Government is working along lines of economy.

I quite understand that there were some objections to this Board from certain quarters, but the producers of grain, who are the people interested, are prepared to foot whatever bills are necessary in connection with it. If a sufficient charge is levied the board can carry itself, and it will be self-supporting in every respect so far as the general public is concerned.

I believe the trouble is that a certain decision had to be reached by the Government before this board was established and it was possibly a very embarrassing one for the Government to make. There was the very strongest pull for this new Court of Appeal to he established in Winnipeg, and equally strong pull for its establishment at the head of the lakes, and strong supporters of the Government were in favour of one or the other proposal. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was not here at the time. Certainly he would not bother his head looking up the discussion, but these rival claims were put forward very strongly on the floor of Parliament. In this difficult situation the Government possibly decided to drift along and make no decision, on the pretext of economy, which would appeal to the people at this particular time. Perhaps it would be a very proper expenditure to have this court constituted, if the people of the West desire it, and especially this year when there is so much wheat that is not up to standard. I presume that the appeals are from the decision of the first set of men who examine the grain. I do not profess to be an expert in this matter, but I understand there has been a great deal of complaint about the decisions of those who have the last say as to the grade in which the grain should fall, and the grain growers are anxious to have a final court of appeal. That was the argument made last winter. If the toll taken from the grain growers themselves is sufficient to pay for the expenses, there is not the same justification for the Government depriving them of this court of appeal. I trust it was not because the Government did not care to decide upon the venue of this court, and that the minister, if this court is not going to cost the Government anything, will let the people have the benefit of it, and decide as he

may deem proper whether it shall be established at Winnipeg or at the head of.the lakes.	.
Sir GBORG'E FOSTER: I think amongst the growers the view is favourably entertained that there should be a court of appeal. The Government does not minimize the value of the opinion of the West, which is not, of course, unanimous, nor has it declared that such legislation shall not be brought into effect. It was considered better, however, after pretty careful study, to give the matter a little more consideration and let it stand over for the present at least. With reference to my hon. friend's political idea, how often we interpret others by what we would do ourselves in a similar position! I can see as plainly as possible that my hon. friend would grasp at such a shrewd way of getting out of a political difficulty, and therefore he imputed it to myself. I can assure him that that was not a deciding factor in the least degree. I was perfectly prepared to give a decision if the time came, as to where this board of appeal should have had its locus in quo. It was the idea of economy, and of prudence in making expenditures, which led to the decision of the Government. Due consideration wall be given to the matter, and next session we will have a chance to talk it over again.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Oape Breton North and Victoria) moved:
subsubtopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION INTO NON-RAILWAY SECTIONS OF MARITIME PROVINCES.
speechtext:
Whereas on the 16th of March, A.D., 1914, this Honourable House passed the following Resolution which was accepted by the Government,-
" Mr. McKenzie moved that in the opinion of this House the time has arrived for the extension of the Intercolonial Railway of Canada into the non-railway sections of the Maritime Provinces within reasonable range of the said railway." See pages 1736, 1737, 1738, 1739 and 1740 of Hansard for the said year, A.D., 1914.
Be it therefore resolved that, in the opinion of this House, the proposals of the said Resolution of the 16th of March, A.D., 1914, should be carried forward to completion at the earliest possible date.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, at this stage of
this short session, I do not purpose saying very much about this resolution moved as it is. During my long experience in this House, although I repeatedly brought to the
54J
attention of the House the matter of the extension of railways in the Maritime Provinces, this was the first time that a resolution along the lines that I had been suggesting from year t-o year was accepted by the Government. On the 16th of March, ,1914, the House accepted the proposition that the day had then arrived for the extension of the Intercolonial railway of Canada into the non-railway sections of the Maritime Provinces within reasonable range of that railway. In August of the same year war broke out, and since then all our resources and energies have been devoted to the prosecution of the war. During those war years I did not say anything about the railway at all, as I thought it was only fair and reasonable to allow the Government to centralize and converge all their energies on the one great question. Sometimes the leader of the Government and others ascribe to us motives and notions which must be political all the time and say that we are all the time talking for political advantage. I can put forward as some proof of the absence of such motives my entire silence during those years upon this very vital question to me. I suppose if I had wanted to make political capital from year to year, I could have continued bringing this question up, hut I said nothing about the matter while the war was on and while our energies and thoughts and every faculty which we could bring to bear towards advancing the cause only, were engaged in the prosecution of the war. Now that the war is over and we are back again to peace and harmony and re-establishment, and doing everything we can towards the advancement of the country, I think it is proper and right for me to advance this question and once more to ask the Government to give attention to the development of railways in that part of the country from which I come and which has hitherto been largely neglected.
Tt is true 'that wre have in the Island of Cape Breton one line of railway, an extension of the Intercolonial across the Strait of Canso, connection having been made between Port Mulgrave and Port Hawkesbury by a good ferry boat. That road extends across the island down to .the city of Sydney, a distance of about ninety miles. Any person acquainted with the geography of the island of Cape Breton will readily understand that no one railway can possibly- satisfy or give proper accommodation to that island, for the reason that that large and important island is divided into two sections by the Bras d'Or lakes. That

is a large arm of the sea running right through the island from the mouth of the Big Bras d'Or on the Atlantic to the St. Peter's canal, where in the old days and before the canal there was a narrow neck of probably half a mile or three-quarters of a mile in width, which has since been cut by the canal. Taking the Bras d'Or lakes with the extension of the canal out to St. Peter's bay, the island of Cape Breton is practically two islands. Therefore, this Government railway which we now have can give accommodation only to one side, and we have accommodation for which we are very thankful largely on the south side of the Bras d'Or lakes, that is, as far as some parts of the Bras d'Or lakes are concerned. The leader of the Government (Sir George Foster) has been through the island of Cape Breton and possibly he has a fair idea of how the road runs; but to the people who have never visited the island and who do not know the manner in which the Bras d'Or lakes cut up the island, it is impossible to explain the insufficiesncy of one line . of railway to accommodate this large section of country, a section of country which has tremendous mineral wealth, coal in inexhaustible quantities, iron and steel, also great possibilities in lumber and still greater possibilities in fisheries. For that reason we think we should have a further development of the railways in the island of Cape Breton. In the fisheries of Nova Scotia and particularly of the northern end of the province, which includes the island of Cape Breton, there is the greatest'opportunity for the development of wealth that we have to-day in any part , of Canada. It is not too much to say that while something like $8,000,000 or possibly $9,000,000 worth of fish was taken out of the water of Nova Scotia last year, we are just touching the industry, just picking up pebbles on the seashore, as one might say, as compared with what can be done. If we had a railway extension along the sea-coast where those fishing villages are, where millions of tons of fish are to be had for the mere taking of them, we would then be in a position to cater to that trade and to get this fish commodity to the market in a marketable shape. In my riding of Victoria and North Cape Breton, not to mention the rest of the -island, there must be, following the sinuosities of the shore, something like 200 miles of magnificent seacoast fisheries, and it is sad to relate that in those 200 miles there is not one-half mile of railway. The only way in- which people can get their fish to market will be by battling with the storms along 
that stormy coast in the summer time, and in the winter time, although there is splendid fishing during that season of the year, there is no means of communication at all. My proposition is that the Government should at once, for the benefit not only of Cape Breton, hut of the whole country, extend a line of railway right along both sides of the island of Cape Breton touching those fishing villages -and fishing centres, and in that .way putting a great wealth and a great food product, the best in. the world, within easy reach of the Canadian people. It is only to-day, Sir, that an American .gentleman came to this city asking for certain information from the Customs Department and other departments of the Government in connection with a fish factory or purchasing establishment to be put in operation in the riding from which I come, and that gentleman informs me that his people intend to invest some $50,000,000 dn the development of fisheries in that part of the country. In that way, Americans, if not ourselves, are beginning to realize the great importance of getting in touch with the fisheries of that part of the province of Nova Scotia.
During the years 1909, 1910, 1911 and 1912 the now Prime Minister, who was in Opposition until 1911, myself, the hon. member for Guystoorough (Mr. 'Sinclair), who is here, the hon. member for Inverness (Mr. Chisholm) and the former member for Richmond, N.S., were working vigorously together for the purpose of carrying forward some railway improvements in the province of Nova Scotia. The Hon. Mr. Borden, who was the senior member for Halifax, was appealing strongly for a road from Dartmouth to Dean Settlement, a distance of about 90 miles. I was looking for a connection between my own riding of Victoria and the main line, having had then in mind a short link of about 22 miles. My hon. friend from Guysborough was looking for a railway system connecting his county with the main line and the members for Richmond and Inverness were looking for the developments necessary to bring their own counties into touch with the great arteries of commerce.
All of that was provided for and a start was made in the early part of 1911. But fortunately, or unfortunately, there was a change of Government. The line of differentiation was drawn very sharply between what was the Liberal road and what was the Conservative road. The Dean Settlement road, which was in the county of the Prime Minister, was built, but the roads in my county and in the counties of the other

gentlemen whom I have mentioned were dropped and nothing was done for (them. Anybody who knows Nova Scotia will know that no part of the county of Halifax needed a road as badly as the county of Victoria.
I have often brought to the notice of the Prime Minister that ft was not fair partnership or quite sportsmanlike on his part, that, in view of the fact that we were all helping to build these roads and standing by him when he was in Opposition, when fortune came his way and he had an opportunity to build our roads as well as his own, he dropped ours and went on with his own. He always promised us that he would do better and that he would help along these projects. Unfortunately he is not here now,' but he has often heard the story before and if he were here to-day and listened to this complaint-and, if you please, accusation- it would not be the first time that he had heard it put forward.
However, be that as it 'may, the Dean Settlement railway is built and it is in operation. I am not at all sorry because the people of that section of the country have the advantage, and it does not have to be built a second time. I would like to be assured that the Government would make provision for the extension of the road in the county of Victoria and through the various large fishing centres in the county to the extreme north where it is necessary to have this work done. I am sure that the right hon, the acting leader of the Government will appreciate a situation such as we have in the county of Victoria. The northern settlements of Victoria would be about 150 years old, if not older. Some of the very earliest settlements in (Canada were to be found here being made up of a splendid, strong, sturdy class of people, fishermen and farmers along that coast. They have always contributed their share to the building up of this country in money and in other ways. But up to this time, while roads are being extended to the Pacific coast and in all directions, while the benefits of civilization, advancement and progress are coming to every other part of the country, these people are left out in the cold with no railway facilities at all. I do not think I am asking too much when I ask the Government to now carry forward the idea which they, accepted some five years ago. They then agreed that this work was necessary and I am now putting forward the proposition that the idea which was accepted in March 1914 should be re-affirmed and that the request made at that time should be
implemented by the building of these roads.
I shall not elaborate this question very much farther because it does not require any elaboration. It is absolutely necessary that these roads should be built and the only possible excuse would be the inability of the Government because of some financial reasons which have nothing to do with the work. I trust, however, that this project will be found to be so deserving, worthy and practicable that there will be no hesitation on the part of the Government in proceeding with the work.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED EXTENSION INTO NON-RAILWAY SECTIONS OF MARITIME PROVINCES.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to support the proposition of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie). He very properly asks Parliament to carry out the resolution that it passed in 1914:	This is the
resolution :
That in the opinion of this House the time has arrived for the extension of the Intercolonial Railway of Canada into the non-railway sections of the Maritime Provinces within reasonable range of the said railway.
The resolution itself is perfectly plain and it can only have one meaning. The carrying out of this resolution was interrupted, as my hon. friend has said, on account of the war. But the war is now over and the time has come when the Government can fairly be asked to deal with this question. Taking the province of Nova Scotia alone, there are, properly speaking, only two nonrailway counties in it. I refer to the counties of Victoria and Guysborough. I submit that the claims of these two counties are stronger than the claims of any other section in Canada for railway extension. We are not asking for any favours from the Government; we are simply asking for fair play.
Speaking for the county of Guysborough, let me point out that the people of that county have been contributing to the building of railways in other parts of Canada for the last fifty years. Along the line of the projected branch line from Sunnybrae: in the county of Pictou to Mulgrave in the county of Guysborough, there are 40,000 people who would be accommodated by the building of the line. It is known that this country has spent on railway construction since Confederation over $400,000,000 without including the expenditure in connection with the Canadian Northern Railway. When you have a population of 40,000 and estimate the whole population of Canada at about
8,000,000 it will be seen that if these people paid their full share which they certainly did it would be about $2,000,000 contributed

to the building of railways in other parts of Canada.
If you make an estimate of the liability incurred in connection with the Canadian Northern system, you will find it would amount to another $400,000,000, so that by giving railway extension to my constituency the Government would simply be paying back a part of the money we have already contributed towards extending railways in other parts of Canada.
I would also point out that this proposal can be defended on its merits. It would be a good investment for the Dominion to build that branch line into my constituency. There are great resources to be developed in that part of the country-agricultural, mining, timber and fishery resources. The leader of the Opposition stated a moment ago that there are great possibilities connected with the fishing industry on the eastern coast of Canada. That statement is quite true, but the fishing industry on that coast has never had a fair chance owing to the lack of the necessary transportation facilities. You cannot carry on a successful fresh fish business without quick means of transportation, and we have never had these means of transportation in Eastern Canada so as to give our fishermen a fair chance to develop this important industry. Wherever these facilities have been granted the results have justified any expenditures that have been made. A good many years ago the Government granted a small subsidy to connect the town of Canso with the Intercolonial railway at Mulgrave by a steamboat service, the distance being about twenty-seven miles. A boat was placed on that route and that was the first opportunity that the fishermen of that vicinity had of putting their fresh fish on the Canadian market. The business began to grow, and I venture to say that for the expenditure that has been made there is no business development in Canada that shows better results than the shipment of fresh fish from the ports of Canso and Mulgrave since those facilities were granted. I have a statement here which I wish to place on Hansard so that the Government may have an opportunity of studying this matter and understanding what a splendid investment this would be if they should decide to embark in it. After the facility referred to was given to the fishermen on that coast, as I have already said, the business began to grow, and it has grown year by year giving the following results.

Showing a steady growth in this trade from the time the boat was put on in 1895. You will notice that in 1895 the Intercolonial freight receipts on these shipments of fish amounted to only $4,805, while in the year 1917 they reached a total of $111 483.17. I have not at hand the figures for the year 1918 or for the part of the present year that ig past, but I am informed that the growth during this period is fully up to that of 1917. Now this business has been handicapped by the fact that the railway is 27 miles away from the point of shipment. Canso is situated at one of the best fishing points on the coast. It juts out into the Atlantic, very near the fishing banks, and there is no part of the coast of Eastern Canada where the fishing industry can be better developed than at the town of Canso; and if the railway could be extended to that point I submit there would be a very large development in that business. If the fish dealers of Canso were able to place their fresh fish on board iced cars at Canso and ship same to western points in Canada, or to the United States, in good condition, without transhipping it by boat at Mulgrave or other points, it would be an immense advantage. It would tend toward developing that trade and building it up into one of

the great industries of Eastern Canada. This fact was recognized by the late Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) has told the House how it was dealt with.
For a good many years- the building of branch lines by the Intercolonial Railway was -not favoured by either political party. But in 1910 the House -adopted the policy that in future the Intercolonial Railway, instead of depending on small companies to build their branch lines, would undertake the work themselves, and immediately following that decision the late Government decided to build -three branch lines in the province of Nova Scotia; one in the county of Guysbo-rough, connecting Guysborough and other points along that coast with the Intercolonial at Sunny Brae; another in the county of Halifax terminating not on the coast, but in a country district called "Dean's Settlement" and connecting with the Intercolonial Railway at Dartmouth in the county of Halifax; the third projected branch line was in the constituency represented by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition. Provision was made for the building of those branch lines, one million dollars being voted for the construction of the branch line in the county of Halifax, another million dollars for the building of the branch in my constituency, the Government also purchased from the Nova Scotia Steel Company a short line of railway from Fer-rona to Sunny Brae at- -a cost of $100,000. That branch was to form part of the Guysborough line and is now owned and operated by the Intercolonial Railway, but the road was never extended. My hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has stated the facts. The late Government did not take into account whether a constituency was represented by -a Liberal or by a Conservative, they viewed the matter in a broad non-partisan spirit as effecting eastern Nova Scotia generally, and they found that in order to provide railway accommodation for the population there it was necessary to build the three branch lines I have mentioned. When the present Government came into power they struck from the estimates the money provided for building the branch line in Victoria, and they cancelled the contract that had been made for building the branch line in the county of Guysborough and struck the million dollars from the estimates. They retained the contract for the branch line in the county of Halifax and went on with its construction. The line has since been completed and I believe it is a prosperous branch of the Intercolonial. I am informed that it
is developing a large traffic in that prosperous district in the' eastern portion of Halifax county. But the counties of Guysborough and Victoria have had to wait for -their much needed railway development, for no other reason than the fact that they exercised their right of sending members of the Opposition to this Parliament. Now, that is not a very credit-able action on the part of the Government, and I think it is time they wiped out the reproach, for it is a reproach, that such a condition of things should prevail in this country.
I am quite aware that the Government are not able to spend as much money now as formerly on account of the financial condition of the country. But at the last session of Parliament a large sum of money was voted for railway extension, and it will be remembered that the late Minister of Public Works (Mr. Carvell) made this statement during the session which closed last July:
We propose to spend $10,00-0,00-0 or $12,000,000 this year,-that is 1919-on branch lines in Canada, and every mile is west of the Great Lakes.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is no good reason for that discrimination. Why should our railway extensions all be west of the Great Lakes? The province of Nova Scotia has a population about the same as that of the province of Saskatchewan, and surely the claims of the people of Nova Scotia for railway accommodation are just as strong as are the claims of the people of Western Canada. I can see no argument at all why they should not be. Indeed, I think that I could build up an argument to show that the claims of Nova Scotia are stronger, because it is a much older settlement, and its people have borne the burdens of this country for a longer period than have the people of the Western Provinces. 1 have already pointed out that they contributed their resources for the last fifty years towards the general development of the Dominion and the construction of railways in the other provinces. Therefore, there can be no reason why a preference should be given to Western over Eastern Canada in the matter of building branch lines of railway. The ancestors of the population of the county that I have the honour to represent came there at the time of the American Revolution, about one hundred and fifty years ago. As I said before, I do not object to the development of Western Canada, but f submit that the -people of	Eastern

Canada have an equal right to the building of branch lines. How, then, can we .justify ourselves in voting $10,000,000 or $12,000,000 during the current year to build railways in Western Canada without voting one dollar for the same purpose in Eastern Canada?
In regard to the financial embarrassment of the Government, it will be noticed that the Government have been spending money right and left for several years past and they continue to do so. If the Government was sincerely practising economy, the case would be very- different and we would be more inclined to excuse them for not taking this step at the present time; but when we find such items in the public accounts as I am about to enumerate, we have to abandon the idea that this railway development is refused on the grounds of economy. For example, $10,000,000 was paid to MacKenzie and Mann when we did not owe them ten cents. That is one very large item, and it would be sufficient to 'build quite a number of small branch lines. On Canadian Registration the Government spent $646,000-an expenditure that in my view was absolutely useless to the people of Canada. On the Department of Public Information last year the Government expended $81,414 in order to publish a small newspaper that is really of no use to anybody and could be very well dispensed with.

I am glad to 'hear it. I pointed out last session that we were spending $10 an hour on that useless newspaper; and if ojur criticism on this side of the House has had the effect of stopping that wasteful expenditure, I am very much pleased to know it. Now, in the face of these extravagances, and many others that I could mention, it is difficult to convince the people of my constituency that the Government have no money wherewith to build these branch lines. We have been very patient in regard to this railway development in the county of Guysborough-the patience of Job was nothing compared with the patience we have exercised in regard to this matter.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce is a reasonable man; I ask him, in all fairness, whether I have not made out a case for some action on the part of the Government in regard to this matter? The minister was a member of the Government which struck from the Estimates a few years ago the million dollars which was voted to complete
[Mr. J, H. Sinclair.!
this branch line in Guysborough, and in that way he is responsible. He was a member of the Government which cancelled the contract that was made for the building of that branch line. The time has come when fair play should be done to my constituency in this matter. We have had promises that when the war was over this item would be restored to the Estimates and 5 p.m. the work would go on. Now the war is over; the Government has commenced the construction of branch lines in other parts of Canada, and they should now implement their promise in regard to the extension of railways in my constituency. I do not wish to press the matter too strongly to-day, but I trust that the minister will, bring this matter before his colleagues and that the promise given by the Minister of Railways when this item was struck from the Estimates will now be carried out.
