speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria) moved:
speechtext:
For a copy of all contracts made or entered into between the Government of Canada or any department thereof or any person or persons acting for or on behalf of the Government or any department thereof and the Dominion Can-ners. Limited, of Hamilton and Simcoe, Ontario, at any time since the 1st of August, A.D., 1914, and the 1st of August, A.D., 1919, and of all reports, letters, correspondence and all other documents in the possession or under the control of the Government, relating to or having any bearing upon any dealings, negotiations, contracts or business transactions of any kind whatsoever between the Government as aforesaid and the Dominion Canners, Limited, or any person or persons acting on behalf of said company, and especially, copies of reports made to the Government or any department thereof, by The Milton Hersey Company, Limited, Montreal, R. R. McColl, Esq., Government Inspector, Simcoe, Ontario, and H. H. Holland, Government Supervising Inspector, in reference to or having any bearing upon contracts, dealings and transactions between the Government as aforesaid and the Dominion Canners, Limited, during the period hereinbefore mentioned, and also of all reports made to the Government as aforesaid by any commission or commissions or any person or persons whatsoever appointed or authorized by the Government to inquire into and report upon the dealings, transactions and contracts between the Government and the Dominion Canners, Limited, or any person or persons acting on their behalf during the period from the 1st of August, A.D., 1914, to the 1st of August, 1919.
He said: I should have liked to make this notion when there was a larger attendance of members present, but as we are so near the end of the session, as I understand, and practically all the remaining days are to be Government days, members on this side of the House cannot very well select the time to make a motion.
The motion itself sets forth the correspondence, contracts, and other documents for which we are asking, and I shall state very briefly my reasons for making this motion. I am not taking any grave responsibility in connection with the facts that are placed in my hands regarding this matter.
I understand, however, that the manufac-

ture of war materials by the Dominion Canners, Limited, is not a new subject to the Government, but that irregularities and difficulties with that company have already once or twice been brought to the notice of the Government. I am informed by a friend of the company that a commission has been appointed to inquire into the dealings between the Dominion Canners, Limited, and the Government, which commission has not yet reported. I did not know anything about that.until informed of it after I had put the notice on the Order Paper. The facts which have been brought to my notice, and which I think will be disclosed in the papers that I hope will be brought down, are to the effect that bad material has been manufactured by the Dominion Canners, Limited, and sent to our soldiers at the front. I am informed that what the company sold to the Government as pork and beans was but a part of what they undertook to supply, that there were beans in the cans, but no pork, that when there should have been good beans and good pork very often there was no pork and only bad beans-rotten, defective beans, and rotten, defective cans- that instead of containing pork and beans alone a very large percentage of stones were from time to time found in the cans. Of course, there were not supposed to be any stones at all, but by a close calculation of the number of stones found in the cans that were examined it was found that something like seven or eight carloads of stones were shipped to the boys at the front as pork and beans. There is evidence that thefts were committed on the Customs Department, and I am informed that an attempt was made to patch up the trouble by the payment of a large amount of money to the Customs Department. These alleged irregularities, and, as I may call them, thefts are alleged to have been brought about by the importation of large quantites of pork with the supposed intention of using it in the manufacture of pork and beans, on which pork when it went out of the country there was to be a drawback under the regulations. It is alleged that large quantities of that pork were not used in the cans, but for other purposes, and that the Government paid drawback to the company in large amounts upon pork which was used in Canada, and was therefore not entitled to drawback. I understand that an investigation was instituted by the Customs Department and that four men were sent some time last February to Simcoe and Hamilton, that they made an investigation and discovered these irregularities, and I am told by a friend of the

company that a very substantial amount of money was paid back to the Department to make good these irregularities or in other words, if I am properly informed, this fraud and theft upon the Government, and I am informed that nothing further was done than to receive amount of moneys and to hush the thing up. That is not sufficient, and conduct of that kind should not escape without the widest possible proofs and with the punishment of parties who would attempt to have any complicity or participation in conduct of that kind. It has been shown by the inspectors that irregularities of this character were going on from time to time, not so much by the importation of pork which was not properly used, as the inspectors did not seem to have anything to do with that particular phase of the trouble, but there is in the possession of the Government a report made by four officials last February, as I understand, showing those irregularities as regards the customs. I have in my hand a letter signed by the Milton Hersey Company, Ltd., who were officials of the Government for the examination of goods produced not only by this company but by other companies as well. This letter, which is addressed to the Dominion Canners, Ltd., Hamilton, Ontario, reads:
Dear Sirs:-In reference to a sample of pork and beans taken at random by our Inspector at your Simcoe plant on 27th ult., we have analysed this sample for moisture, etc., and find the can contained six pebbles. There is something seriously wrong with the method employed at this factory for picking out defective beans, pebbles, etc., on the packing belt.
We would suggest that it is probably because the belt is overloaded, and these pebbles being heavier than the beans would naturally settle to the bottom of the load on the belt.
To remedy this trouble, we would respectfully suggest that some other method be devised to do away with the trouble, as it is a very serious matter.
We would be glad to hear from1 you as to what means you are taking in this connection.
Yours very truly,
Milton Hersey Co., Ltd.,
(Sgd.) J. G. Ross,
Chief Supervising Inspector.
This is another letter addressed by the same company of examiners, the Milton Hersey Company, to one of the inspectors of the Government, Mr. R. R. McColl, who was, as I understand, with the Dominion Canners at Simcoe as an examiner for the Government:
Dear Sir:-We are enclosing here two small pebbles. In the last tin of pork and beans from you there were five such pebbles. The
others we are sending to the Dominion Canners direct to call their attention to the same.
If you need more help to watch the inspection more closely, and to see that they are canning beans instead of gravel, please advise Mr. A. C. Neilson, 394 Sunnyside Avenue, Toronto, Ontario, so that he can give you an assistant. Yours truly,
Milton Hersey Company, Ltd., (Sgd.) J. G. Ross,
Chief Supervising Inspector.
That is a second letter, and only one of many letters that were sent complaining about the packing of gravel, as this concern says, instead of beans. It was contended that this factory was in a filthy, dirty condition and not fit to be used as a place where human food' was being put up. There is a further report to Mr. R. R. McColl from Mr. A. ~H. Holland, supervising inspector. I take it-and I think I am right-that Mr. McColl and -Mr. Holland were both Government officials inspecting the product of this factory. Mr. Holland evidently made an investigation for himself as to the condition of the place, and he writes this letter to Mr. McColl:
Dear Sir,

With reference to the inspection yesterday at the factory of the Dominion Can-ners, Simcoe, we have brought the following points to your attention.
1.	Zinc soaking tanks with a coating of slime on the interior lining. These to be cleansed in your presence.
2.	Soaking barrels in a sour condition. These to be replaced or given a thorough scalding of hot water.
3.	Deposits of slime on the floor and decaying material between the floors at points where the floors have given way.
4.	Packing belt sour. This belt must be cleaned with hot water, and should he attended to nightly.
5.	Condition of the floor in the blanching room and also the lower floors, as a result of the drippings from the soaking floor. These floors to be thoroughly scalded nightly with a view to do away with the sourness.
6.	Pork to be removed from tbe corner where water is dripping on it and be placed on paper on the floor in some dry position.
Kindly let me hear from you in this respect. We understand Mr. Innes is in town to-day and will see the War Office. We have already reported to them with reference to this plant.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) A. H. Holland,
Supervising Inspector.
This investigation of the supervising inspector was brought about by reports made to him and to others in regard to the conditions of this factory. One of the awful conditions was that the sewer from this factory, which sewer was connected with all the water-closets in the factory , was blocked, and that liquid material from that sewer came back into the lower stories of the building, flooding the material that was

being used for canning. When that flood subsided it is reported-and I have sworn statements in regard to the matter-that the material, pork and the stuff that was under this water was shovelled up and put through the process of being canned and was then sent to our boys at the front. If there is an investigation into this matter and if those papers are brought down, I am sure that those things will be shown. Not only was the material shorhweighted, no pork where there should be pork, no beans where there should be beans, but everything was done in an improper and unfit way, and our boys had to put up with that material and to eat stones and the contents of poisoned cans when they should have been getting proper food. I have here affidavits to this effect from many people. I do not purpose taking up the time of the House in reading them, but I purpose making a reference to them so that the Government and hon. gentlemen of this House will know that I am not manufacturing this story; that I have it on the declarations of men who are better known to some hon. gentlemen in this House than they are to myself. There is a very lengthy statement here by a Mr. Thomas Puzey, who was in the employ of this factory, I believe, at Simcoe. He tells a horrifying story about the condition of that establishment and about the shortage of pork.
Sir SiAM HUGHES: Shortage of what?

Pork. A can that was supposed to contain pork and beans did not contain pork at all. There are declarations here made by men and women who were working in the factory to the effect that they could not put the pork into these cans because they were passing too rapidly on the belt, that they had no time and that it could not possibly he done. Where this condition would occur you would have no pork at all. It was subsequently discovered that pork was not being put into the cans that were being handled in this way. Cans coming out of the factory would contain a certain weight of pork if they were put up honestly. The weight of pork was checked up and it was discovered that it was not sufficient to supply the number of cans which were turned out. In that way the Government and the people were paying for hundreds of tons of pork which they never received and large profits were being made in ,gn improper manner.

What is the date
of the manufacture?

I think it went back
as far as 1915 and up to within a short time of the end of the war. There was a contract for 86,000,000 pound tins. I am not informed exactly as to when they finished the contract but it was during the years 1917 and
1918-I think 1916, and possibly as far back as 1915. A report of the facts has been made to the Government. I am informed that a report containing these matters has been in the hands of the President of the Council (Mr. 'Rowell). Reports have been made to hon. members supporting the Government coming from that section of the country complaining about these conditions but nothing has been done. I do not mind telling you that I am informed that this is a source of trouble among the friends of the Government, that the man who at last came to me with the information is a friend of the Government, and that he had exhausted every means of getting some friend of the Government to bring this matter to the notice of the country. But having failed he came to me with these sworn statements and I regard it as my duty to bring the matter to the notice of the Government. It is said that hundreds of thousands of dollars have been improperly extracted or obtained from the Government in this way.
Is there any evidence that the people who were evidently parties to this fraud, reported it at the time, or drew any one's attention to it?

I have letters of the
inspectors who were reporting as to the defective way in which these beans were put up and one inspector writes to the subordinate inspector asking him to see that they put beans and not garbage into the tins. That letter was written away back in 1916. I am further informed-and I believe it is true-that the Department of Customs bad a complaint that they were being robbed, that they were paying a drawback on pork which had no right to have a drawback. They sent four inspectors to see about it and I am informed that in view of these irregularities moneys were paid to get over this difficulty, that the company was allowed to go on and that no further notice was taken of the matter.
I stated that there were declarations upon oath from these men. Thomas Puzey, who was an employee and who made a declaration under oath; and T. P. Pope complained about his business; W. Gurr of Simcoe makes a sworn declaration or a declaration before a commissioner. There are also declarations by H. R. Henderson, A.

G. Pendergast, Ada Pendergast, Mamie Plummer, Thomas H. Plummer, Harry Mansfield, C. Tucker, William H. Trern-bley, John Fraser, Mary A. Collver, Lila Stegmeier, Harry E. Watson, George W. Post, J. George Wood, Thomas Gurr, Jack Eade, Jonathan Peteh, J. Petch and then there is some correspondence. These are sworn statements, or declarations under the provisions of the Act. These are living witnesses who will be available to the Government when the correspondence is brought down if they think it proper to inquire into this matter. This man R. E. McColl, who is a well-known gentleman in Simcoe, says that he found it impossible to prevent them from using this filth and dirt that was lying around the place; that at night they would gather that up notwithstanding all his vigilance. He claims that they would take the rubbish, that even material from the sewer basins would be gathered up, put into boxes and put through the machinery again for the purpose of being canned for the use of our boys. I presume there are many gentlemen in this House who know Mr. McColl. I do not know him. He comes from the county of Simcoe. He had been appointed inspector which is some evidence that he. was a man of some standing. This is one of his letters addressed to the Milton Hersey Company of Montreal:
Simcoe,., Ont., April 28, 1917. .Milton Hersey Co., Ltd.,
Montreal.	'
Dear Sirs :-Regarding the letter from Dominion Canners and the carelessness of the inspector, Mr. R. L. Xnnes, the General Manager, Dominion Canners from the head office Hamilton was here yesterday and I took the topic up with him, and he will he back on Monday 30th after having investigated the matter and who wrote the same-
I do not quite understand that.
I invite the closest investigation as regards my work. As to the inspection of the beans, Mr. Neilson and I have used every civil means to have the same adjusted and they yet fail to comply. I will relate last night's episode.
At 8.30 p.m. I forbade them using anything which was on the floor and it was shovelled into boxes and set by the door apparently to be removed from the premises this morning.
At 6.40 this morning I found the same on the top floor ready to be poured from the spouts into the machines.
You can readily see that my hours mean from before 7 a.m. until 9.3 0 p.m.
I cannot see it in any other way, and I know that the letter you claimed to have received is too true, as regards getting past the inspector.
Now, gentlemen, how far are you prepared to
back me in this, as I intend to fight this to a finish; but not after May 15th at the present salary.
Yours truly,
R. R. McColl, Inspector.
Now there is evidence from the inspector that this business was going on of boiling up, canning, and sending away stuff which certainly should not have been sent as human food to any person, much less to the boys at the front. It will be found that there are declarations here, sworn to by returned soldiers, testifying as* to the quality of the commodity which they received from 'Canada with the label of 'this company on it. I do not wish for one moment to say anything in this connection bd^ond just what is necessary in order to bring the matter to the notice of the Government, so that not only shall the correspondence ]pe brought down, but that the fullest investigation shall take place into tlhe ease. I am told, Sir, that material evidence, which should have been investigated, has been laid by some officers of the Government with the Attorney General of the province of Ontario, but that nothing has been done. I am told that even the English Government, or its officials, have reported to our Department of Justice complaining about these matters, and that the latter passed the matter on to the department of the Attorney General at Toronto, but still nothing has been done. Now it is not at all too late to take action-it is too late, in a way, in 'the case of those who have been eating this poisonous stuff. Many of them, I am told, were sick; some of them came home with broken teeth, owing to their teeth fastening themselves upon these stones. That cannot be remedied, but surely we have not yet reached a day in Canada when we are going to allow criminals to escape because, forsooth, they managed to evade the eye and the arm of justice at the very moment when they should have been held up. It is quite possible that the evidence was not available, and I am not saying whether it is available yet or not, hut I have read out the names of about a dozen people or so, wtho are living in this province, and who have made declarations before the proper officers that they can prove the enormity that has been practised upon the public and upon our soldiers in connection with this establishment. I trust, therefore, Sir, that not only will these papers be brought down, but that the facts, or any facts that the Government think they could obtain in this connection, will be fully gone into and the proper party punished, whoever that party may be.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. gentleman, I think has been misinformed as to the existence of a contract between the Canadian Government and the parties to whom he has referred. I have no knowledge of the existence of any such contract with the Canadian Government. If there be any contract between the parties and the Canadian Government, and any correspondence relating thereto, we will be glad to bring it down. I do understand, however, that there was a contract with the British Government and that with regard to that contract there were certain complaints made as to the manner of its fulfilment, that the British Government made very considerablS inquiry, and that counsel retained on their behalf pursued the matter further. Those counsel were retained through, the Department of Justice at the request of the British Government.

Was the contract
made through the Imperial Munitions Board or direct with the British Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall make inquiry and ascertain, but any knowledge that came to me of the existence of the contract came from the British Government who requested that counsel should be retained to act for them in connection with the differences that arose and the complaints which they had to make with regard to the manner of the fulfilment of the contract. I may say that though I do not claim to have been made aware of the nature of the complaint, I did learn of what appeared to be the substantial complaint, and in connection with this I heard nothing of such statement as there being stones in the pork. Unless my memory is entirely at fault, and I certainly think the fact would have impressed itself on my mind had there been such; I heard of no complaint of the kind. The principal differences were, if my memory serves me, as to the quantity furnished. I know that was one of the complaints, but I have no recollection of a complaint that there were stones in the pork. However, as I have said, if there be any contract, or anything in the nature of a contract with the Canadian Government, or any correspondence relating to the matter at all that will be proper to bring down, it will be brought down.

Would it not be
competent for this Government to bring down the contract between the British Gov-

eminent and Canadian citizens in which the Imperial Munitions Board was concerned, more especially as the Government went out of its way on a former occasion to bring in an American contract with the British Government and there was no opposition whatever to it? I do not see any reason whatever why there should not be inquiry made into the doings of the imperial Munitions Board with regard to any Canadian contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In answer to the hon. gentleman's question, let me say that if it was a matter of bringing down a contract, or contracts, with the British Government, it would be necessary for us to obtain the consent of that Government to do so, and in the second place it ought to be in connection with some matter into which this Parliament was entitled to enter and examine.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. leader of the Opposition desires to take advantage of his right to reply. As this will close the debate, any other hon. member who wishes to speak must do so now.
I would like to ask whether the Department of Trade and Commerce have received any complaints from the British Government concerning these matters alleged by the leader of the Opposition.
The department over which I preside has received no representations at all with reference to this# matter so far as I have followed the statements made by the leader of the Opposition.
Motion agreed to.
Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 25 respecting Patents of Invention.
Explain, please.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The purpose of the Bill is to afford a remedy for persons holding patents of inventions who by reason of war conditions may have been prevented from fulfilling the requirements of the Patent Act. By this Bill it is intended to confer power upon the minister in appropriate cases and where the facts are established to revive a patent when the failure to comply with the statutory requirements was attributable to war circumstances. Provision is made in such instances for the protection of persons who while the patent had lapsed may have begun the manufacture or sale of the patented article. I may say that in the Treaty of Peace provisions are made for such a revival in regard to the rights of nationals of ours in Germany or of German nationals in this country where patents have lapsed under similar conditions. The purpose of this legislation is to give a like remedy in cases of patents held by people in this country where the lapse has been attributable to war conditions, but with re-[DOT] gard to which there arises no question as between our nationals and enemy nationals, and therefore, those eases would not be
governed by the Peace Treaty nor would they be susceptible of being dealt with by any order or regulation made under the Act providing for the carrying out of its provisions.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

On motion of Lion. Arthur Meighen (Minister of the Interior) Bill No. 15 to amend the Dominion Lands Act was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
At six o'clock, Committee took recess.
After Recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
On section 1-right of making entry restricted to persons on active service in military forces of Canada of His Majesty or His Allies, or of any British Dominion or colony.
Will the minister explain this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These amendments are necessitated by the conclusion of peace, or by the anticipated early conclusion of peace in a legal sense. The first, second and third sections are the law to-day, but they are the law by virtue of Orders in Council passed under the War Measures Act. The Bill merely makes permanent that legislation. The three sections contain nothing of startling consequence. They merely provide that when land is thrown open for homestead entry, one day's priority shall be given to returned soldiers.
What is the meaning of "one day's priority"?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
When lands are thrown open for entry, advertisement is given that such and such lands will, on such and such a day, be open for homestead entry. Then the Dominion Lands Act applies and the first eligible entrant to reach the counter -or rather to gain admittance-at the hour on which the entry takes effect, gets the entry. Now, this first section provides that the first day upon which lands are thrown open for entry shall be reserved for returned soldiers as defined by the Soldier Settlement Act. The Orders in Council defined "returned soldier" rather differently -more briefly and more roughly. Now that we are putting it into permanent form, the

definition of the term "settler" in the Soldier Settlement Act is .adopted and any man or any woman who comes within that definition may apply on the first day. Then if no one gets entry on that first day all others come in the second day and the first eligible applicant gets the entry. That is the effect of the first clause.
The second clause provides that the ordinary rule compelling any man who has an entry to go into possession of his homestead within six months-extendable to twelve months at the option of the minister -'Shall not .apply. Many entries are secured by men, while on active service, by proxy and otherwise, and it would be unfair to compel these men to go into possession within six months. Similarly, many returned men are not able, by reason of disablement or otherwise, to go into possession within six months. Under the Orders in Council, certain latitude has been allowed all along as respects such men, and this makes permanent this latitude.
Mr. MoMASTEE:	Is there any limited
time within which they must go into possession?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not on the part of returned men, as yet. On the part of others, the minister may extend the six months' period that the Act allows to a total of twelve months, but not beyond that.

While everybody is perfectly in sympathy with the idea of giving the returned man a preferential position, should there not be some limitation as to time in respect of his obligation to enter into possession? It seems to me that it might retard the development of the country to allow these homesteads to be granted, and perhaps not to be occupied for several years.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would be wise if it were practical, but when one considers the case of the disabled man one immediately conies to the conclusion that a time cannot be fixed. He may be disabled for a year, a year and a half, even for a longer period, and however desirable it may be to get the land into occupation, it is unjust to him to cancel his entry because he has not gone into possession within the six months. So that a discretion has been allowed in this respect, and I have known of no complaint of abuse of that discretion. I have known of no complaint reaching the department of any soldier being retained too long in the right of entry before actually exercising his right of possession.

Section agreed to.

On section 3-requirement of erection of house not necessary if residence acquired by service.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That covers the case
of a man whose residence duties have been performed by 'Virtue of his service overseas. If his residence duties are so performed it is easily seen that there is no use in requiring him to put up a house. This makes permanent that amendment to Dominion Lands Act.
This does not contemplate giving the soldier who had not made his entry prior to enlistment credit for the time he served?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

Does the minister not think some provision should be made in that regard? Large .numbers of men who did not exactly know the position enlisted prior to making entry for their land; others knew that in order to get credit for residence duties, entry had to be made prior to enlistment, so they deferred their enlistment until they had first made their entry. The former donned the khaki and had probably gone overseas while the other men were looking for their homesteads. In all fairness to those men who took up their homesteads after enlistment but prior to going overseas, the privileges accorded under this section should be extended to them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I admit that a plausible case can be made for my hon. friend's contention. It has been urged upon me very strongly and upon the department-indeed, it was urged upon the House last session, particularly by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. L. Thomson)

that that concession should be made. It is true that what is at first sight a very strong case can be made in favour of the argument that at least the same rights should be given to the man who felt that the first duty was enlistment and the second that of making entry as are given to the man who took the reverse procedure-made the entry first and enlisted next. But a review of the whole * situation will convince any one-at least, any one charged with responsibility-that such a concession would now be not only wholly untenable, but wholly dangerous- indeed, what is worse, wholly wrong. The question first came up when the concession was given to actual bona fide homesteaders who had their entry that their service* should count as residence. It was then urged that the same should be done for

those who enlisted and afterwards entered. But it appeared at once that if that principle were established and announced, virtually every one who enlisted would make entry, because he would know that his enlistment would count as residence, and in all probability by the time he got through his service he would have performed all the duties on the homestead except those that he could hire to be performed, and he would just "be in'* the difference between the value of the homestead and the cost of the hiring. Consequently, to have acceded to the suggestion would have meant virtually the blanketing of our available homestead lands in Canada by men who for the most part did not intend to homestead at all, who merely saw a chance to make that equity out of a homestead quarter-section. It would be unreasonable to argue that thousands-yes, possibly hundreds of thousands-would not have done that, because it would be plainly in their interest to do it, and in doing it they would be put to very little, if any, inconvenience. So when that contingency confronted the minister of the day-it was before my occupancy of this position-on the advice of the officers of the department he decided that it could not be done for the reason that instead of resulting in bona fide soldier homesteaders it would result in blanketing the land against bona fide homesteaders and in favour of the men who merely wanted a certain cash equity out of it. When that decision was arrived at, rightly or wrongly,- in my judgment rightly-it had, of course, to be announced, and all in the army and out of it who communicated with the department were so informed, to the number of many thousands. They were told: "You, having enlisted, are in the army, and are not a homesteader at all. There is no use your making an entry if you count on your army service as residence, because that will not be done." Similarly, press notices went out, and those thousands of men were thus informed officially, necessarily informed officially, rightly informed officially, that it was no use for them on that expectation making a homestead entry.
Now we come to the situation as it confronts us this session, and indeed as it confronted us last session. We are asked to recede from that position and to say: "It is true we notified the whole army it would not do you any good, We were afraid if we did -not do that our lands would be blanketed. We told you that, but we really did not mean it, and we will count your entries." WThat would these men have said
who got the notices sent out in answer to their query, and who did not make entry in consequence? Their complaints would be lodged, yes by the tens of thousands. And what would be our answer? We could have no answer at all. So while a very plausible and apparently a very strong case can be made, a consideration of all the circumstances in the history of this matter convinces us, I think, that to make the concession now would be unreasonable, dangerous, and indeed, wrong.
About what time were those notices issued?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would be at the time the concession to the bona fide 'homesteader was actually made, about December, 1915.
Then all who enlisted subsequent to that could have made homestead entry and qualified, could they not?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. They could make homestead entry after enlisting but not have the residence counted.
But there would be nothing after December, 1915, to prevent a man entering for a homestead previous to enlisting? So all these men could have made entry before enlisting if they saw fit?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is true.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-application to court by alien entrant for decision that he is qualified and fit to receive letters patent:

Does this mean that if the judge of the Supreme Court of the province has given a decision in favour of the applicant getting his patent, the case must then go beore the Secretary of State for approval before the patent is issued?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, that is the effect of it. I might explain to the committee something about this clause, because it is an important one. It is an attempt to solve a really difficult problem. A substantial portion of our western, homesteads are held by men who are of alien enemy birth, and who at present, indeed, are technically alien enemies; and in reality many of them are pretty much alien enemies, too. These men obtained their entries while the law was in a certain state. They obtained their entries when under the law they were required to put in the three years term of residence, six months in each year, to do improvements, to take out their naturalization papers, after which they would be entitled to a patent. Those coming in be-



fore the passing of the Naturalization Act of 1914 were allowed to take out naturalization papers after three years; subsequently that was amended to five years, but the difference between the three and the five-year period is not very material to this explanation. The point is that they came, made their entries, and gained their rights as to the homestead land; they made, as it were, a contract with the country under a certain state of law. Then the war intervened, and following the war a new Naturalization Act was passed last session by which an alien enemy could not secure naturalization for a period of ten years subsequent to .the war. That is provided by ' sub-subclause (b) of subclause 4 of clause 8 of the Naturalization Act of this year. So these men find themselves in this position: they made entry for their land when the law required certain duties of them, one factor of those duties being the obtaining of naturalization before the patent was issued. Then by reason of the war the new Naturalization Act intervened precluding them from taking out naturalization for ten years, and of course during the war most of the judges held that they had not power to grant naturalization. They had power under the old Act, and under the Act of 1914 the Secretary of State had the power, but my information is that that power was not exercised by him during the war. The plight, therefore, in which these men found themselves can be easily understood. It is argued in respect of many that no concession should be made, that numbers of them so conducted themselves as to merit no consideration on the part of the country. There may be something in that contention as applied to some, but as applied to a very great many it cannot be argued that any such state of affairs exists. Then the difficulty that confronted us was this, to endeavour to establish some system whereby those not undeserving could be considered in applications for patents, and whereby those against whom a sound complaint should be made should not be considered. This is an attempt to effect that end. It is an attempt to enable Superior Court judges to decide just as they decide whether a man is entitled to naturalization,-and if a -judge certifies that but for this sub-subclause (b) a certain applicant would be entitled to naturalization, that is to say, entitled on all grounds save only that he has not been ten years here, as provided by that sub-subelause, then he -may issue a certificate accordingly, and that certificate 
enables the Secretary of State to dispose of the case.
The hon. member for An-tigonish and Guys-borough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) says: Should not that certificate be final?-why should a discretion thereafter rest with the Secretary of State? That is easily answered. The Naturalization Act of 1914 and the Act of 1918, both framed in unison with the -British Act and similar Acts in all the other, dominions, leave the prerogative of naturalization in the Secretary of State. The old principle of the judicial prerogative was withdrawn both in this country and throughout the Empire, and the Secretary of State was vested with the powers and unrestrained discretion as to naturalization. Consequently, in this Bill that principle must be carried forward. The final discretion must rest with him, but barring exceptional reasons that might -appear or be represented to him, he naturally would be guided by the certificate issued by the Superior Court judge. Therefore, provision i-s made in this section to enable the deserving alien enemy who is forbidden to naturalize, none the less to make his application for patent and, if found fit, to procure his patent, notwithstanding his lack of naturalization ; and at the same time it [DOT] provides that, if for any reason an applicant has so conducted himself as to show that he is not likely to be a good British subject in this country, he cannot, -merely because he has put in the time, come and demand a patent to his homestead. All -that I can say for this is that it seemed the best and fairest machinery that was devisable. I did not think it right that men should be kept for years out of their patents if they were ready to become naturalized. Many of them are not naturalized; many of them will not even apply for naturalization; but if they were ready to apply and to become naturalized, and there was no reason why they -should not, but for the sub-Subclause, then it did not seem fair that they should be kept out of their patent for all those years. While it would be possible to leave them in possession and still to withhold the patent, yet the withholding of the patent itself is a very serious impediment to the progress of a man as a settler and farmer, and an impediment that, unless there were special -reasons to the contrary, did not seem to me to be justified.

The only thing that strikes me is the discretion that is given to the Secretary of State under subclause (8) of clause 4, which subclause reads:

The Secretary of State of Canada may thereupon, in his absolute discretion, issue a certificate in form K that the said alien entrant is or is not qualified to receive a patent, and shall send the same to the Minister of the Interior.
I have not been able to follow up the procedure which is to take place before the judge, but I take it that the Department of the Interior or the Government will be represented at each hearing that will take place before a judge and will see that the facts are fully brought out. I must take it for granted that the judge who will hear the evidence will be perfectly fair as regards the facts and law, and that he will, to the best of his judgment, give a decision on the law and the facts, particularly the facts relative to the conduct of the applicant. Supposing that the judge gives to John Brown a certificate that he is entitled to get his patent. I find no material at all that is submitted to the Secretary of State except the certificate of the judge, and it is somewhat extraordinary that absolute power is left with the Secretary of State to reverse -the finding of that court. I do not know whether he can reverse it both ways or not. If the judge refuses to grant the application, I suppose that is the end of the matter. But should the judge give the certificate, it is somewhat strange that the overruling power should be in a man who has no opportunity of hearing the facts at all. Certainly there must be something upon which that discretion can be exercised. It certainly cannot be the whim or the caprice of the Secretary of State, or something that he may have heard about the man, or something not substantially proven. I would like some explanation from the minister as to what facts besides the certificate of the judge are to go before the Secretary of State on which he is to exercise his discretion. The minister, of course, knows very well what is meant by judicial discretion. Judicial discretion must be exercised according to law. There is no free right given to a judge to use discretion. There are lots of places where a judge can use his discretion about decisions, and costs, and cases, and all that sort of thing, but there must always be underlying the discretion a good legal reason. When discretion is to be exercised here, there must he some legal basis for the exercise of that very important discretion, and I should not like to place (too much power in any minister or any governmental official to overrule the findings of a court.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The papers that will come before the Secretary of State are referred to in subclause (7) of clause 4, the clause under consideration. Subclause (6), however, first provides that;
The applicant shall produce to the court such evidence that he is qualified and fit to be granted his patent under this Act as the court may require, and shall also personally appear before the court for examination.
And so forth. Then subclause 7 says:
Upon the decision of the court being given a certified copy of such decision shall be submitted by the Clerk of the Court to the Department of the Secretary of State of Canada, together with the application and such other papers, documents and reports as may be required by any regulations made hereunder.
That is to say, any regulation made hereunder -as to what is necessary to be submitted must be complied with by the clerk o'f the court before whom the case is tried. Necessarily, all evidence then submitted to the judge would be part of the further-submission to the Secretary of State, and any reports on any special matter that-might be covered by the regulations would also have to come to the Secretary of State, That answers one portion of the hon. gentleman's question as to what would be the material before the Secretary of State. Then there might be further material. Very frequently, in the past at all events, these naturalization certificates have been granted rather formally and, I fear, sometimes hastily, -and subsequently to the granting of them material comes to light which might have seriously affected the grant in the first place. Provision might easily be made for -that to come to the Secretary of State, or, indeed, it might come without any provision at all. It is quite true that section 4 leaves the absolute discretiolf in the Secretary of State as.to the granting of a certificate of right. I pointed out when I was on my feet before that that is essential because that is the principle not only of our Naturalization Act, but of the British Act, the Australian Act and the New Zealand Act. All of them are founded, from the lower strata to the top, on the very same provisions. In the Act itself, if the hon. gentleman will look at the following clauses, he will find that subolause (3) of clause 2 of the Naturalization Act passed just last session reads:
The grant of a certificate of naturalization to any such alien shall be in the absolute discretion of the Secretary of State of Canada, and he may, with or without assigning any reason, give or withhold the certificate as he thinks most conducive to the public good, and no appeal shall lie from his decision.
That subclause merely follows the Act of 1914, and, may I repeat, the -corresponding

Act passed in the Mother Country and the other British Dominions of the Empire. A reference to section 4 brings out the following reading:
The Secretary of State of Canada may in his absolute discretion, in such cases as he thinks fit, grant a special certificate of naturalization to any person with respect to whose nationality as a British subject a doubt exists.
And so on. The final prerogative, unrestrained, rests with the Secretary of State in the main Act. It would be perfectly impossible to argue that if the final prerogative should rest with him as to the naturalization of people generally it ought not to rest with him as to the naturalization of alien enemy homesteaders'. We would be departing from what is, I think, a fundamental principle of the whole naturalization law of Canada if the Act should provide otherwise than it does.

Before this clause goes through I would like to ask the minister if the application of this Act will prevent the transfer of property to aliens on purchase?
I know of many aliens who have lived in this country for sixty or seventy years who have not become naturalized. Can they purchase farm lands and' obtain a proper transfer and title from private individuals if this Bill become law?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No; the Bill which is under consideration now has no effect whatever on the law as to aliens holding title to land. Aliens always could hold title to land in Canada, but they could not get what we call our free homestead patent until they became naturalized.
Bill reported.

subtopic: HEAD OF EAST BAY-CHRISTMAS ISLAND MAIL SERVICE.

speechtext: The House returned to the Order for " Notices of Motion ":

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria) moved:
subtopic: HEAD OF EAST BAY-CHRISTMAS ISLAND MAIL SERVICE.
speechtext:
For a copy of all correspondence between the Post Office Department and the postmistress at the Head of East Bay, Cape Breton County, Nova Scotia, in regard to the mail service between the Head of East Bay and Christmas Island, and also of all other letters, petitions and correspondence received by the Post Office Department relative to this matter, since the 1st of January, A.D., 1915, to date.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is not a matter of very wide importance but it is very important locally to a certain section of the people of the county of Cape Breton. There is a mail route about forty miles long between Christmas Island and the Head of 
East Bay. Christmas Island is one of the railway stations on the Intercolonial Railway about two miles from the Grand Narrows. From there the mails go to the shores of East Bay and then along East Bay about thirty miles to the head of the bay, going one day and coming the next. The Head of East Bay is within twelve miles of Sydney. The mails used to go out from Sydney every second morning and connect with the service at the head of East Bay. The mail carrier started from the Head of East Bay on his way back distributing the mail at each post office between the Head of East Bay and Christmas Island. That is what happened on one day. On the next day the mail carrier would start with his mail from Christmas Island and distribute the mail all the way up to East Bay. The result was that the people over that forty or forty-five miles were getting a daily mail service, one originating in Sydney and the other at Christmas Island.	^
Some time ago-possibly over a year ago -the postmistress at the Head of East Bay refused to distribute this mail; that is refused to distribute the mail that was coming out from Sydney for the offices along the route which I have just mentioned, stating that she was not getting enough money and would not do the work for the amount that she was receiving. This long route extending over forty-five miles was cut down from a daily mail to three mails a week simply because this woman said she was not getting enough money and would not do the work.
I have been in correspondence with the department, with the officials both in my own province and here, for a little over a year now trying to get this matter put right. Still it goes on in the same way, the department refusing to give this woman the money she wants and this woman refusing to do the work until she is paid the money. I am sorry that the Postmaster General is not represented here. We usually find the hon. the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) looking after his affairs in the House. But, we have here the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) who is representing the Government. I wish to appeal to him and to say that it seems to be a most extraordinary condition of things that any person filling a position such as this in a country district would be permitted for a moment to block the operation of the administration in this way. If this woman will not do the work, surely there are other people who will. I can understand that in the settlement in

which she lives nobody would care to say that he would take the office which she holds but if she were removed from office for refusing to do her duty, I do not think there would be any trouble in getting other people to take the office rather than to see the business of the country interfered with.
Now this does not require any further explanation except that spme five or six hundred families, perhaps more, who had been receiving six mails a week, I suppose for the last thirty years, have been during two years or so cut down to three mails a week, not because of any policy determined on by the Government or by the department, but simply because this postmistress, who used to distribute the mails coming out of the city of Sydney, says she will not do this work. Therefore, this body of people along a route of forty or forty-five miles, and having nine or ten post offices, must put up with three mails a week instead of six. I appeal to the Government that such a thing should not be tolerated and that if this woman, Mrs. McNeill, will not do the work, somebody else should be appointed to carry it on. It is my duty to press this matter strongly and insist upon this postmistress either doing her work or getting out; she must certainly do one or the other. I am not particular whether she gets out or not, but if she will only do the work I would certainly prefer to see her stay. The post office has been at her house for a very long time, and so far as I know there never was any trouble with the performance of her work until she took this notion in her head that she was not sufficiently paid. The department tell me they cannot pay her any more than they pay other people and that there must be uniformity in the salaries paid to keepers of post offices. That is all right, I have no concern about that; but what I am concerned about is that the people of my county should receive proper treatment and get the mail service they have been accustomed to for the last thirty or thirty-five'years. I, therefore, move this resolution so as to lay the whole matter, before the Government, and I hope that the condition of things described will not be tolerated, or permitted to last, very much longer.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: HEAD OF EAST BAY-CHRISTMAS ISLAND MAIL SERVICE.
speechtext:
I am feo much impressed with the speech of my hon. friend that I have decided to recommend to the House that the motion be passed. I feel all the more keenly with respect to the matter because I think that in my own county there are cases similar to the one he has
described, to the numlber of three or four. It is not, however, the perversity of woman that is the trouble in Portage la Prairie- I presume that circumstance is peculiar to the Scotch constituency of my hon. friend. The difficulty out our way is that we cannot get anybody to deliver the mails as often as the people want. I find the whole community demanding in tones of thunder, if they can reach me, that the mail shall be delivered, but not one person is ready to deliver them. I presume the circumstances are very much the same in the county of Cape Breton. Whether any postmaster can be found or not is something that will be better known to 'the Postmaster General than to myself. I will draw the attention of my colleague to the motion.

subtopic: HEAD OF EAST BAY-CHRISTMAS ISLAND MAIL SERVICE.
speechtext:
As the minister has
opened up the question somewhat by referring to cases in 'has own constituency, I might refer him to similar cases in my constituency, but the reason there for the non-delivery of mails is entirely different. The reason is because this Government will not pay the courier sufficient to meet expenses apart altogether from leaving anything to live on.

Motion agreed to.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Meighen, the House adjourned at 8.50 p.m.
Tuesday, October 7, 1919.
The House met at Three o'clock.

Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) ; Subject to the consent of the House I would ask to be allowed to introduce two Bills which are on the Votes and Proceedings of to-day, but which have not reached the Order Paper. This is merely in order to expedite the business of the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
These Bills can be introduced at this stage only by unanimous consent.
Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No, 26, to amend the Canada Temperance Act.
We are entitled to the same treatment as if this were in order. The minister will probably explain the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Certainly. The purpose of this Bill is to extend the provisions of the Canada Temperance Act so as to make it possible that, if upon a plebiscite vote of the electors of an entire pro-

vince, [DOT]which plebiscite would be taken upon a petition based on a resolution of the Legislative Assembly, the majority of the electors declare that they desire that the importation of liquor into that province or the manufacture of liquor in that province, or both, should be absolutely prohibited, then under the provisions of this Bill such manufacture, or such importation, or both, would be prohibited by a proclamation which would be issued in accordance with the proceeding provided for in the Canada Temperance Act. This is in effect extending the principle of the Canada Temperance Act so as to enable the majority of the electors of a province to create a situation under which the manufacture of liquor in that province or the importation of liquor into that province would become absolutely prohibited.
Does that mean that if the Ontario Government, for example, has not requested, we are going to decide merely on the referendum?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There will be no referendum except upon a petition based upon a resolution of the legislature of the province concerned. The machinery would be set in motion at the request of the legislature of the province.
Would that ipSo facto come into force in the case of the Ontario Temperance Act, now the law in Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. As I understand it, the present law in force in Ontario does not deal with the question of the importation or manufacture of liquor.
But does not the Ontario Temperance Act cover that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It does not cover the questions of importation into a province or manufacture in a province. The provinces take the position that they cannot deal with those questions. Without discussing that point, I may say that this would be a method whereby, in virtue of Dominion legislation becoming operative by the vote of the electors of a province, importation into that province or manufacture in it would be prohibited.
Then Ontario would have to have a special referendum in regard to this question in order to avail itself of this Bill ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Upon a petition this [DOT]Government would hold a referendum in
-	4*
pMr. Doherty.]
the area of the province on whose behalf the petition was made.

Does the
minister provide for this coming into effect on a majority of the total votes cast, or on a majority of the voters on the list?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is a provision ol the Canada Temperance Act which, I think, provides simply for a majority.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister oi Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 27, to amend an Act in aid of provincial legislation prohibiting the sale or use of intoxicating liquors.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: BILL, TO AMEND AN ACT IN AID OB PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION PROHIBITING THE SALE OR -USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
speechtext: This motion also requires unanimous consent.

subsubtopic: BILL, TO AMEND AN ACT IN AID OB PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION PROHIBITING THE SALE OR -USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
speechtext: I do not object, subject to an explanation being given by the minister as if this procedure were in order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: BILL, TO AMEND AN ACT IN AID OB PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION PROHIBITING THE SALE OR -USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
speechtext: The purpose of this Bill is to amend the Act in aid of provincial prohibitory legislation by making its provisions, which now extend only to the importation of liquor into a province to be used in violation of the laws of that province, to the manufacture within the province of liquor to be used in violation of the laws of that province. That is one provision. The other provision that is made by it re-introduces into the Act a clause which was contained in the Bill as it was passed by the House of Commons, but which the Senate rejected. This clause is accompanied by a modification which we hope may make it acceptable. The clause in question provides that a violator of the provisions of the Act may be tried for the offence either in the province into which the liquor was sent, which we may call the prohibition province, or in the province in which the offence was actually committed. The Senate on two occasions rejected that clause.

subsubtopic: BILL, TO AMEND AN ACT IN AID OB PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION PROHIBITING THE SALE OR -USE OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
