On section 1-aliens not to have ifirearms or weapons without a permit:

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: Why is 'this Act restricted merely to aliens? Does the Minister of Justice not think that a pistol in the hands of a British subject will do as much harm as in the hands of an alien? What is 'the particular reason why aliens should be selected in order to have this law imposed upon them?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
I might say that as regards Ipistols, or any weapon susceptible of being concealed on the person, there is no distinction between the law as applicable to a British subject or as applicable to an alien, nor does this provision make one. At the last session of (Parliament a provision intended to make this distinction between British subjects and aliens was enacted, namely, that the prohibition of carrying weapons without a license in the case of British subjects was limited to weapons of a nature which could be concealed upon the person. But the intention of that legislation was to make, with regard to aliens, a general disposition requiring a license for the carrying of any firearms. In enacting that legislation, the clause as it is now proposed in this Bjll was passed, but it contained the words-I have not the statute before me; they brought me the wrong volume, but I have sent for the right statute-if I remember right, " as before described," or -similar words, which produced the effect of limiting the prohibition upon them of carrying firearms without a license to precisely the same class of weapons as was referred to in the prohibition upon people generally-that is to say, limited the application of the clause to the carrying of weapons susceptible of being concealed on the person. That was not the intention of Parliament, as I understand it; there would be no object in repeating a special provision about aliens if you

left them precisely in the same position as British subjects. This amendment simply drops those words limiting the application of the provision to the carrying of weapons that may be concealed upon the person, and makes it applicable to the weapons mentioned in the clause without regard to whether they are susceptible of being concealed on the person or not.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: When this question was raised at the last session I declared my opposition to it, and I am still of the same opinion. I think it is wrong in principle that we should have one law for the alien and another law for the British subject; it is against all principles of British law. We know that under the old Roman system, in the days of the republic and later of the empire, they had one law for the alien and another law for their own citizens, but I thought we had developed a little since that time. It appears, however, that the Government does not seem to be of that view, and we are now going back to the days of the Antonines and Caligula.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: I must voice my objection to any such law as this being placed on the statute book-I can see no necessity fox it at all. Such a provision may have been necessary during war time-I am doubtful if it was, but there may have been excuse for it-but I can see absolutely no excuse for it at the present time. We have probably as large an alien population in Saskatchewan as in any other province in Canada, and I see no reason for .any such provision. If these people are not fit subjects for this country then we ought to get rid of them altogether. If they are fit persons to live here then they should be treated the same us anybody else-if they are not fit persons, do not admit them to the country at all.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
I most heartily endorse the remarks of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. In the riding which I have the honour to represent there are a large number of aliens-men who came out to this country forty, fifty and sixty years ago as infants, and who have been since they reached the age of twenty-one voting and exercising every function of a Canadian citizen during all the intervening years. These people have become possessed of farms throughout the riding, and they have all the necessary equipment of home life possessed by citizens of British origin. Now these people will be interfered with in the exercise of 'their rights to a very large extent, and it is absolutely unfair to those

of them who have been brought up in this country from infancy, who have been educated in our schools, and some even in our colleges, 'agricultural and other colleges, that they be denied the right 'they have been led to believe they were justly entitled to. I beg, Mr. Chairman, to register as strenuous objection to the passage of this measure as it is possible for me to do. Such a law would be all right if it were intended to be applied to criminals and that class of people who are segregated in the cities and large centres; but to make it apply at this present time, in the manner in which it is proposed- to be 'applied, will cause a great deal of hardship and a great tffeal of inconvenience to and arouse a great deal of dissatisfaction among a class of people who >are just as good British subjects as any hon. gentlemen in this Chamber.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: Might I point out to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pedlow) that if the people to whom he refers are just as good Brit'sh subjects as anybody else they cannot possibly be aliens, and there is no more to be said. Might I further point out that the class of people to whom I believe he intends to refer to have the simplest possible remedy in their own hands. If they have lived in this country for years, as he says, and exercised the franchise and a variety of other privileges, it is absolutely open to -them to cease to be aliens at any moment they choose-

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: Allow me to finish my phrase-at any moment they choose.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: After the expiration of ten years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
At all events so soon as peace shall have been proclaimed, and any suspension of the granting of naturalization resulting from the war shall have disappeared. So that class of people are under an exceedingly temporary disability in any event. Now let me point out, in answer to both the hon. member for Renfrew -and the hon, member for Maple Creek that this is not an absolute prohibition upon these people, but having weapons, the law only requires of them that they should show all these good qualities which are ascribed to them by being willing to ask the proper authority for a permit. Then every man that possesses these good qualities will have no difficulty -about getting one. Now as to the reference of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Jacobs) about going back to the days of Caligula and the rest, might I just suggest this: that when people come into this

country and establish themselves here one of two things is true-either they have been in the country long enough to obtain naturalization, and then they will not come under this Act, or they have not been here long enough to obtain naturalization. Then I put it to the hon. gentleman if it is being quite as bad as Caligula to say, with regard to people who have newly come into the country and who have not as yet given those guarantees of residence and so forth which we consider necessary to make them citizens: before you go around carrying firearms you will get a permit from the proper authority who will make inquiry as to whether you are a suitable person to be entrusted with such permit- or not. Undoubtedly I think the records of our criminal courts would show that crimes of violence are disproportionately frequent .among newly-arrived aliens. It is no reflection upon all aliens to say that. But there the fact stands, and these crimes of violence result from the greater readiness with which certain classes of aliens resort to the use of weapons than do our own people.
Now, the purpose of this legislation is simply to afford protection against those evils, and the " awful thing " that it imposes upon every respectable alien desirous of carrying a fire-arm is that he should go to a proper authority and ask for a permit. We im,pose absolutely the same obligation upon all. our subjects as regards weapons that may be concealed upon the person, and the slight distinction we make, for the reasons that I have pointed out, is simply that in the one instance we extend the obligation to the carrying of fire-arms of the description mentioned generally. I think that with a little reflection the hon. gentleman will see that while it may be important to consider the feelings of the alien, it is a matter of the-very first importance to do everything in our power to protect our communities against crimes of violence perpetrated by means of these weapons; and in many instances we are doing a good service to the alien himself, or to any other person concerned, in depriving him of the carrying of the weapon that he may be too ready to use, with very grave consequences not only to those who may be his victims, but to himself.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
I appreciate very much the lengthy explanation made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), but it fails to cover the point raised by me, perhaps because he is not acquainted with all the facts, or perhaps because I have not made
myself thoroughly understood in regard to the subject. He has referred to the days of Caligula. I once read of a student who had not been .very industrious in preparing for his examination, and in reply to the question:	"Who was Caligula? State
briefly what you know about him;" he wrote, being absolutely ignorant of Caligula's personality: "The less said about this man the better."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman had better address that to his neighbour (Mr. Jacobs).

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
It seems to me that the less said about certain Bills initiated by the Government recently, more particularly those applying to aliens, the better. But to get back to the subject. I received just this morning from one_of my constituents a letter from which I wish to read the following extract, and it will illustrate the point I desire to make:
In the autumn of 1902 Mr. Lawson, barrister, etc., of Eganville went around the back townships making out naturalization papers, but it appears they never came before the judge, or were otherwise shelved somewhere.
This refers to a man who has lived in the country sixty years, and explains why he was never properly naturalized; and that may apply to hundreds, perhaps thousands of residents, not in South Renfrew but in the county. Naturalization is one of the first requisites to obtain consideration before a judge; in the absence of a naturalization paper it would be impossible to obtain such consideration. This man could not obtain naturalization for ten years, notwithstanding the fact that he has lived in this country so many years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: May I correct the hon. gentleman so he may not continue under a misunderstanding? It is not essential to have naturalization papers to get this permit. If a man were naturalized he would not be an alien any longer, and therefore he would not come under this provision at all. *

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
The Minister of Justice
does not quite understand me, Mr. Chairman. This man fully understood that he was naturalized. The naturalization process was engineered by some politician a quarter of a century or more ago-long before I had any connection with the political life of the constituency I represent; but this man, believing he was naturalized, was not naturalized; in fact, there is no record of his naturalization anywhere. A
874	[DOT]

man of that type will not be granted a license although he may apply for one.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
The purpose of this
Bill is, among other things, to permit men of that class to get permits to carry these weapons. What is forbidden is the carrying of firearms without a permit; that is all. Any man who can satisfy the proper authority that he ought to have a permit, whether he is an alien or otherwise, will be entitled to carry firearms.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
I would like to refer to a
statement made by the Minister of Justice in connection with this Bill. He stated that those who were referred to by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) if they can show that they have been good citizens for many years, can obtain permission to carry firearms by applying for naturalization, and then, having become naturalized citizens, they will be the same as all other citizens and this provision will not apply to them. That is the point to which I wish to take exception. If it were only possible for people who are to-day technically aliens to apply to this Government and to obtain naturalization papers, I would raise no particular objection. But I would like to refer to the amendment to the Naturalization Act which was piloted through the House last session by the Solicitor-General (Mr. Guthrie). At that time I protested against the clause which made it necessary for men of alien enemy birth to reside in Canada for another ten years before tfhey could obtain naturaliza-tibn. I do not desire to>
burden the House again with the whole story, but I did refer at that time particularly to certain people of alien enemy birth residing in the riding which I represent and -also in other ridings. These mien had lived there as the (member for South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) stated, for ten, fifteen, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty and even sixty years, and many of them were under the impression that their fathers had become naturalized British subjects, but could not prove it, and who, although they have lived in Canada for that period of years and have always conducted themselves as good British subjects and carried out their duties as citizens, having in many instances been elected to act as magistrates and mayors .and councillors, find themselves in the position of being unable to procure naturalization under the amendment to the Naturalization Act of last session. I protested against that, and I pointed to the fact that in the session of 1917 the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden)
[Mr. Pedlow. 1
stated he would make provision, and he did (make provision later on by Order in Council, whereby these peotple, old residents in Canada-I am not speaking of newcomers- could obtain naturalization by making their application to a judge, (who would report to the Secretary of State, after which, if the reports were satisfactory, certificates were to be issued. In the riding of North Waterloo, some ninety-three petitions of that kind were handed in because of the Order in Council promised by the Prime Minister himself. Those ninety-three applications were approved by the judge, they were sent to the Secretary of State, but the naturalization papers were never issued.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: An oversight.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
It was not an oversight,
Mr. Chairman-but I shall not go over all that again. These people have not received their naturalization papers. No one in this House or outside of it can produce one particle of evidence to show that these people are not, to all intents and purposes, British subjects. But they are not technically so, and the Act of last session made it impossible for men who have been here for so many years, to receive their naturalization papers unless they live here another ten years. I made a plea that if these men were all right in every respect, the time during which they had already lived in Canada should be credited to them so far as the ten year period was concerned. The Prime Minister said that it could not be done, because it was the desire of the House to pass a Naturalization Act that would enable the naturalization certificates to be recognized all over the Empire. He also admitted, as did the President of the Council (Hon. Mr. Rowell) that the condition of which I complained worked an injustice on many good people living in this country. The Prime Minister further promised that he would make application to the British Government to have that state of affairs remedied so that these people could obtain their naturalization papers without having to live here another ten years. The point I wish to make is this:	the Minister of
Justice says that all an alien who has conducted himself properly, has to do to escape the provisions of this Act is to present himself for naturalization. But that is not the case with these particular people; they have to live here another ten years before they can get their naturalization papers, and that is an injustice. So far as my own riding is concerned, we have there-unfortunately for them, and I think, unfortunately for the community at large-three or four hundred

people, perhaps more, who come under that description. I am not referring to people who came from: Germany within [DOT] the last ten or fifteen years; I refer to old residents who have all along considered themselves Canadians and who ought to be made Canadians by the issuance to them of naturalization papers.
Mr. McGIBiBO'N (Muskoka):	What was
the attitude of these people towards Canada during the last war?

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: I will answer that by saying that some of the men to whom naturalization was refused had sons fighting for Canada in that very war.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: How did the majority of them vote?

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: They voted right. .

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: It was a secret ballot, and moreover they were not allowed to vote at all. I wish to ask whether any members of the Government .are able to give any information on the question whether justice is going to be done to these people. I might say further to the minister that the Government need not worry very much about the alien in this country. I do not think that, having regard to the very stringent regulations that have been made, very many aliens desire to come to Canada. Not only that; as I come down in the train from Western Ontario I see every Sunday night hundreds of aliens leaving this country because they think it is no longer a free country. The action now contemplated is quite in harmony with the spirit of oppression which has prevailed in connection with the Government of this country during the last three or four years. I make no plea on behalf of any one who is not absolutely entitled to Canadian naturalization, but I do object to the laying of further disabilities on good Oanadian people who are virtually British subjects. I say that it is an injustice and I desire to protest against it.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
I am opposed to this measure and I wish to register my objection; the legislation proposed is not only unnecessary; it is vicious. The minister has told us that provision is already made for the case of carrying concealed weapons, yet he is now attempting to provide for the case of an alien who carries a gun on his shoulder. Men do not go abroad in that way to commit an offence. It is difficult to understand the attitude of the Government in regard to the alien. The Government profess to be in favour of the League of Nations;
brilliant pictures have been set before us during this session with regard to the great results that are to follow from the institution of this League. We are to have " Peace on earth, good will toward men," but we are busy week after week placing laws on our statute-book that are annoying and objectionable to our colleagues in the League of Nations. I find it difficult to understand why the Government are so anxious to encumber the statute-book with unnecessary legislation of this kind. Many people from the United States come into Nova Scotia to have a day's shooting in the woods; it will be necessary for them, if I understand this Bill aright, to obtain a license before they may carry a gun in 'any part of this, country for the purpose of shooting a partridge or having a little sport in the woods. I repeat that this legislation is absolutely unnecessary, and dt is my view that the Bill should not obtain the consent of the House.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: I understand that under the existing laws, persons going into Nova Scotia, as my hon. friend suggested, for the purpose of shooting, have to. get a license.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
But if this Bill
passes they will have to get two licenses.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: From whom are permits to carry firearms or have them in possession to be obtained? Are they in sufficient numbers. to cause no inconvenience to persons who set about to obtain such permits?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
I have not before me the statute which prescribes the persons from whom the permits1 are to be obtained, but I have a very clear recollection that when we passed the original provision we endeavoured to meet every possible need and to obviate any inconvenience in the obtaining of permits. With regard to what the member for Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) has said, if he had as much to do with seeing the regrettable consequences from the promiscuous possession of firearms as we necessarily have to do in dealing with the different criminal cases which, under the guise of applications for clemency, come before us, I think he would realize that even some slight inconvenience to a gentleman who came across the border should hardly weigh in the balance when we are considering the importance of trying to exercise efficient control over the indiscriminate carrying of arms of this description. The hon. gentleman intimates that people who go abroad with guns on their shoulders are

not dangerous. If he had to weigh t/he pros and cons of exercising clemency in favour of people who have committed murder with guns which they carried over their shoulders when they were not shooting them, off, he would realize, perhaps, that there are more important things at issue than the difficulty which he apprehends. This legislation is not directed against aliens of any particular class. It is not directed against the alien enemy in particular. If it does happen that persons who are aliens or of alien enemy origin suffer what appears to them an injustice-and I am prepared to admit there appears to be very hard cases- in consequence of the legislation of last session, I do not think we can gain anything by trying to carry on a discussion as to the wisdom or justice of legislation which Parliament enacted last session upon a subject different from this.
I am sure that any promise which the hon. member states the Prime Minister made with regard to endeavouring to bring about a situation where that injustice might be remedied or mitigated, will be carried out. But so far as this particular legislation is concerned it is not directed against enemy aliens in particular. I have already indicated the motives that inspired it. In talking about aliens and the unfortunate prevalence of crimes of violence among certain classes of them, it is only just to say that I had not in mind, and the facts would not have justified me in having in mind any particular aliens of enemy origin. I think that perhaps among aliens of some other races we would find a greater readiness to resort to the use of firearms. The hon. gentleman will understand that I do not want to specify, or make invidious distinctions between different races. I only want to say to him, as he seems to be so *specially interested, and naturally so, by reason of the population of his county, in the hardship imposed upon that particular class that I was not seeking to make any reflections upon that class in particular, but the fact remains, and the records of our criminal courts show it, that among the alien population we get a much larger proportion of crimes of violence than we do among our own population.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
I should like to mention that there has been a fairly widespread demand for this legislation, throughout the province of Ontario at least. I know that petitions have come to me from practically all the larger places in Western Ontario asking this Par-

liament to pass legislation absolutely to prohibit the use or possession of such weapons by aliens- not to permit the carrying of these weapons oniy under license, but absolutely to prohibit. I can recall resolutions from the following Boards of Trade and City Councils in Western Ontario : Windsor, Chatham, Welland, Hamilton, Brantford, Stratford, Port Arthur, Fort William, Kingston, Belleville, and Guei.ph. I do not remember any from east of Kingston, but certainly the western portion of the province has made rather a pronounced request upon this subject. Let me give an instance of the conditions which exist in my own home town. At the assizes held in the month of May last, presided over by Sir William Mulock, Chief Justice of one of the courts of Ontario, there were on the opening day of the court confined in the Guelph jail fourteen criminals, thirteen of whom were aliens. The chief justice, addressing the grand jury, specifically referred to the proportion of aliens, a great many of whom were charged with crimes of violence, two being mfirder. Two men, both aliens, have been condemned to death in Guelph, and in both cases the instrument of the crime was a shotgun. An altercation of some kind had taken place, and the man ran into his house for a shotgun, and shot his victim. I could enumerate a fairly large number of such cases in Western Ontario during the past five or six years. The vast majority of these crimes have been *committed by aliens, and it is for that reason there has been this pronounced demand from the cities of Western Ontario. I do not know how it is in other portions of the Dominion, but in my humble judgment the law is a very wise one and will oause no injury to any one.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: I should like to ask the Acting Secretary of State a question in regard to the matter I spoke of before, and that is whether any action has been taken with regard to the naturalization of the people * to whom I have referred, and to whom it wa-s admitted to me that naturalization should be granted. At the last, session I made a special request privately of the Prime Minister that at least those men whose applications had been properly approved by the judge should be granted naturalization, leaving the other cases over for the future pending action, by the British Government. Has anything been dona with regard to that?

I do not know whether this is in order, but I may say that I am

not aware of any such action having been taken. I have been Acting Secretary of State only for the past ten days, and action might have been taken without my having any knowledge of it.

I am not aware whether there is similar legislation in England, but if they have similar conditions in England I have sufficient confidence in their wisdom to believe that they have provided similar legislation.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: What- would the minister regard as similar conditions? Surely he -does not pretend that we have more aliens in this country than they have in the United Kingdom. In 'the city of London alone there are probably more aliens than in the whole of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.

I aim not aware of the comparative number of aliens in the two countries. I have exposed the reasons why I think this legislation is good legislation for this country. If it should be demonstrated to me that either wisely or
4 p.im. unwisely the legislative authorities in Great Britain have not thought it to be good legislation for their country, I would not look upon that as a reason why I should not provide what seems to me to be a highly necessary legislation for our own' country under existing conditions.

speechtext: The original section is to be found in the Statutes of 1913, and at the last session that original provision was amended by adding a provision intended to produce the effect of this one. There are 'two reasons why we want to amend it, the reason I have already given and also because the description of weapons that were prohibited was not as extensive as in the present provision which covers any offensive weapon.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
Before we decide upon the question under consideration, I would like to call the attention of the Government once more to the position of the

case to which I have already referred. If this Bill passes as presented to the House, these men who, as I have already staled, have lived in the country for forty, fifty or sixty years, who believe themselves to be in every respect British subjects, who have no doubt in their homes the usual equipment for hunting, fishing and other amusements, will be up against this propostion, that agents of the Government are going around the country informing upon them because they have weapons in their homes without a license. It requires some time for these men to obtain a license. It may take weeks or months, and in the meantime the arms will' be in their homes, and they will be subject to all kinds of annoyance from that class of individuals whom one meets in every community, I do not care whether they are " bootleggers," or as the hon. member for Park-dale modified the term, men who carry razors in their boots; they are all in the same class of undesirable citizens. I do not see any reason why the amendment should not be adopted by this House. If those of British origin do not carry weapons, then they will not be under any restrictions in regard to the matter. Let this apply to all citizens equally. If those of British origin and those of Canadian birth are immune, then they have nothing to complain of, and we should let the law apply to all people, and then they will all come under the same law. I have much pleasure in supporting the amendment.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Renfrew South (Mr. Pedlow) wants a law that will apply to all citizens of the country, including even those who belong to that highly respectable society known as the Society of Friends, sometimes called the Quakers. But there was a time when the hon. gentleman did not hold quite so comprehensive a view, when he thought and voiced the opinion that there were in this country certain people who should not come under all' the laws and should not assume all the responsibilities of citizens of Canada, but should be excused from certain responsibilities and activities in defending this Dominion because of their certain pecu-lar religious beliefs. It is exceedingly surprising that a gentleman of the quiet, peaceful demeanour of the hon. member for Renfrew South should be assuming such a warlike attitude in this matter. I am very, much surprised that he should have taken that attitude, for of all men in the House of Commons, he is the one man who should be trying to prevent every citizen in this

country from having in his possession anything in the nature of firearms more dangerous than a popgun. But here we find him .advocating in this House that, no matter who the man. is who comes into this country, no matter how short a time a man has been in this country, he may load up with knives, pistols, shotguns and all that sort of thing, and be. ready to go on the warpath, I suppose, whenever he feels so inclined. That is a very fine attitude for the hon. member for Renfrew South.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: The hon. member for Renfrew South surprised me a moment ago by supporting the amendment and by evidently desiring to see people armed with defensive and dangerous weapons. I was surprised and I gave the reason for my surprise, namely, that I had always regarded the hon. gentleman as one of a peculiarly, peaceful, gentle and loving disposition. But not only has he surprised me by advocating the use of firearms by foreigners who come into this country but he has assumed a very belligerent attitude in his own person. In fact when he arose in that hostile manner a moment ago, I got down behind the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell), feeling that I would be safe, fearful lest the quiet-appearing gentleman might have some of these firearms in his possession and might take a shot at me with something more dangerous than his tongue. There is not an hon. gentleman opposite, not even the philosopher from-

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: Brome.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
Not the philosopher from Brome, the one who is alongside of him, the philosopher from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). There is not an hon. gentleman, not even the philosopher from

Brome (Mr. McMaster), nor the philosopher who has moved the amendment (Mr. Jacobs), who would take any exception to the legislation which has been on the Statute Book for years requiring a foreigner coming into this country to reside here for a matter of three years as the law used to be before he could take out his naturalization papers. If hon. gentlemen want to be perfectly consistent, they ought to argue that a foreigner, as soon as he lands on Canadian soil, should be regarded as a Canadian citizen and not be required to live here for three years before being permitted to take out his naturalization papers. What was the purpose of putting that three-year provision in the Act? 'Hon. gentlemen opposite agreed to that and 'said that it was a proper provision. Was that showing a perfect trust and confidence in an alien as soon as he came into this country, or did it not indicate on the part of this Parliament that they thought it was a proper safeguard to take, that these people coming from foreign lands into Canada should live here for a time and get into the ways of this country before they were recognized as citizens and given full citizenship? These gentlemen who argue that you should not treat these foreigners or aliens in a different manner from that in which we treat the native-born Canadian or British subject are inconsistent. If they want to be consistent and argue along that line in regard to having weapons in their possession, they should go the whole distance and remove any restriction as regards length of residence before their citizenship is acknowledged.
What is asked in this Bill? Simply that an alien coming into this country, or an alien living in this country who has not already taken out his citizenship, and who wishes to have in -his -possession firearms or other wea-pons, shall go a short di-stance to some person in his own locality -and ask for a permit to carry a weapon. He is not -asked to come to this Government, to travel a long distance, but he goes to some person who knows him very well indeed, and that person knows whether he -i-s a proper kind of -a man to give a permit to. I-t is a proper safeguard. I-t is -an intimation to the alien that, for a -certain length of time or until he acquires his- citizenship, he is not to be treated in exactly the same way a-s a British subject who is fulfilling all the responsibilities of citizenship. I -commend very -strongly the Bill; I think it is -a move in the righ-t direction. Many crimes have been committed in this country when men were
in a passion. They got in the way of carrying guns- and in a fit o-f passion they used them. It is no -argument at all to tell us that American citizens who aTe coming to this country will come under this provision. Very properly they should come under it. There -have been very many crimes committed on the other side of the line just for lack of some such law -as tih-i-s. Men in the heat of passion have committed crimes which they regretted -all their lives. This is a vety proper provision and it should receive the unanimous support of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
I think the point is well taken.
Mr. McKENZIE.: I wish to call the attention of the minister to the effect of this legislation. This is an innovation and provision should be made to prevent an abuse of the law. I am not finding fault with the Minister of Justice for enacting the law but it is capable of abuse. It has been disclosed to us here to-day that there are alien people who have lived in Canada for sixty years, perhaps longer, who are peaceful and law-abiding. One of these men perhaps has a gun in his house. Perhaps it has been there for a great many years. It is not used very much but perhaps it is used once in a while for sport. This law makes thatpeaoe-loving citizen subject to be penalized and prosecuted in the courts. He has no unlawful intent whatever but he just has a gun in his possession. He never intended to do anything hurtful, he is not a dangerous citizen; nevertheless, this law which we are passing to-day leaves him open to be penalized before the court and to be subjected to a fine or imprisonment or both. In a case of this kind should there not be some restriction as to the opportunity for prosecution?
I think if a permit were required from the Minister of Justice, or from the Attorney General of the province, before such prosecution should foe instituted, it would give some safeguard. I would then feel satisfied that no person would foe prosecuted unless there was some real justification for it. If some such restriction as I have mentioned were to be required wherever these proceedings were to foe instituted in any of our courts I would then feel that possibly no great injustice would result.
Mr. DOHERTY': I can appreciate the desire to avoid this law being applied in a way to give rise to abuses, or to unnecessary hardship, but I might point out that in effect we have a great many dispositions of the law which people may innocently so to speak, or ignorantly at all events, offend against and foe liable under the law to punishment. But I think that in any case such as the leader of the Opposition suggests, in the first place you have this protection-that the magistrates., having all the

circumstances before them, would give consideration to those circumstances in the infliction of the penalty. In the second place, there is the further protection: I think I might undertake to guarantee that in cases with circumstances such as indicated, either my hon. friend the Solicitor General or myself would be very ready to recommend the remission of the penalty. I can understand that there are conceivable cases where a man might he arrested under such circumstances; but I may say this-as showing how slight after all the danger is-that we have in force under the War Measures Act an- Order in Council practically to the same effect. From my personal knowledge-at all events from my official knowledge-I am aware that in the enforcement of that law the police officers who are charged with carrying it out gave warning; they did not jump upon a farmer who happens to have a firearm in his house and arrest him the first time they came across him. In such a case they invariably pointed out to him the nature of .the offence and I think in most cases the man got his permit and that was the whole of it. Yet it is a law that is susceptible, perhaps, of abuse. On the other hand, it is a law which the persons who will be employed in enforcing will have no interest in making operate harshly, and I think we may safely leave the matter without providing a special safeguard. Take a law that is applicable to all of us, the law against carrying concealed weapons. It is quite easy to suppose that any one of us might quite innocently, and for a perfectly innocent purpose, on some particular occasion have a weapon in our possession. Of course if that were so we would be liable to be prosecuted and to be punished; but I fancy that the courts charged with the application of the law would take into consideration the circumstances in measuring any penalty that ought to be imposed. I may say this too, that leaving the matter without any special restriction it has been found to be of very great advantage in dealing with criminal classes. With regard to the .provision of general disposition, I think also it would be found that the application of this disposition, in tlhe large number of cases, would foe with regard to people who for some other reason have rendered themselves liable to having their premises looked into. While I appreciate the fact thatlthere may be some occasional cases of the kind the hon. gentleman refers to, still it hardly seems to me to be so probable as to necessitate our making some specific disposition for protection in such cases. It would be

very difficult indeed, I think, or at least would be very cumbersome, if a police officer discovering an offender in the case of an offence of this kind had to hold his hand until communication could be had with the Attorney General of the province or with the Attorney General of Canada. I think it might oiperate to defeat the law in many instances. On the whole I do not think there is more reason to anticipate the danger of abuse of this law than in the case of innumerable other laws that stand upon the statute book and which people may ignorantly or innocently offend against.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: I was not in the Chamber during the early part of the discussion and therefore I would like to ask what the machinery is hy which permits are to be issued. Who are to issue, the permits and are they to be good only for a specific time? If so, for how long?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
The provision about the issuing of permits- is to be found in the Criminal Code-. It provides:
Upon sufficient cause being shown, any officer of the Royal North West Mounted Police, or Commissioner of Dominion Police, or Superin- ' tendent of Provincial Police, or stipendiary, or district magistrate or police magistrate, or acting police magistrate, or sheriff, or chief constable, of any city, incorporated town, or district municipality, may grant any applicant therefor, as to whose discretion and good character he is satisfied, a permit in Form 76 for such period not exceeding twelve months as he deems'fit.
That is the provision for the obtaining and for the duration of the permit.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: That would- mean- that a fresh permit would he required at the expiration of the twelve months?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: Yes, the man would require to obtain a fresh permit at the end of the twelve months, as every one would require to do if he wanted to carry a weapon that was -susceptible of being concealed. We thought we had made ample provision so as to render it easy to find an- officer who would grant the permit; and that after all, as compared with the evils resulting from the possession of these arms, it was a trifling inconvenience even if a man had to go once a year and get his permit renewed.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: One other question: an ordinary justice of the peace is not qualified to issue the -permit?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
No, but the chief constable of any city, or any incorporated town or -district municipality may grant it.
I think at the time the section was passed we endeavoured to enumerate a sufficient number of authorities so that it would be possible anywhere throughout the country with comparative ease to obtain- this permit. Of course I can- understand that in- sparsely settled districts there- may be greater difficulty in obtaining the permit than- in more populous districts. It was not at the time thought wise to authorize every justice of the peace to do it because, to speak frankly- I am speaking now of the province I kno-w best-even in the older provinces justices of the peace are almost as- numerous as king's counsel, and I do not know that it is always a certificate of discretion- that a man should happen to be named a justice of the peace. It was therefore deemed better to limit the power to the -officers that were mentioned in- the -statute, it being thought at the same time that that would practically meet the requirements of almost all, if not all, the communities of the Dominion.

speechtext:
While I am in sympathy with the general purpose of this amendment, I might point out that there are districts in Western Canada where it will impose very considerable hardship on some of the people who come to this country. Take for instance, American citizens who -come to Canada to take up land and make their -homes

they are individually liable to the provisions o-f this section. Now there are many districts in the West where such a person would be required to travel probably fifteen, twenty or thirty miles to secure a permit to have in his possession a shot-gun to shoot prairie chickens or gophers.
It does -seem to me that that is rather a severe application of the principle, and I would suggest to the Minister of Justice that it might be worth while to consider some amendment, either by extending the scope of the previous amendment so that a justice of the peace would have authority to issue these permits o-r -by making some other provision to meet the cases that I know exist.

Of course, I would not compare my knowledge of the West with that of my hon. friend, but I should think such places must be comparatively rare and will be- ' come still more so. speechtext: In that regard, Mr. Chairman, it must be remembered that every district has a justice of the peace, and it seems to me that such an officer should be just as well qualified to issue these permits, as, for instance, a police constable.

speechtext: Do the old provisions of this subsection (dl) enable a magistrate to give a permit to carry a rifle or a shot-gun?

speechtext: Does the section name the things for which the permit can be given?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
Yes. As regards the
form, the hon. gentleman will notice that it is to be " as near as may be in the same form." The section provides that a man shall not carry these particular weapons " without having a permit therefor." That is, a permit for the particular kind of weapons that are mentioned here, and the form of permit being as near as may be in conformity with the form for other weapons, I would be under the impression that it would specify the weapon which the man desired to be authorized to carry. I was just looking for the form

speechtext: It was not the form I had in mind. I take it that the old section specifies the arms for which a permit can be granted, and if that section does not cover the arms mentioned here, then it is certainly not susceptible to any extension; it will be strictly construed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
If I correctly grasp the effect of this particular section, it requires a permit for one or the other of the different

weapons mentioned. " A permit therefor;" that is a permit for some one of these weapons. Without going back to the other sections, this section itself would require, for instance, if I were an alien and wanted to have a rifle, that I should have a permit for a rifle. And it is said with regard to the form in which that permit is to be issued that it shall be " as near as may be in the same form as in the case of other permits." If the other permits deal with other weapons, and I require under this a permit for a rifle, I would think that that is sufficient to prescribe that the weapon must be specified in the form. Then I turn to the form and I find this:
Permission is hereby given so and so to carry-
And then there is a blank, in regard to which it is said:
(Insert character of weapon).
I think that form will find its application to this present section, and that whoever issued a permit would insert in it the particular weapon which comes under this section and which the party applying for the permit desires to carry.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
I do not wish the
Minister of Justice to suppose I am raising a point which is not well founded. The form' is nothing. It must comply with the statutory provision, or at least if the form is different from the provision it must give way as there must not be anything in the form wider than the statute. I wanted to know if the statute upon which that form is based provides for the granting of a permit for carrying a rifle. If it does not, when I come before a magistrate for a permit to carry a rifle, he refers to the Act- and although I am not familiar with it I take it that it enumerates certain weapons for which a permit can be given. If he does not find a rifle or a shotgun enumerated, he would say, "I have not authority to give you a .permit for a rifle or shotgun, because the statute does not specify it."

When this Bill is passed this particular section which "we -are now discussing will be added to and become part of the original statute, and the section will then provide for permits for carrying rifles, and under this particular section, which will then form part of that statute, we have the provision 'that "a permit therefor," that is, for carrying any of these weapons, may be issued toy all the .persons who are men-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, does not the hon. minister believe that the term "offensive weapon" should be more clearly defined? Many objects which are not by their nature offensive weapons may become so under certain circumstances.
Mr. McM AS'TER: A razor.
Mr. MeKENZIB: An axe.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: Or a knife, or the electrical battery of the hon., member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat).

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext: It might be very difficult to undertake to give an absolutely comprehensive definition of what is an offensive weapon. After all, the words have an ordinary everyday conversational meaning, and I do think we can trust the courts to determine whether under the particular circumstances of a case a certain weapon can be properly described as an offensive weapon. I am not certain whether in the Criminal Oode as it stands there is any definition of an offensive weapon, although the term "offensive weapon" is not finding its W'ay into the Criminal Code for the first time under this section, for the other sections of the Act deal adequately with offensive weapons without a special definition of the term. In any event, "offensive weapons".is defined in subsection 24 of the interpretation clause.

subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
Take the case of a
man from the United States who is travel, ling through Canada en route to Newfoundland and who is carrying with him firearms for the purposes of his sport in Newfoundland; would this law apply in such a case? It would be rather a hardship if such a person was a criminal during the time that he was passing through Canada simply because he had firearms in his possession.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: ALIENS CARRYING FIREARMS.
speechtext:
I think that the law
would, strictly speaking, apply to persons of that class. As I pointed out in answer to the member for Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) while some gentlemen travelling through this country may possibly-(although I do not think it at all probable- be disturbed by some policeman because they are carrying weapons of this kind, still, I do not think that the inconvenience that they may be subjected to compares at all in gravity with the importance of our having the general protection. It is very often the fellow who comes in from another country carrying arms who is the most
56J
dangerous man to deal with. We have to count somewhat on this law being carried out, as other laws are carried out and enforced, with common sense; and I doubt whether any officer would be so officious as, upon an explanation of circumstances of that kind, to insist upon making an arrest. In any case, if inconvenience followed, I think we would be quite able to remedy it. As I say, it is probable thaMf you take the letter of the law a man under the circumstances related by my hon. friend might find himself an offender. On the other hand, how are you going to undertake to protect everybody who for one reason or another may be in his intentions just as innocent as that gentleman who came across the border? If you undertake to do that, it will be very difficult indeed to make a law that will be effective. For example, under th6 general law against carrying concealed weapons, any citizen of Canada is liable to be stopped by a policeman on the street and searched to see whether he has concealed weapons or not. That is liable to happen to any of us; still, it never happens. I do not think, therefore, that we have reason to apprehend as a serious actual danger that*any very grave consequences will follow on the fact that under the letter of the law what is suggested might happen. If it did happen in a few cases, I do think that our own protection is more important than the convenience of these visitors.

On motion of Hon. N. W. Rowell (President of the Privy Council) the House went into Committee on the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Resolved, That it is expedient to provide in the proposed Act to amend the Royal Northwest Mounted Police Act (Bill 22), now before the House, that section 51 of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police Act, Chapter 91 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, as enacted by section 13 of Chapter 69 of the Statutes of 1919, be amended so as to provide that the Governor in Council may as to him seems fit grant a pension to the widow and a compassionate allowance to each of the children of any officer who having completed ten years' service, was at the time of his death on full pay or who having completed ten years' service was at the time of his death in receipt of a pension; and that section 21 of said Chapter 91 toe amended so as to increase the salary of the Commissioner of Police to .$5,000.

subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I cannot see any more reason why a pension of this kind should be paid in the case of a mounted policeman after ten years' service than in the case of any other servant of the Government engaged in any other occupation. The life of a mounted policeman is a very pleasant one, as I understand it. It is an outside life, with no particular danger, consisting largely of going round the ooun-5 p.m. try on horseback, or by rail, or in any other way thought proper for the discharge of his duties. Compare that life with a conductor or a brake-man on the railroad. A brakeman's life is very much harder than that of a policeman, and no matter how long he stays with the road, whether as brakeman or conductor, he gets no pension unless he contributes to some benefit or insurance fund. I mention the brakeman just as one instance. The same is true of civil servants. Some may say that they have a particularly good time and have nothing >to do. I do not agree. Civil servants are doing very useful work, and a great many of them are very capable men. We could not get along without them, although we might get along with considerable fewer than we have, and I can see no good reason why at the end of ten years' service a pension should be granted to the widow of a mounted policeman and her children for the rest of their lives, and not given in the case of other employees of tihe Government.
Perhaps the minister will explain why he singles out a policeman and makes him the ward of the Government in this very satisfactory and kindly way over other servants who are similarly employed.
Mr. ROWEtLL: This Bill does not introduce any new principle. The law has been, I should imagine, ever since the Mounted Police was established, that a pension should be provided for the members of the force after they had served a certain definite period, on a scale which bears a direct relation to the years of service. It is based on the number of years they serve, and the amount of the pension varies according to the length of service. I quite concede that a strong argument may be made for some kind of a pension system for the Civil Service as a whole, but we are dealing now with a pension system which has been established for decades, and the object of this is to correct what appears to be an anomaly in the existing law. As the law now stands, if the
officer has completed ten years of service and retires or is retired under the special conditions mentioned in the Act a very limited pension may be given to him, and in case of his death, if he is in receipt of a pension, the widow and children may be allowed by the Governor in Council a pension not to exceed one-half of what the pensioner was drawing. This is not a pension as of right; it is a pension to meet cases of need. There are cases where under those conditions the Governor in Council would grant a small pension to the widow and children. While that is the law in case the man had retired after ten years and was drawing a pension, yet the law appears to be that if he dies after ten years' service and at the time of his death was still in the service drawing full pay, there is no power to provide any pension for the widow and children. The object of the amendment is [DOT]to put the widow ana children of a Mounted Policeman who has served more than ten years and who is still in service at the time of his death in the same position as the widow and children of a Mounted Policeman who had served ten years and then retired and who was in receipt of a pension at the time of his death. In other words, we could not see why the widow and children of the man who had served ten years and who died in the service should be left in a less advantageous position than the widow and children of a man who had retired after having served just the same length of time, but was on pension at the date of his death.

subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: They could not be the widow and children of a man who was still in the service.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
To put it more accurately, a man who was in the service at the time of his death. This question has arisen on an actual case that has just come 'to our attention. A very efficient officer who had served over ten years has died, leaving a widow and three small children penniless. If he had been retired a year ago on account of ill health-and-he had been in ill health for some 'time-and had been in receipt of a pension, we could, under the existing law -have given his wife and children a pension to a very limited amount; but he was not retired; he died in the service. Therefore, as the law stands, we cannot make any provision for the widow and children, and this is- simply to empower the Governor in Council to make the same provision for the widow and children of a man who dies in the service after ten years of service as we can do in the case of the man

who has already retired and was in receipt of a pension.

subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Supposing a policeman who had not necessarily been ten years in the service was killed in the discharge of his duty. Is any provision made by the law for his widow and other dependents by way of pension, gratuity, bonus or anything of that kind.?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.

I regret to say I cannot
answer that offhand. I do not recall that there is any provision and yet there may be in such a case. My recollection is that he must serve ten years 'before he becomes entitled to a pension.

On motion of Hon. Charles J. Doherty (Minister of Justice) Bill No. 25, respecting patents of invention, was read a second time and the House went into Committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair..
On section 1,-minister to have power to extend time in certain cases for doing any act, etc., under Patent Act.

We are quite familiar with cases of this kind where parties from time to time claim that a patent has lapsed because of some unforeseen circumstance. They used to come before Parliament and apply for special leave to renew the patent. We have had many applications of that kind. Private Bills were in-

troduced for the purpose. The parties interested had an opportunity to be heard before the Committee on Private (Bills. One circumstance may arise in connection with a patent that parties have begun to produce the article which is supposed to be covered by the patent. They have invested a large amount of money for the purpose of manufacturing the article and they have got fully under way in the business. I find no provision here that all the parties who may be interested in a patent must be called before the minister and fully heard. I think we should provide for a case of that kind so that if a man who has allowed his rights, or his application, to lapse comes back for restoration, any person who may be involved in the production of the article covered by the patent shall be heard because he certainly would have an interest as well as the man who is claiming the patent rights.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will lefer to section 3 he will see that the situation is contemplated and that provision is made for it. Section 3 deals precisely with the case that my hon. friend has in mind. For failure to do something a patent has lapsed. Some one else goes into the business and starts to manufacture. No doubt the rights or interests of that party who, when he started out was doing that which was perfectly lawful, must be taken into consideration. Provision is made that:
In any case .... where a patent has become void .... and during the period when such patent was void any person has commenced lawfully to manufacture, use or sell the invention covered by such patent, the patentee or proprietor of the patent shall not he entitled to any claim, action or demand in respect of such manufacture or sale, or the use of the article so manufactured or sold; and moreover the minister upon hearing the parties and considering all the facts and circumstances of the case may impose such terms and conditions (including if he so deems advisaMe, permission to continue such manufacture, use or sale), to which his order shall be subject, as the minister may deem, reasonably necessary for the protection of persons who have commenced lawfully to manufacture, use or sell the Invention covered by the patent.
That provision was intended to meet the case which the hon. gentleman has in view and it seems to me that unless something more satisfactory can be suggested it is sufficient.

The only thing that I wish to bring to the notice of the minister particularly is the question of notice. It is quite possible that the application may be placed before the minister, or before
the deputy minister, when the facts on one *side would be presented and a perfunctory notice, or attempt at notice, given. I would suggest to the minister, however, that provision should be made so that it would be clearly proven to the satisfaction of the minister that all parties interested were notified of the hearing. Sometimes provision is made for gazetting such notice but that is no notice to the ordinary man. Only *about one-twentieth of one per cent of the Canadian people read the Canada Gazette, and if notice by publication is to be necessary at all it should be in some newspaper where the interested parties reside and where it would most naturally come to their attention. Or else provision should be made for such other regulation as the minister might deem necessary in order to make it certain that the parties concerned would have proper and sufficient notice that such a hearing was to take place.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I fancy that the minister, in the exercise of his powers, inasmuch as he is required to hear the parties, would see the propriety of notice being given. I think we can trust any minister administering an Act of this kind to see that sufficient notice is given. It is difficult to prescribe just the kind of notice that would be suitable to' each case but I would be glad to make this suggestion: That after the word "parties" in the eighteenth line the words be added "after such notice as he may deem requisite and sufficient."

Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 4-proviso respecting rights under Treaty of Peace:

I notice in the section the words "British Empire" and I wish to suggest to the minister how wise it would be to employ the words "*associated British *commonwealths" or some such phrase instead of "British Empire." No later than the day before yesterday I had an example of how dangerous it is to continue the employment of these, words. I had the privilege of talking with an old friend, who for many years has been employed in religious work in India, and he said that the feelings of educated East Indians were very much aroused through our prohibition of Asiatic emigration even from India. In discussing the matter with him I asked whether this feeling of soreness was directed merely against Canada, or whether it was not also directed against the British Government.

He expressed to me .the idea that it was also directed against the British Govern* ment because the very words "British Empire" connoted the idea that Canada was in a position of inferiority to Great Britain, and that legislation by us, and for which we are in fact solely responsible, was, through the mere nomenclature of our organization, considered to be legislation for which the people of Great Britain and Ireland were responsible. Now that we have, by our signing of the Peace Treaty, declared ourselves to the rest of the world as being a sovereign nation, or a nation reaching out to sovereignty, I ask the minister is it not a mistake to continue the employment of words which connote an entirely different idea.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I doubt if it rests with us to change the name even though we may be of opinion that the relations of the nations, the group of nations, that constitute what is designated as the British Empire, have grown to be such that perhaps the word " Empire " is not a suitable designation. I think there is a good deal to be said for that proposition; hut though we may entertain that view, still the British Empire is the name toy w'hich this group of nations is known, and I hardly think that we could take upon ourselves, of our own authority, to change that name. The whole question which the hon. gentleman raises might in this connection be avoided, and perhaps it would have been a more logical thing to have done, by not singling out the British Empire at all. Inasmuch as the provision speaks of " the Treaty of Peace between the Allied and Associated Powers, on the one part, and Germany on the other." If we used the language "any other power with which the said Allied or Associated Powers are or have been at war " then we would not raise the question at all. I do not attach great importance to the point myself, but I think it will make the phrase more correct as we describe the Treaty with Germany as being a treaty between the Allied and Associated Powers on the one part and Germany on the other, and the war as having been between the Allied and Associated Powers on the one part, and Germany on the other. Such being the case, it would be more correct, as it occurs to me now, to take that phrasing which would avoid the question which the hon. gentleman raises. Therefore I beg leave to move:
To amend clause 4 by striking out the words " British Empire is " in the thirty-seventh line on page 2 of the Bill, and replacing the said

words by the following, " said Allied and Associated Powers are," and by replacing the word "has" in the same line by the word "have."

It seems to me that the member for Brome (Mr. McMas-ter) proposes to make some change in the statute which affects our standing as a Dominion, associated with the British Empire, and I do not agree with.him at all in that direction until there has been a full discussion of the question in this House, and I hope I will be present at 'that discussion. I would not at all agree with him that we are to define in such a roundabout way our future in connection with the Empire even in an Act of Parliament of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have not defined it at all.

I have no objection to the minister's suggestion; but the hon. gentleman (Mr. McMaster) is framing a constitution for this country in a roundabout way, and I hope, subsequently there will be a full discussion of the whole proposition.
I would like to ask the minister what effect this legislation will have on German patents. Unfortunately I was not here at the beginning of his address.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The real purpose of this legislation is to make provision for questions that may arise between our own nationals. With regal'd to German patents, that is to say, either to patents issued in Germany and held by our nationals, or patents issued by us and held by German nationals, what will happen to them is governed by the Treaty of Peace, and that is the reason why we have inserted a clause here that nothing in this Act is to affect anybody's rights as provided for in the Treaty.
Mr. CURRIE; But that does not answer the question I was going to ask the minister. During the war a number of German patents were taken out in this country and machines were built after the designs of those patents. Under this law will the Germans he able to come in and claim a royalty on all such machines operated during the war? I know of two or three German machines that had to be built here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This amendment does
not affect that case at all. The rights of parties in the case the hon. gentleman (Mr. Currie) refers to would be governed and determined by the conditions of the Treaty, and not by this Act.

For instance, there is a
German patent for the separation of minerals, such as silver and gold, by means of oil. That patent right was obtained in Canada by a German group, and they also secured the patent in the United States. They then transferred the Canadian rights to the United States, and throughout the whole war those people were threatening suits and doing everything they possibly could to prevent the production of silver and gold in the Canadian north country. Now, what effect will this Bill have on their position when the case comes before the courts on the question of their right to royalties on the patent? It is a serious matter involving millions of dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This Bill will have absolutely no effect whatever. The question is with regard to the rights to patents in this country held by German nationals on the one hand, or to patents in Germany held by our nationals on the other hand, and this very clause is inserted 'because those rights are governed by the Treaty stipulations. On a suitable occasion I would be very glad to give the hon. gentleman what I understand to be the effect of the Treaty with regard to those rights. But to make my hon. friend's mind perfectly at ease, I may say that those questions are not governed by this Act, and that is what section four says; they are governed by the stipulations of the Treaty. Although I have not the text of the Treaty before me, I think I would be safe in saying for his information that if he will refer to it he will find that although under the terms of that Treaty patent rights are or may be revived, any such revival is to be subject to such provisions as we, any of the Allied or Associated Powers, may deem fit to make for the protection of people who while the German patents .were in abeyance have acquired interests with regard to them. I think he will find that the Treaty amply provides for the protection of our nationals in cases of til at kind.

Glancing through this
Bill, it seems to me that it is really intended for the revival of German patents. The officials of the Government may issue a patent to a man or may renew a latent patent. For instance, in the case of a German patent which existed before the war and lapsed here during the war,, a German can come along, and although we may have been using the machines covered by that patent, he can say, " Well, owing to the war I was unable to renew this patent. I want it renewed now." Thereupon the
minister must cause an inquiry to be made, and if the Treaty permits it he may renew that German's patent without regard to any rights that may have accrued to Canadians in the meantime. I believe it is a great mistake tying up our patent and copyright law to these foreign countries, and for that reason I would like to know if it is the intention of the minister to bring in a revision of the whole Bill next session. There are lots of things in our Patent Act that require attention.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There may be; I have not given it consideration. But may I point this out, that if the hon. gentleman will read the first section of this Bill he will find that it is intended principally for any distinguished soldier like himself who because he was absent at the war may have failed to comply with some requirements and as time went by he forfeited his patent lights. Now, we want power to remedy that state of things.

That does not apply to
Germany.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As regards the Germans, we have made it very clear that the Treaty settles their rights, and therefore we say that this Act will have no application to any rights that are governed by the Treaty. The hon. gentleman need have no apprehension on that point.

All right, if the hon.
minister says so.
What is the meaning in the thirty-eighth line " at war with regard to industrial property"?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There ought to be a comma after the word " war." I move that section 4 be amended by inserting a comma after the words "at war" on line 38.

Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
