On th.e motion of Hon. Hugh Guthrie (for the Minister of Agriculture) the House went into Committee on the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the 'Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to provide,-
1.	That the manufacture in Canada and importation into Canada of oleomargarine be permitted until the thirty-first day of August, 1920 ; and the offering for sale, the sale and the having in possession for sale of oleomargarine be permitted until the first day of March, 1921.
2.	That no person shall import oleomargarine into Canada or shall manufacture oleomargarine in Canada without having first obtained a license to do so, and such license may be cancelled for the violation of any of the provisions of the proposed legislation or regulations made in pursuance thereof.
3.	That oleomargarine imported into Canada under the provisions of the proposed legislation he imported free of customs duty.
4.	That no person shall sell, offer for sale, or have in his possession for sale any oleomargarine, unless the packages containing it are marked or labelled as prescribed.
5.	That the Governor in Council may make regulations as to the importation, manufacture, inspection and sale of oleomargarine, the Issue of licenses, the seizure and confiscation of apparatus and materials used in the manufacture of oleomargarine in contravention of the provisions of the proposed legislation, and for the efficient enforcement and operation of the proposed Act; and further that penalties may he imposed for violation of the Act.

This resolution proposes to extend the Orders in Council which have been in force since July, 191V, in regard to the manufacture, importation and sale of oleomargarine. The Orders in Council as originally passed were perhaps a little indefinite as to the length of time during which they should remain in effect. The first Order in Council was passed on October 23, 1917, and provided that it should have effect for the period during which the then abnormal condition should continue, the conclusion of such period to be determined by the Minister of Agriculture with the approval of the Governor in Council, and it was 'passed as a war measure only. This Order in Council was supplemented by a subsequent one passed on July 18, 1918, rescinding the first Order in Council. The chief difference between, the two is that the regulations- attached to them differ rather materially, the regulations passed in connection with the second Order in Council being the more stringent. The Order in Council of July 18, 1918, has not yet expired, but as it was passed under the War Measures Act it might he said that it might

expire almost any time now, and it has therefore 'been deemed proper to introduce this resolution to continue the Order in Council in effect until the 31st of August next. Importation and manufacture therefore, are permitted until 31st August next, which is' about ten months, and provision is made for the sale for a further period until March 21. 1921. The regulations, I assume, as set out in the resolution are in general terms about the same as the regulations now in force.

What is the objection to
making this legislation permanent, rather than extending it from time to time by Order in Council?

There are two opinions
upon that question. The matter was pretty thoroughly debated in the House during the session of 1918, and the House was by no means of one opinion. Many men consider that oleomargarine is not a proper article of food. Others take the ground that its permanent adoption in this country would be a serious blow to the dairying interests of Canada. There is a great deal to be said in favour of each of these views. Personally, I see no very great objection to making the policy permanent. However, the Government has not- gone that far, and until the matter has been more fully discussed and things become more normal all the Government seeks to do by this resolution is to extend the present Orders in Council. I have no doubt the time will come, and in the near future, when the Government or the House will have to determine upon a policy in regard to oleomargarine.

This is where our
much-vaunted Department of Health could come into play and tell us whether oleomargarine is fit to be used for human food, whether it is wholesome or otherwise. I see my good friend from South Toronto (Mr. Sheard) here, who is quite an authority on matters of this kind, and who took a very prominent and eloquent part in promoting the Department of Health. Possibly he will give us some side lights, if not head light, on this question. If a Health Department is required at all, and there is- no doubt that it is, I think this is a ease where the Minister of Health or an officer of the Health Department could be of service to the Government and the country. I should like to know whether oleomargarine is a wholesome food. Perhaps the Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) can tell us its ingredients. I will be perfectly honest and tell my hon. friend that

I do not know them myself. I tried to eat oleomargarine once, and I would not try it a second time. I do not know that I would have tried it once if I had known what it really was. It certainly did not agree with me at all, but that is neither here nor there. If oleomargarine is nutritious, and a suitable and proper food for the men, women and children of this country to use, if it nourishes the body properly, and is obtainable cheaper than butter, its use should be encouraged; but if it is not a wholesome food and does not nourish the body properly it is too dear at any price.
I think that before laymen like myself should give their sanction to its adoption as a food, we should have some reliable information from some department of the Government as to the value and safety of introducing this commodity into the country. This is not a new question at all, although oleomargarine to myself is new. I do not know that it is very much used in the part of the country from which I come, but it may be. I trust the Solicitor General will satisfy the House, that, so far as he knows, oleomargarine is a proper commodity to be introduced as a food.

As the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) has been gracious enough to make some reference to myself I think, I may say that I did intend to say a word or two on this subject. At the outset let me say that among the fats there are three basic or neutral fats, olein, margarine and stearin. Their essential difference is the difference in the temperature at which they remain fluid. Olein is a fluid at ordinary temperatures. Stearin is solid at all ordinary temperatures. Margarine is betwixt and between; thus, it would be fluid on a hot summer's day, and solid at an outside temperature such as we have had to-day. The purity of these fats determines absolutely whether they are deleterious or otherwise. The very moment a fat begins to decompose-it makes absolutely no difference whether it is olein, stearin or margarine, certain acids are produced, most of which are poisonous, and all of which are strongly odorous. The quantity of acids produced by decomposition is practically the same in the case of all fats. Therefore, as to whether or not oleomargarine, which, as its name indicates, is a mixture of the food fat olein and the semi-food fat margarine, is deleterious as a food product depends upon the condition of purity and of freshness at the time they were made into oleomargarine. Thus you can get almost as poisonous results
from butter made in a creamery from a Jersey herd as you can from oleomargarine; but the fact remains that in making oleomargarine you can collect various qualities and varieties of fats which you would not be able to do in handling the butter fat only. Butter is butter fat out of the milk, and therefore it is limited to one variety of fat; whereas, olein may be oil from many sources, it may be vegetable oil or it may be animal oil; and so with margarine, it may be fats obtained from a series of animals; and the mixture of these two fats constitutes oleomargarine. I think that clarifies to some extent the question whether oleomargarine is deleterious or noxious as a food product. It depends very largely upon who prepares it, how it is prepared and how long and in what condition it has been kept. It is, therefore, for the Government to provide conditions under which its preparation and supervision will ensure to the public the purest form of fat admixture, so that it will contain no decomposing elements from fat.
But there is another feature and, to my mind, a very important one which should be presented. If oleomargarine can so closely resemble butter that the ordinary consumer cannot tell the difference, and if the price would necessarily, probably, be one-half the price of ordinary creamery butter, and if oleomargarine serves all the purposes both as to food and other conditions which butter serves, I can see very urgent reason and justification for oleomargarine being made a proper article of commerce. Why we should, as consumers, pay tremendous prices for creamery butter in order to keep up the reputation and record of a dairy herd is something that I cannot understand. Therefore, I would urge the Government to favour and to foster the manufacture and development of oleomargarine in Canada under proper supervision for the very purpose of bringing down the price of butter, as it will do, because it ''will be a substitute for butter. Those who want to pay the price of butter may do so; they will pay for all the care, the record, the housing of a dairy herd, for example, and that is a very expensive proposition, and it will all be embraced in the original manufacturing cost of creamery butter from that source. There is this point about the matter, however, that there is in oleomargarine a proneness to decomposition which probably is wider in its field of operation and more extensive in its results than is the case with butter but that can be very easily and readily controlled.

Those are 'the facts .as far as I know them, and sufficient, I think, to clear up the point as to the value or otherwise of oleomargarine as an article of diet.
I am well aware that the agricultural interests of the country are generally opposed to the use and sale of oleomargarine, because it is, as I said, a substitute for butter, and they feel that whatever provides a. substitute in a sense competes with dairy interests. That is true, but the substitution of an article of food which ordinarily will serve the purpose of butter and which only under extreme circumstances can be distinguished from butter is, I think, an economic argument for the sale and production of oleomargarine, (which argument- ought to weigh with those who are legislating for the common good. I have every desire to assist the dairy interests in 'this country as far. as they can possibly be assisted, but if that entails the purchase of a costly product where a cheaper product can be substituted, I question if that is good economics for this country to follow.

I should like to give the House a summary as my memory serves me on the oleomargarine question. Thirty years ago there was probably no question that caused such a great fight throughout the United States, especially the agricultural states, as that of legalizing the manufacture of oleomargarine in that country.
Practically all the New England States with the exception of Rhode Island and Connecticut were against it. At that time butter of the finest quality was selling throughout the United States for about 15 cents a pound. It had to be splendid butter at that. Much of it was being sold as low as ten and twelve cents a pound. After several strenuous years of fighting, the law was adopted by which oleomargarine could be manufactured and sold in the United States. The law provided that any one selling oleomargarine had to pay a tax of $60. From the day it was manufactured and put on the market in the United States dairy and creamery butter advanced in price gradually, never declining for one moment because oleomargarine was on the market. The price increased and it was always from two to five cents higher than the price oi Canadian butter.
I do not wish to go into the question of the wholesomeness of oleomargarine but I know that the -manufacture of oleomargarine was a good thing for the dairying interests. They purchased the separated milk from the farmers and creameries, and churned it and they bought a certain percentage of butter which was mixed in the manufacture of oleomargarine. As time went on they improved and perfected the process until no expert could tell the difference in taste

and flavour except when the oleomargarine was put in comparison with the very best butter. Taking into consideration diseased cattle, impure milk and carelessness of milkers, I believe that oleomargarine will compare favourably with a great deal of the butter that is turned out throughout the United States.
As regards Canada I would not do or favour anything in this House that would work agaiinst the interests of the farmers. But how has it worked out here? Since oleomargarine has been on the market in Canada dairy butter has gradually risen until it nets the farmer at the present time close to 60 cents a pound. I know that the farmers were unanimously against the adoption of the proposal to admit of the manufacture and sale of oleomargarine and that petitions against it were circulated throughout the eastern townships in which I live during the year prior to the permission being given. It is my impression that if we allow oleomargarine to be sold we will be doing the greatest good to the greatest number of people, and I do not believe personally that it will be against the interest of the farmer. However, I will not commit myself against the will or interests of the farmers on this question.

I presume that there have been some representations made to the Government expressing a desire that the permission to sell oleomargarine be extended for a further period. I realize that there are many interests to be considered and that the Government has in its wisdom seen fit to throw around this permission such protection as it deems necessary to at least see that people are supplied with what they would consider to be a pure and staple food. Notwithstanding the steps that may be taken in this direction, it has a disturbing influence on the farming community. I do not think it wise at a time like this to introduce measures that have a tendency to upset the minds of the agricultural community. The production of dairy products in this country unfortunately is shrinking rather than increasing. There seems to be a distinct reaction throughout the country, largely due to the unsettled state of the markets and the lack of assurance of fair prices for his products that would give to the farmer adequate remuneration for his* effort in the industry. This has possibly been -more marked in regard to cheese, also a dairy product, but with regard to butter it has likewise been in evidence. A large quantity of butter has been- produced, we admit-possibly an increasing quantity-but
our export market has increased and the export market sets the value for the product of our own country. The opinion has been expressed that the manipulation of butter by the cold storage companies, in with, holding it from the market, is the cause alone of the unusually high price, but I am very strongly of the opinion that this theory is entirely wrong and that the cause of the prevailing high price is the export demand.
I was not in when the minister introduced the Bill and I did not hear upon what grounds he based its introduction but I think it is unfortunate that we have from term to term of Parliament these disquieting measures and matters being constantly brought up. I wonder whether the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie), who has proposed this legislation, has come to the conclusion that the first day of March, 1921, will be the final limit of time and whether this will be the last time the country will be disturbed by legislation on this matter. I am not disposed to view with favour this constant meddling that creates so much disturbance amongst the agricultural community. I think that we should devote our attention to the encouragement of the producer and the farmer in the effort to increase the supply of butter, so that we may have a pure article in abundance in our own country and at the same time have a large amount for export. If we do so we will be considering the best interests of our country from the standpoint of supplying our people with a pure food and of increasing the standard of our butter in the markets of the world, thus building up a reputation that in the years to -come will stand us in good stead.
I do not know, as I say, just what arguments have been presented for a continuance of the privileges- permitted under the motion; nevertheless I think it is dangerous and undesirable to be constantly tinkering and dealing with this matter. I think the needs of the great agricultural community might more properly be considered in the best interests of the country than the small amount that might be saved to the consumer by the admission of oleomargarine to -Canada, because I think the consumer throughout the country is earning a wage that enables 'him to ipay the higher price for that useful article of food, butter. I think it is unfortunate that even in the family of the poor man it should be necessary to substitute oleomargarine for that more wholesome food, butter. I trust, Sir, that whatever may happen to this resolution to-night, this will be the last we will

hear of any effort to continue the sale of such a product in this country.
Mr. MeOOIG: Mr. Chairman, before you declare the resolution carried, I might add something to what has already been said by the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat in the way of warning the Government about taking action on matters of this kind without giving such matters thorough consideration. Having regard to a pamphlet which has been printed and circulated by the Ontario Government among the farmers in my constituency, at this particular time, when an election is in progress, there undoubtedly are two opinions on many of the questions pertaining to agriculture and affecting the consumer upon which action by the Federal Government has been taken in recent years. The consuming population in Ontario are anxious to get butter and food generally as cheaply as they possibly can, and the Government should do everything they can to lessen the spread in price between what the producer receives and what the consumer pays, and do their utmost to enable the people in the cities to obtain cheap food stuffs. I regret that I was not in the House when this motion was in-

troduced, and I am therefore somewhat handicapped by reason of not having heard the arguments advanced in favour of extending the time for the importation of oleomargarine into Canada and its manufacture here. I would like to remind the House that all the dairymen's associations throughout the country have, I believe, protested against such action. No very serious objection was taken to the admission into Canada of this substitute for butter when it was first authorized, I think in April, 1918, by reason of the fact that we were at war and that there was a very great demand from overseas for butter. I then pointed out what I considered to be unfair and unjust features of the measure, namely, that it permitted the manufacturers of oleomargarine to incorporate butter to any extent they saw fit into these oleo oils and other things which constitute margarine. In this connection the evidence given by the general manager of one of the largest concerns manufacturing oleomargarine in Canada, given here a few weeks ago before a special committee, was somewhat significant, when he pointed out that they were purchasing all the June make of butter they could get for the reason that it was so highly coloured and added a colouring to the oleomargarine, and that if the people really imagined they were eating butter and had something of the exact colour of butter, it would make the article much more palatable to them. I think the committee will agree that it is hardly just to try to reach the consumer unfairly, and to take advantage of the merits of an important food product that has been manufactured in this country for many years-a product in regard to which the manufacturers have spent many millions of dollars in providing plant and equipment and the stock and stabling necessary for carrying on dairying throughout this country. Let hon. gentlemen read the Dairy Act and they will find it contains the strictest provisions in regard to the manufacture of butter and dairy produce in any of the factories of Canada, and that there is no possibility of these products being adulterated, heavy penalties being prescribed for any violation of the law in that respect. It is a common thing to find that people are being fined for what might be considered very slight infringement of the provisions of the Act regarding the manufacture of dairy produce. Yet we permit to be brought into and manufactured in this country something that is being placed in the market, not on its merits, remember-if it were

so placed no one would take any exception -but as a deceptive counterfeit that the manufacturers are endeavouring to place before the people as a substitute for this wholesome article of food which is surrounded with such stringent restrictions.
I ask the committee if they consider it is fair that one body of manufacturers in this country should be singled out and restricted, as the farmers and dairymen are, by the Dairy Act, and other manufacturers permitted to purchase pure butter, or any grade of butter they see fit. Not only that, but churning it in milk in order to take the flavour of the milk, so as to make it palatable to the people, and then incorporate it into this grease and place it on the market? It is well known that there is no substitute for butter as a wholesome article of food. Butter is the most wholesome article of food that there is to be found to-day and nothing that the ingenuity of science and skill can devise -can take its place.
Then I ask why by the legislation passed a little more than a year ago we permit the manufacturers of oleomargarine to purchase millions of pounds of butter and incorporate it in this grease, then churn it in milk, and put the resulting product up in prints exactly the size of butter and enclose it in wrappers identical with those used for wrapping butter, except that they are forced by law to state on those wrappers that the product is oleomargarine. But when the wrapper is taken off, owing to the colour imparted to the oleomargarine by the methods I have just stated, the people are deceived and do not know exactly what they are eating, although it is against the law not only in the United States but in this country to so colour this grease that it is indistinguishable from butter. In many a boarding house and restaurant throughout the country to-day I venture to state one is very often given oleomargarine instead of butter. It is true that a card must be displayed somewhere indicating that oleomargarine is being sold. I contend, Sir, that at this particular juncture when it is necessary to increase the production of our food supplies that this is not the time to extend the period for the importation and manufacture of this article. Margarine is sold at a much lower price in the Old Country, but here the manufacturers contend that they cannot sell it unless there is an admixture of from 20 to 35 per cent of pure butter. It is evident that this was not the idea in the minds of hon. members when they put the legislation through permitting the importation and
manufacture of oleomargarine. It was boosted as an article that could compete successfully with any other similar article placed on the market, that it -was being manufactured from wholesome oils of various kinds, and that it was a common article of food in the Old Country. But the high price of oleomargarine has been severely criticised, and it has been felt that the Food Board should have controlled the price as well as it did the price of some other food commodities. We have not noticed that the Board of Commerce has been very active in this regard. It will be found that the price of foodstuffs for stock is higher to-day than it probably ever was before, and yet in face of those conditions it is proposed to extend the time for the importation and manufacture of this counterfeit article, which its manufacturers are not able to sell on its merits, but only when treated in the way I have described.
I am sorry I did not know that this Bill was coming up to-day, Mr. Chairman, or I would have had some data to give to the House in regard to oleomargarine. I remember a sworn statement made by the manager of one of the packing houses in regard to this article before a committee of this House a short time ago when he admitted that without the oleomargarine being coloured by the admixture of butter it would be practically unsaleable because of the fact that people would realize they were not eating butter. I have pointed out before that it is somewhat significant that during the last year and a half so many of these Bills that have proved such a handicap to agriculture have been permitted to pass this House. I pointed that out particularly with regard to foodstuffs. I have at the present time a Bill before the House which is designed to regulate the millers of this country in regard to the manner in which they have been adulterating bran *and shorts, two of the most important feeding stuffs for the production of dairy produce, and I am not too sanguine yet as to whether that measure will become law. As I say, it is rather significant that all these measures should have been introduced while we had a certain member of the Government charged with the duty of looking after the Department of Agriculture.
I want to say, Mr. Chairman, that I object to the extension being made in this form. If we are going to permit margarine to come into this country and be manufactured here, and if that is the desire of hon. members, I have no objection, provided you do not permit its manufacturers to incorporate in their product a staple ar-

tide of food surrounded with such stringent regulations as is the manufacture of butter, in order that oleomargarine may be given an appearance indistinguishable from butter. Too many restrictions have been imposed on the producers of butter to permit a substitute of this kind to come in unchecked under the guise of an Act of Parliament to enable its manufacture to deceive the people. If we are going to have stringent regulations with, regard to one class, then I say, Mr. Chairman, that we should have just as stringent regulations with regard to all other classes in the community; .and I say further, Sir, that when our dairymen object as strenuously as they have objected to this legislation, their voice is entitled to some consideration at the hands of this Committee and of this House.

While we are on this subject, Mr. Chairman, I would like to call the attention of the minister in charge of this Bill to complaints that come from the public very often not only about the impurities of oleomargarine, but the impurities of butter itself, not perhaps impurities in the first instance, but it is said that butter is put through certain processes in the stores after it has left the hands of the dairymen and is worked up in such a way that a far greater percentage of water is in the butter than it should naturally contain, and in that way -merchants who are handling butter are guilty of selling something to the consumer that is not really what it is represented to be. I do not. know which department of the Government should look after this, hut it is certainly something that should receive proper attention. I merely mention this matter so that steps may be taken to insure that when a man buys a pound of butter

As for the manufacture of oleomargarine, I presume that we have. Canadian factories now manufacturing this article. The only thing that I would suggest to the minister is that, if manufactured at all, oleomargarine should be manufactured under the most stringent system of inspection so that the very best article of its class will be produced. Presumably the manufactured article that is imported is subject to inspection of some kind, but I suppose in any event if it is not the sort of article that it should toe people will not buy it. I would like to see some system of inspec-

Such action on the part of any one who keeps a public eating place is certainly fraudulent, dishonest and unfair.

: The regulations in regard to the importation and sale of oleomargarine are far more stringent than those with regard to the importation and sale of butter; it is necessary, I think, that that should be the case. Regulation 16 covers such a case as that mentioned by my hon. friend. It reads :	.	.

1 am not an expert on oleomargarine. But I have been told by those who know something about the matter, that since the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine was permitted in Canada there has been no great increase in the consumption of the product; in fact within the past six to ten months there has rather been a notable decrease in the consumption. On the other hand, I am informed that there has been an increase in respect of butter and that butter has maintained, if not actually increased, its price since the Order in Council was passed permitting the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine. From this it is to be inferred that the entrance into this market of oleomargarine and its manufacture in Canada have not to any appreciable extent injured buttermaking as an industry. I agree with the member for Uarleton (Mr. Boyce) in his remarks on that subject. Prior to the passing of the Order in Council, people who
could not procure butter had to go without it or use drippings as a substitute. These people are now the present consumers of oleomargarine, the cost of which, I believe, is about half the cost of butter. If these people were deprived of their opportunity to purchase oleomargarine it is doubtful whether they would be able to purchase butter at present prices. It is for the benefit of that class of the people that the extension of this order is now asked. Personally I do not think that it will adversely affect the dairy industry. The extension is only for a limited time-eleven months for importation and fourteen months for sale. I think that is a rather reasonable proposal and I trust that the committee will accept it.
How much oleomargarine has been imported into Canada and how much has been manufactured in Canada since the Order in Council was passed?

This matter was handed to me only during the course of the afternoon; I tried to get those figures for this evening, but was unable to do so. I will have them before the House on the second reading of the Bill.

Mr. Chairman, I
do not think that any one will take exception to the importation of oleomargarine into Canada under present conditions, provided there is no attempt to incorporate butter into this article in order to deceive the people.
I think that that is obviously unfair to those who are engaged in the manufacture of butter. In the regulations regarding the -manufacture of oleomargarine - it is provided that no person other than a manufacturer of oleomargarine shall mix oleomargarine with butter. As the matter stands, you are simply destroying a very important industry in this country; there is no getting away from that fact. You may say that more butter is being manufactured to-day than some years ago, but do not forget that butter has been commanding a very high price during the war, a price it will not command later on when prices generally will reach a lower level than at present. You may also argue that oleomargarine is permitted to enter the country and to be manufactured only for a short time, but 'at the end of that time you will find it will be very much more difficult -to cut off the manufacturing of it than ft would be now, because then the manufacturers will be pointing to the capital they have invested in their plants



for turning out this product. I think it would .be well before we pass this resolution to understand thoroughly the nature of the Bill permitting the manufacture of oleomargarine in this country. I doubt whether very many members of this House realize the very wide powers that were granted when the measure was put through enabling this adulteration to take place. Personally I have not the slightest objection to oleomargarine being imported and manufactured in this country on its merits, but I do object to millions of pounds of good butter being incorporated with it often a total loss, for oleomargarine will not keep in cold storage. That has been amply demonstrated. It has to be quiekly consumed 'because of the milk that is incorporated in it in ordeT to deceive the palates of the people. I think we .should also be informed how many millions of pounds of butter have been used in the manufacture of oleomargarine in this country since the legislation was passed a little over a year ago. We should also know how much of this oleomargarine has been destroyed as unfit for food as a result of attempting to carry it in cold storage. The conservation of food is a very important matter, and I therefore think we should have information on this point before we pass the resolution.
I mentioned before that only the manufacturers of oleomargarine were permitted to adulterate, and I said, why not allow the dairymen to do the same. I do not think, however, that such a proposal would meet with the approval of the dairymen of this country, because on account of the extreme care that has been exercised in order to standardize our butter and improve its quality, it has obtained a place for itself in the markets of the world that is invaluable. The province of Quebec, I believe, is the largest producer of butteT in the Dominion, and their butter has a very high reputation, which I do not think.it would be well to jeopardize.
I again say that we should be furnished with further information before we pass this resolution, particularly with regard to the quantity of butter that is being incorporated into this article of food. Why cannot oleomargarine be sold on its merits in this country as in other countries, if it is the superior article of food that some people would have us believe? You can purchase oleomargarine in the Old Country for about half the price you have to pay in Canada, largely because the people of this country, having been accustomed to a wholesome article of food, will not consume oleomar-

gadine, unless they are deceived as they have been deceived by incorporating butter, by churning it in milk, and by putting it up in identically the same pound prints as butter is sold in. Why should it be permissible to put this stuff up and sell it in that way? The object is quite apparent.
The Solicitor General says that the card must be displayed in some conspicuous place in restaurants and eating houses where oleomargarine is used. Quite true, but you have to search diligently'for these cards, and youwill then find them in letters one and a half inches in length in a large dining room perhaps fifty or one hundred feet in length. That is not displaying the card conspicuously. In other cases you may find it on a shelf partially concealed by some article of furniture. It may be that the people are complying with the law in that respect. I should like to know how many fines have been imposed during the past year for the violation of this law. Possibly it is enforced somewhat in the same manner as the Act dealing with the adulteration of bran and shorts, through which adulterations thousands of animals have been poisoned and, so far as I can learn, in not a single instance has any one been prosecuted for violating the law in that respect. Some hon. members may think this a small matter to take so much interest in, but it is a very important matter when we consider how essential increased production is in order that we may overcome the difficulties confronting this country to-day. Now you are not increasing production (by permitting this stuff to foe brought in and butter to be incorporated with it, because you are taking away from the people a good wholesome article of food and mixing it up with this oleomargarine, and it is a question whether the people receive any benefit as a result. I have no personal knowledge of the matter, but I have made inquiries, -and from the information I could obtain in the absence of the Overseas Minister, Wandsworth jail, prior to the war, was a civil institution, but was subsequently taken over by the Imperial military authorities and used as a military detention barracks, at all events up to the end of 1917- 1 am not sure whether it has been since used for the purpose or not. Some Canadian military prisoners, who were convicted of offences and sentenced to undergo detention for more than fourteen days, were sent to Wandsworth detention camp, but as far as I have been able to ascertain there is no evidence of any brutal treatment being meted out to them. I am informed that a Canadian officer was, in 1916, detailed on Canadian guard to assist the Government at the detention barracks, and, as my hon. friend who is a medical officer in the Canadian army medical corps must be aware, no prisoner was allowed to undergo punishment without a medical certificate that he was fit to undergo the punishment imposed. I can understand that discipline in the detention barracks was probably fairly severe, but the article in question, which was an entirely anonymous report from supposed soldiers, did: not give any names, and as far -as 1 can ascertain no brutal treatment was meted out to any Canadian soldier.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: I would like to inquire if the leader of the Government is able to give us definite information to-day as to when we may expect prorogation, and further, if any definite conclusion has been reached as to whether the House will sit on Monday (Thanksgiving Day) or not?

On making inquiry I think it is absolutely impossible for us to do our duty and get through business this wedk. Mr. Calder's Committee, which is a very important one as hon. gentlemen know, will not be able to report as soon as expected, and the membership of the House desires to be present when that report is submitted. I do not think it is possible therefore to anticipate getting away this week. That being the case, I think probably we had better intermit Thanksgiving Day for the business of the House and devote our hearts and our minds seriously to thanksgiving for the many mercies that are vouchsafed to us, particularly in comparison with other countries and other peoples. With regard to other legislation I am not in a position to make an announcement to-day. In reference to this I might extend the advice to both sides that the Whips and members should conjointly arrange to be present and have as large an attendance as possible for the important legislation which is coming up in the later days of the session. I think our duty is not to slight legislation for the sake of getting away a few days earlier than we otherwise [DOT]might be able to do. The session has not been a long one, and I should invite the Whips on both sides to make arrangements to have during next week as full an attendance of members as possible.
Is the leader of the Government intimating that further legislation is coming down?
I have no announcement to make in reference to that, but an announcement will be made probably to-morrow as to what, if any, legislation will yet be brought down.

Mr. Speaker, I
wish to refer to what may be regarded as a question of privilege. In the Halifax Chronicle of October 4, the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) is reported under Parliamentary Proceedings to have stated as follows:
Mr. Mowat of Toronto rather scored off the Opposition Leader when he recalled that in his own peaceful bailiwick the militia had h>
