If the hon. member for Parkdale is correctly reported, I must say that there is not a scintilla of truth in that statement, nor the slightest foundation for it. There were no riots in Nova Scotia, no militia were called out, and no expense of this kind were incurred or attempted to be collected. When the hon. member spoke the other day he made reference to something that took place thirty-six years ago, but he is reported as having referred to an event of three weeks ago. I do not wish to have any stain like that on my province, and therefore I deem it to be my duty to set the matter right.

Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 21 respecting the Canadian Wheat Board.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I dislike making extended remarks on the motion for the second reading of this Bill, but some statements I made in the House on the resolution seem to have been misunderstood, and I therefore think it necessary to take up a few moments of the time of the House in answering some of the questions which have been put by way of criticism and comment. The President of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange took a newspaper report of my speech and considered that if it was true I misrepresented the situation, insofar as the farmers' market was concerned in the West, both absolutely and comparatively, as taken in relation with the farmers' market in the United States. Generally in the criticisms a number of questions have been asked, which I think are quite in order, and I desire to make a reply to them before we go into Committee of the Whole.
In the first place, the question is put as to why the exchange market was opened up in Winnipeg, and why it was afterwards closed. A great many opinions have been

expressed as to the reasons for both steps. I am free to say that if the Government had had the same information before the market was opened up as it had shortly afterwards, probably the market would not have been opened up at all; but we all depend for our sources of information on agencies, and we have to take from them what information we get from time to time, and in these confused and abnormal conditions information sometimes develops quite rapidly and changes the point of view of the seeker for enlightenment on the general question. As far as I am myself concerned, as the head of the Department of Trade and CoTnmerce, and as far as the Government is concerned, there is no doubt that we were not at all anxious to undertake any controlled system of the marketing of wheat this year. We had experience of the controlled system of marketing during the two preceding years when the war was on, and when I think by general consent, even though some felt that their business and their privileges were largely curtailed by the fact of Government control and operation, it was conceded that nothing else was possible during those times. When the Armistice was declared and peace came in sight the natural desire, both of the Government and of the grain trade, reverted again with all its force that the shackles should be taken off and control should not be exercised, and I was of the opinion, as was the Government, that quite probably very great freedom, if not complete freedom, might be given to the Grain Trade, so that it could resume its normal and accustomed channels for carrying on its various operations. A delegation was sent by the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, which visited London while I was there, and I was in communication with that delegation. The opinion of that delegation was entirely in favour of the open market, of resuming the former methods of carrying on the grain business in this country and for export purposes.
Is the minister referring to the delegation that I accompanied ?
Yes.
Well, I wish to disassociate myself entirely from that view. I was not agreeable to the opening up of the grain market at any time.
Possibly I have confused the delegations. There were two, were there?
Probably the minister might separate them by saying there was-a delegation from the Grain Exchange.

I am speaking ot the delegation from the Grain Exchange. Whether my hon. friend was on that or not, I do not remember; I do not suppose he was. As he now says he was not, I will confine myself to the delegation from the Grain Exchange which was in favour of the open market for the current crop. I may say that the grain trade in Great Britain and also the Royal Wheat Commission were favourable to that idea if it could possibly be carried out. Then I say in reference to the criticism that the Government were desirous on their own part that control should have place rather than the normal methods of carrying on the business.
It certainly is no't a thing which a Government wishes to undertake; it is a thing which primarily belongs to those who are experienced in the business and understand it from a practical point of view. However, as matters1 progressed, it became more and more evident that if there were an open market and normal methods were reverted to, there would- be slight prospect of a speedy sale for the farmers' wheat-if, indeed, it would be possible in the lapse of time to market the wheat at all by the old methods. This condition arose from several considerations. In the first place, there was a lack of speedy decision amongst the purchasing powers of the Allies-, and several considerations contributed to that lack of speedy decision. Two or three of these are the following: Until the crops attained a certain state of maturity it was impossible to estimate what would be the requirements of the European countries, measured by what quantities these countries could produce for their own needs. Until the crops had progressed to a certain stage towards maturity no one could make a fair estimate of what amount would be contributed by the production of the European countries themselves towards their own possible.consumption. On the other hand-, it was impossible to estimate. accurately what would toe the surplus of wheat in the producing and exporting countries until a certain stage of maturity had been reached. Consequently, the British Government, the Wheat Commission, the Allies themselves, did not go into the market; they -held off on account of the two very important considerations which I have mentioned before making cdn-

tracts or entering into arrangements for the supplying of their needs.
There was also the consideration of finance, rvhich I spoke of the other day. It was impossible for them to gather up a sufficient amount of cash with which to buy for their needs. Credits were necessary and those credits had to be arranged as between Governments. The question of the wherewithal to pay and the credits to be made where cash payments were impossible-as they would be in the majority of cases-was, therefore, a third and very important consideration in coming to a conclusion in the matter. All these considerations had the direct effect of keeping out of contracts and actual engagements those European countries which would ultimately require more or less, the quantity to be determined later.
The impression being entertained that it was possible to carry on the business of fbe grain trade in Canada and for export by a reversion to the old methods, permission was given for the opening of the exchange and it was opened. Subsequent information led the Government, after careful consideration, to the conclusion that it was impossible satisfactorily to market the grain crop of the farmers of Canada on the old open system. Practically without exception, the European countries, as they did last year, make their purchases of grain and the necessary arrangements in connection therewith under Government control. There are no open exchanges in Europe where prices are fixed. There was and is no organized system of individual or corporate buying, owing to the conditions (to which I have already referred. The Government, therefore, came to the conclusion that we would have to revert to control; that Government supervision would have to be exercised and that Government facilities for moving the crop would have to be made available. The grain exchange was open for a short time; then it was closed at the request of the Government. Hon. members connected with the grain trade are quite familiar with what took place ait that time. There was a speculative rise in the price of grain. I do not know how far that advance went, but it was continuous and it was considerable, and the Government felt that thpse speculative advances -and the conditions under which they were brought about produced an unhealthy situation as well for the farmer who wished to market his grain as in respect- of the possible buying sources in -the Old Country. If one looks into the transactions during -that time in the Exchange,
[Sir George Foster.!
he will find that the number and amount of actual sales were very small indeed. The price went up and that gave the farmer the idea that that -was an indication of the price at which he could sell his product. We did not think that it was an indication of the price, and if it was not an indication of the real price that the farmer could get, the running up of prices -by speculative operations was not in the interests of- the farmer; it tended to create erroneous impressions on the part of the farmer as to w-hat he would ultimately get and to bring about discontent when those anticipations were disappointed.
Again, suppose that the market had been kept open and that speculative prices had gone up to |2.50, $2.75 or $3 a bushel, what would have been the effect upon .possible buyers in Europe? The quotations of exchange would have been taken as the price to be paid by parties on the other side for Canadian wheat. These buying parties, therefore, would say: We cannot undertake to buy from Canada at $2.50, $2.75, $3 a bushel-indeed, at any price that -was indicated -by the Exchange-because we can get it much cheaper elsewhere.
It would consequently have thrown them off from any pursuit of the Canadian market at all. Therefore, it would have a doubly bad effect, first, on the- farmer at home, raising in his mind the idea by means of a speculative quotation that he should get higher prees for his wheat than he possibly could, and, secondly, in the throwing off of those who were seeking wheat supplies 'because of the high quotations which were made on the exchange itself. Ilf there is a farmer who says.: The Government did me an injury because when wheat went up on the exchange, the exchange was closed and I was precluded from selling my wheat at that price; again I revert to my statement that if he had attempted to sell his wheat, and if all the farmers had attempted to sell their wheat at the speculative price quoted on the exchange during those weeks, they would have been able to sell no proportion of their wheat at all. Those were simply speculative prices. The farmer says, and the critics of the Government plan say: You closed the market and the farmer now is down to the initial price of $2.15, with the prospect of getting what he can out of the surplus of the marketing of his crop; but on the other side of the line the United States farmer is getting $2.50, $2.60, $2.75, $2.80, $2.90, $3 a bushel for his wheat, and I can give you the market quotations at Minneapolis and at other points where those

prices are being paid. And the farmer says: Why should the Canadian farmer not get an equal price as his product is of an equal or of a better quality than the wheat produced on the United States side of the line? The answer to that is this, that the market on the other side of the line is not open to the farmers of Canada. Whether you had an open exchange or an open market or not, the United States market is closed to the seller of Canadian wheat and to the seller of Canadian flour. Consequently, whatever methods you had of marketing in Canada, the farmer who produces wheat in Canada cannot, under the circumstances of to-day, market his wheat in the United States, and, therefore, he cannot share in the same rate as the United 'States farmer gets. I think that is clear 'enough, and I leave that statement as to that part of the matter at that.
It was stated that my remarks led to the conclusion that the Canadian farmer got $2.15 as an initial payment at the station to which he brought his wheat. I do not think the members of the House understood me in that way, and I do not think those who are conversant, with the grain trade and with the system we have been pursuing for the last three years misunderstood me. But if any one. did understand the matter in that way, my statement in regard to that is this, that I was speaking of the wheat business on the basic price which had been settled by the Canadian Wheat Board and of the basic price which had been settled by the United States Government on the other side of the line; that all of us, I supposed knew if that basic price were paid at a certain point, there would be a variation in the price paid on that basis at every point distant more or less from the basic point, and that you would have to take freight and charges between the station point and the basic point in calculating what the farmer would get. It was never my intention, as it was foreign to the information which I possess, to state that $2.15 was received by the western farmer at every station to which he brought his grain. (So much with reference to that.
I have been criticised also-and maybe there is ground for the criticism-for leading up to the impression that in the United States the farmer got no more than the $2.26 which was fixed by the United States Government as what they would pay the farmer, that price being based, I think, on the Chicago price. Well, maybe my remarks were not sufficiently guarded to avoid an impression of that kind, but you cannot have everything in your mind at the same
time. I was pursuing the argument as to what the Government had fixed and what the aspect of the farmer was towards the Government's fixed price. To make the explanation which would at once carry the whole of the truth, I may say that $2.26 is both the maximum and the minimum price fixed and paid by the United States Government for export wheat, and it was with reference to export market that I was speaking at that time; that the United 'States will pay no more and, we suppose, will pay no less, and that every bushel of wheat, whether it be in the form of wheat or of wheat flour, that goes out of the United States for export to European countries, goes out on the basis of that fixed price of $2.26. But there is in the United States domestic market a freedom of millers to compete one with another above the fixed price of $2.26. They
may	not	pay	less:	, but they maypay	as much	more	as they choose,and	that	accounts	for the fact thatyou	have	in	the	United States at
various market points, without the competition of the millers for special grades under special circumstances, wheat going up to as high a price as $2.75, $2.90 and $3.00. But if that be the case in the United States, as I stated before, it is impossible . for the Canadian farmer to benefit by that condition in the United States, no matter under what system, free or controlled, the grain trade was carried on in our country. iSo, though this is not pleasing to the farmer, at the same time, it is not the fault of the Government, it is owing to conditions fixed by the United States Government, which has fixed a price for its surplus and for its wheat, and which will not allow importations of wheat or of flour into that country to interfere with the very heavy responsibility that it took, and with the marketing of its surplus at, if possible, nothing below the price that is paid for it to the United States farmer. Some might argue that if you had the open system in Canada and gave the millers the right to compete one with another, you would have a similar condition of things in this country, and that the farmer would get a higher price for his wheat through the competition of the millers. That may seem to be so, but to my mind it is not and cannot possibly be so owing to the different conditions. Supposing that the millers had the right of competition in an open market and that they did so compete, the inevitable consequence would be that, if they paid more than the fixed price which obtains, the consuming population of Canada would have to pay that much more for their



flour. In the United States, if you take the quotations of flour, you will find that they run from $1.25 to $2.00 per barrel higher than quotations for similar brands in the Dominion of Canada. That is, if for any special reasons the millers pay $3 for their wheat, they must work out the profit to themselves on the brands of flour that they make from that wheat, and that causes a higher price for flour to the whole of the consumers of the country. That would take place provided that competition amongst the millers in Canada did bring about the result of the farmers getting higher prices for the wheat that they sold to the millers. But there is in Canada another condition which is a very important and serious one, namely, that to-day there is very little market; indeed, I might say that at certain times there is absolutely Ino market for (wheat flour (from Canada. I explained that the other day. Your Italian, your Greek, your Frenchman, your United Kingdom man-all of these people want wheat because they want the offal and secondary products from that wheat, and they are the ones to say what and, if possible, to get what they want. Before the war, if I am not mistaken, the wheat flour export of this country was some three to four millions of barrels. During the war it ran up to eight, nine or ten million barrels. To-day, under the conditions I have just mentioned, if is difficult to get an order for wheat flour for export from Canada at all and the Canada Wheat Board are putting forth some of their best and shrewdest efforts in order to mingle certain of the orders for flour along with orders for wheat as well so- as to provide some export market for the Canadian millers and help them' in that direction. But if, in the open market, the millers were left to find a market for themselves in European countries for flour, it would be very difficult indeed for them to do- so. Consequently, they would not be anxious to buy more wheat from the Canadian farmer than was necessary for their own home consumption. They would tread very warily before they would pay competitive prices in order to store up an amount of flour for export a market for which they had a very poor prospect of getting. Therefore, they would march slowly, and they would buy from the farmer from day to day, week to week, or month to month, what was necessary to provide for the home consumption demand which would be small.
If you sum up the trend of these observations the situation sizes itself up in this

[DOT]way: Here is your Canadian farmer with his wheat threshed out in September and October. He wants an immediate market for that wheat. He wants as large a price as possible and he wants cash payment for his wheat. Under the conditions which existed there was no source from which this cash might be expected. I was at the centre of. operations there for several months and I never could get the buying authorities, or the prospective buying authorities, in European countries to make any decision as 'to when they would be in the market or as to the price they would be willing to offer. Therefore, you have this situation, that unless somebody came to the front and supplied a method by which the cash was ready for the immediate purchase of the grain, and the immediate payment to the farmer, you would have a condition of things which would be very detrimental to the farmers themselves.
Their crop wais garnered, their sales would be few and far between, comparatively, and the cash they demanded would be difficult to find. In that 'position you would have no work for your railways for, unless the grain starts to go out promptly upon its being ready for sale, the railways lose -their best opportunity for carrying. That was [DOT]another item which led up to the conclusion reached by the Government. As it is the Government steps in and cash for the immediate purchase of the wheat is provided for. The banks take on the payments, the purchases1 -are made promptly and they are paid for in cash. Up to the present moment, I think I am justified in saying that at least 50 per cent of the total surplus of the Canadian farmers has already been sold and to that extent the money is provided in so far as it is required for prompt and speedy payment when the farmer sells his grain. I am satisfied that with no organized buying with credits, under the conditions that existed and with all these things government controlled on the other side of the water, which in the main they were, it would have been impossible to have had speedy and cash transactions in the wheat of the Canadian farmer under any other system than that which has been provided by the Government.
There was a lot of misconception-I am not going to call it by a harsher name-I might say that it was misrepresentation-of the Government's position in reference to this matter. In the first place it was stated, and held to with the most wonderful tenacity that I ever experienced in this country,

that the Government had fixed a price of ?1.75 and that that was all they were going to pay or that was going to he allowed to be paid to the Canadian farmer. That all existed in the fertile, and not inocuous, imagination of some people who wanted that argument in order to use it to the detriment of somebody or of some Government. That is the only remark that I am going to make in regard to the matter. Neither by myself, by any member of the Government or by the Government as a whole, was there any decision or supposition or suggestion as to the fixing of a price of SI.75. Yet that has been made to do duty against the system which has been brought in by the Government, and to this day it is held more or less firmly by quite too many of the people of this country.
Then again, when the price was fixed, it was not a price fixed by the Government itself. It was a. price which was fixed as the initial payment by the Canadian Wheat Board. I want to correct the misrepresentations which are abroad in reference to the relations between the Government and the old Board of Supervisors of last year and the preceding year and the present Canada Wheat Board. When the Government placed in the hands of the Board of Grain Supervisors in 1917 and 1918 the management of the marketing of the grain of Canada it left it with these gentlemen and it did not interfere with what they did. In the same way in relation to the Canada Wheat Board, the Government tried to get the best representative men that it could, and having got that board it leaves the matter in their bands and it does not interfere with what they do.
If representations are made to the Government, they will be submitted to the Canada Wheat Board, by whom they will be considered. The millers, the producers, the consumers and the varied interests are all represented on that board, and I do not) think that its capacity or calibre has been adversely criticised with any success; nor indeed has it been largely criticised in any event. The board having once been appointed, comprised of practical men, the Government leaves them unhampered to do the work that has been entrusted to them and for the performance of which they are empowered. Now, the board took the situation into retrospective consideration, and they decided that the initial payment should be $2.15. But, as a matter of fact, this had to be approved by council, and council did approve of it immediately, as the 584
recommendation of the board's mature consideration. In regard to the criticism that is made against that action, I think it is well that I should say something. The general trend of criticism is to this effect:
" You have your $2.15, which is all you will get." I may mention just what the scheme is. The Board of Wheat Commissioners shall market the whole crop at the best possible advantage, shall pay the costs, and return shall be made, upon the basis of the quantity which each producer has sold, of any amount in excess of the $2.15 paid initially. The general trend of the criticism, as I say, is to induce the farmers to believe that they will get the $2.15, or the proportional amount wherever they have their grain, and no more. The contention is: " It will all be squandered and nothing will be left." There are participation certificates that every purchaser gets which entitle him to his proportionate return from the pool-his return proportionate to the quantity of grain that is sold. These certificates are negotiable and the farmer may sell them; and the whole force of such criticism, wherever it originates, tends to confirm in the farmer's mind the idea that he has all that he will get. Probably he lends a too-willing ear to the broker or the buyer who says to him: "You have your participation certificate for which you will never get much; but I am prepared to pay you a certain sum for it and will take my chances of loss." Now, it is but human nature that if that impression is forced upon	the	farmer, that	he	is	notlikely to get anything more, he will take	what	is offered to	him	by	the
broker or dealer and consequently part with his certificate. I would advise farmers to hold their participation certificates. Taking my view from the amount of grain that has already been marketed and the prospects for marketing all the rest of it, I would urge upon the farmer the importance of retaining the certificate and would counsel him not to part with it for a song. It will be a substantial advantage to him. No one can tell exactly how much the advantage will be, but looking at the matter in the light of present experience, the advantage will be considerable. I merely mention this as a sort of caution or warning in this respect; for undoubtedly I do not think that any man is doing the most good to the farmer in disseminating the idea that he is not going to derive any greater advantage than the initial payment of $2.15. I think I have met quite a large number of the objections that have been raised, and it is not my in-

tention to multiply words unnecessarily in connection with this matter. But I think I should touch upon the United States system. There is competition in the United States over the $2.26 fixed basic price for domestic purposes. The millers may buy and pay more; the bakers may also buy and pay more; but if either miller or baker buys and pays more than $2.26 for whatever surplus of wheat or flour he finds on hand he has to go to the United Grain Corporation to dispose of it and will be paid for that surplus on the basis of the fixed price of $2.26 and not upon the basis of the price that he has paid to the farmer in his competition with other millers or bakers. So that it is fair to say that everything which is exported of wheat and wheat products out of the United States goes on the export basis of $2.26 as the maximum price which is to be paid. There are other sources for European countries in the obtaining of grain than Canada. Australia is opened up by better conditions and its trade has a very large surplus. The Argentine is also open and at rates which are far lower than those quoted from the United States or from Canada. Neutral and allied countries can therefore turn to these sources, and it seems to be fairly settled, as a result of this condition, that the United States is ready to sell to any European customer who desires to buy, provided cash or credits are forthcoming at $2.26, or probably a shade under that price. My opinion is that the farmer in Canada, for the export grain which goes out of the country either in the shape of wheat or of flour, will get a larger price than that fox what he has to market. Consequently, looked at in that light, and taking into consideration the advantages of quick market, steady market, and cash market, it seems to me-and I believe it will so prove -that it will be ultimately concluded that the system adopted by the Government after very careful consideration has saved the situation in Canada so far as the disposal of its grain is concerned. The question is asked: why did you turn down the grain trade; why did you shut them off from participation in the work? Well, it is unfair to say that the grain trade has been precluded from their usual work. Under this present system to-day, after all the criticisms that have been made as to what the Wheat Board would do in the way of machinery, what are the facts of the case? Your street buyer is at work as usual; your track buyer is at work as usual; your elevator buyer is also at his customary work; the elevator storage system is doing pre-f9ir George Foster.]
cisely what it did before or would do under an open system, and is doing it in exactly the same way. The commission man is also getting his commission and in buying and selling. The broker gets his brokerage, -probably not as much as he wants or would like to have, but he is getting it the same as before. The insurance man is getting insurance contracts as he previously did, and the banker is making his advancements as of yore. Every particle of machinery in the grain trade is functioning to-day just as it did before or would do under an open and unrestrained market, with the exception of this fact, that under the present system speculative prices and profits are absolutely shut out and the farmer receives the actual return for his grain, minus the actual expenses of carrying on the marketing of the grain.
Now speculators or grain traders' profits are legitimate things because these men take risks and if they take risks they must pay themselves by the price that they get compared with- the price that they pay. Therefore, it is their interest to pay the lowest possible price for what they buy and to get the highest possible market price for what they sell, and they make out of that margin their expenses and their profits, and sometimes those profits are very substantial. Expenses go on the same as before and not to a greater extent if to as great an extent; but profits are absolutely shut out to the trader and consequently the return, is by that much the greater and should be the more satisfactory to the farmer himself.
But the question is asked: Is this to be a permanent system? My answer to that is an- emphatic no. It is not a system that the Government coveted to have. A tremendous amount of difficulty, of criticism, and of bad feeling is inevitably aroused when a government takes hold of a thing of this kind and carries it through. No government courts a proceeding of that kind; and it was only the force of circumstances, and their conviction that nothing else could be done to save the situation well, that induced the Government to take the system of supervision and control this year. It is not the intention to make it permanent. We believe that this year is the last year during which the same system of government control will be carried out in the same way. Whatever the country, [DOT] through its legislature, may determine to do with the nationalization of the wheat or the grain business hereafter, is a different matter but I have answered the question

whether this is to he a permanent system or not. I apologize to the House for taking up so much time-
Go on.

-hut I felt it was necessary to make some of these points in order that adverse criticism, which is not well-founded, should not be allowed to prejudice either the farmer or any one else. I cannot think of any other points to deal with, but as we go through with the Bill in committee I shall he glad to answer any questions that may be asked.

We have had a repetition to-day of what was heard in this House in the latter part of 1910 and in 1911- that is a very eloquent and clever speech as a substitute for satisfactory trade conditions. We had in the years 1910 and 1911 the prospects of a 'magnificent trade between Canada and the United States. A population of less than eight millions of people then had the opportunity of exchanging freely with one hundred millions of people the products which the people of Canada could produce in abundance. The opportunity was at our door, it was obtainable, it was within our reach. I remember well the speeches on that occasion of the hon. gentleman who to-day leads the Government, and who, at that time, headed the forces of the Tory party in the movement to break down those relations that were being built up and which really did exist between the Government of the United States and the Government of Canada. He and his party succeeded in making the people of Canada believe that it was a bad thing to have freedom of trade between our country and the great country to the south of us. He made the people of Canada believe that if we had wheat or cattle to sell to the United States it was a mistake to send it immediately across the border to the neighbouring republic; that it was a greater advantage for us to use our railroads, and the ships that might be available, and send that freight out of the country and across the Atlantic. That was the system of trade which the hon. gentleman and his party thought was a good thing for Canada in preference to trade with the United States. It was not very long after the hon. gentleman and his party came into power when they made it their boast that they had acquired, or obtained, for the people of the Canadian West this freedom of trade-that they had obtained in a better way, as they said, the reciprocity which was so much coveted by the Canadian people and that it
was a fixture for them; they had found it in a better way. To-day, Sir, we are told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the doors of the United States are closed against any trading in any way. The doors are closed against our wheat and our flour, there is no foreign market for these products of ours, and we are in the position, according to the minister, where we must find money ourselves-put our hands down in our pockets and find the money-and send it over to a trading commission in England who will buy our own flour with with our own money. That is the substitute, Sir, that is the alternative, which is brought about in this country by the policy or hon. gentlemen opposite, led by the Minister of Trade and Commerce from 1911 up to the present, on that question of trade. It is for the Canadian people-

Would the hon. gentleman state whether or not he is opposed to the giving or extension of credits to buying countries, who are not able at the present time to pay cash, in order to help our export trade and consequently employment in Canada itself? Is he opposed to that principle?

We are not dealing
with that question to-day.
Oh, oh.
The hon. gentleman is making an argument upon it.

I hear the exclamations of hon. gentlemen opposite. They are watching with interest and care for the slightest consolation they may receive from the gentlemen on the treasury benches who lead them, and lead them they know not where. I say to the right hon. gentleman, who at present leads the Government, that I am in favour of an honest, straightforward and wholesome trade for this country, and that I am opposed to his asking me, or asking the ordinary man in Canada, to find money and to send that money to Europe to buy the goods of this country in order to keep up war prices for the ordinary consuming people of this Dominion. I give the complete answer to the hon. gentleman that I am not in favour of artificial trade of that kind. I am in favour of selling our goods to the people of the United States who have themoney to buy those goods and who are willing to send the money here; but the hon. gentleman and his party have 'brought about a condition, have brought about such relations with the hundred millions of people on the other side of the line, that we cannot trade with

them, which puts us in a position that we must find our own money and with our own money trade with ourselves without anything coming in in return for it-the goods going out bought with Canadian money, and nothing coming in in return except old bonds which we cannot sell, that we might get from Koumania, Poland, and other places. If my hon. friend is anxious to put up good Canadian money-which we must borrow and which we must go down on our knees to obtain from the United States-and then put that up against very *doubtful Roumanian, Polish and other foreign bonds in return for our goods or if that is his system of trade I am against it absolutely and entirely.
I hope, Sir, that my 'answer to the hon. gentleman (Sir George Foster) is satisfactory 'and that it will not -be a laughing matter for lion, gentlemen opposite who think that a clever question was thrown across the floor by their leader. I do not so regard it; there is nothing clever about it. We have a very clever speech, and very poor trade. This country, Sir, is looking for good trade, and is very indifferent about speeches. That is the situation which confronts us (to-day.
For many years, Sir, it was difficult to get the American people to talk trade with us. Since 1872 great statesmen like the late Sir John Macdonald, Sir Charles Tup-per and Sir Wilfrid Laurier and others have made unsuccessful attempts to establish, proper trade relations with our neighbours to the south. At last, in 1910-11, it was the good fortune of our hon. friend Mr. Fielding, associated with the Hon. Mr. Paterson, to get the ear of the American people to establish proper, efficient and satisfactory trade relations with them. That opportunity was put at the door of the Canadian people. Ruit 'hon. gentlemen opposite thought they could play upon the prejudices of our people, so they told them: Why are you going to turn round the railroads that we have built? Are you going to destroy our trade across the continent? Are you going to shove everything we have down south and be a mere adjunct to the United States? Under which flag are- you going to be, under the British flag, or are you going to sell yourselves and your loyalty for trade with the United States? That appeal had its effect, and that nonsense, Mr. Speaker, carried the day against the very best interests of the (people of this country. That, Sir, 'has been bearing its results, until today the (Minister of Trade and Commerce- no less a person; it is not the Minister of

Labour, it is not the Minister of Customs, it is not any other minister who may not know about the trade relations of this country with the United States or with any other country who had made the speech which we have 'listened to this afternoon but it is the Minister of Trade and Commerce, whose business it is to know these things, and yet he comes down to us, Sir, with the poorest, kind of a story that could possibly be presented to any country or to any Parliament. He tells us that we cannot trade with the people of the United States-that we have plenty of wheat but we cannot sell it. I have a telegram in my hand which I received from a man in the province of Saskatchewan-[DOT]

We can get $3.01-or 86 cents added to $2.15 *-we could get that for our wheat if we were allowed to sell it across the (border. There is a great deal going across, but only by truck loads.
That is the difference to-day, Mr. Speaker. The farmers of the West (by reason of the short-sighted policy, which, of course, brought hon. gentlemen opposite into power, are placed in this trade condition, that although they could get $3.01, or about $3 a bushel for their wheat if there were proper trade relations between the two countries, they are bound down to this $2.15-and they may or may not get the whole of that amount. That shortsighted policy, Sir, a policy which was not in the 'best interests of the farmers or of any other class in Canada, was foisted upon the Canadian people in 1911 by representations from hon. gentlemen opposite which were not borne out by the fadts, but which representations were well coloured in speeches such as the one made to-day by the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government. To me, Sir, having heard such speeches during the election of 1911, and knowing the result of that

election and having to some extent suffered in consequence, it is some satisfaction to stand here to-day and to see hon. gentlemen obliged on the floor of this House to acknowledge that they were wrong when they advised the people to refuse to trade with the Americans, to decline the offer of reciprocity-that they were wrong from start to finish, and that they must now go to the people and tell them that instead oi getting money from the United States and elsewhere for the goods they have to sell, they must sell those goods through a trade mission beyond the seas, and take bonds in exchange-in short finance the purchase.
Will my hon. friend allow me another question? I do not want to interrupt him unless he is perfectly willing.
Certainly.

I want to ask my hon. friend this question, and I think it is necessary for the proper understanding of the subject matter of this debate. He has read a telegram, the purport of which is quite evident. When the tariffs of the two countries provide for the free passage of wheat and the products of wheat between Canada and the United States, why is it that the Canadian farmer under that tariff arrangement cannot take his wheat in and get his $3.01 the same as the United States farmer? My hon. friend understands my question. What he was arguing for, so far as wheat and the products of wheat are concerned is what has actually been the tariff -condition during the last year or more. Now, what I want to ask my hon. *friend is this: Why is it, that being the tariff condition, that the Canadian farmer cannot put his wheat into that market and get the price that the United States farmer does? Will my hon. friend say now exactly what is the reason?

Let me say to my right hon. friend that it is very difficult for an ordinary private member of the House as I am to follow the twists and turns and changes of this Government. They have bungled everything from start to finish. They have switched off from themselves to boards and commissions and private parties everything that they could do themselves. When the minister and his deputy and the men around him who are responsible to this House should have this matter in hand and be able to give us the information first hand, they switch it off to a commission, absolutely independent, and that commission has made regulations
which rendered it impossible to send wheat out of this country, and has brought about the absurd conditions which exist to-day.
I suppose I shall be called to task if I again go back to ancient history and quote Scripture. But I may be permitted to say that the attitude of the right hon. gentleman reminds me of the answer given by him that aforetime was blind: "One thing I know, that whereas I was blind, now I see."
Arrangements had been made for good trade relations between Canada and the United States; these arrangements were ready to be taken advantage of, but hon. gentlemen opposite destroyed them and we have not those trade relations to-day. No amount of ingenuity; no amount of questioning; no amount of turning around and putting it this, that or the other way, can alter the fact that we had an opportunity of bringing about good trade relations, permanent and lasting, but that that opportunity was destroyed by hon. gentlemen, who are responsible for the unsatisfactory conditions which exist to-day. How that condition came about the right hon. gentleman knows very much better than I do. This Government is responsible to the people; it is suposed to bring about proper trade conditions and to be far-sighted enough to see what is best for the country. Hon. gentlemen who comprise the Government are supposed to have something in their minds more comprehensive, more conducive to the production of dollars and cents within the country, than the mere desire to keep themselves in power absolutely regardless of the trade and development of the country. Representations were made by hon. gentlemen in 1911 as I have intimated, and the fruit of their success is now before us; the chickens have come home to roost. Instead of bringing money to those whom they represent, hon. members from the West have to sit back and take the speech of my right hon. friend, which I suppose they will send to the constituents in place of wheat and wheat prices. If any of our good friends from the West go back to their ridings and say to the farmers: I have in one hand $3 a bushel for your wheat and I have in the other hand the speech of the Right Hon. Sir George Foster, Minister of Trade and Commerce; which will you have? Every one of those farmers will say: Give me the $3 for my wheat and keep the speech for yourself. When the Liberal party were in power they put forth every effort in a proper way to make a good bargain for

the country so far as trade is. concerned- particularly for the people of the West- a bargain which would have brought about development of the country and happiness and prosperity in every line of trade and commerce in the West as well as in every part of Canada. But the people have chosen to put their trust in hon. gentlemen opposite, and the result is the condition which we have to-day. It is to be hoped that the day is not far distant when the hon. gentleman will submit themselves and their conduct and their administration to the people, and that a change will take place which will once more put us on the road to happiness and prosperity.
