speechtext: The expression may not be very desirable, but I do not understand that it reflects upon hon. gentlemen. I rather take it that the hon. member who has the floor is intimating that hon. gentlemen opposite are mistaken.

and, from the depths
not only of an ignorance profound, but

of an ignorance so profound that they do not know their own policy. They are profoundly ignorant, I say, with regard to their own policy, because the leader of the Opposition, when he spoke a few minutes ago about their policy of 1911 being the correct and proper policy for this country, entirely lost sight of the fact that the very party of which he is temporary leader, and of which he sought to be the permanent leader, in their convention at Ottawa a couple of months ago repudiated that policy in 1911 and asserted that it was not right for this country.
No.
Isn't that true?
No.

It is absolutely true, and I will prove it in a few minutes. In the policy of 1911 the Liberal party went on record as advocating free trade between the two countries in natural products, but affirmed that in their opinion no changes should be made in the tariff on manufactured articles. In that policy, which, according to the leader of the Opposition, was so perfect, they proposed no changes in the duties on manufactured articles except a slight change in the duty on agricultural	implements-a	change which
brought the duty down to less than the present duty on agricultural implements. That was the only change they favoured. Is that in accordance with the platform which they laid down at their convention in Ottawa in the month of August last? No, Mr. Speaker; they wanted to appeal to the residents of cities and towns. They had become aware of the fact-it had at last filtered into the grey matter of their systems -that the farmers refused in 1911 to be put up against the competition of the world in what they had to produce and sell and at the same time to be obliged to pay duty on the articles that they had to buy in order to work their land. The farmers said: " If you are going to oblige us to compete with the United States, with Argentina, with all the countries on the face of the earth, in what we produce and have to sell, we ask you to carry the proposal a step further and remove the duties on the things that we have to buy." The farmers were absolutely dissatisfied; and that has at last got into the brains of hon. gentlemen opposite. At their convention in August last, they said: Our policy in 1911 was wrong, unfair and unjust.
If the hon. member l\as at hand the platform of the National Liberal Convention, will he kindly refer to the Fielding resolution?

The hon. gentleman
knew before he put the question, that I had not the platform in my hand; I have nothing in my hand, not even notes. He knew, therefore, that it was safe to ask the question.
The hon. gentleman, if he has any regard for the truth-and I am sure he has-will not undertake to say, nor will any other hon. gentleman, undertake to say that the platform of 1911, boasted of by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie), is the same as the platform laid down at the recent Liberal convention held in this city in the month of August. The platform lad down in 1911 was- a platform which distinctly told the manufacturers of this4 country: We will not interfere with you. And that platform did not interfere with the manufacturers1 in any particular except in the one that I mentioned, namely, agricultural implements, and then only to a very slight extent. They said to the people of Canada: You can go on under the curse and burden of protection which the Liberal party had been cursing from Dan to Beer-shaba, speaking politically, ever since there was'such a thing as a Liberal party. Talk about twistings and turnings ! The leader of the Opposition cannot follow this Government in its twistings and turnings' The leader of the Opposition in regard to twistings could hide behind a corkscrew. Twistings and turnings! The Liberal party has had as many fiscal policies in this country as there are Liberal representatives sitting behind their leader. Every man has had-a policy of his own.
The leader of the Opposition waxed indignant this afternoon over the situation created in this country because the reciprocity pact of 1911 was not' adopted, because we did not open our doors and let things pass freely between this country and the United States. Did he want to open the doors as regards coal? Has he ever wanted to open the doors as regards coal? Why, as regards coal and steel and those products which happen to pertain to his particular part of the country, the leader of the Opposition would erect a tariff as high as Hainan's gallows; you could not make it too high to suit that hon. gentleman when it touches his particular part of the country. As regards manufactured articles, one of the gentlemen who went down to Washington to negotiate this treaty was mighty particular that his special industry should not be
touched. He sat on the biscuit box, and he said: Take the tariff off what the farmer has to sell, but you must not interfere with the duty on biscuits; and so it was all along the line. The chief whip of the Liberal party (Mr. Robb) is not exactly an out-and-out free trader when his industry is touched, as I suppose hon gentlemen have frequently noticed, and the same may be said of all hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House.
Paper.
Hear, hear.

It might be better for
hon. gentlemen opposite if they waved the flag a little more, although the flag might not be in very good hands if it were in the hands of some of them. I do not know why they should be throwing this up as a reproach. If we on this side of the House have in the past seen fit to announce that

we believe in one flag, is that such a terrible thing? Do not hon. gentlemen opposite believe in that? If they do, then what is the point against us on this side? If they believe as we believe in one flag for this country, why do they not wave the flag also? If hon. gentlemen opposite could appeal to the people and make the people feel and believe that they were just as earnest for the protection of that flag as we were, we would not have anything over them in that regard.
As regards this other question, to pass away from the small things to which I have referred as indicating the personalities of hon. gentlemen opposite, and particularly the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) who, in his argument on this matter, is the campaign leader, the " pork and beans" member of this House and repfe-sentative of the people-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member is exceeding the hounds of Parliamentary language. If he desires to refer to an hon. member, he knows how to do so.
Give him a little rope and he will hang himself.

If I hang myself, it will not be with a " paper " cord, I will tell my hon. friend (Mr. McCrea) that. As regards trade matters, my hon, friend has hanged himself a good many times, for he has preached free trade on every article until his particular pocket had been touched, and then, he has been a very strong protectionist. I might have been more explicit; but since I have referred to " pork and beans ", I will come back to that. It is not such a very great way from wheat to pork and beans after all. I do not suppose, in view of the absolutely ridiculous statement made by the leader of the Opposition as regards the way in which this country had treated its soldiers overseas in shipping them rotten pork and beans, we should be surprised at anything the hon. gentleman says in this House.
That is not the subject under discussion,
That is what I meant when I referred to him as the " pork and beans " representative of this House. Perhaps I was not just as select in my reference as I should have been, and I apologize.
You are improving.

As regards this matter of wheat and the fixing of the price of wheat, if I remember correctly

and I think

I do-wheat was made free by this Government as passing between Canada and the United States, and I am not aware that this Government is responsible for any change in those conditions. If any change arose in those conditions which were brought about by this Government enabling Canadian farmers to ship their wheat into the United States and American farmers to ship their wheat into Canada, it was brought about, not by this Government, as was insinuated by the leader of the Opposition, but by the action of the United States itself. That is the situation as I understand it, but I want to add in regard to this matter of wheat, another word which I think is pertinent to this discussion.
I think action should be taken in this country looking towards the greater manufacturing of the wheat of Canada into flour, looking towards the exportation of Canadian flour rather than to the exportation of Canadian wheat. I think the Government should bestir itself and try to have wheat exported from Canada, not as wheat, but as flour.
I suggested some time ago in this House that I thought the Government would be justified in providing transportation and carrying flour made from Canadian wheat, to be shipped from Canadian ports, absolutely free across the ocean to Liverpool. I want to repeat that suggestion here today in all seriousness. I do so for several reasons. I believe they will be justified in adopting a policy of that kind, because, in the first place, it would have a tendency to divert the Western Canadian crop to Canadian railways. Much of it now goes over American railways and is shipped from American ports. The more of it that can be sent over Canadian railways the more we will be helping to solve the railway problem of this country, providing freight for our railways and work for our railway men and elevator men. Secondly, I believe they would be justified in encouraging wheat to be ground in Canadian mills, because that would be an encouragement to the milling industry. Thirdly, I believe they would be amply justified because if it was ground in Canada and exported in the shape of flour we would have the bran and shorts in this country which we stand very much in need of especially in the older Eastern Provinces. From the standpoint of the assistance which will be given in building up our railway lines, affording traffic to our railways and giving employment to Canadian railway men, helping our milling industry and more particularly because it would give the farmers, and especially the dairymen of Ontario, Quebec and the Mari-

time Provinces, in large quantities and at low prices, the bran and shorts which they stand so much in need of in tiheir business,
I believe this or any government would be justified in taking steps to bring about the change I suggest; that is to provide transportation which would encourage the milling of wheat in Canada and by transporting Canadian flour from Canadian ports free across the ocean to Liverpool. These are things which I think are of more importance to the people and to the interests of this country than is a consideration of why the Liberal party did not succeed in the election of 1911.
Mr. J. A. RiOBB (Qhateauguay-Hunting-don): Mr. Speaker, the debate has taken on a somewhat wide range. I do not purpose .following my hon. friend from Frontenae (Mr. Edwards') through his discussion of the duty on coal and steel when we have before us a Bill which deals primarily and only with wheat. But inasmuch as the hon. member has made a reference to certain resolutions passed at the Liberal Convention held in this city in the month of August, will the House have patience with me while I put on Hansard a resolution which was adopted at that convention? I hold in my hand a copy of the resolution on reciprocity adopted at that convention. It is as follows:
That the Reciprocity Agreement negotiated with the United States by the Liberal Government of Canada in 1911 was a measure which realized the hopes that had been entertained and efforts made for better trade relations between Canada and the neighbouring republic by the statesmen of both political parties in the Dominion from the beginning of the Dominion's history.
That the Agreemeftt was fair and just to both countries and well calculated to promote the good relations so desirable;
That the action of the Conservative party under the leadership of Mr. now Sir Robert Borden in opposing and defeating the Agreement was a sacrifice of the best interests of Canada for distinctly partisan ends.
That the insincerity of the movement of the Conservative leaders on that question has been abundantly evidenced by the fact that after coming into office they proceeded to make some of the very tariff changes a denunciation of which was their chief ground in the elections of 1911.
That the action of the Conservative leaders in preventing the consummation of so excellent an arrangement between the two countries deserves and should still receive, whenever the opportunity occurs, the severe condemnation of the Canadian people.
That the Reciprocity Agreement was approved in 1911 .by the Congress of the United States and the law giving such approval still remains on the American Statute book.
That if the proposal lately made in the Congress to repeal the said law he carried out the
people of Canada will have cause to complain, since the Americans have kept the law unimpaired for the long term of eight years during which Canada has made no move to avail herself of its provisions.
That while, for these reasons, this Convention can take no exception to the proposal so made at Washington, we as Liberals again place on record our appreciation of the object of the said Agreement and our faith in the principles of friendly international relations underlying it, and we express our earnest hope that in both countries such principles will he upheld, and that a favourable moment may come when there will be a renewed manifestation by the two Governments of a desire to make some similar arrangement.
That was the resolution adopted at the Liberal convention.
I would like to .ask my hon. friend a question in regard to the duties on manufactured articles. Was not the lowering of duties on manufactured articles referred to in that platform?

As I said at the opening, the question before the House this afternoon is the question of wheat and I do not propose to be dragged into a discussion of coal, steel, or other subjects of that kind. But at some other time, or at any time, we upon this side will be prepared to discuss with hon. gentlemen opposite our attitude on the tariff as compared with the programme-the wobbling programme-of this Government which has, in fact, no programme to-day in the face of eight by-elections throughout this country.

I stated that the attitude of the party, of which my hon. friend is a member, in 1911 in regard to manufactured articles, was not the same as the attitude laid down in the platform in August last. Was I right or wrong in making that statement?

In 1911 my hon. friend argued that the policy of the Liberal party was the destruction of the trade and commerce of this country. After listening this afternoon to the eloquent speech of my right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce and Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster), and then subsequently listening to the speech of my hon. leader (Mr. McKenzie), I looked across the floor to see which of the western representatives upon the other side was going to give us a repetition of the speeches we heard in this House for very many years in defence of western ideals as regards the price of wheat. Those of us who have sat in this House for some years can well remember the eloquent speeches delivered by representatives of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta,

when they were urging on the Government of the day a policy of larger and widei markets with the United States. We can recall how eloquently they argued respecting the difference in prices. They told us what was the difference in the total price of a carload of wheat or barley in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta as compared with the price prevailing in Minneapolis. To-day we have an admission from the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) that there is a considerable difference in price, ranging from 40c. to 60c. a bushel, representing from four hundred to six hundred dollars on a car of a thousand bftshels of wheat; and I have perforce to ask myself now, looking across the floor of the House, where are the men who formerly advocated in this House the ideals of Western Canada? Mr. Speaker, the conclusion very obviously is that they have either taken to the woods, or are sitting in this Chamber in the condition of a certain meek and submissive creature: "As a sheep before her shearers is dumib, so he openeth not his mouth."
The Acting Prime Minister has said that wheat cannot be got into the United States. Wheat is higher in the United States to-day than in Canada, and you cannot export it into that country, and he asks the reason why. Well, I have the answer for him in an official document issued by this Government. In the first place, I have the Government's Order in Council of the 18th of August, 1919. In that Order in Council the Canadian Wheat Board is created and is given certain powers, one of which, under letter M," has for its object the prohibition of the export out of Canada or the importation into Canada of any wheat or wheat products otherwise than in accordance with the regulations and orders of the board. Now, the board were not very long in taking advantage of the powers conferred upon them, because regulation No. 36-an order from the Canadian Wheat Board, acting under the authority given them by the Order in Council says that no wheat or wheat products, shall be exported out of Canada or imported into Canada without a license or permit of the board. That is why wheat is not permitted to go into the United States to-day; but it is not a new policy on the part of this Government. The questions is asked: Why all this discussion to-day upon the question of wheat? Have we not had free wheat in this country? Did the Conservative party not give free wheat, which was the keystone of the arch of reciprocity? Yes, they did, by Order in Council on the 16th of April, 1917, 
after the western farmer had sold his crop, which was then in the hands of the millers and grain dealers. We have the evidence of honourable gentlemen who were then members of this House as to why that Order in Council was passed. There is the statement of a then member of the House representing Saskatchewan-and his remarks may be found in Hansard-that the then Solicitor General had made a trip through the West. There were prospects of an early general election, and his friends in the West had told him: "You must grant reciprocity in wheat. You must conform to the regulations of the United States tariff so that we may have free wheat and get our wheat into the United States. Otherwise, you will not be able to elect one supporter west of the Lakes." That is not my statement. It is the statement of a gentleman who was then a member of this House and is now a member of the Senate, created a senator by this Government. This Order in Council was therefore passed on the 16th of April 1917, and the general elections did take place. The Union Government was created, the Union Government party having captured the organization of both parties. I repeat, Sir, that the Union Government party had captured the organization of both parties throughout Canada, and the position of the Government was consequently fairly safe. The wheat issue was no longer a very grave one in the West, and the Government thought they might very well step in and uphold the policy they preached in 1911 and repeatedly championed in this House when resolutions demanding free wheat were introduced by representatives of the West. And so, on the 4th of December, 1917, another Order in Council was passed practically nullifying that of seven and a half months previously. That other Order in Council prohibited the export or import of wheat, so that from that day until this there has been no reciprocity in wheat between Canada and the United States. That is exactly the situation in regard to wheat, and western members may assemble in private caucus and adopt all the resolutions they like, but the fact remains that this Government, which has prevented the free movement of wheat between Canada and the United States, is in power to-day, sustained in that power by the representatives of the western provinces. Now, if the western provinces are sincere in their desire for free interchange of wheat, they can obtain that interchange by adhering to the ideals which they have enunciated and advocated repeatedly as the ideals of Western Canada.

I shall leave that phase of the subject.' I do not purpose to labour the point any further. I think that the country will admit, and indeed the Acting Prime Minister has admitted to-day, that there is no reciprocity in wheat between Canada and the United States. The minister has also admitted that wheat is higher in the United States than in * Canada, and I leave the question between him and his western supporters to settle. But there is another question in connection with this Bill that affects us in Eastern Canada very materially. I was obliged to leave the Chamber for awhile and I am not sure whether the minister made reference . to the tax of 15 cents.
iSir GEORGE FOSTER: I left those details for the Committee.

Well, I shall still make my statement. Under the regulations of the Wheat Board all millers-not only merchant millers, but grist millers-are licensed, and the miller is made the tax collector for the Government. That is to say, any miller licensed is notified by the Canadian Wheat Board that he must collect 15 cents upon every bushel of wheat brought to him by a farmer, whether or not the farmer grows barely sufficient wheat to suffice his family, without any commercial intentions; and unless he does this his license will be cancelled. The Acting Prime Minister will not contradict that statement. Now,, what does this mean? It means that this Government, who are supposed to advocate a reduction in the cost of living and who have preached greater economy and greater production, organizing campaigns to urge the farmers to grow sufficient food for their own families with a little extra for export, are imposing upon the people a tax of from 68 to 75 cents a barrel on flour. This is exactly the position of affairs, and the Government will have to revise their arguments in defence of the Wheat Board if they intend to convince the people of Eastern Canada, who are attempting to feed their families by growing wheat on their own farms, that this is an economical administration.
Perhaps the minister will be able to make a statement that will be satisfactory to the country and we await that statement with interest. I know that the minister will say that this fifteen cents is the profit for the handling of the crop and that later the balance left in the hands of the Canadian Wheat Board will be handed out to the farmers. Let us see how that is going to work out. Take a farmer who, perhaps,
, grows twenty, thirty, or fifty bushels of wheat for the use of his own family. At the
end of probably two years

because there has been no statement made yet of the handling of the 1917-18 crop, so we cannot anticipate that the 1919-20 crop will be handled any quicker-at the end of two years the millers will have to hunt up all these farmers throughout the country to give them, maybe, seventy-five cents, a dollar, or a dollar and a half, which will be at the utmost the extent of their share of the participation certificates. That is putting a generous estimate upon it, a more generous estimate than is entertained in Western Canada, because I am told by reputable western grain men that you can buy whole rafts of these participation certificates in Winnipeg to-day at two cents per bushel. That is the estimate the western farmer has with respect to the value of the participation certificate; and I hope tnat when the minister goes into detail on this subject he will be able to clear up the situation and remove some of the restrictions put upon the trade of Eastern Canada. As regards Western Canada and the price of wheat, I can only repeat, in closing, that those of us who have sat in this House for so many years and heard the eloquent appeals for larger and wider markets for the products-of the farms of the West are compelled today to believe that Western Canada has been abandoned by its. own friends.
Hon. J. D. REI'D: I would not have risen to speak on this question had it not been for the statements made by the leader of the Opposition and the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat with reference to the situation at the present time as between Canada and the United States in regard to the importation and exportation of wheat. I do not intend going back to the history of the political fight that took place in Canada in 1911 further than to say this: At that time the reciprocity agreement was proposed between the United States Government and that of the Dominion and the issue between the two parties in Canada was this: The then Opposition took the ground that if we allowed the importation of wheat and wheat products from the United States free of duty, it would interfere with the manufacturing of wheat in Canada. The wheat would probably be taken to the country to the south and the American millers would get the advantage of manufacturing there, while the American farmers would profit by the use of wheat products for fattening their cattle. Furthermore, United States wheat and wheat products would enter this country and injure our own Canadian mar-

kets. The result of the election at that time was that the people of Canada expressed the belief that the agreement as proposed by the then Government was not in the interests of this country, and accordingly the Conservative Government came into office. Now the two honourable gentlemen in question have declared that that Government had done nothing to accomplish the free interchange of wheat and wheat products between Canada and the United States. For the life of me I cannot understand the ground for that statement or why it should be said that is the law at the present time. I believe the two hon. gentlemen in question are thoroughly familiar with the provisions of the present Canadian law in force against the United States. The hon. member (Mr. Eobb) waves a paper which he holds in his hand and says that is the law. I will come to that in a few minutes. The hon. gentleman knows there was a law on the statute books of the United States whereby wheat, wheat flour, and semolina, should be admitted from Canada into that country free of duty provided we adopted a similar law here. The honourable gentleman, as well as the leader of the Opposition, knows that and both gentlemen are also aware that this Government passed a law for the free admission into Canada of wheat, wheat flour and semolina from the United States. That law was ,put into force on April 17, 1917, and is in force to-day, and the farmers of this country have had the advantage of it. In view of that fact I am unable to see why these two hon. gentlemen should make such statements as they have made here today.
Now as to the Order in Council prohibiting the exportation of wheat products to the United States. This Government gave power to a board to prohibit the exportation from or the importation into this country of the several products referred to, without a license. That is given as the reason why exportation of these products to the United States cannot now take place. Now the hon. gentleman (Mr. Eobb) must know more than he is suggesting. He must be aware that the United States Government enacted a law prohibiting importations into that country of wheat or wheat products, and that is the reason why-Canadian farmers cannot now export those products to the neighbouring republic. If the hon. gentleman was sincere why did he not give that explanation. I want to say to him that if that law was not in force in the United States a similar law would

not be in 'operation in Canada. First of all, the United States enacted that wheat, wheat flour, and semolina should be allowed into that country free of duty provided Canada would pass a similar law. When we did so the United States Government annulled the existing law and passed another statute prohibiting such importations without a license, and they will not even grant a license. Do hon. gentlemen opposite think that is a fair or right course to pursue?
With a barrier like that erected against us, nothwithstanding the fact that their tariff allows free importation, are we to sit still and let the United States take * all the products that our farmers require for feed and exclude our wheat? In passing, I may say that the reason the United States Government give for passing that law is that they guaranteed to their own people a very high price for wheat, and consequently they made up their minds that they would not allow wheat from any other country to enter the United States until they had made their own people use all their domestic wheat.

I have quoted authority for an Order in Council passed by this Government on the 4th December, 1917, and another passed on 4th September, 1919, whereby this Government placed an embargo on the exportation of wheat to, or the importation of wheat from, the United States. Will the hon. member quote his authority from Washington?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I can get the information, but as the matter has come up quite unexpectedly this afternoon, it is impossible for me to furnish it to my hon. friend at once. But I want to ask him if he will say he never heard of any order issued by the American Government whereby they prohibited importation without license?

We have had a statement from my right hon. friend, the acting Prime Minister, this afternoon that there is a small quantity of wheat going into the United States, and that wheat is from forty to sixty cents a bushel higher in the United States than in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask the hon. member on his honour as a gentleman if he ever heard of an order of that kind being issued by the United States Government. I take it for granted that if he does not answer he has heard something of such an order.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to be discourteous to my hon. friend. I read in to-day's papers that the millers of Minneapolis are threatening to shut down unless restrictions against Canadian wheat are removed.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Then the hon. member admits that he has heard of it to-day. That law has been in force quite a long time. Might I ask him through you, Mr. Speaker, if he ever heard of an order of that kind until he read it in the newspapers to-day?

I have a letter in this file from the Canada Food Board telling our millers that they could not export flour into the United States in quantities over twenty-five barrels. I have never had any communication from Washington in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I take it that the hon. member has not heard of it until to-day. But I feel, Mr. Speaker, that he has not given me a direct answer, for this reason: He states that he has had no communication from Washington. That does not answer my question at all, and I leave it just there, because I feel that any miller in Canada-I am not referring to the hon. member particularly-knows all the laws in so far as the importation and exportation of wheat is concerned. Therefore the position the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) and the hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) are taking to-day is embodied in a ispeech that can be sent broadcast throughout the West to the effect that the whole trouble has arisen because this Government passed an Order in Council prohibiting the export of wheat, and that that is the reason why there is a difference of 86 cents per bushel. I want to tell the hon. member that the United States tariff allows wheat, wheat flour and semolina to enter without restriction, provided Canada makes a similar provision, that a reciprocal law has been placed on the Statute Books of Canada, and that if the United States will remove the order they issued that those articles of food shall not be imported without license, then the farmers of Western Canada can get that difference in price.
No, because your Order in Council still exists.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
There is not a farmer in the West or in any other part of Canada who can prove that that Order in Council interfered to the extent the hon. member has stated. I could name quite a number of other oases where the United States
Government have enacted laws, and when the time came for them to be put into effect the Government would take some means of nullifying their operation. Let us see just exactly what position the Government is in at the present time with reference to wheat and wheat products. In the West the farmers want to send their wheat across to the United States, for they want the difference in price, and I do not blame them at all; but I repeat again that it is the fault of the United States Government that that market is not available to them. All our farmers want us to keep our bran and shorts here, because they cannot possibly raise pork at the price they are getting for it if they allow those by-products of wheat to go into the United States. What are we to do? Are we to allow the United States Government to prevent any bran or shorts coming into this country? Are we to sit still and say to the United States Government: "You have issued an order preventing the byproducts from your wheat or from any wheat that we send over coming in here; but we think we should allow our byproducts to enter the United States for the benefit of your farmers." Talk about reciprocity in wheat, wheat flour and the other products of wheat! The hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) in my opinion, Mr. Speaker, probably understands this matter better than any other member, and understanding it as well as he does, there is not any other member can go before a meeting and, if I may use the word, so completely confuse the issue that no one would understand really what it means. Therefore I believe that in putting this matter before the House to-day the hon. member has done so more particularly for the purpose of placing his views before the farmers of Western Canada in order to confuse the issue and lead them to impute to this Government the whole blame for the condition of things against which they complain.
. Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Marquette): Mr. Speaker, I should like to participate in this debate for a short time before a decision on the resolution is reached. Unquestionably the discussion has taken a very wide range; it has launched out into the consideration of a question which was a live issue in this country nine or ten years ago. To me as a Westerner, and as a man who believed profoundly in reciprocity with the United States, and believes in it yet, the discussion has been decidedly interesting. My recollection, however, of the discussion of reciprocity in 1911 as it took place in East-

ern Canada, is that it had not very much to do with the merits of the question-I mean to say that the election was not fought on the real merits of the question. In the province of Quebec the election was fought upon issues that were as foreign to reciprocity-well, as the Mikado of Japan is to a Laplander; on issues that when the political history of this country comes to be written, will stand revealed as probably the most sordid that ever were placed before the Canadian people. In Ontario the question was not debated to any great extent; my recollection is that extraneous issues were introduced and that the judgment of the people was not at all upon the question of reciprocity. I maintain, Sir, that Western Canada to-day is in favour of reciprocity; I believe that Canada from one end of the country to the other is in favour of it, and that this would be amply demonstrated if a dispassionate verdict could be obtained from the people.
I have always been amazed-and I take this opportunity of discussing the question a little bit, since the debate has taken such a wide range-I have been amazed that the benefits of reciprocity did not appeal to the people of Ontario and Quebec more than they did. The fact that they did not appeal to them is due, as I say, to the fact that the question itself was not discussed. Two-thirds of the population of the United States lies east of a line drawn north and south through Chicago; the greater part of the population east of that line is in the New England States and in New York and Pennsylvania. Adjoining the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, therefore, we have this dense population, and here in these provinces we can produce the finest quality of butter, cheese, milk, lambs, hogs, hay- everything, in fact, that a great consuming population requires in order to maintain itself.
Mr. P. iMcGIBBON (Muskoka):	If this
subject was not discussed on its merits in Ontario or Quebec, was it so discussed in Manitoba?
The question was discussed in Manitoba.
And what was the result?

The 21st, I
think.

The 21st of July. There
was very little trading in wheat upon the exchange, practically none; the trading was within very narrow limits, and yet the price of wheat went up in the short space of eight or ten days from $2.24, if my memory serves me correctly, to $2.42. What induced the market to go up? It was the result of speculative influences operating upon it. Let us bear in mind that our Canadian millers have to regulate the price of their flour upon the price they pay for wheat, and if a Canadian miller were protecting sales of flour by buying wheat on the open market, as was the legitimate custom in the past, at $2.42, he would have to raise the price of his flour correspondingly. But what would have happened, supposing the market had remained open? The price would probably have gone to $3 per bushel; and after the grain started to move, and when our private exporters in Canada found themselves up against the difficulty of selling wheat abroad, what would have happened? The price would have dropped in just as short a period of time from $3 to probably less than $2 per bushel, and you would have had a universal cry in this country, not only from farmers, but from consumers, that permission was given to speculators to come in and rig the market, and a state of disorganization would have resulted that could have been avoided only by the course the Government took.
I was rather curious why the control was asked for the period of eighteen months, and I was gratified to hear the statement from the Minister of Trade and Commerce that it was not the policy of the Government to continue this control. I take it that this period of eighteen months is asked for in order that the board may have ample time to clean up all their transactions for the present year.

That is it. It does not anticipate nor is it meant to provide that they shall carry on active operations of control of the market for eighteen months, but it is to provide that if after the season is over, there are odds and ends which have to be fixed up, they may have that period of time in which to fix them up.

The explanation of the Minister of Trade and .Commerce quite satisfies me in that respect, and it will probably be necessary to have that length of time.
One other word. It is, of course, unknown what surplus the wheat board will have when its business is completed; but as I said a moment ago, I have complete confidence in the integrity and honour of the executive and, indeed, of the whole board. I am satisfied of this, that they will sell the Canadian wheat crop at the very highest price that can be secured in the markets of the world; that there will be careful administration of the business, and that if there is any surplus to distribute after their operations are over, every producer of wheat who holds a participation certificate, will get his share of it. The hon. member for Chateauguay-Huntingdon (Mr. Robb) referred to the fact that participation certificates were to-day being traded in at two cents per bushel, and he cited this as evidence that probably the farmers had not a great deal of confidence as to what share of surplus they would get in the final distribution. I have no doubt that.his statement is true, but I think such farmers are following a rather short-sighted course in disposing of their certificates. Of course, if a man is in a position where he requires ready money and he has participation certificates covering several thousand bushels of wheat and he can realize two or three cents a bushel upon those certificates, naturally the temptation is strong to do so; but my view, from what I know of the situation, is that the final distribution will give the Canadian farmer considerably more than two cents per bushel. These matters of control are all difficult and inevitable in a period of war, and they are inevitable for a period after such a war as we have passed through, owing to the disturbance of trade that exists throughout the world. But I hope, and I am sure we all hope that within a period of another year at any rate these restrictions may be removed, and that as time goes on the visible evidences of the aftermath of the war will disappear and we shall get back to normal conditions once more.
Was the hon. gentleman in favour of the fixation of the price of wheat in December, 1918 on the same basis as was fixed by the United States, namely, $2.26?

I have no hesitation in answering that question. I was not in 
favour of a fixed .price for wheat, nor of a fixed price for wheat eiqual to that of the United States, because I thought there was the .possibility that the Canadian treasury might be called upon to make up to the farmers of Canada a very considerable difference, and I did not think the Canadian treasury should be called upon to do that. That is why I was opposed to the fixing of a price equal to that in the United 'States. But the Canadian Wheat Board, with the information that is before them, knowing the crops that have been produced in the wheat producing countries this year, knowing the quantity of wheat that will be required in Europe, have been able to determine pretty accurately to what degree the available wheat will go around. Consequently, they fixed their advance price at $2.15, because that is all it is in reality, upon a conclusion reached after an examination of all the facts, that afforded to them reasonable satisfaction that the Government would not be called upon to put up anything to implement the $2.15 per bushel price. Therefore, I think they acted with good judgment and in the best interests of the country.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time. The House went into Committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-powers of Canadian Wheat Board continued for eighteen months:
The minister was to give us an explanation of thi-s provision.

I will tell the Committee exactly my position in reference to the fifteen cents. I will premise what I have to say by the observation that on the Canadian Wheat Board there are three millers-Mr. W. T. Black, of the Ogilvie eastern mills; Mr. William T. Matheson, of Winnipeg, and Mr. Watts, of the Ontario Millers' Association.
Mr. MAHAiRG: Mr. Watts'is the agent for the Ontario millers.

Yes, he represents the Ontario millers and particularly the small millers. So that there are three practical, able and experienced millers, and they have made these regulations as. being the best under all the circumstances to conserve the object and purpose and to carry out the plans of the Canadian Wheat Board. The millers are looked upon as licensees from the board, and they are required to pay in fifteen cents for every bushel that they buy. That goes to the Wheat Board

and goes into the fund for the participating tickets. These men then give a participation ticket to every person from whom they buy and the person who sells to them and from whom they buy holds that participation ticket. At the end he gets his proportion of the sale. I asked for a memorandum explaining that matter. I do not have it amongst my papers, but I will undertake to say that the Bill will not get its third reading until I have their explanation before me. I had expected to have it by now. If I were a practical miller I might know more about it, but I am not anid I have to get my information from others. It is not the purpose of the board to be over particular with the smaller millers, but they do exact this from all of the larger millers. I do not know that the millers of the eastern provinces or of the province of Quebec are being particularly disturbed with regard to the matter.

If this tax, and the board itself, are found necessary as a piece of machinery to carry on the grain trade of the West, where grain is such a substantial commodity of commerce, I have no criticism to make, I take it for granted that what was necessary was done, but what I do object to is that in the eastern provinces, such as Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, where grain is not a commercial article at all, where it is not sold or bought to any perceptible degree,* the system here proposed will apply. Thousands of farmers have a little grain of their own which they bring to the mill to be ground and which they carry back home in the shape of flour. Under this regulation they are met at the mill door with a fifteen cent tax on every bushel they bring in, they have to pay that and it means in money a tax of 75 cents a barrel on their flour. I take it that it never was the intention to apply the tax to men of that kind. The board is not for the purpose of doing anything of that kind. This whole machinery was never intended to apply to the small concerns which I have just mentioned, which are not commercial entities but which are dealing with small farmers who have wheat of their own and which they grind for their own purposes. The thing is so clear in the mind of the minister that I am sure I need not say anything more but I would ask that the necessary remedy be applied so that these farmers will not have to pay this tax. If that is brought about my purpose is accomplished.
59i

I have communicated with the chairman of our board in reference to this particular grievance which my hon. friend has voiced. There has already been a modification. I am assured that the regulation had to be general in order to prevent abuses, but that it is not the intention to make it burdensome in the case of gristing. In that -case, however, wherever a farmer is so treated in taking his grist to the mill, the process is that -the miller who is the buyer, buys the wheat and returns the -grist. The seller, the man who brings the wheat to be ground, gets -a participation ticket and will get a refund at the -end of the transaction.

That is quite correct but the minister must see that he has introduced; through this b-o-ard conditions that will' prove most detrimental to small grist mills-throughout Canada, not only in Quebec and in the- Maritime Provinces but in Ontario as well. I know that very -strong representations h-ave been made to Mr. Watts as representing small millers of Ontario. These regulations are going to throw the business of the country into the hands of large mills. The small miller is going to quit. He will not bother with all these details. He will not take the trouble of going through this process with his customers; he will quit that sort of work. I hope the minister will follow it up and see that a remedy is provided. There is one other point. I noticed in th-e speech made before the Winnipeg Exchange by Dr. Magi 11, the secretary of the Exchange, who was sent to England, he -states that Mr. Lloyd Harris, chairman of the Canadian Trade Mission, said that it was his duty to sell Canadian wheat to England and neutral countries. Further he said that a cable had been sent by Sir Robert Borden to the Hon. Arthur Sifton telling him among other things to sell 50,000,000 to
75,000,000 bushels of our wheat. I would like to inquire from the minister what quantity of this year's crop has been sold and, I was going ,to s-ay, at what price? Perhaps it would not be fair to -ask the price but there could not be -any objection to the minister making a -statement as to the quantity of our wheat that had already been sold.

I am glad my hon. friend has mentioned that because I noticed -a criticism -spread widely and [DOT]broadly, not in the form of an insinuation even, but in the form of -an absolute assertion, that the Government was gambling in wheat, that, gambling in wheat it had

made its sales, that when the Winnipeg Exchange was opened the price went down, that the Government feared that it would be met with these gambler losses and that therefore it shut up the Winnipeg Exchange.
Now, what 'are called reputable papers have made that statement, and in one there is the broad headlines:	"The Crucifixion
of the Farmer." The question is therefore opportune because it allows me to nail that criticism.	.
The minister had the papers under control at that time.

I do not think so. Those are very late papers. The Government was intensely anxious to get market for this year's crop for the farmer. When Mr. Harris went over there as chairman of the Trade Mission he went with the idea of securing as large an export market as he could for products Canadian, and endeavoured to obtain markets for wheat as well as other products. That was particularly within his line. He was perfectly justified in doing it and was encouraged, and the contract with the Greek Government for the sale to them of about tewlve million bushels of wheat throughout the year was one which was engineered and brought, about by the Canadian Trade Mission under Mr. Harris. That is all the wheat that was sold previous to the sales made by the Canadian Wheat Board. When we were over there, and later when Mr. -Sifton went over the second time, they were in communication all the time with members of the British Government and with the wheat commission to find out if possible what proportion of our surplus Great Britain and the Allies would take. That was a perfectly legitimate thing to do. Unfortunately, we were not able, for the reasons I mentioned this afternoon, to -get any definite offer, either as to the quantity they would take or the price they would foe prepared to pay. Then came the decision of the Government, under the circumstances, to put the matter in the hands of the Wheat Board, and since it has been in their hands they have had the sole arrangements and work of trying to find an export market for our wheat. They have co-operated through and with Mr. Harris, but it is the Wheat Board as constituted here that is doing the selling. No member of the Government, and no friends of any member of the Government, so far as I know, ever undertook to gamble in wheat on the basis of the criticism which has been circulated in the West.

Under the provisions of the Order in Council of July 31, 1919, enabling - the commission to fix the price and profit on wheat and by-products, have prices been fixed with regard to the by-products known -as -bran -and shorts? If so, what are the prices and what is the spread between the two?

The Wheat Board have acted upon that authority and have fixed the price to the miller. They have also fixed the price of the prodiu-ots of the mill. I cannot give the figures but I can obtain them from my hon. friend.

Can the minister give me an answer to the question that is put in this tele-gram I have in my hand? I need not read it. A certain farmer in Saskatchewan wants me to ask the minister what will re-ally -be -the ultimate price of wheat to the farmer. 1 do not mean the $2.15. After distribution -and so forth what -are the prospects -as to the ultimate price?

My hon. friend will see that -it is impossible to answer that question. The surplus will be somewhere about one -hundred million bushels. Of that surplus fifty iper cent is already disposed of. It is not wise that those prices should be made public. Half of it is yet to be sold -and that sale -may continue fo-r -two, three, five or six months, and it is therefore impossible to tell what the ultimate aggregate will be of prices received. Then the matter of expenses is an indefinite thing, although it is being carefully watched by the -board. If I were a farmer and were not in a position that compelled me to take two cents now instead of twenty cents later, I would no-t sell my participation certificate for -any two cents.
W-as there -any difference in the condition of the world's wheat markets w-hen the grain exchange was -permitted to resume open trade and when it was closed after about two weeks' operations?

There was, in this Tespect, that -there w-as both -a desire and a prospect that dealing -in wheat might be -put upon the old basis or something approaching the old basis. But it developed in -the latter part of the consideration of the question that with the lack of cash -and the necessity for credits, it would be impossible to carry out our business on the open plan-, When that information came to the Government it was -thoroughly considered, and it was decided that it would

be better to work the Winnipeg Exchange to a close.
