Hon. Mr. DOHERTY moved the second reading of Bill No. 28 to permit the temporary importation, manufacture and sale of oleomargarine in Canada.
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, if it is not the intention of the minister to speak on the matter I would like to offer a few remarks rather than permit the resolution to pass without any discussion. When the Bill for this purpose was first introduced and passed about a year and a half ago as a war measure I understood that it would end with the war. Now it is proposed to extend its operation for another year and certain of its provisions until the year 1921. I doubt if the importance of this measure has as yet dawned on some members of the House. The cost of living is certainly a very troublesome question with many people, and anything that would tend to reduce that cost would naturally be welcomed. I doubt, however, whether this Bill tends to accomplish anything in that direction. On the contrary I think it is encouraging a practice in this country that should not be encouraged, something that is not honest and straight and above board. It is an endeavour to injure-I will not say destroy, because it cannot be destroyed-an old-established industry in this country, one that is founded upon a substance that nothing else can take the place of. I am satisfied that in the course of time that fact will dawn upon the people of this Dominion, indeed I believe it has already done so, because a few years ago you could buy the very best dairy or creamery butter for 30 and 35 cents per pound whereas I presume to-day it will command about 55 cents. The increase in the price of butter has not been at all comparable with the increase in the price of other food commodities and other necessaries of life. Oleomargarine has been sold, and I believe is still being sold, for about 34 and 35 cents a pound, or nearly double the price at which it has been sold for in Great Britain. Many people laboured
under the impression that with the admission of what is called a substitute for butter-but it is not at all a substitute for butter-the cost would be made so low that it would be purchased in tremendous quantities. When the resolution upon which this Bill is founded was before the House on Tuesday night, I asked for some information regarding the amount of butter that had been used by the manufacturers of oleomargarine in Canada for the purpose of incorporating into oleomargarine and rendering the stuff palatable so that they would be enabled to dispose of it. So far I have not received any information on the subject from the Government-whether they have that information or not I do not know. I am also unable to find out from them the number of manufacturers who are engaged in the manufacture of oleomargarine in Canada, although I think we ought to have this information before proceeding with the present Bill. On that ground I took exception to the measure the other night, before dividing the Committee on it, but I was unable to obtain the desired information. I must say I am a little surprised that the second reading of this Bill should be proceeded with without the information in question being presented to the House.
It was promised by the Government.

I do not know whether the Government promised to give that information or not, but it is quite apparent there is a strong desire on the part of many members for it. As a matter of fact, somewhere in the neighbourhood of 800,000 pounds of butter was used by one of the manufacturers of oleomargarine in Canada last year, and that is too great a quantity of butter to be wasted in trying to make palatable a commodity which is not at all acceptable to the people without the butter it contains. Where has the agitation for the use of oleomargarine arisen? I believe it originated in this very city. Resolutions on the subject have been passed by some of the women's organizations in Ottawa. Some of the prominent ladies of Ottawa have identified themselves with the movement, and their plea is that the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine in Canada should be permitted in the interest of poor people and so that the children of that class may have this nourishing food. Let me remind the ladies who were instrumental in forcing this matter upon the attention ot the Government that the children who have grown up in Canada and have made a world-

wide reputation for themselves during the war, which they did in competition with the men oi all the other nations of the world, did not grow up on oleomargarine; they were nurtured on and nourished by the pure unadulterated butter that was consumed in their homes. If hon. gentlemen would take the trouble to follow the investigations of those who have made a study and analysis of oleomargarine, and have thoroughly tested it, as many of the medical experts have, they would find it is not a substitute for butter, and that were it not for the quantity of butter incorporated into it good reason exists for doubt whether the commodity should be allowed to reach young and growing children at all. Doctor E. B. MacCallum, of Johns Hopkins University, has made a thorough investigation into oleomargarine and the results of that inquiry were published in many of the medical and scientific magazines of the country some time ago. Dr. MaoCallum, author of a notable contribution to the animal study of America, points out the effect that oleomargarine has on children and on others to whom it has been given.
He also makes a comparison between skim milk and whole milk, and emphasizes the fact that butter fat is the natural food not only for children but for the young of all animals, and that there is no substitute for it. He mentions that in the rural districts near Copenhagen, where children had been fed exclusively on a diet of separator skim mil'k, a certain eye trouble manifested itself, but that it promptly disappeared on the children being given whole milk, the disease being essentially the result of fat starvation. I am not going to discuss that feature, but I wish to call the attention of the House to the opinion given by another Canadian-born in Western Ontario-who has attained a very high position in the United States and who has been closely identified with the dairying industry there since his youth. I refer to Dr. G. L. McKay. He says:
Milk fat differs from other fats from the fact that it contains certain life-giving substances that are essential for promoting the growth of the young. The all-wise Creator has placed this substance in the milk fat of all animals. The same substance, we are told .by .prominent physiologists, is found in the leaves of some plants.
He quotes, certain, prominent medical authorities as follows:
Dr. Halliburton, the celebrated Condon writer on foods, has recently completed an important investigation of the numerous 'butter substitutes on the British market particularly with reference to the fat soluble growth factor. He found

by feeding experiments on animals that what he calls the " accessory growth substance," which is present in milk fat in great abundance, is absent from the majority of oils of vegetable origin. Nut-butter and lard substitutes are also destitute of growth substances. Dr. Halliburton states that the results of his investigations show the importance of butter as an essential pair of the diet of a nation at war. In his opinion, war imposes different standards of diet on people. In the case of children he thinks that the growth substance of fat must be supplied, and the way to accomplish this is to provide an abundance of fresh milk.
Dr. Harvey Wiley stated in a recent issue of Good Housekeeping:
As far as I am concerned, I should never gi/e my children nut margarine, oleoma rgarine, or any other margarine, as a substitute for butter. Butter contains a vital principle necessary to the growth of children which none of its substitutes possess. I should never give children nor grown persons in my family food products containing a preservative such as benzoate of soda.
These are the views of recognized medical authorities throughout .the world. Dr. MaeKay .points to the fact that nations at war demand butter rather than a substitute of this kind. And it is apparent that our soldiers when they demonstrated to the whole world what Canadians could do as fighting men, were giving the greatest possible recommendation to good, pure, wholesome butter,-a fact that should not escape the attention of hon. members to-night when it is proposed to continue a measure which apparently was drafted by those who were anxious to manufacture oleomargarine rather than by those interested in providing a real food substitute.
I may be reminded of the restrictions that have been provided to insure the purity of this compound. But do not let us forget that the men who are engaged in the manufacture of margarine admit that they cannot produce it without the incorporation of from 20 to 35 per cent of butter or milk. We had evidence before a Committee of this House last session from the manager of the Harris Abattoir company, which I believe last year manufactured about 8,000,000 pounds of oleomargarine, regarding the composition of the margarine that is manufactured in Canada. He stated that 55 per cent is oleo oil, 15 per cent is creamery butter, 15 per cent is cotton seed oil, and there is a certain percentage of neutral lard, which percentage he was unable to give. He also stated: :
This is all mixed in a mixer and reduced to a liquid and mulsifled in milk and takes on 15 per cent of the milk.
This is rather a remarkable process. The cotton seed oil and the other fats are

churned in milk to make the product palatable so that it can be disposed of. But in addition to that he said, in answer to a question which I put to him:
It is necessary to purchase this highly coloured June butter-
As hon. members are aware, the spring grass imparts a high colour to the butter manufactured at that season of the year. The witness added that this butter is purchased in immense quantities in order to give a suitable colour to this grease and so make it saleable. I put to him this question:
Is it not a fact? You realize that if it was sold without any colouring it would be unsaleable?
He replied:
It would not be so palatable, it would be like eating lard.
The largest manufacturer of oleomargarine in this country states emphatically that were it not for the deceptive colouring of the oleomargarine, even with the butter in it, to eat it is something like eating lard. This article is being sold at forty and forty-one cents a pound, according to his sworn evidence before the Committee.
This gentleman also gives some evidence with regard to the quantity of butter they were buying to be mixed with this cottonseed oil and the other ingredients. He states:
March 31st, or on the last Thursday, we always end our charges, the last Thursday in March. They are divided into dairy and creamery: dairy 1&5,0>00 pounds; creamery, 3,6'59,000 pounds. The average cost of dairy was 37.36 and the average cost of creamery was 45 cents per pound.
That is the price that was being paid by these manufacturers of oleomargarine at that time for butter to be manufactured into oleomargarine. Yet you will find people saying: Why is butter such ah unreasonable price. He states further:
But we have to buy a certain quantity in any event. Of course, we want that June butter for the oleomargarine because it is a butter witli a little colour and we need it for the oleomargarine. You know we are not allowed to put any colouring matter into the margarine, so we have to use this June butter.
I think it is well that the House should know what is going on in connection with the manufacture of margarine in Canada.
There is a wrong impression abroad with regard to the prices being obtained for milk or milk products. I have here a statement by the secretary-treasurer of one of the oldest cheese factories in Canada, established fifty years ago. I believe that the first cheese factory in Canada was established at this point, a small village called Salford. He says that the highest price producers received for imilk for the manufacture of cheese in fifty years was in 1918- $1.90 per hundred pounds. Nearly all the cheese factories in that district have now been closed up, I might say, as a result of the price of cheese having been fixed and kept down lower than other dairy produce. I have pointed out that the buttermaking branch of the dairy industry may meet with the same fate unless something is done to encourage rather than hamper and discourage those who have been endeavouring to carry on. In view of the professions that we have heard from hon. members, particularly from this side of the House, with regard to the necessity of a protective tariff in this country, I think it is a most remarkable thing that we should not only eliminate protection in respect of a certain commodity, but that we should encourage the importation into and manufacture in Canada of a deceptive counterfeit in order to destroy an old-established industry. It is little to be wondered at that many of those who are engaged in that business to-day feel that if they are to be singled out in this way; if that is the attitude of the people of Canada with regard to the business they are interested in; if they are not to receive the same treatment or the same consideration as that which is accorded to other manufacturers, then they are prepared to set their good judgment aside so far as tariff arrangements are concerned and take chances with the rest of the world.
I would like to know whether the National Dairy Council has been consulted in regard to this matter or whether they have made any protests against the continuance of this measure. This is a body which represents the dairy interests of Canada, and I believe it has an executive here in Ottawa. I mention this because I believe that the chief pressure that was brought to bear in regard to this legislation originated with certain women's organizations in Ottawa. I have remarked before, and I still believe, that there is no place in Canada where you can so quickly get out of touch with the true sentiment of the people of Canada as you can right here in Ottawa. I am firmly convinced that that is a fact. I believe that the large majority of people who live in this city are not actuated by the same objects or motives in life and have not the same incentive to exercise their own initia-

all others not so engaged. The fixing of the price of cheese closed up many cheese factories in Ontario. The oleomargarine legislation of the last session of Parliament, the Daylight Saving Bill, the fixing of an eight-hour day for labour over which the Government has control, have all seriously affected dairymen. Dairy help is not to be had in the face of a generil day's labour of from 12 to 14 hours. Such acts are hardly consistent with the policy advocated of greater production and must inevitably result in lessening the dairy output. It is not surprising that the Canadian farmer is beginning to advocate Free Trade when the actual producers of wealth in Canada are singled out and restrictions placed on them in this way. If this is to continue I can foresee very interesting times ahead for some .people. While the war was on, the privileged classes were not called upon to deny themselves ice cream, however great the need was at the front for dairy products. I do not think there is another productive and necessary industry in Canada which has been quite so difficult to carry on during the past four years as that of dairy farming. There are few indeed where the returns have been less, considering the labour involved where the same hours constitute a day as a basis of comparison. It may be said that such regulations were necessary in order to secure butter for export to Great Britain for the soldiers. This result could have been arrived at just as easily by fixing a price on a par with that prevailing elsewhere and would have been an incentive to greater production. Such general handicaps on an essential industry may well cause one to ask one's self if the very thing our soldiers are fighting abroad to destroy is not in evidence at home.
It is with deep regret that I feel called upon to pen these lines and only a keen sense, to me at least, of the doubtful wisdom of this tampering influence, causes me to do so.
Tours sincerely,
D. Sutherland.
I can foresee what the result of all these restrictions is going to be. It is going to lessen the output of what ought to be one cf the most profitable, substantial and beneficial industries of this country. ,We had before the House this afternoon a measure in regard to disposing of the Canadian wheat crop. You can produce wheat and dispose of it in that manner but a time will arrive when your land will fail to produce and you will have to turn in some other direction. There is no other branch of the agricultural industry that will enable you to carry on and maintain the fertility of your soil so well as stock farming of which dairying is one of the most important branches. It is true that you may obtain cheap lands that are rich and fertile, and you may for a time, exploit the richness that has been stored up there for centuries, but the time will quickly arrive when you will have to adopt different methods.
The effect of allowing oleomargarine to come into this country, or to be manufactured, is to discourage, discredit and de-
TMr. Sutherland.!
stroy this industry. I remarked the other night that I would take no exception whatever to the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine provided it is confined to the ingredients which are supposed to be put into it and they do not use the dairy products of this country in their manufacture of this material. Do not-as was done by the Order in Council which was first passed on the recommmendation of the Food Board -permit them to incorporate butter in it, nor to incorporate milk to the extent of 15 per cent of their output in order to make it palatable, it is well known that there has been much oleomargarine that has become unfit for food and had to be destroyed as it will not keep in cold storage or elsewhere by reason of the fact that it contains matter introduced with a view to deceiving the consumer which does not mature.
I would like to call attention to the regulations which were passed and which will doubtless be referred to. Precautions have been taken to make it appear that only wholesome food was contained in oleomargarine, and clause after clause was adopted with that object in view. Subsection 10 of the regulations provides:
Oleomargarine shall not be manufactured In Canada in any premises of or connected with a butter factory.
Why should it not be permitted to be manufactured on any premises connected with a butter factory? If you permit the manufacture'rs of oleomargarine to mixbutter and incorporate it with oleomargarine, surely it is just as fair to show the same consideration to the one as the other? It provides further that no preservative except salt shall be used for oleomargarine without the written permission of the Canada Food .Board, and no person other than a. manufacturer of oleomargarine shall mix oleomargarine and butter. We are granting exclusive rights to a close corporation to acquire butter by millions of pounds or in as large quantities as they like and mix it with another substance in order to produce an article of food which they can palm off on the public yet deny this privilege to the dairymen. Reference was made by the Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) the other night to the regulation providing that in restaurants where this butter substitute is used this fact shall be declared on a card prominently displayed and in letters of not less than an inch and a half in length. Well, some day when hon. members have a little time at their disposal they can go into some of these restaurants, and occasionally they will find a card stuck up in a place where it would fail to attract very much

attention unless one were looking for it, because letters of an inch and a half in length are not apt to strike the eye very readily in a large restaurant or dining room, and one card is all that it is necessary to display.
Now, this is not the only country that has to contend with this question. In France they prohibit the artificial coloration of oleomargarine and do not permit its sale in stores that sell butter. Yet we permit it to be put up in packages of exactly the same size as those containing the best dairy butter. Its wrappers are precisely the same, with the exception that the word " oleomargarine " is printed on the wrappers. The boxes in which this product is put up are identical in size with those used for butter, and you will find further that oleomargarine is being quoted in the newspapers in the same column in which the prices of butter appear. I do not think that this should be permitted. Oleomargarine should not be considered as a dairy product at all. If it has any merit then it should be sold on its merits and should not be disposed of in the way I have described. In Germany the mixing of butter with oleomargarine is not allowed, and the sellers are not permitted to put it up in butter shapes. It is apparent that an endeavour has been made, not only in this country but elsewhere, to get it on the market under the guise of butter and with a similar trademark. I think the Government would be well advised to revise the regulations so as to prevent the incorporating of butter into margarine. The manufacturers of this substance should not be permitted to churn it in milk and should not be in a position to deceive the people by putting it on the market in the manner contemplated in this legislation. The present law in Canada gives them too much latitude. If the Government see fit to amend the regulations so as to prohibit the incorporation of butter and milk into this commodity I will have nothing further to say on the subject, nor do I think that the dairymen of the country will raise any objections in connection with it. But so long as this legislation remains in its present form, you may rest assured, Mr. Speaker, that there will be strong objection and efforts will be put forth to obtain some redress for what at the present time can only be considered as a rank injustice to people who are deserving of better treatment and who are engaged in- a legitimate business.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR (Antigonish and Guysborough):

speechtext:
It is very seldom that I have an opportunity to agree with anything said by the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. I have followed his remarks very closely and I thought for some time that I was going to be able to agree with him entirely. But before he concluded he had to get in his little dig about the big interests, rather a favourite line of argument with the hon. gentleman, something which I do not think is at all necessary to introduce into this discussion. The matter can be discussed on its .merits, and while I believe there are two sides to the question-entirely apart from the interest of those who are engaged in the manufacture of oleomargarine-I believe the Government will deal fairly with the subject in the light in which they see proper to deal with it. From my point of view I must express my concurrence with the remarks so earnestly uttered by the honourable member for South Oxford.
I think, Sir, that the time should not be extended for permitting the manufacture
and importation of margarine. I believe margarine was first made immediately following the Franco-Prussian war. There was then practically no butter to be had to meet the needs of the people of France, and this product was devised to supply the deficiency. In England, where hundreds of millions of pounds of this article have been used for many years, as also in France, the manufacture and use of margarine is hedged round by very drastic restrictions. In England, I believe, there is an absolute prohibition against the use of butter in the manufacture of oleomargarine without changing the name; if butter is incorporated the product is known as butter-ine. The United States Government have endeavoured to place restrictions about this article, but according to reports from that country they have failed. I placed on Hansard a session or two ago some figures- I regret to say I have not them at hand now -which were taken from the records of the United States, tending to show that out of hundreds of millions of .pounds of margarine used in the United States over 90 per cent was sold to the public as butter. In England and in France the Governments have also gone to great trouble in order to .prevent, as far as it was possible, the same thing occurring there. The action taken by those three governments, and also by the governments of other countries where margarine is used, is to my judgment a clear indication that they consider the article inferior to butter and something which should not be supplied to the consuming pupblic under any false pretences. The natural colour of margarine is white, and unless some artificial means is used to change the colour, of course it can always be distinguished from butter. In the United States the storekeepers will supply you with so many capsules of colouring matter according to the amount of margarine you have purchased, so that if you wish you may make it look like butter. That puts the purchaser in this position, that if he does not want his gues'ts to know they are eating margarine, he goes out into the kitchen, puts some colouring matter into the margarine until it resembles butter, and then his guests may not know that they are not eating butter.
I do not believe that this article is as good a food as butter. But the principal reasons why I object to. the further use of it in Canada are these: Our dairymen have gone to enormous expense in order to build up their dairy herds, and as a result Canadian cheese and butter have acquired a

reputation second to none in the markets of the world. I think, Sir, it is poor encouragement to those men, encouraged by the Dominion and Provincial Governments, to make that expenditure in order to procure the very best breeds of cattle and to improve their dairy herds in every respect, to force them to compete with this article called margarine. Moreover, in view of the fact that we have a tariff duty of four cents a pound on butter coming into this country, I think it is a breach of faith with our farmers and dairymen that this article should be allowed to enter free of duty and compete with their product. It is not fair play at all.
In regard to the statement made about the high price of butter, I firmly believe there is no article of food to-day that goes on any man's table, whether he is a rich or a poor man, which gives as much in food value for the money paid for it as does butter, and that the price paid by the consuming public to-day is not a high price when you consider its food value. I also believe that the price at which butter is sold is not an excessive price if the farmer or dairyman is to be encouraged to remain in business.
My hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) has said that certain restrictions have been placed upon the farmer in regard to what he produces and sells, which restrictions, to say the least, are not very encouraging to him to continue his farming or dairying operations. The action some time ago of " that man O'Connor " in fixing the price of milk-in undertaking to give a verdict before he had heard any evidence- was one knock at the farmer. This, it seems to me, is another knock. There is nothing that tends so much to keep up the fertility of the soil as dairying, and there is a large amount of money invested in the industry. We evidently have butter to>
spare, because we are exporting butter, and one of the reasons why we are forced to look overseas for a market is because of the introduction into this country of a substitute for that butter in the shape of margarine.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when this measure was first introduced it was regarded by the farmers as a war measure. Our farmers realized at the time that the introduction of margarine was not in their interest, but they accepted the situation loyally because they regarded the measure as one of the necessities imposed by war conditions. Now the war is over, at all events hostilities have ceased, and we are endeavouring to get Pack to normal.

There would be more justification for taking action with a view to reducing the price of many other articles which the people of this country have to buy than there is for permitting the continued manufacture in and importation of oleomargarine into this country, thereby lessening the profits of farmers and dairymen who are producing butter. Oleomargarine has been in use for many years in the United States and in other countries of the world. Of course, these countries are more densely populated than Canada and have a smaller rural or agricultural population than we have. But I believe that Canadian Governments were influenced by two considerations in the past in prohibiting up to a short time ago the manufacture or importation of oleomargarine. ' First, they evidently thought that margarine was not as wholesome a food as butter; second, they believed that it was incumbent upon the government of the country to give proper encouragement to the dairy interests with a view to their keeping more cattle and producing more milk. The importation and manufacture of margarine was permitted and accepted because the war was on. But the war is now over and in the interests of one of our greatest industries-an industry which has made wonderful progress in Canada, and an industry we are all proud of, the dairy industry-I do think that the time has arrived for prohibiting the further importation of this article, or its manufacture, in Canada.
Suppose the price of butter became prohibitive to some people, would the hon. member then argue that oleomargarine should not be manufactured or imported into this country?

I do not know just what the hon. gentleman means by the price of butter becoming prohibitive. I suppose that meat at one cent a pound is prohibitive to a man who has not a cent, and the same may be said of butter at fifty or sixty cents a pound. An article of food or any other article becomes prohibitive only when the consumer has not the money with which to buy the article. I think there is no likelihood of butter becoming so scarce in Canada as not to meet the needs of the public at reasonable prices. Believing that the dairy industry should be encouraged and that dairymen should receive a price for their product which will encourage them to keep more cattle, I am opposed to the sale of oleomargarine in this country.

Mr. Speaker, before I left for Ottawa to attend the session at the beginning of this year a number of farmers in my riding arranged an interview with me, which, of course, I was glad to give. They were engaged in dairy farming

I have done a little at it myself for eighteen years; sometimes a good deal; we milked twenty-six cows on our ranch one summer-and naturally, in a protectionist country, they thought, I suppose, that I would be friendly to what were, in a measure, my own interests. They laid their case before me, and I said: "Gentlemen, you have brought your pigs to the wrong market; I am a free trader." That is the fundamental reason for my giving a very hearty support to the measure which the Government has most sensibly introduced. There is only one thing wrong with the Bill, and that is the use of the word "temporary" in the title. I would make the importation, the manufacture and the sale of this product part of the expanding commerce of a great country, and I would make it go on just as long as anybody wanted to import it who is a Canadian and as long as anybody wanted to buy it and to eat it who is a Canadian. That is the fundamental ground upon which I support the measure.
Why, Mr. Speaker, if oleomargarine is brought into Canada, who brings it? A Canadian importer. And to whom does that importer sell it? To Canadian consumers. And yet we have hon. gentlemen in this House who would contend that this is a free country suggesting that we should prevent importers from importing and consumers from consuming. Personally, Sir, I have no sympathy with that point of view. Of course, I judge that hon. members knew that before I rose to speak. The fact of the matter is, you cannot have any real freedom under a protective tariff. We- beguile ourselves into thinking that we are free men; we are nothing of the sort. When one person, or ten persons, say to another person: "You must not spend your hardly-earned money to buy something which you want to buy," they unwarrantably interfere with the liberty of the subject. That is my fundamental objection to all protective tariffs. No one. who lives in a protective country, flatter himself and his country as he may, has yet come down to the fundamentals of freedom.
Mr. Speaker, a certain amount of fat is absolutely necessary for the proper sustenance of a healthy human being, and the nearer you get to the North Pole the more fat you need. I remember reading
in an authentic book of travel an account of the arrival of a whaler amongst the Eskimo. A little boy, as is the custom of youngsters when whalers go there, came to the side of the vessel. In these regions they not only use large quantities of fat, but they take enormous quantities at one time when they have the chance, and they store it. Nature teaches them, of course, that they need the fat and that they can store it; .and they eat it in proportions that would hurt the stomach even of the average Canadian-although the average Canadian has a pretty good, healthy .appetite about three times a day. Well, this little fellow came to the whaler; the men on board knew what he wanted, and they tried him out with some huge chunks of fat meat. With extraordinary rapidity the little fellow consumed the whole thing .and looked the happier for having done it-and then looked for more. They they tried him out with a few tallow candles that they did not need particularly, and the candles followed the chunks of fat meat. Finally they gave him a piece of soap; the soap went the same road, and the little fellow looked happiest after he had consumed the soa.p. Now, I recall that incident of travel-which is very well authenticated; it is told by Herbert Spencer in one of his books-to enforce my statement that a certain amount of fat is needed by the human being, and the more the farther north we are.
My second reason for supporting this Bill, in addition to the fundamental one with which I started out, is that although we are not so far north as the Eskimo, this is a pretty cold climate, and I should be very slow to put any obstacle in the way of our people getting a good, healthy appetite for fat, even if it is not always of the best variety. There has been some talk of consumption of oleomargarine reducing the quality of our population. I do not think it would reduce it to anything like the extent that doing without the fat altogether would.
When I listened to the hon. member for Oxford South (Mr. Sutherland) dilating on the terrible compositions that are sold as oleomargarine, I could not help having a little dread that if the consumption of material of such a nature became so great as he seemed to fear, we might produce youngsters of the kind that the TSskimo boy was. But after thinking the matter out, I consider that that is highly unlikely, although if there were anything in my hon. friend's further contention that the consumption of oleomargarine, horrible com-

pound as it is, is going to drive dairymen out of dairying and put down the whole butter and dairy industry in this country- and he went almost as far as that-then I must say that the natural conclusion is that the appetite of our people is already very considerably degraded in this matter. The stuff tastes like lard; yet my hon. friend says that Canadians are going to take to it ,so heartily that they are going to drive the dairy people out of business.

I am sure the hon. gentleman would not like to do me an injustice. I think I made it quite clear that what I objected to was the incorporation, along with these other things that go to make up oleomargarine, of 30 per cent of milk and butter.

I have no wish to misrepresent my hon. friend, but there is the fact that he gave a somewhat horrifying account of these compositions, and I jokingly expressed a fear as to the effect they might have on our people. I, of course, believe in a certain amount of oversight, not too much of it, by medical boards or any other hoards, over the food people use. Under ordinary freedom, however, people will protect themselves fairly well in civilized countries against adulteration. As a matter of fact, the oleomargarine that is sold in the old country has, I know, nothing approaching the qualities that have been represented by my hon. friend. I have a friend who was in the old country towards the end of the war for some weeks, and who was one of the better-to-do Canadians and staying with people of his own class in the old country. After he had been there -about ten days, he said: "Before I leave you, I want to congratulate you on the excellent quality of butter you are getting at this advanced period of the war." The lady of the house said: "We have not tasted butter in this house for eighteen months. What you are eating is oleomargarine." That could not have tasted like lard; I think the quality of the stuff could not have been so very bad. We all know that for weeks together the soldiers never saw butter in the trenches. The scarcity was so great that sometimes they ate large quantities of oleomargarine, and they did not seem to take any hurt; on the contrary, they canje back a pretty healthy looking -set of fellows.
The fact of the matter is that we are too selfish in this country; we look at everything from the point of view of classes, and we fail to take into consideration the case of the other fellow. I want to put in a

word for the town fellow, and I do it the more readily because I come from the country and can get all the butter I want. What is more, although I took up the business late in life, with the people I have, we make such good butter that we do not fear competition from oleomargarine. We have such a demand that we could sell ten times the quantity any day in the week -and any week in the year. That is the kind of Canadian we need, the man who produces such stuff that he does not fear competition. But what are the facts? The fact is that butter is very scarce in Canada, and there is a reason for that. It is not the fanciful reason that oleomargarine is driving people out of the dairy business. I know why dairying is becoming less in my part of the country. As soon as a man gets big enough in the farming and stock-raising business to keep enough cattle to live off his -steers, he cannot get his boys or his hired help to sit down and milk cows. That is the fact of the matter about Western- Canada. I-f a man gets big enough in the business to keep cattle so as to live off selling the beef, the boys, whether they are his own boys or hired help, rebel to -such an extent that they go out of that line of business into another which is probably better for the country -and better for themselves. They produce in a bigger way quantities of material which sell for larger prices. They make -more money and probably do more good to the industry of the country. But I repeat that butter is a scarce commodity in Canada, and the reason for that is what I have stated. We have a large country of very great resources; we have the greatest possible-facilities for young people, if they have the go in them, to get into bigger lines of business, and dairying, especially the milking, is -a very irksome game. I know, because I have done more or less of it for eighteen, years, and it is not a pleasant experience, with the thermometer at 90 degrees in the shade, to have a cow take her tail, not in the most -cleanly condition, and wipe it through both your eyes. As long as I can deal in steers, I am not going to do -any more of that than I can help. I sympathize with -the young fellows, and that is why so far as I -am concerned-and my experience is. that of scores of hundreds of men, my neighbours, all through the great cattle province of Alberta-we get out of dairying as soon as we can and produce cattle. Not only is butter scarce in this country, but as it is scarce, the price naturally is high, high at any rate compared with the price of oleomargarine. Butter being

hard to get and fat being needed in human food, and the price of oleomargarine being so much lower, I say that we men in Canada want to be just a little bigger, be prepared to stand on our own feet and let our butter fight its way by its quality, but give the town dweller a little reasonable freedom to get cheaper material if he wants to buy it as it has been introduced by Canadians for the purpose of sale.
Something was said about the big interests as the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) pointed out. Well, there are big interests in the farming and dairying business. There was a candidate on the opposite side to myself in Alberta at the last election who posed, by the way, as a great free trader for many years and who was generally a free trader; but in the first week of the active campaign of 1917 he talked exactly as the hon. member for Oxford South (Mr. Sutherland) and his supporters have done tonight, against the introduction of oleomargarine, until his opponent, whom I shall not name in this House, found out that this farmer and free trader had, fortunately for himself, made a large amount of money in real estate in Edmonton and had about $17,000, I think, invested in a dairy company in Edmonton. That little incident only shows how readily, even	a farmer	and afree	trader will fight	where	hisown interests are concerned. The successful candidate in that election naturally used this fact, and the moment he used it, it was so effective with the audiences that the farmer and free trader returned to his old faith so far as oleomargarine was concerned, because he stopped talking against oleomargarine there and then. There are interests and interests; there are interests behind the opposition to this Bill as well as possibly interests in favour of the other side of	the argument.	I want toclose	as I began by	saying that
we want to have a little reasonable consideration for other people; we want to have a little reasonable regard to the other fellow's point of view. There was a time when there were 70 or 80 percent of the people of Canada engaged in agriculture. Now there are only about 48 per cent so engaged. The majority of the people are town or urban dwellers, and I must say that so far from seeing anything to object to in the argument of those ladies -Lady Pope among the others-who were quoted by my hon. friend, I very much admire their point of view. Theirs is not a political point of view; it is not a party
point of view; it is the sympathetic attitude of women, moving in a plane of society where they can get butter, towards the poor who have to pinch and reckon about their weekly budget in the districts of our cities where they have a hard time to make ends meet and just manage to keep out of debt at the end of the year. It is a shame that we should have such conditions! in this country. With the multitude of our resources and less than two people to the square mile, everybody should be well off in Canada. Everybody should be well off and I trust that one of these days we shall have conditions under which they will be well off. That will not be; by restricting your commerce; it will not 'be by putting embargoes on all kinds of endeavour; it will not be by restricting importations, manufactures and sales'. Importations always mean exportations, manufactures and sales, and these are what we want to clear off our war debt and make us all wealthy. I am glad to have.this opportunity of supporting a really good Government measure and saying a word for the town dweller and a humble word for the substitute for butter which I understand is generally a very good one.

Mr. Speaker, I have very much pleasure in agreeing for once at least with the hon. member (Mr. M. 'Clark), who has just taken his seat. The hon. member for Red Deer is always interesting, logical and consistent. Whether we agree with him in his doctrine altogether we must agree with him on this question. I agree with him very heartily when he says that we should keep our hands off the poor man's living. We have just closed a very trying war and we are entering upon a period, in the fall of th'e year, when we expect a lot of unemployment and a great deal of hardship. I think that at this time it would be a great mistake if we did not extend to the poor man the privilege of buying a substitute for butter when he cannot afford the real article. I cannot conceive of any man buying a pound of the oleomargarine that is made in this country if he could afford to buy 'butter. I would like to have seen the Government go farther; I would like to have seen them importing into this country, if they could, the brand sold in England and which is far superior to the article sold in Canada. I myself went through a similar experience to the one referred to by the last speaker. I ate oleomargarine over there for four months before I knew the difference; I had looked upon it as one of the very choicest



brands of fresh butter. If we could get an article like that in this country for the poor man, who has to raise four or five of a family on about $2.50 or $3 a day with the present cost of living, we would do him a great service indeed.
In regard to the other branch of this argument which has been adduced by my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), I would like to call the attention of the House to the fact, which was admitted by him, that since the introduction of oleomargarine into this country butter has not decreased, but increased, in price. As long as that condition of affairs exists I do not see any danger to the great dairying industry of this country, and I think that until the danger does appear on the horizon we should at least give the poor man a chance.	*
I must differ from my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) as to the nourishment that butter contains. I do not look upon butter as of any great value at all with reference to nourishment. Its principal use is in making bread palatable. The average person probably does not use more than an ounce of butter per day. That amount of fat could be very easily and quickly substituted if we were simply looking at the nutritive values or the heat producing properties of fat. But, as I said, I do not look upon butter as such. It is simply used upon bread to make that great staple article of our diet a little more palatable and possibly a little more digestible. I for one am very glad that the Government had the courage to extend this legislation and to give to people who are not able to buy the pure article of butter as a diet a chance to get a substitute. I would like to see a better substitute provided. I can see no reason personally why butter should not be incorporated with oleomargarine. There is a very serious and substantial objection to the reverse taking place. I do not think that butter should be adulterated by the addition of anything to it, but if you have a cheaper, more inferior article which is less in demand and if you can make it more palatable and nourishing and give it a certain amount of heat producing value for the poor man who cannot afford to get butter, I do not see why it should not be done.

Mr. Speaker, as one who is interested in the dairying industry I listened with great delight and pleasure to the address delivered by my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland). He seemed to understand his sub-

ject very well and he gave us a good explanation in regard to the whole business. I was also pleased to hear the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), a doctor by profession, yet understanding the interests and welfare of the dairymen. I was again pleased to hear that eloquent orator from Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) giving his views. Some of them were fairly good. We have heard a good deal in this House about that hon. gentleman being nearly always on the wrong side. But he was not altogether on the wrong side to-night except when he was telling you about milking twenty cows out in the cold and frost and the like of that. If he did that he must have kept a very poor dairy. In our part, the place where we milk the cows is just as warm as where you are now, and if it is not you need not attempt to keep a dairy.
I was very pleased, indeed, to hear the eloquent doctor from Muskoka (Mr. McGib-bon) giving expression to his views in regard to oleomargarine at the front.
I was surprised to learn that he was given oleomargarine at the front, because our best butter was commandeered and sent overseas in order that our men in the trenches should be supplied with a good, fresh article. What necessity, therefore, existed for oleomargarine? The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) told us of an incident in some part of the country where some one was given soap to eat. Well, I would sooner eat good, clean soap any day in preference to oleomargarine. Now, the question that is of greatest importance is this: Why should the dairymen and farmers of this country be placed at a disadvantage? What do we find in connection with any of our exhibitions? Take as an example the exhibition held in the city of Ottawa a month ago. There was a great pure food show in connection with that exhibition. But was oleomargarine to be found among any of the exhibits? Not at all. It would not be allowed inside the door, for the good reason that it is unfit for human food. I do not think that it is in the interests of any section of the country to discriminate against the farmers, and if you put hampering restrictions on the dairy industry you will certainly hurt the country to a great extent. Millions of dollars have been invested in pure bred stock, and millions in buildings erected for the housing of that stock-buildings that are a distinct credit to the country; and a very large amount of money has been expended in getting men to inspect our butter and milk in order to keep these products up to a high standard.

If we permit this spurious article to oust the genuine product we shall make a grave mistake and shall put a serious handicap upon the farmers of the country. Seventy per cent of the population formerly engaged in agriculture, whereas to-day, I believe, only thirty per cent are farmers; and it is of the utmost importance that this latter percentage shall not further decrease. We should give the farmers every possible encouragement, for as we are all aware, agriculture is the backbone of the country, and where there is not progressive agriculture you do not find success along other lines. If you want to ascertain the potentialities of a country, look at its industries. We have an important industry in agriculture and we should do everything within our power to develop it. I regret having spoken so long on this subject, but some curious things have been said and wrong views advanced in favour of this spurious article which has been largely exploited in the United States. I do not think we should spend our money on something that is undoubtedly deleterious. Would any man or woman think for a moment of giving a child this harmful product? I do not think so. The proper care of children demands the purest food, and this oleomargarine or any artificial food of a similar nature will not tend to robust health. Let our children have absolutely unadulterated butter. I hear hon. gentlemen on the other side talking about a reasonable rate in connection with butter, and I desire to say that butter is one of the most reasonably-priced articles on the market at the present time. In conclusion, I would ask hon. members this question: Would it not be better, if people cannot afford butter for a while, to do without it rather than to spend their money on something that will surely hurt them?

Mr. Speaker, two years ago, it was any privilege to lay on the Table a petition signed by 29,000 farmers of the province of Quebec, protesting against the importation, .sale and manufacture of oleomargarine in *this country. At the time, it was represented in this House that the importation of oleomargarine would be allowed only temporarily, to carry through the hard times of the war. Several agricultural associations in Ontario and Quebec agreed to withdraw their opposition, in views of the circumstances and the promise that was made at the time: That measure was to be in force for one year only. The time has now expir-60} 1
ed and the Government, instead of redeeming their pledge, are now trying to further extend the delay.
I do not concur in the views expressed by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) when lie insinuated, a few minutes ago that the farming community was actuated by selfish motives.
Why, for the last few years has the Dominion government, as well as the provincial, asked the farmers to speed up production, to put more land under cultivation, to raise more stock and to increase their output :n every way? To help the people of Europe. The farmers responded to that appeal frcm their leaders and the result was that all over the country of late years production increased by leaps and bounds. The position taken by the farmers to-day is altogether justified. They say: " You urged us to promote the dairying industry, to enlarge our dairy herds, to turn out more butter and more cheese. We complied with that request, and now that we have made the n -cessaiy preparations, you are allowing the s.i'e on our maket of a counterfeit article, which is being .sold in competition with that same product in the manufacture of whieft we have invested an enormous amount of labour, skill and capital".
Mr. Speaker, considerable capital is invested in the dairying industry of this country. Our dairy herds represent many millions of dollars. To feed that stock, extensive pastures are required in summer, and enormous quantities of feed and hay in winter. The value of that pasturage and of those feeding .stuffs is also very large. The production of butter and cheese represents a heavy investment on the part of those engaged in the business. The statement is sometimes made that butter is too high, that cheese is too dear. Butter is not selling too high; its price is in keeping with that of all other staple commodities. If the price of agricultural products is higher today, it is because the farmers are paying three times more for everything they have to buy.
We are called upon to fix the price of butter, the price of cheese, the price of all agricultural products, and yet no one suggests that the prices of manufactured articles *should be fixed. Why such discrimination? Why do you confine yourself to addressing the farmers and telling them: " You shall produce this and that commodity, but you shall not exact for it more than such and such price." We want you to increase your production, but we propose fixing the price at which you shall have to sell your goods."

Oleomargarine, strickly speaking is not unwholesome, and I am not prepared to deny its value as a food; I am free to admit that its consumption may be found beneficial in the household.
But the consumer should understand that when he buys a pound of butter, he is really buying a pound of butter, but when he buys a pound of margarine, oleomargarine or butterine or any other similar products, he never can tell what he is buying. To make a pound of butter, money and time are required, but in the manufacture of oleomargarine, which is mixed with various ingredients, adulteration enters to a large degree. Butter is selling now at the price it is worth, hut oleomargarine is selling for more than it is worth, .so .that the consuming public is cheated to that extent.
Farmers are appealed to and asked to increase their dairy output. I know whereof I speak, having devoted my attention to the dairy industries for several years past and I know what it costs to manufacture good butter and good cheese. We have had to conduct many a campaign, we have carried on a considerable propaganda, through the press, by means of lectures, meetings, conventions and in every possible way, in order to impress upon the minds of our farmers the benefit accruing to them from keeping on their farms more cattle and improving their dairy herds, because it has been proved beyond the shadow of a doubt that without good stock, farming would be a failure. It took us four or five years to educate the farmer; we have impressed on his mind the importance of keeping the best breeds of cattle, keeping only select animals, from a well known breed and the best milk producers. In short, we have encouraged the farmer, we have induced him to tread that path, and now you are barring his progress, by putting hampering restrictions on the dairy industry, you are thwarting his hopes, his projects, in allowing those butter substitutes to be palmed off on the public. I cannot coincide in the opinion of the Government in introducing this measure. If you want to handicap the farmer, instead of giving him all the latitude required, you should make a clean breast of it.
The farmer has to pay abnormal prices for the feedstuffs which he has to buy for his stock, and for his fertilizers; the food bill of his family is growing, on account of the war having .pushed up food prices, and now you come and tell farmers "We are going to allow that butter substitute which is styled oleomargarine to enter into an unfair competition with your products.''

Not only have you allowed oleomargarine to be imported into the country, but the people who manufacture and sell this product have taken advantage of this in adulterating it by the addition of several ingredients, the result of which is that the consumer is being cheated. It has been ascertained that a mixture of butter and oleomargarine in equal proportion had been palmed off on the public as butter, so that the consumer was under the impression that he was buying butter at 60 cents or 55 cents a pound, when as a matter of fact he was only getting oleomargarine which could easily have been obtained retail on the market at from 25 to 30 cents a pound.
Margarine which is now selling on the market is waging an unjust war on butter in the matter of prices, because it is fetching just as high prices as butter, so that the consuming public who most should benefit from it are the least benefited, and here again the public is being cheated.
The Government, when they introduced this measure, two years ago, I believe, had undertaken to keep it under a strict control, and among several other regulations, it had been provided that no body could sell oleomargarine without obtaining a certificate from the Minister of Agriculture. Had those regulations been enforced, I might perhaps say that it would not have proved so injurious to the country; but when I bear in mind that, in the city of Montreal, scarcely two weeks ago, several thousand pounds of oleomargarine were seized which were being sold in the guise of butter, I wonder whether, under such circumstances, it would not he better for the consumer to pay a higher price for good butter than a little less for margarine or adulterated butter..
These are the grounds on which I oppose this measure and I intend to fight it. I will combat it on behalf of my electors, on behalf of the eight hundred agricultural societies and the 29,000 farmers of the province of Quebec who have protested, by way of petitions, against this measure being introduced. The Government then asked us to be forbearing. We have exercised forbearance. Now, the war is over, the world is making a fresh start in the various branches of industry; activity is renascent, and it is high time that the interests of the farmers should be taken into consideration and that they should not be the only class whose activities this House aims at controlling.

To be consistent, I feel it incumbent upon me to take the position I took a couple of

nights ago when this matter was last before the House. We have had a very interesting statement from the hon. member for Red Deer as to the capacity of an Eskimo boy to consume certain impure fats, and he wound up by telling us that the final dose was a piece of soap. When the hon. gentleman was telling that story I was wishing he had followed it a little further and told us what effect the soap had on the boy. The hon. gentleman has pro-"claimed the principle of free trade, and because he is a free trader he thinks that is a reason why, even in the matter of foods of this character, we should consent to allow our market to be flooded with deleterious products in order that the principle he espouses may he maintained. Sir, I do not think the members of this House will altogether agree with him. When legislation on this subject was first introduced very strong expressions in opposition to it came from all parts of the country where dairying was carried on to any extent, and even amongst the consuming classes the call for it was not general. But, if I remember correctly, the outstanding reason given for the introduction of the measure at the time was the dire need of our soldiers at the front, and of Great Britain, for all the butter we could spare. As a result of that situation rationing went into force under the direction, of the Food Board, and we were restricted in the amount of butter we could consume. As a matter of fact a large quantity of butter, held in cold storage at that time, was withdrawn from the home market in order that the need of the men at the front might be supplied. I do not presume that at this stage, and at this hour of the night, I shall be able to add any new arguments to the very able presentation which has been made by my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) and others who have spoken on this subject. The hon. gentleman said, and I think rightly, that one of the very strong objections to permitting the use of oleomargarine in the country is the fact that we allow, without any restriction, a large quantity of pure butter to be mixed with it in order to make the camouflage as perfect as possible and to convince people that they are buying a really proper substitute for butter.
This is wrong because it draws into its manufacture a very large quantity of a pure food to be mingled with a spurious article in order that a lower price may be obtained from the consumer. He said that if regulations would prevent the use of butter to produce this spurious article
his objections to some extent would be overcome. One very great objection he urged, and which I believe has considerable merit, is the fact that the Act permits this oleomargarine to be put up in prints and wrapped in paper and put on the market to all appearances in the same form as butter. That I think is wrong. It seems to me that oleomargarine should be so stamped and wrapped that it cannot in any way pass for an imitation of butter.
When we were discussing this matter a few nights ago the Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) in response to a query of mine, drew attention to the method of advertising in hotels and restaurants where margarine was used. A sign may be displayed in a prominent place in a hotel, in the vestibule, for instance, and yet it would not be prominent to the guests at the time. they were at their meals. I would require-hotel and restaurant keepers to advertise-on their bill of fare: "We serve margarine"' or "We serve 'butter or margarine," if they-serve butter as well. I think if their patrons had their choice they would almost invariably order butter. We have very stringent laws in order to maintain the purity of our foods, laws that are in the interests of our people, and it seems to me it ought to be made impossible to serve oleomargarine as a substitute for butter.
But the outstanding objection from my point of view, and it has been already expressed by other hon. gentlemen, is the-disturbing effect of attempted price control on the agricultural and dairy industry-of this country. I submit that if we spent as much energy in endeavouring to reduce-the price that the farmer has to pay for his stock-feed -as we have in trying to procure cheap food for the consuming public,, we would be serving a more useful purpose and one of more economic advantage to this country. An hon. gentleman has said that the price of butter, notwithstanding the use of margarine, has advanced to some-extent. I submit, Sir, that the price of butter has not advanced in proportion to its increased cost of production. Both butter -and cheese productions are declining, -and our dairying industry is at the present time in a state that should cause anxiety to this Government. I do not know -how it is to be prevented, but as a matter of fact, as I pointed out the other night, not only has the cost of production of milk increased by reason of the increased cost of feedstuffs, but to-day owing to the price that evaporating milk factories can afford to pay for milk being so -much higher-

than the cheesemaker or the butter man can afford to pay in order to compete at present prices, the milk is finding its . way to those factories, and the production of both cheese and butter is materially decreasing.
I can only say, Sir, that from all parts of my own district, which, like my hon. friend's constituency-we are from neighbouring counties-is very largely engaged in the dairying industry, I have received strong opposition to the continuance of this measure. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) is of the opinion that the Government might have gone further and made this a permanent arrangement; and I do think it was unfortunate that the Government has found it necessary to bring the subject so repeatedly before the House. It creates a disturbance in the dairying industry, and if it could be dealt with definitely so that farmers and dairymen would know where they were at, it might relieve some of the anxiety that is felt amongst them.
One hon. member referred to the small quantity of butter consumed by an individual each day. While butter is a very rich article of food, I submit that the amount that any individual or any family uses in a year is not such as to be a serious burden.
Mr. JACOBS; At 80 cents a pound?
Mr. GLASS; Even at 80 cents a pound, wages are high enough to justify the price for the proportion people use. This, Sir, seems to me very much like daylight saving. We are divided in this House to some extent into those who represent the consumers and the labouring class in the cities and those who represent the agricultural class and the producers in the country. We may talk as much as we like and have all the regulations that commissions may impose on the agricultural interests of this country, but, Sir, there is only one way by which the cost of food can become lower, and that is by increased production. That statement has been enunciated in this House time and again, and it has been publicly admitted by prominent statesmen of Great Britain. But, I submit that so far as butter is concerned, the tendency of the legislation now in question will be to restrict production rather than increase it. It is all very well to say that the price of butter has been well maintained, no doubt it has been; but notwithstanding that I say that the price of butter has not advanced in proportion to the cost of the feed which the dairymen has to buy for his stock. I do not think this legislation is in the interests of the country generally. I do not

think any large demand has come from the consuming public for its continuance, and I am going to move, seconded by the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), this amendment:
That this Bill be not now read the second time, but this day six months.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. H. KEEFER (Port Arthur and Kenora):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to
say a few words in reply to the member for East Middlesex (Mr. Glass). The hon. member finds fault with the Government for bringing this subject up more than once. But this is the first time that the subject has been brought up in any way by the Government. What my hon. friend is thinking about, no doubt, is the debate which took place in 1918 when a motion was made by a private member respecting the matter, based upon the action of the Food Board in recommending the passing of an Order in Council permitting the importation and manufacture of oleomargarine. The object of that Order was not to send more butter to the troops overseas. The price of butter had risen to fifty cents or more a pound at that time and the people with smaller incomes were complaining that they were unable to purchase necessary substances containing fat. An Order was therefore passed permitting the manufacture and sale in Canada of oleomargarine, as well as its importation free of duty. If my hon. friend had seen some of the letters that came to the Food Board from people with large families and small incomes expressing their appreciation of the action of the board, I rather think that he would not, even with the price of butter as it is, endeavour to keep margarine out of this country. According to the Toronto Globe of to-day's date, the price of butter is 55 cents and of margarine 35 cents. I represent a constituency largely composed of working men and I consider it a hardship that the dairy interests should, by any such process as this, endeavour to prevent these poorer families from being able to buy what is not so much a substitute as it is a competitor of butter The amount of margarine that has been manufactured since this Order was passed is considerable. In my judgment the manu facture should not stop. Why is it that 'Canada, prior to the war and to the passing of that Order in Council, was the only country in the world, the only dairy country particularly, which prohibited the manufacture and importation of margarine." Denmark permits it; Holland, New Zealand, Australia, England, Germany, France and the United States permit it The navy uses

it, but hon. gentlemen say:	"No, it shall
not be manufactured or sold in this country." Why do they say that? I think that the dairy interests have been carefully watching this matter with a view to keeping its competitor out. The dairy interests would be perfectly justified in doing that, but I fail to see why the farmer should object to the manufacture within the country of margarine. The farmer sells the beef fats and the lard from the hog which are refined and used in the manufacture of margarine. If he cannot sell these products to that market he necessarily will have to sell them at a lower price. We have heard complaints about the farmer not being able to sell his hides outside the country; are the farmers going to ask in the same breath that they be not allowed to sell within the country the other products of the animal? It seems to be utterly illogical. I could understand that the dairy interests might not want to have margarine manufactured and sold in competition with their products, but I cannot understand why the farmer should oppose the manufacture of margarine; if he does so he interferes with his own pocket.
Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that the farmer is not a dairyman?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly the farmer is a dairyman-that is, he sells his milk to the cheese and butter factories. If the producers do not require his milk for butter, he sells it for cheese, for condensed milk, to the co-operative factories, or anywhere else. But the demand for butter will never be interfered with by the importation, manufacture and sale of margarine except to the extent to which it is used by the poorer people who cannot afford to pay for butter. Are we going to compel these people to buy a more expensive article simply for the purpose of protecting the dairy interests? I do not think the House should be asked to do that. As I say, I fail to understand why, prior to the war, we were the only country in the world that prohibited the manufacture of this article. There must be some ulterior reason for it.

The hon. gentleman who ha.s moved the amendment (Mr. Glass), which, if passed, will destroy the Bill before the House, and those who support him have at least the merit of consistency in the position they are taking. I have gathered from the remarks of the hon. gentleman in this
Chamber and elsewhere that he believes in the principle of protection; that he believes in imposing customs tariffs on t'he implements and equipment that farmers, and particularly t)he dairy farmers, require in their industry. Consequently, in taking the position that the dairy farmer should be protected in the sale of his butter, my hon. friend is consistent. For the same reason I .am consistent in opposing the resolution that my hon. friend has moved. I believe in freedom. I believe that the farmers of this country, the dairy farmers and others, should be permitted to purchase the equipment they require for the carrying on of their industry in the cheapest possible market and that no restrictions should be thrown around the consumers in the purchase of the food they require to keep body -and soul together.
I do not share the apprehension which hon. members who are opposed to the Bill seem to entertain that this measure will work a serious hardship to the dairy industry. Our dairy industry has developed very well during the last ten or fifteen years, when we consider the development of the country; and it is only during that period that much attention has been given to it. Our cheese occupies a pre-eminent position in the markets of the world to-day, and I am eonvinced that our butter can occupy the same position. Denmark is perhaps the banner country of the world in the production of high quality butter. The Danish farmers have risen to that position and have maintained it in the face of all competition and notwithstanding the fact that oleomargarine is manufactured in and imported into Denmark. If the Danish farmer can do that, do my hon. friends contend that the Canadian farmer has less initiative, less ability or less skill in meeting similar competition? I venture to say that they will not.
If my hon. friends hope to build up an export business in butter from this country, our farmers will be compelled to build up that export business in the face of the competition of oleomargarine consumption in almost every country of the world. If they have to face this competition in Great Britain, France, United States and everywhere else where we sell our Canadian butter, surely they can stand the competition in our own home market.
I have this suggestion to offer in connection with this Bill. that it is highly important that proper provisions should be made and proper regulations framed to ensure that oleomargarine is sold

as oleomargarine and not as anything else. That is due to the public. I understand that in the regulations now governing the sale of this commodity every pound print of oleomargarine, when sold, has to be clearly and' unmistakably labelled " oleomargarine." One thing further. It is well known that oleomargarine, or whatever it may be called, is composed of several different elements. It is, therefore, incumbent upon the inspectors of the Government to see that only wholesome elements enter into the production of it; but when that is done, when the public are protected in this way, I am for the importation of oleomargarine into this country and the sale of it to the people of this country who want to use it. Let me say in conclusion, that I take that position in order to be consistent, in order that the people of this country, many of whom we know have a hard enough struggle with the present high cost of foodstuffs and the high cost of living generally, may be able to get a food that is admittedly wholesome at a cheaper price than they would probably have to pay were they restricted to the use of butter.
Amendment (Mr. Glass) negatived on division.

With very great reluctance I have to detain the House one moment with regard to a matter of privilege. I was informed last evening that when I happened not to be in the House my accuracy had been impugned by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau). I have in my hand a copy of Hansard containing the speech in which that accuracy was impugned, and I propose to read to the House the passage in question.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) quoted the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier as having said: "Well, no great mistake could be made if the Grits should undertake to fight the enemy with the devil's fire."
The hon. gentleman followed the quotation by saying:
That cannot be found in the speech delivered on the Address in reply to the speech from the Throne in 1906 by the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
As a matter of fact it can and is to be found there. I cast no douibt upon my hon. friend's honesty in his excursions into Hansard, but those excursions were not extensive enough. There were two debates on the Address in the year 1906, and it is in the second debate in that year that those words are to ibe found just as I quoted them. They will be found on page 38 of the Hansard for 1906-7, but under the date of November 23, 1906. That was when the words were uttered. I apprehend that the month of November, 1906, was in the year 1906, so that my hon. friend was, as I say, a little impatient in his excursion into the records of Hansard and he was only one hundred per cent wrong. The hon. gentleman went On to say:
My leader asked the hon. member for Red Deer this question:
Mr. McKenzie: Would the hon. gentleman mind giving me the page of Hansard and the subject in connection with which Sir Wilfrid Laurier said he was no purist?
The hon. member for Red Deer replied:
It was in the debate on the Address in the year 1906. I have not the page, unfortunately.
Whether it is the fault of the accoustics of the Chamber or that advancing years are affecting my hearing, in perfect good faith- and I am sure the leader of the Opposition will accept my statement-I understood his query to relate to the only quotation to which II really referred in that portion of my remarks. I did not gather that he asked for another statement which I had referred

to and had not quoted. I quoted the one very carefully, having copied it froim Han. sard; the other came to me as a matter of common knowledge to members of Parliament who have sat in this House for many years. I ask my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) to accept in perfect good faith my statement that I understood him to be asking as to the previous quotation.
