speakeroldname: Mr. S. W. JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier) :
speechtext: I desire to ascertain if the Government has arrived at any decision with regard to the payment of wages earned by enemy aliens interned during the war and numbering about ten thousand. During the last session I was informed by the Government that these men were to receive twenty-five cents per day for their work, but it had not then been decided as to whether this sum would be set off against the cost of their upkeep or for other purposes. Inasmuch as many of these men are now being daily deported, it is important to know whether the money due will be paid.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman has put his question.

Ilf you will permit me, Mr. Speaker, I desire to ask a further question before I resume my seat, and that is as to whether the Government intends to set off the amount due to these people for upkeep -for board and lodging-or whether it is the intention to use it to pay the indebtedness due to Canadian nationals by enemy nationals.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With regard to the question of what course has been taken as to the payment of the allowances that were made for work done, I am not in a position to answer the question at this moment, but I will make a note of it and furnish the hon. gentleman with the information later. As to the intention of paying the debts due by enemy nationals to Canadian nationals, there are provisions in the Treaty dealing with the manner in which such debts are to be arranged. Just how they would be dealt with depends upon the determination whether this country should adopt what is called the Enemy Debts Scheme, or should decline to avail itself of it. In any event I think whether by one method or another it is open to us to realize any indebtedness that may be owing by German nationals to our nationals; and it is likewise open to

us to utilize money so collected, including the result of the liquidation of the assets of German nationals in this country in payment of claims by our own nationals against those nationals. The particular method of doing that, as I have said, will depend on whether it be determined to adopt -the Enemy Debts Scheme as contained in the Treaty, or to proceed without adopting it.
Do I understand that these men are being deported, and that -their money is being held back pending decision by the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As regards details of
the payment of wages, as I have already told the hon. gentleman, I am not in a position to give definite information, but I will make inquiries and advise him.

On motion of Hon. A. K. MACLEAN, the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to provide in the proposed Act to amend the Civil Service Act, 1918 (Bill 18), now before the House, that the chairman of the commission shall be paid a salary of seven thousand dollars, and each of the other commissioners six thousand dollars; such salaries to be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.
Explain.

Bill No. 18, being the Bill amending the Civil Service Act, was,
as hon. gentlemen will remember, referred to the Special Committee, and one of the recommendations of that committee is to the effect that in respect of salary the members of the Civil Service Commission be placed in the position of deputy ministers, that is, that they receive $6,000 per year, with an extra allowance to the chairman. The amendment could not be pressed in the House without this resolution being first passed.

What is the
present salary?
$5,000 to the commissioners and $6,000 to the chairman. This amendment would make the salaries $6,000 and $1,000 additional to the chairman.

We have already made provision for increasing (the number of Civil Service Commissioners; now we are increasing their salaries. The first notice on the Order Paper when we came here for this session was with respect to increasing the salaries of these commissioners. Would we lose these men if we did not increase their salaries? If not, what is the real object of this increase?

I did not say that we would lose the services of the commissioners if we dlid not increase their salaries. As these commissioners, under the .statute, have the same rank and status as deputy ministers, it was thought that as a matter of justice their salaries should correspond with those of the deputy ministers. Further, in view of the importance of the very extensive work which they have to do, it was thought by the Committee that it was only fair to give them the salaries mentioned in the resolution.

How are these salaries determined? I raised the same question when the .salary of the chairman of the Board of Commerce was being determined by the House. We have a Commissioner of Taxation? What salary does he receive? If he is not paid as high a salary as that which is mentioned here, why not? His services are of a very important and very exacting nature. Is 'there any standard that governs the compensation for services rendered by commissioners and deputy ministers, or is each case determined on its own basis?

My hon. friend's question is a very wide one; I could hardly undertake to answer it at this stage. It would more properly come up when we are

considering the Bill and the amendments thereto. The duties of the members of the Civil Service Commission are very important. They are obliged' to do a good deal of work-work -that is, .to some extent at least, of a disagreeable nature. I think it is very desirable that the members of the commission should be placed in an absolutely independent position, and that Parliament should now by statute fix the salaries at the amounts proposed.

In my judgment, the Commissioner of Taxation performs very important duties-the most important performed by any one in the employ of the Government. I understand that he is in receipt of a salary which is not anything like the amount named here in respect of the Civil Service Commissioners. I do not see why the Government should not deal with him as they are proposing to deal with these commissioners.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not think that the hon. member's remarks are in order. The resolution under consideration provides increased salaries for the Civil Service Commissioners. The rule is quite clear that the discussion should be strictly relevant to the item or resolution under discussion, The hon. member would be in order in making a comparison, but he is not justified in asking at this stage for an increase in salary for any other employee in the public service.

Mr; Chairman, I do- not want to be understood as deprecating in any way the services of these commissioners; as a matter of fact, I have no doubt that they are doing a meritorious work and doing it to the best of their ability. But I think we should have a very full statement of the grounds on which Parliament is being asked to increase these salaries. An increase of salaries is the most common parliamentary experience that we have had this year-I think I am well within the bounds of accuracy when I make that statement-and a reason frequently given has been the rise in the cost of living. But that reason does not carry me very far as a member of Parliament. It is notorious, for instance, that members of Parliament are paid much too small an indemnity, but there is no question of increasing the indemnity of members of Parliament because of the cost of living. Well, I do not object. I am not asking for that increase; I assume there is good reason for not proposing it, because the cost of living is bound to come down some time. In fact, the Government

are taking very elaborate steps to bring down the cost of living. They have appointed a Board of Commerce-incidentally spending $26,000 a year in salaries for that Board-to bring down the cost of living with a bludgeon. But while they appoint a Board of 'Commerce to bring down the cost of living with a bludgeon, they. at the same time come before Parliament and ask for an increase in the salaries of these gentlemen referred to in the resolution. I repeat that we should have a full statement o>f the grounds on which these increases are asked for. There has got to be an end to this sort of thing. Everybody who feels any responsibility in connection with the financial welfare of our country is preaching economy. A couple of days ago the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) told a committee which is sitting upstairs that the financial condition of Canada, while not critical, is serious. Well, Mr. Chairman, if I were a sick man and I was told that my condition was not critical, but serious, I should not feel that I would be much worse if it was critical. My mind would be just as serious as the adjective; "serious " would be serious enough for me. We all know that the financial position of the country is very serious, and in the face of that the Government ought to give the fullest reasons for doing so when they come forward with proposals to increase salaries, not only on this occasion, but day after day. I assure the Government that the returned soldier will be watching what is happening in matters of this kind. The committee which is dealing with the reestablishment of the soldier will report and Parliament will have to take some action. We are acting as though we had oceans of money to spend and no need to exercise any care about it whatsoever; we talk economy, but we practice extravagance. I want to appeal to my hon. friend (Mr. A. K. Maclean) in this matter. I have the utmost regard for him-I think he knows it-and I want to appeal to him especially, because, when we both sat on the Opposition benches a few years ago, I cannot remember one of the excellent speeches he made as Opposition financial critic in which he did not put this need for economy at the very forefront of his remarks. I should like to have the assurance from him that that need is still in the forefront of his mind and of the mind of the Government of which he is so able and distinguished a member. I would like to have the assurance that they are really giving this matter very serious consideration, because it is by far the most important

matter that ought to occupy the mind of the people of Canada to-day.

I do not rise to object to this proposed increase; I do not think the salaries named are excessive in any way. But II desire to point out that a few months ago we passed a Pension Bill, under which three commissioners were appointed, and that the salaries of tHfese men, at least two of whom had seen honourable service at the front, were fixed at $5,000. I think that we should be consistent. I do not believe that the Civil Service Commissioners have any more important work to do or duties to fulfil than have the pension commissioners.
We should 'have some information as to that. Comparisons, it is said are odious; but still people will make them, and if we are going to give the members of the Civil Service Cbmmission increases in salaries and not do the .same with regard to the members of the Pensions Board, which has to deal with the pensions of the five hundred thousand boys who went overseas, we are inviting criticism which we shall undoubtedly get.

The minister told us that he wanted to place these men in an independent position. Would he tell ns if they are not already in an independent position? I can readily see that, while we might feel like placing every civil servant in Canada to-day in an independent position, yet that would cost a very great sum of money, and I do not think the country is in a position to expend such a :sum. Last year we threw away from $100,000 to $150,000, which we were asked to shove through this House in the dying hours of the session and which was thrown into the waste basket, and now we have another appropriation which we are asked to put through, and I do not know whether it will go into the waste basket or not. We should be a little more careful of the people's money which we are handling here. 'If anybody should receive an increase in salary, it is those who are drawing low salaries and not those who are receiving high salaries. There are in the Dominion of Canada to-day, many men who are quite capable of taking these positions and who would be willing to take them at $5,000 or $6,000. I am not saying that I am in favour of this increase in salary, because I am not. We are in many cases at the present time paying salaries for positions that we could well do without. What are we going to tell the people of this country when we put the soldiers in positions inferior to those in which the salary is high?

Whilst dealing with the general principles enunciated by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) and the hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Best), I may say that it is a notorious fact that the Dominion of Canada is underpaying its principal .men, just as it is a public shame that the judges of the Dominion of Canada should be in receipt of the small salaries that, are being paid to them. The Civil Service Commissioners are filling one of the most important positions in the Dominion to-day. They are replacing the hon. member for Red Deer; they are replacing the hon. member for Dufferin. In that they are the dictators as to who should hold positions and who should not, they decide what we were individually deciding in the past, and the work that is incumbent upon them is greater in proportion than that of any other department or of the deputy head of any department in the public service. There is a difference between them and the deputy head to-day in that, the deputy head is receiving $6,000 or more, whereas these gentlemen who have to deal with the deputy heads are being paid less. Whilst we are indeed to practice economy, and whilst members of Parliament are willing to bear the difficulties of representing their constituencies for $2,500, it is not the duty of Parliament to see that the public service shall be underpaid. It is not economy, in my opinion, that you should seek to have men perform onerous duties at a less salary than that which they are able to earn, and I heartily support the motion as being one that is reasonable and just.

There will he no disposition on my part, and, I am sure, none on the part of any hon. gentleman to refuse acquiescence to the statement of the hon. member for Red Deer. I think it will be conceded by everybody that the Government must practice economy in every possible way and must avoid, if possible, all unnecessary additions to onr public expenditure. There can be no room for argument in respect of that matter. The whole purpose of the classification of the Civil .Service is twofold. First, it puts into the hands of the Civil Service Commission the matter of employment of the Government employees, numbering 60,000. By the statute, the Civil Service Commission has become; the employe ment agency of the Government; it has to do with promotion of the employees in the public service; the members of the Civil

Service Commission are, by the Bill which will be before us shortly, given power to classify the service, to amend the classifications which they may make, and, in fact, to establish schedules of compensation which shall be received by members of the public service. This, of course, is .subject to approval by the Governor in Council. When you place upon a body of men responsibilities and duties (not at all pleasant) of this character, they should at least be placed in the same position as a deputy minister.
The position of a member of the Civil Service (Commission is certainly one of the most disagreeable positions in the public service to-day. They must, of necessity, come into conflict even with the 'Government and members of Government; they are constantly in conflict with members of Parliament, and they are more or less the subject of criticism, a great deal of which is unfair, from the public generally. Under the statute, they have the rank of deputy minister. At the last session of Parliament, I think, deputy ministers were given a salary of $6,000, instead of $5,000. The proposal is to put the members of the Civil Service Commission in that position, and I think it is better that we do that now rather than that representations should come to the Government through members of Parliament or otherwise in respect of this matter, and personally, I should like to see it closed, and, I hope, once and for all. While I admit the necessity for the strictest economy, much stricter than we have perhaps shown in the recent past, being displayed in the future, still I think the proposal is not unreasonable.
Are these officials subject to the income tax?
I think so. I have no information to the contrary.
Yes.
The minister says that under the regulations these gentlemen have the rank of a deputy minister. Who decides as to the rank?

I do not know
that I could give any other meaning than quoting the words the hon. member used, namely, that the statute says that they had the rank of a deputy minister.
How can a common man get into that rank?

Perhaps when the classification is before us it would be a more suitable occasion to ask about the work of the commissioners, but I suppose when we

are raising the salary of an officer of the Government, that is a proper time to ascertain what service that person is giving to the country. I fully realize what the minister says, namely that a great responsibility devolves upon these men and that they have a great deal of work to do, but last session we had in this House \^;ry interesting discussions along the line of extra charges and the bringing in of other commissioners to do their work. I would expect the commissioners to make appointments themselves. When the Government or any department of Government wants, an officer, I would expect the duty of the 'Civil (Service Commission would be to select and appoint that officer and pass him over to the department. If they do that, they are doing their work, as I understand it; they are earning their money,. But there was placed before the House last session abundant evidence that, instead of doing this work themselves, they involved an expenditure running into thousands of dollars in bringing in other people to decide for them who the men should be that should be appointed.
1 do not think that is business-like. I think the commission should decide these things for themselves; otherwise, there is an entire misunderstanding of their duties. If a man is to be appointed to the Customs Department why should not the Civil Service Commission appoint him? Instead of that, we have special commissioners from the East and the West sitting down in solemn conclave, taking evidence, examining documents and credentials, and then reporting to the commission. The last touch, I think, is given to the appointment by the commission. That is the kind of evidence that was given to us last year, and frankly I do not understand that kind of business. When a judge of the Supreme Court hears the evidence he has to decide and file his decision. Whether that decision is right or wrong he has to take the responsibility; he cannot shift it to somebody else, ask them to take the evidence, and then subscribe his name to their decision. That would not be tolerated for one moment. I do not understand why the practice should continue, if it did exist in the past, of the commissioners switching the responsibility of making appointments to somebody else. It would not be proper at this stage to go into the question of the advisability of putting this power in the hands of the commission in the first place. I suppose it is a step in advance; it is said to be, but a great deal was said in the

House the other day against the step with very much of which I agreed. I think it is an absolute impossibility for the commission to make satisfactory appointments to the Civil Service all over the country. But that is apart from this matter. I should like to know upon what principle the commission shifts the responsibility of making a selection among applicants to outside agencies.

If the facts were actually as stated by the leader of the Opposition, his objection would have some foundation, but as a matter of fact, except in a few instances, the Civil Service Commission makes all the appointments. The commission does not call in any outside help in the case of an appointment to the Customs or Post Office Departments, but a board is sometimes appointed to advise the commission in the selection of an applicant for a technical position requiring technical knowledge. This practice exists in Great Britain and in the United States, and I' do not see how it can intelligently be avoided.
Suppose there are a hundred applicants for a position in the Geological Survey, all of whom have been trained in geology, I think it would be too much to expect the commission to have such a wide range of knowledge as would enable them to determine the most competent man among all those applicants. I am sure'the leader of the Opposition must have been misinformed if he imagines for one moment that the Civil Service Commission delegates to other people the authority given them by the statute to make appointments. It is only in a few rare cases such as I have indicated that outside help is called in. I trust with this explanation my hon. friend will not press that point further.

I would remind the
minister of the discussion that took place in this House last session, led off by the hon. member for Frontenac and backed up by the hon. member for West Toronto, in which certain cases were specifically referred to and names given, I believe. The appointment was mentioned, for instance, of a man to do Government advertising in newspapers and periodicals. Surely a capable commission, with all the testimonials before them, could select a man for that purpose. If not, it is hopeless to trust them to do anything. In that case, however, they called to their assistance two newspaper men, whose names were given to the House,
the editor of the Ottawa Journal, and the then editor of The Toronto Times-two respectable men, but what special knowledge would they have of a stranger's special -qualifications for this work? Other similar cases were mentioned. Certainly no highly technical scientific knowledge was required for that position. Although it might be said that a man who. was going around the country picking out the best newspapers, the best Tory newspapers, of course, in which to advertise some business of the Government was scientific work from the party viewpoint, I doubt whether it could be considered scientific even from that point of view. I can understand the commission calling in outside help where the position requires real scientific knowledge, but the minister has not satisfied me that the position in question was of a scientific character. I insist that it was a selection that should have'been made by the commission themselves.

The minister has said that the commission take the responsibility of appointing postmasters. That is not the experience I have. I got a return the other day which sets forth the way in which rural postmasters are appointed, and in that return there is correspondence to the effect that the Postmaster Gen-4 p.m. eral has the last say in the appointment of rural postmasters. I would think the Post Office Inspector would be the best man to make the appointment. It is impossible for the Civil Service Commission sitting at Ottawa to know who is the best man; they must take advice from somebody, and they do take advice from some outside source. It would be impossible for the commission to do anything else. They do not know the different applicants, but it has been the experience of most of us on this side of the House that it is friends of the Government who are appointed to these rural postmasterships. Why is it that they do not even occasionally happen to choose a Liberal for these positions? We are all satisfied that somebody gives advice, and in the nature of things that must be so. If the Post Office Inspector of the division was given the responsibility of appointing the rural postmasters, I think he would be the best man, if the Government or the commission would throw the responsibility on him and back him up in his appointments. The inspector knows the district better than anybody else, and can locate the post office in the proper place, but he does not make the appointment. He is appealed to and gives



some advice, but he has not the final say, and as long as that is the practice, outside influence will enter into the appointment. When the minister said that the Civil Service Commission alone were responsible for_ the appointment of officials to the Post Office Department, he evidently had not appreciated what was laid before the House a few days ago.
Does my hon. friend mean to say that the Postmaster General in this particular case recommended that certain appointments be made?

I moved for the correspondence between the post office inspectors, the Government and the Civil Service Commission relating to the appointment of rural postmasters. There was general correspondence and instructions given to the post office inspectors throughout the Dominion, coming chiefly from the department-some from the Civil Service Commission, but largely from the department- and that correspondence plainly said that the last word was with the Postmaster General.

I think I can very safely assure my hon. friend that no matter what is in the return that is not correct. The Postmaster General is never consulted about these matters and should not be consulted. I am sure the Civil Service Commission will not permit that. It is a fact that the Civil Service Commission does consult the post office inspectors with respect to appointments in the different provinces. The Civil Service Commission must obtain knowledge from some source or other because it is quite obvious that they could not make appointments to rural post offices without some information gathered from somewhere. Accordingly they are driven to what seems the soundest course, namely, getting the advice and assistance of the post office inspector. I know that advice is frequently given by the inspector of the province from which my hon. friend comes, because the matter has on several occasions 'been brought to my attention by reason of individual cases having been mentioned in the House. Otherwise I would have no knowledge of it. I have always failed to appreciate the soundness of the objection which the leader of the Opposition makes to the commission availing itself of expert assistance when positions relate to some complicated duties. For instance, it has happened that legal men have had to be appointed to the Civil Service. In such cases, when the appointment relates to the

service in Ottawa, a member of the Exchequer Court, a member of the county court and some practising barrister are usually called in. That would seem to be a sound and businesslike procedure. I do not understand how it can be questioned. The Civil Service Commission are not bound to accept the opinion which is expressed by this board, because it must, of course, in the end accept the responsibility for the appointment. All it does is to ask that the applicants, or a certain number of them who seem to be better qualified than the others, should present themselves to this board for a test. When that is completed the Board simply .advises the Commission as to which of the applicants in its judgment is the best qualified for the position. I do not think there can possibly be any objection to that course of procedure. I think it would be unfair to prevent the Civil Service Commission, from doing this. The services are always rendered gratuitously to the Commission. Nobody has been paid for services of this kind. The .leader of the Opposition refers to ia case which was discussed at the last session of Parliament involving the question of the employment of a publicity agent. He was not required for an advertising position, which is altogether different from publicity work. Advertising is a business by itself. Persons 'spending a great deal of money in advertising secure the services of experts because they have found that if they allowed everybody to write their advertisements they would be wasting money.

I have at the present time a case in point in my own riding and I think I can commend the action of the Civil Service Commission. There is a postmaster to be appointed in my riding. There are many applicants. I am told that the post office inspector at Quebec will go down there and see those who are making application. for the position. The best man will be chosen. I think that is a propeT way to do it and I can only say that it should be recommended for the future.

I would ask the minister to correct me if I have not understood his position correctly. I understood him to state that it is the duty of .the Civil Service Commission to establish the schedules of pay. I think he is not quite correct in that. That has been their duty heretofore but my understanding of their duties in the future is that they will have more to do with applying the schedules already-provided by the classification experts after these schedules have been endorsed by the

House. In that case their duties should not be so exacting, or onerous in the future as they have been in the past.

The classification of the Civil Service is not a thing that can ever end. New positions are being created and the duties and responsibilities of such new positions must be standardized. New duties may be added to the present duties involving the fresh classification of duties and responsibilities which also affects the range of salaries. Generally speaking, my hon. friend (Mr. Pedlow) is right that when the classification in the main has been adopted that part of the work should be very much less onerous upon the commission.

I wish to emphasize what I said before, that if we are going to have efficiency, development and experience in the commission, they must do things themselves. If they are going to waive aside anything that presents a difficulty to them and call in another commission under them to decide the point for them, they will lose great opportunities of development and of acquiring experience for themselves. We know that all of us possibly prefer to call in a doctor of ten or twelve years' experience in preference to a young man who has just gone through some university and who has only had a few months' experience. Both doctors may have gone through the same course at college, but one has had ar practical experience that the other has not had. Our commissioners are never going to get practical experience if they are going to switch the responsibility to some board. What we want is a commission which will get the experience and knowledge that come from doing things themselves. They may make a mistake, and they naturally will make mistakes. Human nature is disposed to get away from difficulties and switch them to somebody else. We want them to take the responsibility of doing disagreeable things. When we take positions we must learn that we must deal with these things, face them and try to do our duty even if they are disagreeable and irksome. I would say one word particularly in view of the fact that the chairman of the commission is here to-day. I wish him to have my views at first hand. I must say that I have always had the highest regard for him both in this House and outside of it.
I wish to say in his hearing that it is always a most marvellous thing to me that whenever they make any appointment in the part of the country I come from they invariably strike a Tory. Once in a while it might be an accident but when accidents occur they usually happen on both sides of the political fence, and right and left. If this is an accident it is a continuous accident in only one direction. I would have a great deal more regard for the commission and their friends if I found that sometimes they made a mistake and appointed a Liberal to a position. While they continue persistently selecting Tories I can only come to the conclusion that we have the same old Tory machine and the same old system of patronage, and that the commission is merely an instrument in the hands of the other patronage machines.
Resolution read the first and second time, concurred in, and referred to Committee of the Whole to be considered in connection with Bill No. 18.

I wish to move
that 2 (a) be added as a new paragraph:
